stem: A patient on warfarin presents with major, life-threatening bleeding and a high INR. What is the most appropriate reversal treatment?

options.A: Intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
options.B: Oral vitamin K and withhold warfarin, rechecking INR at 24 hours
options.C: Fresh frozen plasma as the sole reversal agent
options.D: Withhold warfarin and transfuse red cells, rechecking the INR daily
options.E: IV protamine sulfate followed by IV vitamin K

correct_answer: A. Intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
why_correct: Major (life-threatening) bleeding on warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K together with prothrombin complex concentrate, which rapidly replaces the vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors; PCC is preferred over fresh frozen plasma for speed and completeness.
why_wrong: B. Oral vitamin K works too slowly for life-threatening bleeding; immediate factor replacement with PCC plus IV vitamin K is required. C. FFP is slower and less complete than PCC and is not the agent of choice when PCC is available. D. Red cells replace blood loss but do not reverse anticoagulation; urgent reversal is needed. E. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
pearl: Major warfarin bleeding is reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K — vitamin K alone is too slow when the bleeding is life-threatening.
thinking: Warfarin + major life-threatening bleeding + high INR ↓ Needs immediate factor replacement plus sustained reversal ↓ IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate
exam_trap: B, oral vitamin K alone — vitamin K does reverse warfarin, so it seems sufficient. But oral vitamin K works too slowly for life-threatening bleeding; immediate factor replacement with PCC (plus IV vitamin K) is required.
takeaway: Major warfarin bleeding is reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K — vitamin K alone is too slow when the bleeding is life-threatening.

stem: During labour, after the membranes rupture, the cord is felt below the presenting part in the vagina and the fetal heart rate drops. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Start an oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery
options.B: Replace the cord above the presenting part and keep monitoring
options.C: Continuous CTG monitoring and await spontaneous delivery
options.D: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange immediate delivery
options.E: Apply fundal pressure and encourage pushing to speed vaginal delivery

correct_answer: D. Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange immediate delivery
why_correct: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency; pressure on the cord is relieved (manually elevating the presenting part, maternal positioning), the cord kept warm and moist, and the baby delivered immediately, usually by caesarean.
why_wrong: A. Oxytocin increases contractions and cord compression, worsening fetal hypoxia. B. Handling the cord causes vasospasm and worsens fetal hypoxia; pressure is relieved and the baby delivered urgently, not left to labour. C. With fetal bradycardia, waiting risks fetal death; immediate delivery is required. E. Fundal pressure increases cord compression; the presenting part is elevated and urgent delivery (usually caesarean) arranged.
pearl: Cord prolapse means relieve the pressure and deliver now — do not handle or replace the cord.
thinking: Cord palpable below the presenting part + fetal bradycardia ↓ cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency ↓ relieve compression and deliver immediately
exam_trap: B, push the cord back in — instinct says to replace it. But handling the cord causes vasospasm and worsens fetal hypoxia; the cord is not replaced — pressure is relieved and the baby delivered urgently.
takeaway: Cord prolapse means relieve the pressure and deliver now — do not handle or replace the cord.

stem: A pregnant woman is found to carry group B Streptococcus on a swab in the current pregnancy. What is the most appropriate intrapartum management to reduce early-onset neonatal infection?

options.A: Elective caesarean section for all carriers
options.B: A course of oral antibiotics now, in the antenatal period

why_correct: Group B Streptococcus carriage in the current pregnancy is managed with intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis (benzylpenicillin) during labour to reduce early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis; antenatal treatment does not prevent recolonisation.
why_wrong: A. GBS carriage is not an indication for caesarean section. B. Antenatal oral antibiotics do not prevent recolonisation by the time of delivery; the effective measure is intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis. C. GBS colonisation can cause early-onset neonatal sepsis, so intrapartum prophylaxis is offered. E. Topical antiseptics do not reduce early-onset GBS disease.
pearl: GBS prophylaxis is given intravenously during labour, not as an antenatal course — the protection has to be present at delivery.
thinking: GBS carriage in current pregnancy ↓ risk is early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis ↓ intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin from onset of labour
exam_trap: B, treat antenatally with oral antibiotics — eradicating the organism in advance seems logical. But antenatal treatment does not prevent recolonisation by the time of delivery; the effective measure is intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis during labour.
takeaway: GBS prophylaxis is given intravenously during labour, not as an antenatal course — the protection has to be present at delivery.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with sudden severe pain in her right eye. She reports blurred vision, seeing haloes around lights and feeling nauseated. Examination reveals a red eye, cloudy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Routine ophthalmology referral and lubricating eye drops meanwhile
options.B: Chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily and review in 48 hours
options.C: Urgent ophthalmology referral and pressure-lowering drugs
options.D: High-dose oral prednisolone today and an urgent ESR and CRP check
options.E: Dilating drops (tropicamide 1%) to examine the fundus fully

correct_answer: C. Urgent ophthalmology referral and pressure-lowering drugs
why_correct: This is acute angle-closure glaucoma, a sight-threatening emergency caused by a sudden rise in intraocular pressure. Immediate pressure reduction and urgent ophthalmology involvement are required to prevent permanent visual loss.
why_wrong: A. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency, not for routine referral. B. This is not infective conjunctivitis. D. Steroids with ESR and CRP are for giant cell arteritis, which does not cause a fixed mid-dilated pupil with corneal clouding. E. Dilating the pupil worsens angle closure.
pearl: Painful red eye + haloes + fixed mid-dilated pupil = acute angle-closure glaucoma.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Painful red eye + haloes + fixed mid-dilated pupil = acute angle-closure glaucoma. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: Do not mistake acute angle-closure glaucoma for conjunctivitis.
takeaway: Acute angle-closure glaucoma → urgent ophthalmology referral and immediate pressure-lowering treatment.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 2 hours of crushing central chest pain radiating to his left arm. His ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.E: IV morphine and await cardiology review

why_correct: Inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF). Primary PCI is the gold-standard reperfusion strategy when deliverable within 120 minutes of first medical contact — superior vessel patency and mortality benefit over thrombolysis.
why_wrong: B: thrombolysis is reserved for when PCI is unavailable within 120 minutes. C: aspirin is adjunctive, not definitive reperfusion. D: CABG is not first-line acute reperfusion. E: symptom relief without reperfusion is inadequate.
pearl: Inferior STEMI — check V3R/V4R for right ventricular involvement; avoid nitrates if RV infarction present.
thinking: Identify territory from leads: inferior = II,III,aVF; anterior = V1-V4; lateral = I,aVL,V5-V6.
exam_trap: Choosing thrombolysis when PCI is available — the clinical context implies a PCI centre.
takeaway: Primary PCI is first-line for STEMI when deliverable within 120 minutes.

stem: A 45-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer presents with progressive dyspnoea, hypotension (BP 88/60), and elevated JVP. Heart sounds are muffled. ECG shows electrical alternans. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds) plus electrical alternans confirms cardiac tamponade — a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate pericardiocentesis to relieve pericardial pressure.
why_wrong: B. Fluid may temporise but does not relieve tamponade. C. Diuretics reduce preload and worsen haemodynamics in tamponade. D. Thoracotomy is not indicated when pericardiocentesis can relieve tamponade. E. Steroids do not relieve acute tamponade.
pearl: Electrical alternans (beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation) on ECG is highly specific for large pericardial effusion with tamponade.
thinking: Tamponade = obstructive shock. The only definitive treatment is drainage.
exam_trap: Giving furosemide — this worsens tamponade by reducing preload in an already preload-dependent state.
takeaway: Cardiac tamponade requires immediate pericardiocentesis — diuretics are harmful.

stem: A 70-year-old man collapses. ECG shows P waves at 80 bpm with no fixed relationship to broad QRS complexes occurring at 38 bpm. He is haemodynamically compromised. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.A: IV atropine 500 micrograms (up to 3 mg total in incremental doses)

why_correct: Complete (third-degree) heart block with haemodynamic compromise requires immediate transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous or permanent pacing — the most rapidly available intervention.
why_wrong: A: RCUK 2025 advises not giving atropine in high-degree AV block with a wide QRS — it is ineffective and may worsen the block. B: a 1 mg IV bolus is the cardiac arrest dose; in bradycardia adrenaline is used only as a 2–10 mcg/min infusion interim measure. D: permanent pacemaker requires assessment and planning. E: observation is inappropriate in haemodynamic compromise.
pearl: In complete heart block, atropine may accelerate atrial rate but rarely improves ventricular rate — transcutaneous pacing is preferred.
thinking: P waves and QRS complexes marching independently = complete heart block.
exam_trap: Giving maximum-dose atropine expecting it to work reliably in complete heart block.
takeaway: Haemodynamically unstable complete heart block: immediate transcutaneous pacing.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Serum amylase is 1400 U/L (normal <100). CXR is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: IV fluids, analgesia, and nil by mouth
options.D: Oral clear fluids and outpatient follow-up

correct_answer: A. IV fluids, analgesia, and nil by mouth
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis management: IV fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia (IV opioids), with oral intake resumed early as tolerated (no prolonged nil by mouth; enteral rather than parenteral nutrition if needed, NICE NG104). Assess severity using Glasgow/APACHE score. Routine antibiotics are not indicated.
why_wrong: B: cholecystectomy is performed electively during the same admission after recovery from gallstone pancreatitis. C: ERCP is for gallstone pancreatitis with biliary obstruction or cholangitis. D: admission is required. E: antibiotics are not routine — only for infected necrosis.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol account for over 80% of acute pancreatitis in the UK.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis: supportive care first; ERCP only for biliary obstruction or cholangitis.
exam_trap: Routinely prescribing antibiotics — not indicated in uncomplicated pancreatitis.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis: IV fluids, analgesia, NBM — antibiotics only for infected pancreatic necrosis.

stem: A 50-year-old man is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His first retinal screen is normal. What is the recommended screening interval?

options.E: At diagnosis and then at 5 years

why_correct: NICE recommends annual retinal photography for all patients with diabetes (type 1 and 2) with no or background retinopathy. Screening aims to detect sight-threatening retinopathy before symptoms develop.
why_wrong: A: 2-yearly is not the UK standard. C: 6-monthly is used for higher-risk or active disease. D: retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced — do not wait for symptoms. E: 5-yearly is far too infrequent.
pearl: Pre-proliferative and proliferative retinopathy are sight-threatening and require ophthalmology referral.
thinking: All diabetic patients need annual eye screening — retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced.
exam_trap: Only screening when symptomatic — by then significant vision loss may have already occurred.
takeaway: Diabetic retinopathy: annual digital fundus photography regardless of symptoms.

stem: A 72-year-old woman suffers a vertebral fragility fracture after minimal trauma. DXA T-score is -2.8. No contraindications to medication. What is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Calcium and vitamin D with annual DXA scan
options.E: Alendronate plus calcium and vitamin D

correct_answer: E. Alendronate plus calcium and vitamin D
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly) plus calcium and vitamin D is first-line for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women. Bisphosphonates reduce vertebral and hip fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Calcium and vitamin D are adjuncts and do not adequately treat established osteoporosis. B. Strontium ranelate is rarely used because of cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk. C. HRT is not first-line osteoporosis treatment at 72 because of its risks. D. Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and is not first-line.
pearl: FRAX tool calculates 10-year fracture probability to guide treatment decisions.
thinking: Fragility fracture = osteoporosis treatment regardless of T-score. T-score <-2.5 = osteoporosis.
exam_trap: Prescribing calcium/vitamin D alone — adjunctive to bisphosphonate, not sufficient alone for treatment.
takeaway: Osteoporosis with fragility fracture: alendronate plus calcium and vitamin D.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation has BP 158/105, 2+ proteinuria, and headache. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
options.B: Bed rest, IV fluids and repeat BP in 4 hours on the antenatal ward
options.C: Oral labetalol and twice-weekly day-unit review as an outpatient
options.D: Immediate caesarean section before controlling the BP or giving magnesium

correct_answer: A. Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
why_correct: Severe pre-eclampsia: admit, antihypertensives (labetalol IV or oral nifedipine), magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis (eclampsia prevention), and plan for delivery (a senior obstetric decision: at 34-36+6 weeks birth is planned when there are severe features such as ongoing severe headache or visual disturbance, uncontrolled BP or worsening bloods).
why_wrong: B. Bed rest and fluids do not control BP and risk fluid overload. C. Severe hypertension with proteinuria and headache requires admission, not outpatient care. D. BP must be controlled and magnesium sulphate given before delivery. E. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia.
pearl: MgSO4 reduces eclampsia risk by 50% in severe pre-eclampsia. Diazepam is not recommended for eclamptic seizures.
thinking: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP control + MgSO4 + delivery planning.
exam_trap: Giving diuretics — pre-eclampsia causes vasoconstriction and relative hypovolaemia; diuretics worsen organ perfusion.
takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia: antihypertensives + MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis + plan for delivery.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker presents with calf pain on walking 200 metres that relieves within 5 minutes of rest. ABI is 0.65. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Supervised exercise, smoking cessation and antiplatelet therapy
options.B: Angioplasty and stenting of the femoral artery
options.D: Rest, leg elevation and compression stockings
options.E: Naftidrofuryl oxalate first, with review in 3 months

correct_answer: A. Supervised exercise, smoking cessation and antiplatelet therapy
why_correct: Intermittent claudication (stable PAD, ABI 0.4-0.9): first-line management is supervised exercise programme (improves collateral circulation and walking distance), risk factor modification (smoking cessation, statins, antihypertensives), and antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 75 mg preferred in PAD per NICE CG147 / TA210).
why_wrong: B. Revascularisation is for failed supervised exercise or critical limb ischaemia. C. Anticoagulation is not standard for stable claudication. D. Elevation and compression worsen arterial insufficiency. E. Naftidrofuryl is considered only when supervised exercise has not helped and revascularisation is unsuitable.
pearl: ABI <0.9 = PAD. ABI <0.4 = critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). ABI >1.4 = non-compressible vessels (diabetes).
thinking: Claudication + ABI 0.65 = stable PAD. Conservative management first.
exam_trap: Anticoagulating claudication — warfarin has no benefit in stable PAD and increases bleeding risk.
takeaway: Intermittent claudication: supervised exercise + smoking cessation + antiplatelet therapy first-line.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness. Blood tests show potassium 2.7 mmol/L. She has recently started a loop diuretic. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Loop diuretics increase distal sodium delivery and promote renal potassium loss, and a potassium of 2.7 mmol/L confirms hypokalaemia as the cause of this patient's muscle weakness.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia is not the characteristic electrolyte effect of loop diuretics. C. Hypermagnesaemia is not expected. D. Hyperkalaemia is associated with potassium-sparing drugs such as spironolactone, the opposite effect. E. Hypernatraemia is not the characteristic direct effect of loop diuretics.
pearl: Loop and thiazide diuretics both cause renal potassium wasting, so electrolytes should be monitored after starting or increasing the dose, particularly in patients also taking digoxin, where hypokalaemia increases toxicity risk.
thinking: Muscle weakness + recent loop diuretic start + low potassium on testing ↓ diuretic-induced renal potassium loss ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: Candidates may overthink the electrolyte pattern, but a clear low measured potassium value combined with a known potassium-wasting drug makes hypokalaemia the straightforward answer.
takeaway: Loop diuretics waste potassium — always check electrolytes after starting or uptitrating one.

presentation: Confidentiality for a Competent Young Person
stem: A 14-year-old girl tells her doctor that she is sexually active and asks for contraception. She specifically asks the doctor not to tell her parents. She demonstrates understanding of the information and consequences of treatment. What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Keep her confidence unless there is a safeguarding concern
options.B: Inform her school nurse so she has support within school
options.C: Inform her parents as she is under 16 years of age
options.D: Contact the police as she is under the legal age of consent
options.E: Defer contraception until she agrees to tell her parents

correct_answer: A. Keep her confidence unless there is a safeguarding concern
why_correct: A young person who demonstrates sufficient understanding can consent to confidential care, including contraception; confidentiality should be maintained unless there is a genuine safeguarding concern requiring disclosure.
why_wrong: B. Sharing information with the school nurse without consent or a safeguarding reason breaches confidentiality. C. Being under 16 does not entitle parents to a competent young person's confidential information. D. Sexual activity at 14 does not automatically require police involvement; disclosure is guided by safeguarding assessment. E. She should be encouraged to involve her parents, but contraception should not be made conditional on it if she is Fraser competent.
pearl: When assessing a young person for contraception, clinicians should also consider exploitation or safeguarding risk factors, such as a significant age gap with the partner.
thinking: 14-year-old + demonstrates understanding + requests confidentiality ↓ competent young person entitled to confidential care ↓ Maintain confidentiality unless safeguarding concern
exam_trap: Candidates may default to 'must tell the parents' given her age, but competent young people are entitled to confidential care unless a genuine safeguarding issue arises.
takeaway: A competent young person's confidentiality should be maintained unless there's a safeguarding concern.

stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted after a fall. He takes several medications, including an antihypertensive and a sedative. Which intervention is particularly appropriate to reduce his future falls risk?
why_correct: Medications such as antihypertensives and sedatives are important, reversible contributors to falls in older adults through hypotension, sedation and impaired balance, so a structured medication review is a key intervention.
why_wrong: B. Alcohol increases sedation and falls risk rather than reducing it. C. Prolonged bed rest causes deconditioning and increases frailty and future falls risk. D. Visual impairment is a modifiable falls risk factor and should be assessed, not ignored. E. Restricting fluids can cause dehydration, which itself increases falls risk.
pearl: A falls risk assessment in older adults should cover medication review, vision, gait and balance, cardiovascular causes (including postural BP), and home hazards.
thinking: Fall + multiple medications including antihypertensive/sedative ↓ Reversible drug-related contributors to falls ↓ Medication review
exam_trap: A candidate might focus solely on investigating a medical cause for the fall, overlooking that reviewing potentially culprit medications is a key, readily actionable intervention.
takeaway: In an older patient after a fall, always review medications that can cause hypotension or sedation.

stem: A patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, profound weakness and hypotension. What emergency should be suspected?
why_correct: In a patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency, acute vomiting, abdominal pain, profound weakness and hypotension represent an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis, a life-threatening emergency.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid storm occurs in severe thyrotoxicosis, not adrenal insufficiency. B. Pulmonary embolism can cause shock but does not fit this specific clinical context as well as adrenal crisis. D. Acute glaucoma causes severe eye pain and visual disturbance, not this systemic picture. E. DKA is associated with hyperglycaemia and ketoacidosis, not primary adrenal insufficiency.
pearl: Adrenal crisis requires immediate treatment with intravenous hydrocortisone and fluids; delay can be fatal, so treatment should not wait for confirmatory blood results.
thinking: Known adrenal insufficiency + vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, hypotension ↓ acute cortisol deficiency, life-threatening ↓ Adrenal crisis
exam_trap: Candidates may consider sepsis as the primary diagnosis, but in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency, any acute illness with hypotension should first trigger treatment for adrenal crisis.
takeaway: In known adrenal insufficiency, acute vomiting with hypotension is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 30-year-old man develops persistent bloating and foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea after drinking untreated water while travelling. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Prolonged bloating with foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea after drinking untreated water is characteristic of giardiasis, which causes malabsorption.
why_wrong: A. Influenza is a respiratory infection, unrelated to water exposure. C. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms, not diarrhoea. D. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea rather than greasy, foul-smelling stools. E. Shigella usually causes inflammatory or bloody diarrhoea, not greasy malabsorptive stools.
pearl: Greasy, offensive stools and bloating that persist after travel should prompt testing for Giardia, which can cause prolonged symptoms if untreated.
thinking: Untreated water exposure + persistent bloating + greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea ↓ small-bowel malabsorption from a protozoal parasite ↓ Giardiasis
exam_trap: Candidates may think of cholera given the water exposure, but cholera causes watery, not greasy, diarrhoea; the fatty, malabsorptive stool is specific to giardiasis.
takeaway: Greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea with bloating after contaminated water points to giardiasis.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is found to have a low bone mineral density on a DXA scan. Which lifestyle measure is particularly important in reducing future fracture risk?

options.B: Increasing caffeine to five cups daily
options.C: Avoiding sunlight to prevent skin cancer
options.D: Bed rest after any minor fall or strain
options.E: Restricting dairy foods and calcium intake

correct_answer: A. Weight-bearing exercise and falls prevention
why_correct: Weight-bearing exercise helps maintain bone density, and falls-prevention strategies directly reduce the likelihood of a fragility fracture, making this combination particularly effective in someone with low bone mineral density.
why_wrong: B. High caffeine intake does not protect bone and may increase calcium loss. C. Avoiding sunlight can worsen vitamin D status and bone health. D. Bed rest accelerates bone loss and deconditioning. E. Restricting calcium intake worsens bone health.
pearl: Osteoporosis management is about more than medication — weight-bearing activity and falls-prevention measures meaningfully reduce fracture risk.
thinking: Low bone mineral density on DXA ↓ fracture risk is driven by both bone fragility and fall likelihood ↓ Weight-bearing exercise and falls prevention
exam_trap: Candidates focused purely on pharmacological bone treatment may underweight the practical importance of exercise and falls prevention in reducing fracture risk.
takeaway: Reducing fracture risk means building bone strength and preventing falls, not just treating density alone.

stem: A 28-year-old man develops fever, headache and a widespread maculopapular rash after returning from a tropical country. He also has thrombocytopenia and mild jaundice. Which diagnosis should be considered particularly urgently?
why_correct: Fever after travel to a tropical region must be treated as malaria until excluded, particularly with associated thrombocytopenia and jaundice, since severe malaria can progress rapidly and be fatal if treatment is delayed.
why_wrong: B. Hay fever does not cause fever, rash or thrombocytopenia. C. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause systemic febrile illness. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause fever or thrombocytopenia. E. Migraine does not explain the systemic and haematological features described.
pearl: Thrombocytopenia and jaundice accompanying fever after tropical travel should heighten, not lower, suspicion of malaria, as these are recognised features of the disease.
thinking: Fever + rash + thrombocytopenia + jaundice after tropical travel ↓ malaria must be urgently excluded regardless of the atypical rash ↓ Malaria
exam_trap: Candidates may be misled by the rash into thinking of a different tropical infection, but the combination of travel history and fever still makes malaria the diagnosis that must be urgently excluded.
takeaway: Fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise.

stem: A 34-year-old man has persistent unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent nosebleeds. What is an important diagnosis to exclude?
why_correct: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with recurrent nosebleeds is a red-flag combination that must prompt exclusion of nasal or sinonasal malignancy, particularly when symptoms are unilateral and persistent.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis affects joints and is unrelated. C. Plantar fasciitis affects the foot and is unrelated. D. Irritable bowel syndrome affects gastrointestinal function and is unrelated. E. Tension headache does not cause unilateral nasal obstruction.
pearl: Unilateral (rather than bilateral) nasal symptoms, especially with recurrent epistaxis, are a red flag that should prompt specialist ENT assessment to exclude malignancy.
thinking: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction + recurrent nosebleeds ↓ unilateral, persistent pattern is a red flag rather than typical bilateral allergic symptoms ↓ Nasal malignancy must be excluded
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute this to simple allergic rhinitis, missing that unilaterality and persistence are the key red-flag features that distinguish this from a benign, typically bilateral, process.
takeaway: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction with recurrent nosebleeds needs exclusion of nasal malignancy.

stem: A 71-year-old man has urinary urgency, frequency and nocturia. He has no dysuria or haematuria. Which condition is most likely to cause these lower urinary tract symptoms?
why_correct: Urgency, frequency and nocturia without dysuria or haematuria in an older man are typical lower urinary tract symptoms of benign prostatic enlargement.
why_wrong: A. Epididymo-orchitis causes painful scrotal swelling. B. Acute pyelonephritis usually causes fever and flank pain. C. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain. D. An obstructing ureteric calculus causes severe loin-to-groin pain.
pearl: Absence of dysuria or haematuria helps distinguish uncomplicated benign prostatic enlargement from infective or malignant causes of lower urinary tract symptoms, which still warrant exclusion.
thinking: Older man + urgency, frequency, nocturia + no dysuria/haematuria ↓ typical bladder outlet obstruction pattern ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
exam_trap: Pyelonephritis might be considered because of urinary symptoms, but the absence of fever, flank pain or dysuria argues against an infective process.
takeaway: Frequency, urgency and nocturia without dysuria or haematuria in an older man suggests benign prostatic enlargement.

stem: A 55-year-old man suddenly develops slurred speech and weakness of the left side of his body. He remains conscious. Which vascular territory is most likely to be affected if the dominant hemisphere is involved?
why_correct: The middle cerebral artery supplies large areas of the lateral cerebral hemisphere and commonly produces contralateral weakness with language disturbance when the dominant hemisphere is involved.
why_wrong: A. The renal artery supplies the kidney, not the brain. B. Posterior cerebral artery infarction more typically causes visual deficits. C. The external carotid artery does not supply the cerebral hemisphere. E. Basilar artery disease can cause brainstem syndromes but is not the typical territory for this hemispheric presentation.
pearl: The middle cerebral artery is the most commonly affected vessel in ischaemic stroke and, when the dominant hemisphere is involved, typically produces aphasia alongside contralateral weakness.
thinking: Sudden focal weakness and speech disturbance + dominant hemisphere involvement ↓ typical distribution of large-vessel hemispheric stroke ↓ Middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: Posterior cerebral artery is sometimes chosen for any stroke question, but it classically produces visual field deficits rather than the motor and language pattern described here.
takeaway: Contralateral weakness with language disturbance in dominant hemisphere stroke points to middle cerebral artery territory.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has gradually worsening back pain and loses height over several years. Imaging shows a vertebral compression fracture without significant trauma. What is the most likely underlying condition?
why_correct: Gradual height loss and back pain from vertebral compression fractures occurring with little or no trauma are characteristic of osteoporosis.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis primarily affects joints rather than causing vertebral compression fractures. C. Gout causes crystal-induced arthritis, not fracture. D. Septic arthritis causes an acutely inflamed joint, not a chronic compression fracture. E. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without structural vertebral collapse.
pearl: Vertebral compression fractures are often asymptomatic or attributed to 'normal ageing' back pain, so height loss over time is a useful clue to underlying osteoporosis.
thinking: Gradual height loss + back pain + minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture pattern ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute chronic back pain in an older patient simply to degenerative disease, but the minimal-trauma vertebral fracture and height loss specifically indicate osteoporosis.
takeaway: Height loss with a minimal-trauma vertebral fracture points to osteoporosis.

stem: A 29-year-old tall, thin man develops sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. Breath sounds are absent on the affected side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness with absent breath sounds on the affected side in a tall, thin young man are classic for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
why_wrong: A. Stable angina causes exertional central chest discomfort, not sudden unilateral pleuritic pain with absent breath sounds. B. Acute pericarditis causes positional chest pain without unilateral absent breath sounds. C. Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain but does not typically cause absent unilateral breath sounds. E. Pneumonia usually causes fever and focal crackles rather than absent breath sounds.
pearl: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall, thin young men, often related to the rupture of subpleural blebs, and is a key differential in any young adult with sudden pleuritic chest pain.
thinking: Tall, thin young man + sudden pleuritic chest pain ↓ breathlessness ↓ absent breath sounds on one side ↓ Spontaneous pneumothorax
exam_trap: A candidate might consider pulmonary embolism given pleuritic pain, but the specific finding of absent breath sounds on one side points more directly to a pneumothorax.
takeaway: Sudden pleuritic pain with absent unilateral breath sounds in a tall, thin young man suggests spontaneous pneumothorax.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge. There is no fever or breast tenderness. What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: Spontaneous, unilateral, bloody nipple discharge without fever or tenderness is a recognised red-flag feature requiring urgent assessment to exclude breast malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Gynaecomastia refers to male breast enlargement, unrelated to nipple discharge assessment in this context. C. A breast abscess causes a painful, inflamed, tender lump, not painless bloody discharge. D. Lactational engorgement occurs during breastfeeding and does not typically cause bloody discharge. E. Mastitis usually causes pain, erythema and systemic symptoms, which are absent here.
pearl: Unilateral, spontaneous, blood-stained nipple discharge is a breast cancer red flag even when a discrete lump cannot be felt, and warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for triple assessment.
thinking: Spontaneous unilateral bloody discharge ↓ no fever or tenderness to suggest infection ↓ red-flag breast symptom ↓ Breast malignancy
exam_trap: A candidate might dismiss the discharge as benign engorgement, but the specific combination of spontaneous, unilateral and bloody discharge without infective features is a recognised red flag for malignancy.
takeaway: Spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge is a red flag for breast malignancy.

stem: A man presents with a urethral discharge that is thick and purulent. Which infection is particularly associated with this presentation?
why_correct: A thick, purulent urethral discharge is particularly characteristic of gonococcal urethritis, compared with the typically scantier discharge of other causes.
why_wrong: A. HPV causes genital warts or is asymptomatic, not urethral discharge. B. Syphilis classically causes a painless chancre initially, not purulent discharge. C. Candidiasis does not typically cause a purulent urethral discharge in men. E. Herpes causes painful vesicles or ulcers rather than a purulent discharge.
pearl: A thick, purulent discharge favours gonorrhoea, while a thinner, mucoid discharge is more typical of chlamydial urethritis, though co-infection is common and both should be tested for.
thinking: Man with urethral discharge + thick and purulent character ↓ typical of gonococcal infection ↓ Gonorrhoea
exam_trap: Candidates might assume chlamydia given it is more prevalent overall, but the specifically purulent (not mucoid) nature of the discharge points to gonorrhoea.
takeaway: A thick, purulent urethral discharge is classically gonococcal.

stem: A patient taking warfarin develops significant bleeding. Which treatment can be used to rapidly reverse the anticoagulant effect?

options.D: Protamine sulfate given by slow intravenous injection
options.E: IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate

correct_answer: E. IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate
why_correct: Significant warfarin-associated bleeding requires urgent reversal with vitamin K together with rapid clotting-factor replacement, such as prothrombin complex concentrate, to restore haemostasis quickly.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not warfarin. B. Naloxone reverses opioids, not warfarin. C. Idarucizumab specifically reverses dabigatran, not warfarin. D. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
pearl: Vitamin K alone takes hours to correct the INR, so clotting-factor concentrate is added when rapid reversal is needed for serious or life-threatening bleeding.
thinking: Warfarin + significant bleeding ↓ needs both rapid and sustained reversal ↓ Vitamin K with appropriate coagulation-factor replacement
exam_trap: Candidates might select vitamin K alone as sufficient, but for significant bleeding this is too slow on its own and needs to be paired with clotting-factor replacement for rapid reversal.
takeaway: Major warfarin bleeding needs vitamin K plus clotting-factor replacement for rapid reversal.

stem: A 61-year-old man has chronic lower back pain and an X-ray showing vertebral compression. Which condition increases the risk of this type of fracture?
why_correct: Osteoporosis reduces bone density and strength, predisposing to vertebral compression fractures, sometimes after minimal or no trauma.
why_wrong: A. Migraine is unrelated to bone fragility. B. Asthma does not itself increase fracture risk in this way. D. Otitis externa is unrelated. E. Irritable bowel syndrome does not directly cause vertebral fractures.
pearl: Vertebral compression fractures from osteoporosis can occur with minimal trauma and may present only as chronic back pain or height loss rather than an acute injury.
thinking: Chronic back pain + vertebral compression on imaging ↓ fragility fracture pattern ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: Candidates might look for a traumatic cause, but osteoporotic vertebral fractures often occur with little or no preceding injury.
takeaway: Vertebral compression fractures in older adults should prompt evaluation for osteoporosis.

stem: A 41-year-old man develops severe muscle spasms and sensitivity to light and sound after being bitten by an unvaccinated dog while travelling abroad. Which infection should be suspected?
why_correct: Neurological symptoms including muscle spasms and marked sensory hypersensitivity following a bite from an unvaccinated animal abroad are highly concerning for rabies.
why_wrong: B. Lyme disease follows tick exposure rather than an animal bite. C. Malaria follows exposure to malaria-endemic mosquitoes rather than a bite injury. D. Tetanus follows wound contamination and causes rigidity, but lacks the characteristic sensory hypersensitivity of the animal-bite syndrome described here. E. Influenza does not cause this characteristic neurological syndrome.
pearl: Post-exposure rabies prophylaxis should be considered promptly after any bite from a potentially rabid animal abroad, since once clinical rabies develops it is almost always fatal.
thinking: Animal bite from unvaccinated dog abroad + spasms + sensory hypersensitivity ↓ classic rabies exposure and prodrome ↓ Rabies
exam_trap: A candidate might think of tetanus given the spasms, but the animal-bite context abroad and sensory hypersensitivity point specifically to rabies.
takeaway: Neurological symptoms after an animal bite abroad should raise concern for rabies and prompt post-exposure prophylaxis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman develops tingling around her mouth and painful muscle spasms several days after neck surgery. Blood tests show low calcium. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Perioral tingling and painful muscle spasms with confirmed low calcium after neck surgery reflect hypoparathyroidism from inadvertent parathyroid gland damage or removal.
why_wrong: A. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia rather than hypocalcaemic symptoms. B. Cushing syndrome causes features of glucocorticoid excess rather than hypocalcaemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia rather than perioral tingling and spasms. E. Phaeochromocytoma causes catecholamine-related symptoms such as palpitations and sweating.
pearl: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia after neck surgery should be treated promptly, as untreated severe hypocalcaemia can progress to tetany or seizures.
thinking: Recent neck surgery + perioral tingling + painful spasms + confirmed low calcium ↓ parathyroid injury impairing calcium regulation ↓ Hypoparathyroidism
exam_trap: A candidate might consider diabetes insipidus given the surgical context, but the specific combination of perioral tingling, spasms and confirmed hypocalcaemia points to parathyroid injury, not posterior pituitary dysfunction.
takeaway: Perioral tingling and spasms with low calcium after neck surgery indicates hypoparathyroidism.

stem: A patient is being transferred between clinical teams.  Which information is particularly important during handover?

options.A: The admission diagnosis and original presenting complaint
options.B: Past medical history and full social circumstances at home
options.C: Only a complete list of the regular medications
options.D: Demographics, next of kin details and current ward location
options.E: Active problems, current plan and outstanding tasks

correct_answer: E. Active problems, current plan and outstanding tasks
why_correct: Effective handover should communicate the information needed for safe ongoing care, including active problems, plans, risks and outstanding actions.
why_wrong: A. The admission diagnosis may not capture current problems or plans. B. Background history alone does not communicate current care needs. C. Medication information is important but insufficient on its own. D. Identification and contact details alone do not support safe ongoing care.
pearl: Safe handover communicates active problems, the current plan, and outstanding tasks - not just a static history or identifiers.
thinking: Each wrong option isolates a single narrow element; the correct answer must be the one that captures ongoing, actionable clinical information.
exam_trap: Candidates can be drawn to the medication list as sounding safety-critical, overlooking that it is only one part of what a safe handover requires.
takeaway: Handover is about now and next, not just who and what happened before.

stem: A patient has experienced harm following a clinical incident. The doctor explains what is known, expresses regret for the harm and discusses what will happen next.  Which principle is being demonstrated?
why_correct: Open disclosure involves communicating openly with patients about incidents causing harm, including what is known and what will happen next.
why_wrong: A. Informed refusal concerns declining treatment. B. Screening concerns testing people without symptoms. C. Therapeutic privilege is a separate and very limited concept. D. Randomisation relates to research methodology.
pearl: Open disclosure means communicating transparently with a harmed patient about what is known, expressing regret, and explaining next steps - distinct from related but unrelated concepts like therapeutic privilege.
thinking: This is a definitions-matching question. Identify the behaviours described and match them to the one option that is a communication principle rather than a research or consent concept.
exam_trap: Therapeutic privilege is a tempting distractor because it also concerns what is told to a patient, but it refers to withholding information, the opposite of open disclosure.
takeaway: Open disclosure: explain, apologise for the harm, and say what happens next.

stem: A patient agrees to a procedure only after being threatened that treatment will otherwise be withheld.  Which element of valid consent is missing?
why_correct: Consent must be given freely, without coercion or undue pressure.
why_wrong: A. Confidentiality is a separate professional duty. B. Documentation is important but does not define voluntariness. C. Capacity concerns the ability to make the decision. E. Diagnosis is separate from consent.
pearl: Consent obtained under threat or coercion fails on voluntariness even if the patient has full capacity and understanding.
thinking: The stem explicitly describes a threat. Match this to the consent element concerned with freedom from pressure, rather than capacity or documentation.
exam_trap: Candidates confuse voluntariness with capacity, since both relate to decision-making, but capacity is about mental ability, not external pressure.
takeaway: Consent under threat is not consent - voluntariness is the missing ingredient.

stem: Which of the following is part of assessing whether an adult has capacity to make a particular decision?

options.A: Ability to understand, retain, use/weigh information and communicate
options.B: Whether the treating doctor agrees with the decision they have reached
options.C: Whether the decision is the one most clinicians would advise them to make
options.D: Whether they have a physical disability or another long-term health condition
options.E: Whether they are under the age of 65 at the time the decision is made

correct_answer: A. Ability to understand, retain, use/weigh information and communicate
why_correct: These are central elements of the functional assessment of decision-making capacity.
why_wrong: B. Capacity is not determined by agreement with the clinician. C. An unwise or unusual decision does not itself demonstrate incapacity. D. Physical disability or a long-term condition does not automatically imply lack of capacity. E. Capacity is not determined by age alone.
pearl: The functional test of capacity asks whether a person can understand, retain, use/weigh information, and communicate a decision - not whether the decision itself seems sensible.
thinking: Recall the four-stage functional test and match it directly against the correct option; all other options describe irrelevant factors that must not be used to judge capacity.
exam_trap: Candidates may be tempted by whether the decision is medically sensible, confusing unwise decisions with incapacity.
takeaway: Capacity is about the process of deciding, not the content of the decision.

presentation: Refusal of Treatment by a Capacitous Patient
stem: A patient with capacity refuses a recommended operation because they accept the risk of deterioration.  What should the doctor do?

options.B: Ask the police to authorise treatment
options.D: Declare the patient to lack capacity because they refused
options.E: Perform the operation against the patient's wishes

correct_answer: A. Respect an informed, voluntary refusal
why_correct: A competent adult has the right to refuse treatment, even when the decision exposes them to serious harm.
why_wrong: B. Police do not normally authorise routine medical treatment. C. Employers have no automatic role in treatment decisions. D. An unwise decision does not by itself establish incapacity. E. Treatment without valid consent is generally unlawful.
pearl: An unwise decision does not equal incapacity; a capacitous adult can refuse even life-saving treatment.
thinking: Confirm the patient has capacity, then recognise that the correct response is simply to respect the refusal once informed and voluntary - treating or declaring incapacity because you disagree is not permitted.
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes select declaring the patient to lack capacity because the decision seems irrational, conflating disagreement with incapacity.
takeaway: Capacity gives the right to make unwise choices, not just wise ones.

stem: A DNACPR decision is documented for a patient who is approaching the end of life.  What does DNACPR specifically mean?

options.A: Escalation to intensive care is no longer an available option
options.B: Active treatment should be withdrawn and comfort care started
options.C: CPR is not attempted in cardiac or respiratory arrest
options.D: Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration are stopped
options.E: The patient should be transferred to a hospice for care

correct_answer: C. CPR is not attempted in cardiac or respiratory arrest
why_correct: DNACPR concerns CPR specifically and does not automatically mean that other appropriate treatments should be withheld.
why_wrong: A. A DNACPR decision does not by itself preclude escalation to critical care; this is a separate decision. B. Other appropriate treatments may continue; DNACPR does not mean withdrawal of active care. D. Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration require separate consideration. E. A DNACPR decision does not determine the place of care.
pearl: DNACPR applies only to CPR in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest; it does not restrict any other treatment, including nutrition, hydration, or antibiotics.
thinking: Treat this as a pure definition check. Any option that extends DNACPR beyond resuscitation is a scope-creep distractor.
exam_trap: Candidates frequently believe DNACPR implies withdrawal of all active treatment, when it is specific to resuscitation attempts alone.
takeaway: DNACPR is about one thing only: not attempting CPR.

stem: A patient has died in hospital and is potentially suitable for organ donation. Which of the following describes the appropriate process?

options.A: Donation proceeds automatically without family discussion or clinical assessment
options.B: The treating doctor decides alone without involving the family or the donation team
options.C: Hospital management decides based on current transplant waiting-list pressures
options.D: Early SNOD involvement under the consent law, with family discussion
options.E: Donation requires a signed donor card found with the patient

correct_answer: D. Early SNOD involvement under the consent law, with family discussion
why_correct: Organ donation in all four UK nations follows a legal consent or deemed-consent framework. The specialist nurse for organ donation (SNOD) is involved early to check the person's recorded decision, support the family and assess suitability.
why_wrong: A. Even under deemed consent, suitability assessment and family discussion are required. B. Donation follows a structured process involving the donation team and, where applicable, the family. C. Hospital management has no authority to authorise donation on this basis. E. The NHS Organ Donor Register, family discussion and deemed consent also apply; a donor card is not required.
pearl: Even under deemed/opt-out consent systems, donation still requires suitability assessment, specialist nurse involvement, and sensitive family discussion - it is never automatic.
thinking: This question tests process knowledge rather than pattern recognition. Eliminate the extreme automatic/unilateral options first, then the option requiring a donor card which is outdated given deemed consent frameworks, leaving the structured, multi-step process.
exam_trap: Candidates under time pressure may pick the option implying automatic donation under deemed consent, forgetting that family discussion and suitability assessment are still required.
takeaway: Deemed consent does not mean no conversation: donation is always a structured, supported process.

presentation: Immediate First Aid for Needle-Stick Injury
stem: A healthcare worker sustains a needle-stick injury from a potentially infected patient.  What should they do first?

options.A: Wash the area promptly with soap and running water
options.B: Ignore it if the wound is small
options.C: Cover it with adhesive and continue working without reporting
options.D: Apply bleach directly to the wound

correct_answer: A. Wash the area promptly with soap and running water
why_correct: Immediate first aid includes washing the affected area with soap and running water, followed by prompt occupational-health assessment.
why_wrong: B. Even apparently minor exposures require assessment. C. Prompt reporting and risk assessment are important. D. Bleach should not be applied to tissue. E. Aggressive squeezing is not recommended.
pearl: The first step after any sharps injury is simple first aid - wash with soap and running water - followed promptly by occupational health risk assessment.
thinking: This is a first-step question: look for the simple, immediate, harm-reducing action rather than anything that delays or ignores the exposure.
exam_trap: Candidates may be tempted by more dramatic-sounding actions such as squeezing or bleach, which are actually discouraged.
takeaway: Wash first, assess fast - never squeeze or bleach a sharps injury.

presentation: Post-Exposure Risk Stratification for Hepatitis B
stem: A healthcare worker sustains a significant blood exposure from a patient known to have hepatitis B.  What determines the need for post-exposure management?

options.A: The worker's HBV immunity status and the exposure risk
options.B: Whether the source patient also has hepatitis C antibodies
options.D: The time since the worker's last tetanus vaccine booster
options.E: The source patient's age and length of admission

correct_answer: A. The worker's HBV immunity status and the exposure risk
why_correct: Hepatitis B post-exposure management depends on the nature of exposure and the exposed person's vaccination and immune status.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis C status of the source does not determine hepatitis B post-exposure management. C. Blood group does not determine hepatitis B prophylaxis. D. Tetanus status is relevant to wound management, not hepatitis B prophylaxis. E. The source patient's age and length of admission do not determine prophylaxis.
pearl: The need for hepatitis B post-exposure management depends on the exposed worker's own vaccination/immunity status combined with the nature of the exposure - not on patient or worker demographics.
thinking: Filter out every option that is clinically irrelevant to leave the only biologically meaningful factor: immune status plus exposure risk.
exam_trap: Irrelevant-sounding but plausible distractors can tempt candidates searching for a clever answer instead of the straightforward correct one.
takeaway: Hepatitis B post-exposure management hinges on the worker's immunity, not on coincidental details.

stem: A patient develops an acute stroke and subsequently coughs whenever they attempt to swallow water.  What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Coughing during swallowing after stroke suggests impaired swallowing and risk of aspiration.
why_wrong: B. GORD causes heartburn and regurgitation, not coughing on swallowing water after an acute stroke. C. Gallstone disease causes biliary colic, not coughing on swallowing. D. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and/or diarrhoea, not coughing when swallowing water. E. IBS causes abdominal pain and altered bowel habit.
pearl: Coughing on swallowing after a stroke signals dysphagia with aspiration risk and should trigger swallow assessment before oral intake continues.
thinking: This is a straightforward sign-recognition question: cough with swallowing in a stroke patient has one clinically important explanation, and none of the gastrointestinal distractors fit the stroke context.
exam_trap: Candidates distracted by gastroenteritis or bowel-related options may not connect coughing on swallowing specifically to aspiration risk.
takeaway: Coughing when swallowing after a stroke means screen for aspiration, not gut disease.

presentation: Pain Out of Proportion - Necrotising Fasciitis
stem: A patient develops rapidly progressive severe limb pain, swelling and systemic toxicity. The pain is much greater than expected from the visible skin changes.  What diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Severe pain disproportionate to apparent skin findings, rapid progression and systemic toxicity are major warning signs of necrotising fasciitis.
why_wrong: A. Tinea is a superficial fungal infection. B. Chronic venous disease is usually gradual rather than rapidly     destructive. C. Osteoarthritis is chronic and does not cause systemic toxicity. E. Eczema does not cause rapidly progressive systemic toxicity.
pearl: Pain disproportionate to visible skin findings, combined with rapid progression and systemic toxicity, is the critical early warning sign of necrotising fasciitis and demands urgent surgical referral.
thinking: The phrase pain much greater than expected from the visible skin changes is the single most important red flag in the whole stem - it should override reassurance from relatively unimpressive-looking skin and prompt immediate escalation.
exam_trap: Candidates anchor on the skin appearance looking mild and underestimate severity, missing that disproportionate pain is the defining clue precisely because the skin can look deceptively unremarkable early on.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to the skin is the red flag for necrotising fasciitis - never wait for the skin to look as bad as the pain feels.

stem: A patient develops a unilateral area of spreading, warm, tender erythema on the lower leg with fever.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute spreading warmth, tenderness and erythema with systemic symptoms are typical of cellulitis.
why_wrong: A. Vitiligo causes depigmented patches. B. Alopecia areata causes non-scarring hair loss. C. Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals rather than persistent     tender spreading erythema. D. Psoriasis causes chronic scaly plaques.
pearl: Unilateral spreading warmth, tenderness, erythema and fever over the lower leg is the classic presentation of cellulitis.
thinking: This is a straightforward pattern-match: acute, unilateral, spreading, warm and tender skin changes with systemic fever point directly to cellulitis.
exam_trap: Candidates distracted by the word spreading sometimes consider psoriasis, but psoriasis is chronic and scaly rather than acutely warm and tender.
takeaway: Warm, tender, spreading redness with fever on one leg is cellulitis.

stem: An elderly patient develops an acutely painful, swollen knee. Joint aspiration identifies calcium pyrophosphate crystals.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition causes acute crystal arthritis known as pseudogout.
why_wrong: A. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals. B. Osteoarthritis is degenerative rather than an acute crystal     arthritis. C. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis. D. Septic arthritis is caused by infection rather than crystals.
pearl: Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition and is confirmed on aspiration by identifying these crystals, distinguishing it from urate-driven gout.
thinking: The stem gives the crystal identity directly, so this becomes a direct recall match rather than pattern recognition from symptoms alone.
exam_trap: Candidates may default to gout from the clinical picture of an acute hot joint without registering that the crystal described is pyrophosphate, not urate.
takeaway: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals on aspiration mean pseudogout, not gout.

stem: A man feels as though he has been kicked in the back of the ankle while playing tennis. He is unable to push off normally with the affected foot.  What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Acute gouty arthritis of the ankle

why_correct: Sudden posterior ankle pain with a sensation of being kicked and impaired plantarflexion is characteristic of Achilles tendon rupture.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not cause sudden tendon rupture symptoms. C. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. D. An ankle sprain usually follows an inversion injury and affects the lateral ligaments. E. Plantar fasciitis causes gradual heel pain.
pearl: A sudden kicked-in-the-back-of-the-ankle sensation with inability to push off is the classic history for Achilles tendon rupture.
thinking: The characteristic sensation description plus loss of plantarflexion push-off strength together point specifically to tendon rupture rather than a ligamentous ankle sprain.
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse this with an ankle sprain, but a sprain involves the lateral ligaments after twisting, not a posterior kick sensation with loss of push-off.
takeaway: The kicked-in-the-back-of-the-ankle feeling with no push-off power is an Achilles rupture.

stem: A footballer twists their ankle during a tackle and develops pain and swelling around the lateral malleolus. They can still walk.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An inversion-type injury commonly damages the lateral ankle ligaments and causes local pain and swelling.
why_wrong: A. Achilles rupture causes posterior ankle symptoms and impaired     push-off. B. Septic arthritis is not caused by an acute twisting injury. C. Hip fracture does not explain isolated lateral ankle symptoms. D. Gout is an inflammatory crystal arthritis.
pearl: An inversion injury with pain and swelling around the lateral malleolus, with preserved ability to walk, is typical of a lateral ankle sprain rather than a fracture or tendon rupture.
thinking: Note the mechanism, the location, and the retained ability to weight-bear - together these favour a ligamentous sprain over fracture or Achilles pathology.
exam_trap: Candidates may overcall this as a fracture purely because of the swelling, missing that retained walking ability and typical inversion mechanism favour a sprain.
takeaway: Inversion injury with lateral swelling but able to walk is a classic ankle sprain.

stem: An elderly woman falls onto an outstretched hand and develops a displaced distal radius fracture with a characteristic “dinner-fork” deformity.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement producing a dinner-fork deformity is a Colles fracture.
why_wrong: A. Radial head fractures involve the elbow. B. A Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar     displacement. C. Clavicle fractures affect the shoulder girdle. D. Scaphoid fracture causes wrist pain and anatomical snuffbox     tenderness.
pearl: A Colles fracture is a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture producing the classic dinner-fork deformity after a fall onto an outstretched hand.
thinking: The deformity description is diagnostic by name - dinner-fork is specific to dorsal displacement, which should be distinguished from a Smith fracture's opposite, volar displacement.
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse Colles with Smith fracture since both are distal radius fractures from a fall; the direction of displacement is the key differentiator.
takeaway: Dinner-fork deformity after a fall onto an outstretched hand is a Colles fracture.

stem: A patient has diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness. Blood tests show low vitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase.  What condition is most likely?
why_correct: Vitamin D deficiency can cause defective bone mineralisation, producing bone pain, proximal weakness and biochemical evidence such as raised alkaline phosphatase.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis causes joint-related mechanical pain. C. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. D. Septic arthritis is an acute joint infection. E. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis.
pearl: Diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, low vitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase together indicate osteomalacia - defective mineralisation of bone in adults.
thinking: Combine the biochemical picture with the clinical picture to land on a mineralisation disorder rather than an inflammatory or degenerative joint disease, none of which explain the biochemistry.
exam_trap: Candidates may be tempted by osteoarthritis because of bone/joint pain wording, overlooking that OA does not cause this biochemical derangement or proximal muscle weakness.
takeaway: Bone pain, proximal weakness, low vitamin D and raised ALP point to osteomalacia.

stem: A patient with a history of smoking develops proximal leg weakness and reduced reflexes. The weakness improves temporarily after repeated muscle activity.  Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Proximal weakness with reduced reflexes and facilitation after repeated activity is characteristic of Lambert-Eaton syndrome, which is associated with small-cell lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness but reflexes are usually preserved. B. A multiple sclerosis relapse produces central neurological deficits rather than this characteristic neuromuscular pattern. C. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, without improvement on repeated activity. D. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes acute ascending weakness with areflexia but no facilitation after exercise.
pearl: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal weakness with reduced reflexes that paradoxically improve with repeated muscle activity, and is strongly associated with small-cell lung cancer in smokers.
thinking: The two features that separate this from myasthenia gravis are the reduced reflexes and the improvement of strength with repeated activity; combined with the smoking history, this points to a paraneoplastic neuromuscular junction disorder.
exam_trap: Candidates frequently default to myasthenia gravis because both cause fatigable-sounding weakness, missing that reflexes are reduced and strength improves, not worsens, with repetition in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
takeaway: Reduced reflexes that improve with repeated effort in a smoker point to Lambert-Eaton syndrome, not myasthenia gravis.

stem: A man has a painless enlargement of one side of the scrotum. The swelling allows light to pass through it on transillumination.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A hydrocele is a collection of fluid around the testis and classically transilluminates.
why_wrong: A. Epididymo-orchitis causes painful inflammatory swelling. B. An inguinal hernia may produce a groin/scrotal swelling but does     not characteristically transilluminate. D. Torsion causes acute pain. E. A solid testicular tumour does not typically transilluminate.
pearl: A painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates is a hydrocele - a fluid collection around the testis.
thinking: Transillumination is the single diagnostic clue here: fluid collections transilluminate while solid masses and most hernias typically do not, immediately narrowing the differential.
exam_trap: Candidates may consider an inguinal hernia since it can also cause scrotal swelling, but hernias do not characteristically transilluminate the way a pure fluid collection does.
takeaway: A scrotal swelling that lights up on transillumination is a hydrocele.

stem: An elderly patient with poor access to water develops marked thirst and confusion. Blood tests show a sodium concentration of 153 mmol/L.  What is the most likely abnormality?
why_correct: A sodium concentration above the normal range represents hypernatraemia, commonly associated with a deficit of free water.
why_wrong: A. Hypermagnesaemia concerns magnesium. C. Hypocalcaemia concerns calcium. D. Hypokalaemia concerns potassium. E. Hyponatraemia is a low sodium concentration.
pearl: A sodium concentration above the normal range defines hypernatraemia, commonly due to inadequate free water intake, especially in elderly or dependent patients.
thinking: This is a direct laboratory-value match: identify that the stated sodium level is elevated and match this to the one electrolyte option concerning sodium excess.
exam_trap: Candidates occasionally confuse hyper- and hyponatraemia under time pressure, especially when the clinical picture could superficially fit either.
takeaway: Thirst, confusion and poor water access with a raised sodium level is hypernatraemia.

stem: A patient with prolonged diarrhoea develops muscle cramps and cardiac arrhythmias. Blood tests show a low magnesium concentration.  What is the most likely abnormality?
why_correct: Low magnesium can cause neuromuscular symptoms and cardiac arrhythmias and may occur after prolonged gastrointestinal losses.
why_wrong: A. Hypermagnesaemia is an elevated magnesium concentration. B. Hypercalcaemia has a different clinical pattern. D. Hypernatraemia reflects excess sodium relative to water. E. Hyperkalaemia concerns potassium rather than magnesium.
pearl: Prolonged diarrhoea can cause significant magnesium loss, producing muscle cramps and cardiac arrhythmias from hypomagnesaemia, which often needs correcting alongside potassium.
thinking: Trace the mechanism from the clinical context to the stated low magnesium level, matching neuromuscular and cardiac symptoms to this specific electrolyte.
exam_trap: Candidates may consider hyperkalaemia because of the cardiac arrhythmia mention, overlooking that the stem explicitly states a low magnesium level driving the presentation.
takeaway: Diarrhoea-related cramps and arrhythmias with low magnesium mean hypomagnesaemia.

presentation: Irreducible Femoral Hernia at Risk of Strangulation
stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with a painful groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is irreducible. What is the main concern?

options.C: Large saphena varix in the groin

why_correct: Femoral hernias have a relatively narrow neck and are particularly prone to incarceration and strangulation.
why_wrong: B. An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle. C. A saphena varix is usually compressible and associated with venous disease. D. A lipoma is not typically acutely painful and irreducible. E. Lymph nodes do not usually produce a cough impulse or acute obstructive symptoms.
pearl: Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and have a narrow neck that makes them especially prone to irreducibility and strangulation, warranting urgent surgical review.
thinking: Combine the anatomical landmark with the clinical red flag to recognise both the hernia type and its urgent surgical risk.
exam_trap: Candidates may focus only on the anatomical position and underestimate the urgency implied by painful and irreducible, which signal possible strangulation.
takeaway: An irreducible, painful groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is a femoral hernia at risk of strangulation.

stem: A patient develops a large collection of clear fluid beneath a surgical wound several days after surgery. There is no significant erythema or systemic illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A seroma is a collection of serous fluid that can occur after surgery, particularly where tissue planes have been extensively dissected.
why_wrong: A. A haematoma contains blood. C. Dehiscence is separation of the wound edges. D. An abscess contains infected material and usually causes     inflammatory signs. E. Cellulitis is diffuse infection of the skin and subcutaneous     tissues.
pearl: Seromas are sterile fluid collections that form in dead space after extensive tissue dissection (e.g. mastectomy, hernia repair) and usually resolve with observation or aspiration unless infected.
thinking: Clear fluid with no erythema and no systemic upset rules out infection and haematoma in one step; dehiscence requires wound-edge separation, which is not described, so seroma is the best fit.
exam_trap: Candidates may jump to 'abscess' because of the word 'collection', missing that pus, not clear fluid, defines an abscess.
takeaway: Clear fluid with no inflammation after surgery is a seroma, not infection.

stem: A patient has separation of a recently closed abdominal wound with protrusion of abdominal contents. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Saline-soaked sterile dressing and urgent surgical review
options.C: Apply an abdominal binder and arrange routine review
options.D: Replace the contents manually and re-close at the bedside
options.E: Apply a dry dressing and review on tomorrow's ward round

correct_answer: B. Saline-soaked sterile dressing and urgent surgical review
why_correct: Wound dehiscence with exposed abdominal contents is a surgical emergency. The exposed viscera should be protected with sterile saline-soaked dressings while urgent surgical assessment is arranged.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics alone are insufficient. C. Compression may damage exposed viscera, and routine review delays an emergency. D. The contents should not be reduced and closed at the bedside; this requires theatre. E. Dry dressings adhere to bowel, and delaying assessment risks bowel injury and contamination.
pearl: Exposed bowel is never pushed back blind: cover it with saline-soaked gauze to prevent desiccation while arranging immediate surgical review.
thinking: Recognise 'protrusion of abdominal contents' as evisceration, a surgical emergency, then pick the option that protects the bowel with a moist dressing while escalating rather than one that treats superficially or delays.
exam_trap: Distractors offering a dry dressing or 'review tomorrow' tempt candidates who underestimate how urgent exposed viscera really are.
takeaway: Evisceration: cover it moist and call the surgeons now.

stem: A 55-year-old man notices a bulge from his rectum when straining. It is initially reducible but has gradually become more prominent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rectal prolapse is protrusion of rectal wall through the anal canal, often becoming more apparent with straining.
why_wrong: A. An inguinal hernia presents in the groin. B. An abscess causes painful swelling and infection. C. Thrombosed haemorrhoids produce a painful perianal lump. E. A fissure causes painful defecation rather than prolapse.
pearl: Full-thickness rectal prolapse typically occurs in older patients with chronic straining and pelvic floor weakness, and shows concentric mucosal folds on examination, unlike prolapsing piles.
thinking: A reducible-then-progressive rectal bulge on straining is the classic natural history of prolapse; thrombosed haemorrhoids would instead be acutely painful and fixed, not gradually enlarging.
exam_trap: Candidates may pick haemorrhoidal thrombosis because both protrude through the anus, missing that thrombosed piles are acutely painful rather than a straining-related bulge.
takeaway: A gradually enlarging, straining-induced rectal bulge is prolapse, not piles.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has very heavy menstrual bleeding and a pelvic mass. Ultrasound shows a well-defined mass arising from the uterine wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Uterine fibroids are benign smooth-muscle tumours and commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged or irregular uterus.
why_wrong: A. An endometrioma is an ovarian manifestation of endometriosis. C. A cervical polyp arises from the cervix rather than the uterine     wall. D. Ectopic pregnancy requires a pregnancy. E. Ovarian cancer usually presents with abdominal distension, pelvic     symptoms or altered bowel/bladder symptoms.
pearl: Fibroids are the commonest pelvic tumour in women and classically cause heavy menstrual bleeding with a mass arising from, not separate to, the uterine wall.
thinking: The mass arises from the uterine wall itself, which immediately excludes ovarian or cervical origins, leaving fibroid as the only uterine-wall option among those listed.
exam_trap: Endometrioma is a tempting distractor for any pelvic mass with heavy bleeding, but it is ovarian, not uterine, in origin.
takeaway: A mass arising from the uterine wall with menorrhagia is a fibroid.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has severe cyclical pelvic pain and deep pain during sexual intercourse. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?
why_correct: Endometriosis commonly causes cyclical pelvic pain and deep dyspareunia.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial vaginosis causes abnormal vaginal discharge rather than     cyclical deep pelvic pain. B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. C. Fibroids more commonly cause heavy menstrual bleeding and     pressure symptoms. D. Appendicitis causes acute rather than typically cyclical pelvic     pain.
pearl: Deep dyspareunia plus cyclical pelvic pain is the classic endometriosis pairing, though laparoscopy remains the diagnostic gold standard because imaging can be normal.
thinking: Cyclical timing plus deep dyspareunia together exclude cystitis and bacterial vaginosis, which are not cyclical, pointing instead to endometrial tissue outside the uterus.
exam_trap: Fibroids are a common wrong pick because they also cause pelvic symptoms, but they classically cause heavy bleeding and pressure rather than deep dyspareunia.
takeaway: Cyclical pain plus deep dyspareunia points to endometriosis.

stem: A woman presents with amenorrhoea, breast tenderness and a positive pregnancy test. She subsequently develops vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate first investigation to establish the location and viability of the pregnancy?
why_correct: Ultrasound is used to establish pregnancy location and assess viability when early pregnancy complications are suspected.
why_wrong: B. Serum hCG supports assessment of a pregnancy of unknown location but cannot itself establish location or viability. C. Sigmoidoscopy is irrelevant to the immediate problem. D. CT is not the first-line investigation in early pregnancy. E. CA125 is not used to establish early pregnancy location.
pearl: Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to locate a pregnancy and assess viability whenever bleeding or pain complicates early pregnancy.
thinking: Amenorrhoea, positive hCG and then bleeding and pain raise concern for miscarriage or ectopic; ultrasound is the only listed test that can answer both the location and viability questions directly.
exam_trap: CA125 is a tempting distractor as an 'ovarian' test, but it has no role in dating or locating a pregnancy.
takeaway: Bleeding in early pregnancy: ultrasound first, to confirm location and viability.
