options.C: Pulmonary lesions commonly cause cranial diabetes insipidus
options.D: Hypoxia directly blocks free-water excretion by the kidneys
options.E: Some lung disorders trigger inappropriate ADH release

correct_answer: E. Some lung disorders trigger inappropriate ADH release
why_correct: Certain pulmonary disorders, including some malignancies, can be associated with inappropriate ADH secretion.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia does not mimic SIADH and is not the link here. B. Lung disease does not directly increase PTH. C. Pulmonary lesions do not commonly cause cranial diabetes insipidus, which produces the opposite picture. D. Hypoxia does not directly block renal free-water excretion; the problem is inappropriate ADH.
pearl: Pulmonary conditions, including infections and malignancies (notably small cell lung cancer), are recognised causes of SIADH via ectopic or inappropriate ADH secretion.
thinking: Connect the new pulmonary lesion to SIADH through the known paraneoplastic/infective mechanism of inappropriate ADH release, rather than unrelated absolute statements about diabetes insipidus or calcium.
exam_trap: Overly absolute distractors ('always causes...') are a signal to eliminate them, since pulmonary disease is only sometimes, not invariably, linked to SIADH.
takeaway: New lung lesion plus hyponatraemia — think SIADH, especially small cell lung cancer.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with painless visible blood in his urine. There is no evidence of urinary infection. What important diagnosis must be excluded?
why_correct: Unexplained visible haematuria, particularly in an older adult, requires assessment for urinary tract malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Prostatic enlargement can bleed, but haematuria should not be attributed to it until malignancy is excluded. C. Exercise-induced haematuria is a diagnosis of exclusion after malignancy is ruled out. D. IgA nephropathy is more typical in younger adults, often after an infection. E. Calculi usually cause pain, and the priority remains to exclude malignancy.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria in an adult, especially over 45, must be investigated urgently to exclude urothelial or renal malignancy.
thinking: Recognise painless visible haematuria without infection as a red-flag symptom requiring a suspected cancer pathway referral rather than reassurance.
exam_trap: Candidates may wait for other urinary symptoms before referring, but painless haematuria alone is sufficient to trigger urgent investigation.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria = cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 30-year-old man has gradual onset of unilateral scrotal pain, dysuria and fever. The epididymis is tender. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Gradual scrotal pain with urinary symptoms, fever and epididymal tenderness is typical of epididymitis.
why_wrong: A. Torsion is usually sudden and severe. B. Hydrocele is generally painless. C. Varicocele is usually chronic and non-acute. E. Testicular cancer is usually painless.
pearl: Epididymitis typically presents with gradual unilateral scrotal pain, dysuria, fever and a tender epididymis, in contrast to the sudden severe pain of torsion.
thinking: Use the time course (gradual vs sudden) and associated urinary/infective symptoms to distinguish epididymitis from testicular torsion, which is the key differential to exclude.
exam_trap: Torsion must always be actively excluded in acute scrotal pain; relying solely on a gradual onset history without examination/imaging risks missing a torsion.
takeaway: Gradual scrotal pain with fever and dysuria favours epididymitis; sudden severe pain favours torsion until excluded.

stem: A 33-year-old woman develops diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and bloating after consuming wheat-containing foods. She has also lost weight. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, weight loss and a relationship with gluten-containing foods should raise suspicion of coeliac disease.
why_wrong: B. Biliary colic causes episodic right upper abdominal pain. C. Renal colic causes acute flank pain. D. Lactose intolerance is specifically related to lactose rather than gluten. E. Appendicitis is an acute illness.
pearl: Coeliac disease should be considered in patients with chronic GI symptoms and weight loss triggered by gluten-containing foods; diagnosis requires serology (anti-tTG) while still eating gluten.
thinking: Link the gluten-symptom relationship and weight loss to coeliac disease rather than lactose intolerance, which relates specifically to dairy rather than wheat.
exam_trap: Lactose intolerance is a common distractor since both cause bloating/diarrhoea, but the wheat-specific trigger points to gluten, not lactose.
takeaway: GI symptoms plus weight loss triggered by wheat — think coeliac disease, test serology before gluten withdrawal.

stem: A 76-year-old man develops abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation. His abdomen is markedly distended. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Abdominal distension, vomiting and inability to pass stool or flatus are characteristic features of intestinal obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Urinary retention causes suprapubic distension and inability to pass urine, not vomiting and absolute constipation. C. Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea rather than absolute constipation. D. IBS does not cause absolute constipation with marked distension and vomiting. E. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain without distension or absolute constipation.
pearl: Abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus) form the classic triad of intestinal obstruction.
thinking: Recognise the triad of distension, vomiting and absolute constipation as mechanical bowel obstruction rather than an unrelated non-abdominal diagnosis.
exam_trap: Distractors from unrelated systems (ENT, joints, urinary) are included to test basic pattern recognition rather than close differentials.
takeaway: Distension + vomiting + absolute constipation = bowel obstruction.

stem: A 70-year-old man develops sudden severe abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension. He has a previous history of abdominal surgery. What is a common cause of intestinal obstruction in this setting?

options.B: Gallstone ileus in the terminal ileum

why_correct: Previous abdominal surgery is a major risk factor for adhesive small-bowel obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Gallstone ileus is a rare cause of obstruction and is not linked to previous surgery. C. Mesenteric lymphadenitis causes abdominal pain, mainly in children, not mechanical obstruction. D. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea rather than distension with obstruction. E. Biliary colic does not cause intestinal obstruction.
pearl: Adhesions from previous abdominal surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.
thinking: Use the history of prior abdominal surgery as the key clue pointing to adhesions as the cause of obstruction, ahead of other less common causes.
exam_trap: Hernias are another common cause of obstruction and may be considered, but a clear surgical history makes adhesions the best-supported answer here.
takeaway: Previous abdominal surgery + obstruction = think adhesions first.

stem: A 29-year-old woman develops a circular, expanding erythematous rash on her thigh several days after returning from a hiking trip. She recalls removing a tick. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Erythema migrans is the characteristic expanding rash associated with early Lyme disease following a tick bite.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis is related to exposure to an irritant or allergen. B. Urticaria produces transient raised wheals. C. Psoriasis typically produces persistent scaly plaques. D. Cellulitis is usually a painful, hot, more diffuse bacterial skin infection.
pearl: Erythema migrans is an expanding erythematous 'bullseye' rash appearing days after a tick bite and is diagnostic of early Lyme disease.
thinking: Connect the tick exposure history and the specific expanding, circular rash morphology to erythema migrans rather than more generic skin infections.
exam_trap: Cellulitis is a common distractor, but it is usually more acutely painful, hot and does not have the classic expanding annular/target appearance.
takeaway: Expanding rash after a tick bite = erythema migrans, treat as Lyme disease.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops fever, headache and a widespread maculopapular rash after returning from sub-Saharan Africa. He has not taken malaria prophylaxis. Which investigation is particularly important?
why_correct: Fever after travel to a malaria-endemic region is malaria until excluded, particularly without prophylaxis.
why_wrong: B. Faecal calprotectin assesses intestinal inflammation. C. Bone densitometry assesses bone mineral density. D. Spirometry assesses airflow. E. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury.
pearl: Fever in a returning traveller from a malaria-endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, regardless of prophylaxis use.
thinking: Prioritise the travel history and lack of prophylaxis as the key safety-critical clue pointing to urgent malaria testing over other investigations.
exam_trap: Non-specific distractors testing unrelated organ systems are there to test whether candidates recognise the travel-fever red flag.
takeaway: Fever + travel to malaria-endemic area = test for malaria urgently.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a painless, slowly enlarging lump on the back. It is smooth, soft and mobile beneath the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass is characteristic of a lipoma.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis is a diffuse skin infection rather than a discrete mobile lump. C. An abscess is usually painful, inflamed and fluctuant. D. Squamous cell carcinoma is usually a lesion arising from the skin surface. E. Melanoma is a pigmented malignant skin lesion.
pearl: A lipoma is a soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous lump composed of mature adipocytes and is the most common benign soft tissue tumour.
thinking: Apply classic lump examination findings — soft, mobile, painless, slow-growing — to identify a benign lipoma rather than a malignant or inflammatory lesion.
exam_trap: Any lump description can trigger cancer-related anxiety in exam questions, but the specific soft/mobile/painless triad is reassuringly benign.
takeaway: Soft, mobile, painless lump = think lipoma.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has a painful fluctuant lump in the axilla with surrounding erythema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful, fluctuant, erythematous lump is characteristic of a collection of pus.
why_wrong: A. Melanoma is a malignant melanocytic skin lesion. C. Seborrhoeic keratosis is a benign superficial skin lesion. D. Fibroadenoma occurs in breast tissue and is usually painless. E. Lipomas are usually soft, mobile and painless.
pearl: A painful, fluctuant, erythematous lump represents a collection of pus (abscess) and usually requires incision and drainage.
thinking: Use the clinical hallmarks of infection — pain, fluctuance, surrounding erythema — to identify an abscess rather than a benign, painless mass.
exam_trap: Lipoma and fibroadenoma are distractors chosen because they are common lumps, but both are classically painless and non-fluctuant.
takeaway: Painful, fluctuant, erythematous lump = abscess, think incision and drainage.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of nasal congestion and sneezing every spring. Her eyes are itchy and watery. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Seasonal sneezing, nasal congestion and itchy watery eyes are typical of seasonal allergic rhinitis.
why_wrong: A. Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis usually causes facial pain/pressure and purulent symptoms. C. Nasal fracture follows trauma. D. A nasal foreign body is mainly relevant to children and usually causes unilateral symptoms. E. Non-allergic rhinitis is not seasonal and is not associated with itchy, watery eyes.
pearl: Seasonal allergic rhinitis presents with recurrent sneezing, nasal congestion and itchy, watery eyes occurring at the same time each year, typically from pollen exposure.
thinking: Use the seasonal recurrence pattern and ocular itching/watering to distinguish allergic rhinitis from infective or structural nasal causes.
exam_trap: Bacterial sinusitis is a common distractor, but it typically causes facial pain/pressure and purulent discharge rather than itchy eyes and seasonal recurrence.
takeaway: Seasonal sneezing with itchy, watery eyes = allergic rhinitis.

stem: A 44-year-old man develops a painful swelling of the parotid gland, particularly when eating. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent salivary swelling and pain triggered by meals is characteristic of obstructed salivary flow, often due to a stone.
why_wrong: B. Otitis externa affects the external ear. C. Pleomorphic adenoma causes a slowly enlarging painless mass not related to meals. D. A dental abscess causes tooth pain and facial swelling not specifically triggered by eating. E. Sjögren syndrome causes dry eyes and mouth with persistent, often bilateral, gland enlargement.
pearl: Salivary gland swelling and pain that worsens with eating suggests ductal obstruction, commonly by a stone (sialolithiasis).
thinking: Connect the meal-related trigger (increased salivary flow against an obstruction) to a salivary duct stone rather than thyroid or dental pathology.
exam_trap: Thyroid disease is a plausible-sounding distractor, but it does not characteristically cause pain specifically triggered by eating.
takeaway: Parotid swelling that worsens with eating = think a salivary duct stone.

stem: A 70-year-old woman develops gradual pain and stiffness in both knees that is worse after prolonged walking and improves with rest. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Mechanical joint pain and stiffness associated with activity are typical of osteoarthritis.
why_wrong: B. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects the shoulder and hip girdles. C. Gout typically causes acute inflammatory attacks. D. Acute rheumatic fever has a different systemic presentation. E. Septic arthritis is usually acute, painful and associated with systemic illness.
pearl: Osteoarthritis causes mechanical joint pain and stiffness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, typically in older patients.
thinking: Use the activity-related pain pattern and patient age to favour a degenerative mechanical cause over inflammatory or infective arthritis.
exam_trap: Polymyalgia rheumatica is a tempting distractor in an older patient, but it classically affects the shoulder and hip girdles with marked early morning stiffness, not isolated knee pain.
takeaway: Activity-related knee pain relieved by rest in an older adult = osteoarthritis.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a newly diagnosed DVT asks why anticoagulation has been prescribed. What is the main purpose?

options.A: To lower blood viscosity and improve venous return
options.B: To treat the inflammation within the affected vein wall
options.C: To reduce platelet aggregation within the deep vein
options.D: To prevent clot extension and embolisation
options.E: To dissolve the existing clot rapidly within days

correct_answer: D. To prevent clot extension and embolisation
why_correct: Anticoagulation reduces further thrombus formation and the risk of embolisation while the body's fibrinolytic system breaks down the clot.
why_wrong: A. Anticoagulants do not act by reducing blood viscosity. B. Anticoagulants are not anti-inflammatory. C. Anticoagulants act on coagulation factors, not platelet aggregation. E. Anticoagulants do not directly dissolve existing clot as thrombolytic therapy does.
pearl: Anticoagulation in DVT prevents clot extension and embolisation while the body's own fibrinolytic system gradually breaks down the existing clot.
thinking: Distinguish the role of anticoagulants (preventing further clot formation/embolisation) from thrombolytics (actively dissolving clot) to select the correct mechanism.
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes believe anticoagulants dissolve existing clots like thrombolytics do, which is incorrect.
takeaway: Anticoagulants prevent clot growth and embolisation; they don't dissolve existing clots.

stem: A 34-year-old healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a needle that was used on a patient whose HIV status is unknown. What should the healthcare worker do first?

options.A: Suck the wound immediately to remove contaminated blood
options.B: Scrub the wound with an alcohol-based disinfectant gel
options.C: Wait for the source patient's blood results before acting
options.D: Wash the affected area with soap and running water
options.E: Cover the wound with a dressing and finish the shift

correct_answer: D. Wash the affected area with soap and running water
why_correct: Immediate washing of the exposed area is an important first step following a needlestick injury, followed by prompt occupational-health assessment.
why_wrong: A. Sucking the wound is not recommended. B. Scrubbing or applying disinfectants such as alcohol may damage tissue and is not recommended. C. First aid and reporting should not wait for source results. E. The wound should be washed immediately and the injury reported promptly.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, the wound should be encouraged to bleed gently and washed immediately with soap and running water, then reported for risk assessment.
thinking: Follow standard first-aid sequence for sharps injuries: wash first, then seek occupational health assessment, rather than sucking, scrubbing with alcohol, or delaying care.
exam_trap: Scrubbing with alcohol gel or waiting for the source patient's results can seem sensible, but first aid is simply washing with soap and running water, then urgent reporting and assessment.
takeaway: Needlestick first aid: wash with soap and water immediately, then report and seek assessment.

presentation: Hepatitis B Exposure With Documented Immunity
stem: A healthcare worker is exposed to blood from a patient known to have hepatitis B. The worker has completed an appropriate hepatitis B vaccination course and has documented immunity. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: HIV PEP should be started for this exposure
options.B: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is routinely required
options.C: The worker should stop clinical work until tested
options.D: Vaccination protects poorly against this route
options.E: Documented immunity substantially reduces the risk

correct_answer: E. Documented immunity substantially reduces the risk
why_correct: Effective hepatitis B vaccination with documented immunity provides strong protection against occupational exposure.
why_wrong: A. HIV PEP depends on HIV risk and is unrelated to hepatitis B exposure. B. HBIG is not routinely needed for a worker with documented immunity. C. Exposure does not require withdrawal from clinical work. D. Vaccination provides effective protection against occupational exposure.
pearl: A healthcare worker with documented immunity from completed hepatitis B vaccination has substantially reduced risk following exposure and usually needs no further intervention.
thinking: Interpret 'documented immunity' as sufficient reassurance rather than triggering unnecessary additional treatment or restriction of duties.
exam_trap: Absolute distractors (permanent avoidance of patients, automatic HIV treatment) should be eliminated as disproportionate responses to a hepatitis B exposure with known immunity.
takeaway: Documented hepatitis B immunity greatly reduces risk after exposure.

stem: A patient with sickle cell disease becomes acutely confused and develops a focal neurological deficit. What complication should be urgently considered?
why_correct: Sickle cell disease increases the risk of cerebrovascular complications, including stroke.
why_wrong: B. Tension headache does not cause focal neurological deficits. C. Peripheral neuropathy does not usually cause an acute focal cortical syndrome. D. Migraine does not adequately explain a new focal deficit in this high-risk context. E. Bell's palsy causes isolated lower motor neurone facial weakness.
pearl: Sickle cell disease significantly increases the risk of ischaemic stroke, particularly in children and young adults, due to vaso-occlusion in cerebral vessels.
thinking: Recognise acute confusion with a focal neurological deficit in a known sickle cell patient as a vaso-occlusive cerebrovascular event requiring urgent imaging and exchange transfusion.
exam_trap: Migraine or peripheral neuropathy may be considered, but a new focal deficit in sickle cell disease must be treated as stroke until proven otherwise.
takeaway: New focal neurological deficit in sickle cell disease = stroke until excluded.

stem: A man with haemophilia develops a painful swollen knee without significant trauma. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Bleeding into joints is a characteristic complication of severe haemophilia.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis is generally chronic and mechanical. C. Meniscal degeneration does not explain spontaneous joint swelling in this context. D. Gout causes inflammatory arthritis but is not the typical explanation in haemophilia. E. Cellulitis affects skin and soft tissue rather than causing primary joint bleeding.
pearl: Spontaneous or minor-trauma joint bleeding (haemarthrosis) is a hallmark complication of haemophilia and can lead to chronic arthropathy if recurrent.
thinking: Connect a swollen, painful joint without significant trauma in a known haemophiliac directly to bleeding into the joint space rather than degenerative or infective causes.
exam_trap: Septic arthritis/cellulitis should still be considered in a hot joint, but the absence of trauma plus known haemophilia points strongly to haemarthrosis.
takeaway: Atraumatic joint swelling in haemophilia = haemarthrosis.

stem: A patient with haemophilia is found to have a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Which abnormality is most likely?
correct_answer: E. Factor VIII or IX deficiency
why_correct: Haemophilia A and B result from deficiencies of factor VIII and IX respectively and characteristically prolong the APTT.
why_wrong: A. Increased fibrinogen is not the underlying defect. B. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT rather than the APTT. C. Platelet count is generally normal in haemophilia. D. Vitamin K deficiency mainly prolongs the PT and is not the defect in haemophilia.
pearl: Haemophilia A and B are caused by deficiencies of factor VIII and IX respectively, both of which prolong the APTT while the PT remains normal.
thinking: Link the intrinsic pathway factors (VIII, IX) to the APTT test, recalling that haemophilia spares the extrinsic pathway (and therefore the PT).
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse haemophilia's coagulation factor defect with a platelet disorder, but platelet count and function are typically normal in haemophilia.
takeaway: Haemophilia prolongs APTT (intrinsic pathway, factor VIII/IX) with a normal PT.

stem: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency develops numbness in both feet and difficulty walking. Which complication is particularly important?
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological dysfunction, including peripheral neuropathy and posterior column dysfunction.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 deficiency does not cause hyperthyroidism. C. Acute glaucoma is unrelated. D. Hearing loss is not a characteristic consequence. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological impairment, including peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
thinking: Link numbness and gait difficulty in B12 deficiency to its known neurological effects (posterior column and peripheral nerve involvement) rather than unrelated distractors.
exam_trap: Candidates may focus only on the hematological (macrocytic anaemia) features of B12 deficiency and overlook the important, sometimes irreversible, neurological complications.
takeaway: B12 deficiency can cause serious, potentially irreversible neurological damage — treat it promptly.

stem: A patient has fatigue, recurrent infections and easy bruising. Full blood count shows low haemoglobin, neutrophils and platelets. What does this pattern represent?
why_correct: Pancytopenia means reduction in red cells, white cells and platelets.
why_wrong: B. Only neutrophils are reduced in isolated neutropenia. C. Leukocytosis means an increased white-cell count. D. Polycythaemia means increased red-cell mass. E. Only the platelet count is reduced in isolated thrombocytopenia.
pearl: Pancytopenia refers to a simultaneous reduction in red cells, white cells (neutrophils) and platelets, producing fatigue, infection risk and bruising.
thinking: Match the triad of symptoms (fatigue, infections, bruising) to reduction across all three cell lines, rather than an isolated cytopenia.
exam_trap: Isolated cytopenia distractors (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia alone) explain only part of the clinical picture, not the full triad described.
takeaway: Fatigue + infections + bruising with low Hb, neutrophils and platelets = pancytopenia.

stem: A 46-year-old healthcare worker develops persistent wrist pain after repeatedly performing a manual task at work. The symptoms worsen during the activity and improve during periods away from work. What is an appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Advise permanent change of job before assessment
options.B: Assess work exposure and consider a work-related cause
options.C: Review again if symptoms persist for a year
options.D: Attribute the symptoms to age-related osteoarthritis
options.E: Start methotrexate for presumed inflammatory arthritis

correct_answer: B. Assess work exposure and consider a work-related cause
why_correct: Symptoms related to repetitive occupational activity should prompt assessment of workplace exposures, ergonomics and appropriate management.
why_wrong: A. A permanent job change is not required before assessment. C. Early assessment can prevent progression and prolonged disability. D. The temporal relationship with work makes occupational factors relevant, and osteoarthritis is unlikely to explain this pattern. E. There are no features of inflammatory arthritis to justify methotrexate.
pearl: Symptoms that worsen with repetitive occupational activity and improve away from work should prompt assessment for a work-related musculoskeletal disorder and review of ergonomics/exposure.
thinking: Use the temporal pattern (worse with activity, better away from it) to recognise an occupational cause, then choose the option that assesses rather than dismisses or over-treats.
exam_trap: Options offering an immediate firm diagnosis (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis) or an extreme management step (permanent work avoidance) are tempting but unjustified from the history alone.
takeaway: Symptoms that track with work exposure deserve an occupational assessment, not a snap diagnosis.

stem: A 4-year-old child is repeatedly found with bruises on the shins after playing outdoors. There are no bruises elsewhere and the child is otherwise well. Which feature would make non-accidental injury more concerning?

options.A: A single bruise over the shin
options.B: A minor graze on the elbow
options.C: A small bruise after playing football
options.D: Bruising on the torso, ears or neck
options.E: A bruise over the knee after falling

correct_answer: D. Bruising on the torso, ears or neck
why_correct: Bruising in unusual locations, particularly protected areas, should raise concern for possible non-accidental injury and requires appropriate safeguarding assessment.
why_wrong: A. Shin bruising is common in active children. B. Minor elbow injuries are common in childhood. C. Sports-related bruising has a plausible accidental mechanism. E. Knee bruising can occur after ordinary falls.
pearl: Bruising on unusual or well-protected body sites (torso, ears, buttocks, neck) in a child who is not independently mobile or playing roughly should raise concern for non-accidental injury.
thinking: Contrast the described benign shin bruising (common in active children) with the safeguarding red flag pattern of bruising in protected or unusual sites.
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes over-flag ordinary accidental bruising (shins, knees after falls) as concerning, when the real red flag is bruise location and the child's developmental stage.
takeaway: Shin bruises in an active child are normal; bruises on ears, torso or buttocks are not.

stem: A 6-year-old child tells a teacher that someone at home has hurt him. He appears frightened when discussing it. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: Listen calmly and follow safeguarding procedures
options.C: Ask detailed leading questions to clarify the events
options.D: Promise to keep the disclosure secret to maintain trust
options.E: Investigate the allegation personally before informing anyone

correct_answer: B. Listen calmly and follow safeguarding procedures
why_correct: Safeguarding concerns should be taken seriously, documented appropriately and escalated through established procedures.
why_wrong: A. Direct confrontation may increase risk and is not the clinician's role. C. Leading questions can contaminate the account; detailed questioning is for trained professionals. D. Confidentiality cannot be promised where safeguarding is involved. E. Professionals should not conduct their own investigative interview instead of following safeguarding pathways.
pearl: When a child discloses possible abuse, listen calmly without leading questions, take it seriously, and follow local safeguarding procedures rather than investigating or promising secrecy.
thinking: Eliminate options that involve promising confidentiality, confronting the alleged perpetrator, or self-investigating, since safeguarding pathways exist precisely to avoid these pitfalls.
exam_trap: Promising to 'keep it secret' feels supportive but is unsafe and professionally inappropriate once a safeguarding concern has been raised.
takeaway: Listen, believe, and refer through safeguarding channels — never promise secrecy or investigate alone.

stem: A patient with depression reports hearing a voice telling him that he is worthless and should die. The hallucination occurs only during periods of severe depression. What is this presentation called?
why_correct: Psychotic symptoms occurring in the context of a severe depressive episode are consistent with psychotic depression.
why_wrong: A. Schizoaffective disorder involves psychotic symptoms that also occur outside mood episodes. B. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions. D. Panic disorder causes episodic intense anxiety. E. Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition.
pearl: Mood-congruent hallucinations or delusions occurring only during severe depressive episodes define psychotic depression, a severe subtype requiring prompt psychiatric treatment.
thinking: Note that the hallucination content is mood-congruent (worthlessness, death) and occurs only alongside severe depression, distinguishing it from primary psychotic or manic illness.
exam_trap: Candidates might label any hallucination as schizophrenia; the temporal link to depressive episodes and mood-congruent content are what define psychotic depression instead.
takeaway: Hallucinations that appear only during severe depression and match depressive themes are psychotic depression.

stem: A 38-year-old man experiences intrusive thoughts that he might deliberately harm his child. He finds the thoughts distressing and has no desire or intention to act on them. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Unwanted, distressing intrusive thoughts that are inconsistent with the person's wishes are characteristic of obsessions.
why_wrong: A. A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus. B. Mania is characterised by elevated/irritable mood and increased activity. C. The patient explicitly has no intention to act on the thought. D. A delusion is a fixed false belief rather than an intrusive unwanted thought.
pearl: Unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts of harming a loved one, causing distress with no intention to act, are intrusive obsessions, not a sign of true risk or psychosis.
thinking: Key discriminators are distress and the explicit absence of intent/desire to act — these features define an obsession rather than a genuine homicidal plan or delusion.
exam_trap: A naive reading might treat any thought of harming a child as an immediate risk/safeguarding emergency, but ego-dystonic, distressing intrusive thoughts without intent are a recognised OCD symptom.
takeaway: Distressing harm-related thoughts the person doesn't want to act on are obsessions, not intent.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is distressed after witnessing a serious road traffic collision. Three months later she has recurrent intrusive memories, avoids driving and becomes highly distressed when she hears braking noises. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent re-experiencing, avoidance and heightened distress following a traumatic event are characteristic of PTSD.
why_wrong: A. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions. B. Adjustment disorder does not characteristically produce persistent trauma re-experiencing. C. Panic disorder involves recurrent panic attacks. D. GAD involves excessive worry across multiple areas of life.
pearl: Persistent re-experiencing (intrusive memories), avoidance and hyperarousal beginning after a traumatic event, lasting beyond a month, define PTSD.
thinking: Use the trauma trigger (RTC), the specific symptom triad (intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal-type distress) and the three-month duration to confirm PTSD over adjustment disorder.
exam_trap: Adjustment disorder is the main distractor, but it does not characteristically feature persistent re-experiencing/flashback-type symptoms tied to a specific trauma trigger.
takeaway: Trauma exposure plus intrusive memories, avoidance and hyperarousal = PTSD.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after taking an overdose of paracetamol. He says he does not want to live. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Discharge immediately if he denies current symptoms
options.C: Tell his family to supervise him without further assessment
options.D: Urgent assessment of medical toxicity and suicide risk
options.E: Ignore the overdose because it was impulsive

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment of medical toxicity and suicide risk
why_correct: A deliberate overdose requires assessment of both physical toxicity and immediate risk of further self-harm.
why_wrong: A. Absence of immediate symptoms does not exclude serious toxicity or suicide risk. B. Routine follow-up is inadequate after a significant self-harm episode. C. Family supervision alone is insufficient. E. Impulsivity does not make the episode clinically insignificant.
pearl: Every deliberate overdose requires urgent assessment of both medical toxicity (e.g. paracetamol levels, treatment nomogram) and ongoing suicide risk before any decision about discharge.
thinking: Recognise that neither medical risk nor psychiatric risk can be assessed in isolation — both must be addressed urgently regardless of apparent symptom severity or impulsivity.
exam_trap: A common error is to discharge based on absence of current symptoms, forgetting that paracetamol toxicity is often delayed and risk assessment is still required.
takeaway: After any overdose: assess toxicity risk and suicide risk together, urgently.

stem: A screening programme is being considered for a common disease. Which feature supports the use of screening?

options.A: There is an identifiable early stage of disease
options.B: Outcomes are similar with early or late treatment
options.C: No effective treatment is currently available
options.D: The disease is usually mild and self-limiting
options.E: The screening test has a high false-positive rate

correct_answer: A. There is an identifiable early stage of disease
why_correct: Screening is more useful when disease can be detected before symptoms and early treatment improves outcomes.
why_wrong: B. If early treatment gives no better outcome, screening has no rationale. C. Without effective treatment or intervention, screening has limited benefit. D. Screening should address a meaningful health problem. E. A high false-positive rate causes harm and unnecessary investigation.
pearl: Effective screening requires a detectable early/latent stage of disease, an accurate test, and an effective intervention that improves outcomes when applied early.
thinking: Apply the classic Wilson-Jungner principles to filter out options describing the absence of these requirements (no treatment, inaccurate test, no benefit from early treatment).
exam_trap: All the wrong options are essentially negations of screening criteria; the trap is picking a feature that sounds relevant but actually argues against screening.
takeaway: Good screening needs an early detectable stage, an accurate test, and effective early treatment.

stem: A woman receives a positive screening test for a disease. She is worried that this proves she definitely has the disease. What should she be told?

options.A: A positive screening test usually requires further diagnostic assessment
options.B: Screening tests always establish the diagnosis
options.D: No further testing is ever required
options.E: A positive screening result means treatment must start immediately

correct_answer: A. A positive screening test usually requires further diagnostic assessment
why_correct: Screening identifies people at increased probability of disease; diagnostic testing may be required to establish the diagnosis.
why_wrong: B. Screening and diagnostic testing have different purposes. C. Screening tests are not perfectly specific. D. Further assessment may be necessary. E. Treatment should not automatically follow an unconfirmed screening result.
pearl: A positive screening test indicates increased probability of disease, not a confirmed diagnosis, and usually needs further diagnostic testing before treatment decisions.
thinking: Recall that screening tests are chosen to be sensitive but not perfectly specific, so positives require confirmation rather than triggering immediate treatment.
exam_trap: Patients (and sometimes candidates) conflate a positive screen with a certain diagnosis; the correct framing is 'increased risk requiring further testing'.
takeaway: A positive screening test raises suspicion — it doesn't confirm disease.

stem: A study reports that a new treatment reduces the risk of a complication from 10% to 5%. What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction = 10% − 5% = 5 percentage points.
why_wrong: A. This is the original baseline risk. C. This represents the relative risk reduction expressed as a percentage. D. This is the sum rather than the difference. E. This is not the difference between the two risks.
pearl: Absolute risk reduction is the simple arithmetic difference between the control event rate and the treatment event rate (10% − 5% = 5%).
thinking: Subtract the treatment group risk from the control group risk directly; do not express it as a ratio or percentage of the baseline, which would instead give relative risk reduction.
exam_trap: The 50% option represents the relative risk reduction, a common distractor when candidates mix up absolute versus relative risk calculations.
takeaway: ARR = control risk minus treatment risk, as a simple percentage-point difference.

stem: A treatment reduces an event rate from 20% to 10%. What is the relative risk?
why_correct: Relative risk = risk in treatment group ÷ risk in control group = 10% ÷ 20% = 0.5.
why_wrong: A. This is not the calculated ratio. B. This is the absolute difference expressed as percentage points. C. This is the baseline percentage rather than a relative risk. D. This is the reciprocal of the relative risk.
pearl: Relative risk is calculated as the event rate in the treatment group divided by the event rate in the control group (10% ÷ 20% = 0.5).
thinking: Divide treatment-group risk by control-group risk in that order; do not invert the ratio or confuse it with the absolute difference between the two rates.
exam_trap: Inverting the calculation (control ÷ treatment) gives 2, a tempting wrong answer for candidates who mix up numerator and denominator.
takeaway: RR = treatment risk ÷ control risk — keep the order consistent.

presentation: Duty of Candour After a Prescribing Error
stem: A doctor realises that they have made a prescribing error that reached the patient but caused no apparent harm. What is the appropriate professional response?

options.A: Discuss it only with friends outside the healthcare team
options.B: Inform the patient, apologise and report the incident
options.C: Alter the medical record to remove evidence of the error
options.D: Report it internally but not tell the patient
options.E: Say nothing to the patient as no harm occurred

correct_answer: B. Inform the patient, apologise and report the incident
why_correct: Professional practice requires openness about errors, appropriate apology and use of systems designed to support patient safety and organisational learning.
why_wrong: A. Informal discussion does not replace appropriate professional reporting and communication. C. Altering records dishonestly is unacceptable. D. Openness requires telling the patient as well as reporting the error. E. Lack of apparent harm does not justify withholding the information.
pearl: Even a harmless prescribing error must be disclosed to the patient with an appropriate apology and reported through local incident-reporting and learning systems (duty of candour).
thinking: Eliminate options involving concealment, record alteration or blaming others, since professional guidance requires openness and honesty regardless of whether harm occurred.
exam_trap: 'No harm occurred' can tempt candidates into thinking disclosure is optional; duty of candour principles apply even to near-misses and low-harm errors.
takeaway: No harm doesn't mean no disclosure — always be open, apologise, and report errors.

stem: A patient presents with sudden onset of facial weakness, arm weakness and aphasia. Which symptom particularly suggests involvement of the dominant cerebral hemisphere?
why_correct: Aphasia indicates dysfunction of dominant cortical language areas, usually in the left cerebral hemisphere.
why_wrong: A. Nystagmus can occur with vestibular or cerebellar dysfunction. C. Vertigo commonly arises from vestibular or brainstem/cerebellar disorders. D. Ataxia is particularly associated with cerebellar dysfunction. E. Tremor has multiple possible neurological causes and is not specifically a dominant cortical language sign.
pearl: Aphasia specifically indicates dysfunction of the dominant hemisphere's language areas (usually the left hemisphere in most people, including most right-handed individuals).
thinking: Distinguish aphasia (a cortical language deficit) from cerebellar or vestibular signs (ataxia, vertigo, nystagmus), which localise to different neuroanatomical regions.
exam_trap: Ataxia and nystagmus can be mistakenly linked to hemisphere dominance when they actually reflect cerebellar or brainstem/vestibular pathology instead.
takeaway: Aphasia points to the dominant hemisphere, usually the left side of the brain.

stem: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome develops increasing difficulty breathing. What complication is most important to monitor for?
why_correct: Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause rapidly progressive respiratory muscle weakness requiring urgent respiratory support.
why_wrong: B. There is no history suggesting asthma; breathing difficulty in GBS reflects neuromuscular weakness. C. Attributing breathlessness to anxiety risks missing life-threatening ventilatory failure. D. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: Guillain-Barré syndrome can progress to respiratory muscle weakness and ventilatory failure, so respiratory function (e.g. forced vital capacity) must be closely monitored.
thinking: Recognise that ascending paralysis in GBS can reach the respiratory muscles, making respiratory monitoring and potential ventilatory support the critical complication to anticipate.
exam_trap: Unrelated distractor options are included to test whether candidates correctly link the underlying disease process to its most dangerous complication rather than picking an implausible option.
takeaway: In GBS, always monitor respiratory function — ventilatory failure is the feared complication.

stem: A 62-year-old man develops a tremor, slow movements and difficulty initiating walking. His symptoms are predominantly unilateral at first. Which feature is most characteristic of Parkinson's disease?
why_correct: Bradykinesia is a core clinical feature of Parkinson's disease, typically accompanied by rigidity and/or resting tremor.
why_wrong: A. Visual aura is associated with migraine rather than Parkinson's disease. B. Acute severe headache suggests other diagnoses. C. Isolated sensory loss is not characteristic of Parkinson's disease. E. Sudden paralysis suggests an acute neurological event such as stroke.
pearl: Bradykinesia — slowness of movement with progressive reduction in amplitude/speed on repetitive action — is the core defining feature of Parkinson's disease, alongside tremor and rigidity.
thinking: Recognise bradykinesia as the cardinal diagnostic feature required for a Parkinson's disease diagnosis, distinguishing it from acute neurological events or sensory syndromes listed as distractors.
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes equate Parkinson's with tremor alone, but bradykinesia (not tremor) is the obligatory core feature in diagnostic criteria.
takeaway: Bradykinesia, not tremor alone, is the defining feature of Parkinson's disease.

stem: A 43-year-old man has dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the beginning. He has regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, regurgitation and weight loss are characteristic of achalasia.
why_wrong: B. Peptic ulcer disease does not usually cause this pattern. C. Pancreatitis does not cause chronic dysphagia. D. Gallstones do not cause dysphagia. E. Mechanical obstruction such as cancer classically causes progressive dysphagia beginning with solids.
pearl: Achalasia causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss, due to failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and loss of peristalsis.
thinking: Note dysphagia affecting solids and liquids simultaneously from onset, which differentiates a motility disorder like achalasia from the progressive, solids-first pattern of mechanical obstruction.
exam_trap: Oesophageal cancer is the main distractor; the simultaneous solid/liquid dysphagia from the start (rather than progressive) is the key discriminating clue here.
takeaway: Dysphagia to solids and liquids together from the start, with regurgitation, suggests achalasia.

stem: A patient with chronic reflux asks about lifestyle measures that may reduce symptoms. Which advice is appropriate?

options.A: Lie down for 30 minutes after meals to aid digestion
options.B: Avoid large meals and identify personal triggers
options.C: Have the main meal of the day shortly before going to bed
options.D: Stop all exercise to reduce intra-abdominal pressure
options.E: Drink more coffee after meals to aid gastric emptying

correct_answer: B. Avoid large meals and identify personal triggers
why_correct: Lifestyle measures can help reflux symptoms, including avoiding large meals and individual triggers.
why_wrong: A. Lying down soon after eating can worsen reflux. C. Large late meals can worsen reflux. D. Stopping exercise is unnecessary; weight loss and activity help. E. Caffeine can aggravate reflux symptoms.
pearl: Lifestyle advice for reflux includes avoiding large meals, identifying and avoiding individual trigger foods/behaviours, weight management, and avoiding lying down soon after eating.
thinking: Select the option promoting sensible, evidence-based behavioural change and eliminate options that would clearly worsen reflux (lying flat after eating, smoking, large late meals).
exam_trap: The other options are deliberately the opposite of good advice, testing whether candidates can correctly identify genuinely helpful versus harmful lifestyle measures.
takeaway: Smaller meals, trigger avoidance, and staying upright after eating help manage reflux.

stem: A patient with intestinal obstruction develops severe continuous abdominal pain, fever and increasing tachycardia. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Increasing continuous pain, fever and systemic deterioration in bowel obstruction raise concern for compromised bowel blood supply and strangulation.
why_wrong: A. Uncomplicated ileus does not cause fever, severe continuous pain and worsening tachycardia. B. IBS does not cause systemic toxicity. D. Simple constipation with overflow does not typically cause fever and this acute deterioration. E. Functional dyspepsia does not cause intestinal obstruction or systemic deterioration.
pearl: Severe continuous (rather than colicky) abdominal pain, fever and tachycardia in bowel obstruction suggest bowel ischaemia or strangulation, a surgical emergency requiring urgent intervention.
thinking: Note the shift from the typical colicky pain of simple obstruction to continuous pain with systemic signs of sepsis/shock, which signals compromised bowel viability.
exam_trap: Candidates may under-recognise worsening systemic signs in known obstruction as 'just worsening obstruction' rather than specifically flagging strangulation, which needs emergency surgery rather than conservative management.
takeaway: Continuous pain, fever and tachycardia in bowel obstruction = suspect strangulation, operate urgently.

stem: A young adult with multiple sclerosis develops diplopia because one eye fails to adduct appropriately when looking laterally. Which structure is classically affected in internuclear ophthalmoplegia?

options.B: Facial nerve nucleus in the pons

why_correct: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, which coordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements.
why_wrong: B. Facial nerve nucleus lesions cause facial weakness, not failure of adduction. C. Optic nerve lesions cause visual impairment. D. The cerebellar vermis and flocculus have roles in coordination, balance and smooth eye movements, not isolated failure of adduction. E. A PPRF lesion causes an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy rather than isolated failure of adduction.
pearl: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failure of adduction on lateral gaze with contralateral abducting nystagmus) localises to a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, classically from demyelination in multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Recognise the specific pattern of impaired adduction on lateral gaze as INO, then recall the brainstem tract (MLF) that coordinates conjugate horizontal gaze rather than cranial nerves supplying the eye directly.
exam_trap: Candidates may pick optic nerve or facial nerve because the complaint is 'the eye doesn't move/see properly', missing that INO is a conjugate-gaze pathway problem, not a nerve palsy.
takeaway: Failed adduction on lateral gaze in a young adult = MLF lesion (think MS).

stem: A patient with a known intracranial mass develops a new focal seizure. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.E: Peripheral nerve damage causing focal jerking

correct_answer: C. Abnormal discharges from irritated cortex
why_correct: Structural brain lesions can disrupt cortical networks and produce focal seizures.
why_wrong: A. Anaemia is not the mechanism of a focal structural seizure. B. Hypoglycaemia can cause seizures but does not explain a focal seizure from a known mass. D. Systemic hypotension causes syncope or global ischaemia rather than a focal cortical seizure. E. Peripheral nerve damage does not generate focal cortical seizures.
pearl: Structural intracranial lesions can irritate adjacent cortical tissue, producing abnormal electrical discharges that manifest as focal seizures.
thinking: Recognise that a 'new focal seizure' in a patient with a known mass points to a structural/cortical mechanism, and eliminate systemic metabolic or peripheral explanations.
exam_trap: Insulin/hypoglycaemia is a plausible-sounding distractor for seizures generally, but it doesn't explain a focal seizure arising from a known structural brain lesion.
takeaway: A known mass plus a new focal seizure = irritated cortex generating abnormal electrical activity.

stem: A patient has a slowly growing extra-axial intracranial tumour arising from the meninges. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Meningiomas arise from the meninges and are typically extra-axial tumours.
why_wrong: A. Astrocytomas arise from glial cells within the CNS. C. Pituitary adenomas arise from the pituitary gland. D. Medulloblastoma is a malignant cerebellar tumour, especially in children. E. Glioblastoma is an aggressive glial tumour within brain tissue.
pearl: Meningiomas arise from the meninges and are classically slow-growing, extra-axial intracranial tumours.
thinking: Match 'extra-axial' and 'arising from the meninges' directly to meningioma, and eliminate intra-axial glial tumours such as astrocytoma and glioblastoma.
exam_trap: Astrocytoma and glioblastoma are common distractors because they are also brain tumours, but both arise from glial cells within the brain (intra-axial), not from the meninges.
takeaway: Slow-growing extra-axial tumour from the meninges = meningioma.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes develops retinal microaneurysms and haemorrhages. What underlying process is responsible?

options.C: Optic nerve compression by a pituitary mass

why_correct: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal microvasculature and produces diabetic retinopathy.
why_wrong: B. Corneal infection and scarring affect the cornea, not the retina. C. Optic nerve compression produces visual field loss and disc pallor, not retinal microaneurysms. D. Lens dislocation does not cause diabetic retinopathy. E. Microaneurysms and haemorrhages reflect microvascular rather than large-vessel disease.
pearl: Chronic hyperglycaemia causes diabetic microvascular damage to retinal vessels, producing microaneurysms and haemorrhages in diabetic retinopathy.
thinking: Attribute retinal microaneurysms and haemorrhages in a diabetic patient to microvascular damage rather than to local ocular causes like infection or trauma.
exam_trap: Candidates might consider acute trauma or infection given the eye findings, but the chronicity and diabetes history point squarely to microvascular disease.
takeaway: Retinal microaneurysms in diabetes = microvascular damage from chronic hyperglycaemia.

stem: Which symptom is particularly characteristic of anterior uveitis?

options.D: Painless gradual loss of peripheral vision

why_correct: Anterior uveitis commonly causes photophobia, ocular pain and a painful red eye.
why_wrong: A. Sudden painless monocular blindness suggests a vascular retinal emergency. C. A curtain-like defect suggests retinal detachment. D. Gradual peripheral field loss is more characteristic of chronic glaucoma. E. Isolated eyelid swelling has a different differential diagnosis.
pearl: Photophobia alongside ocular pain and redness is a hallmark feature of anterior uveitis.
thinking: Match photophobia with a painful red eye to anterior uveitis, and separate this from retinal detachment (painless field loss) or glaucoma (gradual peripheral loss).
exam_trap: Curtain-like visual field loss is a strong distractor pointing to retinal detachment, but the question asks about a symptom of uveitis specifically, which is photophobia.
takeaway: Photophobia with a painful red eye points to anterior uveitis.

stem: A patient has involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Nystagmus is involuntary rhythmic movement of the eyes.
why_wrong: B. Strabismus is ocular misalignment. C. Ptosis is drooping of the eyelid. D. A scotoma is an area of visual field loss. E. Diplopia is double vision.
pearl: Nystagmus is involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes and can arise from vestibular, cerebellar or ocular pathology.
thinking: Directly match 'involuntary rhythmic oscillation of the eyes' to nystagmus, as opposed to strabismus (misalignment) or ptosis (eyelid drooping).
exam_trap: Strabismus is a frequent mix-up since both are eye movement/position abnormalities, but strabismus is static misalignment, not rhythmic oscillation.
takeaway: Rhythmic, involuntary eye movement = nystagmus.

stem: A healthcare worker sustains a needle-stick injury from a used needle. What is the appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Scrub the wound with a nailbrush and alcohol hand gel, then report it at the end of the shift
options.B: Cover the wound with a dressing and report it to occupational health within the next week
options.C: Soak the wound in dilute bleach solution for several minutes, then cover with a waterproof dressing
options.D: Wash the area with soap and running water and seek urgent occupational-health assessment
options.E: Wash the area, then arrange a blood test for HIV and hepatitis B and C in six weeks’ time

correct_answer: D. Wash the area with soap and running water and seek urgent occupational-health assessment
why_correct: Immediate washing followed by prompt assessment allows appropriate evaluation for blood-borne virus exposure and time-critical post-exposure measures.
why_wrong: A. Scrubbing can damage tissue, alcohol gel is not used for wound care, and reporting should not wait until the end of the shift because post-exposure measures are time-sensitive. B. Waiting a week delays risk assessment beyond the window for post-exposure prophylaxis. C. Caustic substances such as bleach should not be applied to the wound. E. Delayed testing alone omits urgent risk assessment and time-critical post-exposure measures.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, the area should be washed with soap and running water (without aggressive squeezing) and urgent occupational health assessment sought for blood-borne virus risk evaluation.
thinking: Apply the standard first-aid and reporting pathway for sharps injuries, rejecting both over-aggressive wound manipulation and any delay in seeking assessment.
exam_trap: Some candidates choose aggressive cleaning (scrubbing, alcohol or bleach) or delay reporting, but the wound should simply be washed with soap and running water and urgent occupational-health assessment sought, as post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical.
takeaway: Needlestick: wash with soap and water, then seek urgent occupational health review, don't delay or squeeze.

stem: A patient has progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Contrast imaging shows a dilated oesophagus with narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Achalasia causes impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes right lower abdominal pain. C. Crohn's disease does not characteristically produce this oesophageal pattern. D. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting and early satiety rather than classic dysphagia. E. Peptic ulcer disease primarily affects the stomach or duodenum.
pearl: Achalasia causes impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, leading to dysphagia for both solids and liquids with a dilated oesophagus and 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction on imaging.
thinking: Use the simultaneous dysphagia for both solids and liquids plus dilated oesophagus with distal narrowing to identify a motility disorder (achalasia) rather than a mechanical obstruction.
exam_trap: Candidates may expect a mechanical cause given the narrowing seen on imaging, but the simultaneous solid-and-liquid dysphagia points to a motility problem, not a structural stricture.
takeaway: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids with a dilated oesophagus = achalasia.

stem: A patient with sudden severe abdominal pain has free gas visible beneath the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray. What does this finding suggest?
why_correct: Free intraperitoneal gas can result from perforation of a hollow gastrointestinal organ.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria and oedema. B. Cystitis affects the urinary bladder. C. Uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux does not cause pneumoperitoneum. D. Constipation and faecal impaction do not produce free intraperitoneal gas.
pearl: Free gas beneath the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray in a patient with sudden severe abdominal pain indicates perforation of a hollow abdominal viscus.
thinking: Directly link free intraperitoneal gas on imaging to perforation of a hollow organ, excluding conditions (renal, urinary, benign GI) that do not cause pneumoperitoneum.
exam_trap: Simple constipation is a plausible-sounding but incorrect distractor, as it does not produce free intraperitoneal gas.
takeaway: Free sub-diaphragmatic gas = perforated hollow viscus until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient develops fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. What condition should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain form the classic Charcot triad of acute cholangitis.
why_wrong: B. Diverticulitis commonly causes left lower abdominal pain. C. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain. D. Cystitis causes lower urinary tract symptoms. E. Appendicitis typically causes right lower quadrant pain.
pearl: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain form Charcot's triad, which is classic for acute cholangitis (biliary tract infection, often due to obstruction).
thinking: Recognise the three-part triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) as Charcot's triad pointing directly to acute cholangitis.
exam_trap: Acute appendicitis and diverticulitis are distractors causing abdominal pain but do not typically present with jaundice as part of the classic triad.
takeaway: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain = Charcot's triad, suspect acute cholangitis.

stem: The appendix is most commonly located in which position relative to the caecum?
why_correct: The retrocaecal position is the most common anatomical position of the appendix.
why_wrong: A. A subhepatic appendix is an anatomical variant. C. The appendix is associated with the caecum, not the spleen. D. The appendix is not normally intrathoracic. E. A pelvic appendix is also a common variant but not present in all patients.
pearl: The retrocaecal position is the most common anatomical location of the appendix relative to the caecum.
thinking: Recall standard anatomical teaching on the most frequent appendix position, rejecting absolute statements ('in all patients') for less common variants.
exam_trap: Pelvic position is a real but less common variant, and absolute wording ('in all patients') should be a red flag for an incorrect option.
takeaway: Retrocaecal is the most common appendix position.

stem: A patient with heavy proteinuria and marked oedema develops a venous thromboembolism. Which renal syndrome is associated with increased thrombotic risk?
why_correct: Nephrotic syndrome is associated with increased thrombotic risk, partly because anticoagulant proteins can be lost in the urine.
why_wrong: A. Hypertension alone does not explain the syndrome. B. Nephritic syndrome is not classically associated with the same degree of thrombotic risk. D. Cystitis does not characteristically produce systemic hypercoagulability. E. Renal colic is caused by urinary tract obstruction, usually by a stone.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, partly due to urinary loss of natural anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin.
thinking: Link heavy proteinuria and oedema (nephrotic syndrome) with the known complication of hypercoagulability and thrombosis.
exam_trap: Nephritic syndrome is a tempting but distinct distractor; it is not classically associated with the same degree of thrombotic risk as nephrotic syndrome.
takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome raises thrombosis risk via loss of anticoagulant proteins in urine.

stem: A patient has a functioning arteriovenous fistula for haemodialysis. Which action should be avoided in that arm?

options.E: Checking the access site before dialysis

why_correct: Blood pressure cuffs and unnecessary venepuncture should generally be avoided in an arm containing a dialysis AV fistula to protect the access.
why_wrong: A. Monitoring for infection is important. C. Inspection is appropriate. D. A thrill can provide information about fistula function. E. Assessment before dialysis is appropriate.
pearl: Routine blood pressure measurement and unnecessary venepuncture should be avoided in the arm with a functioning dialysis AV fistula, to protect vascular access.
thinking: Identify which listed action could compress or damage the fistula (a BP cuff) versus the routine, appropriate monitoring actions (inspection, checking for a thrill, infection checks).
exam_trap: Candidates might assume all hands-on assessment of the fistula arm should be avoided, but visual inspection and palpating for a thrill are appropriate and important, only cuff compression should be avoided.
takeaway: Never use a blood pressure cuff on the arm with an AV fistula.

stem: Why do renal transplant recipients require long-term immunosuppressive treatment?

options.B: To stimulate red-cell production by the new kidney
options.C: To prevent rejection of the transplanted kidney
options.E: To reduce the risk of post-transplant infections

correct_answer: C. To prevent rejection of the transplanted kidney
why_correct: Immunosuppression reduces the recipient's immune response against the transplanted organ.
why_wrong: A. Increasing blood pressure is not the purpose. B. Immunosuppression does not stimulate erythropoiesis. D. It does not dissolve renal stones. E. Immunosuppressive drugs increase, rather than reduce, susceptibility to infection.
pearl: Long-term immunosuppressive treatment after renal transplantation reduces the recipient's immune response against the transplanted kidney, lowering the risk of rejection.
thinking: Match the therapeutic goal (preventing immune attack on the graft) directly to reducing rejection risk, excluding unrelated physiological effects listed as distractors.
exam_trap: 'Prevent all bacterial infections' is a tempting but incorrect distractor, since immunosuppression actually increases susceptibility to infection.
takeaway: Immunosuppression after transplant reduces rejection risk, but increases infection risk.

stem: An older man with longstanding lower urinary tract symptoms develops recurrent urinary tract infections and worsening urinary retention. What complication of benign prostatic enlargement may be responsible?
why_correct: Prostatic enlargement can obstruct urinary outflow, causing residual urine, retention and recurrent infection.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis does not cause chronic urinary obstruction. B. An oesophageal stricture affects swallowing. D. Glaucoma affects the eye. E. Pneumothorax affects the pleural space.
pearl: Benign prostatic enlargement can cause bladder outlet obstruction, leading to residual urine, recurrent urinary tract infections and worsening retention.
thinking: Connect longstanding LUTS from prostatic enlargement to bladder outlet obstruction as the unifying mechanism behind recurrent UTIs and retention.
exam_trap: Unrelated systemic conditions (glaucoma, pneumothorax) are distractors from other organ systems entirely and can be excluded immediately.
takeaway: BPH causing recurrent UTIs and retention = bladder outlet obstruction.

stem: A teenage boy develops sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea. What is the most important reason for urgent treatment?

options.A: Untreated torsion commonly progresses to epididymo-orchitis
options.B: It is primarily a gastrointestinal disorder
options.C: Most episodes resolve without intervention within hours
options.D: Testicular viability can be lost if torsion persists
options.E: Torsion causes bilateral infertility within the first hour

correct_answer: D. Testicular viability can be lost if torsion persists
why_correct: Twisting of the spermatic cord compromises testicular blood supply, making torsion a time-critical surgical emergency.
why_wrong: A. Torsion is an ischaemic, not infective, process. B. It is a urological emergency. C. Torsion should not be expected to resolve spontaneously, and delay risks testicular loss. E. Infertility is not an inevitable early consequence; the urgency relates to ischaemia of the affected testis.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency because twisting of the spermatic cord compromises testicular blood supply, and viability can be lost if torsion persists.
thinking: Recognise sudden severe unilateral testicular pain in a teenager as a time-critical vascular emergency, prioritising urgent surgical exploration over watchful waiting.
exam_trap: Assuming the pain is 'usually self-limiting' is the dangerous trap, as delay in treating torsion risks loss of the testis.
takeaway: Sudden testicular pain in a teenager is torsion until proven otherwise, and time is testis.

stem: A patient has visible haematuria associated with significant proteinuria and red-cell casts. Where is the bleeding most likely to originate?
why_correct: Proteinuria and red-cell casts strongly suggest a glomerular source of haematuria.
why_wrong: A. External skin bleeding is not true urinary haematuria. B. Bladder bleeding does not typically produce red-cell casts. C. Prostatic bleeding does not produce a glomerular urinary sediment. D. Urethral bleeding would not explain red-cell casts.
pearl: Haematuria with significant proteinuria and red-cell casts localises the bleeding to the glomeruli, indicating a glomerular cause rather than a lower urinary tract source.
thinking: Combine proteinuria and red-cell casts as specific markers of glomerular pathology, ruling out lower tract sources (bladder, urethra, prostate) that would not produce these findings.
exam_trap: Bladder neck or prostate are tempting lower-tract answers for haematuria, but neither produces red-cell casts or significant proteinuria, which are glomerular-specific findings.
takeaway: Proteinuria plus red-cell casts localises haematuria to the glomeruli.

stem: A patient reports that visible blood is most noticeable at the beginning of urination. Which anatomical source is more likely?
why_correct: Blood occurring predominantly at the beginning of the urinary stream suggests a urethral source.
why_wrong: A. Renal bleeding is more likely to produce blood throughout the urinary stream. B. Bladder bleeding is typically associated with haematuria throughout the stream. C. Renal pelvic bleeding similarly tends to produce blood throughout the stream. E. Ureteric bleeding generally produces blood throughout the stream.
pearl: Visible blood that is most noticeable at the start of urination (initial haematuria) suggests a urethral source of bleeding, as opposed to bleeding throughout the stream from higher up the urinary tract.
thinking: Use the timing of haematuria within the urinary stream (initial vs. throughout vs. terminal) as a localising clue, assigning 'initial' haematuria to the urethra.
exam_trap: Candidates may assume all haematuria originates from the kidney or bladder, missing that the timing pattern (initial-stream blood) specifically localises to the urethra.
takeaway: Blood at the very start of the stream points to a urethral source.

stem: A boy has a foreskin that has been retracted behind the glans and cannot be returned to its normal position. The glans is swollen and painful. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans, causing swelling and potentially compromising blood flow.
why_wrong: A. Hypospadias concerns the position of the urethral opening. C. Hydrocele is a fluid collection around the testis. D. An epididymal cyst is a benign cystic swelling. E. Phimosis is inability to retract the foreskin.
pearl: Paraphimosis occurs when a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans and cannot be reduced, causing painful glans swelling and requiring urgent reduction.
thinking: Match an irreducible, retracted foreskin with glans swelling to paraphimosis, distinguishing it from phimosis, which is inability to retract the foreskin in the first place.
exam_trap: Phimosis is the classic opposite-direction distractor; phimosis is a non-retractable foreskin, while paraphimosis is a retracted foreskin that cannot be returned.
takeaway: Retracted foreskin stuck behind a swollen glans = paraphimosis, needs urgent reduction.

stem: A man develops inflammation, redness and soreness of the glans penis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis and can cause redness, soreness and irritation.
why_wrong: A. Varicocele is dilatation of scrotal veins. B. Epididymitis causes scrotal/testicular pain. D. Torsion causes acute severe testicular pain. E. Hydrocele is a fluid collection around the testis.
pearl: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis, presenting with redness and soreness, and can have infective, irritant or dermatological causes.
thinking: Match 'inflammation, redness and soreness of the glans' directly to balanitis, distinguishing it from testicular or scrotal conditions listed as distractors.
exam_trap: Epididymitis is a distractor involving the epididymis/testicle rather than the glans itself, and should be excluded based on the anatomical site affected.
takeaway: Inflammation localised to the glans penis = balanitis.

stem: A teenage boy has sudden severe unilateral testicular pain and clinical suspicion of testicular torsion. What is the appropriate management?

options.D: Reassurance and review in one month

correct_answer: A. Urgent surgical assessment and exploration
why_correct: Testicular torsion is a time-critical surgical emergency because prolonged vascular compromise can result in testicular loss.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics do not treat torsion, and epididymo-orchitis should not be assumed when torsion is suspected. C. Imaging should not delay surgical exploration, and a routine outpatient scan is inappropriate. D. Delaying treatment risks irreversible ischaemia. E. Topical corticosteroids do not treat torsion.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency requiring exploration within hours to save the testis.
thinking: Recognise sudden severe unilateral testicular pain in a young male as torsion until proven otherwise, then go straight to urgent surgical review rather than imaging or waiting.
exam_trap: Candidates are tempted to order imaging first, but clinical suspicion alone should prompt urgent surgical exploration without delay.
takeaway: Torsion = urgent theatre, not a work-up.

stem: Which feature most strongly favours testicular torsion rather than epididymo-orchitis?
correct_answer: E. Sudden onset of severe pain
why_correct: Testicular torsion classically presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain.
why_wrong: A. Fever over several days favours infection. B. Urinary frequency can occur with urinary infection. C. Dysuria is more suggestive of infection. D. Gradual onset is more typical of epididymo-orchitis.
pearl: Sudden, severe pain favours torsion, while gradual onset with urinary symptoms favours infection.
thinking: Contrast the tempo of onset and associated urinary/systemic features between the two conditions to separate a surgical emergency from an infective cause.
exam_trap: Fever and dysuria can mislead towards infection even when sudden severe pain should point to torsion.
takeaway: Sudden pain is torsion until proven otherwise.

stem: A man has a history of bilateral undescended testes that were not corrected during childhood. Which long-term problem is particularly associated with this history?
why_correct: Prolonged exposure of undescended testes to higher intra-abdominal temperatures can impair spermatogenesis.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer disease is unrelated. B. Diverticulitis is unrelated. D. Asthma is unrelated. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: Untreated bilateral cryptorchidism is associated with impaired spermatogenesis and reduced fertility.
thinking: Recall that the intra-abdominal/inguinal position keeps the testis at a higher temperature, which is detrimental to sperm production over time.
exam_trap: Candidates may default to malignancy risk and forget the more directly tested fertility complication.
takeaway: Undescended testes: heat impairs sperm, impairs fertility.

stem: A woman has repeated episodes of symptomatic urinary tract infection. Which factor should be specifically considered during assessment?
why_correct: Sexual activity is a recognised risk factor for recurrent urinary tract infection in women.
why_wrong: A. Psoriasis is unrelated. B. Otitis externa is unrelated. D. Migraine aura is unrelated. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: Sexual activity is a well-recognised trigger for recurrent urinary tract infection in women.
thinking: Focus on genitourinary and behavioural factors rather than unrelated systemic conditions when assessing recurrent UTI.
exam_trap: Distractors list unrelated conditions (psoriasis, migraine) to test whether candidates can filter relevant risk factors.
takeaway: Ask about intercourse when UTIs keep recurring.

stem: A patient has recurrent urinary infections despite treatment. Why may a urine culture be useful?

options.A: To quantify the degree of proteinuria
options.B: To estimate the glomerular filtration rate
options.C: To detect malignant cells shed from an occult bladder tumour
options.D: To identify the organism and its antibiotic sensitivities
options.E: To exclude renal stones as the underlying cause of infection

correct_answer: D. To identify the organism and its antibiotic sensitivities
why_correct: Culture can identify the organism and provide antimicrobial susceptibility information, particularly when infection is recurrent or complicated.
why_wrong: A. Proteinuria is quantified with a urine albumin:creatinine or protein:creatinine ratio. B. GFR is estimated from serum creatinine. C. Malignant cells are assessed by urine cytology, not culture. E. Stones require imaging; culture cannot exclude them.
pearl: Urine culture identifies the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivities in complicated or recurrent UTI.
thinking: Match the investigation to its purpose: culture is about organism identification and susceptibility, not unrelated organ systems.
exam_trap: Obviously irrelevant distractors are included to test basic investigation-indication matching.
takeaway: Culture guides antibiotics, especially when infections recur.

stem: A patient with pyelonephritis remains febrile despite appropriate antibiotics. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent fever despite appropriate treatment can indicate a renal or perinephric abscess, particularly if there is an underlying obstruction or other risk factor.
