exam_trap: A, paralytic ileus — it also causes obstructive features, but it is typically painless or mildly uncomfortable and does not cause increasing tenderness with tachycardia.
takeaway: Obstruction with continuous pain, tachycardia and tenderness: suspect strangulation.

stem:
A patient has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. Coeliac disease is suspected.

What is important before testing?

options.A: Start a gluten-free diet now to see if symptoms improve
options.B: Stop iron supplements for two weeks before serology
options.C: Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
options.D: Diagnose clinically if symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet
options.E: Reduce gluten intake to once weekly before testing

correct_answer: C. Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
why_correct: Coeliac serology and biopsy rely on an immune response to gluten, so NICE NG20 advises eating gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before testing.
why_wrong: A. A gluten-free diet before testing can give false-negative serology and histology. B. Iron supplements do not affect coeliac serology and need not be stopped. D. Response to a gluten-free diet is not diagnostic; serology, with biopsy where indicated, is needed. E. NICE advises gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before testing; once weekly is insufficient.
pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy need ongoing gluten exposure; advise eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing to avoid false negatives.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Tests depend on an immune response to gluten ↓ Removing gluten can cause false negatives ↓ Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
exam_trap: A, starting a gluten-free diet now — it feels helpful, but it can give false-negative serology and histology, making a firm diagnosis difficult.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease while the patient is still eating gluten.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy presents with fever and severe neutropenia.

What should be assumed until assessed otherwise?

options.A: Drug fever to be treated with paracetamol
options.B: Viral illness to be reviewed in 48 hours
options.C: Dehydration to be managed with oral fluids at home
options.D: Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
options.E: Tumour fever to be treated with naproxen

correct_answer: D. Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
why_correct: Fever in a patient on chemotherapy with severe neutropenia must be treated as neutropenic sepsis; NICE recommends immediate assessment and empirical IV antibiotics within one hour.
why_wrong: A. Fever with neutropenia should not be attributed to drugs; it must be treated as sepsis; antipyretics alone may mask deterioration. B. Delaying assessment risks rapid deterioration and death. C. Dehydration does not explain fever, and home management without assessment is unsafe. E. Tumour fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be assumed in a neutropenic patient.
pearl: Fever in a patient on chemotherapy with neutropenia is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; give empirical IV antibiotics within one hour without waiting for results.
thinking: Receiving chemotherapy ↓ Fever with severe neutropenia ↓ Infection can progress rapidly with few signs ↓ Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
exam_trap: A, drug fever treated with paracetamol — drugs can cause fever, but assuming it delays antibiotics, and antipyretics alone may mask deterioration.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy with neutropenia: treat as neutropenic sepsis with urgent IV antibiotics.

stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.

What simple investigation is important early in assessment?
why_correct: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding should have an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded (NICE NG126).
why_wrong: A. HbA1c is not relevant to this acute presentation. B. Serum calcium is not a priority investigation here. D. Spirometry is irrelevant to abdominal pain and bleeding. E. An ECG does not address the possibility of pregnancy-related causes such as ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding needs an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be considered.
thinking: Woman of reproductive age ↓ Lower abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding ↓ Ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage must be considered ↓ Pregnancy test
exam_trap: E, ECG only — it is a quick bedside test, but it does not address pregnancy-related causes such as ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Pain and bleeding in a woman of reproductive age: do a pregnancy test early.

stem:
A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake.

What should be considered?

options.A: Normal pregnancy sickness to be managed with dietary advice at home
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
options.C: Gestational diabetes requiring a glucose tolerance test
options.D: Gastroenteritis to be treated with oral rehydration at home
options.E: Diabetes insipidus requiring a water deprivation test

correct_answer: B. Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
why_correct: Persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to keep food or fluids down suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs assessment of hydration, electrolytes and ketones, and antiemetics with fluids where required (RCOG guidance).
why_wrong: A. Dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake go beyond normal nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. C. Gestational diabetes does not cause persistent vomiting with dehydration. D. Persistent vomiting with dehydration in pregnancy suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, and home oral rehydration is inadequate when intake cannot be maintained. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not persistent vomiting.
pearl: Hyperemesis gravidarum differs from normal pregnancy sickness by dehydration or inability to keep food and fluids down; it needs assessment, antiemetics and fluids where required.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Persistent vomiting with dehydration ↓ Unable to maintain oral intake ↓ Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
exam_trap: A, normal pregnancy sickness — nausea and vomiting are common in pregnancy, but dehydration and inability to maintain intake go beyond it and need assessment.
takeaway: Vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration: hyperemesis gravidarum, not ordinary pregnancy sickness.

stem:
A pregnant woman with hypertension develops severe headache and visual disturbance.

What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
options.B: Reassure her that headaches are always normal in pregnancy
options.C: Give only paracetamol and discharge without assessment

correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
why_correct: Severe headache and visual disturbance in a hypertensive pregnant woman are features of severe pre-eclampsia, so NICE NG133 requires urgent same-day assessment and management to prevent eclampsia and other complications.
why_wrong: B. Headache with hypertension can signal severe pre-eclampsia. C. Analgesia without assessment risks missing severe pre-eclampsia. D. Blood pressure is central to the assessment. E. A six-month delay would be dangerous.
pearl: Severe headache or visual disturbance in a hypertensive pregnant woman are features of severe pre-eclampsia and need same-day assessment to prevent eclampsia and other complications.
thinking: Pregnant with hypertension ↓ Severe headache ↓ Visual disturbance ↓ Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
exam_trap: C, paracetamol and discharge — headache is common in pregnancy, but with hypertension and visual symptoms it may signal severe pre-eclampsia.
takeaway: Hypertension in pregnancy with headache or visual disturbance: urgent same-day assessment.

stem:
A pregnant woman has an eclamptic seizure.

Which treatment is central to immediate management?
why_correct: NICE NG133 recommends IV magnesium sulfate for eclampsia, to treat seizures and prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate for treating and preventing eclamptic seizures. B. Labetalol treats severe hypertension but does not treat or prevent eclamptic seizures. D. A benzodiazepine may be used for a prolonged seizure, but magnesium sulfate is the central treatment. E. Levetiracetam is not used for eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is recommended.
pearl: Magnesium sulfate is the central treatment in eclampsia, both to stop seizures and to prevent recurrence; severe hypertension is controlled alongside it.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Eclamptic seizure ↓ Magnesium sulfate treats and prevents eclamptic seizures ↓ Magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: B, IV labetalol — blood pressure control is part of management, but labetalol does not treat or prevent eclamptic seizures.
takeaway: Eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice.

stem:
A pregnant woman reports a significant reduction in fetal movements compared with normal for her.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Advise her to count kicks at home for 24 hours
options.B: Review at the next routine antenatal appointment
options.C: Advise lying on her left side and drinking something cold
options.E: Book a growth scan for the following week

correct_answer: D. Arrange same-day maternity unit assessment
why_correct: Reduced fetal movements may indicate fetal compromise, so RCOG guidance advises prompt maternity assessment the same day, according to gestation and the local pathway.
why_wrong: A. Home kick-counting delays assessment of possible fetal compromise and is not recommended. B. Waiting for the next appointment delays assessment of possible fetal compromise. C. Trying to stimulate movements by lying down or cold drinks is not recommended and delays assessment. E. A scan next week delays assessment of possible fetal compromise.
pearl: A significant reduction in fetal movements may signal fetal compromise; advise same-day maternity unit assessment rather than home monitoring or waiting.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Significant reduction in fetal movements ↓ May indicate fetal compromise ↓ Same-day maternity unit assessment
exam_trap: C, lying on the left side and drinking something cold — a common folk remedy, but trying to stimulate movements delays assessment and is not recommended.
takeaway: Reduced fetal movements: same-day maternity assessment, not home monitoring.

stem:
A term pregnancy is found to have a persistent breech presentation.

Which option may be considered in appropriate circumstances?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering external cephalic version from 36 weeks (nulliparous) or 37 weeks (multiparous) for uncomplicated breech presentation, to increase the chance of vaginal birth.
why_wrong: A. Internal podalic version is reserved for delivery of a second twin and is not used for a singleton breech. C. McRoberts manoeuvre is used for shoulder dystocia. D. Ventouse delivery requires a cephalic presentation and is not used for breech. E. Cervical cerclage is used to prevent preterm birth and does not correct presentation.
pearl: For an uncomplicated breech presentation at term, offer external cephalic version to turn the baby and increase the chance of vaginal birth, if there are no contraindications.
thinking: Term pregnancy ↓ Persistent breech presentation ↓ Turning to cephalic increases the chance of vaginal birth ↓ External cephalic version
exam_trap: A, internal podalic version — it also changes fetal presentation, but it is reserved for delivering a second twin, not a singleton breech.
takeaway: Persistent breech at term: offer external cephalic version if there are no contraindications.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding three years after her last menstrual period. She does not take hormone replacement therapy.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Trial topical vaginal oestrogen and refer if the bleeding recurs
options.B: Arrange a routine gynaecology appointment within 18 weeks
options.C: Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
options.D: Repeat cervical screening and refer if the result is abnormal
options.E: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review in three months

correct_answer: C. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment for endometrial cancer; NICE NG12 (updated 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to hormone replacement therapy (HRT), with transvaginal ultrasound and further investigation as indicated.
why_wrong: A. Atrophy cannot be assumed; postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer. B. A routine referral delays diagnosis; NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT. D. Cervical screening does not assess the endometrium. E. Tranexamic acid treats the symptom and delays investigation for malignancy.
pearl: Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT in a woman aged 55 or over warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to exclude endometrial cancer.
thinking: 62-year-old woman ↓ Vaginal bleeding three years after menopause ↓ Not taking HRT ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial assessment
exam_trap: A, vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophy — atrophy is common, but it cannot be assumed; endometrial cancer must be excluded first.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding not explained by HRT: suspected cancer pathway referral.

stem:
A woman who experiences migraine with aura asks about combined hormonal contraception.

What is the important principle?

options.A: It is acceptable if a low-dose 20-microgram ethinylestradiol pill is used
options.B: It is contraindicated because of increased ischaemic stroke risk
options.C: It is suitable provided her blood pressure and BMI are both normal
options.D: It is suitable if she takes low-dose aspirin 75 mg daily alongside it
options.E: It is preferred because it reduces menstrual migraine

correct_answer: B. It is contraindicated because of increased ischaemic stroke risk
why_correct: Under UKMEC, migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk, so CHC should not be used.
why_wrong: A. A lower estrogen dose does not remove the stroke risk; migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal contraception. C. Normal blood pressure and BMI do not offset the stroke risk associated with migraine with aura. D. Aspirin does not make CHC acceptable in migraine with aura. E. CHC is contraindicated in migraine with aura, whatever its effect on menstrual migraine.
pearl: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk; offer progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods instead.
thinking: Migraine with aura ↓ Request for combined hormonal contraception ↓ Oestrogen adds to ischaemic stroke risk ↓ Contraindicated (UKMEC 4)
exam_trap: A, a low-dose 20-microgram pill — lower oestrogen sounds safer, but no dose removes the stroke risk; migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined methods.
takeaway: Migraine with aura: never prescribe combined hormonal contraception.

stem:
A woman requests emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Offer levonorgestrel if within 24 hours, otherwise decline
options.B: Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
options.C: Arrange a pregnancy test first and offer EC if it is negative
options.D: Advise waiting for the next period before deciding on EC
options.E: Offer a copper IUD at the next routine clinic in four weeks

correct_answer: B. Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
why_correct: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly after assessing timing and cycle, with options including the copper IUD (most effective) or oral levonorgestrel or ulipristal acetate, following FSRH guidance.
why_wrong: A. Levonorgestrel can be used up to 72 hours, ulipristal up to 120 hours and a copper IUD up to 5 days, so presenting after 24 hours does not exclude emergency contraception. C. A pregnancy test cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and should not delay emergency contraception. D. Waiting for a period loses the window for emergency contraception. E. A copper IUD for emergency contraception must be fitted within 5 days of intercourse or of the earliest expected ovulation.
pearl: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly; the copper IUD is most effective, and oral ulipristal acetate or levonorgestrel are options depending on timing and circumstances.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Request for emergency contraception ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
exam_trap: C, a pregnancy test first — it seems prudent, but it cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and only delays effective treatment.
takeaway: Emergency contraception: assess timing and offer it promptly; do not delay for tests.

stem:
A patient presents with a new sexually transmitted infection and asks whether they should have HIV testing.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Offer HIV testing if they report a partner from a high-prevalence area
options.B: Defer HIV testing for three months to cover the window period
options.C: Test for HIV with the routine bloods without discussing it
options.D: Reserve HIV testing for those with symptoms of seroconversion
options.E: Offer HIV testing with appropriate information and consent

correct_answer: E. Offer HIV testing with appropriate information and consent
why_correct: BASHH and NICE recommend offering HIV testing to everyone attending for STI assessment, with appropriate information and consent, because a new STI indicates risk of HIV.
why_wrong: A. HIV testing should be offered to everyone attending for STI assessment, not limited by partner characteristics. B. Testing should be offered now, with a repeat test after the window period if needed. C. Testing requires informed consent and should not be done covertly. D. Waiting for symptoms leads to late diagnosis and worse outcomes.
pearl: Everyone attending for STI assessment should be offered an HIV test with information and consent; a new STI indicates risk, and a repeat after the window period may be needed.
thinking: New sexually transmitted infection ↓ Shared transmission routes mean HIV risk ↓ HIV testing is offered to everyone assessed for STIs ↓ Offer testing with information and consent
exam_trap: B, deferring for three months to cover the window period — it sounds logical, but testing should happen now, with a repeat later if needed, to avoid delayed diagnosis.
takeaway: New STI: offer HIV testing now with consent; repeat after the window period if needed.

stem:
A patient with depression says they have been thinking about ending their life.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer routinely to talking therapies and review in four weeks
options.B: Ask directly about intent, plans and immediate safety
options.C: Increase the antidepressant dose and review in two weeks
options.D: Avoid asking about plans to prevent planting the idea
options.E: Give a crisis line number and end the consultation

correct_answer: B. Ask directly about intent, plans and immediate safety
why_correct: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plans and access to means is essential in risk assessment and does not increase risk (NICE NG225).
why_wrong: A. A routine referral without assessing risk may miss serious and imminent danger. C. Changing medication without assessing suicidal intent and safety is unsafe. D. Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and is essential for assessment. E. Signposting without assessing risk is inadequate.
pearl: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plans and access to means does not increase risk and is essential to judge how urgently the patient needs help.
thinking: Direct assessment of suicidal ideation and intent is an important part of depression assessment.
exam_trap: D, avoiding questions about plans — a common fear, but asking directly does not plant the idea and is essential for assessing risk.
takeaway: Suicidal thoughts: ask directly about intent, plans and access to means.

stem:
A patient with depression says they have a specific suicide plan and intend to act on it today.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Refer to the community mental health team for a routine appointment
options.B: Agree a no-suicide contract and review the next day
options.C: Increase the antidepressant dose and arrange GP review this week
options.D: Give crisis line details and arrange review within a week
options.E: Treat as immediate risk and arrange urgent mental health assessment

correct_answer: E. Treat as immediate risk and arrange urgent mental health assessment
why_correct: A specific plan with intent to act today indicates immediate high risk, needing urgent mental health assessment and measures to keep the patient safe.
why_wrong: A. A routine referral ignores immediate high risk. B. No-suicide contracts are not effective and do not keep the patient safe. C. A dose increase does not address imminent risk. D. Signposting with delayed review is unsafe when there is a plan with intent to act today.
pearl: A specific suicide plan with intent to act today indicates immediate high risk; arrange urgent mental health assessment and keep the patient safe in the meantime.
thinking: Depression ↓ Specific suicide plan ↓ Intent to act today ↓ Immediate risk needing urgent mental health assessment
exam_trap: B, a no-suicide contract — it seems to secure commitment, but such contracts are not effective and do not keep the patient safe.
takeaway: Plan plus intent to act today: urgent mental health assessment and immediate safety measures.

stem:
A patient starts an antidepressant. Two weeks later they report increased agitation and new suicidal thoughts.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
options.B: Stop the antidepressant abruptly and review in one month
options.C: Reassure that early side effects settle and review in four weeks
options.D: Double the dose to speed up the antidepressant response
options.E: Add a benzodiazepine for agitation and continue as planned

correct_answer: A. Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
why_correct: Agitation and new suicidal thoughts soon after starting an antidepressant need urgent reassessment, as NICE warns of increased risk early in treatment, particularly in younger people.
why_wrong: B. Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms and does not address the risk. C. New suicidal thoughts need urgent reassessment, not routine review. D. Increasing the dose without assessment may worsen agitation and risk. E. Treating agitation symptomatically without reassessing suicide risk is unsafe.
pearl: Agitation or new suicidal thoughts soon after starting an antidepressant need urgent reassessment, as risk can rise early in treatment, particularly in younger people.
thinking: Recently started an antidepressant ↓ Two weeks later: increased agitation ↓ New suicidal thoughts ↓ Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
exam_trap: C, reassurance that early side effects settle — some early effects do settle, but new suicidal thoughts need urgent reassessment, not routine review.
takeaway: New suicidal thoughts after starting an antidepressant: urgent reassessment.

stem:
A patient presenting with depression reports previous episodes of several days of markedly increased activity, reduced need for sleep and impulsive behaviour.

What should be considered?

options.A: Simple unipolar depression without further assessment

why_correct: Previous episodes of elevated activity, reduced need for sleep and impulsivity suggest hypomania or mania, so bipolar disorder should be considered; this matters because antidepressant monotherapy can trigger mania.
why_wrong: A. A history suggesting hypomania or mania should not be labelled unipolar depression without assessment. B. Generalised anxiety disorder does not explain episodes of elevated activity and reduced need for sleep. D. Dementia does not explain episodic mood elevation with reduced sleep. E. OCD is characterised by obsessions and compulsions, not manic episodes.
pearl: Always ask about past hypomanic or manic episodes before treating depression; bipolar disorder changes management, as antidepressant monotherapy can trigger mania.
thinking: Presenting with depression ↓ Past episodes of increased activity and reduced need for sleep ↓ Impulsive behaviour suggests hypomania or mania ↓ Bipolar disorder
exam_trap: A, simple unipolar depression — it fits the current presentation, but past episodes of elevated activity suggest bipolar disorder and must be assessed.
takeaway: Depression with past episodes of elevated mood or activity: consider bipolar disorder.

stem:
A patient with suspected mania is behaving dangerously and has become unable to care for themselves.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Arrange urgent specialist mental health assessment
options.B: Start a hypnotic and review in the GP surgery next week
options.C: Refer routinely to the community mental health team
options.D: Advise the family to monitor them and call if worse
options.E: Start an antidepressant for underlying low mood

correct_answer: A. Arrange urgent specialist mental health assessment
why_correct: Mania with dangerous behaviour and inability to self-care needs urgent specialist mental health assessment, which may include crisis team input or consideration of the Mental Health Act.
why_wrong: B. Treating insomnia with delayed review ignores serious risk from dangerous behaviour. C. A routine referral is unsafe given the immediate risk. D. Relying on family monitoring ignores dangerous behaviour that needs urgent action. E. Antidepressants can worsen mania and do not address the immediate risk.
pearl: Mania with dangerous behaviour or inability to self-care needs urgent specialist mental health assessment; crisis team input or a Mental Health Act assessment may be needed.
thinking: Suspected mania ↓ Dangerous behaviour ↓ Unable to care for themselves ↓ Urgent specialist mental health assessment
exam_trap: C, routine community mental health team referral — specialist input is right, but a routine timescale is unsafe given the immediate risk.
takeaway: Mania with risk to self or others: urgent specialist mental health assessment.

stem:
A young adult develops new auditory hallucinations, persecutory beliefs and marked social withdrawal.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Refer to primary care talking therapies for social anxiety
options.B: Refer promptly to early intervention in psychosis services
options.C: Start an antidepressant and review in four weeks
options.D: Arrange a routine community mental health review in three months
options.E: Start an antipsychotic in primary care and monitor response

correct_answer: B. Refer promptly to early intervention in psychosis services
why_correct: New hallucinations, persecutory beliefs and withdrawal suggest possible first-episode psychosis; NICE CG178 recommends urgent referral to early intervention in psychosis services.
why_wrong: A. Hallucinations and persecutory beliefs are not explained by social anxiety; possible psychosis needs specialist assessment. C. These features suggest psychosis rather than depression, and delayed review risks harm. D. Delayed referral worsens outcomes; NICE recommends urgent referral to early intervention in psychosis services. E. NICE advises against starting antipsychotics in primary care before specialist assessment.
pearl: Suspected first-episode psychosis should be referred urgently to early intervention in psychosis services; avoid starting antipsychotics in primary care before specialist assessment.
thinking: Young adult ↓ New auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs ↓ Marked social withdrawal ↓ Possible first-episode psychosis: refer to early intervention services
exam_trap: E, starting an antipsychotic in primary care — it seems to treat the problem early, but antipsychotics should not be started before specialist assessment.
takeaway: Possible first-episode psychosis: refer urgently to early intervention in psychosis services.

stem:
A patient receiving long-term antipsychotic treatment is attending for review.

Which area should be monitored?

options.A: Weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
options.B: Thyroid function and vitamin D levels

correct_answer: A. Weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
why_correct: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk, so NICE CG178 recommends regular monitoring of weight, BMI, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c and lipids.
why_wrong: B. Thyroid monitoring is relevant to lithium rather than routine antipsychotic monitoring, and vitamin D is not a core parameter. C. Visual acuity and intraocular pressure are not the key monitoring parameters for antipsychotics. D. Bone density and urinary calcium are not routine antipsychotic monitoring. E. Hearing and peak flow are not the parameters affected by antipsychotics.
pearl: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, so monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c and lipids regularly during long-term treatment.
thinking: Long-term antipsychotic treatment ↓ Risk of weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia ↓ Increased cardiovascular risk ↓ Monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
exam_trap: B, thyroid function — thyroid monitoring is familiar in psychiatry, but it relates to lithium, not routine antipsychotic monitoring.
takeaway: Long-term antipsychotics: monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids.

stem:
A patient repeatedly experiences intrusive thoughts of causing harm to others and is extremely distressed by the thoughts. They have no intention of acting on them.

What is an important clinical principle?

options.A: Inform the police, as the thoughts indicate a risk to others
options.B: Distinguish obsessional intrusive thoughts from intent and assess risk
options.C: Arrange urgent admission under the Mental Health Act
options.D: Advise the patient to suppress the thoughts when they occur
options.E: Diagnose psychosis and start an antipsychotic medication urgently

correct_answer: B. Distinguish obsessional intrusive thoughts from intent and assess risk
why_correct: Distressing, unwanted intrusive thoughts of harm that the patient resists are typical of OCD and are not the same as intent; risk should still be assessed appropriately, but the thoughts should not be misread as dangerousness.
why_wrong: A. Distressing intrusive thoughts that the patient resists do not indicate intent, and reporting without real risk breaches confidentiality. C. There is no indication of risk or a mental disorder that warrants detention. D. Thought suppression tends to worsen obsessions; CBT with exposure and response prevention is used. E. Intrusive thoughts recognised as one's own are not psychotic.
pearl: Unwanted, distressing intrusive thoughts of harm that the patient resists are typical of OCD and differ from intent; assess risk, but do not misread them as dangerousness.
thinking: Repeated intrusive thoughts of harming others ↓ Extremely distressed by them ↓ No intention to act ↓ Distinguish obsessional thoughts from intent and assess risk
exam_trap: A, informing the police — thoughts of harm sound alarming, but distressing intrusive thoughts the patient resists do not indicate intent, and reporting would breach confidentiality.
takeaway: Distressing, resisted thoughts of harm suggest OCD, not intent; assess risk proportionately.

stem:
A patient with an eating disorder presents with marked weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations.

What is important?

options.A: Delay physical assessment until psychological treatment is complete
options.C: Use BMI alone to determine whether treatment is required
options.D: Assume the patient is medically stable
options.E: Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability

correct_answer: E. Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability
why_correct: Weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations in an eating disorder may indicate medical instability (e.g. bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance), which needs urgent physical assessment using MEED guidance.
why_wrong: A. Physical risk must be assessed urgently, not delayed for psychological treatment. B. Discharge without observations would be unsafe. C. BMI alone does not reflect medical risk, and patients can be unstable at any BMI. D. Abnormal observations suggest instability.
pearl: Patients with eating disorders can be medically unstable at any BMI; weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations need urgent physical assessment, including electrolytes and ECG.
thinking: Eating disorder ↓ Marked weakness and dizziness ↓ Abnormal observations ↓ Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability
exam_trap: C, using BMI alone — BMI is a familiar severity marker, but it does not reflect medical risk, and patients can be unstable at any BMI.
takeaway: Eating disorder with abnormal observations: assess for medical instability, not BMI alone.

stem:
A patient with Parkinson's disease develops new visual hallucinations.

What should be considered initially?

options.A: Diagnose Parkinson's disease dementia and start donepezil
options.B: Look for medical and medication-related causes
options.C: Start haloperidol to control the hallucinations
options.E: Refer for assessment of new-onset schizophrenia

correct_answer: B. Look for medical and medication-related causes
why_correct: New hallucinations in Parkinson's disease may be caused by intercurrent illness or dopaminergic medication, so the first step is to look for medical causes and review treatment (NICE NG71).
why_wrong: A. Dementia should not be diagnosed before medical and medication-related causes have been excluded. C. Haloperidol can severely worsen parkinsonism and should be avoided. D. Abrupt withdrawal of Parkinson's medication risks acute akinesia and a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. E. Schizophrenia should not be assumed when common medical and drug-related causes exist.
pearl: New hallucinations in Parkinson's disease should prompt a search for intercurrent illness and a review of medication, especially dopaminergic drugs, before other diagnoses are made.
thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ New visual hallucinations ↓ Intercurrent illness or dopaminergic drugs are common triggers ↓ Look for medical and medication-related causes
exam_trap: C, haloperidol — it treats hallucinations in other settings, but it can severely worsen parkinsonism and should be avoided in Parkinson's disease.
takeaway: Hallucinations in Parkinson's disease: look for illness and medication causes; avoid haloperidol.

stem:
A patient with myasthenia gravis develops rapidly worsening dysphagia, weak cough and breathlessness.

What is the priority?

options.A: Increase pyridostigmine and review in clinic next week
options.B: Arrange speech and language therapy review of swallowing
options.C: Urgent respiratory function assessment and escalation
options.D: Start nasogastric feeding and review the next day
options.E: Start high-dose prednisolone and discharge home

correct_answer: C. Urgent respiratory function assessment and escalation
why_correct: Rapidly worsening bulbar weakness, weak cough and breathlessness suggest myasthenic crisis, which needs urgent assessment of respiratory function (e.g. FVC) and escalation to critical care.
why_wrong: A. Increasing anticholinesterase with delayed review ignores impending respiratory failure and may precipitate cholinergic crisis. B. A swallow assessment does not address the respiratory risk. D. Feeding support does not address the respiratory risk and delays escalation. E. Starting high-dose steroids can transiently worsen weakness, and discharge would be dangerous.
pearl: Bulbar weakness, weak cough and breathlessness in myasthenia gravis suggest crisis; assess respiratory function such as FVC and escalate to critical care rather than adjusting oral treatment.
thinking: Myasthenia gravis ↓ Rapidly worsening dysphagia and weak cough ↓ Breathlessness ↓ Possible myasthenic crisis: urgent respiratory assessment and escalation
exam_trap: A, increasing pyridostigmine — it is the usual symptomatic drug, but delayed review ignores impending respiratory failure and extra dosing may precipitate cholinergic crisis.
takeaway: Myasthenia with bulbar and respiratory symptoms: assess FVC and escalate urgently.

stem:
A patient with suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome develops increasing difficulty swallowing and a weak cough.

What is the priority?

options.A: Start high-dose oral prednisolone and observe on the ward
options.B: Monitor oxygen saturation, as hypoxaemia shows respiratory failure
options.C: Arrange outpatient nerve conduction studies within a month
options.D: Refer for speech therapy and routine physiotherapy on the ward
options.E: Urgent respiratory assessment with serial FVC monitoring

correct_answer: E. Urgent respiratory assessment with serial FVC monitoring
why_correct: Bulbar weakness and a weak cough in Guillain-Barré syndrome suggest risk of respiratory failure, so urgent assessment with serial FVC monitoring and early critical care involvement are needed.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barré syndrome, and ward observation alone does not address respiratory risk. B. Oxygen saturation falls late in neuromuscular respiratory failure, so serial FVC is needed to detect deterioration early. C. Outpatient investigation ignores the immediate respiratory risk. D. Therapy referrals do not address the risk of respiratory failure.
pearl: Bulbar weakness and a weak cough in Guillain-Barré syndrome signal risk of respiratory failure; serial FVC monitoring and early critical care involvement are essential.
thinking: Suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome ↓ Increasing difficulty swallowing ↓ Weak cough ↓ Urgent respiratory assessment with serial FVC monitoring
exam_trap: B, monitoring oxygen saturation — it seems a direct measure, but saturation falls late in neuromuscular respiratory failure; serial FVC detects decline earlier.
takeaway: Guillain-Barré with bulbar signs: serial FVC and early critical care input.

stem:
A patient suddenly develops unilateral weakness and dysarthria. Their capillary glucose is 2.1 mmol/L.

What should be considered?

options.C: Hypoglycaemia as a potential stroke mimic
options.D: Stroke is impossible in a patient with hypoglycaemia

correct_answer: C. Hypoglycaemia as a potential stroke mimic
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can cause focal neurological deficits that mimic stroke, so glucose must be checked and corrected, then the patient reassessed (NICE NG128).
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness, not limb weakness and dysarthria. B. Parkinson's disease does not cause sudden focal weakness. D. Stroke can coexist with hypoglycaemia, so deficits that persist after correction still need stroke assessment. E. Migraine should not be assumed while a correctable cause is present.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia can cause focal deficits that mimic stroke; correct the glucose and reassess, and if deficits persist continue stroke assessment, because the two can coexist.
thinking: Sudden unilateral weakness and dysarthria ↓ Low capillary glucose ↓ Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke ↓ Correct glucose and reassess: a potential stroke mimic
exam_trap: D, stroke is impossible with hypoglycaemia — tempting once a cause is found, but stroke can coexist, so deficits persisting after correction still need stroke assessment.
takeaway: Focal deficit with low glucose: treat the hypoglycaemia, then reassess for stroke.

stem:
A patient suddenly develops painless loss of vision in one eye.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Routine optician review in the next few weeks
options.B: Refer to the eye clinic within two weeks
options.D: Start chloramphenicol drops and review in a week

why_correct: Sudden painless monocular vision loss may indicate retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis or retinal detachment, which need same-day urgent ophthalmology assessment (and stroke pathway assessment where retinal artery occlusion is suspected).
why_wrong: A. A delay of weeks could lead to permanent vision loss. B. Waiting up to two weeks is inappropriate for sudden vision loss, which needs same-day assessment. D. Topical antibiotics do not treat the causes of sudden painless vision loss. E. Cataract causes gradual, not sudden, vision loss.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss needs same-day ophthalmology assessment; consider retinal artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis and retinal detachment.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Painless loss of vision in one eye ↓ Possible retinal artery occlusion, GCA or detachment ↓ Same-day urgent ophthalmology assessment
exam_trap: B, eye clinic referral within two weeks — it sounds prompt, but two weeks is far too long for causes in which sight can be lost within hours.
takeaway: Sudden painless monocular visual loss: same-day ophthalmology assessment.

stem:
A previously well adult develops sudden hearing loss in one ear over 24 hours. There is no impacted wax, otitis externa or middle-ear infection.

What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Arrange routine audiology in one year
options.C: Reassure and review in six months

why_correct: NICE NG98 recommends immediate referral (to be seen within 24 hours) for sudden hearing loss developing over 3 days or less within the past 30 days when not explained by external or middle-ear causes, because early treatment may improve recovery.
why_wrong: A. A year's delay is inappropriate. B. Ear drops do not treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss. C. Delayed review may miss the window for treatment. D. Waiting for spontaneous recovery may reduce the chance of recovery with prompt treatment.
pearl: Sudden hearing loss developing over three days or less, not explained by external or middle-ear causes, needs immediate specialist referral, as early treatment may improve recovery.
thinking: Sudden hearing loss developing over 3 days or less, when not explained by an external or middle-ear cause, requires immediate specialist assessment. NICE specifies assessment within 24 hours when it developed within the preceding 30 days.
exam_trap: D, waiting for spontaneous recovery — some cases do recover, but waiting may lose the window in which prompt treatment improves the outcome.
takeaway: Sudden unexplained hearing loss: immediate specialist assessment, not watchful waiting.

stem:
A patient develops sudden unilateral hearing loss together with ipsilateral facial weakness.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Immediate assessment for an acute neurological cause
options.B: Olive oil ear drops and review in two weeks
options.C: Routine ENT referral for audiometry within six weeks
options.D: Routine audiology referral for hearing aids
options.E: Diagnose Bell's palsy and start prednisolone

correct_answer: A. Immediate assessment for an acute neurological cause
why_correct: Sudden hearing loss with ipsilateral facial weakness may indicate a neurological cause such as stroke, so it needs immediate specialist assessment, following stroke pathways if stroke is suspected.
why_wrong: B. Ear drops do not address possible serious pathology. C. A routine referral is inappropriate when stroke or another acute neurological cause is possible. D. A hearing-aid assessment ignores possible serious pathology. E. Bell's palsy does not cause sudden hearing loss; this combination needs assessment for stroke or another acute cause.
pearl: Sudden hearing loss with facial weakness or other neurological signs may reflect an acute neurological cause such as stroke; assess immediately and follow stroke pathways if suspected.
thinking: Sudden hearing loss associated with facial weakness is an immediate referral situation; stroke pathways should be followed if stroke is suspected.
exam_trap: E, Bell's palsy with prednisolone — facial weakness makes it tempting, but Bell's palsy does not cause sudden hearing loss; this combination needs assessment for stroke.
takeaway: Sudden hearing loss plus facial weakness: immediate assessment for a neurological cause.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin presents with persistent epistaxis.

What is important?

options.A: Stop warfarin permanently and switch to aspirin
options.B: Give IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex routinely
options.C: Continue warfarin and review the INR at the next clinic
options.D: Control the bleeding and check severity and INR
options.E: Pack the nose and discharge without checking the INR

correct_answer: D. Control the bleeding and check severity and INR
why_correct: Persistent epistaxis on warfarin needs first aid and haemorrhage control alongside assessment of haemodynamic status and an urgent INR, because over-anticoagulation may be driving the bleed and determines whether dose adjustment or reversal is needed (NICE CKS Epistaxis; BNF warfarin guidance).
why_wrong: A. Warfarin should not be stopped permanently by reflex; the indication and bleeding severity must be weighed, and aspirin would further impair haemostasis. B. Reversal is guided by the INR and bleeding severity and is not given routinely for epistaxis. C. Persistent bleeding needs the INR checked now, not at the next clinic. E. Anticoagulation directly affects bleeding severity, so the INR must be checked.
pearl: Bleeding on warfarin is managed in two parallel strands: stop the bleed (first aid, packing or cautery) and check haemodynamic status and the INR now, because the INR decides whether to adjust, withhold or reverse.
thinking: Persistent epistaxis ↓ Patient is anticoagulated with warfarin ↓ Over-anticoagulation may be driving the bleed ↓ Control bleeding, assess severity and check INR urgently
exam_trap: B, IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex — reversal sounds decisive, but it is guided by the INR and bleeding severity, not given routinely, and may cause unnecessary thrombotic risk.
takeaway: Bleeding on warfarin: control the bleed and check the INR now; let the INR and severity guide reversal.

stem:
A patient suddenly develops difficulty speaking and finding words.

What should be assumed until assessed otherwise?

options.A: Possible stroke or transient ischaemic attack
options.C: Migraine with aura, to be confirmed if headache follows
options.D: Early Alzheimer's disease with expressive language decline
options.E: Primary progressive aphasia needing memory clinic review

correct_answer: A. Possible stroke or transient ischaemic attack
why_correct: Sudden-onset speech or language disturbance (dysphasia) is a focal neurological deficit, so it should be treated as a possible stroke or TIA until proven otherwise and assessed immediately using a validated tool such as FAST (NICE NG128).
why_wrong: B. A functional cause cannot be assumed for a sudden focal deficit, and doing so risks missing a stroke during the window for treatment. C. Migraine aura is a diagnosis of exclusion in a sudden-onset deficit, so stroke must be assumed until assessed. D. Alzheimer's disease causes gradual decline, not a sudden-onset deficit. E. Primary progressive aphasia develops gradually, not suddenly.
pearl: Any sudden-onset focal deficit, including word-finding difficulty or dysphasia, is a stroke or TIA until proven otherwise; rapid recognition with a tool such as FAST protects the window for reperfusion.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Speech and word-finding difficulty is a focal deficit ↓ Vascular cause must be assumed first ↓ Possible stroke or TIA
exam_trap: C, migraine with aura — aura can cause transient speech disturbance, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion; a sudden focal deficit must be treated as stroke or TIA first.
takeaway: Sudden focal neurology, including dysphasia, means stroke or TIA until proven otherwise.

stem:
An adult develops rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness over three weeks.

What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Urgent neurological assessment of bulbar and respiratory function
options.B: Outpatient neurology referral for nerve conduction studies and EMG
options.C: Check vitamin B12, thyroid function and CK, and review in two weeks
options.D: Start oral prednisolone 40 mg and review in neurology clinic in one week
options.E: Refer to community physiotherapy and review muscle strength in a month

correct_answer: A. Urgent neurological assessment of bulbar and respiratory function
why_correct: Rapidly progressive symmetrical limb weakness over days to weeks suggests an acute neuromuscular disorder such as Guillain–Barré syndrome, which can cause respiratory failure and bulbar compromise, so immediate neurological assessment with monitoring of forced vital capacity and swallow is required (NICE NG127 Suspected neurological conditions). Source: NICE recommends immediate referral for rapidly progressive symmetrical limb weakness.
why_wrong: B. Outpatient investigation delays recognition of possible respiratory and bulbar failure. C. Waiting two weeks risks missing a condition such as Guillain-Barré syndrome progressing to respiratory compromise. D. Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and delay appropriate assessment. E. Routine physiotherapy delays diagnosis of a potentially life-threatening neuromuscular cause.
pearl: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness over days to weeks suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome, where the danger is silent respiratory and bulbar failure; monitor forced vital capacity and swallow, not oxygen saturation alone.
thinking: Weakness progressing over weeks ↓ Symmetrical pattern ↓ Suggests acute neuromuscular disease such as Guillain–Barré ↓ Risk of respiratory and bulbar failure ↓ Urgent neurological assessment
exam_trap: B, outpatient nerve conduction studies and EMG — these help confirm the diagnosis, but an outpatient pathway delays recognising impending respiratory or bulbar compromise.
takeaway: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness needs immediate assessment of breathing and swallow.

stem:
A patient is suspected of having bacterial sepsis and blood cultures are indicated.

When should blood cultures generally be obtained in relation to antimicrobial treatment?

options.A: After the first antibiotic dose, to avoid delaying treatment
options.B: Before antimicrobials, if this causes no significant delay
options.C: At 24 hours, to assess the clinical response to initial treatment
options.D: Once the patient's temperature exceeds 39°C on two occasions
options.E: Before antimicrobials, even if this delays them by several hours

correct_answer: B. Before antimicrobials, if this causes no significant delay
why_correct: Blood cultures should be taken before the first dose of antimicrobial, because antibiotics reduce culture yield, but this must not cause a clinically significant delay in giving antibiotics to a patient with suspected sepsis (NICE NG253).
why_wrong: A. Taking cultures after antibiotics reduces yield; they should be taken first if this causes no significant delay. C. Cultures taken 24 hours after antibiotics are likely to be falsely negative and too late to guide initial treatment. D. The need for cultures does not depend on a temperature threshold. E. Antibiotics should not be significantly delayed in order to obtain cultures.
pearl: Take blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose because antibiotics reduce culture yield, but never let obtaining them cause a clinically significant delay in treating suspected sepsis.
thinking: Suspected bacterial sepsis ↓ Antibiotics reduce culture yield ↓ Antibiotics must not be delayed ↓ Cultures before antimicrobials if no significant delay
exam_trap: E, before antimicrobials even if this delays them by several hours — it correctly values culture yield, but delaying antibiotics in sepsis increases harm.
takeaway: Cultures before antibiotics, but never at the cost of a significant delay to treatment.

stem:
A patient is about to receive a unit of red blood cells.

What is essential immediately before starting the transfusion?

options.A: Start the transfusion before checking the patient
options.C: Complete the required bedside identity and compatibility checks
options.D: Assume the unit is correct because it arrived from the blood bank
options.E: Ask another patient to confirm the blood group

correct_answer: C. Complete the required bedside identity and compatibility checks
why_correct: Immediately before any blood component is given, a bedside check must confirm positive patient identification against the wristband and match it with the details, blood group and compatibility label on the unit, because ABO-incompatible transfusion from identification errors can be fatal (BSH administration of blood components guideline; SHOT).
why_wrong: A. Starting before checking removes the final safeguard against a wrong-patient transfusion. B. A surname alone is insufficient; at least first name, surname, date of birth and unique identifier must be checked. D. Errors can occur at any stage, so the bedside check is mandatory regardless of where the unit came from. E. Another patient cannot verify someone else's identity or blood group, and this is unsafe.
pearl: The bedside check is the final safeguard against ABO-incompatible transfusion: match the patient's positive identification and wristband against the unit's details, blood group and compatibility label.
thinking: Red cell transfusion about to start ↓ Identification errors can cause fatal ABO incompatibility ↓ Final safeguard is at the bedside ↓ Complete bedside identity and compatibility checks
exam_trap: D, assuming the unit is correct because it came from the blood bank — errors can occur at any stage, so the bedside check is mandatory every time.
takeaway: Every unit needs a full bedside identity and compatibility check immediately before starting.

stem:
A patient develops fever, chills, back pain and hypotension shortly after a blood transfusion begins.

What should be done first?

options.A: Slow the transfusion rate and give oral paracetamol now
options.B: Give IV chlorphenamine 10 mg and continue the transfusion
options.C: Continue but increase observations to every 15 minutes
options.D: Stop the transfusion and assess the patient urgently
options.E: Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg and continue at a slower rate

correct_answer: D. Stop the transfusion and assess the patient urgently
why_correct: Fever, rigors, loin/back pain and hypotension shortly after a transfusion starts suggest an acute haemolytic (ABO-incompatible) reaction or bacterial contamination, so the transfusion must be stopped immediately, the patient assessed using ABCDE with IV access maintained, and identity and unit checked (BSH transfusion reactions guideline).
why_wrong: A. Slowing the rate may suit a mild febrile reaction, but fever with hypotension and back pain needs the transfusion stopped. B. Continuing delivers more of the component causing the reaction. C. Continuing risks a potentially fatal haemolytic or septic reaction. E. Steroids do not treat haemolysis or bacterial contamination, and continuing worsens the reaction.
pearl: Fever, rigors, loin or back pain and hypotension soon after a transfusion starts suggest acute haemolytic reaction or bacterial contamination: stop the transfusion, keep IV access, assess ABCDE and recheck identity and unit.
thinking: Transfusion just started ↓ Fever, chills, back pain and hypotension ↓ Suggests acute haemolytic reaction or bacterial contamination ↓ Stop the transfusion and assess urgently
exam_trap: A, slowing the rate and giving paracetamol — this may suit an isolated mild febrile reaction, but hypotension and back pain signal a severe reaction needing the transfusion stopped.
takeaway: Severe transfusion reaction signs: stop the transfusion first, then assess ABCDE.

stem:
A patient presents with dysuria and urinary frequency.

Which urinalysis finding supports a urinary tract infection?

options.B: Raised urine specific gravity with proteinuria
options.C: Positive ketones with an acidic pH
options.D: Blood on dipstick with negative nitrites and leukocytes
options.E: Glucose and protein detected on the dipstick

correct_answer: A. Positive nitrites and/or leukocyte esterase
why_correct: Nitrites (from bacterial reduction of nitrate) and leukocyte esterase (from white cells) support a urinary tract infection when interpreted with typical symptoms such as dysuria and frequency; nitrite positivity is the more specific finding (UKHSA guidance on diagnosing UTI).
why_wrong: B. Specific gravity and protein are non-specific findings that do not establish infection. C. Ketonuria reflects fasting, ketoacidosis or vomiting rather than infection. D. Haematuria without nitrites or leukocytes is non-specific and does not support UTI. E. Glycosuria suggests hyperglycaemia or a low renal threshold, not infection.
pearl: Nitrites, from bacterial conversion of nitrate, and leukocyte esterase, from white cells, support UTI when they fit typical symptoms; nitrite positivity is the more specific of the two.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency suggest UTI ↓ Dipstick should show markers of bacteria or white cells ↓ Nitrites and leukocyte esterase are those markers ↓ Positive nitrites and/or leukocyte esterase
exam_trap: D, blood with negative nitrites and leukocytes — haematuria can accompany UTI, but on its own it is non-specific and, without nitrites or leukocytes, does not support infection.
takeaway: Nitrites and leukocyte esterase, with typical symptoms, support a UTI.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin develops significant gastrointestinal bleeding.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Treat the bleed urgently and reverse warfarin according to severity
options.B: Withhold one dose of warfarin and recheck the INR tomorrow
options.C: Give oral vitamin K and restart warfarin once the bleeding has settled
options.D: Continue warfarin and give a PPI to protect the stomach
options.E: Arrange outpatient endoscopy and continue warfarin

correct_answer: A. Treat the bleed urgently and reverse warfarin according to severity
why_correct: Significant GI bleeding on warfarin needs ABCDE resuscitation and urgent treatment of the bleed, with warfarin withheld and reversal guided by severity: major bleeding is reversed with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate (BNF; NICE CG141).
why_wrong: B. Withholding a single dose is inadequate for significant bleeding, which needs urgent resuscitation and reversal guided by severity. C. Major bleeding on warfarin is reversed with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, not oral vitamin K alone. D. Continuing warfarin would worsen the bleeding. E. Significant GI bleeding needs urgent assessment and inpatient endoscopy, with warfarin withheld.
pearl: Major bleeding on warfarin: resuscitate, withhold warfarin and reverse according to severity, with IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate for major bleeds, alongside definitive treatment of the bleeding source.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Significant GI bleeding ↓ Anticoagulation is worsening a major bleed ↓ Treat the bleed urgently and reverse according to severity
exam_trap: C, oral vitamin K and restart once settled — vitamin K is part of reversal, but oral vitamin K alone is too slow for major bleeding, which needs IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex.
takeaway: Significant bleeding on warfarin: resuscitate, stop warfarin and reverse according to severity.

stem:
A 58-year-old patient presents with severe abdominal pain. They are pale, tachycardic and hypotensive, with marked abdominal tenderness.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange CT abdomen and review the result the next morning
options.B: Give analgesia and admit for review on the morning ward round
options.C: Arrange an urgent outpatient ultrasound later this week
options.D: Resuscitate urgently with senior surgical involvement
options.E: Give IV antibiotics and refer to the gastroenterology team

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate urgently with senior surgical involvement
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with pallor, tachycardia, hypotension and marked tenderness indicates shock from a possible surgical emergency (e.g. ruptured AAA, perforation, ischaemia), so ABCDE resuscitation and immediate senior surgical involvement take priority over establishing the exact diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Reviewing imaging the next day misses a time-critical emergency. B. Waiting for a morning ward round could be fatal in a shocked patient. C. Outpatient imaging is inappropriate for a shocked patient with an acute abdomen. E. Shock with an acute abdomen needs resuscitation and senior surgical review, not a gastroenterology referral.
pearl: Shock with an acute abdomen is a surgical emergency: resuscitate using ABCDE and involve a senior surgeon immediately, because the exact diagnosis, such as ruptured aneurysm or perforation, matters less than speed.
thinking: Shock plus severe abdominal pain and peritoneal features is an emergency. Stabilisation and escalation take priority over establishing the exact diagnosis first.
exam_trap: A, CT abdomen reviewed the next morning — imaging may help localise the cause, but deferring review leaves a shocked patient untreated during a time-critical emergency.
takeaway: Acute abdomen with shock: resuscitate and get senior surgical help now.

stem:
A patient's creatinine rises significantly from their previous baseline over a short period.

What does this indicate?

options.A: Chronic kidney disease requiring annual monitoring
options.B: Normal variation that should be rechecked in three months
options.C: Dehydration that should be managed without further tests
options.D: Progressive ageing-related decline in renal function
options.E: Possible acute kidney injury; assess for the cause

correct_answer: E. Possible acute kidney injury; assess for the cause
why_correct: A rapid rise in creatinine from baseline (e.g. 50% or more within 7 days, or 26 µmol/L within 48 hours) meets the KDIGO criteria for AKI, which needs assessment of prerenal, renal and postrenal causes (NICE NG148).
why_wrong: A. CKD is defined by abnormalities persisting for more than 3 months, not an acute rise. B. A significant rise from baseline is a clinically important change that needs prompt action. C. Volume depletion is one possible cause, but prerenal, renal and postrenal causes need assessment. D. Ageing causes a gradual, not acute, decline in renal function.
pearl: AKI is defined by a rise in creatinine from baseline over a short period or a fall in urine output; the change from the patient's own baseline matters more than the absolute value.
thinking: Creatinine rises significantly ↓ Compared with the patient's own baseline ↓ Over a short period ↓ Meets the pattern of acute kidney injury ↓ Assess for prerenal, renal and postrenal causes
exam_trap: C, dehydration managed without further tests — volume depletion is a common cause, but assuming it skips assessment for renal and postrenal causes such as obstruction.
takeaway: An acute creatinine rise from baseline is AKI until proven otherwise; look for the cause.

stem:
A patient with severe hyperkalaemia has ECG changes consistent with myocardial membrane instability.

What treatment takes immediate priority?

options.A: IV insulin and glucose before any other treatment
options.B: Oral potassium binder to remove potassium
options.C: Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg as the sole treatment
options.D: IV calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium
options.E: IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis

correct_answer: D. IV calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium
why_correct: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium (gluconate or chloride) stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes and reduces arrhythmia risk, while insulin–glucose is then used to shift potassium into cells (UK Kidney Association hyperkalaemia guideline).
why_wrong: A. Insulin-glucose shifts potassium into cells but does not stabilise the myocardium; with ECG changes, IV calcium is given first. B. Potassium binders act slowly and do not protect the heart. C. Salbutamol is an adjunct that shifts potassium and does not stabilise the myocardium. E. Bicarbonate is not first-line and does not stabilise the myocardium.
pearl: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium comes first because it stabilises the myocardium within minutes; it does not lower potassium, so insulin–glucose follows to shift potassium into cells.
thinking: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, cardiac membrane stabilisation is an immediate priority.
exam_trap: A, IV insulin and glucose first — it is a key treatment for lowering potassium, but it does not protect the heart; with ECG changes, IV calcium is given first.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first to protect the heart, then shift potassium.

stem:
A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration and marked hyperglycaemia. Blood tests show metabolic acidosis and ketonaemia.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis together define diabetic ketoacidosis, and vomiting, abdominal pain and dehydration are typical features in type 1 diabetes (JBDS DKA guideline).
why_wrong: A. The patient is markedly hyperglycaemic, not hypoglycaemic. B. The patient has type 1 diabetes and the presentation is a metabolic emergency, not uncomplicated disease. C. Hyperthyroidism does not produce ketoacidosis with marked hyperglycaemia. E. Gastroenteritis does not cause marked hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis.
pearl: DKA is defined by the triad of hyperglycaemia or known diabetes, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis; vomiting and abdominal pain are common presenting features that can mimic an abdominal illness.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes ↓ Vomiting, abdominal pain and dehydration ↓ Marked hyperglycaemia ↓ Ketonaemia with metabolic acidosis ↓ Diabetic ketoacidosis
exam_trap: E, simple viral gastroenteritis — vomiting and abdominal pain fit, but gastroenteritis does not explain marked hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia and acidosis.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis together mean diabetic ketoacidosis.

stem:
A patient is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis.

Why must potassium be monitored closely?

options.A: Insulin shifts potassium out of cells, so hyperkalaemia worsens with treatment
options.B: DKA causes a total body potassium excess that insulin treatment then corrects
options.C: Acidosis lowers serum potassium, which then rises once insulin is started
options.D: Body potassium is depleted though serum potassium may be normal or high
options.E: Replacement is started once serum potassium falls below 2.5 mmol/L

correct_answer: D. Body potassium is depleted though serum potassium may be normal or high
why_correct: In DKA, total body potassium is depleted, but acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium may initially be normal or high; insulin then drives potassium into cells, causing a rapid fall, so close monitoring and replacement are required (JBDS DKA guideline).
why_wrong: A. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so serum potassium falls during treatment. B. Total body potassium is depleted in DKA, not in excess. C. Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells and raises serum potassium; insulin then lowers it. E. Potassium is usually added to fluids once the level is 5.5 mmol/L or below and the patient is passing urine; waiting for 2.5 mmol/L would be dangerous.
pearl: In DKA, total body potassium is low even when the serum level looks normal or high; insulin drives potassium into cells, so levels can fall rapidly and need close monitoring and replacement in fluids.
thinking: DKA treatment ↓ Total body potassium is depleted ↓ Acidosis and insulin deficiency keep serum potassium normal or high ↓ Insulin drives potassium into cells ↓ Body potassium depleted though serum may be normal or high
exam_trap: A, insulin shifts potassium out of cells — it reverses the physiology: insulin drives potassium into cells, so the risk during treatment is hypokalaemia, not worsening hyperkalaemia.
takeaway: DKA depletes body potassium; expect serum potassium to fall once insulin starts.

stem:
A patient with suspected sepsis requires IV antibiotics. Blood cultures can be obtained immediately without causing a significant delay in treatment.

What should be done?

options.A: Give antibiotics now and take blood cultures after 24 hours
options.B: Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics
options.C: Give antibiotics and take cultures if fever persists
options.D: Take blood cultures, then give antibiotics without delay
options.E: Take cultures and wait for a temperature spike before antibiotics

correct_answer: D. Take blood cultures, then give antibiotics without delay
why_correct: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics where this causes no significant delay, because prior antibiotics reduce culture yield, and the result allows treatment to be targeted (NICE NG253).
why_wrong: A. Cultures taken after antibiotics have low yield, and here they can be taken first without significant delay. B. Waiting for culture results before antibiotics delays urgent treatment by days. C. Prior antibiotics reduce culture yield, so cultures should be taken first. E. Antibiotics in suspected sepsis should not wait for a temperature spike.
pearl: When cultures can be taken immediately, take them first and then give antibiotics without delay; this preserves culture yield, allowing later targeting, without compromising time-critical treatment.
thinking: Suspected sepsis needing IV antibiotics ↓ Cultures obtainable without significant delay ↓ Antibiotics reduce culture yield ↓ Take cultures, then give antibiotics immediately
exam_trap: A, antibiotics now and cultures after 24 hours — giving antibiotics promptly is right, but cultures taken a day later have low yield and are too late to guide treatment.
takeaway: Cultures first if no delay results, then antibiotics straight away.

stem:
A patient develops sudden confusion and weakness. Capillary glucose is 2.1 mmol/L.

What should be done?

options.A: Activate the stroke pathway before correcting glucose
options.B: Arrange an urgent CT head and treat the glucose afterwards
options.C: Give insulin to stabilise glucose control
options.D: Start aspirin 300 mg for presumed ischaemic stroke
options.E: Treat the hypoglycaemia and reassess the deficit

correct_answer: E. Treat the hypoglycaemia and reassess the deficit
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke with focal deficits and confusion, so the low glucose must be treated promptly and the patient reassessed; a deficit that persists after correction then needs stroke assessment (NICE NG128).
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia is a stroke mimic and must be corrected first before reassessing the deficit. B. Correction of hypoglycaemia should not be delayed for imaging. C. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycaemia. D. Assuming ischaemic stroke ignores a treatable stroke mimic.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic that can cause confusion and focal weakness; check capillary glucose in every suspected stroke, treat a low level, then reassess before activating the stroke pathway.
thinking: Sudden confusion and weakness ↓ Looks like stroke ↓ Capillary glucose is very low ↓ Hypoglycaemia is a stroke mimic ↓ Treat the hypoglycaemia and reassess
exam_trap: A, activating the stroke pathway first — speed feels right in suspected stroke, but hypoglycaemia is a treatable mimic and must be corrected before reassessing the deficit.
takeaway: Always check glucose in suspected stroke; correct hypoglycaemia first, then reassess.

stem:
A patient has pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and unexplained hypoxaemia.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Treat as pneumonia with oral antibiotics and review
options.B: Treat as musculoskeletal pain with NSAIDs
options.D: Assess for PE using the Wells score pathway
options.E: Diagnose acute pericarditis and start colchicine

correct_answer: D. Assess for PE using the Wells score pathway
why_correct: Pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and unexplained hypoxaemia raise suspicion of PE, which should be assessed using the two-level Wells score with D-dimer or CTPA as indicated (NICE NG158).
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics without assessment may treat the wrong condition and delay diagnosis of PE. B. Musculoskeletal pain does not explain hypoxaemia and tachycardia. C. Outpatient echocardiography delays assessment of a potentially life-threatening PE. E. Pericarditis does not explain unexplained hypoxaemia, and PE must be assessed.
pearl: Pleuritic chest pain with tachycardia and unexplained hypoxaemia should prompt structured PE assessment with the two-level Wells score, leading to D-dimer or CTPA as indicated.
thinking: Pleuritic chest pain ↓ Tachycardia ↓ Hypoxaemia with no other explanation ↓ Raises suspicion of PE ↓ Assess using the Wells score pathway
exam_trap: A, pneumonia with oral antibiotics — pleuritic pain can accompany pneumonia, but treating without assessment risks missing PE, which explains unexplained hypoxaemia and tachycardia.
takeaway: Pleuritic pain, tachycardia and unexplained hypoxaemia: work through the PE pathway.

stem:
A patient presents with unilateral swollen, painful calf and has a clinical assessment suggesting DVT is likely.

What is the appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a D-dimer and discharge if it is negative
options.E: Advise compression stockings and review in a week

correct_answer: D. Arrange a proximal leg-vein ultrasound
why_correct: When the two-level DVT Wells score suggests DVT is likely, NICE recommends a proximal leg-vein ultrasound within 4 hours (or interim anticoagulation if it cannot be done within that time) (NICE NG158).
why_wrong: A. When DVT is likely, a proximal leg-vein ultrasound is needed; a negative D-dimer alone does not exclude DVT in this group. B. Nothing suggests cellulitis, and antibiotics do not treat DVT. C. CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism, not the leg veins. E. Delaying assessment risks propagation of thrombosis and PE.
pearl: When the two-level Wells score says DVT is likely, go straight to a proximal leg-vein ultrasound, giving interim anticoagulation if the scan cannot be done promptly; D-dimer cannot rule out DVT in this group.
thinking: Unilateral swollen, painful calf ↓ Clinical assessment says DVT likely ↓ D-dimer cannot exclude DVT when likely ↓ Proximal leg-vein ultrasound
exam_trap: A, D-dimer and discharge if negative — D-dimer is a valid rule-out test, but only when DVT is unlikely; when DVT is likely, imaging is needed.
takeaway: DVT likely: proximal leg-vein ultrasound; DVT unlikely: D-dimer first.

stem:
A patient has a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism and an appropriately performed D-dimer test is positive.

What does the result mean?

options.A: PE is excluded because the clinical probability is low
options.B: Repeat the D-dimer in 48 hours before any imaging
options.C: PE is confirmed and anticoagulation alone is sufficient
options.D: PE is confirmed and thrombolysis should be considered
options.E: PE is not excluded and needs imaging, usually CTPA

correct_answer: E. PE is not excluded and needs imaging, usually CTPA
why_correct: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: a negative result in a low-probability patient helps exclude PE, but a positive result can be due to many conditions, so further assessment, usually CTPA, is required (NICE NG158).
why_wrong: A. A positive D-dimer does not exclude PE; only a negative result in a low-probability patient helps rule it out. B. Repeating the D-dimer delays diagnosis and does not resolve a positive result; imaging is needed. C. D-dimer rises in many conditions (e.g. infection, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy), so a positive result does not confirm PE. D. A positive D-dimer does not confirm PE, and thrombolysis is reserved for confirmed PE with haemodynamic instability.
pearl: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: a negative result in a low-probability patient helps exclude PE, but a positive result only means PE has not been excluded and imaging, usually CTPA, is needed.
thinking: Low clinical probability of PE ↓ D-dimer positive ↓ D-dimer is sensitive but not specific ↓ PE neither confirmed nor excluded ↓ Proceed to imaging, usually CTPA
exam_trap: A, PE excluded because probability is low — low probability tempts, but only a negative D-dimer in this group helps rule PE out; a positive result requires imaging.
takeaway: Positive D-dimer does not confirm PE; it means imaging is needed.

stem:
A patient with asthma becomes increasingly breathless and has difficulty speaking in full sentences.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Give a salbutamol inhaler and review at the next GP appointment
options.B: Treat as potential acute severe asthma and assess urgently
options.C: Arrange routine asthma review and increase the inhaled steroid
options.D: Treat as a panic attack with breathing control techniques
options.E: Start oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours

correct_answer: B. Treat as potential acute severe asthma and assess urgently
why_correct: Inability to complete sentences in one breath is a feature of acute severe asthma, which requires urgent assessment (PEF, SpO2, heart and respiratory rate) and immediate treatment with oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and steroids (BTS/SIGN acute asthma guidance).
why_wrong: A. A single inhaler dose with delayed review is inadequate for possible acute severe asthma, which needs urgent assessment. C. Routine review and stepping up maintenance therapy ignores a potentially life-threatening exacerbation. D. Inability to complete sentences is a severity marker of asthma and should not be attributed to panic. E. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated in asthma exacerbations and delaying review is unsafe.
pearl: Inability to complete sentences in one breath is a marker of acute severe asthma: assess urgently with PEF, SpO₂, pulse and respiratory rate, and treat immediately with oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and steroids.
thinking: Known asthma ↓ Increasing breathlessness ↓ Cannot complete full sentences ↓ Feature of acute severe asthma ↓ Treat as potential acute severe asthma and assess urgently
exam_trap: D, panic attack with breathing control — distress can look like anxiety, but difficulty speaking in sentences is a recognised severity marker of asthma, not panic.
takeaway: Asthma with inability to complete sentences is acute severe asthma until proven otherwise.

stem:
