why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes pain in proportion to skin changes; disproportionate pain with systemic toxicity suggests necrotising infection. C. Gout causes acute joint inflammation, not rapidly spreading limb pain with systemic toxicity. D. DVT causes limb swelling but not rapidly worsening disproportionate pain with systemic toxicity. E. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender cord along a vein without systemic toxicity.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression and systemic toxicity suggest necrotising soft-tissue infection; it needs urgent surgical review and IV antibiotics.
thinking: This is a surgical emergency; do not wait for extensive skin changes before escalating.
exam_trap: A, simple cellulitis — redness and swelling suggest it, but pain disproportionate to skin changes with systemic toxicity points to necrotising infection.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to skin signs plus systemic toxicity: suspect necrotising infection.

stem:
An 82-year-old becomes acutely confused in hospital. Their attention varies markedly during the day and they are lucid at some times and disorientated at others.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute onset, impaired attention and fluctuating cognition are characteristic of delirium.
why_wrong: A. Learning disability is lifelong and does not explain a new acute fluctuating confusion. B. Schizophrenia rarely presents for the first time in an 82-year-old with acute fluctuating inattention. C. Depression may affect concentration but does not usually cause acute fluctuating confusion and disorientation. E. Stable dementia causes gradual decline without acute onset or marked fluctuation in attention.
pearl: Delirium has an acute onset with inattention and fluctuating cognition; look for precipitants such as infection, drugs, dehydration, pain, constipation and urinary retention.
thinking: 82 years old in hospital ↓ Acute confusion ↓ Attention fluctuates during the day ↓ Lucid intervals ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: E, stable dementia — it causes confusion in older adults, but its decline is gradual, without acute onset or marked fluctuation in attention.
takeaway: Acute onset plus fluctuating attention means delirium; search for the cause.

stem:
A patient following a stroke coughs repeatedly when drinking thin fluids.

What complication is particularly important to consider?
why_correct: Dysphagia after stroke can result in aspiration of food or fluids into the airway.
why_wrong: A. DVT is a risk after stroke but is not explained by coughing on swallowing fluids. B. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye and is unrelated to coughing on drinking. C. Gout causes acute joint inflammation and is unrelated to swallowing difficulties. D. Otitis externa is an ear infection unrelated to dysphagia.
pearl: Coughing when drinking after a stroke suggests dysphagia with aspiration risk; a swallow screen is needed before oral intake, with specialist speech and language assessment if it fails.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ Coughs when drinking thin fluids ↓ Unsafe swallow (dysphagia) ↓ Fluid entering the airway ↓ Aspiration
exam_trap: A, deep-vein thrombosis — a recognised complication after stroke, but it does not explain coughing on swallowing; aspiration does.
takeaway: Coughing on drinking after stroke means dysphagia — think aspiration.

stem:
A patient with advanced cancer has troublesome pain despite regular analgesia.

What is the appropriate general principle?

options.A: Assess the pain and optimise symptom control
options.B: Tell the patient pain is unavoidable
options.C: Ignore pain because the illness is advanced

correct_answer: A. Assess the pain and optimise symptom control
why_correct: Palliative care aims to relieve distressing symptoms and improve quality of life.
why_wrong: B. Most cancer pain can be improved with careful assessment and treatment. C. Pain management is central to palliative care regardless of disease stage. D. Stopping all analgesia would worsen symptoms and could cause opioid withdrawal. E. Open communication about symptoms is essential to effective palliative care.
pearl: Uncontrolled cancer pain needs reassessment of its cause and type, then optimised analgesia, often adjusting opioids or adding adjuvants; specialist palliative care input can help.
thinking: Advanced cancer ↓ Pain despite regular analgesia ↓ Palliative goal is symptom relief ↓ Reassess and adjust treatment ↓ Assess the pain and optimise symptom control
exam_trap: B, telling the patient pain is unavoidable — it may seem honest in advanced disease, but most cancer pain can be improved with careful assessment and treatment.
takeaway: Uncontrolled pain in advanced cancer: reassess and optimise, never accept it.

stem:
A patient with advanced progressive illness is approaching the end of life and may develop pain, breathlessness, agitation or secretions.

What is the purpose of anticipatory medicines?

options.A: To replace all communication with the patient
options.B: To prepare for likely symptoms that may develop
options.C: To treat every symptom prophylactically regardless of need
options.D: To avoid involving community healthcare professionals

correct_answer: B. To prepare for likely symptoms that may develop
why_correct: Anticipatory prescribing allows appropriate symptom-relief medicines to be available if symptoms arise.
why_wrong: A. Ongoing communication with the patient and family remains essential. C. Medicines are prescribed in advance but given only when symptoms arise, not prophylactically. D. Anticipatory prescribing supports community teams to manage symptoms promptly at home. E. Anticipatory medicines are for symptom control, not to deliberately shorten life.
pearl: Anticipatory ('just in case') medicines for pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea and secretions are prescribed in advance so symptoms can be treated promptly, but given only when needed.
thinking: Approaching the end of life ↓ Likely symptoms: pain, breathlessness, agitation, secretions ↓ Delays in obtaining drugs cause distress ↓ Prepare for likely symptoms
exam_trap: C, treating every symptom prophylactically — prescribing in advance sounds like routine dosing, but these medicines are given only if symptoms arise.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines are prescribed in advance and given only when symptoms arise.

stem:
A patient asks what a DNACPR decision means.

Which explanation is accurate?

options.A: It means the patient will not be admitted to the intensive care unit
options.B: It means treatment will now focus on end-of-life and comfort care
options.C: It applies to CPR in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest
options.D: It means the patient has lost the capacity to make their own decisions
options.E: It means antibiotics and IV fluids will be withheld

correct_answer: C. It applies to CPR in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest
why_correct: DNACPR concerns CPR; it does not automatically mean that other appropriate treatments should be withheld.
why_wrong: A. Escalation to intensive care is a separate decision and is not determined by a DNACPR decision. B. DNACPR does not mean a move to end-of-life care; other appropriate treatment continues. D. DNACPR does not imply loss of capacity; patients with capacity remain involved in decisions. E. Antibiotics, fluids and other treatments may still be given where appropriate.
pearl: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment, including antibiotics, fluids and escalation where suitable, continues. Not for CPR does not mean not for treatment.
thinking: Patient asks about DNACPR ↓ The decision concerns CPR only ↓ Other treatment decisions are separate ↓ Applies to CPR in cardiac or respiratory arrest
exam_trap: B, a move to end-of-life comfort care — a common misunderstanding, but DNACPR does not stop other appropriate active treatment.
takeaway: DNACPR means no CPR — it does not mean no treatment.

stem:
A patient is admitted to hospital with a medication list that differs from the medicines they report taking at home.

What should be done?

options.C: Ask the patient to choose whichever list they prefer without checking
options.E: Reconcile the medicines using reliable sources

correct_answer: E. Reconcile the medicines using reliable sources
why_correct: Medication reconciliation helps identify omissions, duplications and prescribing errors during transitions of care.
why_wrong: A. Prescribing both lists risks duplication and toxicity. B. Ignoring the discrepancy risks omissions, duplications and prescribing errors. C. Reconciliation requires verification from reliable sources such as GP records, not unchecked patient choice. D. Stopping all medicines automatically can cause harm, for example from omission of time-critical drugs.
pearl: Admission and discharge are high-risk points for medication discrepancies.
thinking: Hospital admission ↓ Listed medicines differ from those taken at home ↓ Risk of omission or duplication ↓ Verify with reliable sources ↓ Reconcile the medicines
exam_trap: C, letting the patient choose a list — the patient knows what they take, but reconciliation requires verification against reliable sources such as GP records.
takeaway: Medication discrepancies on admission: reconcile using reliable sources.

stem:
A patient is started on antibiotics while awaiting microbiological results.

The results later identify an organism susceptible to a narrower antibiotic.

What is an appropriate stewardship principle?

options.A: Continue the empirical regimen for the full course
options.B: Escalate to a broader agent to ensure full cover
options.D: Add a second agent to provide synergistic cover
options.E: Extend the course to prevent later recurrence

correct_answer: C. Narrow treatment when clinically appropriate
why_correct: Antibiotic therapy should be reviewed and narrowed where appropriate to reduce unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.
why_wrong: A. Continuing an unnecessarily broad empirical regimen ignores the microbiology result. B. Escalating to a broader agent promotes resistance and C. difficile infection. D. Adding antibiotics without indication increases adverse effects and resistance. E. Antibiotics should have a defined duration and be reviewed, not extended without reason.
pearl: Reviewing antibiotics once cultures return is a core stewardship step: switch to a narrower agent when clinically appropriate and set a clear stop or review date.
thinking: Empirical antibiotics started ↓ Microbiology identifies a susceptible organism ↓ A narrower agent will work ↓ Narrow treatment when clinically appropriate
exam_trap: A, continuing the empirical regimen — completing what was started feels safe, but staying broad ignores the result and adds resistance and C. difficile risk.
takeaway: Use microbiology results to narrow antibiotics whenever clinically appropriate.

stem:
A blood culture grows an organism that is a common skin contaminant, while the patient is clinically well and other cultures are negative.

What should the clinician do?

options.C: Interpret the result in its clinical context
options.D: Assume every positive culture represents bloodstream infection

correct_answer: C. Interpret the result in its clinical context
why_correct: Some organisms commonly represent contamination, although true infection must be considered according to the organism and clinical circumstances.
why_wrong: A. Lifelong antibiotics are not indicated for a likely contaminant in a well patient. B. Endocarditis requires clinical and microbiological criteria such as multiple positive cultures, not a single probable contaminant. D. Skin contaminants commonly grow in blood cultures without true infection. E. Blood culture results are important and should not be ignored.
pearl: A single culture growing a skin commensal in a well patient with other cultures negative is often contamination; true infection is more likely with multiple positive sets or prosthetic material.
thinking: Blood culture grows a common skin contaminant ↓ Patient clinically well ↓ Other cultures negative ↓ Likely contamination, but not assumed ↓ Interpret in clinical context
exam_trap: D, assuming every positive culture is a bloodstream infection — a positive result feels definitive, but skin contaminants commonly grow without true infection.
takeaway: Interpret a positive blood culture by organism, number of sets and the clinical picture.

stem:
A patient with suspected bloodstream infection requires blood cultures.

Which principle is important when obtaining them?

options.C: Collect them from an unclean surface

why_correct: Aseptic technique reduces contamination and improves the reliability of microbiological results.
why_wrong: B. Reusing needles is unsafe and risks infection. C. Unclean surfaces increase contamination risk. D. Labelling from memory risks misidentification; samples should be labelled at the bedside. E. Touching prepared sterile equipment introduces contamination.
pearl: Contaminated blood cultures lead to unnecessary antibiotics and longer stays; use aseptic non-touch technique, clean the skin and bottle tops, and label at the bedside.
thinking: Suspected bloodstream infection ↓ Blood cultures needed ↓ Contamination gives misleading results ↓ Use appropriate aseptic technique
exam_trap: D, labelling later from memory — it seems harmless once the sample is taken, but it risks misidentification; samples should be labelled at the bedside.
takeaway: Blood cultures: aseptic non-touch technique and bedside labelling.

stem:
A healthcare worker has just examined one patient and is about to examine another.

What is an important infection-prevention measure?

options.B: Wear the same gloves for both patients
options.D: Change gloves without considering hand hygiene
options.E: Wash hands only at the end of the shift

why_correct: Hand hygiene is a fundamental measure for preventing healthcare-associated infection.
why_wrong: B. Wearing the same gloves between patients transfers microorganisms. C. Antibiotics have no role in preventing transmission between patients. D. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, which is required before and after glove use. E. Hand hygiene is needed between patients, not only at the end of a shift.
pearl: Hand hygiene between patients is the most important single measure against healthcare-associated infection; gloves must be changed between patients and never replace it.
thinking: Examined one patient ↓ About to examine another ↓ Hands may carry organisms between them ↓ Perform appropriate hand hygiene
exam_trap: D, changing gloves without hand hygiene — fresh gloves seem enough, but hands are contaminated during glove removal, so hand hygiene is still needed.
takeaway: Between patients: change gloves and clean hands, every time.

stem:
A healthcare worker is about to perform a procedure involving potential contact with body fluids.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Reuse disposable gloves if they appear intact
options.B: Re-sheath needles carefully when wearing gloves
options.C: Use gloves instead of hand hygiene
options.D: Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure
options.E: Wear gloves for all patient contact

correct_answer: D. Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure
why_correct: PPE should be selected according to the foreseeable risk of exposure.
why_wrong: A. Disposable gloves are single-use and must not be reused. B. Needles should not be re-sheathed; gloves do not remove the need for safe sharps practice. C. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. E. Gloves should be used according to risk, not for every interaction.
pearl: Choose PPE by the task: gloves and apron for contact with blood or body fluids, adding eye protection or a fluid-resistant mask if splashing is likely; gloves never replace hand hygiene.
thinking: Procedure with possible body fluid contact ↓ Standard precautions apply ↓ PPE depends on the anticipated exposure ↓ Select PPE according to risk
exam_trap: E, gloves for all patient contact — it seems safer, but unnecessary glove use is not recommended; PPE should match the anticipated exposure.
takeaway: Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure for each task.

stem:
A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a potentially contaminated needle.

What should they do?

options.A: Suck the wound, apply an alcohol-based scrub and then report the injury
options.B: Squeeze the wound hard and scrub it with a brush under hot running water
options.C: Apply a waterproof dressing and report the injury at the end of the shift
options.D: Wash the area and follow the occupational exposure pathway promptly
options.E: Wash the area and arrange a GP blood test for HIV in three months' time

correct_answer: D. Wash the area and follow the occupational exposure pathway promptly
why_correct: Prompt first aid, reporting and risk assessment are important after occupational exposure.
why_wrong: A. Sucking the wound is not recommended; it should be encouraged to bleed and washed with soap and running water. B. Scrubbing or squeezing hard may damage tissue; gentle bleeding and washing are advised. C. Delayed reporting may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis, which should ideally start within hours. E. Waiting 3 months misses urgent risk assessment and possible prophylaxis.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage gentle bleeding and wash with soap and running water without sucking or scrubbing, then report at once for risk assessment and possible PEP.
thinking: Needlestick from a possibly contaminated needle ↓ First aid: encourage bleeding and wash ↓ Urgent risk assessment for time-critical PEP ↓ Wash and follow the exposure pathway promptly
exam_trap: C, a dressing and reporting at the end of the shift — finishing the shift seems practical, but the delay may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
takeaway: Needlestick: bleed, wash, report immediately — never wait until the shift ends.

stem:
A patient has symptoms strongly suggestive of infectious pulmonary tuberculosis.

Which infection-control principle is important?

options.A: Admission to an open bay with standard infection-control precautions
options.B: Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
options.C: Allow normal movement around the ward once antibiotics have been started
options.D: Treat with amoxicillin and review in 2 weeks
options.E: Nurse in a single side room with the door kept open for easy observation

correct_answer: B. Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate infection-control precautions to reduce transmission.
why_wrong: A. An open bay increases the risk of airborne transmission. C. Patients with pulmonary TB remain infectious for a period after starting treatment (usually about 2 weeks of effective therapy), so unrestricted movement around the ward increases the risk of airborne transmission. D. Amoxicillin does not treat TB and delays diagnosis. E. A side room door should be kept closed to reduce airborne spread.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs respiratory isolation in a side room with the door closed and appropriate respiratory protection, with specialist infection-control input.
thinking: Symptoms suggest infectious pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission ↓ Others on the ward at risk ↓ Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
exam_trap: E, a single room with the door open — a side room seems sufficient, but an open door allows airborne spread; the door should be kept closed.
takeaway: Suspected infectious TB: respiratory isolation with the side-room door closed.

stem:
A patient presents with fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash. Measles is suspected.

What is an important immediate principle?

options.A: Await measles IgM serology results before starting any infection-control measures
options.B: Isolate the patient and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
options.C: Manage in the main waiting room wearing a surgical mask
options.D: Treat as bacterial cellulitis with oral flucloxacillin and review after 48 hours
options.E: Delay notification to the health protection team until laboratory confirmation

correct_answer: B. Isolate the patient and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
why_correct: Measles is highly transmissible, so infection-control and public-health measures are important.
why_wrong: A. Infection control should start on clinical suspicion, not wait for serology. C. Measles is airborne and highly transmissible, so a shared waiting room risks spread. D. The features suggest measles, not bacterial cellulitis. E. Measles is notifiable on clinical suspicion; notification should not wait for confirmation.
pearl: Measles is highly transmissible; isolate on clinical suspicion, keep the patient out of shared waiting areas and notify the health protection team without waiting for laboratory confirmation.
thinking: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash ↓ Measles suspected ↓ Airborne, highly infectious and notifiable ↓ Isolate and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
exam_trap: E, delaying notification until laboratory confirmation — confirmation seems prudent, but measles is notifiable on clinical suspicion so public-health action can start quickly.
takeaway: Suspected measles: isolate and notify on suspicion — do not wait for results.

stem:
A patient has suspected C. difficile infection with diarrhoea.

Which measure is particularly important?

options.A: Allow use of the shared bay bathroom with cleaning at the end of each day
options.B: Transfer the patient to another ward to reduce spread on the current ward
options.C: Routine detergent cleaning of the bed space and shared equipment once daily
options.D: Prophylactic oral antibiotics for all the other patients in the same bay
options.E: Isolation and hand hygiene according to infection-control procedures

correct_answer: E. Isolation and hand hygiene according to infection-control procedures
why_correct: C. difficile spores can spread in healthcare environments, making appropriate infection-control measures essential.
why_wrong: A. Shared bathrooms increase the risk of spore transmission to vulnerable patients. B. Transfer spreads infection risk to another area and does not replace isolation. C. Spores persist on surfaces and need sporicidal cleaning, not routine detergent. D. Antibiotics do not prevent transmission and can increase C. difficile risk.
pearl: Suspected C. difficile diarrhoea needs prompt isolation, ideally with dedicated toilet facilities, soap-and-water hand washing, gloves and aprons, and sporicidal cleaning.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile ↓ Diarrhoea spreads spores ↓ Spores persist on surfaces and hands ↓ Isolation and hand hygiene per infection-control procedures
exam_trap: C, routine detergent cleaning once daily — it is the normal standard, but C. difficile spores survive detergent and need sporicidal cleaning.
takeaway: C. difficile: isolate, wash hands with soap and water, clean with sporicidal agents.

stem: When should a patient's blood sample normally be labelled?

options.A: Before sampling, using pre-printed labels prepared at the start of the shift
options.B: At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
options.C: At the nurses' station after all of the patient's samples are taken
options.D: In the laboratory reception using the request form
options.E: On return to the ward office, using the printed patient list for the bay

correct_answer: B. At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
why_correct: Correct identification and contemporaneous labelling reduce the risk of sample misidentification.
why_wrong: A. Pre-labelling before seeing the patient is unsafe and increases wrong-blood-in-tube errors. C. Delayed labelling away from the patient increases misidentification risk. D. Samples must be labelled at collection, not later by the laboratory. E. Labelling must occur at the bedside, not later away from the patient.
pearl: Wrong-blood-in-tube errors can cause fatal transfusion reactions; positively identify the patient and label each sample at the bedside straight after taking it, never in advance.
thinking: Blood sample taken ↓ Risk of misidentification ↓ Labelling must link sample to patient at collection ↓ At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
exam_trap: A, pre-printed labels prepared before sampling — it feels efficient, but pre-labelling is a classic cause of wrong-blood-in-tube errors.
takeaway: Label samples at the bedside after positive patient identification, never in advance.

stem:
A study reports a risk ratio of 1.4 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.1–1.8.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The confidence interval shows that 95% of patients have the disease
options.B: The reported confidence interval does not include 1
options.C: The result cannot be interpreted without knowing the mean
options.E: The risk ratio must equal exactly 1.4 in every patient

correct_answer: B. The reported confidence interval does not include 1
why_correct: For a ratio measure such as a risk ratio, 1 represents no relative difference. The reported interval lies entirely above 1.
why_wrong: A. The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimate, not the proportion of patients with disease. C. The risk ratio can be interpreted without a mean. D. A statistically significant association does not prove causation. E. The risk ratio is a group summary estimate and does not apply exactly to each individual.
pearl: For a risk ratio, 1 means no difference; an interval lying entirely above 1 indicates a statistically significant increase in risk, but an association still does not prove causation.
thinking: Risk ratio is a ratio measure ↓ No effect = 1 ↓ 95% CI 1.1–1.8 lies entirely above 1 ↓ The confidence interval does not include 1
exam_trap: D, the study proves causation — a significant result is tempting to over-read, but excluding 1 shows only a statistically significant association.
takeaway: Ratio confidence interval entirely above 1: significant increase in risk, not proof of causation.

stem:
A treatment reduces the risk of an event from 4% to 2%.

What is the relative risk reduction?
why_correct: Relative risk = 2% ÷ 4% = 0.5, so relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.5 = 50%.
why_wrong: A. 2% is the absolute risk reduction, not the relative risk reduction. B. 25% does not correspond to the calculation (4 − 2) ÷ 4. D. 75% would require the risk to fall from 4% to 1%. E. 100% would require the risk to fall to zero.
pearl: Relative risk reduction is the absolute risk reduction divided by the baseline risk; it sounds impressive but says nothing about how common the event was to begin with.
thinking: Relative risk reduction compares the reduction with the original risk.
exam_trap: A, 2% — this is the absolute risk reduction (4% minus 2%), the figure candidates calculate first; the relative reduction expresses that 2% as a share of the 4% baseline.
takeaway: RRR = (control risk − treated risk) ÷ control risk; ARR is the simple difference.

stem:
A treatment reduces the risk of an event from 4% to 2%.

What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction = 4% − 2% = 2 percentage points.
why_wrong: A. 0.5% does not reflect the difference between 4% and 2%. B. 1% underestimates the 2-percentage-point difference. D. 4% is the baseline risk, not the reduction. E. 50% is the relative risk reduction, not the absolute reduction.
pearl: Absolute risk reduction is the plain difference in event rates between groups, and its reciprocal gives the number needed to treat, so here 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50.
thinking: Baseline risk 4%, treated risk 2% ↓ Question asks for the absolute, not relative, change ↓ Subtract: 4% − 2% ↓ ARR = 2%
exam_trap: E, 50% — it is the striking number from the same data, but it is the relative risk reduction (2% ÷ 4%), not the absolute difference in risk.
takeaway: ARR is a subtraction; RRR is a division by the baseline risk.

stem:
A highly specific screening test is applied to a population in which the target disease is extremely rare.

What problem can occur?

options.A: Sensitivity of the test falls to a low level
options.B: Most negative results will be false negatives
options.C: Specificity falls because there are few cases
options.D: Most positive results may be false positives
options.E: The test will miss most cases of the disease

correct_answer: D. Most positive results may be false positives
why_correct: When disease prevalence is very low, even a highly specific test can produce more false-positive than true-positive results among those testing positive.
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity is not altered by disease prevalence. B. In a low-prevalence population negative predictive value is high, so most negatives are true negatives. C. Specificity is not altered by disease prevalence. E. Missing cases depends on sensitivity, which is not changed by low prevalence.
pearl: Predictive values depend on prevalence: in a rare disease even a very specific test gives a low positive predictive value, because false positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives.
thinking: Disease extremely rare ↓ Almost everyone tested is disease-free ↓ A small false-positive rate across many healthy people still gives many false positives ↓ Most positive results may be false positives
exam_trap: E, the test will miss most cases — tempting because rarity feels like a detection problem, but missing cases reflects sensitivity, which prevalence does not change.
takeaway: Low prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV; sensitivity and specificity stay fixed.

stem:
In a clinical trial, the person recruiting a participant cannot predict which treatment group the participant will enter.

What methodological feature does this describe?
why_correct: Allocation concealment prevents recruiters from knowing the upcoming allocation and reduces selection bias at enrolment.
why_wrong: B. Intention-to-treat refers to analysing participants in their allocated groups. C. External validity concerns generalisability of results to other populations. D. Blinding of outcome assessment concerns those assessing outcomes, not recruitment. E. Loss to follow-up refers to participants who drop out after enrolment.
pearl: Allocation concealment protects the randomisation sequence until the moment of enrolment, preventing selection bias; it is achievable in every trial, unlike blinding.
thinking: Recruiter cannot predict the next allocation ↓ This applies at enrolment, before treatment starts ↓ Protects the random sequence from selection bias ↓ Allocation concealment
exam_trap: D, blinding of outcome assessment — both hide group information, but blinding applies after allocation to assessors, whereas concealment hides the sequence from recruiters before enrolment.
takeaway: Concealment hides the next allocation before enrolment; blinding hides the group afterwards.

stem:
In a clinical trial, 30% of participants in one treatment group cannot be contacted for final outcome assessment.

What is a major concern?
why_correct: Differential or substantial loss to follow-up can distort the observed treatment effect.
why_wrong: A. Recall bias concerns inaccurate recall of past exposure, not loss to follow-up. B. Specificity is a diagnostic test property unrelated to loss to follow-up. C. Loss to follow-up can introduce, not eliminate, bias and imbalance. E. Loss to follow-up does not mean randomisation failed.
pearl: Substantial or unequal loss to follow-up causes attrition bias, because those who drop out often differ in prognosis from those who remain; intention-to-treat and sensitivity analyses help limit it.
thinking: 30% of one arm lost before final assessment ↓ Dropouts may differ systematically from completers ↓ Remaining groups are no longer comparable ↓ Attrition bias
exam_trap: E, guaranteed randomisation failure — loss to follow-up happens after randomisation, so allocation itself was not compromised; the problem is a biased comparison of those left.
takeaway: Large or unequal dropout after randomisation means attrition bias.

stem:
A study finds that people who drink more coffee have higher rates of a particular disease. However, smokers are also more likely to drink large amounts of coffee and smoking is associated with the disease.

What is smoking in this example?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both the exposure and outcome and may distort the apparent association between coffee consumption and disease.
why_wrong: B. A confidence interval describes statistical uncertainty. C. Randomisation is a method of allocation, not a variable in this association. D. A placebo is an inactive comparator used in trials. E. The outcome is the disease, not smoking.
pearl: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome and is not on the causal pathway between them; it can create or hide an apparent association.
thinking: Coffee drinking associated with disease ↓ Smoking linked to coffee drinking ↓ Smoking independently linked to the disease ↓ Smoking is a confounder
exam_trap: E, the outcome — smoking is closely tied to the disease, but the outcome measured is the disease itself; smoking is a third variable distorting the coffee–disease link.
takeaway: Associated with both exposure and outcome, and not on the causal path: confounder.

stem:
An observational study finds an association between two variables.

Which conclusion is justified?

options.A: Confounding has been excluded by the study design
options.B: It may be causal, but other explanations must be considered
options.C: The association demonstrates a causal relationship
options.D: Reverse causation can be excluded by the statistical analysis
options.E: The association proves that the exposure preceded the outcome

correct_answer: B. It may be causal, but other explanations must be considered
why_correct: Observational associations can result from causation, confounding, bias or chance.
why_wrong: A. Confounding is a key limitation of observational studies and cannot be excluded by design. C. Association does not prove causation. D. Reverse causation remains possible in observational data. E. An association alone does not establish temporal sequence.
pearl: Any observed association can reflect chance, bias, confounding, reverse causation or true causation; observational designs cannot exclude the alternatives, so causal claims need cautious, cumulative evidence.
thinking: Observational design, not randomised ↓ Exposure was not allocated by investigators ↓ Chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation remain possible ↓ May be causal, but alternatives must be considered
exam_trap: C, the association demonstrates causality — tempting when the link is strong, but without randomisation confounding and bias cannot be excluded, so association never proves cause.
takeaway: Association is not causation; consider chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation.

stem:
Researchers assess blood pressure and body weight in 10,000 adults during a single health survey.

What does this study primarily measure?

options.E: Prevalence at a point or period in time

correct_answer: E. Prevalence at a point or period in time
why_correct: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at a particular time rather than following participants prospectively.
why_wrong: A. Effectiveness of an intervention requires an interventional design such as a trial. B. Incidence requires follow-up over time to identify new cases. C. Relative risk requires following exposed and unexposed groups over time, as in a cohort study. D. Survival requires a cohort followed over time.
pearl: A cross-sectional study is a single snapshot of exposure and outcome together, so it measures prevalence; it cannot establish incidence or which came first.
thinking: Single survey of 10,000 adults ↓ Measurements taken once, with no follow-up ↓ Cross-sectional design ↓ Measures prevalence at a point or period
exam_trap: B, incidence of hypertension over time — blood pressure is measured, but incidence needs a disease-free group followed for new cases; one survey only captures existing cases.
takeaway: One-off snapshot survey means cross-sectional study, which measures prevalence.

stem:
A population contains 10,000 people who are disease-free at the beginning of a year. During that year, 100 develop the disease.

What does the 100 new cases represent?
why_correct: Incidence describes new cases arising in a population over a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Specificity is a diagnostic test measure. C. Positive predictive value describes the probability of disease after a positive test. D. Prevalence includes all existing cases, not only new cases. E. Sensitivity is a diagnostic test measure.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases arising in a population at risk over a defined period; here 100 new cases among 10,000 disease-free people in a year gives an incidence of 1% per year.
thinking: 10,000 people disease-free at the start ↓ Followed for one year ↓ 100 new cases develop ↓ New cases over time define incidence
exam_trap: D, prevalence — candidates mix the two, but prevalence counts all existing cases at a time point; here the group started disease-free and only new cases were counted.
takeaway: New cases over time = incidence; all existing cases at a time = prevalence.

stem:
A survey finds that 300 of 10,000 adults currently have a particular condition.

What measure is being estimated?
why_correct: Prevalence describes the proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or period.
why_wrong: B. Incidence measures new cases over a period, not existing cases. C. A hazard ratio compares event rates over time between groups. D. NNT describes how many patients need treating to prevent one outcome. E. Relative risk compares risk between exposed and unexposed groups.
pearl: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time; it reflects both how often the condition arises and how long it lasts.
thinking: Survey at one time point ↓ Counts adults who currently have the condition ↓ Existing cases ÷ population ↓ Prevalence
exam_trap: B, incidence — tempting as the other basic frequency measure, but incidence requires counting new cases over a period of follow-up, not current cases in a survey.
takeaway: Current cases ÷ population at a point in time = prevalence.

stem:
During an outbreak, 100 people develop a particular infection and 5 of them die from it.

Which measure describes the proportion of affected patients who die from the disease?
why_correct: Case fatality describes deaths among people who have the disease.
why_wrong: B. Cumulative incidence measures new cases in an at-risk population over a period. C. Population mortality rate uses the whole population as the denominator, not only those with the disease. D. Attack rate is the proportion of an exposed population who develop the disease. E. Period prevalence measures existing cases in a population over a period.
pearl: Case fatality uses only those with the disease as the denominator, so it reflects disease severity; a mortality rate uses the whole population at risk.
thinking: 100 people develop the infection ↓ 5 of them die ↓ Denominator is affected people only ↓ Case-fatality proportion (5%)
exam_trap: C, population mortality rate — it also counts deaths, but its denominator is the whole population, not just those who developed the infection.
takeaway: Deaths among the diseased = case fatality; deaths among the population = mortality rate.

stem:
A footballer changes direction suddenly, hears a pop in the knee and develops rapid swelling.

Which injury should be considered?
why_correct: A twisting injury with a popping sensation and rapid haemarthrosis is characteristic of ACL injury.
why_wrong: A. Frozen shoulder affects the shoulder joint. B. Gout causes an acute inflammatory arthritis, not a traumatic pop with immediate swelling. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a wrist nerve entrapment unrelated to knee injury. E. Achilles tendinopathy causes heel pain, not acute knee haemarthrosis.
pearl: Rapid knee swelling within hours of injury suggests haemarthrosis, most often from an ACL tear; a pop during a twisting, pivoting movement is the classic history.
thinking: Sudden change of direction ↓ Audible pop in the knee ↓ Rapid swelling suggests haemarthrosis ↓ ACL injury
exam_trap: B, gout — the only other option causing an acutely swollen joint, but gout is inflammatory, not traumatic, and does not follow a pop with immediate swelling.
takeaway: Twist, pop and rapid swelling of the knee: think ACL rupture.

stem:
A patient develops shoulder weakness after lifting a heavy object. Passive shoulder movement is relatively preserved, but active abduction is markedly impaired.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Significant weakness of active movement with relatively preserved passive movement suggests a rotator cuff problem.
why_wrong: A. Cervical myelopathy causes progressive upper motor neurone signs, not acute weakness after lifting. B. Gout typically causes acute painful swelling, not isolated loss of active abduction after lifting. C. Frozen shoulder restricts both active and passive movement, particularly external rotation. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand, not shoulder movement.
pearl: Weak active abduction with preserved passive range points to a rotator cuff tear; frozen shoulder restricts both active and passive movement, especially external rotation.
thinking: Weakness after heavy lifting ↓ Passive movement relatively preserved ↓ Active abduction markedly impaired ↓ Failure of the tendon unit ↓ Rotator cuff tear
exam_trap: C, frozen shoulder — a common shoulder diagnosis, but it limits passive as well as active movement, whereas here passive range is preserved.
takeaway: Active lost, passive preserved: cuff tear; both lost: frozen shoulder.

stem:
A man with previous gout develops acute pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after a period of heavy alcohol consumption.

What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute podagra is a classic presentation of gout. Alcohol can precipitate attacks.
why_wrong: A. Septic bursitis affects a bursa, typically the olecranon or prepatellar, not the first MTP joint itself. B. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, not acute first MTP involvement after alcohol. D. Osteoporosis causes fragility fractures, not acute joint inflammation. E. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, not acute toe pain.
pearl: A hot swollen joint should not automatically be assumed to be gout; septic arthritis may need exclusion.
thinking: Previous history of gout ↓ Acute painful swelling of the first MTP joint ↓ Triggered by heavy alcohol intake ↓ Gout
exam_trap: A, septic bursitis — infection must be kept in mind with any hot swollen area, but septic bursitis affects bursae such as the olecranon, not the first MTP joint itself.
takeaway: Podagra after an alcohol binge in known gout is gout until shown otherwise.

stem:
A patient has persistent hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality but inappropriately concentrated urine. There is no obvious evidence of volume depletion or fluid overload.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: SIADH causes inappropriate antidiuretic hormone activity, leading to water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine and hypernatraemia, not hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. B. Diabetes mellitus does not typically cause euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. C. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia, not hyponatraemia. D. Adrenal insufficiency should be excluded but typically causes hypovolaemia and hyperkalaemia, so it does not best fit euvolaemic hyponatraemia.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine, once hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretics are excluded.
thinking: Hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality ↓ Urine inappropriately concentrated ↓ Patient clinically euvolaemic ↓ Inappropriate ADH activity ↓ SIADH
exam_trap: D, Addison's disease — it must be excluded before diagnosing SIADH, but it typically causes hypovolaemia and hyperkalaemia, not the euvolaemic picture described.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine: SIADH, after excluding mimics.

stem:
A patient with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe limb and back pain without another obvious cause.

What is this most consistent with?
why_correct: Acute severe pain caused by vaso-occlusion is a characteristic complication of sickle cell disease.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes gradual mechanical joint pain in older people, not sudden severe limb and back pain in sickle cell disease. C. Fibromyalgia causes chronic widespread pain and is not an acute severe presentation in sickle cell disease. D. Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis must be considered if there is fever or a single hot joint, but it is not the cause in every case and the stem gives no such features. E. Gout typically causes acute monoarthritis of a single joint such as the first MTP joint, not diffuse limb and back pain.
pearl: Vaso-occlusive crisis is the commonest acute presentation of sickle cell disease; give prompt, adequate analgesia, often opioids, and look for triggers such as infection or dehydration.
thinking: Known sickle cell disease ↓ Sudden severe limb and back pain ↓ No other obvious cause ↓ Vaso-occlusive pain episode
exam_trap: D, septic arthritis in every case — infection must be considered with fever or a single hot joint, but nothing here suggests it and diffuse pain fits vaso-occlusion.
takeaway: Sudden severe bone pain in sickle cell disease: vaso-occlusive crisis; treat pain fast.

stem:
A student with infectious mononucleosis asks when they can immediately return to contact sports.

What is the most important consideration?
why_correct: Splenomegaly can occur in infectious mononucleosis, creating a risk of splenic rupture with trauma.
why_wrong: A. Glaucoma is not a complication of infectious mononucleosis. B. Appendicitis is not a specific risk of glandular fever; the concern with contact sport is splenomegaly and rupture. C. Cataract is not a recognised complication of infectious mononucleosis. D. Renal stones are not associated with infectious mononucleosis.
pearl: Splenomegaly is common in glandular fever, so contact sport and heavy lifting are avoided for several weeks after the illness to reduce the risk of splenic rupture.
thinking: Infectious mononucleosis ↓ Spleen often enlarged and fragile ↓ Contact sport risks trauma to it ↓ Risk of splenic injury
exam_trap: B, risk of appendicitis — an abdominal surgical risk sounds plausible, but it is not linked to glandular fever; the danger with contact sport is splenic rupture.
takeaway: Glandular fever: avoid contact sport for weeks because of splenic rupture risk.

stem:
A teenager develops fever, headache, vomiting and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Oral antibiotics at home with a GP review in 48 hours' time
options.C: Observe at home and return if the rash continues to spread
options.D: Treat as a viral illness with antipyretics and fluids at home
options.E: Emergency treatment for suspected meningococcal disease

correct_answer: E. Emergency treatment for suspected meningococcal disease
why_correct: A rapidly progressive non-blanching rash with systemic illness is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment and escalation.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are unsafe because meningococcal disease can be fatal within hours. B. A dermatology referral would dangerously delay treatment of possible meningococcal septicaemia. C. Observing at home delays immediate antibiotics and escalation, which are time-critical. D. A rapidly spreading non-blanching rash with systemic illness must not be assumed to be viral.
pearl: Suspected meningococcal disease outside hospital needs parenteral benzylpenicillin as soon as possible, provided it does not delay transfer, with emergency hospital admission.
thinking: Fever, headache and vomiting ↓ Rapidly spreading non-blanching rash ↓ Meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise ↓ Emergency treatment for suspected meningococcal disease
exam_trap: D, treat as a viral illness — many febrile rashes are viral, but a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash with systemic illness must be treated as meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Fever plus a non-blanching rash: treat as meningococcal disease immediately.

stem:
A sexually active patient has a new sexual partner but has no symptoms.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Defer STI testing until symptoms develop to avoid false positives
options.B: Test for HIV alone as the main asymptomatic screening test
options.C: Offer a full STI screen without taking a sexual history
options.D: STI testing may be appropriate even without symptoms
options.E: Give empirical doxycycline as prophylaxis without testing

correct_answer: D. STI testing may be appropriate even without symptoms
why_correct: Many STIs are asymptomatic, so risk assessment and appropriate screening are important.
why_wrong: A. Many STIs, including chlamydia and gonorrhoea, are frequently asymptomatic, so waiting for symptoms misses infection. B. Screening should be guided by risk and usually includes chlamydia and gonorrhoea as well as blood-borne viruses. C. A sexual history is essential to assess risk and decide which tests are needed. E. Antibiotics are not given as prophylaxis without testing or a specific indication such as being a contact of a confirmed infection.
pearl: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are often asymptomatic, so a new partner is a reason to offer testing guided by a sexual history, including blood-borne virus tests such as HIV.
thinking: Sexually active with a new partner ↓ No symptoms ↓ Many STIs are asymptomatic ↓ Take a sexual history and offer appropriate testing
exam_trap: A, defer testing until symptoms develop — sounds proportionate, but many infections never cause symptoms yet still cause complications and onward transmission.
takeaway: No symptoms does not mean no STI: offer risk-based testing.

stem:
A young adult is diagnosed with uncomplicated genital chlamydia.

Which additional consideration is important?

options.E: No need to discuss sexual partners

why_correct: Management of chlamydia includes consideration of sexual partners to reduce ongoing transmission and reinfection.
why_wrong: B. Chemotherapy has no role in managing chlamydia. C. Appendicectomy is not indicated for uncomplicated genital chlamydia. D. Anticoagulation has no role in chlamydia management. E. Failing to discuss partners risks reinfection and onward transmission.
pearl: Every chlamydia diagnosis should trigger partner notification, testing and treatment of recent partners, and advice to avoid sex until both have completed treatment, to prevent reinfection.
thinking: Uncomplicated genital chlamydia diagnosed ↓ Partners often infected without symptoms ↓ Risk of reinfection and onward spread ↓ Partner notification and testing
exam_trap: E, no need to discuss sexual partners — may seem to respect privacy, but untreated partners lead to reinfection and transmission; partner notification is confidential and essential.
takeaway: Treat the patient and trace the partners in every STI.

stem:
A patient has urethral discharge and dysuria. Gonorrhoea is suspected.

Which service is particularly appropriate for definitive assessment and management?
why_correct: Suspected gonorrhoea requires appropriate testing and management through sexual health services, including consideration of antimicrobial resistance.
why_wrong: A. Routine urology is not the appropriate service for testing, treatment and partner notification in suspected gonorrhoea. C. Dermatology is not the appropriate service for suspected urethral gonorrhoea. D. General surgery has no role in managing urethral discharge from suspected gonorrhoea. E. Gastroenterology is unrelated to the assessment of urethral discharge.
pearl: Suspected gonorrhoea is best managed in a sexual health clinic, which offers culture for antimicrobial sensitivities, test of cure, partner notification and screening for other STIs.
thinking: Urethral discharge with dysuria ↓ Suspected gonorrhoea ↓ Needs culture, sensitivities, test of cure and partner notification ↓ Sexual health service
exam_trap: A, urology clinic — urinary symptoms point candidates towards urology, but routine urology does not provide STI testing, resistance-guided treatment or partner notification.
takeaway: Suspected gonorrhoea: refer to sexual health for testing, treatment and partner notification.

stem:
A woman with previous pelvic inflammatory disease develops difficulty conceiving.

Which complication of PID may explain this?
why_correct: PID can cause tubal inflammation and scarring, increasing the risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
why_wrong: B. Otitis externa is unrelated to PID or fertility. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome is unrelated to PID or fertility. D. Thyroid failure is not caused by PID, although thyroid dysfunction can affect fertility independently. E. Cataract is not a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease.
pearl: PID inflames and scars the fallopian tubes, raising the risk of tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain; the risk rises with each episode.
thinking: Previous pelvic inflammatory disease ↓ Inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes ↓ Impaired transport of egg and sperm ↓ Tubal damage causing subfertility
exam_trap: D, thyroid failure — thyroid dysfunction can independently affect fertility, but it is not a complication of PID; the link here is tubal scarring.
takeaway: PID damages the tubes: infertility and ectopic pregnancy follow.

stem:
A pregnant woman with severe persistent vomiting develops confusion and difficulty walking.

Which deficiency-related complication should be considered?
why_correct: Prolonged vomiting can cause thiamine deficiency and neurological complications, particularly if carbohydrate is given without appropriate vitamin replacement.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged vomiting does not cause calcium excess, and the picture fits Wernicke's encephalopathy. B. Vitamin D toxicity is not caused by vomiting; confusion and ataxia in hyperemesis suggest thiamine deficiency. C. Vitamin K excess is not a consequence of vomiting and does not cause confusion and ataxia. D. Iron overload does not result from hyperemesis and does not cause this neurological picture.
pearl: Prolonged vomiting in pregnancy can deplete thiamine and cause Wernicke encephalopathy; give thiamine before or with any glucose-containing fluids in a woman with persistent vomiting.
thinking: Pregnant with severe persistent vomiting ↓ Prolonged poor intake depletes thiamine ↓ Confusion and difficulty walking ↓ Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency
exam_trap: A, calcium excess — hypercalcaemia can cause confusion, but vomiting does not raise calcium; confusion with ataxia after prolonged vomiting points to thiamine deficiency.
takeaway: Hyperemesis with confusion or ataxia: think Wernicke and give thiamine.

stem:
A man with lower urinary tract symptoms has an abnormal, hard, irregular prostate on digital rectal examination.

What should this finding prompt?

options.A: Reassurance that this is normal ageing

correct_answer: C. Assessment for possible prostate cancer
why_correct: A hard or irregular prostate is a concerning finding requiring appropriate investigation for malignancy.
why_wrong: A. A hard, irregular prostate is not a feature of normal ageing or benign enlargement, which is typically smooth. B. Antifungal treatment has no role for a suspicious prostate finding. D. Cystitis does not cause a hard, irregular prostate, and the finding needs cancer assessment. E. Renal colic causes loin pain and does not explain an abnormal prostate on DRE.
pearl: A hard, irregular or nodular prostate on DRE warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral; benign enlargement typically feels smooth and firm.
thinking: Lower urinary tract symptoms ↓ DRE finds a hard, irregular prostate ↓ Benign enlargement feels smooth ↓ Suspicious for malignancy ↓ Assess for prostate cancer
exam_trap: A, reassurance that this is normal ageing — prostate enlargement with age is common, but benign enlargement is smooth; hardness and irregularity suggest cancer.
takeaway: Hard, irregular prostate on DRE: refer on a suspected cancer pathway.

stem:
A patient with known ureteric stone develops fever, rigors and systemic illness.

What is the important concern?

options.A: Uncomplicated renal colic needing analgesia alone
options.C: Simple lower UTI suitable for oral antibiotics at home
options.D: Infected obstructed kidney needing urgent urological assessment
options.E: Viral illness coinciding with renal colic

correct_answer: D. Infected obstructed kidney needing urgent urological assessment
why_correct: Infection behind urinary obstruction can progress rapidly to sepsis and requires urgent management.
why_wrong: A. Fever and rigors with a stone indicate infection behind obstruction, not simple renal colic. B. Appendicitis does not explain systemic sepsis in a patient with a known ureteric stone. C. Systemic illness with an obstructing stone needs urgent drainage assessment, not oral antibiotics at home. E. Fever and rigors with a known stone must be assumed to be infected obstruction rather than a coincidental virus.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: give antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent, as antibiotics alone cannot drain the infected system.
thinking: Known ureteric stone ↓ Fever, rigors and systemic illness ↓ Infection behind an obstruction ↓ High risk of sepsis ↓ Infected obstructed kidney needing urgent urology
exam_trap: A, uncomplicated renal colic needing analgesia — the stone fits colic, but fever and rigors mean infection behind obstruction, which needs urgent drainage.
takeaway: Stone plus fever means infected obstructed kidney: decompress urgently.

stem:
An older man presents with acute painful inability to pass urine and a palpable, distended bladder.

What is the immediate management priority?

options.A: Tamsulosin and review in a week without catheterisation
options.B: Fluid restriction and oral analgesia with later review
options.C: Urgent CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder first
options.E: Warm bath and await spontaneous voiding

correct_answer: D. Bladder decompression with urinary catheterisation
why_correct: Acute urinary retention requires prompt bladder drainage and subsequent assessment of the underlying cause.
why_wrong: A. Alpha-blockers may support a later trial without catheter but do not relieve acute retention. B. Fluid restriction does not relieve acute retention and delays definitive treatment. C. Imaging is not part of immediate management and delays bladder drainage. E. Waiting prolongs pain and risks bladder and renal damage.
pearl: Acute urinary retention is relieved by urethral catheterisation with the residual volume recorded; an alpha-blocker may then be started before a trial without catheter.
thinking: Older man unable to pass urine ↓ Painful, palpable distended bladder ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Immediate bladder decompression by catheterisation
exam_trap: A, tamsulosin and review without catheterisation — alpha-blockers do help, but only to support a later trial without catheter; they do not relieve acute retention.
takeaway: Painful acute retention: catheterise first, investigate the cause later.

stem:
A patient develops marked peripheral oedema and heavy proteinuria.

Which additional finding is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome?
why_correct: Heavy urinary protein loss can produce hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism is not part of nephrotic syndrome; urinary loss of binding proteins does not cause it. B. Neutropenia is not a feature of nephrotic syndrome. C. Hypercalcaemia is not characteristic of nephrotic syndrome; total calcium is often low because of hypoalbuminaemia. E. Polycythaemia is not a feature of nephrotic syndrome.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is the triad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, usually with hyperlipidaemia and a raised risk of thrombosis and infection.
thinking: Heavy proteinuria ↓ Marked peripheral oedema ↓ Urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin ↓ Hypoalbuminaemia completes the nephrotic triad
exam_trap: C, hypercalcaemia in every case — candidates may recall calcium changes, but total calcium is usually low in nephrotic syndrome because albumin is low.
takeaway: Nephrotic = heavy proteinuria + low albumin + oedema.

stem:
A urine dipstick repeatedly shows significant protein.

What is an appropriate next principle?

options.A: Diagnose nephrotic syndrome and start steroids
options.E: Attribute it to contamination and stop testing

correct_answer: B. Quantify and investigate the proteinuria
why_correct: Persistent proteinuria requires confirmation/quantification and assessment for an underlying renal or systemic cause.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome needs nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, so it cannot be diagnosed from a dipstick alone. C. Proteinuria is not an indication for antibiotics without evidence of infection. D. Persistent proteinuria can indicate significant renal disease and needs prompt quantification. E. Repeated proteinuria should not be dismissed as contamination; it needs quantification with an ACR or PCR.
pearl: Dipstick proteinuria should be quantified, usually with a urine albumin:creatinine ratio, alongside eGFR, testing for haematuria and blood pressure, to look for kidney disease.
thinking: Repeated significant dipstick protein ↓ Persistent, not a one-off finding ↓ Dipstick is only semi-quantitative ↓ Quantify with ACR or PCR and investigate the cause
exam_trap: A, diagnose nephrotic syndrome and start steroids — proteinuria is part of it, but nephrotic syndrome needs heavy quantified proteinuria plus hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
takeaway: Persistent dipstick proteinuria: quantify it and look for the cause.

stem:
A renal transplant recipient says they have stopped taking their immunosuppressant because they feel completely well.

What is the most important concern?
why_correct: Immunosuppressive medication is required to reduce the risk of immune-mediated rejection of the transplanted organ.
why_wrong: A. Cataract is not caused by stopping immunosuppression and does not develop within hours. B. Ankle sprain is unrelated to immunosuppressant non-adherence. C. Appendicitis is not a specific consequence of stopping immunosuppression. D. Migraine is not the important risk of stopping transplant immunosuppression.
pearl: Transplant recipients need lifelong immunosuppression; non-adherence is a major cause of rejection and graft loss, and rejection can be silent until kidney function falls.
thinking: Renal transplant recipient ↓ Stopped immunosuppression because feeling well ↓ Immune response against the graft unchecked ↓ Risk of transplant rejection
exam_trap: A, cataract within hours — long-term steroid use can cause cataracts, but that follows taking, not stopping, treatment and never develops within hours.
takeaway: Stopping transplant immunosuppression risks rejection, even when feeling well.

stem:
A patient receiving haemodialysis has an arteriovenous fistula in the forearm.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Use the fistula for routine blood samples given its high flow
options.B: Avoid unnecessary venepuncture and BP measurement in the fistula arm
options.C: Measure blood pressure on the fistula arm as it is easier
options.D: Check the fistula only at dialysis sessions
options.E: Apply a tight bandage over the fistula overnight to protect it

correct_answer: B. Avoid unnecessary venepuncture and BP measurement in the fistula arm
why_correct: Protecting the vascular access is important. Unnecessary compression or trauma can compromise the fistula.
why_wrong: A. The fistula should not be needled for samples except by trained dialysis staff as part of agreed practice. C. Blood pressure cuffs on the fistula arm can compress and damage the access, so this should be avoided. D. Patients should check the thrill daily, as changes may indicate stenosis or thrombosis. E. Prolonged tight pressure can cause fistula thrombosis.
pearl: An AV fistula is the patient's lifeline for dialysis: no blood pressure cuffs, venepuncture or cannulas in that arm, and avoid tight clothing or sustained pressure.
thinking: Haemodialysis via a forearm AV fistula ↓ Access is vulnerable to compression and trauma ↓ Damage risks thrombosis and loss of access ↓ Avoid venepuncture and BP cuffs in that arm
exam_trap: A, use the fistula for routine blood samples — its high flow makes sampling tempting, but needling outside dialysis practice risks damage, infection and thrombosis.
takeaway: Protect the fistula arm: no cuffs, no needles, no tight pressure.

stem:
A patient with an AV fistula reports that the usual buzzing sensation has disappeared and the arm looks swollen.

What should this raise concern for?

options.C: Dialysis steal syndrome from high flow

why_correct: A change or loss of the normal thrill/bruit, particularly with swelling, can indicate vascular access dysfunction and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Lymphoedema does not cause loss of the fistula thrill. B. Loss of a previously present thrill is not part of normal maturation, during which the thrill typically strengthens. C. Steal syndrome causes a cold, painful hand from high flow, not loss of the thrill. E. Cellulitis may cause redness and swelling but does not explain loss of the thrill.
pearl: A healthy fistula has a palpable thrill and audible bruit; loss of the thrill suggests thrombosis and needs urgent referral to the dialysis or vascular access team to salvage it.
thinking: AV fistula with usual buzzing ↓ Thrill has disappeared ↓ Arm now swollen ↓ Flow interrupted ↓ Fistula dysfunction or thrombosis
exam_trap: C, dialysis steal syndrome — a recognised fistula complication, but steal causes a cold, painful hand from excess flow, not loss of the thrill.
takeaway: Lost thrill in an AV fistula means thrombosis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A woman requires a urine sample for culture because of suspected urinary infection.

Which collection principle reduces contamination?

options.A: Collect a clean-catch midstream urine sample
options.B: Collect the first part of the stream into the pot
options.C: Transfer urine from a bedpan into the container
options.D: Leave the sample at room temperature overnight before sending
options.E: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after voiding

correct_answer: A. Collect a clean-catch midstream urine sample
why_correct: Appropriate collection technique helps reduce contamination and improves the reliability of urine culture results.
why_wrong: B. First-void urine contains more urethral and skin contaminants and is used for chlamydia testing, not culture. C. Bedpan urine is contaminated and unsuitable for culture. D. Delay at room temperature allows bacterial overgrowth, giving unreliable results. E. Urine from a toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
pearl: A clean-catch midstream sample avoids the first portion of urine, which washes out urethral and skin organisms; send it promptly or refrigerate it to prevent bacterial overgrowth.
thinking: Suspected UTI needing urine culture ↓ First part of the stream carries urethral and skin contaminants ↓ Midstream portion is cleaner ↓ Clean-catch midstream sample
exam_trap: B, collect the first part of the stream — first-void urine is right for chlamydia NAAT testing, but for culture it carries more contaminants.
takeaway: Culture needs midstream urine; chlamydia testing needs first-void urine.

stem:
A person with diabetes becomes sweaty, shaky and confused.

Which problem should be considered immediately?
why_correct: Sweating, tremor and confusion are common manifestations of hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: A. Anaemia causes fatigue and breathlessness rather than acute sweating, shakiness and confusion. C. Hyperthyroidism can cause tremor and sweating but develops gradually and is not the immediate concern in a person with diabetes. D. Hypercalcaemia causes thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion but not acute sweating and tremor. E. Hyperlipidaemia is asymptomatic and does not cause acute symptoms.
pearl: In any person with diabetes who becomes sweaty, shaky or confused, check capillary glucose immediately; treat with fast-acting glucose if conscious and able to swallow safely.
thinking: Person with diabetes ↓ Sweating and tremor are adrenergic warning signs ↓ Confusion suggests neuroglycopenia ↓ Hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise
exam_trap: C, hyperthyroidism — it causes tremor and sweating, but develops gradually; acute symptoms in a person with diabetes mean hypoglycaemia first.
takeaway: Diabetes plus acute sweating or confusion: check the glucose now.

stem:
An older woman develops sudden-onset back pain without significant trauma. She has lost height over several years.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Mechanical lumbar muscle strain after lifting
options.B: Acute pyelonephritis causing loin and back pain
options.E: Lumbar disc prolapse with nerve root compression

why_correct: Sudden back pain, height loss and low-trauma presentation in an older person can indicate vertebral fragility fracture.
why_wrong: A. Muscle strain does not explain progressive height loss in an older woman. B. Pyelonephritis causes fever and loin pain, not sudden back pain with height loss. D. Ankylosing spondylitis presents earlier in life with inflammatory back pain, not a new sudden pain in an older woman. E. No radicular symptoms are described, and disc prolapse does not explain height loss.
pearl: Vertebral fragility fractures often follow minimal or no trauma, and progressive height loss or kyphosis may be the only clue; they should prompt osteoporosis assessment.
thinking: Older woman with sudden back pain ↓ No significant trauma ↓ Progressive height loss over years ↓ Fragility fracture ↓ Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture
exam_trap: A, mechanical muscle strain — the commonest back pain, but it does not explain sudden pain without lifting or years of height loss in an older woman.
takeaway: Sudden back pain plus height loss in an older woman: vertebral fragility fracture.

stem:
A patient with severe hyperkalaemia undergoes an ECG.

Which ECG finding may occur?

options.A: Isolated prolonged QT interval as the classic finding
options.E: Persistent ST elevation confined to one coronary territory only

why_correct: Hyperkalaemia can cause tall, peaked T waves and, with increasing severity, progressive conduction abnormalities.
why_wrong: A. A prolonged QT interval is associated with hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia and drugs rather than being the classic sign of hyperkalaemia. C. Delta waves indicate ventricular pre-excitation such as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. D. Saw-tooth flutter waves indicate atrial flutter. E. ST elevation confined to one coronary territory suggests myocardial infarction, not hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Hyperkalaemia ECG changes progress from peaked T waves to flattened P waves, prolonged PR, broad QRS and a sine-wave pattern; ECG changes need urgent IV calcium for cardiac protection.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Altered ventricular repolarisation ↓ Earliest characteristic ECG change ↓ Tall peaked T waves
exam_trap: A, isolated prolonged QT — QT changes are classic for electrolyte disturbance, but prolonged QT points to hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia, not hyperkalaemia.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia: peaked T waves first, then broad QRS and sine waves.

stem:
A young woman with a very low body weight has a heart rate of 42/min and feels faint.

What is the most appropriate concern?

options.B: Medical instability from an eating disorder
options.D: Benign physiological sinus bradycardia of athletes
options.E: Postural hypotension from a recent viral illness

correct_answer: B. Medical instability from an eating disorder
why_correct: Severe bradycardia and presyncope in someone with significant nutritional restriction can indicate serious medical compromise and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Vasovagal syncope does not explain sustained profound bradycardia with very low body weight. C. Hypothyroidism typically causes weight gain and does not explain severe underweight. D. Bradycardia with presyncope and very low weight should not be assumed to be athletic physiology. E. A viral illness does not explain profound bradycardia with very low body weight.
pearl: In eating disorders, bradycardia, hypotension, syncope and electrolyte disturbance signal medical instability needing urgent medical assessment and possibly admission.
thinking: Very low body weight ↓ Heart rate 42/min ↓ Feels faint ↓ Cardiovascular compromise from starvation ↓ Medical instability from an eating disorder
exam_trap: D, benign athletic bradycardia — slow heart rates are common in fit young people, but presyncope with very low weight signals danger, not fitness.
takeaway: Low weight plus bradycardia and faintness: treat as medically unstable.

stem:
A patient with Parkinson's disease reports constipation, reduced sense of smell and sleep disturbance.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Loss of smell suggests an alternative diagnosis to Parkinson's
options.B: These symptoms are unrelated to the underlying Parkinson's disease
options.C: Parkinson's disease can cause significant non-motor symptoms
options.D: Parkinson's disease affects motor function alone, not other systems
options.E: Constipation points to a separate bowel disorder needing colonoscopy

correct_answer: C. Parkinson's disease can cause significant non-motor symptoms
why_correct: Parkinson's disease has both motor and non-motor manifestations, including autonomic, sleep and sensory symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Loss of smell is a recognised early feature of Parkinson's disease. B. Constipation, anosmia and sleep disturbance, including REM sleep behaviour disorder, are common in Parkinson's disease. D. Parkinson's disease also causes non-motor symptoms such as constipation, anosmia and sleep disturbance. E. Constipation is a common, often early, non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease and does not by itself need colonoscopy.
pearl: Non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, such as anosmia, constipation and REM sleep behaviour disorder, can precede motor signs by years and often affect quality of life most.
thinking: Known Parkinson's disease ↓ Constipation, reduced smell and sleep disturbance ↓ Autonomic, sensory and sleep systems involved ↓ Recognised non-motor symptoms
exam_trap: A, loss of smell suggests an alternative diagnosis — anosmia can have other causes, but in Parkinson's disease it is a common early feature.
takeaway: Parkinson's disease is more than a movement disorder: ask about non-motor symptoms.

stem:
A patient with peripheral arterial disease develops severe foot pain at rest, particularly at night, and has a non-healing toe ulcer.

What does this suggest?

options.A: Severe limb ischaemia needing urgent vascular assessment
options.C: Painful diabetic neuropathy needing neuropathic analgesia

correct_answer: A. Severe limb ischaemia needing urgent vascular assessment
why_correct: Rest pain and tissue loss indicate severe arterial insufficiency and require urgent vascular assessment.
why_wrong: B. Spinal stenosis causes exertional leg symptoms relieved by flexion, not rest pain with tissue loss. C. Neuropathy does not explain rest pain with a non-healing ulcer in known arterial disease. D. Cellulitis can coexist but does not explain ischaemic rest pain. E. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain on first steps, not rest pain with tissue loss.
pearl: Ischaemic rest pain, often worse at night and eased by hanging the leg down, or tissue loss means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
thinking: Known peripheral arterial disease ↓ Severe foot pain at rest, worse at night ↓ Non-healing toe ulcer ↓ Severe limb ischaemia ↓ Urgent vascular assessment
exam_trap: C, painful diabetic neuropathy — night-time foot pain fits neuropathy, but in known arterial disease rest pain with a non-healing ulcer means critical ischaemia.
takeaway: Rest pain or tissue loss in arterial disease: urgent vascular referral.

stem:
A patient has a bite wound over the knuckle sustained during a fight.

Why is this injury particularly important?

options.A: It is mainly a cosmetic concern requiring closure
options.B: Human bites carry a lower risk than animal bites
options.C: Primary suturing is needed to reduce infection
options.D: Human bites can cause serious infection and deep injury

correct_answer: D. Human bites can cause serious infection and deep injury
why_correct: Human bites, particularly over the hand, have a significant risk of infection and may involve tendons or joints.
why_wrong: A. A fight bite is a high-risk wound, not mainly cosmetic. B. Human bites, particularly to the hand, carry a high risk of infection. C. Bite wounds over the knuckle are usually left open; primary closure increases infection risk. E. Rabies prophylaxis is not indicated for a human bite in the UK.
pearl: A fight bite over the knuckle can penetrate the MCP joint or tendon sheath; it needs exploration, irrigation, antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav and often hand surgery review.
thinking: Wound over the knuckle from a fight ↓ Clenched fist striking teeth ↓ Mouth flora inoculated into joint or tendon ↓ Human bites cause serious infection and deep injury
exam_trap: C, primary suturing reduces infection — closing seems tidy, but suturing a contaminated hand bite traps bacteria; these wounds are usually left open.
takeaway: Knuckle wound after a punch is a fight bite: explore, irrigate, give antibiotics.

stem:
A patient accidentally splashes a strong chemical into one eye.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Apply an eye patch without irrigation
options.B: Immediate, copious irrigation of the eye
options.D: Cover the eye and wait for an ophthalmology appointment
options.E: Rub the eye to remove the chemical

correct_answer: B. Immediate, copious irrigation of the eye
why_correct: Chemical ocular exposure is an emergency. Immediate irrigation is the priority to reduce ongoing tissue damage.
why_wrong: A. Patching without irrigation traps the chemical against the eye. C. Steroid drops are not first-line and should not delay irrigation. D. Delaying irrigation allows ongoing chemical damage. E. Rubbing can worsen corneal injury and spread the chemical.
pearl: Chemical eye injury, especially from alkalis, needs immediate copious irrigation before anything else, continued until the pH is neutral, then urgent ophthalmology review.
thinking: Strong chemical splashed into the eye ↓ Damage continues while chemical remains ↓ Time-critical emergency ↓ Immediate, copious irrigation
exam_trap: D, cover the eye and await ophthalmology — specialist review is needed, but waiting allows continued chemical damage; irrigate first, then refer.
