A young woman notices a painless lump near the vaginal opening. It is located at the posterolateral aspect of the vaginal introitus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bartholin cysts occur near the posterolateral vaginal opening and may be painless unless infected.
why_wrong: A. Cervical polyps arise from the cervix and are seen at the os, not the introitus. B. Fibroids are uterine and not located at the introitus. C. Ovarian cysts are pelvic and not palpable at the vaginal introitus. D. Vulval carcinoma is uncommon in young women and usually presents as an ulcer or plaque rather than a smooth cyst at the gland site.
pearl: Bartholin glands lie at the posterolateral vaginal introitus; cysts are painless unless infected, and a new lump at this site in an older woman needs assessment to exclude cancer.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Painless lump near the vaginal opening ↓ Posterolateral introitus = Bartholin gland site ↓ E, Bartholin cyst
exam_trap: D, vulval carcinoma — tempting for any vulval lump, but it is uncommon in young women and usually presents as an ulcer or plaque.
takeaway: A painless posterolateral introital lump in a young woman is a Bartholin cyst.

stem:
A woman develops a very painful swelling near the vaginal opening with difficulty sitting and walking.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Infection of a Bartholin gland cyst can produce a very painful vulval swelling.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian cysts are pelvic and do not cause a vulval swelling. B. An uninfected Bartholin cyst is usually painless. C. Fibroids are uterine and do not cause a vulval swelling. D. A cervical polyp is not palpable near the vaginal opening and is not painful.
pearl: A Bartholin abscess is an acutely painful, tender swelling at the introitus that makes sitting and walking difficult; treat with drainage, for example Word catheter or marsupialisation.
thinking: Very painful swelling ↓ Near the vaginal opening ↓ Difficulty sitting and walking ↓ Infected Bartholin gland ↓ E, Bartholin abscess
exam_trap: B, uninfected Bartholin cyst — tempting as it occurs at the same site, but uninfected cysts are usually painless; severe pain means abscess.
takeaway: A very painful swelling at the vaginal opening is a Bartholin abscess.

stem:
A woman develops a persistent itchy or irregular pigmented lesion on the vulva.

What is the appropriate concern?

options.E: Recurrent bacterial cystitis with vulval irritation

correct_answer: D. Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer
why_correct: Persistent, atypical, pigmented or changing vulval lesions require assessment for neoplasia.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain rather than a persistent vulval lesion. B. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. C. Candidiasis causes itch and discharge but not a persistent irregular pigmented lesion, which needs assessment for neoplasia. E. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms, not a persistent irregular pigmented vulval lesion.
pearl: Any persistent, itchy, irregular or pigmented vulval lesion needs examination and biopsy to exclude VIN, vulval cancer or melanoma.
thinking: Persistent itchy vulval lesion ↓ Irregular and pigmented ↓ Possible premalignant or malignant change ↓ D, VIN or cancer
exam_trap: C, candidiasis with excoriation — tempting because of the itch, but thrush does not cause a persistent irregular pigmented lesion.
takeaway: A persistent irregular or pigmented vulval lesion needs assessment for neoplasia.

stem:
A pregnant woman is found to have hyperglycaemia during routine antenatal testing despite having no symptoms.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first recognised during pregnancy may represent gestational diabetes.
why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and is rare. B. Addison disease tends to cause hypoglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria with normal blood glucose. E. Hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy is most likely gestational diabetes, not necessarily type 1 diabetes.
pearl: Gestational diabetes is often asymptomatic and found on testing; it raises risks of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia and needs glucose testing after birth.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Hyperglycaemia on routine antenatal testing ↓ No symptoms ↓ First recognised in pregnancy ↓ C, gestational diabetes
exam_trap: E, type 1 diabetes only — tempting as a cause of hyperglycaemia, but asymptomatic hyperglycaemia found on antenatal testing most likely reflects gestational diabetes.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes.

stem:
A patient with a recent dental infection develops bilateral submandibular swelling, a raised tongue and difficulty swallowing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the floor of the mouth and submandibular spaces, often originating from a dental infection.
why_wrong: B. Viral pharyngitis causes sore throat but not bilateral submandibular swelling with tongue elevation after dental infection. C. Aphthous ulcers are small painful mucosal ulcers and do not cause bilateral submandibular swelling with an elevated tongue. D. A parotid tumour typically causes a slowly growing preauricular mass, not acute bilateral submandibular swelling. E. Gingivitis is a localised gum inflammation and does not spread to the submandibular spaces or elevate the tongue.
pearl: Ludwig's angina is bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually from a lower molar infection; airway protection takes priority alongside IV antibiotics.
thinking: Recent dental infection ↓ Bilateral submandibular swelling ↓ Raised tongue and dysphagia ↓ Spreading floor-of-mouth cellulitis ↓ Ludwig's angina
exam_trap: C, peritonsillar aphthous ulcer — 'peritonsillar' echoes quinsy, but aphthous ulcers are small mucosal lesions and do not cause bilateral submandibular swelling.
takeaway: Dental infection plus bilateral submandibular swelling and a raised tongue = Ludwig's angina.

stem:
A patient develops painful swelling in front of the ear that becomes worse when eating.

Which salivary gland is most likely affected?
why_correct: Parotid inflammation causes painful preauricular swelling, which can become more noticeable during eating.
why_wrong: A. The thyroid lies in the anterior neck, is not a salivary gland and does not swell in front of the ear with eating. B. The tonsil is lymphoid tissue in the oropharynx and does not cause preauricular swelling with eating. C. The submandibular area is below the jaw and a lymph node is not a salivary gland. E. The lacrimal gland lies in the superolateral orbit and produces tears, not saliva.
pearl: The parotid lies in front of the ear; parotid inflammation or duct obstruction causes preauricular swelling that is often worse with eating as saliva production rises.
thinking: Painful swelling in front of the ear ↓ Worse when eating ↓ Salivary gland stimulated by meals ↓ Preauricular site ↓ Parotid gland
exam_trap: C, submandibular lymph node — meal-related swelling suggests salivary disease, but the submandibular area is below the jaw and a lymph node is not a salivary gland.
takeaway: Preauricular salivary swelling = parotid; swelling below the jaw = submandibular.

stem:
A patient repeatedly develops painful swelling beneath the jaw during meals, which settles afterwards.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.E: Periapical dental abscess of a molar

why_correct: Meal-related swelling and pain are typical of obstruction of a salivary gland duct by a stone.
why_wrong: A. A parotid tumour usually presents as a persistent preauricular mass that does not fluctuate with meals. C. Thyroiditis causes anterior neck pain and swelling unrelated to eating. D. Reactive cervical lymphadenitis causes tender nodes that do not swell and settle with each meal. E. A dental abscess causes persistent localised pain and swelling that does not come and go with meals.
pearl: Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland; pain and swelling at mealtimes that settle afterwards is the classic history.
thinking: Swelling beneath the jaw ↓ Comes on with meals ↓ Settles afterwards ↓ Intermittent duct obstruction ↓ Submandibular salivary stone
exam_trap: D, reactive cervical lymphadenitis — tender nodes below the jaw are common, but they do not swell and settle with each meal.
takeaway: Meal-related swelling below the jaw = submandibular stone.

stem:
A healthy young adult develops a small, painful, shallow ulcer inside the mouth that resolves spontaneously.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Aphthous ulcers are common, painful, shallow oral ulcers that usually heal spontaneously.
why_wrong: A. Ludwig's angina is a spreading floor-of-mouth cellulitis with systemic illness, not a small self-limiting ulcer. B. A dental abscess causes toothache and localised swelling, not a shallow mucosal ulcer. C. Oral squamous cell carcinoma typically causes a persistent, non-healing ulcer, often in older smokers or drinkers, not one that resolves spontaneously. D. Herpes zoster causes a painful unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution rather than a single shallow ulcer.
pearl: Aphthous ulcers are small, painful, shallow and self-limiting; any mouth ulcer that fails to heal should prompt review for malignancy.
thinking: Healthy young adult ↓ Small, painful, shallow oral ulcer ↓ Heals by itself ↓ Aphthous ulcer
exam_trap: C, oral squamous cell carcinoma — candidates fear missing cancer, but malignant ulcers persist and do not resolve spontaneously.
takeaway: Painful, shallow and healing = aphthous; persistent = exclude cancer.

stem:
A patient has a persistent ulcer on the side of the tongue that has not healed after several weeks.

What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: A persistent non-healing oral ulcer, particularly on the lateral tongue, requires assessment for malignancy.
why_wrong: A. A salivary stone causes meal-related glandular swelling, not a non-healing ulcer on the tongue. B. Viral gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea and does not produce a persistent tongue ulcer. C. Aphthous ulcers usually heal within about two weeks, so persistence for several weeks should not be attributed to them without excluding malignancy. E. Otitis media is a middle-ear infection unrelated to a tongue ulcer.
pearl: An unexplained oral ulcer that persists beyond about three weeks warrants a suspected cancer referral; the lateral tongue is a classic site for squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Ulcer on the side of the tongue ↓ Not healed after several weeks ↓ Benign ulcers usually heal sooner ↓ Oral malignancy
exam_trap: C, aphthous ulcer only — aphthous ulcers are common, but they usually heal within a couple of weeks; persistence must not be attributed to them.
takeaway: A non-healing tongue ulcer is cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine testing suggests a urinary tract infection.

Why is treatment particularly important?

options.A: UTI in pregnancy usually resolves without treatment
options.B: Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
options.C: Untreated UTI commonly causes fetal neural tube defects
options.E: Pregnancy protects against urinary tract infection

correct_answer: B. Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
why_correct: Urinary infection during pregnancy can progress to upper urinary tract infection and requires appropriate assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. UTI in pregnancy should be treated, as untreated infection risks pyelonephritis and preterm labour. C. Neural tube defects relate to folate deficiency or first-trimester folate antagonists, not untreated UTI. D. Ovarian torsion is not a complication of urinary infection. E. Pregnancy increases rather than protects against urinary infection because of urinary stasis and ureteric dilatation.
pearl: Treat UTI in pregnancy promptly with an antibiotic suitable for pregnancy and send a urine culture; untreated infection can ascend to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm labour.
thinking: Pregnant woman with dysuria and frequency ↓ Urine test suggests UTI ↓ Urinary stasis and ureteric dilatation in pregnancy ↓ Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
exam_trap: A, UTI usually resolves without treatment — some uncomplicated UTIs settle outside pregnancy, but in pregnancy treatment is needed because of the risk of ascending infection.
takeaway: UTI in pregnancy always needs treatment and a urine culture.

stem:
A pregnant woman with severe prolonged vomiting has poor oral intake and develops confusion and unsteadiness.

Which nutritional deficiency is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Prolonged vomiting and poor intake can cause thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes a bleeding tendency rather than confusion and unsteadiness. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum bleeding and poor wound healing, not acute confusion and ataxia. D. Iron deficiency causes anaemia and fatigue but does not explain acute confusion and ataxia suggestive of Wernicke encephalopathy. E. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not acute encephalopathy.
pearl: Wernicke encephalopathy can complicate severe vomiting in pregnancy; give thiamine before glucose-containing fluids in at-risk patients.
thinking: Pregnant with prolonged severe vomiting ↓ Poor oral intake ↓ Confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Wernicke encephalopathy ↓ Thiamine deficiency
exam_trap: D, iron deficiency only — common in pregnancy and causes fatigue, but it does not cause acute confusion and ataxia.
takeaway: Severe vomiting in pregnancy plus confusion or ataxia: think thiamine and Wernicke's.

stem:
A patient with sarcoidosis develops polyuria and thirst. Blood tests show hypercalcaemia.

What is the mechanism?

options.C: Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
options.D: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption in the small bowel
options.E: Increased calcitonin secretion by thyroid C cells

correct_answer: C. Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
why_correct: Activated macrophages within granulomas can increase conversion of vitamin D to its active form, increasing calcium absorption.
why_wrong: A. PTHrP is produced by some malignancies; in sarcoidosis PTH and PTHrP are suppressed, and hypercalcaemia is driven by calcitriol. B. Renal calcium wasting would lower serum calcium; hypercalciuria in sarcoidosis is a consequence of increased absorption, not the cause of hypercalcaemia. D. Granulomatous calcitriol production increases rather than reduces intestinal calcium absorption. E. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium, and increased secretion would not cause hypercalcaemia.
pearl: Granuloma macrophages convert vitamin D to active calcitriol independently of PTH, so PTH is suppressed; sarcoid hypercalcaemia typically responds to corticosteroids.
thinking: Sarcoidosis ↓ Polyuria, thirst and hypercalcaemia ↓ Granulomas activate vitamin D ↓ More intestinal calcium absorption ↓ Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
exam_trap: A, PTHrP from granulomas — PTHrP is a familiar cause of hypercalcaemia, but it comes from malignancy; in sarcoidosis the driver is calcitriol.
takeaway: Sarcoid hypercalcaemia is driven by granuloma-derived calcitriol, with PTH suppressed.

stem:
A patient with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis presents with a persistent cough.

Which infection-control measure is particularly important?

options.D: No precautions until treatment is completed
options.E: Standard precautions are sufficient in all circumstances

why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate airborne/respiratory infection-control measures to reduce transmission.
why_wrong: A. Reverse isolation protects immunocompromised patients from infection and does not prevent onward spread of TB. C. Contact precautions alone do not prevent airborne transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. D. Patients with suspected infectious pulmonary TB should be isolated from the outset, not only after treatment. E. Standard precautions alone are insufficient for suspected infectious pulmonary TB, which requires airborne precautions.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs airborne precautions from the outset: a single room, with negative pressure where indicated, and respirator masks for staff.
thinking: Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Persistent cough ↓ Spread by the airborne route ↓ Appropriate respiratory isolation
exam_trap: E, standard precautions are sufficient — they cover routine care, but TB is airborne and needs respiratory isolation from the point of suspicion.
takeaway: Suspected infectious TB: isolate with airborne precautions straight away.

stem:
A patient with known sarcoidosis develops a painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Sarcoidosis can cause ocular inflammation, including uveitis.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes redness and discharge but not marked photophobia or blurred vision. C. Retinal detachment causes painless visual loss with floaters or a curtain effect, without a painful red eye. D. Cataract causes gradual painless visual loss without photophobia or a red eye, although it may complicate chronic uveitis. E. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and does not affect vision or cause photophobia.
pearl: Uveitis is a common eye manifestation of sarcoidosis; a painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Known sarcoidosis ↓ Painful red eye ↓ Photophobia and blurred vision ↓ Intraocular inflammation ↓ Uveitis
exam_trap: A, conjunctivitis only — the commonest red eye, but it does not cause marked photophobia or blurred vision.
takeaway: Painful red eye with photophobia in a systemic disease = uveitis.

stem:
A patient with multiple myeloma develops worsening renal function.

Which mechanism can contribute?
why_correct: Monoclonal light chains can cause renal injury, including cast nephropathy.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma causes anaemia with relatively reduced erythropoietin, and excess erythropoietin does not cause renal injury. B. Increased insulin secretion is not a feature of myeloma and does not cause renal impairment. D. Myeloma and its treatment tend to increase rather than reduce uric acid, and reduced uric acid would not damage the kidneys. E. Bile production has no role in myeloma-related renal impairment.
pearl: In myeloma, free light chains form casts that block the tubules (cast nephropathy); hypercalcaemia, dehydration and nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs worsen renal injury.
thinking: Multiple myeloma ↓ Worsening renal function ↓ Excess monoclonal light chains filtered ↓ Tubular cast formation and toxicity ↓ Light-chain nephrotoxicity
exam_trap: D, reduced uric acid production — urate does matter in myeloma, but it tends to rise, and reduced uric acid would not damage the kidneys.
takeaway: Renal injury in myeloma is mainly light-chain cast nephropathy.

stem:
An otherwise well older adult is found to have a monoclonal paraprotein during investigation of abnormal blood tests. There is no anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia or bone disease.

Which condition may explain this finding?

options.A: Polyclonal rise from chronic liver disease

correct_answer: B. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
why_correct: MGUS is characterised by a monoclonal protein without the clinical features of symptomatic plasma-cell malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Chronic liver disease causes a polyclonal rise in immunoglobulins, not a monoclonal paraprotein. C. Acute leukaemia presents with cytopenias and blasts, not an isolated paraprotein in a well person. D. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia due to marrow failure and is not associated with a paraprotein. E. Haemophilia is an inherited clotting-factor deficiency and does not produce a monoclonal paraprotein.
pearl: MGUS is a paraprotein without myeloma-defining features (CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions); it needs monitoring because of a small ongoing risk of progression.
thinking: Otherwise well older adult ↓ Monoclonal paraprotein found ↓ No CRAB features ↓ Not symptomatic myeloma ↓ Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
exam_trap: A, polyclonal rise from chronic liver disease — raised immunoglobulins are common, but liver disease causes a polyclonal rise, not a monoclonal band.
takeaway: Paraprotein without CRAB features in a well patient = MGUS; monitor it.

stem:
A patient with known lymphoma reports unusual pain in an enlarged lymph node shortly after drinking alcohol.

What diagnosis is classically associated with this finding?
why_correct: Alcohol-induced pain in affected lymph nodes is an uncommon but classically described feature of Hodgkin lymphoma.
why_wrong: B. Multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating disease and does not involve lymph node pain. C. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease and does not cause alcohol-induced lymph node pain. D. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis, not lymph node pain after alcohol. E. Ulcerative colitis causes bloody diarrhoea and is not associated with alcohol-induced nodal pain.
pearl: Alcohol-induced lymph node pain is rare but highly characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma; B symptoms and pruritus are other recognised features.
thinking: Known lymphoma ↓ Enlarged lymph node ↓ Pain after drinking alcohol ↓ Uncommon but classic sign ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: D, gout — alcohol famously triggers gout attacks, but gout affects joints, not lymph nodes.
takeaway: Lymph node pain after alcohol is the classic Hodgkin clue.

stem:
A healthy adult develops unilateral calf swelling after a long-haul flight.

Which factor has increased the risk of venous thromboembolism?
why_correct: Prolonged immobility causes venous stasis and increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.
why_wrong: B. Exercise improves venous return and does not increase VTE risk. C. Short sleep alone is not a recognised VTE risk factor; the relevant factor is immobility during the flight. D. Mild seasonal rhinitis does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism. E. Dietary calcium intake is not a risk factor for venous thromboembolism.
pearl: Long-haul travel raises VTE risk mainly through immobility and venous stasis (Virchow's triad); unilateral calf swelling afterwards warrants assessment for DVT.
thinking: Healthy adult ↓ Long-haul flight ↓ Prolonged sitting causes venous stasis ↓ Unilateral calf swelling suggests DVT ↓ Prolonged immobility
exam_trap: C, short sleep alone — disrupted sleep is common on flights, but it is not a VTE risk factor; immobility is.
takeaway: Long flights raise VTE risk through immobility and venous stasis.

stem:
A patient develops a tender, erythematous cord along a superficial vein in the leg.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Cellulitis of the lower leg skin
options.D: Acute limb ischaemia from arterial embolism

why_correct: A painful, palpable superficial venous cord with local inflammation is characteristic of superficial thrombophlebitis.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute inflammatory joint pain, not a linear cord along a vein. B. Cellulitis causes diffuse spreading erythema rather than a tender cord following the course of a superficial vein. D. Arterial embolism causes an acutely cold, pale, pulseless limb rather than a tender red venous cord. E. Chronic osteomyelitis is a bone infection with deep pain and sinuses, not a superficial venous cord.
pearl: Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender red cord along a superficial vein; consider ultrasound, as it can coexist with or extend into deep vein thrombosis.
thinking: Tender, erythematous area ↓ Palpable linear cord ↓ Follows a superficial vein ↓ Superficial thrombophlebitis
exam_trap: B, cellulitis of the lower leg — both cause red tender skin, but cellulitis spreads diffusely rather than following the line of a superficial vein.
takeaway: A tender red cord along a superficial vein = superficial thrombophlebitis.

stem:
A patient with chronic venous disease develops bilateral lower-leg swelling that is worse towards the end of the day and improves with elevation.

Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic venous insufficiency causes venous hypertension, often producing dependent oedema that improves with elevation.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome can cause oedema but is not the explanation in every case, and the history points to chronic venous disease. B. Acute lymphatic obstruction is uncommon, usually unilateral and does not characteristically improve with elevation in a patient with venous disease. C. Arterial embolism causes an acutely ischaemic limb, not bilateral dependent oedema. E. Hypoglycaemia does not cause leg oedema.
pearl: Venous oedema is dependent: worse at the end of the day and better with leg elevation; skin changes such as haemosiderin staining reflect sustained venous hypertension.
thinking: Chronic venous disease ↓ Bilateral leg swelling ↓ Worse by evening, better with elevation ↓ Gravity-dependent venous pressure ↓ Venous hypertension
exam_trap: A, nephrotic syndrome in every case — it does cause bilateral oedema, but 'every case' is wrong and the history points to venous disease.
takeaway: Dependent oedema relieved by elevation in venous disease = venous hypertension.

stem:
A patient develops chronic swelling of one leg. The swelling is persistent and the skin gradually becomes thickened.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent limb swelling with progressive skin thickening can occur with lymphatic dysfunction.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic causes acute loin-to-groin pain and does not cause leg swelling. C. Cellulitis is an acute infection with erythema and warmth, although recurrent episodes can complicate lymphoedema. D. An arterial ulcer is a painful punched-out ulcer in an ischaemic limb, not chronic swelling with skin thickening. E. Acute gout causes an acutely painful inflamed joint, not chronic limb swelling with skin thickening.
pearl: Lymphoedema causes chronic swelling with progressive skin thickening and fibrosis; it predisposes to recurrent cellulitis, and compression with good skin care is the mainstay.
thinking: Chronic swelling of one leg ↓ Persistent rather than acute ↓ Progressive skin thickening ↓ Impaired lymphatic drainage ↓ Lymphoedema
exam_trap: C, cellulitis only — swelling with skin change suggests infection, but cellulitis is acute with warmth and erythema; it complicates lymphoedema rather than explaining it.
takeaway: Chronic limb swelling with thickened skin = lymphoedema; watch for cellulitis.

stem:
A patient with long-standing dysphagia to solids and liquids frequently wakes at night coughing after bringing up undigested food.

Which condition best explains this?
why_correct: Food retained in the oesophagus can be regurgitated, particularly when lying down.
why_wrong: B. Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain and does not cause dysphagia to both solids and liquids. C. Gallstone disease causes biliary colic and does not cause dysphagia or nocturnal regurgitation. D. Gastroenteritis is an acute illness with vomiting and diarrhoea, not long-standing dysphagia with regurgitation of undigested food. E. Acute pancreatitis causes acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, not chronic dysphagia.
pearl: Achalasia classically causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids, with regurgitation of undigested food and nocturnal cough; oesophageal manometry confirms the diagnosis.
thinking: Long-standing dysphagia ↓ Both solids and liquids ↓ Night-time regurgitation of undigested food ↓ Food retained in the oesophagus ↓ Achalasia
exam_trap: B, peptic ulcer disease — an upper GI diagnosis that tempts, but it causes epigastric pain, not dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation.
takeaway: Dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation = achalasia.

stem:
An elderly patient develops difficulty initiating swallowing and repeatedly coughs immediately after attempting to drink water.

Which type of swallowing problem is most likely?
why_correct: Difficulty initiating swallowing with coughing or choking immediately after swallowing suggests oropharyngeal dysfunction.
why_wrong: A. Oesophageal dysphagia causes a sensation of food sticking after swallowing has started, rather than difficulty initiating swallowing with immediate coughing. B. Irritable bowel syndrome affects bowel habit and does not cause swallowing difficulty. D. Biliary obstruction causes jaundice and does not affect swallowing. E. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting of undigested food and early satiety, not difficulty initiating swallowing.
pearl: Difficulty starting a swallow with immediate coughing or choking suggests oropharyngeal dysphagia, often neurological such as after stroke, with aspiration risk; arrange a swallow assessment.
thinking: Elderly patient ↓ Difficulty initiating swallowing ↓ Coughs immediately after drinking ↓ Problem in the oropharyngeal phase ↓ Oropharyngeal dysphagia
exam_trap: A, oesophageal dysphagia — a common type of dysphagia, but it causes food sticking after the swallow starts, not difficulty initiating it with immediate coughing.
takeaway: Trouble starting a swallow plus immediate coughing = oropharyngeal dysphagia.

stem:
A patient has recurrent dyspepsia and testing confirms Helicobacter pylori infection.

Why is eradication important?

options.A: It treats coeliac disease and gluten intolerance
options.B: It reduces the risk of peptic ulcer disease
options.C: It causes permanent immunity to gastroenteritis
options.D: It prevents all forms of colorectal adenocarcinoma
options.E: It prevents gallstones and acute cholecystitis

correct_answer: B. It reduces the risk of peptic ulcer disease
why_correct: H. pylori is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease and contributes to gastric malignancy risk.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is an immune response to gluten and is treated with a gluten-free diet, not H. pylori eradication. C. Eradication does not confer immunity to gastroenteritis. D. H. pylori eradication does not prevent colorectal cancer. E. H. pylori is not a cause of gallstones or cholecystitis, and eradication does not prevent them.
pearl: H. pylori eradication heals peptic ulcers and prevents their recurrence, and also lowers gastric cancer risk; test with a urea breath test or stool antigen test off PPIs.
thinking: Recurrent dyspepsia ↓ H. pylori confirmed ↓ H. pylori drives peptic ulceration ↓ Eradication reduces the risk of peptic ulcer disease
exam_trap: D, prevents all colorectal adenocarcinoma — H. pylori is linked to gastric cancer, which tempts, but eradication has no role in colorectal cancer.
takeaway: Eradicate H. pylori to treat and prevent peptic ulcer disease.

stem:
An older patient develops sudden painless passage of a large amount of fresh blood per rectum.

Which condition can cause this presentation?
why_correct: Diverticular haemorrhage can cause sudden, often painless, significant lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and does not cause large-volume rectal bleeding. B. An anal fissure causes painful defecation with small amounts of bright red blood, not painless large-volume bleeding. C. Haemorrhoids usually cause small-volume bright red bleeding on the paper or in the pan rather than sudden large-volume haemorrhage. D. Peptic ulcer bleeding usually causes haematemesis or melaena; it produces fresh rectal blood only with very brisk bleeding and haemodynamic compromise.
pearl: Diverticular bleeding is a common cause of sudden, painless, large-volume fresh rectal bleeding in older adults; it often stops spontaneously but can be brisk.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Sudden fresh rectal bleeding ↓ Painless and large volume ↓ Diverticular bleeding
exam_trap: C, haemorrhoids only — common and painless, but they usually cause small-volume bleeding on the paper or in the pan, not sudden large-volume haemorrhage.
takeaway: Painless, large-volume fresh rectal bleeding in older adults: think diverticula.

stem:
A patient develops jaundice, dark urine and pale stools with a predominantly cholestatic liver-test pattern.

Which process should be considered?
why_correct: Cholestasis results from impaired bile formation or flow and can cause conjugated jaundice, dark urine and pale stools.
why_wrong: A. A respiratory infection does not explain cholestatic jaundice with pale stools. C. Iron deficiency does not cause jaundice or cholestatic liver tests. D. Hyperthyroidism may mildly derange liver tests but does not cause cholestatic jaundice with pale stools. E. Isolated haemolysis causes unconjugated (acholuric) jaundice without bilirubinuria or pale stools, and liver tests are not cholestatic.
pearl: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the gut; a cholestatic pattern points to impaired bile flow, and ultrasound looks for duct dilatation.
thinking: Jaundice ↓ Dark urine and pale stools ↓ Cholestatic liver-test pattern ↓ Bile not reaching the gut ↓ Impaired bile flow
exam_trap: E, isolated haemolysis — it also causes jaundice, but it is unconjugated, without dark urine, pale stools or cholestatic liver tests.
takeaway: Dark urine, pale stools and cholestatic LFTs = impaired bile flow.

stem:
A patient with established cirrhosis becomes confused and disorientated after developing constipation.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Constipation can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy in patients with advanced liver disease.
why_wrong: A. Acute cystitis can occasionally precipitate confusion, but the history of cirrhosis and constipation points to hepatic encephalopathy. B. Migraine does not cause disorientation precipitated by constipation in cirrhosis. C. Tension pneumothorax causes acute respiratory distress and haemodynamic compromise, not gradual confusion after constipation. E. Acute appendicitis causes abdominal pain and fever rather than confusion precipitated by constipation in cirrhosis.
pearl: Hepatic encephalopathy is often precipitated by constipation, infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance or sedatives; treat the trigger and give lactulose.
thinking: Established cirrhosis ↓ New confusion and disorientation ↓ Constipation as precipitant ↓ More gut-derived toxins absorbed ↓ Hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: A, acute cystitis — infection can precipitate confusion, but cirrhosis plus constipation points directly to hepatic encephalopathy.
takeaway: Confusion in cirrhosis: think encephalopathy and look for the trigger.

stem:
A patient with established cirrhosis develops a new focal liver lesion on surveillance imaging.

Which malignancy is particularly important to consider?
why_correct: Cirrhosis is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, which is why at-risk patients undergo surveillance.
why_wrong: B. A colorectal adenoma is a colonic polyp and is not a focal liver lesion. C. Cholangiocarcinoma can occur in cirrhosis but is much less common than HCC and is not the explanation in every case. D. Renal cell carcinoma does not arise in the liver and is not linked to cirrhosis. E. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma arises in the pancreas and is not the target of cirrhosis surveillance.
pearl: Patients with cirrhosis are offered regular ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma; a new focal lesion needs further cross-sectional imaging.
thinking: Established cirrhosis ↓ Surveillance imaging ↓ New focal liver lesion ↓ Cirrhosis is the main HCC risk factor ↓ Hepatocellular carcinoma
exam_trap: C, cholangiocarcinoma in every case — it can arise in cirrhosis, but it is far less common than HCC, and 'every case' is never right.
takeaway: New liver lesion in cirrhosis: think hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem:
A patient develops an acute hepatitis-like illness after returning from an area with poor sanitation.

Which route commonly transmits hepatitis A?
why_correct: Hepatitis A is commonly transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water via the faeco-oral route.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is rarely transmitted by blood and is not spread only by needlestick injury. B. Sexual transmission of hepatitis A can occur, particularly among men who have sex with men, but it is not the only or principal route. C. Hepatitis A is not spread by inhalation. E. Hepatitis A is not transmitted by mosquitoes.
pearl: Hepatitis A spreads faeco-orally via contaminated food and water, causes acute self-limiting illness without chronic infection, and is vaccine-preventable for travellers.
thinking: Acute hepatitis-like illness ↓ Return from an area with poor sanitation ↓ Contaminated food or water ↓ Faeco-oral transmission
exam_trap: B, sexual transmission only — sexual spread of hepatitis A does occur, but it is not the only or principal route.
takeaway: Hepatitis A and E spread faeco-orally; hepatitis B and C are blood-borne.

stem:
A pregnant woman develops an acute hepatitis-like illness after recent travel to an area where hepatitis E is endemic.

Which infection should be considered?
why_correct: Hepatitis E is commonly acquired through contaminated food or water and can cause severe disease during pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. HIV does not typically cause an acute hepatitis-like illness related to travel to an area endemic for hepatitis E. B. Hepatitis C is blood-borne, usually asymptomatic when acute, and not linked to travel to an area endemic for an enterically spread virus. D. EBV can cause hepatitis but is not linked to travel to an endemic area or to severe disease in pregnancy in this way. E. CMV can cause hepatitis but is not associated with travel to an area endemic for hepatitis E.
pearl: Hepatitis E is mainly spread through contaminated food or water and is usually self-limiting, but it can cause severe disease and acute liver failure in pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Acute hepatitis-like illness ↓ Recent travel to a hepatitis E-endemic area ↓ Enteric virus, severe in pregnancy ↓ Hepatitis E
exam_trap: B, hepatitis C only — a familiar hepatitis virus, but it is blood-borne, usually silent when acute, and not linked to travel to an endemic area.
takeaway: Acute hepatitis in a pregnant traveller: think hepatitis E.

stem:
A patient with untreated appendicitis develops worsening generalised abdominal pain, guarding and systemic illness.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Progressive generalised peritonism and systemic deterioration can indicate perforation of an inflamed appendix.
why_wrong: A. Gastritis causes epigastric discomfort without generalised guarding or systemic deterioration. B. IBS does not cause generalised peritonism and systemic illness. D. Faecal loading and constipation do not cause generalised peritonism and systemic illness complicating appendicitis. E. Haemorrhoids cause rectal bleeding and perianal symptoms, not peritonitis.
pearl: Delay in treating appendicitis raises the risk of perforation; spreading pain, generalised guarding and systemic illness suggest peritonitis needing resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent surgery.
thinking: Untreated appendicitis ↓ Pain becomes generalised ↓ Guarding and systemic illness ↓ Peritoneal contamination ↓ Perforation with peritonitis
exam_trap: D, simple faecal loading with constipation — constipation commonly causes abdominal pain, but not generalised guarding and systemic illness.
takeaway: Appendicitis with spreading peritonism and systemic illness = perforation.

stem:
A patient develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Blood tests confirm acute pancreatitis, and imaging shows gallstones.

Which cause is most likely?
why_correct: Gallstones are one of the common causes of acute pancreatitis and can obstruct the biliary-pancreatic outflow.
why_wrong: A. Achalasia is an oesophageal motility disorder and does not cause pancreatitis. B. Haemorrhoids are unrelated to pancreatitis. C. Coeliac disease is not a common cause of acute pancreatitis, and imaging here shows gallstones. D. IBS is a functional disorder and does not cause acute pancreatitis.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK; abdominal ultrasound to look for gallstones is needed in every case.
thinking: Epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Acute pancreatitis confirmed ↓ Gallstones on imaging ↓ Stone obstructs pancreatic outflow ↓ Gallstone disease
exam_trap: C, coeliac disease — occasionally linked with pancreatitis, but it is not a common cause, and the imaging already shows gallstones.
takeaway: Pancreatitis plus gallstones on imaging = gallstone pancreatitis.

stem:
A patient with severe acute pancreatitis becomes increasingly breathless and hypoxic.

Which systemic complication can occur?
why_correct: Severe acute pancreatitis can trigger systemic inflammation and acute respiratory distress syndrome.
why_wrong: B. COPD is a chronic smoking-related lung disease and does not arise acutely from pancreatitis. C. Simple bronchitis does not explain progressive hypoxia in the context of severe systemic inflammation. D. Pulmonary TB is a chronic infection, not an acute complication of pancreatitis. E. Pleural effusion can occur in pancreatitis, but pleural infection alone does not account for the systemic inflammatory lung injury.
pearl: Severe pancreatitis can trigger a systemic inflammatory response causing ARDS, an important cause of early organ failure; a rising oxygen requirement needs critical care input.
thinking: Severe acute pancreatitis ↓ Systemic inflammatory response ↓ Increasing breathlessness and hypoxia ↓ Inflammatory lung injury ↓ Acute respiratory distress syndrome
exam_trap: E, pleural infection only — pleural effusion is recognised in pancreatitis, but infection alone does not explain systemic inflammatory lung injury.
takeaway: Worsening hypoxia in severe pancreatitis: think ARDS.

stem:
A patient has painless obstructive jaundice and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice can indicate malignant distal biliary obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Acute appendicitis causes right iliac fossa pain and does not cause obstructive jaundice. B. Biliary colic causes episodic pain without a palpable non-tender gallbladder or persistent jaundice. D. Common bile duct stones usually cause painful jaundice, and the gallbladder is typically fibrosed and not palpable (Courvoisier's law). E. Acute cholecystitis causes a tender gallbladder with fever and right upper-quadrant pain, not painless jaundice.
pearl: Courvoisier's law: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones and suggests malignancy, such as carcinoma of the pancreatic head.
thinking: Painless obstructive jaundice ↓ Palpable, non-tender gallbladder ↓ Stones unlikely (Courvoisier's law) ↓ Malignant biliary obstruction
exam_trap: D, obstructing common bile duct stone — the commonest cause of obstructive jaundice, but it is usually painful and the gallbladder is typically fibrosed and impalpable.
takeaway: Painless jaundice plus a palpable gallbladder: think pancreatic or biliary malignancy.

stem:
An adult develops intermittent cramping abdominal pain and episodes of vomiting. Imaging demonstrates telescoping of one segment of bowel into another.

Which diagnosis is this?
why_correct: Intussusception occurs when one segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment.
why_wrong: B. Biliary colic is gallbladder pain and does not cause bowel telescoping. C. Volvulus is twisting of bowel around its mesentery, not telescoping of one segment into another. D. Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and does not cause bowel telescoping on imaging. E. Diverticulitis is inflammation of colonic diverticula and does not produce telescoping on imaging.
pearl: Adult intussusception usually has a pathological lead point, often a tumour, so it generally needs surgery and identification of the cause, unlike most childhood cases.
thinking: Intermittent cramping abdominal pain ↓ Episodes of vomiting ↓ Imaging shows bowel telescoping ↓ Intussusception
exam_trap: C, volvulus — another mechanical cause of obstruction, but it is twisting of bowel around its mesentery, not telescoping.
takeaway: Telescoping bowel = intussusception; in adults, look for a lead point.

stem:
A patient has a painful anal fissure in the posterior midline.

What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Most primary anal fissures occur in the posterior midline and are commonly associated with trauma from passing hard stool.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause painless bleeding and are not the cause of a painful fissure. C. Rectal prolapse causes protrusion of the rectum, not a painful posterior midline fissure. D. Colorectal cancer rarely presents as a posterior midline fissure and is not the cause in every case. E. Crohn disease is associated with atypical or lateral fissures rather than typical posterior midline ones, and is not the cause in every case.
pearl: Primary anal fissures are typically posterior midline and linked to passing hard stool; off-midline, multiple or non-healing fissures should prompt a search for secondary causes.
thinking: Painful anal fissure ↓ Posterior midline position ↓ Typical site for a primary fissure ↓ Linked to hard stool ↓ Idiopathic anal fissure
exam_trap: E, Crohn disease in every case — Crohn disease causes fissures, but these are typically lateral or atypical, and 'every case' is never right.
takeaway: Posterior midline fissure = primary; atypical site = look for a cause.

stem:
An older adult develops involuntary leakage of stool following previous obstetric anal sphincter injury.

Which condition is being described?
why_correct: Involuntary loss of stool is faecal incontinence, and sphincter injury is an important cause.
why_wrong: A. Constipation is infrequent or difficult passage of stool, not involuntary leakage. B. Steatorrhoea is fatty stool from malabsorption, not involuntary leakage. C. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. D. Tenesmus is a sensation of incomplete evacuation, not involuntary loss of stool.
pearl: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is an important cause of faecal incontinence that may present years later; ask directly, as patients often do not volunteer the symptom.
thinking: Previous obstetric anal sphincter injury ↓ Weakened sphincter ↓ Involuntary leakage of stool ↓ Faecal incontinence
exam_trap: D, persistent rectal tenesmus — both are rectal symptoms, but tenesmus is an urge to defecate with little stool, not involuntary leakage.
takeaway: Involuntary loss of stool is faecal incontinence; sphincter injury is a key cause.

stem:
An older woman develops persistent watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy appears macroscopically normal.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Microscopic colitis typically causes chronic watery diarrhoea despite a macroscopically normal colon; diagnosis requires histological assessment.
why_wrong: B. Ulcerative colitis usually causes bloody diarrhoea with visible mucosal inflammation at colonoscopy. C. Acute appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain, not persistent watery diarrhoea. D. Diverticulitis causes acute left iliac fossa pain and fever, not chronic watery diarrhoea with a normal colon. E. Colorectal cancer is usually visible at colonoscopy and is not the cause in every case of watery diarrhoea.
pearl: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal-looking colon, typically in older women; biopsies are needed, and drugs such as NSAIDs and PPIs are recognised triggers.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Persistent watery, non-bloody diarrhoea ↓ Macroscopically normal colonoscopy ↓ Inflammation visible only on histology ↓ Microscopic colitis
exam_trap: B, ulcerative colitis — the classic colitis, but it usually causes bloody diarrhoea with visible mucosal inflammation at colonoscopy.
takeaway: Watery diarrhoea with a normal-looking colon: take biopsies for microscopic colitis.

stem:
A patient taking regular NSAIDs develops melaena and a fall in haemoglobin.

Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: NSAIDs increase the risk of peptic ulceration and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes right iliac fossa pain and does not cause melaena. B. Coeliac disease can cause iron deficiency but does not typically cause melaena. C. IBS does not cause GI bleeding or a fall in haemoglobin. D. Biliary colic causes right upper-quadrant pain, not melaena with a haemoglobin drop.
pearl: Melaena suggests upper GI bleeding; in NSAID users a bleeding peptic ulcer is the leading cause and needs resuscitation, risk scoring and endoscopy.
thinking: Regular NSAID use ↓ Melaena ↓ Falling haemoglobin ↓ Upper GI bleed ↓ Bleeding peptic ulcer
exam_trap: B, untreated coeliac disease — it can cause iron-deficiency anaemia, but it does not typically cause melaena.
takeaway: NSAIDs plus melaena = bleeding peptic ulcer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A man has recurrent pelvic discomfort and urinary symptoms for several months. He has no fever or systemic illness.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent or recurrent pelvic and urinary symptoms without systemic infection can occur with chronic prostatitis.
why_wrong: A. Testicular torsion is an acute emergency with sudden severe testicular pain, not chronic pelvic symptoms. B. Renal colic causes acute episodic loin-to-groin pain, not months of pelvic discomfort. C. Acute pyelonephritis causes fever, loin pain and systemic illness, not months of pelvic discomfort without fever. D. Acute appendicitis is an acute illness and does not cause months of urinary symptoms.
pearl: Chronic prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome) causes months of pelvic or perineal pain with urinary symptoms but no systemic infection; other causes, including malignancy, should be considered.
thinking: Man with several months of symptoms ↓ Recurrent pelvic discomfort ↓ Urinary symptoms ↓ No fever or systemic illness ↓ Chronic prostatitis
exam_trap: C, acute pyelonephritis — urinary symptoms suggest infection, but pyelonephritis is acute with fever and loin pain, not months of afebrile pelvic discomfort.
takeaway: Months of pelvic pain and urinary symptoms without fever: think chronic prostatitis.

stem:
A man with known prostate cancer develops persistent lower-back pain.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Prostate cancer commonly metastasises to bone and can cause persistent bone pain.
why_wrong: B. Epididymitis causes scrotal pain and swelling, not back pain. C. Renal colic causes episodic colicky loin pain rather than persistent lower-back pain. D. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain, not back pain. E. Acute cystitis causes dysuria and frequency rather than persistent back pain.
pearl: Prostate cancer commonly spreads to bone, especially the spine; new back pain needs prompt assessment, and neurological symptoms suggest metastatic spinal cord compression.
thinking: Known prostate cancer ↓ Persistent lower-back pain ↓ Prostate cancer spreads to bone ↓ Spine is a common site ↓ Bone metastases
exam_trap: C, renal colic — back and loin pain overlap, but renal colic is episodic and colicky rather than persistent.
takeaway: Back pain in prostate cancer = bone metastases until proven otherwise; check for cord compression.

stem:
A patient with severe nephrotic syndrome develops sudden unilateral leg swelling.

Why is venous thrombosis an important consideration?

options.C: Thrombosis occurs only in nephritic syndrome

correct_answer: D. Nephrotic syndrome increases thrombotic risk
why_correct: Loss of anticoagulant proteins in the urine and other changes associated with nephrotic syndrome increase thrombotic risk.
why_wrong: A. Proteinuria does not always cause arterial embolism; the main thrombotic risk is venous. B. Nephrotic syndrome causes a hypercoagulable state rather than preventing clot formation. C. Thrombosis is a recognised complication of nephrotic syndrome, not only of nephritic syndrome. E. Oedema does not exclude DVT, and asymmetric swelling should prompt assessment.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable, partly through urinary loss of antithrombin and other anticoagulant proteins; DVT and renal vein thrombosis are recognised complications.
thinking: Severe nephrotic syndrome ↓ Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins ↓ Hypercoagulable state ↓ Sudden unilateral leg swelling ↓ Nephrotic syndrome increases thrombotic risk
exam_trap: E, oedema excludes thrombosis — generalised oedema can mask a DVT, but new asymmetric swelling still needs assessment.
takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome is prothrombotic: asymmetric leg swelling needs DVT assessment.

stem:
A patient with severe hyperkalaemia develops generalised muscle weakness.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.C: Hyperkalaemia affects only the gastrointestinal tract

correct_answer: A. Hyperkalaemia can cause neuromuscular weakness
why_correct: Significant hyperkalaemia can cause muscle weakness and potentially life-threatening cardiac conduction abnormalities.
why_wrong: B. Hyperkalaemia can cause weakness and life-threatening arrhythmias. C. Hyperkalaemia mainly affects skeletal and cardiac muscle rather than only the gastrointestinal tract. D. The patient has hyperkalaemia, so weakness cannot confirm hypokalaemia. E. Weakness can be caused by electrolyte disorders including hyperkalaemia and hypokalaemia.
pearl: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause muscle weakness and dangerous arrhythmias; get an ECG and, if there are changes, give IV calcium to protect the heart before lowering potassium.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Altered membrane excitability ↓ Affects skeletal and cardiac muscle ↓ Generalised weakness ↓ Hyperkalaemia can cause neuromuscular weakness
exam_trap: D, it confirms hypokalaemia — weakness is classically taught with low potassium, but high potassium causes it too, and this patient is hyperkalaemic.
takeaway: Both high and low potassium can cause weakness; always get an ECG.

stem:
A patient develops severe symptomatic hyponatraemia and then has a generalised seizure.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.D: Iron deficiency from occult gastrointestinal loss

correct_answer: B. Cerebral oedema from severe hyponatraemia
why_correct: Severe acute hyponatraemia can cause cerebral oedema and neurological symptoms, including seizures.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia causes weakness and arrhythmias but is not the explanation for a seizure in severe hyponatraemia. C. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion and drowsiness but does not explain this seizure in a patient with severe hyponatraemia. D. Iron deficiency does not cause acute seizures. E. Hypercholesterolaemia and atheroma do not cause acute seizures in this setting.
pearl: Severe or rapidly developing hyponatraemia causes cerebral oedema; seizures need urgent treatment with hypertonic saline under senior guidance, avoiding overly rapid correction.
thinking: Severe hyponatraemia ↓ Water moves into brain cells ↓ Cerebral oedema ↓ Generalised seizure ↓ Cerebral oedema from severe hyponatraemia
exam_trap: C, hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism — another electrolyte cause of confusion, but it does not explain a seizure in severe hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Seizure with severe hyponatraemia = cerebral oedema; correct carefully.

stem:
A 7-year-old becomes extremely distressed whenever their parent leaves and repeatedly worries that something terrible will happen to the parent.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Excessive anxiety concerning separation from an attachment figure is characteristic of separation anxiety disorder.
why_wrong: A. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions rather than distress focused on separation from a parent. C. A specific phobia is a fear of a particular object or situation, not separation from an attachment figure. D. Social anxiety disorder is fear of scrutiny or negative evaluation by others, not fear of separation from a parent. E. Generalised anxiety disorder involves excessive worry across many areas, not distress focused on separation from a parent.
pearl: Separation anxiety disorder is excessive, developmentally inappropriate fear of separation from attachment figures, often with worry that harm will come to them.
thinking: 7-year-old ↓ Extreme distress when the parent leaves ↓ Fears harm will come to the parent ↓ Beyond developmental norms ↓ Separation anxiety disorder
exam_trap: E, generalised anxiety disorder — the child worries a lot, but GAD involves worry across many areas, not worry focused on separation.
takeaway: Anxiety focused on separation from a carer = separation anxiety disorder.

stem:
A teenager experiences marked fear of being judged negatively when speaking in front of classmates and avoids social situations because of this.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent fear of scrutiny or negative evaluation in social situations is characteristic of social anxiety disorder.
why_wrong: A. Separation anxiety disorder involves fear of separation from attachment figures, not fear of being judged. B. Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks rather than fear specifically linked to social scrutiny. D. Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape or help may be difficult, not specifically fear of judgement. E. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions rather than fear of negative evaluation.
pearl: Social anxiety disorder centres on fear of scrutiny or embarrassment, leading to avoidance; cognitive behavioural therapy is the first-line treatment.
thinking: Teenager ↓ Fear of being judged negatively ↓ When speaking in front of classmates ↓ Avoids social situations ↓ Social anxiety disorder
exam_trap: D, agoraphobia — both involve avoidance, but agoraphobia is fear of being unable to escape or get help, not fear of judgement.
takeaway: Fear of negative evaluation by others = social anxiety disorder.

stem:
A patient avoids buses, crowded shops and cinemas because they fear being unable to escape or obtain help if they suddenly become unwell.

Which condition is most consistent?
why_correct: Agoraphobia involves fear or avoidance of situations where escape or help may be difficult if distressing symptoms occur.
why_wrong: A. Social anxiety disorder involves fear of negative evaluation by others rather than fear of being unable to escape. B. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions, not avoidance of places where escape is difficult. C. A specific phobia relates to a single object or situation, whereas this patient avoids multiple situations for fear of being unable to escape. D. Separation anxiety disorder involves fear of separation from attachment figures.
pearl: Agoraphobia is fear of places where escape or help may be difficult, such as crowds and public transport, and often coexists with panic disorder.
thinking: Avoids buses, crowded shops, cinemas ↓ Multiple situations ↓ Fear of being unable to escape or get help ↓ Agoraphobia
exam_trap: A, social anxiety disorder — crowded places tempt, but the fear here is of being trapped without help, not of being judged.
takeaway: Avoidance driven by fear of no escape or help = agoraphobia.

stem:
A patient reports episodes in which they feel detached from themselves or that their surroundings are unreal, particularly during periods of severe stress.

Which term best describes these experiences?
why_correct: Dissociation can involve a sense of detachment from oneself or one's surroundings and may occur during severe psychological stress.
why_wrong: A. Mania involves elevated mood, overactivity and grandiosity, not feeling detached from oneself. C. A delusion is a fixed false belief, whereas this patient describes a subjective sense of unreality. D. Confabulation is the unintentional production of false memories, typically in memory disorders such as Korsakoff syndrome. E. A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus, not a feeling of detachment or unreality.
pearl: Depersonalisation (feeling detached from oneself) and derealisation (surroundings feel unreal) are dissociative experiences, often triggered by severe stress, with insight preserved.
thinking: Feels detached from self ↓ Surroundings seem unreal ↓ Occurs under severe stress ↓ Disrupted integration of experience ↓ Dissociation
exam_trap: E, hallucination — unusual experiences suggest it, but a hallucination is a perception without a stimulus, not a sense of detachment or unreality.
takeaway: Feeling detached or that surroundings are unreal = dissociation.

stem:
A young woman has significantly restricted her food intake because she believes she is overweight despite being markedly underweight.

Which feature is most characteristic of anorexia nervosa?

options.A: Recurrent binge eating without compensatory behaviour

why_correct: Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced or evaluated is a key feature of anorexia nervosa.
why_wrong: A. Binge eating without compensatory behaviour describes binge-eating disorder, not anorexia nervosa. C. Excessive alcohol consumption is not a defining feature of anorexia nervosa. D. Recurrent panic attacks characterise panic disorder, not anorexia nervosa. E. Compulsive checking is a feature of OCD, not anorexia nervosa.
pearl: Anorexia nervosa combines restricted intake, low weight and a distorted view of body weight or shape; always assess physical risk, as complications can be life-threatening.
thinking: Restricts food intake ↓ Markedly underweight ↓ Believes she is overweight ↓ Distorted body image
exam_trap: A, recurrent binge eating without compensatory behaviour — an eating-disorder option that sounds related, but it describes binge-eating disorder, not restriction.
takeaway: Restriction, low weight and a distorted body image = anorexia nervosa.

stem:
A pregnant patient repeatedly eats non-food substances such as soil and has no cultural explanation for the behaviour.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Pica involves persistent eating of substances that are not normally considered food.
why_wrong: A. Binge-eating disorder involves recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food, not non-food substances. B. Anorexia nervosa involves restricted intake and a distorted body image, not eating non-food substances. D. Bulimia nervosa involves binge eating with compensatory behaviours, not eating non-food substances. E. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions rather than eating non-food substances.
pearl: Pica is persistent eating of non-food substances; in pregnancy it is associated with iron deficiency, so check a full blood count and ferritin.
thinking: Pregnant patient ↓ Repeatedly eats soil ↓ Non-food substance ↓ No cultural explanation ↓ Pica
exam_trap: E, OCD — repetitive behaviour suggests compulsions, but OCD involves obsessions and compulsions, not eating non-food substances.
takeaway: Persistent eating of non-food items = pica; check for iron deficiency.

stem:
A patient with long-standing gastro-oesophageal reflux disease undergoes endoscopy.

Which condition is associated with chronic GORD?
why_correct: Chronic reflux can cause metaplastic change in the distal oesophageal epithelium known as Barrett oesophagus.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulitis is a colonic condition unrelated to reflux. B. Appendicitis is not a complication of gastro-oesophageal reflux. D. Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease of the colon and is not caused by GORD. E. Haemorrhoids are anorectal vascular cushions unrelated to reflux disease.
pearl: Barrett oesophagus is metaplasia from squamous to columnar epithelium caused by chronic reflux; it is a precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma and may warrant endoscopic surveillance.
thinking: Long-standing GORD ↓ Chronic acid exposure of the distal oesophagus ↓ Squamous to columnar metaplasia ↓ Barrett oesophagus
exam_trap: D, ulcerative colitis — a chronic inflammatory GI condition seen at endoscopy, but it affects the colon and is not caused by reflux.
takeaway: Chronic GORD can cause Barrett oesophagus, a precursor of adenocarcinoma.

stem:
A patient being treated for diverticulitis remains febrile and develops a tender palpable mass in the left lower abdomen.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Persistent sepsis with a localised tender mass following diverticulitis suggests an intra-abdominal abscess.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain and is not a complication of diverticulitis. B. Coeliac disease is a chronic malabsorptive condition and does not cause a tender mass with persistent fever. C. Haemorrhoids cause rectal bleeding and perianal symptoms, not a febrile abdominal mass. E. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea, not sepsis with a palpable mass.
pearl: Persistent fever or a tender mass despite treatment for diverticulitis suggests an abscess; CT confirms it, and larger collections may need drainage.
thinking: Diverticulitis on treatment ↓ Persistent fever ↓ Tender palpable left lower abdominal mass ↓ Localised collection ↓ Diverticular abscess
exam_trap: C, haemorrhoids — a familiar lower GI problem, but they cause rectal bleeding and perianal symptoms, not fever with an abdominal mass.
takeaway: Diverticulitis not settling, with a tender mass = abscess; arrange CT.

stem:
An older patient with chronic constipation develops marked abdominal distension, abdominal pain and inability to pass stool or flatus.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Sigmoid volvulus causes large-bowel obstruction and is particularly associated with older adults and chronic constipation.
why_wrong: A. Acute hepatitis causes jaundice and malaise, not marked distension with failure to pass flatus. B. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption rather than acute obstruction with absolute constipation. C. Gastric ulcer causes epigastric pain and bleeding rather than large-bowel obstruction. E. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain and does not cause large-bowel obstruction.
pearl: Sigmoid volvulus typically affects older, chronically constipated patients and causes marked distension; uncomplicated cases are often decompressed endoscopically.
thinking: Older adult with chronic constipation ↓ Marked distension and pain ↓ No stool or flatus ↓ Large-bowel obstruction ↓ Sigmoid volvulus
exam_trap: C, gastric ulcer — it causes abdominal pain, but not marked distension with failure to pass stool or flatus.
takeaway: Older constipated patient with massive distension and absolute constipation: sigmoid volvulus.

stem:
A child with known Hirschsprung disease develops sudden abdominal distension, fever and profuse diarrhoea.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, abdominal distension and diarrhoea in a child with Hirschsprung disease are red flags for Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents in early infancy with projectile non-bilious vomiting, not fever and diarrhoea. B. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption rather than an acute febrile illness. D. Lactose intolerance does not cause fever or acute systemic illness. E. Biliary colic is rare in children and does not cause fever with profuse diarrhoea and distension.
pearl: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can occur before or after surgery and may progress to sepsis and perforation; fever, distension and diarrhoea need urgent assessment.
thinking: Known Hirschsprung disease ↓ Sudden abdominal distension ↓ Fever and profuse diarrhoea ↓ Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis
exam_trap: D, lactose intolerance — it causes diarrhoea and distension, but not fever or acute systemic illness.
takeaway: Hirschsprung disease plus fever and diarrhoea = enterocolitis, an emergency.

stem:
A postmenopausal woman develops chronic vulval itching with pale, thin skin and architectural changes.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Lichen sclerosus commonly causes pruritus and pale, thin vulval skin and is associated with an increased risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes causes painful vesicles and ulcers rather than chronic pale atrophic skin. B. Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes itch with thick white discharge and erythema rather than pale thin skin with architectural change. C. A Bartholin cyst is a swelling at the vaginal introitus, not chronic itch with pale skin. D. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin fishy-smelling discharge, not vulval skin changes.
pearl: Lichen sclerosus gives itchy, white, thin 'cigarette-paper' vulval skin with loss of normal architecture; treat with a potent topical steroid and keep under review because of the small risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman with chronic vulval itch ↓ Skin is pale and thin, not red or ulcerated ↓ Architectural change (labial fusion or resorption) points to a chronic scarring dermatosis ↓ Lichen sclerosus
exam_trap: B, vulvovaginal candidiasis — itch makes it tempting, but thrush gives red, inflamed skin with thick white discharge and does not cause pale atrophic skin or architectural change.
takeaway: Chronic vulval itch plus pale, thin skin and scarring means lichen sclerosus until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops new neck pain and neurological symptoms.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause atlantoaxial instability, which may threaten the spinal cord.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms in the hand and does not explain new neck pain. B. Lumbar disc prolapse would not explain neck pain, and the word 'only' ignores cervical involvement in rheumatoid arthritis. C. Gout rarely affects the cervical spine and is not the classic complication here. D. Osteoarthritis of the hip does not cause neck pain or neurological symptoms.
pearl: In long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, new neck pain or neurological signs suggest atlantoaxial subluxation; take care with neck manipulation, including at intubation, and seek urgent imaging and specialist review.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Synovitis can erode the transverse ligament and odontoid peg ↓ New neck pain with neurological symptoms suggests cord compromise ↓ Cervical spine instability
exam_trap: A, carpal tunnel syndrome only — a well-known RA complication, but it causes median nerve symptoms in the hand and cannot explain new neck pain; 'only' ignores a threat to the spinal cord.
takeaway: RA plus new neck pain or neurological signs: think atlantoaxial instability and protect the cervical spine.

stem: Which patient has an important risk factor for osteoporosis?

options.A: An adult with isolated, recurrent bacterial otitis externa
options.B: A patient with uncomplicated myopia wearing contact lenses
options.C: A postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
options.D: A healthy child with normal growth
options.E: A young adult using a steroid nasal spray for hay fever

correct_answer: C. A postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
why_correct: Increasing age, menopause and prolonged systemic corticosteroid use are important osteoporosis risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa, even when recurrent, has no relationship with bone density. B. Myopia and contact lens use have no association with osteoporosis. D. A healthy child with normal growth has no osteoporosis risk factor. E. Intranasal corticosteroids for allergic rhinitis have minimal systemic absorption and are not a meaningful osteoporosis risk factor.
pearl: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are one of the commonest secondary causes of osteoporosis; consider fracture risk assessment and bone protection when prolonged systemic steroid treatment is started, especially after the menopause.
thinking: Look for established osteoporosis risk factors ↓ Postmenopausal oestrogen loss accelerates bone loss ↓ Long-term oral prednisolone adds systemic steroid-induced bone loss ↓ Postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
exam_trap: E, a young adult using a steroid nasal spray — the word 'steroid' tempts, but intranasal steroids have minimal systemic absorption and are not a meaningful osteoporosis risk factor.
takeaway: Systemic, prolonged glucocorticoids plus menopause is a classic high-risk combination for osteoporosis.

stem:
A young adult with inflammatory back pain develops a painful red eye with photophobia.

Which ocular condition should be suspected?
why_correct: A painful photophobic red eye in a patient with an inflammatory systemic condition is characteristic of anterior uveitis.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes a red, gritty eye with discharge but not significant pain and photophobia, and is not linked to inflammatory back pain. B. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring without a red eye. D. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and does not cause photophobia. E. A chalazion is a painless eyelid lump and does not cause photophobia.
pearl: Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra-articular feature of axial spondyloarthritis: a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision need same-day ophthalmology review.
thinking: Young adult with inflammatory back pain suggests axial spondyloarthritis ↓ Painful red eye with photophobia, not just discomfort ↓ This is the classic associated eye inflammation ↓ Acute anterior uveitis
exam_trap: A, conjunctivitis — the commonest red eye, but it causes grittiness and discharge, not significant pain and photophobia; missing uveitis risks sight-threatening complications.
takeaway: Inflammatory back pain plus a painful, photophobic red eye equals anterior uveitis: refer urgently.

stem:
A patient has chronic irritation, crusting around the eyelashes and burning eyes.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Blepharitis causes chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, often with crusting and irritation.
why_wrong: A. Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection with fever, lid swelling and painful eye movements, not chronic crusting. B. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring without lid irritation. C. Acute anterior uveitis causes a painful photophobic red eye rather than eyelid margin crusting. E. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a field defect, not eyelid crusting.
pearl: Blepharitis is chronic eyelid-margin inflammation causing burning, grittiness and crusting at the lashes; mainstay treatment is daily lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid cleaning, usually long term.
thinking: Chronic rather than acute symptoms ↓ Crusting localised to the eyelashes and lid margins ↓ Burning, irritated eyes without red flags ↓ Blepharitis
exam_trap: C, acute anterior uveitis — a cause of eye discomfort, but it presents acutely with pain, photophobia and reduced vision, not chronic crusting of the lash line.
takeaway: Chronic crusty lid margins with burning eyes is blepharitis; treat with regular lid hygiene.

stem:
A patient reports a gritty sensation and intermittent blurred vision that improves after blinking.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Grittiness, irritation and fluctuating vision that improves with blinking are typical of dry eye disease.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a curtain-like field loss rather than grittiness relieved by blinking. C. Optic neuritis causes painful eye movements and reduced vision that does not improve with blinking. D. Cataract causes gradual, persistent blurring that does not improve with blinking. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye, haloes and systemic upset.
pearl: Dry eye disease causes gritty, burning eyes with vision that blurs and then clears on blinking as the tear film is restored; first-line treatment is lubricating eye drops and addressing contributing factors.
thinking: Gritty, irritated eyes ↓ Blurring is intermittent, not persistent ↓ Vision clears after blinking, so the tear film is the problem ↓ Dry eye disease
exam_trap: D, cataract — causes blurred vision, but it is gradual, painless and constant; blinking does not clear it and it does not cause grittiness.
takeaway: Blurring that clears with blinking plus grittiness points to the tear film: dry eye disease.

stem:
A patient develops sudden unilateral hearing loss over several hours. Otoscopy is normal.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Reassure and review in six months

why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time-sensitive and requires urgent specialist assessment.
why_wrong: B. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs same-day assessment because treatment is time-dependent, so delayed review is unsafe. C. Routine audiology alone would delay the urgent ENT assessment needed for sudden hearing loss. D. Ear drops do not treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss and would delay urgent assessment. E. Otitis externa causes ear canal inflammation visible on otoscopy, which is normal here.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss with a normal ear on otoscopy is an ENT emergency; urgent referral allows audiometry, steroid treatment where appropriate and investigation for causes such as a vestibular schwannoma.
thinking: Hearing loss developing over hours ↓ Normal otoscopy rules out wax, effusion and canal causes ↓ Likely sudden sensorineural hearing loss ↓ Time-sensitive, so arrange urgent ENT assessment
exam_trap: C, routine audiology only — a hearing test is part of work-up, but a routine referral wastes the short window in which treatment is most likely to help.
takeaway: Sudden unilateral hearing loss with normal otoscopy needs urgent, same-day ENT referral.

stem:
A patient develops ear pain after frequent swimming. Movement of the tragus markedly worsens the pain.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Pain aggravated by movement of the tragus is characteristic of inflammation of the external ear canal.
why_wrong: A. Cholesteatoma typically causes painless offensive discharge and hearing loss. B. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss rather than ear pain. C. Acute otitis media causes deep ear pain with a bulging tympanic membrane, not pain on tragal movement. D. Otosclerosis causes painless progressive conductive hearing loss.
pearl: Otitis externa is typical in swimmers: canal pain worsened by moving the tragus or pinna, often with discharge; topical treatment and keeping the ear dry are the mainstay.
thinking: Frequent swimming keeps the ear canal moist ↓ Ear pain localised to the canal ↓ Tragal movement markedly worsens pain ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: C, acute otitis media — a common cause of ear pain, but it arises in the middle ear, so moving the tragus does not typically worsen it and swimming is not the classic trigger.
takeaway: Ear pain worse on tragal pressure after swimming is otitis externa, not otitis media.

stem:
A patient has persistent offensive ear discharge and conductive hearing loss.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent offensive otorrhoea with conductive hearing loss is characteristic of cholesteatoma.
why_wrong: A. Acute otitis externa causes painful otorrhoea of short duration rather than persistent offensive discharge with conductive loss. B. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo with no hearing loss or discharge. D. Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss but no ear discharge. E. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss, not offensive discharge.
