Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causes marked polyuria and polydipsia, including by day. D. New-onset type 1 diabetes causes polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss, and typically presents as new (secondary) bedwetting. E. Constipation can contribute to enuresis but is not established by the information given.
pearl: Primary nocturnal enuresis is common and often resolves with time; after lifestyle advice, an enuresis alarm is first-line, with desmopressin when an alarm is unsuitable or short-term dryness is needed.
thinking: Child aged 6 ↓ Never consistently dry overnight ↓ No daytime urinary symptoms ↓ No other cause suggested ↓ Primary nocturnal enuresis
exam_trap: A, secondary nocturnal enuresis — also bedwetting, but secondary means wetting returns after a period of established dryness, which this child has never achieved.
takeaway: Never been dry at night = primary enuresis; wet again after being dry = secondary.

stem: A child has infrequent, hard stools and painful defecation. Examination suggests a palpable stool mass in the abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Infrequent hard stools, painful defecation and palpable stool are typical of childhood constipation.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain and systemic symptoms. B. Hirschsprung disease usually presents much earlier with delayed passage of meconium and bowel obstruction symptoms. D. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting in young infants. E. Intussusception causes acute episodic abdominal pain and may cause bloody stool.
pearl: Childhood constipation is usually functional; treat promptly with an osmotic laxative such as macrogol, disimpacting first if a faecal mass is present, and continue well after regular habit returns.
thinking: Infrequent hard stools ↓ Painful defecation ↓ Palpable stool mass ↓ Faecal loading ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: B, Hirschsprung disease — causes chronic constipation, but usually presents from birth with delayed passage of meconium and distension; this history fits functional constipation.
takeaway: Hard, infrequent, painful stools with palpable faeces = functional constipation; treat with macrogol.

stem: A patient experiences recurrent burning discomfort behind the sternum, particularly after meals and when lying down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Heartburn related to meals and lying down is characteristic of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
why_wrong: A. A perforated ulcer causes sudden severe abdominal pain and peritonism. B. Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes intermittent chest pain and dysphagia rather than meal- and posture-related heartburn. C. Pancreatitis causes severe upper abdominal pain, often radiating to the back. D. Acute coronary syndrome can cause chest pain and must be considered when clinically appropriate, but the meal- and position-related burning pattern described is typical of reflux.
pearl: Typical reflux causes retrosternal burning after meals and on lying down; red flags such as dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding need prompt endoscopic assessment rather than empirical acid suppression alone.
thinking: Recurrent retrosternal burning ↓ After meals ↓ Worse lying down ↓ Acid reflux pattern ↓ Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
exam_trap: D, acute coronary syndrome — retrosternal pain must never be dismissed, but recurrent burning linked to meals and lying flat is the classic reflux pattern.
takeaway: Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying flat = GORD; always screen for red flags.

stem: A patient with longstanding gastro-oesophageal reflux undergoes endoscopy showing replacement of the normal lower oesophageal lining by specialised intestinal-type epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Barrett oesophagus is characterised by metaplastic intestinal-type epithelium replacing the normal squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus, commonly associated with chronic reflux.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer disease affects the stomach or duodenum. C. Achalasia is a motility disorder causing impaired lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes infectious oesophagitis. E. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear associated with forceful vomiting.
pearl: Barrett oesophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the distal oesophagus caused by chronic reflux; it is premalignant for adenocarcinoma, so patients take a PPI and enter endoscopic surveillance.
thinking: Longstanding reflux ↓ Endoscopy of the lower oesophagus ↓ Squamous lining replaced by intestinal-type epithelium ↓ Metaplasia ↓ Barrett oesophagus
exam_trap: C, achalasia — another lower oesophageal disorder that can mimic reflux, but it is a motility problem of sphincter relaxation and does not change the lining epithelium.
takeaway: Intestinal metaplasia in the lower oesophagus is Barrett — premalignant and needs surveillance.

stem: A patient develops sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Blood tests show a markedly raised lipase. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones. What is the most likely cause of the pancreatitis?
why_correct: Gallstones are a common cause of acute pancreatitis, usually through obstruction of the biliary/pancreatic outflow tract.
why_wrong: B. Appendicitis causes right lower abdominal symptoms rather than this pancreatic presentation. C. IBS does not cause pancreatitis or markedly elevated pancreatic enzymes. D. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. E. Coeliac disease causes chronic intestinal inflammation and malabsorption.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol cause most acute pancreatitis in the UK; after gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy is advised during the same admission or soon after to prevent recurrence.
thinking: Sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Vomiting ↓ Markedly raised lipase = acute pancreatitis ↓ Ultrasound shows gallstones ↓ Gallstones as the cause
exam_trap: C, irritable bowel syndrome — causes recurrent abdominal pain, but it never raises pancreatic enzymes or causes pancreatitis; gallstones on ultrasound give the cause.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis with gallstones on ultrasound = gallstone pancreatitis.

stem: A man who has recently stopped heavy alcohol consumption develops severe agitation, confusion, visual hallucinations, fever and marked autonomic overactivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Delirium tremens is a severe, potentially life-threatening manifestation of alcohol withdrawal involving delirium, hallucinations and marked autonomic disturbance.
why_wrong: A. Alcohol intoxication causes central nervous system depression rather than severe withdrawal-related autonomic overactivity. B. Panic attacks are episodic but do not cause persistent delirium. C. Depression does not cause this acute fluctuating confusional state. D. Absence seizures cause brief episodes of impaired awareness rather than prolonged delirium.
pearl: Delirium tremens usually develops a few days after stopping heavy drinking and can be fatal; treat urgently with benzodiazepines and give parenteral thiamine.
thinking: Recently stopped heavy drinking ↓ Agitation, confusion, visual hallucinations ↓ Fever and autonomic overactivity ↓ Severe withdrawal with delirium ↓ Delirium tremens
exam_trap: A, simple alcohol intoxication — alcohol is the obvious link, but intoxication depresses the CNS; agitation, hallucinations and autonomic overactivity after stopping are withdrawal.
takeaway: Delirium with autonomic overactivity after stopping alcohol = delirium tremens, a medical emergency.

stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol dependence develops confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: The combination of confusion, ataxia and ocular abnormalities in a malnourished patient is characteristic of thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Alzheimer's disease causes progressive cognitive decline rather than this acute nutritional syndrome. B. Multiple sclerosis usually causes focal neurological episodes. C. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor. D. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease causes rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus rather than an acute nutritional syndrome of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.
pearl: Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; give high-dose parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) promptly and do not wait for all three features, as the full triad is often absent.
thinking: Alcohol dependence and malnutrition ↓ Confusion ↓ Unsteady gait (ataxia) ↓ Abnormal eye movements ↓ Wernicke encephalopathy
exam_trap: D, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease — causes confusion and ataxia, but it is a rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus; malnourished alcohol dependence points to thiamine deficiency.
takeaway: Confusion, ataxia and eye signs in a malnourished drinker: give parenteral thiamine now.

stem: A patient with longstanding alcohol dependence has persistent severe short-term memory impairment and invents information to fill gaps in memory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic amnestic disorder associated with thiamine deficiency and may involve confabulation.
why_wrong: A. Delirium tremens is an acute withdrawal syndrome with delirium and autonomic overactivity. B. Vascular dementia is associated with cerebrovascular disease and cognitive impairment. C. Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute neurological manifestation of thiamine deficiency. D. Alzheimer's disease causes progressive broader cognitive decline.
pearl: Korsakoff syndrome is a largely irreversible amnesic state after thiamine deficiency, with profound anterograde amnesia and confabulation; prompt thiamine for Wernicke helps prevent it.
thinking: Longstanding alcohol dependence ↓ Persistent severe short-term memory loss ↓ Confabulation fills the gaps ↓ Chronic thiamine-deficiency amnesia ↓ Korsakoff syndrome
exam_trap: C, Wernicke encephalopathy — same cause, thiamine deficiency, but it is the acute picture of confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not chronic amnesia with confabulation.
takeaway: Wernicke is acute and treatable; Korsakoff is chronic amnesia with confabulation.

stem: An older patient with a history of gallstones develops abdominal pain, vomiting and intestinal obstruction. Imaging shows air within the biliary tree and an ectopic gallstone in the bowel. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Gallstone ileus occurs when a gallstone enters the bowel through a biliary-enteric fistula and causes mechanical obstruction; pneumobilia may be present.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes pancreatic inflammation rather than a gallstone obstructing the bowel. B. Biliary colic does not cause intestinal obstruction. C. Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder. D. Appendicitis does not cause this characteristic combination.
pearl: Rigler's triad on imaging — pneumobilia, small-bowel obstruction and an ectopic gallstone — is classic for gallstone ileus; the stone usually impacts at the terminal ileum.
thinking: Older patient with gallstones ↓ Intestinal obstruction ↓ Air in the biliary tree (biliary-enteric fistula) ↓ Gallstone within the bowel ↓ Gallstone ileus
exam_trap: B, biliary colic — the gallstone history tempts, but colic is pain from a stone at the gallbladder outlet; it causes no bowel obstruction or pneumobilia.
takeaway: Bowel obstruction + pneumobilia + ectopic gallstone = gallstone ileus.

stem: A patient with cirrhosis develops haematemesis from dilated veins in the lower oesophagus. What are these veins called?
why_correct: Portal hypertension can produce dilated collateral veins in the oesophagus, which may rupture and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Aortic aneurysms involve the arterial system. B. Mesenteric cysts are fluid-filled lesions within the mesentery. C. Haemorrhoids involve the anorectal region. E. Mallory–Weiss tears are mucosal lacerations at the gastro-oesophageal junction after retching, not dilated veins.
pearl: Suspected variceal bleeding needs resuscitation, terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics before urgent endoscopy with band ligation.
thinking: Cirrhosis ↓ Portal hypertension ↓ Portosystemic collaterals in the lower oesophagus ↓ Dilated veins rupture causing haematemesis ↓ Oesophageal varices
exam_trap: E, Mallory–Weiss tears — also cause haematemesis near the gastro-oesophageal junction, but they are mucosal tears after retching, not dilated veins from portal hypertension.
takeaway: Haematemesis in cirrhosis = varices until proven otherwise; give terlipressin and antibiotics.

stem: A middle-aged woman has persistent itching and cholestatic liver tests. Which chronic autoimmune liver disease should be considered?
why_correct: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease that commonly affects women and can present with pruritus and cholestatic liver-test abnormalities.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes acute abdominal pain and pancreatic enzyme elevation. B. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without cholestatic liver disease. C. Autoimmune hepatitis typically causes a hepatitic, transaminase-predominant pattern rather than cholestatic tests with pruritus. D. Alcohol withdrawal causes autonomic and neurological symptoms rather than chronic cholestasis.
pearl: PBC typically affects middle-aged women with itch and fatigue; a cholestatic picture with positive antimitochondrial antibodies supports the diagnosis, and ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line.
thinking: Middle-aged woman ↓ Persistent itching ↓ Cholestatic liver tests ↓ Autoimmune damage to small bile ducts ↓ Primary biliary cholangitis
exam_trap: C, type 1 autoimmune hepatitis — also an autoimmune liver disease common in women, but it gives a transaminase-predominant hepatitic picture rather than cholestasis with itch.
takeaway: Middle-aged woman with itch and raised ALP: think PBC and check antimitochondrial antibodies.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with new temporal headache develops sudden visual loss in one eye. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?
why_correct: New headache with acute visual loss in an older adult is a red-flag presentation for giant cell arteritis and requires urgent assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment. B. Allergic conjunctivitis does not cause acute visual loss. C. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters and is not associated with new temporal headache. E. Migraine with aura causes transient, reversible visual symptoms rather than sudden persistent visual loss in this context.
pearl: Suspected GCA with visual loss needs immediate high-dose corticosteroids and same-day specialist review; do not delay treatment while awaiting temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound.
thinking: Age 72 ↓ New temporal headache ↓ Sudden visual loss in one eye ↓ Arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy ↓ Giant cell arteritis
exam_trap: E, migraine with visual aura — headache with visual symptoms tempts, but aura is transient and reversible; new headache with persistent visual loss in an older adult is GCA.
takeaway: Older patient with new headache and visual loss: start high-dose steroids for GCA now.

stem: An 80-year-old develops progressive difficulty reading and distortion of straight lines. Which part of the eye is primarily affected?
why_correct: Age-related macular degeneration affects the macula and causes central visual impairment, including difficulty reading and distortion.
why_wrong: A. Lens opacity causes cataract and generally produces gradual visual blurring. B. Iris disease does not cause the characteristic central visual distortion. C. Corneal disease usually causes pain, photophobia or reduced visual clarity. D. Optic-nerve disease causes a different pattern of visual loss.
pearl: Central visual loss with distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) in an older person suggests age-related macular degeneration; sudden distortion warrants urgent referral to exclude wet AMD.
thinking: Age 80 ↓ Difficulty reading = central vision affected ↓ Straight lines distorted ↓ Age-related macular degeneration ↓ Macula
exam_trap: A, lens — cataract is common in older people and blurs vision, but it causes glare and generalised blurring, not distortion of straight lines.
takeaway: Central visual loss with distorted straight lines localises to the macula.

stem: A patient with age-related macular degeneration develops rapid deterioration in central vision. Which process is characteristic of the wet form?

options.B: Ischaemic swelling of the optic nerve head
options.C: Abnormal vessel growth beneath the retina
options.D: Accumulation of drusen with geographic atrophy

correct_answer: C. Abnormal vessel growth beneath the retina
why_correct: Neovascular or wet age-related macular degeneration involves abnormal blood-vessel growth beneath the retina, which can cause rapid central visual deterioration.
why_wrong: A. Lens opacity is cataract. B. Ischaemic swelling of the optic nerve head describes anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, not macular degeneration. D. Drusen with geographic atrophy is characteristic of dry age-related macular degeneration, which progresses gradually. E. Corneal infection causes keratitis.
pearl: Wet AMD is choroidal neovascularisation that leaks and bleeds, causing rapid central loss; it needs urgent ophthalmology referral for anti-VEGF intravitreal injections.
thinking: Known AMD ↓ Rapid deterioration in central vision ↓ Suggests the wet (neovascular) form ↓ New vessels beneath the retina leak and bleed ↓ Abnormal vessel growth beneath the retina
exam_trap: D, accumulation of drusen with geographic atrophy — the hallmark of dry AMD, which progresses slowly; rapid deterioration indicates neovascular change.
takeaway: Dry AMD = drusen and slow atrophy; wet AMD = new vessels, rapid loss, anti-VEGF treatment.

stem: A patient has a constricted pupil, mild drooping of the upper eyelid and reduced sweating on one side of the face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway and classically causes miosis, partial ptosis and anhidrosis.
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy causes lower motor neurone facial weakness. C. Third-nerve palsy typically causes ptosis with a larger, often poorly reactive pupil and abnormal eye movements. D. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye and a mid-dilated pupil. E. Myasthenia can cause fluctuating ptosis but does not produce miosis and facial anhidrosis.
pearl: Horner syndrome is ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from sympathetic interruption; always look for a cause such as an apical lung tumour or carotid dissection.
thinking: Constricted pupil (miosis) ↓ Mild partial ptosis ↓ Reduced sweating on one side of the face ↓ Sympathetic pathway interrupted ↓ Horner syndrome
exam_trap: C, third-nerve palsy — also causes ptosis, but with a dilated pupil and abnormal eye movements; a small pupil with mild ptosis is sympathetic.
takeaway: Ptosis with a small pupil = Horner syndrome; ptosis with a large pupil = third-nerve palsy.

stem: A patient with acute Bell's palsy cannot fully close the affected eye. What is the main immediate ocular concern?
why_correct: Incomplete eye closure can leave the cornea exposed, causing dryness and potentially corneal damage.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis affects the optic nerve rather than eye closure. C. Cataract is unrelated to acute facial nerve palsy. D. Bell's palsy does not directly cause retinal detachment. E. Central retinal artery occlusion is a separate vascular emergency unrelated to incomplete eye closure.
pearl: In Bell's palsy with incomplete eye closure, protect the cornea with lubricating drops and ointment and tape the eye closed at night; refer urgently if eye pain or redness develops.
thinking: Bell's palsy ↓ Orbicularis oculi weakness ↓ Eye cannot close fully ↓ Cornea exposed and dries ↓ Corneal exposure and injury
exam_trap: A, acute ipsilateral optic neuritis — sounds like a neuro-ophthalmic complication, but Bell's palsy affects the facial nerve and eyelid closure, not the optic nerve.
takeaway: Bell's palsy with incomplete eye closure: protect the cornea.

stem: A patient develops acute prolonged vertigo accompanied by hearing loss. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Labyrinthitis causes acute vertigo with auditory symptoms such as hearing loss, reflecting involvement of the cochlear as well as vestibular apparatus.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa does not cause this characteristic prolonged vertigo syndrome. B. Ménière disease causes recurrent episodic attacks rather than this typical acute prolonged presentation. C. Vestibular neuritis typically causes vertigo without hearing loss. D. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo.
pearl: Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis both cause acute prolonged vertigo; added hearing loss means the cochlea is involved, so it is labyrinthitis, and sudden hearing loss needs urgent ENT assessment.
thinking: Acute onset vertigo ↓ Prolonged, not brief or positional ↓ Accompanied by hearing loss ↓ Cochlear plus vestibular involvement ↓ Labyrinthitis
exam_trap: C, vestibular neuritis — gives the same acute prolonged vertigo, but hearing is preserved because only the vestibular nerve is affected.
takeaway: Acute vertigo without hearing loss = vestibular neuritis; with hearing loss = labyrinthitis.

stem: A teenager with infectious mononucleosis asks when they can return to contact sport. What complication is the main reason for restricting contact sport during recovery?
why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis can cause splenomegaly, creating a risk of splenic rupture, particularly with abdominal trauma.
why_wrong: A. Renal stones are not the key complication relevant to contact sport. B. Appendicitis is not the characteristic concern following infectious mononucleosis. C. Cataract is unrelated to infectious mononucleosis. E. Retinal detachment is unrelated.
pearl: Glandular fever often causes splenomegaly, so contact sport and heavy lifting are avoided for several weeks; amoxicillin given during EBV infection classically causes a widespread rash.
thinking: Infectious mononucleosis ↓ Splenomegaly is common ↓ Enlarged spleen is fragile ↓ Abdominal impact in contact sport ↓ Splenic rupture
exam_trap: B, appendicitis — an abdominal emergency that might seem linked to infection, but it is not a feature of glandular fever; the enlarged, fragile spleen is the concern.
takeaway: Glandular fever: no contact sport for several weeks because of splenic rupture risk.

stem: A patient sustains a direct blow to the nose and develops swelling, bruising and tenderness. What injury is most likely?
why_correct: Direct nasal trauma followed by swelling, bruising and tenderness is typical of a nasal fracture.
why_wrong: A. Clavicle fracture causes shoulder-region pain. B. Mandibular fracture causes jaw pain, malocclusion or difficulty opening the mouth. C. Zygomatic fracture causes cheek and orbital symptoms. D. Orbital floor fracture may cause diplopia and altered sensation around the cheek.
pearl: Nasal fracture is a clinical diagnosis; always look for a septal haematoma, and if the nose is deformed, reassess once swelling settles because manipulation is done within a couple of weeks.
thinking: Direct blow to the nose ↓ Swelling and bruising ↓ Nasal tenderness ↓ Nasal bones take the direct impact ↓ Nasal fracture
exam_trap: C, zygomatic fracture — a mid-face injury after a blow, but it causes cheek flattening, infraorbital numbness and trismus rather than isolated nasal signs.
takeaway: Nasal injury: diagnose clinically, exclude septal haematoma, reassess deformity once swelling settles.

stem: A patient sustains nasal trauma and develops bilateral nasal obstruction with a soft, fluctuant swelling of the nasal septum. What is the most important diagnosis?
why_correct: A septal haematoma can occur after nasal trauma and presents with nasal obstruction and a fluctuant septal swelling. It requires urgent treatment to prevent cartilage necrosis and deformity.
why_wrong: A. Sinusitis causes facial pain or pressure and nasal symptoms rather than an acute septal collection. B. A deviated septum is generally a structural, non-fluctuant abnormality. C. Nasal polyps are usually chronic and not related to acute trauma. E. Allergic rhinitis causes congestion, sneezing and rhinorrhoea.
pearl: A septal haematoma needs same-day ENT incision and drainage; untreated it can cause abscess, cartilage necrosis and a saddle-nose deformity.
thinking: Nasal trauma ↓ Bilateral nasal obstruction ↓ Soft, fluctuant septal swelling ↓ Blood collecting over the septal cartilage ↓ Septal haematoma
exam_trap: B, deviated septum — also causes nasal obstruction, but it is a firm, non-fluctuant structural problem; a soft boggy septal swelling after trauma is a haematoma.
takeaway: Boggy septal swelling after nasal trauma = septal haematoma; drain urgently.

stem: A patient is struck in the eye and subsequently develops diplopia, particularly on looking upwards, with numbness over the cheek. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Orbital floor fractures can entrap extraocular muscles, causing diplopia, and may affect the infraorbital nerve, producing cheek numbness.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment. B. Traumatic optic neuropathy causes reduced vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect rather than diplopia on upgaze with cheek numbness. C. A subconjunctival haemorrhage causes painless redness of the eye, not diplopia or cheek numbness. D. An isolated nasal fracture affects the nose and does not cause diplopia on upgaze or cheek numbness.
pearl: Orbital floor blow-out fractures can trap the inferior rectus, limiting upgaze, and injure the infraorbital nerve; advise against nose-blowing and refer to maxillofacial surgery.
thinking: Blow to the eye ↓ Diplopia on upgaze (inferior rectus trapped) ↓ Cheek numbness (infraorbital nerve) ↓ Blow-out injury of the orbit ↓ Orbital floor fracture
exam_trap: B, traumatic optic neuropathy — a serious orbital injury, but it reduces vision with a relative afferent pupillary defect and does not cause diplopia on upgaze or cheek numbness.
takeaway: Diplopia on upgaze plus cheek numbness after a blow to the eye = orbital floor fracture.

stem: A patient suffers facial trauma and develops flattening of the cheek, facial numbness and difficulty opening the mouth. Which fracture is most likely?
why_correct: Zygomatic fractures can cause flattening of the cheek, infraorbital sensory disturbance and trismus.
why_wrong: B. An isolated orbital floor fracture more typically causes diplopia and infraorbital numbness. C. A clavicle fracture is unrelated to facial trauma findings. D. Nasal fracture primarily affects the nose. E. A mandibular condyle fracture can cause malocclusion and restricted jaw movement but does not explain the characteristic cheek flattening.
pearl: Zygomatic fractures cause cheek flattening, infraorbital numbness and difficulty opening the mouth when the depressed arch impinges on the coronoid process; refer to maxillofacial surgery.
thinking: Facial trauma ↓ Flattened cheek ↓ Facial numbness (infraorbital nerve) ↓ Difficulty opening the mouth ↓ Zygomatic fracture
exam_trap: E, mandibular condyle fracture — explains difficulty opening the mouth, but not the flattened cheek or facial numbness.
takeaway: Flat cheek, cheek numbness and trismus after facial trauma = zygomatic fracture.

stem: A patient is struck in the face and develops pain when opening the mouth with malocclusion. What injury should be suspected?
why_correct: Facial trauma followed by malocclusion and pain or difficulty with jaw movement is strongly suggestive of a mandibular fracture.
why_wrong: B. Nasal fracture causes nasal swelling and tenderness. C. Otitis externa causes painful inflammation of the external ear canal. D. Orbital floor fracture primarily causes orbital symptoms such as diplopia. E. Cataract is unrelated to acute facial trauma.
pearl: The mandible often fractures in two places because it forms a ring; look for malocclusion, a step deformity and lower lip numbness, and image with an OPG.
thinking: Blow to the face ↓ Pain on opening the mouth ↓ Malocclusion (teeth no longer meet normally) ↓ Disrupted mandible ↓ Mandibular fracture
exam_trap: D, orbital floor fracture — a common facial fracture after a blow, but it causes diplopia and cheek numbness, not malocclusion.
takeaway: Malocclusion after facial trauma = mandibular fracture until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops severe deep eye pain that radiates to the face. The eye appears intensely red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Scleritis causes severe deep ocular pain and is associated with systemic inflammatory conditions including rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is generally painless. B. Conjunctivitis usually causes superficial irritation and discharge rather than severe deep pain. C. A chalazion is a localised eyelid swelling. E. Cataract causes painless visual impairment.
pearl: Scleritis causes severe, boring eye pain that may wake the patient, with deep tender redness; linked to rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis, it needs same-day ophthalmology review.
thinking: Rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Severe deep eye pain radiating to the face ↓ Intensely red eye ↓ Deep scleral inflammation ↓ Scleritis
exam_trap: B, conjunctivitis — the commonest red eye, but it causes grittiness and discharge, not severe deep pain radiating to the face.
takeaway: Red eye with severe deep pain in rheumatoid arthritis = scleritis; refer urgently.

stem: A patient develops a localised area of red eye with mild discomfort but no visual impairment. The patient is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episcleritis causes superficial, usually mild inflammation and redness of the eye without significant visual impairment.
why_wrong: A. Scleritis causes much more severe deep pain. B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe pain and visual disturbance. C. Keratitis commonly causes pain, photophobia and visual impairment. D. Anterior uveitis causes pain, photophobia and visual disturbance.
pearl: Episcleritis gives sectoral redness with mild discomfort, normal vision and no photophobia; it is usually self-limiting, unlike scleritis, which is severely painful.
thinking: Localised area of red eye ↓ Only mild discomfort ↓ Vision normal ↓ Otherwise well ↓ Episcleritis
exam_trap: A, scleritis — also causes localised redness, but with severe deep pain and possible threat to vision; mild discomfort with normal vision fits episcleritis.
takeaway: Sectoral red eye with mild discomfort and normal vision = episcleritis; severe pain = scleritis.

stem: A patient develops a painful, tender lump at the edge of the eyelid with local redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A stye is an acute, tender infection or inflammation involving an eyelid gland.
why_wrong: A. Subconjunctival haemorrhage causes a painless red patch on the sclera. B. Uveitis causes painful inflammation inside the eye. C. Cataract affects the lens and does not cause an eyelid lump. E. A chalazion is typically painless and chronic.
pearl: An external stye is an acute, painful infection of a gland at the lash margin; warm compresses usually suffice and antibiotics are rarely needed.
thinking: Acute painful lump ↓ At the edge of the eyelid ↓ Tender with local redness ↓ Acute infection of a lid gland ↓ Stye
exam_trap: E, chalazion — also an eyelid lump, but it is a chronic, usually painless blocked meibomian gland rather than an acutely tender lesion at the lid margin.
takeaway: Painful acute lid-margin lump = stye; painless chronic lid lump = chalazion.

stem: A patient develops painful swelling and redness at the inner corner of the eye, with purulent discharge from the lacrimal punctum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dacryocystitis is infection of the lacrimal sac and causes painful swelling near the medial canthus, often with discharge.
why_wrong: A. A chalazion is a painless eyelid lump. B. Orbital cellulitis causes diffuse orbital swelling and systemic illness. D. Scleritis causes severe deep ocular pain. E. Conjunctivitis causes diffuse conjunctival inflammation rather than focal medial-canthus swelling.
pearl: Acute dacryocystitis is a tender swelling at the medial canthus from nasolacrimal duct obstruction; it needs systemic antibiotics, as spread can cause orbital cellulitis.
thinking: Painful swelling at the inner corner of the eye ↓ Local redness ↓ Pus expressed from the lacrimal punctum ↓ Infected lacrimal sac ↓ Dacryocystitis
exam_trap: B, orbital cellulitis — also painful periocular swelling, but it is diffuse with proptosis, painful eye movements and systemic illness; pus from the punctum localises to the sac.
takeaway: Medial canthal swelling with pus from the punctum = dacryocystitis.

stem: A child has reduced vision in one eye despite a normal-looking eye. The reduced vision developed during early childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Amblyopia is reduced visual development in childhood, often affecting one eye, without an adequate structural explanation.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss. C. Cataract causes opacity of the lens. D. Retinal detachment is an acute retinal disorder. E. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye with visual disturbance.
pearl: Amblyopia develops during early visual development from squint, refractive error or visual deprivation; treatment with glasses and patching works best when started early.
thinking: Reduced vision in one eye ↓ Developed in early childhood ↓ Eye looks structurally normal ↓ Abnormal visual development ↓ Amblyopia
exam_trap: C, cataract — a cause of childhood visual loss, but the lens is visibly opaque; reduced vision in a normal-looking eye is amblyopia.
takeaway: Reduced childhood vision in a structurally normal eye = amblyopia; treat early.

stem: A 3-year-old has persistent inward deviation of one eye. What is the main concern if this is left untreated?
why_correct: Persistent childhood strabismus can cause the brain to suppress input from the deviating eye, resulting in amblyopia.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis is an inflammatory optic-nerve disorder. B. Macular degeneration is primarily an age-related retinal condition. D. Retinal artery occlusion is an acute vascular event. E. Strabismus does not directly cause cataract.
pearl: Any persistent squint in a child needs referral to orthoptics or ophthalmology, because the brain suppresses the deviating eye and amblyopia becomes harder to reverse with age.
thinking: Child aged 3 ↓ Persistent inward deviation of one eye ↓ Brain suppresses the deviating eye ↓ Vision fails to develop in that eye ↓ Amblyopia
exam_trap: E, cataract — a childhood eye condition linked with squint, but cataract can cause a squint, not the reverse; the risk of an untreated squint is amblyopia.
takeaway: A persistent childhood squint risks amblyopia — refer promptly.

stem: A patient develops a foreign-body sensation, tearing and discomfort after working with metal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Mechanical exposure to metal followed by foreign-body sensation and tearing strongly suggests a corneal foreign body.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment. C. Acute anterior uveitis causes a painful red eye with photophobia but not a foreign-body sensation after working with metal. D. Glaucoma does not typically cause an acute foreign-body sensation. E. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters or a visual-field defect.
pearl: After metalwork, examine with fluorescein for a corneal foreign body or rust ring; high-velocity injuries such as hammering metal on metal need urgent assessment for penetrating injury.
thinking: Working with metal ↓ Foreign-body sensation ↓ Tearing and discomfort ↓ Particle lodged on the cornea ↓ Corneal foreign body
exam_trap: C, anterior uveitis — also a painful watery eye, but it presents with photophobia and ciliary flush without an injury history; metalwork points to a foreign body.
takeaway: Gritty, watery eye after metalwork = corneal foreign body; think penetrating injury if high-velocity.

stem: Following blunt orbital trauma, a patient develops diplopia and reduced sensation over the cheek. Which nerve is most likely affected?
why_correct: The infraorbital nerve runs through the orbital floor and can be injured in orbital floor fractures, causing numbness over the cheek and upper lip.
why_wrong: A. Glossopharyngeal nerve injury affects swallowing and pharyngeal sensation. B. Optic nerve injury causes visual loss rather than isolated cheek numbness. C. Facial nerve injury causes facial weakness. D. Hypoglossal nerve injury causes tongue weakness.
pearl: The infraorbital nerve runs in the orbital floor, so blow-out fractures cause numbness of the cheek, side of the nose, upper lip and upper teeth.
thinking: Blunt orbital trauma ↓ Diplopia suggests orbital floor fracture ↓ Reduced sensation over the cheek ↓ Sensory nerve in the orbital floor ↓ Infraorbital nerve
exam_trap: C, facial nerve — the main nerve of the face, but it is motor to the facial muscles; injury causes weakness, not cheek numbness.
takeaway: Cheek numbness after orbital trauma = infraorbital nerve injury from a floor fracture.

stem: An elderly patient with diabetes develops severe persistent ear pain and offensive ear discharge. What serious complication should be considered?
why_correct: Severe persistent otitis externa in an older person with diabetes can represent malignant otitis externa, a potentially serious invasive infection.
why_wrong: B. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo. C. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo with auditory symptoms. D. Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss. E. Chronic suppurative otitis media causes painless chronic discharge through a perforation rather than severe persistent pain in an older patient with diabetes.
pearl: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a skull-base osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas, in older people with diabetes or immunosuppression; it needs urgent ENT referral and IV antibiotics.
thinking: Older patient with diabetes ↓ Severe persistent ear pain ↓ Offensive discharge ↓ Invasive canal infection spreading to the skull base ↓ Malignant otitis externa
exam_trap: E, chronic suppurative otitis media — causes persistent discharge, but it is usually painless through a perforation; severe pain in an older person with diabetes signals invasive infection.
takeaway: Severe ear pain and discharge in an older person with diabetes: suspect malignant otitis externa.

stem: A patient has unilateral conductive hearing loss and a blocked sensation. Otoscopy shows a large amount of wax obstructing the external auditory canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Obstructing cerumen can cause a blocked sensation and conductive hearing loss.
why_wrong: A. Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss without visible canal obstruction. B. Ménière disease causes fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss with vertigo. C. Vestibular schwannoma causes sensorineural hearing loss. E. Vestibular neuritis primarily causes prolonged vertigo.
pearl: Impacted wax causes conductive hearing loss and a blocked feeling; soften it first with olive oil or sodium bicarbonate drops, then use irrigation or microsuction if it persists.
thinking: Unilateral blocked ear ↓ Conductive hearing loss ↓ Otoscopy: canal obstructed by wax ↓ Cause directly visible ↓ Impacted earwax
exam_trap: A, otosclerosis — a classic cause of conductive hearing loss, but the canal and drum look normal; visible obstructing wax gives the answer.
takeaway: Conductive loss with wax filling the canal: soften with drops before removal.

stem: A patient with acute otitis media develops sudden relief of ear pain followed by purulent discharge. What complication has most likely occurred?
why_correct: A perforated tympanic membrane can allow infected middle-ear fluid to drain into the external canal, sometimes causing sudden reduction in pressure and pain.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular schwannoma causes progressive sensorineural hearing loss. B. Otosclerosis causes gradual conductive hearing loss. C. Infected cholesteatoma causes chronic painless foul-smelling discharge and hearing loss, not sudden pain relief during acute otitis media. D. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and hearing symptoms.
pearl: In acute otitis media, sudden pain relief followed by discharge means the drum has perforated; most perforations heal spontaneously, so keep water out of the ear and review.
thinking: Acute otitis media ↓ Pressure builds in the middle ear ↓ Sudden relief of pain ↓ Followed by purulent discharge ↓ Tympanic membrane perforation
exam_trap: C, infected cholesteatoma — also causes ear discharge, but it is chronic, foul-smelling and usually painless, not sudden pain relief during an acute infection.
takeaway: Pain relief then discharge in acute otitis media = drum perforation; most heal on their own.

stem: A patient develops a blocked sensation and muffled hearing after an upper respiratory infection. Symptoms worsen during air travel. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Eustachian tube dysfunction can cause pressure and conductive hearing symptoms, particularly during changes in atmospheric pressure.
why_wrong: B. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo with sensorineural hearing symptoms. C. Acute otitis externa causes ear-canal pain, itching and discharge rather than pressure symptoms worsened by air travel. D. Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss unrelated to air-travel pressure changes. E. Vestibular schwannoma causes progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
pearl: Eustachian tube dysfunction after a cold causes muffled hearing and pressure, worse with altitude change; most cases settle, helped by autoinflation or gentle Valsalva manoeuvres.
thinking: Recent upper respiratory infection ↓ Blocked ear, muffled hearing ↓ Worse with pressure change on flying ↓ Poor middle-ear ventilation ↓ Eustachian tube dysfunction
exam_trap: C, acute diffuse otitis externa — can cause a blocked ear, but with canal pain, itch and discharge; pressure symptoms after a cold and on flying point to the Eustachian tube.
takeaway: Blocked ear after a cold, worse when flying = Eustachian tube dysfunction.

stem: A patient develops hoarseness after a viral upper respiratory infection. There is no stridor, dysphagia or respiratory distress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute hoarseness following a viral upper respiratory infection without airway compromise is typical of acute laryngitis.
why_wrong: A. Epiglottitis causes potentially severe airway symptoms. C. Bacterial tracheitis can cause significant systemic illness and airway obstruction. D. Peritonsillar abscess causes unilateral throat pain, trismus and muffled voice. E. Foreign-body aspiration usually has sudden onset with coughing or respiratory symptoms.
pearl: Acute laryngitis is usually viral and settles with voice rest and fluids; hoarseness that persists for more than a few weeks needs ENT assessment to exclude laryngeal cancer.
thinking: Recent viral upper respiratory infection ↓ Hoarseness ↓ No stridor, dysphagia or distress ↓ No airway compromise ↓ Acute laryngitis
exam_trap: A, epiglottitis — a laryngeal-region infection that tempts, but it causes drooling, stridor and respiratory distress, all absent here.
takeaway: Hoarseness after a cold without airway symptoms = acute laryngitis; persistent hoarseness needs ENT.

stem: A patient develops persistent hoarseness following neck surgery. Which structure is most likely to have been injured?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply the intrinsic muscles of the larynx and injury can cause vocal cord palsy and hoarseness.
why_wrong: A. The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement. B. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve supplies the lower lip depressors; injury causes lip asymmetry, not hoarseness. C. The trigeminal nerve supplies facial sensation and muscles of mastication. E. The optic nerve carries visual information.
pearl: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the thyroid gland and is at risk in thyroid and other neck surgery; unilateral injury causes hoarseness, bilateral injury can cause stridor.
thinking: Neck surgery ↓ Persistent hoarseness ↓ Vocal cord palsy ↓ Nerve supplying the intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: B, marginal mandibular nerve — also at risk in neck surgery, but injury causes lower lip asymmetry, not hoarseness.
takeaway: Hoarseness after thyroid or neck surgery = recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

stem: A young adult has irresistible episodes of daytime sleep and brief episodes of sudden muscle weakness triggered by laughter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Narcolepsy can cause excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, with sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions such as laughter.
why_wrong: A. Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition. C. Anxiety does not cause recurrent sleep attacks with cataplexy. D. Obstructive sleep apnoea causes sleep fragmentation and daytime sleepiness but not typical cataplexy. E. Insomnia causes difficulty sleeping rather than irresistible sleep attacks.
pearl: Narcolepsy is excessive daytime sleepiness with cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations; patients must stop driving and inform the DVLA until symptoms are controlled.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Irresistible daytime sleep episodes ↓ Sudden weakness triggered by laughter (cataplexy) ↓ Disorder of sleep-wake regulation ↓ Narcolepsy
exam_trap: D, obstructive sleep apnoea — a common cause of daytime sleepiness, but it does not cause cataplexy; emotion-triggered weakness is specific to narcolepsy.
takeaway: Daytime sleep attacks plus cataplexy = narcolepsy.

stem: A patient has a slow-growing, round lump in the skin with a small central punctum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Epidermoid cysts are common subcutaneous lesions and may have a characteristic central punctum.
why_wrong: A. Dermatofibroma is a firm dermal papule rather than a cystic lump. B. Lipomas are soft, mobile fatty lumps and do not usually have a punctum. C. Abscesses are usually painful and inflamed. D. Melanoma is a malignant pigmented lesion.
pearl: Epidermoid cysts are keratin-filled with a central punctum; inflamed cysts are not excised acutely, and recurrence is common unless the whole cyst wall is removed.
thinking: Slow-growing round lump ↓ Within the skin ↓ Small central punctum ↓ Keratin-filled cyst ↓ Epidermoid cyst
exam_trap: B, lipoma — the commonest benign lump, but it is soft, lobulated and subcutaneous with no punctum.
takeaway: Round skin lump with a central punctum = epidermoid cyst.

stem: A healthcare worker develops a painful cluster of vesicles on a finger after contact with a patient who has an active herpes infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Herpetic whitlow is a painful HSV infection of the finger producing grouped vesicles.
why_wrong: B. Scabies causes an intensely itchy widespread infestation. C. Tinea corporis produces annular scaly lesions. D. Paronychia causes infection around the nail fold and is not characterised by grouped vesicles. E. Cellulitis causes diffuse erythema and swelling.
pearl: Herpetic whitlow is HSV infection of the finger and a recognised risk for healthcare workers; it must not be incised, and the lesion should be kept covered.
thinking: Healthcare worker ↓ Contact with active herpes infection ↓ Painful cluster of vesicles ↓ On a finger ↓ Herpetic whitlow
exam_trap: D, acute paronychia — a painful finger infection, but it is a bacterial nail-fold infection; grouped vesicles mean HSV, which must not be incised.
takeaway: Painful grouped vesicles on a finger = herpetic whitlow; do not incise.

stem: A patient develops recurrent grouped painful vesicles at the border of the lip, often during periods of illness or stress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent grouped vesicles at the lip margin are characteristic of herpes labialis caused by HSV.
why_wrong: A. Aphthous ulcers are painful mucosal ulcers rather than grouped vesicles on the lip margin. B. Angular cheilitis affects the corners of the mouth. C. Oral candidiasis produces removable or adherent white plaques rather than recurrent grouped vesicles. D. Impetigo commonly produces superficial erosions and honey-coloured crusts.
pearl: Herpes labialis is reactivated HSV, triggered by illness, stress or sunlight; topical aciclovir helps most if started at the first prodromal tingle.
thinking: Recurrent episodes ↓ Grouped painful vesicles ↓ At the border of the lip ↓ Triggered by illness or stress ↓ Herpes labialis
exam_trap: D, impetigo — also affects the skin around the mouth, but it causes spreading honey-coloured crusts rather than recurrent grouped vesicles at the lip border.
takeaway: Recurrent grouped lip-border vesicles with illness or stress = herpes labialis.

stem: A patient is prescribed oral alendronate for osteoporosis. Which instruction is appropriate?

options.A: Take it with an antacid to improve its absorption
options.B: Take it at bedtime after the evening meal
options.C: Crush it and mix it with soft food such as yoghurt
options.D: Take it with plenty of water and stay upright
options.E: Take it with milk to protect the stomach lining

correct_answer: D. Take it with plenty of water and stay upright
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonates can irritate the oesophagus and should be taken correctly with water while remaining upright.
why_wrong: A. Antacids can reduce absorption. B. Taking it at bedtime means lying down afterwards, increasing oesophageal irritation, and food reduces absorption. C. Tablets should not routinely be crushed, and food (especially dairy) reduces absorption. E. Milk and calcium reduce absorption; it should be taken with plain water only.
pearl: Take alendronate on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, stay upright for at least 30 minutes and delay food, drinks and other medicines; stop and seek advice if dysphagia or heartburn develops.
thinking: Oral bisphosphonate ↓ Poorly absorbed and irritant to the oesophagus ↓ Needs an empty stomach and plain water ↓ Upright position prevents oesophagitis ↓ Take it with plenty of water and stay upright
exam_trap: E, take it with milk to protect the stomach lining — sounds protective, but calcium in milk binds alendronate and blocks its absorption; plain water only.
takeaway: Alendronate: empty stomach, plain water, stay upright for 30 minutes.

stem: A patient with severe renal impairment receives excessive magnesium-containing medication and develops reduced reflexes and hypotension. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Severe hypermagnesaemia can cause neuromuscular depression, reduced reflexes and hypotension, particularly in renal impairment.
why_wrong: A. Hypomagnesaemia causes neuromuscular irritability and can predispose to arrhythmias. B. Hypercalcaemia has a different clinical pattern. C. Hypernatraemia primarily causes neurological symptoms related to cellular dehydration. E. Hypophosphataemia causes weakness and other metabolic complications but not this characteristic pattern.
pearl: Magnesium is renally excreted, so magnesium-containing antacids or laxatives can accumulate in renal impairment; loss of tendon reflexes is an early warning sign of magnesium toxicity.
thinking: Severe renal impairment ↓ Excess magnesium intake ↓ Reduced excretion, so magnesium accumulates ↓ Reduced reflexes and hypotension ↓ Hypermagnesaemia
exam_trap: A, Hypomagnesaemia — candidates recall that magnesium disorders affect nerves, but low magnesium causes irritability and tetany, not depressed reflexes.
takeaway: Reduced reflexes after magnesium in renal impairment means hypermagnesaemia.

stem: A severely malnourished patient develops profound muscle weakness during nutritional rehabilitation. Which electrolyte disturbance may contribute?
why_correct: Refeeding can cause a rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, producing hypophosphataemia and potentially severe muscle weakness and respiratory failure.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia is not typical. B. Hyperphosphataemia is not the characteristic refeeding abnormality. C. Hypernatraemia is not the defining electrolyte disturbance of refeeding syndrome. E. Hypermagnesaemia is not the characteristic abnormality.
pearl: In refeeding, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells; hypophosphataemia is the hallmark and can cause muscle weakness, respiratory failure and arrhythmias.
thinking: Severe malnutrition ↓ Feeding restarted ↓ Insulin drives phosphate into cells ↓ Low phosphate impairs muscle energy supply ↓ Hypophosphataemia
exam_trap: B, Hyperphosphataemia — candidates know phosphate is involved but reverse the direction; refeeding drops serum phosphate.
takeaway: Weakness during refeeding: think low phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

stem: A patient with SIADH has hyponatraemia. Which urine finding is expected compared with what would normally occur with marked hypotonicity?

options.A: Maximally dilute urine in all cases

why_correct: Excess ADH causes water retention and prevents appropriate urinary dilution, resulting in inappropriately concentrated urine.
why_wrong: A. ADH excess prevents appropriate maximal dilution. B. Haematuria is unrelated. C. Glycosuria is not characteristic of SIADH. D. Urine sodium is not necessarily absent.
pearl: SIADH is euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and continued urinary sodium loss; exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency first.
thinking: Hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality ↓ Normal response is to dilute urine and excrete water ↓ Excess ADH keeps urine concentrated ↓ Inappropriately concentrated urine
exam_trap: A, Maximally dilute urine — this is the normal response to hypotonicity, exactly what SIADH prevents; dilute urine with hyponatraemia suggests primary polydipsia instead.
takeaway: SIADH: low serum osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine.

stem: A patient develops tingling around the mouth and carpopedal spasm several days after total thyroidectomy. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Accidental damage or removal of the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery can cause hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcaemia.
why_wrong: A. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness, not perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. B. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia. E. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia.
pearl: After total thyroidectomy, check calcium routinely; perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm and Chvostek or Trousseau signs indicate hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury, and severe cases need IV calcium gluconate.
thinking: Total thyroidectomy ↓ Parathyroids at risk of injury or removal ↓ Perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm ↓ Hypocalcaemia ↓ Postoperative hypoparathyroidism
exam_trap: A, Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — a classic thyroidectomy complication, but it causes hoarseness, not perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm.
takeaway: Tingling and spasm after thyroidectomy: hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism.

stem: A 45-year-old patient develops progressive involuntary jerky movements, personality changes and cognitive decline. A parent had a similar illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Huntington disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterised by chorea, psychiatric or behavioural changes and progressive cognitive impairment.
why_wrong: A. Multiple sclerosis typically causes episodes of neurological dysfunction separated in time and space. C. Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. D. Essential tremor primarily causes action or postural tremor. E. Myasthenia causes fluctuating fatigable weakness.
pearl: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant with a CAG trinucleotide repeat; anticipation can bring earlier onset in successive generations, and genetic counselling is essential before predictive testing.
thinking: Middle-aged patient ↓ Chorea, personality change and cognitive decline ↓ Affected parent suggests autosomal dominant inheritance ↓ Huntington disease
exam_trap: C, Parkinson disease — a common movement disorder, but it causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor rather than chorea with an affected parent.
takeaway: Chorea, psychiatric change and dementia with an affected parent: Huntington disease.

stem: A patient describes an uncomfortable urge to move both legs, particularly when resting in the evening. Walking temporarily relieves the symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Restless legs syndrome causes an urge to move the legs, usually worse at rest and in the evening, with temporary relief from movement.
why_wrong: A. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness rather than this characteristic sensory urge to move. B. DVT usually causes unilateral swelling and pain. C. Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and other motor features. D. Peripheral arterial disease causes exertional rather than rest-related leg symptoms.
pearl: Restless legs syndrome is linked to iron deficiency, pregnancy and chronic kidney disease; check ferritin and correct iron deficiency as part of management.
thinking: Urge to move the legs ↓ Worse at rest and in the evening ↓ Relieved by walking ↓ Restless legs syndrome
exam_trap: D, Peripheral arterial disease — leg discomfort linked to activity tempts, but claudication comes on with walking and eases with rest, the reverse pattern.
takeaway: An evening urge to move the legs, eased by movement, is restless legs syndrome; check ferritin.

stem: During an episode of cataplexy, which feature is typical?

options.A: Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
options.D: Complete loss of consciousness with prolonged confusion

correct_answer: A. Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
why_correct: Cataplexy consists of sudden transient muscle weakness or paralysis, usually triggered by strong emotion, while consciousness is maintained.
why_wrong: B. Generalised tonic-clonic movements suggest a generalised seizure. C. Progressive memory loss is not cataplexy. D. Prolonged confusion after loss of consciousness suggests another neurological event. E. Persistent unilateral weakness suggests a focal neurological disorder.
pearl: Cataplexy, a sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone with retained awareness, is highly specific for narcolepsy type 1, alongside excessive daytime sleepiness.
thinking: Cataplexy ↓ Triggered by strong emotion such as laughter ↓ Sudden transient loss of muscle tone ↓ Consciousness preserved ↓ Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
exam_trap: D, Loss of consciousness with prolonged confusion — collapse suggests a seizure, but cataplexy preserves awareness and has no post-ictal confusion.
takeaway: Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with full consciousness: think narcolepsy.

stem: A patient becomes markedly unsteady when standing with their feet together and eyes closed, after being relatively stable with their eyes open. What does a positive Romberg test suggest?
why_correct: A positive Romberg test indicates impaired proprioceptive input or vestibular function, with vision compensating while the eyes are open.
why_wrong: B. Aphasia is a language disorder. C. Isolated weakness does not produce the characteristic test finding. D. Facial nerve palsy affects facial movement. E. Lower motor neurone disease is characterised by weakness, wasting and reduced reflexes.
pearl: Romberg tests position sense, not cerebellar function: a patient with cerebellar ataxia is unsteady even with eyes open, whereas sensory ataxia worsens markedly when the eyes close.
thinking: Stable with eyes open ↓ Unsteady when eyes close ↓ Vision was compensating for lost position sense ↓ Positive Romberg ↓ Impaired proprioception
exam_trap: C, Isolated motor weakness — unsteadiness may suggest weakness, but weakness does not worsen specifically when the eyes are closed.
takeaway: A positive Romberg points to sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, not cerebellar disease.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes develops reduced sensation in both feet extending upwards in a symmetrical stocking distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy commonly produces symmetrical distal sensory loss in a stocking distribution.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome causes saddle sensory disturbance and bladder or bowel dysfunction. B. Stroke usually causes an acute focal neurological deficit. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than sensory loss. E. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis typically produces focal or multifocal neurological episodes rather than a symmetrical stocking distribution.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy begins distally and ascends in a stocking distribution; loss of protective sensation raises ulcer risk, so regular foot review with monofilament testing matters.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Symmetrical sensory loss in both feet ↓ Length-dependent stocking distribution ↓ Peripheral diabetic neuropathy
exam_trap: A, Cauda equina syndrome — bilateral lower-limb sensory change tempts, but it causes saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction.
takeaway: Symmetrical stocking sensory loss in diabetes is peripheral neuropathy; protect the feet.

stem: Which nerve root predominantly contributes to knee extension?
why_correct: Knee extension via the quadriceps is predominantly supplied by the femoral nerve, with major contributions from L3 and L4.
why_wrong: A. C5–C6 contributes to upper-limb movements. B. S1–S2 contributes mainly to plantarflexion and other lower-limb functions. C. T1–T2 is associated with upper thoracic and upper-limb innervation. D. L5–S1 is not the principal root contribution to knee extension.
pearl: The knee jerk tests L3–L4 via the femoral nerve, while the ankle jerk tests S1. Quadriceps weakness with a reduced knee jerk points to an L3–L4 root or femoral nerve lesion.
thinking: Knee extension is the movement tested ↓ Performed by quadriceps femoris ↓ Supplied by the femoral nerve ↓ Main root contribution is L3–L4
exam_trap: D, L5–S1 — the familiar lumbar roots of sciatica questions, but they serve ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, not knee extension.
takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk: L3–L4 via the femoral nerve.

stem: A patient has difficulty lifting the front of the foot while walking. Which movement is impaired?
why_correct: Foot drop refers to weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, causing difficulty clearing the foot during walking.
why_wrong: A. Foot drop involves dorsiflexion rather than isolated toe flexion. C. Hip extension is unrelated to the characteristic gait abnormality. D. Plantarflexion weakness is a different motor deficit. E. Knee flexion is not the defining movement affected.
pearl: Foot drop, or weak ankle dorsiflexion, produces a high-stepping gait; common causes include common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck and L5 radiculopathy.
thinking: Cannot lift the front of the foot ↓ Toes catch while walking ↓ Tibialis anterior weakness ↓ Ankle dorsiflexion
exam_trap: D, Ankle plantarflexion — the opposite ankle movement and easily confused; plantarflexion weakness affects push-off, not lifting the forefoot.
takeaway: Foot drop means weak ankle dorsiflexion: think common peroneal nerve or L5.

stem: Which finding is most characteristic of a lower motor neurone lesion?
correct_answer: D. Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
why_correct: Lower motor neurone lesions cause weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations and reduced or absent reflexes.
why_wrong: A. An extensor plantar response indicates an upper motor neurone lesion. B. Spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign. C. Increased tone and brisk reflexes are upper motor neurone features. E. Clonus is associated with hyperreflexia and upper motor neurone lesions.
pearl: LMN lesions give weakness, wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reduced or absent reflexes; UMN lesions give spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus and extensor plantars.
thinking: Lower motor neurone damaged ↓ Muscle loses its nerve supply ↓ Wasting and a broken reflex arc ↓ Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
exam_trap: C, Increased tone and brisk reflexes — often mixed up, but these are upper motor neurone signs; LMN lesions reduce tone and reflexes.
takeaway: LMN: wasting, fasciculation, low tone, reduced reflexes; UMN: the opposite.

stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome develops increasing difficulty breathing and a weak cough. What complication is the greatest immediate concern?
why_correct: Guillain–Barré syndrome can progress to respiratory muscle paralysis, making respiratory function an immediate priority.
why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis does not explain progressive respiratory muscle weakness with a weak cough. B. Asthma causes wheeze and bronchospasm and does not explain progressive weakness with a weak cough. C. Hyperventilation should not be assumed; increasing breathlessness with a weak cough in Guillain–Barré syndrome indicates respiratory muscle weakness. D. Functional dyspnoea should not be assumed in Guillain–Barré syndrome, where breathlessness and a weak cough signal impending respiratory failure.
pearl: In Guillain–Barré syndrome, monitor forced vital capacity regularly; oxygen saturation falls late, and a falling FVC or weak cough needs urgent critical care review.
thinking: Guillain–Barré syndrome ↓ Ascending weakness can reach respiratory muscles ↓ Increasing breathlessness with a weak cough ↓ Neuromuscular respiratory failure
exam_trap: C, Psychogenic hyperventilation — anxiety is common in acute illness, but a weak cough signals respiratory muscle weakness, and blaming anxiety is dangerous.
takeaway: Breathlessness in Guillain–Barré: measure FVC and escalate early.

stem: A previously well older adult suddenly becomes unable to form new memories, repeatedly asking the same questions, while remaining alert and otherwise neurologically intact. The episode resolves within several hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Transient global amnesia causes sudden temporary anterograde memory impairment with repetitive questioning while other neurological functions are relatively preserved.
why_wrong: A. Delirium causes broader disturbance of attention and awareness. B. A generalised seizure would usually involve impaired consciousness and other seizure features. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes sudden severe headache and may cause neurological deterioration. E. Dementia causes persistent rather than transient cognitive impairment.
pearl: Transient global amnesia causes sudden anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning but preserved identity and alertness, resolving within 24 hours; recurrence is uncommon.
thinking: Older adult, sudden onset ↓ Cannot form new memories, repeats questions ↓ Alert and otherwise neurologically intact ↓ Resolves within hours ↓ Transient global amnesia
exam_trap: A, Delirium — acute confusion in an older adult tempts, but delirium impairs attention and awareness, whereas here alertness is preserved and only memory fails.
takeaway: Sudden isolated amnesia with repetitive questions, resolving within a day: transient global amnesia.

stem: An elderly hospital patient becomes acutely confused over one day. Their attention fluctuates and they cannot maintain a conversation. What feature most strongly supports delirium?
correct_answer: D. Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention
why_correct: Delirium is characterised by an acute disturbance in attention and awareness that often fluctuates.
why_wrong: A. Long-term personality change suggests another chronic neurological or psychiatric process. B. Gradual decline over years is more consistent with dementia. C. Isolated stable amnesia does not capture the fluctuating attentional disturbance of delirium. E. Lifelong learning difficulty suggests a developmental condition.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention; screen at-risk older inpatients with a tool such as the 4AT and seek causes like infection, drugs, dehydration, pain, constipation and urinary retention.
thinking: Elderly inpatient ↓ Acute onset over one day ↓ Fluctuating attention, cannot hold a conversation ↓ Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention
exam_trap: B, Gradual memory decline over years — memory problems in older patients suggest dementia, but delirium is acute and fluctuating.
takeaway: Acute onset with fluctuating inattention is the hallmark of delirium.

stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of a limb. Neurological examination shows findings that are inconsistent with recognised neuroanatomical patterns, and investigations do not demonstrate a structural lesion. What diagnosis may explain the presentation?

options.A: Acute ischaemic stroke in the internal capsule

why_correct: Functional neurological disorder can cause genuine neurological symptoms associated with abnormal nervous-system functioning without an explanatory structural lesion; diagnosis is based on positive clinical features of inconsistency or incongruence.
why_wrong: A. Stroke produces a neurological deficit corresponding to a vascular territory or recognised syndrome. B. Motor neurone disease causes progressive upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction. C. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis produces deficits corresponding to demyelinating lesions, usually visible on MRI. E. A peripheral mononeuropathy follows a recognised nerve-distribution pattern.
pearl: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive signs such as Hoover sign, not simply by excluding disease; explain the diagnosis clearly, as symptoms are genuine, and consider specialist physiotherapy.
thinking: Sudden limb weakness ↓ Signs inconsistent with neuroanatomy ↓ No structural lesion on investigation ↓ Genuine symptoms from altered nervous-system function ↓ Functional neurological disorder
exam_trap: C, Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis — tempting because MS signs vary, but its deficits follow anatomy and usually show lesions on MRI.
takeaway: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency.

stem: A patient develops ipsilateral facial weakness together with weakness and sensory abnormalities affecting the opposite side of the body. Where is the lesion most likely located?
why_correct: Crossed neurological signs involving cranial nerve findings on one side and long-tract body findings on the opposite side suggest a brainstem lesion.
why_wrong: A. A lumbar spinal cord lesion cannot produce ipsilateral cranial nerve findings. C. A peripheral nerve lesion does not produce contralateral body weakness. D. Neuromuscular-junction disorders do not produce crossed neurological deficits. E. A purely cerebellar lesion causes coordination abnormalities rather than this classic crossed pattern.
pearl: Crossed signs, a cranial nerve deficit on one side with limb weakness or sensory loss on the other, localise to the brainstem, where cranial nerve nuclei lie beside long tracts serving the opposite side of the body.
thinking: Ipsilateral facial weakness: cranial nerve ↓ Contralateral body weakness and sensory change: long tracts ↓ Crossed signs ↓ Brainstem
exam_trap: E, Cerebellar hemisphere only — the posterior fossa location tempts, but cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, not crossed weakness and sensory loss.
takeaway: Crossed cranial nerve and body signs localise to the brainstem.

stem: A patient develops sudden severe vertigo, inability to walk and marked limb ataxia. Which diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Sudden severe vertigo accompanied by inability to walk or marked neurological signs is concerning for a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo without persistent severe neurological deficits. B. Tension headache does not cause acute cerebellar signs. C. Peripheral neuropathy develops differently and does not cause sudden severe vertigo. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than acute vertigo and ataxia.
pearl: Acute vertigo with inability to walk, limb ataxia or other neurological signs suggests a central cause such as cerebellar stroke; urgent imaging is needed, as swelling can compress the brainstem.
thinking: Sudden severe vertigo ↓ Unable to walk ↓ Marked limb ataxia ↓ Central rather than peripheral cause ↓ Cerebellar stroke
exam_trap: A, Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — the commonest cause of vertigo, but it is brief and positional and does not cause limb ataxia or inability to walk.
takeaway: Vertigo with ataxia or inability to walk is central until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance. Which vascular territory should be considered?
why_correct: Brainstem and posterior-circulation ischaemia can produce symptoms such as diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia.
why_wrong: A. Renal circulation does not cause these neurological symptoms. B. Coronary circulation supplies the heart. C. Middle cerebral artery syndromes more typically affect the lateral cerebral hemisphere. E. Anterior cerebral artery disease predominantly affects medial frontal/parietal regions and the leg.
pearl: Posterior circulation TIA or stroke causes diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo, ataxia and visual field loss; these need the same urgent stroke assessment as anterior circulation events.
thinking: Recurrent transient episodes ↓ Diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance ↓ Brainstem and cerebellar features ↓ Posterior circulation ↓ Vertebrobasilar circulation
exam_trap: C, Middle cerebral artery only — the most familiar stroke territory, but MCA events cause contralateral weakness, sensory loss and aphasia, not diplopia with imbalance.
takeaway: Diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance point to vertebrobasilar ischaemia.

stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of haemolytic anaemia and a family history of similar illness. Which inherited condition causes red cells to become spherical and prone to haemolysis?
why_correct: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing spherical erythrocytes and haemolytic anaemia.
why_wrong: A. von Willebrand disease causes impaired primary haemostasis. B. Haemophilia A is a coagulation-factor deficiency. C. Thalassaemia involves impaired globin-chain production. E. Sickle cell disease causes abnormal haemoglobin and sickling.
pearl: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant and causes haemolysis, jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones; spherocytes on the film with a negative direct antiglobulin test support it.
thinking: Recurrent haemolytic anaemia ↓ Family history ↓ Inherited red-cell membrane defect ↓ Spherical red cells ↓ Hereditary spherocytosis
exam_trap: E, Sickle cell disease — inherited and haemolytic, but the defect is an abnormal haemoglobin causing sickled cells, not spherical cells.
takeaway: Inherited haemolysis with spherical red cells is hereditary spherocytosis.

stem: A boy has recurrent haemarthroses and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Which clotting-factor deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency and classically causes deep bleeding such as haemarthroses.
why_wrong: B. Factor XIII deficiency has a different presentation and routine clotting tests may be normal. C. Factor IX deficiency causes haemophilia B. D. Factor X deficiency is a different, rare inherited bleeding disorder. E. Factor VII deficiency primarily affects the extrinsic pathway.
pearl: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked and mainly affect males; both prolong the APTT with a normal PT and platelet count, and only factor assays separate factor VIII from factor IX deficiency.
thinking: Boy, fitting X-linked inheritance ↓ Recurrent haemarthroses, a deep bleeding pattern ↓ Prolonged APTT ↓ Haemophilia, most commonly type A ↓ Factor VIII
exam_trap: C, Factor IX — also X-linked with haemarthroses and a prolonged APTT, but haemophilia B is less common, so factor VIII deficiency is the most likely.
takeaway: Boy with haemarthroses and a prolonged APTT: haemophilia A, factor VIII.

stem: A young adult presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and reports drenching night sweats. Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Hodgkin lymphoma commonly presents in younger adults with painless lymphadenopathy and may cause systemic symptoms such as night sweats.
why_wrong: A. Multiple myeloma predominantly affects older adults and causes bone, renal and calcium abnormalities. B. Iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than persistent lymphadenopathy. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes thrombocytopenia rather than persistent lymphadenopathy. D. Haemophilia causes bleeding.
pearl: Hodgkin lymphoma often affects young adults; B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss) and alcohol-induced node pain are classic clues, and Reed–Sternberg cells on biopsy confirm it.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Painless cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Drenching night sweats, a B symptom ↓ Lymphoma typical of this age group ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: A, Multiple myeloma — a haematological malignancy, but it affects older adults with bone pain, renal impairment and hypercalcaemia, not painless nodes.
takeaway: Young adult with painless nodes and B symptoms: think Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A patient has a painless cervical lymph node that has progressively enlarged over several weeks. What feature makes malignancy particularly concerning?

options.A: A small mobile node that is shrinking
options.B: Recent mild sore throat that has resolved
options.D: Generalised itch after using a new soap

why_correct: Persistent, progressive, unexplained lymphadenopathy warrants assessment for malignancy among other causes.
why_wrong: A. A shrinking node is less concerning than progressive enlargement. B. A resolving sore throat can cause reactive lymphadenopathy. C. Tenderness may occur with an acute inflammatory process. D. Local skin irritation does not explain progressive lymph-node enlargement.
pearl: Unexplained lymphadenopathy that persists or keeps enlarging, especially if painless, hard or fixed, or with night sweats or weight loss, warrants urgent assessment for malignancy.
thinking: Painless cervical node ↓ Progressively enlarging over weeks ↓ Not explained by recent infection ↓ Malignancy concern ↓ Persistent progressive enlargement
exam_trap: B, Recent sore throat that has resolved — this explains reactive nodes, which settle; it is persistent growth over weeks that raises concern.
takeaway: A painless node that keeps growing needs assessment for malignancy.

stem: A 19-year-old develops fever, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy and marked fatigue. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis is classically caused by Epstein–Barr virus and commonly causes fever, pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and prolonged fatigue.
