pearl: Healthcare workers at risk of exposure to blood and body fluids should be vaccinated against hepatitis B, with a check of antibody response after the course.
thinking: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids ↓ Healthcare workers have occupational exposure ↓ Vaccination protects them ↓ Healthcare workers at occupational risk
exam_trap: C, patients with osteoarthritis only — a chronic condition may sound like a reason to vaccinate, but osteoarthritis carries no blood-borne virus risk.
takeaway: Healthcare workers exposed to blood should be vaccinated against hepatitis B.

stem: A hospitalised patient develops frequent watery diarrhoea after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Antibiotic exposure can disrupt normal bowel flora and allow C. difficile to cause diarrhoea and colitis.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption rather than typically acute post-antibiotic diarrhoea. B. IBS does not cause an acute antibiotic-associated inflammatory diarrhoeal illness. C. UC is chronic inflammatory bowel disease and is not specifically associated with recent antibiotic exposure. E. Crohn disease is chronic inflammatory bowel disease.
pearl: New diarrhoea after broad-spectrum antibiotics in hospital suggests C. difficile infection; send a stool sample, isolate the patient and stop or review the antibiotic if possible.
thinking: Hospitalised patient ↓ Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ Normal gut flora disrupted ↓ Frequent watery diarrhoea ↓ C. difficile infection
exam_trap: C, ulcerative colitis — it causes diarrhoea and colitis, but it is chronic and not specifically triggered by recent antibiotics.
takeaway: Diarrhoea after antibiotics in hospital: suspect C. difficile.

stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile diarrhoea is admitted to hospital. Which infection-control measure is particularly important?

options.A: Sharing a bathroom with other patients
options.C: No hand hygiene if gloves are worn

correct_answer: D. Appropriate isolation and contact precautions
why_correct: C. difficile can spread through contaminated environments and spores, so appropriate isolation and infection-control measures are important.
why_wrong: A. Shared bathroom facilities increase transmission risk. B. Airborne isolation alone is not the relevant precaution. C. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. E. Contaminated equipment can facilitate transmission.
pearl: C. difficile spores survive on surfaces and are not killed by alcohol gel; isolate patients and use gloves, aprons and soap-and-water handwashing.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile diarrhoea ↓ Spores contaminate the environment ↓ Spread by contact ↓ Alcohol gel does not kill spores ↓ Appropriate isolation and contact precautions
exam_trap: B, routine airborne isolation only — isolation is right, but C. difficile spreads by contact, so airborne precautions alone miss the main route.
takeaway: C. difficile: isolate, use contact precautions and wash hands with soap and water.

stem: A patient develops a painful vesicular rash involving the forehead and tip of the nose. What complication should be particularly considered?

options.A: Ramsay Hunt syndrome of the ear
options.C: Tinea pedis of the toe webs

why_correct: Involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve can threaten the eye and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves the facial nerve with vesicles in or around the ear, not the forehead and nasal tip. C. Tinea pedis affects the feet. D. Cellulitis of the leg is unrelated. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes scaly erythema, not a painful dermatomal vesicular eruption.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) suggest nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of eye involvement in shingles; start antivirals and arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Painful vesicular rash ↓ Forehead involvement ↓ Tip of the nose involved ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: A, Ramsay Hunt syndrome — it is also facial shingles, but it involves the facial nerve with vesicles in or around the ear.
takeaway: Shingles on the forehead or nose tip: think ophthalmic involvement and refer urgently.

stem: A child develops painful clusters of vesicles and ulcers throughout the mouth with fever and difficulty eating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Primary HSV infection in children can cause fever with widespread painful oral vesicles and ulcers, often involving the gums.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection with honey-crusted lesions, not widespread intraoral vesicles. B. Candidiasis produces white plaques rather than widespread painful vesicular ulcers. C. Leukoplakia is a persistent white mucosal patch rather than an acute febrile illness. D. Recurrent aphthous ulcers are discrete ulcers without a febrile vesicular illness.
pearl: Primary HSV infection in young children causes herpetic gingivostomatitis: fever, swollen gums and many painful oral ulcers; the main risk is dehydration from poor intake.
thinking: Child with fever and difficulty eating ↓ Painful vesicles and ulcers throughout the mouth ↓ Typical of primary HSV infection ↓ Herpetic gingivostomatitis
exam_trap: D, recurrent minor aphthous ulcers — they are painful mouth ulcers, but they are few and discrete, without fever or widespread vesicles.
takeaway: Fever with widespread painful oral vesicles in a child: herpetic gingivostomatitis.

stem: A young woman develops painful loss of vision in one eye. Colour vision is reduced and the symptoms develop over several days. Which diagnosis is an important consideration?
why_correct: Painful subacute visual loss, particularly with impaired colour vision, is characteristic of optic neuritis and may be associated with multiple sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment commonly causes flashes, floaters or a curtain-like visual field defect. B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe painful red eye and markedly raised intraocular pressure. C. Conjunctivitis causes red eye and discharge rather than this pattern of visual loss. E. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment.
pearl: Optic neuritis causes subacute visual loss with pain on eye movement and reduced colour vision, often with a relative afferent pupillary defect; it can be the first sign of multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Painful loss of vision in one eye ↓ Reduced colour vision ↓ Develops over days ↓ Optic nerve inflammation ↓ Optic neuritis
exam_trap: B, acute angle-closure glaucoma — it causes painful visual loss, but onset is sudden with a red eye, haloes and a hard eye, not reduced colour vision over days.
takeaway: Painful subacute monocular visual loss with poor colour vision: optic neuritis.

stem: A patient with motor neurone disease develops progressive difficulty speaking and swallowing. What is this most consistent with?
why_correct: Motor neurone disease can affect the bulbar muscles responsible for speech and swallowing.
why_wrong: B. Cerebellar stroke can cause coordination problems but does not explain the progressive pattern in established MND. C. Peripheral vascular disease affects circulation. D. Optic neuritis causes visual symptoms. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Bulbar involvement in motor neurone disease causes dysarthria and dysphagia, with risk of aspiration and malnutrition; it needs early speech, swallowing and nutrition planning.
thinking: Motor neurone disease ↓ Progressive speech difficulty ↓ Progressive swallowing difficulty ↓ Brainstem motor nuclei affected ↓ Bulbar involvement
exam_trap: B, cerebellar stroke — it can cause slurred speech, but it is sudden, and progressive speech and swallowing loss in MND reflects bulbar disease.
takeaway: Progressive speech and swallowing problems in MND mean bulbar involvement.

stem: A patient has an unsteady gait that becomes markedly worse when their eyes are closed. Which neurological deficit is most likely contributing?
why_correct: Sensory ataxia due to impaired proprioception becomes worse when visual compensation is removed by closing the eyes.
why_wrong: A. Hallucinations do not explain the gait disturbance. B. Hearing loss does not cause this characteristic pattern. D. Loss of smell does not cause ataxia. E. Facial weakness does not cause sensory ataxia.
pearl: Sensory ataxia from loss of proprioception worsens when the eyes are closed, giving a positive Romberg test; causes include B12 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy.
thinking: Unsteady gait ↓ Markedly worse with eyes closed ↓ Vision was compensating ↓ Position sense is lost ↓ Loss of proprioception
exam_trap: B, isolated hearing loss — inner ear problems can affect balance, but hearing loss alone does not cause gait that worsens with eyes closed.
takeaway: Gait much worse with eyes closed means proprioceptive loss.

stem: Which is a recognised non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease?
why_correct: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease and may occur before prominent motor symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria for a different reason. B. Haemoptysis is respiratory tract bleeding. D. Urticaria is an allergic skin condition. E. Haematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: Parkinson's disease has important non-motor features, including constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and dementia; some can come years before tremor.
thinking: Non-motor feature of Parkinson's needed ↓ Autonomic involvement affects the gut ↓ Slowed bowel motility ↓ Can precede motor signs ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: A, polyuria from diabetes insipidus — urinary symptoms are common in Parkinson's, but they reflect bladder dysfunction, not diabetes insipidus.
takeaway: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease.

stem: A patient experiences an electric-shock sensation travelling down the spine and into the limbs when flexing the neck. What is this called?
why_correct: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock-like sensation triggered by neck flexion and can occur with cervical cord pathology, including multiple sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Murphy sign is associated with acute cholecystitis. B. Babinski sign assesses corticospinal tract function. C. Romberg sign assesses proprioception and balance. D. Tinel sign is used to elicit nerve irritation, often at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.
pearl: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock sensation down the spine and limbs on neck flexion, suggesting cervical cord disease such as multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Electric-shock sensation ↓ Travels down the spine into the limbs ↓ Triggered by neck flexion ↓ Cervical cord pathology ↓ Lhermitte sign
exam_trap: D, Tinel sign — it also produces tingling, but by tapping over a peripheral nerve such as the median nerve at the wrist.
takeaway: Electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion are Lhermitte sign.

stem: A patient develops sudden weakness and loss of sensation affecting the right side of the body. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely responsible?

options.C: Peripheral nerves of the right leg only

why_correct: The cerebral hemispheres predominantly control the opposite side of the body, so a left hemispheric lesion can cause right-sided weakness and sensory loss.
why_wrong: A. A right hemispheric lesion would typically produce left-sided deficits. B. A spinal lesion would depend on its level and pattern. C. A peripheral nerve lesion would not usually affect an entire side of the body. D. Cerebellar lesions mainly cause coordination problems.
pearl: Each cerebral hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, so sudden right-sided weakness and numbness point to a left hemisphere lesion, which may also affect language.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Right-sided sensory loss ↓ Motor and sensory pathways cross over ↓ Lesion is on the opposite side ↓ Left hemisphere
exam_trap: A, right hemisphere — candidates may link the deficit to the same side, but motor and sensory pathways cross, so right-sided signs mean a left-sided lesion.
takeaway: Right-sided weakness and sensory loss point to a left hemisphere lesion.

stem: A patient develops loss of vision in the outer halves of both visual fields. What is this visual-field defect called?
why_correct: Loss of the temporal visual fields of both eyes is bitemporal hemianopia and can result from optic chiasm compression.
why_wrong: A. Monocular blindness affects one eye. C. A central scotoma affects central vision. D. Homonymous hemianopia affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes. E. Diplopia means double vision rather than loss of a visual field.
pearl: Bitemporal hemianopia is loss of the outer (temporal) halves of both visual fields, caused by optic chiasm compression, most often by a pituitary tumour.
thinking: Loss of the outer halves ↓ Both visual fields affected ↓ Temporal fields lost in each eye ↓ Crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm ↓ Bitemporal hemianopia
exam_trap: D, homonymous hemianopia — it also affects both eyes, but it is loss of the same side of the field in each eye from a lesion behind the chiasm.
takeaway: Loss of both outer visual fields is bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression.

stem: Which joint is commonly affected in rheumatoid arthritis but is usually spared in osteoarthritis of the hands?

options.A: Interphalangeal joint of the great toe

why_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis commonly affects the MCP and PIP joints, whereas DIP involvement is less typical.
why_wrong: A. This is not a typical distinguishing hand-joint pattern. B. The first CMC joint is commonly affected by osteoarthritis. D. DIP involvement is characteristic of hand osteoarthritis. E. Distal interphalangeal disease is more typical of osteoarthritis.
pearl: Rheumatoid arthritis affects the MCP and PIP joints and spares the DIPs, while hand osteoarthritis affects the DIPs, PIPs and thumb base.
thinking: Need a joint typical of RA ↓ RA affects MCP and PIP joints ↓ Hand OA hits DIPs and thumb base ↓ MCPs usually spared in OA ↓ Metacarpophalangeal joint
exam_trap: D, distal interphalangeal joint — it is a classic hand-arthritis joint, but DIP disease is typical of osteoarthritis and is usually spared in RA.
takeaway: MCP involvement suggests RA; DIP and thumb-base involvement suggests OA.

stem: Which is a recognised extra-articular feature of rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Rheumatoid nodules are a recognised extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, particularly in established disease.
why_wrong: A. Café-au-lait spots are pigmented skin lesions with different associations. B. Koplik spots occur in measles. D. Xanthelasma is associated with lipid deposition. E. Erythema migrans occurs in Lyme disease.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, painless lumps over pressure areas such as the extensor forearm, more common in seropositive, established rheumatoid arthritis.
thinking: Extra-articular feature of RA needed ↓ RA is systemic ↓ Firm subcutaneous lumps at pressure points ↓ Rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: E, erythema migrans — Lyme disease can also cause arthritis, but erythema migrans is its expanding rash, not a feature of RA.
takeaway: Rheumatoid nodules are a classic extra-articular feature of RA.

stem: Why is septic arthritis treated as a medical emergency?

options.A: It causes persistent hyperuricaemia and gout
options.B: It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
options.C: It usually resolves without treatment within days
options.D: It often progresses to rheumatoid arthritis

correct_answer: B. It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
why_correct: Infection within a joint can rapidly damage cartilage and may lead to bacteraemia and sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Hyperuricaemia is associated with gout, not septic arthritis. C. Untreated septic arthritis does not resolve spontaneously and can cause severe complications. D. It does not cause rheumatoid arthritis. E. Septic arthritis does not cause generalised osteoporosis.
pearl: Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days and cause sepsis; a hot, swollen joint needs urgent aspiration and cultures before IV antibiotics where safe.
thinking: Bacteria in the joint space ↓ Cartilage can be destroyed rapidly ↓ Infection can spread to the blood ↓ Delay worsens outcome ↓ It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
exam_trap: A, causes persistent hyperuricaemia and gout — gout is the main differential for a hot joint, but septic arthritis does not cause hyperuricaemia.
takeaway: A hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until aspirated: treat as an emergency.

stem: Which symptom is particularly suggestive of giant cell arteritis?
why_correct: Jaw claudication is a characteristic symptom of giant cell arteritis and reflects vascular insufficiency affecting the muscles of mastication.
why_wrong: A. Pain triggered by swallowing cold drinks is not characteristic of GCA. B. Fatty-food-related pain suggests biliary disease. C. Jaw clicking may occur with temporomandibular joint disorders. D. Tooth sensitivity suggests dental pathology.
pearl: Jaw claudication is one of the most specific symptoms of giant cell arteritis; start high-dose steroids promptly to protect vision while confirming the diagnosis.
thinking: Possible giant cell arteritis ↓ Arteries to the jaw muscles inflamed ↓ Reduced blood flow when chewing ↓ Pain with use of muscles ↓ Jaw pain on chewing
exam_trap: C, jaw clicking only — it involves the jaw, but clicking points to temporomandibular joint disorder, not ischaemic pain on chewing.
takeaway: Jaw pain on chewing is jaw claudication, suggesting giant cell arteritis.

stem: Which medication is an important risk factor for osteoporosis when used long term?
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy increases bone loss and fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Topical antibiotics do not cause osteoporosis. C. Topical emollients do not cause significant systemic bone loss. D. Inhaled salbutamol is not a major osteoporosis risk factor. E. Paracetamol is not a major cause of osteoporosis.
pearl: Long-term oral corticosteroids are the commonest drug cause of osteoporosis; assess fracture risk and consider bone protection for patients on prolonged courses.
thinking: Medication causing osteoporosis ↓ Taken long term ↓ Must have systemic effect ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation ↓ Oral corticosteroids
exam_trap: D, inhaled salbutamol therapy — long-term inhaler use in asthma may suggest steroids, but salbutamol is a bronchodilator and not a major bone risk.
takeaway: Long-term oral steroids are the classic drug cause of osteoporosis.

stem: Which person is at increased risk of vitamin D deficiency?

options.A: A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
options.C: A person with a balanced diet and adequate sunlight
options.D: A person who regularly spends time outdoors
options.E: A person with isolated seasonal rhinitis

correct_answer: A. A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
why_correct: Reduced exposure to sunlight reduces cutaneous vitamin D synthesis and increases the risk of deficiency.
why_wrong: B. Paracetamol does not cause vitamin D deficiency. C. Adequate dietary intake and sunlight reduce deficiency risk. D. Regular outdoor exposure generally supports vitamin D synthesis. E. Seasonal rhinitis does not itself cause vitamin D deficiency.
pearl: Most vitamin D comes from skin synthesis in sunlight, so people with little sun exposure, such as the housebound, are at risk; supplements may be advised for at-risk groups.
thinking: Vitamin D mostly made in skin ↓ Needs sunlight ↓ Very limited sun exposure ↓ Reduced synthesis ↓ A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
exam_trap: C, balanced diet and adequate sunlight — it mentions the right factors, but describes protection, not risk.
takeaway: Limited sunlight exposure is a key risk factor for vitamin D deficiency.

stem: A young woman develops photosensitive facial erythema over the cheeks and bridge of the nose, sparing the nasolabial folds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A photosensitive malar rash that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
why_wrong: A. Rosacea commonly affects the central face with flushing and papules but has a different pattern and does not spare the nasolabial folds. B. Impetigo typically produces superficial crusted lesions. D. Cellulitis or erysipelas is usually unilateral, painful and associated with warmth and fever. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis commonly affects areas such as the nasolabial folds and scalp.
pearl: The malar (butterfly) rash of SLE is a photosensitive erythema over the cheeks and nasal bridge that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds; check ANA when SLE is suspected.
thinking: Photosensitive facial rash ↓ Cheeks and bridge of the nose ↓ Nasolabial folds spared ↓ Malar rash ↓ Systemic lupus erythematosus
exam_trap: A, rosacea with flushing — it also causes central facial redness, but it brings papules and pustules and does not spare the nasolabial folds.
takeaway: Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds suggests SLE.

stem: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus notices that her skin symptoms worsen after significant sun exposure. What is this feature called?
why_correct: Photosensitivity, in which ultraviolet exposure provokes or worsens skin manifestations, is a recognised feature of SLE.
why_wrong: A. Claudication is exertional pain caused by inadequate blood supply. B. Dactylitis is diffuse swelling of a digit. D. The Koebner phenomenon describes lesions appearing at sites of skin trauma, classically in psoriasis. E. Raynaud phenomenon causes episodic colour changes of digits in response to cold or stress.
pearl: Photosensitivity, where sunlight triggers or worsens skin lesions, is common in SLE; sun protection is an important part of management.
thinking: Patient with SLE ↓ Skin symptoms worsen ↓ Trigger is sun exposure ↓ Ultraviolet light provokes the disease ↓ Photosensitivity
exam_trap: E, Raynaud phenomenon — it is common in SLE, but it is triggered by cold or stress and causes colour change in the digits, not sunlight-provoked rash.
takeaway: Skin worsening after sun exposure in SLE is photosensitivity.

stem: A patient with systemic sclerosis has progressive difficulty swallowing and symptoms of reflux. Which organ system is commonly affected?
why_correct: Systemic sclerosis commonly affects oesophageal motility and can cause reflux and dysphagia.
why_wrong: A. Gallbladder disease is not the typical gastrointestinal manifestation. C. Appendiceal disease is not a characteristic manifestation. D. Middle-ear disease does not explain these symptoms. E. The retina is not responsible for dysphagia or reflux.
pearl: Systemic sclerosis often affects the oesophagus: smooth muscle fibrosis causes poor motility and a weak lower sphincter, leading to dysphagia and reflux.
thinking: Systemic sclerosis causes smooth muscle fibrosis ↓ Swallowing difficulty and reflux ↓ Poor motility and weak lower sphincter ↓ Oesophagus
exam_trap: A, gallbladder only — it is a digestive organ, but it does not cause dysphagia, and the gut organ typical of systemic sclerosis is the oesophagus.
takeaway: Dysphagia and reflux in systemic sclerosis reflect oesophageal involvement.

stem: Which symptom is most characteristic of keratoconjunctivitis sicca in Sjögren syndrome?
correct_answer: D. Gritty sensation in the eyes
why_correct: Reduced tear production commonly causes dry, gritty or burning eyes in Sjögren syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Flashes and floaters raise concern for vitreoretinal pathology. B. Sudden blindness requires urgent assessment for other causes. C. Purulent ear discharge suggests ear infection. E. Severe unilateral orbital pain suggests other acute ocular conditions.
pearl: Sjögren syndrome reduces tear and saliva production, so dry, gritty eyes and dry mouth are typical; Schirmer test measures tear flow.
thinking: Sjögren syndrome ↓ Lacrimal glands damaged ↓ Reduced tears ↓ Dry ocular surface ↓ Gritty sensation in the eyes
exam_trap: E, severe unilateral orbital pain — eye discomfort occurs in dry eye, but it is a bilateral gritty feeling, not severe one-sided orbital pain.
takeaway: Gritty, dry eyes are the typical eye symptom of Sjögren syndrome.

stem: A patient with known heart failure develops bilateral pleural effusions. What is the most likely mechanism?
why_correct: Heart failure raises hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary circulation, promoting transudation of fluid into the pleural space.
why_wrong: A. Bronchial obstruction is not the usual mechanism. C. Infection can cause an exudative effusion but is not the mechanism in uncomplicated heart failure. D. Alveolar destruction is associated with emphysema rather than this mechanism. E. Pulmonary embolism is not present in every patient with heart-failure-related effusions.
pearl: Heart failure causes transudative pleural effusions, usually bilateral, from raised hydrostatic pressure; atypical features such as a one-sided effusion need further investigation.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ Raised venous and capillary pressures ↓ Fluid pushed out into the pleura ↓ Transudate, usually bilateral ↓ Increased hydrostatic pressure
exam_trap: C, bacterial invasion of the pleura — infection does cause effusions, but they are exudates, usually one-sided and not the mechanism in heart failure.
takeaway: Bilateral effusions in heart failure are transudates from raised hydrostatic pressure.

stem: A patient being treated for pneumonia develops increasing breathlessness and persistent fever. Imaging shows fluid adjacent to the infected lung. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Fluid accumulating in the pleural space in association with pneumonia is a parapneumonic effusion.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic interstitial process. B. Pulmonary hypertension is elevated pulmonary arterial pressure. D. Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space. E. Emphysema is characterised by destruction of alveolar walls.
pearl: A parapneumonic effusion is pleural fluid next to a pneumonia; persistent fever or slow recovery should prompt imaging and possibly aspiration to exclude empyema.
thinking: Pneumonia on treatment ↓ Worsening breathlessness ↓ Persistent fever ↓ Fluid next to infected lung ↓ Parapneumonic effusion
exam_trap: D, pneumothorax — it also causes increasing breathlessness, but it is air, not fluid, in the pleural space.
takeaway: Pleural fluid next to a pneumonia is a parapneumonic effusion.

stem: A patient with pneumonia has persistent fever despite antibiotics. Imaging demonstrates a loculated pleural collection containing pus. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: An infected pleural collection containing pus is an empyema.
why_wrong: B. Fibrosis is chronic scar formation. C. A simple effusion is not a purulent infected collection. D. Pneumothorax contains air rather than pus. E. Pulmonary oedema involves fluid within the lungs rather than a purulent pleural collection.
pearl: An empyema is pus in the pleural space; it needs chest drainage as well as antibiotics, and complex or loculated collections may need specialist intervention.
thinking: Pneumonia with persistent fever ↓ Not responding to antibiotics ↓ Loculated pleural collection ↓ Contains pus ↓ Empyema
exam_trap: C, simple pleural effusion — both are fluid in the pleural space, but a simple effusion is not purulent and does not form loculated pus.
takeaway: Pus in the pleural space is an empyema and needs drainage.

stem: Which physical sign may occur in pulmonary fibrosis?

options.D: Pitting oedema as the defining feature

why_correct: Digital clubbing can occur in several interstitial lung diseases, including pulmonary fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Flapping tremor is associated with metabolic encephalopathy. C. Cyanosis may occur in severe respiratory disease but is not the characteristic distinguishing sign. D. Pitting oedema is not the defining physical sign of pulmonary fibrosis. E. Splinter haemorrhages have different causes, including infective endocarditis.
pearl: Pulmonary fibrosis classically causes fine bibasal inspiratory crackles and may cause digital clubbing.
thinking: Pulmonary fibrosis ↓ Chronic interstitial lung disease ↓ Linked with changes in the digits ↓ Recognised sign on hand examination ↓ Digital clubbing
exam_trap: C, central cyanosis only — it can occur in severe disease, but it is not specific and does not characterise fibrosis.
takeaway: Clubbing and fine bibasal crackles suggest pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A patient with bronchiectasis develops an episode of coughing up blood. What is this symptom called?
why_correct: Haemoptysis means coughing up blood originating from the respiratory tract.
why_wrong: A. Epistaxis is bleeding from the nose. B. Haematemesis is vomiting blood. C. Haematuria is blood in the urine. D. Melaena refers to black, tarry stool usually caused by upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: Haemoptysis is coughing up blood from the respiratory tract; bronchiectasis is a recognised cause, and massive haemoptysis is a medical emergency.
thinking: Patient with bronchiectasis ↓ Blood brought up by coughing ↓ Source is the airways, not the gut ↓ Haemoptysis
exam_trap: B, haematemesis — both involve blood from the mouth, but haematemesis is vomited blood from the upper GI tract, not coughed up.
takeaway: Coughed-up blood is haemoptysis; vomited blood is haematemesis.

stem: A 35-year-old non-smoker develops early-onset emphysema, particularly affecting the lower lungs. Which inherited condition should be considered?
why_correct: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency predisposes to premature emphysema, particularly in younger adults and non-smokers.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia causes vascular malformations and bleeding rather than emphysema. B. Cystic fibrosis causes bronchiectasis and recurrent respiratory infection rather than this classic early emphysema presentation. C. Sickle cell disease causes haemolytic anaemia and vaso-occlusive complications. E. Marfan syndrome affects connective tissues and cardiovascular structures.
pearl: Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in emphysema that starts young, affects non-smokers or is basal; check alpha-1 antitrypsin levels.
thinking: 35-year-old non-smoker ↓ Early-onset emphysema ↓ Lower lungs mainly affected ↓ Protease damage without the usual cause ↓ Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
exam_trap: B, cystic fibrosis — it is an inherited lung disease of young adults, but it causes bronchiectasis and infections, not basal emphysema.
takeaway: Early basal emphysema in a non-smoker: test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

stem: Which is an important risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea?
why_correct: Obesity is a major risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause upper-airway obstruction during sleep. B. Hyperthyroidism is not a typical major risk factor. C. Appendicitis has no relevant association. D. Iron deficiency is not a major direct risk factor.
pearl: Obesity is the main risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea; snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness should prompt assessment, and weight loss helps.
thinking: Obstructive sleep apnoea ↓ Upper airway collapses during sleep ↓ Excess neck and pharyngeal tissue narrows it ↓ Main modifiable risk ↓ Obesity
exam_trap: B, hyperthyroidism alone — thyroid disease can be linked with OSA, but it is hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism, that is the recognised association.
takeaway: Obesity is the major risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea.

stem: A patient develops sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain that is worse on inspiration. What symptom pattern is particularly compatible with pulmonary embolism?

options.B: Burning epigastric pain after meals only

why_correct: Pulmonary embolism can cause sudden pleuritic chest pain, particularly when peripheral pulmonary infarction irritates the pleura.
why_wrong: A. Dysphagia suggests oesophageal pathology. B. This suggests gastrointestinal disease. C. Dysuria suggests urinary tract pathology. E. Colicky loin pain suggests renal colic.
pearl: Pulmonary embolism classically causes sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain; assess clinical probability with the Wells score to guide D-dimer or imaging.
thinking: Sudden breathlessness ↓ Sharp chest pain ↓ Worse on inspiration ↓ Pleural irritation from lung infarction ↓ Pleuritic chest pain
exam_trap: B, burning epigastric pain after meals — chest discomfort can be gut in origin, but it is not pleuritic and does not fit sudden breathlessness.
takeaway: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain should raise suspicion of PE.

stem: A patient with longstanding lung disease develops progressive exertional breathlessness and signs of right-sided heart failure. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic lung disease can cause pulmonary hypertension, which may eventually lead to right ventricular strain and right-sided heart failure.
why_wrong: B. Cataract causes visual impairment. C. Appendicitis causes abdominal symptoms. D. Peptic ulcer disease causes gastrointestinal symptoms. E. Carpal tunnel causes median-nerve symptoms.
pearl: Chronic lung disease can cause pulmonary hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction, leading to right heart failure (cor pulmonale); echocardiography is the usual first test.
thinking: Longstanding lung disease ↓ Chronic hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels ↓ Pulmonary pressure rises ↓ Right ventricle strains ↓ Pulmonary hypertension
exam_trap: D, peptic ulcer disease — it is a common illness in this group, but it causes abdominal symptoms, not exertional breathlessness with right heart failure.
takeaway: Chronic lung disease with right heart failure suggests pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A patient with chronic respiratory disease develops peripheral oedema and raised jugular venous pressure due to right ventricular failure. What is this complication called?
why_correct: Cor pulmonale refers to right ventricular structural or functional disease resulting from pulmonary hypertension associated with lung disease.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema through renal protein loss. B. Left ventricular failure primarily causes pulmonary congestion. D. Cirrhosis can cause oedema and ascites through liver disease mechanisms. E. Pericarditis causes chest pain and characteristic inflammatory findings.
pearl: Cor pulmonale is right heart failure caused by lung disease through pulmonary hypertension; COPD is the commonest UK cause, so new oedema and a raised JVP in a chronic chest patient point to the right heart.
thinking: Chronic respiratory disease ↓ Hypoxic vasoconstriction raises pulmonary pressures ↓ Right ventricle fails: oedema, raised JVP ↓ Cor pulmonale
exam_trap: B, left ventricular failure — heart failure is clearly in play, but LVF produces pulmonary oedema and orthopnoea; right-sided failure secondary to lung disease is cor pulmonale.
takeaway: Lung disease plus signs of right heart failure equals cor pulmonale.

stem: A patient has a lung tumour at the apex associated with severe shoulder pain and weakness of the hand. Which type of tumour should be considered?
why_correct: An apical lung tumour can invade structures of the lower brachial plexus and cause shoulder and upper-limb symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Bronchiectasis causes chronic productive cough and recurrent infections. C. Pleural effusion causes respiratory and pleural findings rather than this characteristic apical neurological presentation. D. Mesothelioma is a pleural malignancy. E. Pulmonary embolism causes acute vascular respiratory symptoms.
pearl: A Pancoast tumour at the lung apex invades the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1), giving shoulder pain and hand weakness, and may involve the sympathetic chain to cause Horner syndrome.
thinking: Apical lung tumour ↓ Severe shoulder pain plus hand weakness ↓ Lower brachial plexus invasion ↓ Pancoast tumour
exam_trap: D, mesothelioma — a thoracic malignancy that causes chest-wall pain, but it is a diffuse pleural tumour linked to asbestos, not an apical mass invading the brachial plexus.
takeaway: Apical lung mass with shoulder pain and small-muscle hand weakness: think Pancoast tumour.

stem: A patient with a mediastinal lung tumour develops persistent hoarseness. Which nerve may be affected?
why_correct: Compression or involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve can cause vocal-cord paralysis and persistent hoarseness.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglossal nerve injury causes tongue weakness and deviation, not hoarseness. C. Sympathetic chain involvement causes Horner syndrome, not hoarseness. D. Phrenic nerve involvement causes diaphragmatic paralysis, not hoarseness. E. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula, not hoarseness.
pearl: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, so mediastinal and left hilar tumours can paralyse a vocal cord; persistent hoarseness with a chest lesion needs urgent assessment.
thinking: Mediastinal lung tumour ↓ Persistent hoarseness = vocal-cord palsy ↓ Nerve to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: D, phrenic nerve — it also runs through the mediastinum and can be invaded by tumour, but its palsy causes a raised hemidiaphragm and breathlessness, not hoarseness.
takeaway: Hoarseness with a chest tumour means recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.

stem: A former shipyard worker has progressive breathlessness, chest pain and a pleural mass. Which occupational exposure is classically associated with this malignancy?
why_correct: Asbestos exposure is strongly associated with malignant pleural mesothelioma.
why_wrong: A. Flour dust is associated with occupational asthma. B. Silica exposure is associated with silicosis and increased tuberculosis risk. C. Cotton dust exposure is associated with byssinosis. D. Coal dust is associated with coal workers' pneumoconiosis.
pearl: Mesothelioma is strongly linked to asbestos exposure, often decades earlier, in trades such as shipbuilding, construction and plumbing; take an occupational history in any pleural mass or unexplained effusion.
thinking: Former shipyard worker ↓ Pleural mass, chest pain, breathlessness ↓ Malignant pleural mesothelioma ↓ Asbestos exposure
exam_trap: B, silica only — another classic occupational dust, but silica causes upper-lobe silicosis and raises tuberculosis risk; it is not the cause of pleural mesothelioma.
takeaway: Pleural malignancy plus a shipyard or building-trade history: asbestos.

stem: A worker exposed to silica dust develops chronic breathlessness and upper-lobe nodular lung disease. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Silica exposure can cause silicosis, a pneumoconiosis typically associated with upper-lung involvement.
why_wrong: A. Bronchiectasis causes chronic productive cough and recurrent infections. B. Asbestosis is associated with asbestos exposure and typically produces a different fibrotic pattern. C. Pulmonary embolism is an acute vascular disorder. E. Pleural effusion is fluid accumulation in the pleural space.
pearl: Silicosis follows inhalation of crystalline silica in quarrying, stonework and sandblasting, causing upper-lobe nodular fibrosis, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes and an increased risk of tuberculosis.
thinking: Occupational silica dust exposure ↓ Chronic progressive breathlessness ↓ Upper-lobe nodular lung disease ↓ Silicosis
exam_trap: B, asbestosis — the other famous pneumoconiosis, but it follows asbestos exposure and typically causes lower-lobe fibrosis, often with pleural plaques.
takeaway: Silica gives upper-lobe nodules; asbestos gives lower-lobe fibrosis.

stem: A patient with sarcoidosis is found to have an elevated calcium level. What mechanism can contribute to this?

options.C: Increased production of active vitamin D by macrophages
options.D: Excess parathyroid hormone from a parathyroid adenoma

correct_answer: C. Increased production of active vitamin D by macrophages
why_correct: Activated macrophages in sarcoid granulomas can increase production of calcitriol, increasing intestinal calcium absorption and potentially causing hypercalcaemia.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D deficiency generally reduces calcium absorption. B. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium. D. Primary hyperparathyroidism is a different cause of hypercalcaemia. E. Reduced calcium absorption would tend to lower rather than raise calcium.
pearl: Sarcoid granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase and make calcitriol independently of PTH; PTH is therefore suppressed, which separates this from primary hyperparathyroidism.
thinking: Sarcoidosis with hypercalcaemia ↓ Granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D ↓ Excess calcitriol raises gut calcium absorption ↓ Macrophage production of active vitamin D
exam_trap: D, excess PTH from a parathyroid adenoma — the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia overall, but in sarcoidosis PTH is suppressed because the drive is extrarenal calcitriol.
takeaway: Granulomatous disease raises calcium through macrophage calcitriol, with a low PTH.

stem: A patient with suspected ureteric stone has blood detected on urine testing. Which finding commonly accompanies renal colic?
why_correct: A ureteric stone can cause bleeding from the urinary tract, resulting in microscopic or visible haematuria.
why_wrong: A. Bilirubinuria is associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. B. Glycosuria is not a typical consequence of renal stones. C. Ketonuria is associated with fasting, starvation or metabolic states such as diabetic ketoacidosis. D. Massive proteinuria suggests significant glomerular disease.
pearl: Haematuria, usually microscopic, is found in most patients with renal colic, but its absence does not exclude a stone; low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder is the usual confirmatory test.
thinking: Suspected ureteric stone ↓ Stone injures the urothelium as it passes ↓ Blood detected on urine testing ↓ Haematuria
exam_trap: D, massive proteinuria — dipstick findings blur together, but heavy proteinuria signals glomerular disease; a passing stone causes bleeding, not protein loss.
takeaway: Renal colic usually brings haematuria, but a negative dipstick does not exclude a stone.

stem: Which finding is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome?
why_correct: Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by heavy proteinuria, usually accompanied by hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
why_wrong: A. Isolated haematuria is not the defining feature of nephrotic syndrome. B. Neutropenia is a haematological abnormality. D. Polycythaemia is unrelated. E. Hypercalcaemia is not characteristic.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, usually with hyperlipidaemia; nephritic syndrome instead centres on haematuria, hypertension and falling renal function.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome ↓ Leaky glomerular barrier ↓ Large protein losses in the urine ↓ Heavy proteinuria
exam_trap: A, isolated microscopic haematuria — confuses nephrotic with nephritic; haematuria is the hallmark of nephritic syndrome, whereas nephrotic is defined by heavy protein loss.
takeaway: Nephrotic means heavy protein loss; nephritic means blood in the urine.

stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops marked peripheral and periorbital oedema. What is an important mechanism?
why_correct: Urinary loss of albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure, contributing to fluid movement into the tissues and oedema.
why_wrong: A. Hyperventilation is unrelated. C. Haemolysis does not explain this mechanism. D. Bile production does not cause nephrotic oedema. E. Increased haemoglobin production does not cause nephrotic oedema.
pearl: Urinary albumin loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid shifts into the interstitium; periorbital swelling, often most obvious on waking, is a classic early sign.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome ↓ Heavy urinary albumin loss ↓ Low plasma oncotic pressure ↓ Fluid moves into tissues ↓ Hypoalbuminaemia
exam_trap: C, excess red-cell destruction — haemolysis sounds like a systemic mechanism, but it causes anaemia and jaundice, not oedema; nephrotic oedema follows albumin loss.
takeaway: Nephrotic oedema is driven by hypoalbuminaemia and low oncotic pressure.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes has a small but persistent increase in urinary albumin excretion. What does this suggest?

options.E: Renal colic from a ureteric calculus

why_correct: Persistent albuminuria can be an early manifestation of diabetic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. Retention causes difficulty passing urine and bladder distension. B. Renal cell carcinoma is not diagnosed by isolated low-level albuminuria. D. Urinary infection causes transient proteinuria with symptoms, not persistent low-level albuminuria. E. Renal colic causes acute severe pain.
pearl: Persistent albuminuria, measured by the urine albumin:creatinine ratio, is the earliest marker of diabetic kidney disease and should prompt tighter blood pressure and glucose control, usually with an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Small but persistent rise in urinary albumin ↓ Early glomerular damage ↓ Early diabetic kidney disease
exam_trap: D, recurrent lower UTI — infection can cause proteinuria, but it is transient and symptomatic; persistent low-level albuminuria in diabetes reflects kidney disease.
takeaway: Persistent albuminuria in diabetes means early diabetic kidney disease until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. What contributes to this?

options.B: Increased renal clearance of serum phosphate

correct_answer: E. Phosphate retention and low calcitriol
why_correct: CKD reduces phosphate excretion and active vitamin D production, contributing to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
why_wrong: A. Erythropoietin relates to red-cell production. B. CKD reduces rather than increases phosphate clearance. C. Calcitonin is not the primary mechanism. D. CKD reduces rather than increases intestinal calcium absorption.
pearl: In CKD the kidney retains phosphate and makes less calcitriol, so calcium falls and PTH rises; left untreated this drives renal bone disease and vascular calcification.
thinking: Advanced CKD ↓ Phosphate retained, less vitamin D activation ↓ Low calcium, high phosphate ↓ Parathyroids stimulated ↓ Phosphate retention and low calcitriol
exam_trap: B, increased renal phosphate clearance — sounds like a plausible renal mechanism, but failing kidneys clear less phosphate; retention, not loss, drives the PTH rise.
takeaway: CKD: high phosphate plus low calcitriol leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops a persistent rise in serum potassium. What is the main underlying problem?
why_correct: Advanced kidney disease can impair potassium excretion and lead to hyperkalaemia.
why_wrong: A. Reduced rather than increased effective renal excretion is the problem. B. Sweating is not the principal mechanism. C. Insulin promotes cellular potassium uptake. E. Gastrointestinal secretion does not explain the typical CKD-related hyperkalaemia.
pearl: The kidneys excrete most potassium, so falling GFR causes hyperkalaemia, made worse by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics and acidosis; check an ECG when potassium is high.
thinking: Advanced CKD ↓ Fewer functioning nephrons ↓ Impaired distal potassium secretion ↓ Reduced renal potassium excretion
exam_trap: E, excess gastrointestinal potassium secretion — sounds like a potassium-handling mechanism, but gut losses lower potassium; the rise in CKD reflects failed renal excretion.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia in CKD is a renal excretion problem; review potassium-raising drugs.

stem: A urine dipstick is persistently positive for protein. Which renal structure is primarily responsible for preventing large amounts of protein from entering the urine?
why_correct: The glomerular filtration barrier normally restricts passage of large proteins such as albumin into the filtrate.
why_wrong: A. The ureteric epithelium lines the tube transporting urine from the kidney to the bladder and does not filter protein. B. Collecting duct principal cells regulate sodium and water reabsorption, not protein filtration. C. The urethral sphincter contributes to continence. D. The detrusor muscle contracts during bladder emptying.
pearl: The glomerular filtration barrier of fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes holds back albumin by size and charge, so significant proteinuria usually points to glomerular disease.
thinking: Persistent proteinuria ↓ Large proteins are normally kept out of the filtrate ↓ The barrier sits at the glomerulus ↓ Glomerular filtration barrier
exam_trap: B, collecting duct principal cells — a renal structure that sounds functional, but they handle sodium and water under aldosterone and ADH, not protein filtration.
takeaway: Significant proteinuria means the glomerular filtration barrier is leaking.

stem: Which urinary finding suggests a glomerular source of haematuria?
why_correct: Red-cell casts form within renal tubules and strongly suggest bleeding originating from the glomeruli.
why_wrong: A. A bladder stone can cause lower urinary tract bleeding. C. Dysuria alone suggests lower urinary tract irritation or infection. D. Frequency alone does not establish a glomerular cause. E. Ureteric colic suggests a stone causing obstruction.
pearl: Red-cell casts form when red cells leak through damaged glomeruli and set within tubular protein; together with dysmorphic red cells and proteinuria they point to glomerulonephritis.
thinking: Haematuria ↓ Need to localise where the bleeding arises ↓ Red cells moulded within the renal tubules ↓ Red-cell casts
exam_trap: E, ureteric colic — a common cause of blood in the urine, but stone bleeding arises below the kidney's filtering units and does not form casts.
takeaway: Red-cell casts in the urine mean bleeding from the glomeruli.

stem: A patient has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with evidence of impaired renal acid handling. Which group of disorders is most appropriate?
why_correct: Renal tubular acidosis causes metabolic acidosis due to impaired renal handling of acid or bicarbonate and typically has a normal anion gap.
why_wrong: A. Lactic acidosis is typically a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. B. Respiratory alkalosis is caused by reduced carbon dioxide. D. Metabolic alkalosis is the opposite acid-base disturbance. E. Respiratory acidosis results from carbon dioxide retention.
pearl: A normal anion gap acidosis means bicarbonate loss, from the gut (diarrhoea) or the kidney (renal tubular acidosis); a high anion gap points instead to lactate, ketones, toxins or uraemia.
thinking: Metabolic acidosis ↓ Normal anion gap ↓ Impaired renal acid or bicarbonate handling ↓ Renal tubular acidosis
exam_trap: A, lactic acidosis — the most familiar metabolic acidosis, but lactate is an unmeasured anion that raises the anion gap, so it does not fit a normal-gap picture.
takeaway: Normal anion gap acidosis: think diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis.

stem: An RhD-negative pregnant woman gives birth to an RhD-positive baby. What treatment may be required to prevent maternal Rh sensitisation?
why_correct: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation of an RhD-negative mother following exposure to RhD-positive fetal red cells.
why_wrong: A. Anti-A immunoglobulin is not used for Rh sensitisation. B. Insulin treats hyperglycaemia. C. Vitamin K is involved in coagulation. D. Magnesium sulfate has specific obstetric uses such as seizure prevention in severe pre-eclampsia.
pearl: A non-sensitised RhD-negative mother of an RhD-positive baby is given anti-D, ideally within 72 hours, with a test for fetomaternal haemorrhage guiding whether more is needed; anti-D also follows sensitising events in pregnancy.
thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ RhD-positive baby ↓ Fetal cells may sensitise her, risking haemolytic disease in later pregnancies ↓ Anti-D immunoglobulin
exam_trap: A, anti-A immunoglobulin — the immunoglobulin idea is right, but ABO antibodies are not the issue; preventing RhD sensitisation needs anti-D specifically.
takeaway: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive baby: give anti-D to prevent sensitisation.

stem: A woman develops hyperglycaemia for the first time during pregnancy. What is the most appropriate term?
why_correct: Diabetes first recognised during pregnancy is termed gestational diabetes mellitus when it meets diagnostic criteria for diabetes in pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Reactive hypoglycaemia refers to low rather than high glucose. B. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells and is not defined by first recognition during pregnancy. D. Addison disease causes adrenal insufficiency. E. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causes polyuria due to renal resistance to antidiuretic hormone, not hyperglycaemia.
pearl: Gestational diabetes is screened for with an oral glucose tolerance test in women with risk factors; it raises the risk of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia, and of type 2 diabetes later in life.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Hyperglycaemia for the first time ↓ Pregnancy hormones increase insulin resistance ↓ Gestational diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: B, new-onset type 1 diabetes — it can present at any age, but it is autoimmune beta-cell loss and is not defined by first recognition in pregnancy.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first recognised in pregnancy is gestational diabetes.

stem: A woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy develops regular painful uterine contractions accompanied by progressive cervical change. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Regular contractions accompanied by cervical change before 37 weeks indicate preterm labour.
why_wrong: A. Placenta praevia presents primarily with painless bleeding. B. Braxton Hicks contractions do not cause progressive cervical dilatation. C. Hyperemesis causes severe vomiting. E. Ectopic pregnancy occurs outside the uterine cavity, usually early in pregnancy.
pearl: Preterm labour is regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; key steps include antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection at earlier gestations.
thinking: 30 weeks pregnant ↓ Regular painful contractions ↓ Progressive cervical change ↓ Before 37 weeks ↓ Preterm labour
exam_trap: B, Braxton Hicks contractions — common in the third trimester, but they are irregular and do not change the cervix; progressive cervical change confirms labour.
takeaway: Contractions plus cervical change before 37 weeks equals preterm labour.

stem: A woman at 31 weeks develops leakage of fluid from the vagina before the onset of labour. What is this called?

options.C: Prelabour rupture of membranes at term

correct_answer: B. Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
why_correct: Rupture of membranes before labour and before 37 weeks is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.
why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis causes vomiting. C. Term begins at 37 weeks; rupture at 31 weeks is preterm. D. Placental abruption causes bleeding and abdominal pain. E. Placenta praevia causes painless bleeding.
pearl: P-PROM is confirmed on speculum examination by pooling of amniotic fluid; avoid digital vaginal examination, and give prophylactic antibiotics such as erythromycin and antenatal corticosteroids.
thinking: 31 weeks pregnant ↓ Fluid leaking from the vagina ↓ No labour yet ↓ Before 37 weeks ↓ Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
exam_trap: C, prelabour rupture of membranes at term — the right event at the wrong gestation; term starts at 37 weeks, so rupture at 31 weeks is preterm.
takeaway: Rupture before labour and before 37 weeks is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.

stem: A woman has heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery. What is the most important immediate clinical concern?

options.D: Placenta praevia as a current pregnancy diagnosis

why_correct: Significant bleeding after childbirth is postpartum haemorrhage and requires urgent assessment and management.
why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis occurs during pregnancy. B. Gestational diabetes does not explain acute postpartum bleeding. C. Ectopic pregnancy occurs outside the uterus, usually early in pregnancy. D. Placenta praevia describes placental location during pregnancy rather than the immediate diagnosis of postpartum bleeding.
pearl: In PPH call for help, resuscitate with an ABCDE approach and work through the 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin; uterine atony is the commonest cause, treated first with fundal massage and uterotonics.
thinking: Recent delivery ↓ Heavy vaginal bleeding ↓ Risk of rapid haemorrhagic shock ↓ Postpartum haemorrhage
exam_trap: D, placenta praevia — a classic cause of obstetric bleeding and a PPH risk factor, but it describes placental position in pregnancy, not the diagnosis for bleeding after birth.
takeaway: Heavy bleeding after delivery is PPH: resuscitate and work through the 4 Ts.

stem: Immediately after delivery, a woman develops severe pain, haemorrhage and shock. Examination suggests that the uterus has turned inside out. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Uterine inversion is an obstetric emergency in which the uterus turns inside out, usually shortly after delivery, and can cause severe haemorrhage and shock.
why_wrong: B. Placenta praevia causes antepartum bleeding. C. Ectopic pregnancy is an early pregnancy complication. D. Uterine atony causes haemorrhage but does not produce inversion. E. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain but not postpartum uterine inversion.
pearl: Uterine inversion can cause shock out of proportion to visible blood loss; treat at once by manual replacement of the uterus alongside resuscitation, without first removing an attached placenta.
thinking: Immediately after delivery ↓ Severe pain, haemorrhage and shock ↓ Uterus turned inside out ↓ Uterine inversion
exam_trap: D, uterine atony — the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage, but an atonic uterus is soft and in place; a uterus turned inside out defines inversion.
takeaway: Postpartum shock with an inside-out uterus is inversion: replace it immediately.

stem: A woman with longstanding endometriosis has difficulty becoming pregnant. Which reproductive problem can be associated with endometriosis?

options.A: Complete absence of ovulation in every case

why_correct: Endometriosis is associated with reduced fertility in some women.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis does not inevitably abolish ovulation. B. It does not cause immediate menopause. C. Endometriosis does not inevitably cause infertility. D. Hyperprolactinaemia is not an inevitable consequence.
pearl: Endometriosis can reduce fertility through pelvic adhesions, tubal distortion and ovarian endometriomas, yet many affected women still conceive; delayed conception warrants fertility assessment.
thinking: Longstanding endometriosis ↓ Difficulty conceiving ↓ Adhesions and inflammation impair fertility ↓ Not absolute in every case ↓ Subfertility
exam_trap: C, permanent infertility in every case — tempting because endometriosis and infertility are linked, but many women conceive; absolute wording like 'every case' is wrong.
takeaway: Endometriosis is associated with subfertility, not inevitable infertility.

stem: Which infection is the major causative factor for cervical cancer?
why_correct: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types is the principal cause of cervical cancer.
why_wrong: A. EBV is associated with several malignancies but is not the principal cause of cervical cancer. C. Hepatitis A primarily affects the liver. D. Influenza does not cause cervical cancer. E. HSV-2 was historically investigated as a cause but is not the principal cause of cervical cancer.
pearl: Persistent high-risk HPV, especially types 16 and 18, causes almost all cervical cancer; the UK prevents it through HPV vaccination and HPV-based cervical screening.
thinking: Cervical cancer ↓ Persistent viral infection of the transformation zone ↓ Oncogenic high-risk types ↓ Persistent high-risk HPV infection
exam_trap: E, HSV-2 — a sexually transmitted genital virus once suspected as the cause, but HPV, not herpes, drives cervical neoplasia.
takeaway: Cervical cancer is driven by persistent high-risk HPV infection.

stem: A woman develops recurrent bleeding after sexual intercourse. Which gynaecological malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Postcoital bleeding is an important symptom that can occur with cervical cancer and warrants appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid cancer does not characteristically cause postcoital bleeding. C. Renal cell carcinoma causes urinary symptoms such as haematuria. D. Ovarian cancer more commonly presents with abdominal or pelvic symptoms. E. Endometrial pathology more typically causes abnormal uterine bleeding, particularly intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding.
pearl: Postcoital bleeding needs a speculum examination of the cervix; a cervix that looks suspicious of cancer warrants urgent suspected cancer referral, even after a recent normal screening result.
thinking: Recurrent bleeding after intercourse ↓ Contact bleeding from a friable cervical lesion ↓ Examine the cervix ↓ Cervical cancer
exam_trap: E, endometrial hyperplasia only — a genuine gynaecological cause of bleeding, but it typically gives intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding; contact bleeding points to the cervix.
takeaway: Postcoital bleeding needs the cervix examined to exclude cervical cancer.

stem: A 17-year-old can read a book clearly when it is held close but has difficulty seeing the writing on a distant classroom board. What refractive error is most likely?
why_correct: Myopia causes distant objects to appear blurred while near objects remain relatively clear.
why_wrong: A. Hypermetropia can make near vision more difficult. B. Presbyopia is age-related loss of near accommodation. C. Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision due to unequal refractive power. E. Cataract causes progressive lens opacity rather than isolated difficulty seeing distant objects in a young person.
pearl: In myopia light focuses in front of the retina, blurring distance vision while near vision stays clear; it commonly develops in childhood and adolescence and is corrected with concave lenses.
thinking: 17-year-old ↓ Near reading clear ↓ Distant board blurred ↓ Image focuses in front of the retina ↓ Myopia
exam_trap: A, hypermetropia — the other common refractive error, but long-sighted eyes struggle more with near focus; distance blur with clear near vision is myopia.
takeaway: Short-sighted (myopic) eyes see near clearly but distance poorly.

stem: A child has difficulty focusing on nearby objects but can see distant objects relatively clearly. Which refractive error is most likely?
why_correct: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) can make near vision more difficult because the eye has insufficient refractive power.
why_wrong: A. Presbyopia is an age-related reduction in accommodation. C. Myopia primarily affects distance vision. D. Cataract causes progressive visual impairment from lens opacity. E. Retinal detachment causes visual-field or visual disturbances rather than simple long-sightedness.
pearl: In hypermetropia light focuses behind the retina; children can partly compensate by accommodating, but significant uncorrected hypermetropia can cause squint and amblyopia. Convex lenses correct it.
thinking: Child ↓ Difficulty focusing on near objects ↓ Distance relatively clear ↓ Too little refractive power ↓ Hypermetropia
exam_trap: A, presbyopia — it also causes near-vision difficulty, but it is age-related loss of accommodation from middle age, not a refractive error of childhood.
takeaway: Near blur in a child is hypermetropia; near blur from middle age is presbyopia.

stem: A 52-year-old increasingly needs to hold a book farther away to read it comfortably. Distance vision remains good. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Presbyopia is age-related reduction in the ability of the lens to accommodate for near vision.
why_wrong: A. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye with visual disturbance. B. Retinal detachment causes acute visual symptoms such as flashes, floaters or a field defect. C. Optic neuritis commonly causes painful visual loss, particularly with eye movement. D. Myopia causes difficulty with distance vision.
pearl: Presbyopia is age-related stiffening of the lens that reduces accommodation, typically noticed from the mid-forties; holding print farther away is the classic clue, and reading glasses correct it.
thinking: 52-year-old ↓ Holds the book farther away to read ↓ Distance vision preserved ↓ Lens loses accommodation ↓ Presbyopia
exam_trap: D, myopia — a common refractive error, but myopia blurs distance vision; this patient has good distance vision and failing near focus.
takeaway: Near-vision difficulty from middle age with good distance vision is presbyopia.

stem: What is the purpose of diabetic eye screening?

options.A: Detect cataract before it impairs driving vision
options.B: Measure intraocular pressure to detect glaucoma
options.E: Detect retinopathy before it threatens sight

correct_answer: E. Detect retinopathy before it threatens sight
why_correct: Screening aims to identify retinal changes early so that appropriate management can reduce the risk of sight-threatening disease.
why_wrong: A. Cataract detection is not the specific purpose of diabetic eye screening. B. Intraocular pressure measurement is part of glaucoma assessment, not diabetic eye screening. C. Migraine is not diagnosed by retinal screening. D. Hearing impairment is unrelated.
pearl: The NHS diabetic eye screening programme uses digital retinal photography for people with diabetes aged 12 and over, to find treatable sight-threatening retinopathy before symptoms develop.
thinking: Diabetes damages the retinal microvasculature ↓ Retinopathy is silent until advanced ↓ Regular retinal photography ↓ Detect retinopathy before it threatens sight
exam_trap: B, measuring intraocular pressure for glaucoma — pressure checks feel like routine eye screening, but diabetic eye screening photographs the retina to find retinopathy.
takeaway: Diabetic eye screening exists to catch retinopathy before sight is lost.

stem: An elderly patient develops progressive difficulty reading and recognising faces, while peripheral vision remains relatively preserved. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Age-related macular degeneration primarily affects the macula and therefore central vision.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis usually causes acute/subacute visual loss, often with pain on eye movement. B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye and acute visual disturbance. C. Otitis externa affects the ear canal. D. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden visual loss.
pearl: AMD damages the macula, causing central visual loss that affects reading and faces; sudden distortion or rapid central loss suggests wet AMD, which needs urgent ophthalmology referral for anti-VEGF treatment.
thinking: Elderly patient ↓ Progressive difficulty reading and recognising faces ↓ Central vision lost, periphery preserved ↓ Macular disease ↓ Age-related macular degeneration
exam_trap: D, central retinal artery occlusion — sounds 'central', but it causes sudden, profound painless loss of vision, not gradual central loss with a preserved periphery.
takeaway: Gradual central visual loss with spared peripheral vision in an older person suggests AMD.

stem: A young adult develops subacute visual loss in one eye accompanied by pain when moving the eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Painful monocular visual loss, particularly pain on eye movement, is characteristic of optic neuritis.
why_wrong: B. Presbyopia causes difficulty with near vision in older adults. C. Conjunctivitis causes redness and discharge rather than this pattern of visual loss. D. Retinal detachment usually causes flashes, floaters or a field defect. E. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment.
pearl: Optic neuritis causes pain on eye movement, reduced acuity and colour vision, and a relative afferent pupillary defect; it may be the first presentation of multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Subacute monocular visual loss ↓ Pain on eye movement ↓ Inflamed optic nerve ↓ Optic neuritis
exam_trap: D, retinal detachment — it causes monocular visual loss, but it is painless and heralded by flashes, floaters or a field defect; pain on eye movement points to optic neuritis.
takeaway: Painful eye movement with subacute monocular visual loss is optic neuritis.

stem: A patient with diabetes has gradually worsening, painless visual acuity due to opacity of the crystalline lens. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cataract is opacity of the crystalline lens and commonly causes gradual painless visual deterioration.
why_wrong: B. Optic neuritis usually causes more acute/subacute visual loss. C. Keratitis causes corneal inflammation, usually with pain and photophobia. D. Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden visual loss. E. Acute glaucoma is typically painful with a red eye.
pearl: Diabetes is a recognised risk factor for earlier cataract, which causes gradual painless blurring and glare with a reduced red reflex; surgery is offered when vision affects daily life.
thinking: Patient with diabetes ↓ Gradual painless visual decline ↓ Opacity of the crystalline lens ↓ Cataract
exam_trap: E, acute glaucoma — an important eye emergency, but it presents suddenly with a painful red eye and haloes, not slow painless blurring.
takeaway: Lens opacity with gradual painless visual loss is cataract.

stem: An adult develops severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing and drooling, with relatively little visible abnormality in the throat. What serious diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Severe odynophagia/dysphagia with drooling and potentially minimal oropharyngeal findings should raise concern about epiglottitis because of the risk of airway obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Nasal polyps cause chronic nasal obstruction. B. Otitis externa causes ear pain. C. Cerumen impaction causes hearing symptoms rather than acute airway symptoms. D. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms.
pearl: Suspected epiglottitis is an airway emergency: keep the patient calm and upright, avoid instrumenting the throat, and involve senior anaesthetic and ENT help early.
thinking: Severe sore throat ↓ Dysphagia and drooling ↓ Little to see in the oropharynx ↓ Swelling lies lower, at the epiglottis ↓ Epiglottitis
exam_trap: D, allergic rhinitis — an upper airway condition, but its symptoms are nasal; drooling and severe painful swallowing with a near-normal throat point to supraglottic swelling.
takeaway: Severe sore throat with drooling and a normal-looking throat: think epiglottitis.

stem: A patient develops persistent hoarseness after neck surgery. Injury to which nerve is most directly associated with unilateral vocal-cord paralysis?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies most intrinsic muscles of the larynx and injury can cause vocal-cord paralysis and hoarseness.
why_wrong: A. The optic nerve carries visual information. B. The vestibulocochlear nerve is responsible for hearing and balance. C. The trigeminal nerve supplies facial sensation and muscles of mastication. E. The facial nerve controls facial expression and other functions.
pearl: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the thyroid, so thyroid and other neck surgery can injure it; unilateral palsy causes hoarseness, while bilateral palsy can cause stridor and airway compromise.
thinking: Neck surgery ↓ Persistent hoarseness ↓ Unilateral vocal-cord paralysis ↓ Nerve to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: E, facial nerve — a cranial nerve at risk in head and neck surgery, especially parotid surgery, but it controls facial expression, not the vocal cords.
takeaway: Hoarseness after thyroid or neck surgery suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

stem: A patient has hearing loss with normal inner-ear function but impaired transmission of sound through the external or middle ear. What type of hearing loss is this?
why_correct: Conductive hearing loss results from impaired transmission of sound through the external or middle ear.
why_wrong: A. Sensorineural hearing loss involves the cochlea or auditory nerve. C. Vestibular neuritis affects balance rather than sound conduction. D. Optic neuropathy affects the optic nerve. E. Central visual loss concerns vision.
pearl: Tuning fork tests separate the types: in conductive loss Rinne is negative and Weber lateralises to the affected ear; causes include wax, otitis media with effusion and otosclerosis.
thinking: Hearing loss ↓ Inner ear functions normally ↓ Sound blocked in the external or middle ear ↓ Conductive hearing loss
exam_trap: A, sensorineural hearing loss — the other main category, but it arises in the cochlea or auditory nerve, which the stem describes as normal.
takeaway: External or middle-ear problem means conductive loss; cochlea or nerve means sensorineural.

stem: A patient develops a blocked sensation and muffled hearing during air travel, particularly during descent. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Failure of the Eustachian tube to equalise middle-ear pressure can cause ear blockage and discomfort during changes in atmospheric pressure.
why_wrong: B. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo, not ear blockage with pressure change. C. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and auditory symptoms. D. Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss unrelated to pressure change. E. Peritonsillar abscess causes severe unilateral throat symptoms with referred otalgia, not pressure-related ear blockage during descent.
pearl: On descent cabin pressure rises and a poorly functioning Eustachian tube fails to equalise the middle ear; swallowing, yawning or a Valsalva manoeuvre help, and flying with a cold makes it worse.
thinking: Air travel ↓ Worse during descent ↓ Middle-ear pressure not equalised ↓ Blocked, muffled ear ↓ Eustachian tube dysfunction
exam_trap: C, Ménière disease — it causes aural fullness and muffled hearing, but in spontaneous episodes with vertigo and tinnitus, not triggered by pressure change.
takeaway: Ear blockage triggered by pressure change points to Eustachian tube dysfunction.

stem: A patient has persistent foul-smelling ear discharge and progressive conductive hearing loss. Examination shows abnormal skin/debris in the middle-ear region. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising epithelium in the middle ear and can cause persistent offensive discharge and conductive hearing loss.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular neuritis causes acute vertigo without the characteristic chronic ear discharge. B. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms. C. Presbyopia causes age-related difficulty with near vision. D. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo.
pearl: Cholesteatoma is keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear that erodes bone; persistent foul discharge with conductive loss needs ENT referral, as complications include facial palsy and intracranial infection.
thinking: Persistent foul-smelling discharge ↓ Progressive conductive hearing loss ↓ Skin debris in the middle ear ↓ Cholesteatoma
exam_trap: A, vestibular neuritis — an inner-ear diagnosis, but it causes acute vertigo with no discharge or hearing loss; discharge with keratin debris is cholesteatoma.
takeaway: Foul persistent ear discharge with conductive loss: suspect cholesteatoma and refer.

stem: A patient has recurrent unexpected panic attacks and has become persistently worried about having another attack. They have started avoiding places where they previously experienced attacks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by persistent concern or behavioural change related to further attacks are characteristic of panic disorder.
why_wrong: A. PTSD follows a traumatic event. B. OCD involves intrusive thoughts and/or repetitive compulsions. C. Social anxiety centres on fear of scrutiny or embarrassment in social situations. D. GAD involves excessive worry across multiple domains.
pearl: Panic disorder is recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent fear of further attacks; first-line treatment is CBT or an SSRI, and avoidance can lead on to agoraphobia.
thinking: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks ↓ Persistent worry about further attacks ↓ Avoids places linked to attacks ↓ Panic disorder
exam_trap: D, generalised anxiety disorder — also a chronic anxiety state, but GAD is persistent worry about many everyday matters rather than discrete unexpected panic attacks.
takeaway: Unexpected panic attacks plus fear of the next one equals panic disorder.

stem: A patient has an intense, persistent fear of spiders and avoids situations where they might encounter one. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A specific phobia is marked fear of a particular object or situation, leading to avoidance.
why_wrong: A. Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape or help may be difficult. B. Social anxiety concerns social scrutiny or evaluation. C. OCD involves obsessions and/or compulsions. E. PTSD follows a traumatic event and has characteristic trauma-related symptoms.
pearl: A specific phobia is marked fear of one object or situation, such as spiders, heights or needles, leading to avoidance; graded exposure within CBT is the mainstay of treatment.
thinking: Intense, persistent fear ↓ Single specific trigger: spiders ↓ Avoidance of that trigger ↓ Specific phobia
exam_trap: A, agoraphobia — a phobic disorder with avoidance, but the fear is of situations where escape or help is difficult, not a single object such as spiders.
takeaway: Fear and avoidance tied to one object or situation is a specific phobia.

stem: A patient avoids buses, crowded shopping centres and being far from home because they fear becoming unwell somewhere they could not easily escape or obtain help. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Agoraphobia involves fear or avoidance of situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like or incapacitating symptoms occur.
why_wrong: B. GAD involves excessive worry across multiple domains. C. Social anxiety is centred on scrutiny or embarrassment. D. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions. E. Specific phobia involves a particular object or situation.
pearl: Agoraphobia is fear of situations where escape or help may be difficult, such as public transport, crowds or being away from home; it often accompanies panic disorder.
thinking: Avoids buses, crowds and distance from home ↓ Fears becoming unwell without escape or help ↓ Several situations, not one object ↓ Agoraphobia
exam_trap: C, social anxiety disorder — crowded places can be feared, but its core fear is scrutiny or embarrassment, not being unable to escape or get help.
takeaway: Fear of places where escape or help is hard defines agoraphobia.

stem: A patient who survived a serious road traffic collision repeatedly experiences vivid involuntary memories and nightmares about the crash. Which PTSD symptom cluster does this represent?
