why_wrong: B. Anaphylaxis involves acute severe allergic features such as airway or circulatory compromise. C. Mild post-vaccination fever alone does not indicate bacterial sepsis. D. Minor reactions do not generally contraindicate future vaccination. E. A minor reaction does not indicate vaccine failure.
pearl: Mild fever and injection-site soreness are common, expected vaccine reactions; they settle on their own and do not contraindicate future doses.
thinking: Recent vaccination ↓ Mild fever ↓ Local soreness at injection site ↓ Expected short-lived response ↓ Common minor vaccine reaction
exam_trap: D, contraindication to all future vaccines — tempting out of caution, but minor reactions are not contraindications; only true allergy or anaphylaxis would be.
takeaway: Mild fever and local soreness after vaccination are common and not a reason to stop vaccinating.

stem:
In a clinical trial, participants do not know whether they have received the active treatment or placebo.

What is this an example of?
why_correct: Participants are blinded when they are unaware of which intervention they have received.
why_wrong: A. Randomisation concerns how participants are allocated. B. Allocation concealment concerns preventing foreknowledge of allocation during enrolment. C. Confounding is distortion by another variable. D. Matching is a method used in some observational studies.
pearl: Blinding hides which treatment was received to reduce bias in reporting and assessing outcomes; allocation concealment instead stops anyone predicting the next allocation during enrolment.
thinking: Participants unaware of treatment received ↓ Hides allocation after assignment ↓ Applies to the participants ↓ Participant blinding
exam_trap: B, allocation concealment only — tempting because both involve hiding allocation, but concealment applies during enrolment, before assignment, not after treatment is received.
takeaway: Blinding = not knowing the treatment received; allocation concealment = not knowing the next allocation.

stem:
In a randomised trial, some participants stop taking their allocated treatment but remain included in the analysis according to their original treatment group.

What analysis principle is being used?
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analyses participants according to their original randomised allocation, regardless of whether they completed the assigned treatment.
why_wrong: A. Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome at a point in time. C. Per-protocol analysis generally focuses on participants who adhered to the protocol. D. Case-control studies select participants according to outcome status. E. Ecological studies analyse population-level rather than individual-level data.
pearl: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone in the group they were randomised to, preserving randomisation and reflecting real-world effectiveness, even if they stop treatment.
thinking: Randomised trial ↓ Some stop treatment ↓ Still analysed in original groups ↓ Preserves randomisation ↓ Intention-to-treat
exam_trap: C, per-protocol only — tempting because it is the other common trial analysis, but per-protocol includes only participants who adhered, the opposite of this stem.
takeaway: Analysed as randomised, regardless of adherence = intention-to-treat.

stem:
Researchers measure blood pressure and body weight in 5,000 adults during a single health survey.

What type of study is this?
why_correct: Exposure and outcome-related variables are measured at a defined point in time.
why_wrong: A. This is a population survey rather than a clinical case series. B. There is no longitudinal follow-up. C. No intervention was randomly assigned. D. Participants were not selected according to disease status.
pearl: A cross-sectional study measures exposures and outcomes at one point in time, giving prevalence, but cannot show which came first.
thinking: Large population sample ↓ Single survey ↓ Measured at one point in time ↓ No follow-up and no intervention ↓ Cross-sectional study
exam_trap: B, cohort study — tempting because it involves a large population, but a cohort is followed over time; here measurements are taken once.
takeaway: One snapshot in time = cross-sectional; followed over time = cohort.

stem:
A study finds that people who drink more coffee have higher rates of a particular disease.

What can be concluded from this finding alone?

options.A: The study proves an underlying biological mechanism
options.B: The association is explained entirely by chance
options.C: Coffee intake is associated with the disease
options.D: The disease leads people to drink more coffee

correct_answer: C. Coffee intake is associated with the disease
why_correct: An observational association does not by itself establish causation.
why_wrong: A. A statistical association does not establish mechanism. B. The association may or may not be due to chance; this cannot be concluded from the finding alone. D. Reverse causation is possible but cannot be assumed. E. Causation requires further evidence.
pearl: An observational association does not prove causation; chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation must all be considered before inferring cause.
thinking: Coffee drinkers have more disease ↓ Observational finding ↓ Could be chance, bias or confounding ↓ Cannot prove cause ↓ Coffee intake is associated with the disease
exam_trap: E, coffee consumption causes the disease — tempting from the headline result, but an association alone does not establish causation.
takeaway: Association is not causation; consider chance, bias and confounding first.

stem:
A study finds that people who carry a particular medication prescription have higher mortality. However, the medication is mainly prescribed to people with severe disease.

What could distort the observed association?
why_correct: Disease severity is associated with both receiving the medication and mortality and could therefore distort the observed association.
why_wrong: A. Measurement bias in recording deaths does not explain the link between severity, prescription and mortality. B. Blinding does not explain this association. D. Recall bias concerns inaccurate participant recall and does not explain this association. E. Herd immunity concerns transmission of infection.
pearl: Confounding by indication occurs when the reason a treatment is prescribed, such as disease severity, also influences the outcome, making the treatment look harmful.
thinking: Medication linked with higher mortality ↓ Mainly given to people with severe disease ↓ Severity drives both prescribing and death ↓ Third variable distorts the link ↓ Confounding by disease severity
exam_trap: D, recall bias in prescription histories — tempting because prescriptions are involved, but nothing suggests inaccurate recall; severity explains both exposure and outcome.
takeaway: When the reason for treatment also affects the outcome, think confounding by indication.

stem:
Studies with positive results are more likely to be published than studies with negative results.

What type of bias can this create in a systematic review?
why_correct: Selective publication of studies according to their results can distort the apparent evidence base.
why_wrong: A. Observer effects do not describe selective publication. B. Lead-time bias concerns earlier diagnosis. D. Recall bias concerns inaccurate or differential recollection. E. Verification bias concerns differences in whether reference-standard testing is performed.
pearl: Publication bias occurs because positive studies are more likely to be published, so systematic reviews may overestimate effects; funnel plots can help detect it.
thinking: Positive studies more often published ↓ Negative studies missing from literature ↓ Review sees a skewed evidence base ↓ Publication bias
exam_trap: E, verification bias — tempting because it is another named bias, but it concerns diagnostic studies where not everyone gets the reference test, not selective publication.
takeaway: Selective publication of positive results = publication bias.

stem:
A 52-year-old man has fatigue, abnormal liver function tests and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. He has a bronze skin discoloration and a family history of a similar condition.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Haemochromatosis causes excessive iron accumulation and may present with liver disease, diabetes and skin pigmentation.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease can cause malabsorption but does not explain this classic combination. B. Acute hepatitis A causes an acute hepatitis syndrome. C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without iron overload. D. Primary biliary cholangitis predominantly affects the small intrahepatic bile ducts and has a different typical presentation.
pearl: Haemochromatosis causes iron overload that can present with fatigue, abnormal liver tests, diabetes, skin pigmentation and arthropathy; raised ferritin and transferrin saturation support the diagnosis.
thinking: Middle-aged man with fatigue ↓ Abnormal LFTs and new diabetes ↓ Bronze skin ↓ Family history suggests inherited disease ↓ Haemochromatosis
exam_trap: D, primary biliary cholangitis — tempting because it causes fatigue and abnormal liver tests, but it is cholestatic and does not explain diabetes and bronze pigmentation.
takeaway: Liver disease + diabetes + bronze skin + family history = haemochromatosis.

stem:
A patient develops fever after returning from a malaria-endemic region several weeks earlier.

Why is malaria particularly important to diagnose promptly?

options.B: Malaria is transmitted by contaminated food
options.D: Falciparum malaria can rapidly become severe
options.E: Malaria is the commonest cause of travellers' diarrhoea

correct_answer: D. Falciparum malaria can rapidly become severe
why_correct: Plasmodium falciparum can cause severe and potentially life-threatening malaria.
why_wrong: A. Fever and systemic illness are characteristic; diarrhoea is not the defining feature. B. Malaria is transmitted by infected mosquitoes. C. Untreated malaria can be life-threatening. E. Travellers' diarrhoea is usually bacterial; the importance of malaria lies in its potential severity.
pearl: Any fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area needs urgent malaria testing, as falciparum malaria can deteriorate quickly and can present weeks after return.
thinking: Fever after travel ↓ Malaria-endemic region ↓ Falciparum can become severe quickly ↓ Delay risks death ↓ Falciparum malaria can rapidly become severe
exam_trap: C, malaria usually resolves without treatment — tempting because fever may come and go, but untreated falciparum malaria can be fatal.
takeaway: Fever in a returning traveller = test for malaria urgently.

stem:
A traveller develops acute watery diarrhoea shortly after arriving in another country. They are otherwise well and have no blood in the stool.

What is the most important initial management principle?

options.C: Start intravenous antibiotics in every case

why_correct: Maintaining hydration is the key initial management principle for most uncomplicated acute diarrhoeal illnesses.
why_wrong: A. Inducing vomiting is harmful and inappropriate. B. Stopping fluids increases the risk of dehydration. C. Antibiotics are not required for every case. E. Chemotherapy has no role.
pearl: Most travellers' diarrhoea is self-limiting; the priority is oral rehydration, with antibiotics reserved for selected cases such as severe illness or bloody diarrhoea.
thinking: Acute watery diarrhoea ↓ Otherwise well, no blood ↓ Usually self-limiting ↓ Main risk is fluid loss ↓ Maintain adequate hydration
exam_trap: C, intravenous antibiotics in every case — tempting because many cases are bacterial, but uncomplicated travellers' diarrhoea does not need routine antibiotics.
takeaway: Uncomplicated travellers' diarrhoea: hydration first; antibiotics are not routine.

stem:
A 68-year-old man is diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.2 cm on ultrasound. He has no symptoms.

What is the usual management approach?

options.D: Elective repair solely because an aneurysm is present

why_correct: Small asymptomatic AAAs are generally monitored with ultrasound rather than immediately repaired.
why_wrong: A. Emergency surgery is for rupture or other appropriate emergencies. B. An AAA requires appropriate surveillance. C. Thrombolysis has no role in treating an uncomplicated AAA. D. Size and symptoms influence the decision for elective repair.
pearl: Small asymptomatic AAAs are monitored with ultrasound surveillance; elective repair is considered for large, rapidly growing or symptomatic aneurysms.
thinking: Older man ↓ AAA found on ultrasound ↓ Small and asymptomatic ↓ Rupture risk low at this size ↓ Surveillance with interval ultrasound
exam_trap: D, elective repair solely because an aneurysm is present — tempting because aneurysms can rupture, but repair depends on size, growth and symptoms, not the aneurysm alone.
takeaway: Small asymptomatic AAA = ultrasound surveillance, not immediate repair.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman has repeated episodes of dizziness and syncope. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation with intermittent periods of profound bradycardia.

What underlying problem should be suspected?
why_correct: Alternating atrial tachyarrhythmias and significant bradycardia can occur in sick sinus syndrome (tachy-brady syndrome).
why_wrong: A. Ventricular fibrillation causes cardiac arrest. B. First-degree AV block produces PR prolongation rather than alternating tachyarrhythmia and bradycardia. D. Pericarditis causes inflammatory chest pain and characteristic ECG changes. E. WPW involves an accessory pathway and typically produces pre-excitation.
pearl: Tachy-brady syndrome, with atrial tachyarrhythmias alternating with bradycardia, is a form of sick sinus syndrome and often needs a pacemaker, especially before rate-slowing drugs.
thinking: Older patient with dizziness and syncope ↓ Atrial fibrillation present ↓ Intermittent profound bradycardia ↓ Alternating fast and slow rhythms ↓ Sick sinus syndrome
exam_trap: B, first-degree AV block — tempting as a conduction problem, but it only prolongs the PR interval and does not cause alternating tachyarrhythmia and profound bradycardia.
takeaway: Alternating tachyarrhythmia and bradycardia with syncope = sick sinus (tachy-brady) syndrome.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful red eyes, photophobia and blurred vision. Examination shows an inflamed eye without purulent discharge.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A painful photophobic red eye with visual disturbance is characteristic of anterior uveitis and requires ophthalmological assessment.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment without an acutely painful red eye. C. Allergic conjunctivitis is typically itchy and bilateral. D. Bacterial conjunctivitis usually causes discharge and is less likely to cause significant pain or visual loss. E. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is usually painless.
pearl: Anterior uveitis causes a painful red eye with photophobia, blurred vision and often a small pupil, without discharge; it needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Recurrent painful red eye ↓ Photophobia and blurred vision ↓ No purulent discharge ↓ Intraocular inflammation ↓ Anterior uveitis
exam_trap: D, bacterial conjunctivitis — tempting because it is the commonest red eye, but it causes discharge with normal vision and little pain.
takeaway: Painful, photophobic red eye with blurred vision and no discharge = anterior uveitis.

stem:
A 31-year-old man has recurrent attacks of severe pain and swelling affecting his right knee. Joint aspiration shows calcium pyrophosphate crystals.

What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals cause CPPD, commonly known as pseudogout.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis is caused by infection rather than crystal deposition. C. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory polyarthritis and is not diagnosed by crystals. D. Osteoarthritis is primarily a degenerative joint disease and does not explain the crystals. E. Gout is caused by monosodium urate, not calcium pyrophosphate, crystals.
pearl: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals confirm CPPD; in a younger patient, look for an underlying cause such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism or hypomagnesaemia.
thinking: Recurrent painful swollen knee ↓ Joint aspirated ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate crystals found ↓ CPPD disease (pseudogout)
exam_trap: E, monosodium urate gout — tempting because both are crystal arthritis, but gout is caused by urate crystals, not calcium pyrophosphate.
takeaway: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals = pseudogout; urate crystals = gout.

stem:
A 40-year-old woman has persistent fatigue, abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. She has iron-deficiency anaemia despite taking oral iron.

Which investigation is most appropriate to assess for coeliac disease?
why_correct: Coeliac disease should be assessed initially with appropriate coeliac serology, particularly tissue transglutaminase antibodies.
why_wrong: B. Lactose breath testing assesses lactose malabsorption, not coeliac disease. C. CA-125 is not a test for coeliac disease. D. Faecal elastase assesses exocrine pancreatic function. E. Faecal calprotectin assesses intestinal inflammation and is not the primary test for coeliac disease.
pearl: First-line testing for coeliac disease is IgA tTG with total IgA, taken while the patient is still eating gluten; positive serology is usually confirmed by duodenal biopsy.
thinking: Fatigue, bloating and diarrhoea ↓ Iron deficiency not responding to oral iron ↓ Suggests malabsorption ↓ Coeliac serology first ↓ Tissue transglutaminase IgA
exam_trap: E, faecal calprotectin — tempting as a test for chronic diarrhoea, but it detects intestinal inflammation such as IBD, not coeliac disease.
takeaway: Suspected coeliac disease: test IgA tTG with total IgA while eating gluten.

stem:
A 55-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. His abdomen is distended and bowel sounds are initially increased. He has previously undergone major abdominal surgery.

What is the most likely cause of his small bowel obstruction?
why_correct: Previous abdominal surgery is a major risk factor for adhesive small bowel obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids do not cause small bowel obstruction. B. A perforated ulcer causes peritonitis rather than mechanical small bowel obstruction. C. Crohn disease can cause obstruction but is not suggested here. D. Sigmoid volvulus causes large, not small, bowel obstruction.
pearl: Adhesions from previous abdominal surgery are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in the UK; hernias are the next key cause to check for.
thinking: Abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ Distension with increased bowel sounds ↓ Small bowel obstruction ↓ Previous major abdominal surgery ↓ Postoperative adhesions
exam_trap: D, sigmoid colon volvulus — tempting because it causes obstruction with distension, but it affects the large bowel, not the small bowel.
takeaway: Small bowel obstruction after previous abdominal surgery = adhesions until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 20-year-old man presents with urethral discharge and dysuria. He has recently had unprotected sex with a new partner.

Which infection is a common cause?
why_correct: Chlamydia is a common cause of sexually transmitted urethritis, often presenting with dysuria and urethral discharge.
why_wrong: A. Herpes zoster causes a dermatomal vesicular eruption. B. HPV commonly causes genital warts or asymptomatic infection. C. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis. D. Hepatitis A is primarily transmitted faeco-orally.
pearl: Urethral discharge and dysuria after unprotected sex suggest urethritis, most often from chlamydia or gonorrhoea; test with NAAT and offer partner notification.
thinking: Young man ↓ Urethral discharge and dysuria ↓ Recent unprotected sex with new partner ↓ Sexually transmitted urethritis ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: B, human papillomavirus — tempting as a common sexually transmitted infection, but HPV causes warts or no symptoms, not urethral discharge.
takeaway: Urethral discharge after unprotected sex: think chlamydia (and gonorrhoea).

stem:
A 48-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of facial flushing, sweating and palpitations. During one episode she develops a severe headache and her blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg.

Which tumour should be considered?
why_correct: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and marked hypertension are characteristic of catecholamine excess from phaeochromocytoma.
why_wrong: A. Prolactinoma causes hyperprolactinaemia-related symptoms. C. Parathyroid adenoma causes hypercalcaemia rather than episodic hypertensive attacks. D. Acromegaly causes characteristic somatic changes and metabolic effects. E. Thyroid carcinoma does not typically produce episodic catecholamine symptoms.
pearl: Episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with severe hypertension suggest phaeochromocytoma; first-line testing is plasma or urine metanephrines.
thinking: Recurrent episodes of sweating and palpitations ↓ Severe headache during an episode ↓ Marked hypertension ↓ Episodic catecholamine excess ↓ Phaeochromocytoma
exam_trap: E, thyroid carcinoma — tempting because thyroid disease causes palpitations and sweating, but it does not cause episodic catecholamine surges with severe hypertension.
takeaway: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension = phaeochromocytoma.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman has weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and palpitations. Her TSH is suppressed.

Which result would support primary hyperthyroidism?
why_correct: Primary hyperthyroidism is characterised by excess thyroid hormone with suppression of TSH.
why_wrong: A. Cortisol does not establish the diagnosis. B. TSH is usually suppressed. C. Low free T4 would suggest hypothyroidism or central disease. D. PTH is unrelated to the primary diagnosis.
pearl: In primary hyperthyroidism the thyroid makes excess hormone, so free T4 and/or T3 are raised and TSH is suppressed by negative feedback.
thinking: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor ↓ Palpitations ↓ TSH suppressed ↓ Thyroid overproducing hormone ↓ High free T4
exam_trap: B, high TSH — tempting because TSH drives the thyroid, but in primary hyperthyroidism TSH is suppressed; a high TSH would point to hypothyroidism or a TSH-secreting tumour.
takeaway: Primary hyperthyroidism = low TSH with high free T4 (and/or T3).

stem:
A 54-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the right side of his body and difficulty speaking. Symptoms began 45 minutes ago.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.D: Reassure and arrange routine GP review

why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficits are a medical emergency requiring immediate stroke assessment.
why_wrong: B. There is no evidence of bacterial infection. C. Stroke must be excluded before attributing new focal deficits to migraine. D. Delay risks loss of potentially effective acute treatment. E. Routine imaging is inappropriate for a suspected acute stroke.
pearl: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a stroke until proven otherwise; urgent assessment and brain imaging decide eligibility for time-critical thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Speech difficulty ↓ Started 45 minutes ago ↓ Within the window for reperfusion treatment ↓ Arrange urgent stroke assessment
exam_trap: C, treat as migraine without assessment — tempting because migraine can cause focal symptoms, but stroke must be excluded first as treatment is time-critical.
takeaway: Sudden focal deficit = emergency stroke assessment; time is brain.

stem:
A 61-year-old man develops sudden facial drooping, arm weakness and speech difficulty. His blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.

Why is checking blood glucose important in suspected stroke?

options.D: Glucose measurement determines whether the stroke is haemorrhagic
options.E: Glucose measurement diagnoses the location of the stroke

why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can produce focal neurological deficits resembling stroke and is an important reversible mimic.
why_wrong: A. Imaging remains important when indicated. B. Hyperglycaemia does not invariably cause stroke. D. Glucose does not distinguish haemorrhagic from ischaemic stroke. E. Glucose cannot localise a cerebral lesion.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke with focal deficits, so check capillary glucose early in every suspected stroke; it is quick to test and easily reversed.
thinking: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty ↓ Looks like stroke ↓ Hypoglycaemia can produce similar deficits ↓ Glucose check excludes a reversible mimic ↓ Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke
exam_trap: D, glucose determines whether the stroke is haemorrhagic — tempting as a reason for early tests, but only brain imaging distinguishes haemorrhage from infarction.
takeaway: Always check glucose in suspected stroke to exclude hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman develops a new unilateral facial weakness. She cannot close her left eye and has weakness of both the upper and lower parts of the left side of her face.

Which nerve is affected?
why_correct: The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, including the forehead and lower face.
why_wrong: A. The trigeminal nerve provides facial sensation and motor supply to mastication. B. The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement. C. The vagus nerve has major functions involving the pharynx, larynx and autonomic system. E. The oculomotor nerve controls several extraocular muscles and the pupil.
pearl: Weakness of both the forehead and lower face points to a lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion; upper motor neurone lesions such as stroke usually spare the forehead.
thinking: Unilateral facial weakness ↓ Cannot close the eye ↓ Upper and lower face both affected ↓ Muscles of facial expression involved ↓ Facial nerve
exam_trap: A, trigeminal nerve — tempting because it supplies the face, but it provides facial sensation and the muscles of mastication, not facial expression.
takeaway: Whole-face weakness including forehead = facial nerve (lower motor neurone) lesion.

stem:
A 66-year-old man develops a new unilateral temporal headache and pain when chewing. He also reports transient visual disturbance in the affected eye.

What is the most important immediate concern?
why_correct: The combination is highly concerning for giant cell arteritis, where visual loss is an important complication requiring urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Otitis media does not explain this presentation. B. Tension headache does not typically cause jaw claudication or visual disturbance. D. Sinusitis does not explain the characteristic combination. E. Posterior subcapsular cataract causes gradual visual impairment.
pearl: Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms is an emergency: start high-dose steroids immediately and seek same-day ophthalmology input; never wait for biopsy or ultrasound before treating.
thinking: Age over 50 with new temporal headache ↓ Jaw claudication points to giant cell arteritis ↓ Transient visual disturbance signals ischaemic risk to the optic nerve ↓ Permanent visual loss
exam_trap: E, posterior subcapsular cataract — it is an eye answer in an older patient, but cataract causes gradual painless blurring, not transient visual loss with headache and jaw claudication.
takeaway: Headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms in an older adult mean GCA: protect sight now.

stem:
A 43-year-old man with recurrent dyspepsia is found to have Helicobacter pylori infection.

Why is eradication treatment important?

options.B: It eliminates the need for any future medical review
options.D: It reduces the risk of peptic ulcer disease recurrence
options.E: It always cures gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

correct_answer: D. It reduces the risk of peptic ulcer disease recurrence
why_correct: H. pylori contributes to peptic ulcer disease, and eradication reduces recurrence in affected patients.
why_wrong: A. It does not prevent all gastrointestinal cancers. B. Successful eradication does not eliminate the need for appropriate clinical follow-up. C. Dyspepsia can have multiple causes. E. H. pylori eradication is not a universal cure for GORD.
pearl: H. pylori is a major driver of peptic ulcer disease; eradication with PPI-based combination therapy heals ulcers and greatly cuts recurrence, though it does not cure all dyspepsia or reflux.
thinking: Recurrent dyspepsia ↓ H. pylori confirmed ↓ H. pylori causes mucosal inflammation and ulceration ↓ Eradication removes the driver ↓ Reduced peptic ulcer recurrence
exam_trap: C, permanently prevents dyspepsia — tempting because symptoms often settle, but dyspepsia has many causes, so eradication cannot guarantee it never returns.
takeaway: H. pylori eradication reduces ulcer recurrence; absolute words like all, always and permanently are usually wrong.

stem:
A 73-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops severe itching, fatigue and reduced appetite. His estimated GFR has fallen substantially.

Which substance commonly accumulates in advanced kidney failure?
why_correct: Reduced renal filtration causes accumulation of urea and other nitrogenous waste products, contributing to uraemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Bile salts are primarily handled by the hepatobiliary system. B. Insulin is primarily metabolised by the liver and kidneys but is not the defining retained waste product. C. Oxygen is not retained in kidney failure. D. Haemoglobin does not accumulate as a uraemic toxin.
pearl: Itch, nausea, anorexia, fatigue and confusion in advanced CKD reflect retained nitrogenous waste (uraemia) and can be a reason to plan renal replacement therapy.
thinking: CKD with falling eGFR ↓ Itch, fatigue and poor appetite are uraemic symptoms ↓ Reduced filtration retains nitrogenous waste ↓ Urea
exam_trap: A, bile salts only — tempting because pruritus is classic for cholestasis, but here the itch comes from renal failure, where urea and other nitrogenous wastes accumulate.
takeaway: Itch, anorexia and fatigue in advanced CKD point to uraemia from retained urea.

stem:
A 78-year-old man has chronic bilateral lower-leg swelling, brown skin pigmentation around the ankles and a shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus.

Which type of ulcer is most likely?
why_correct: Venous ulcers typically occur around the medial gaiter region and are associated with chronic oedema and haemosiderin-related pigmentation.
why_wrong: A. Gangrene represents severe tissue ischaemia rather than the typical chronic ulcer pattern described. B. Arterial ulcers are typically distal, painful and associated with poor arterial perfusion. C. Neuropathic ulcers are commonly associated with loss of protective sensation. D. Pressure ulcers occur over pressure points in patients at risk from prolonged pressure.
pearl: Venous ulcers are shallow, in the gaiter area above the medial malleolus, with oedema and haemosiderin staining; check ABPI before compression bandaging to exclude significant arterial disease.
thinking: Chronic bilateral leg swelling ↓ Brown haemosiderin pigmentation at the ankles ↓ Shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus ↓ Venous hypertension pattern ↓ Venous ulcer
exam_trap: B, arterial ulcer — tempting in a 78-year-old, but arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out and distal on the toes or pressure points, without oedema and pigmentation.
takeaway: Medial malleolus, oedema and brown staining mean venous ulcer; check ABPI before compression.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman with asthma is unable to complete sentences because of breathlessness. Her peak expiratory flow is 40% of her best.

How should this presentation be regarded?
why_correct: Under BTS/SIGN acute asthma guidance (retained alongside BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024), inability to complete sentences in one breath or PEF 33–50% of best or predicted defines acute severe asthma; PEF below 33% would make it life-threatening.
why_wrong: A. Stable asthma does not cause inability to complete sentences or a PEF of 40% of best. B. Mild intermittent asthma describes infrequent symptoms with normal function between episodes, not an acute attack with PEF 40% of best. C. Chronic bronchitis is a COPD phenotype and does not explain this acute asthma presentation. E. Viral rhinitis does not cause marked airflow obstruction.
pearl: Grade acute asthma at the bedside: inability to complete sentences or PEF 33–50% is acute severe; PEF below 33%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion or confusion mark life-threatening asthma.
thinking: Known asthma ↓ Unable to complete sentences ↓ PEF 40% of best falls in the severe band ↓ No life-threatening features described ↓ Severe acute asthma
exam_trap: B, mild intermittent asthma — a familiar asthma label, but it describes infrequent background symptoms, not an acute attack with PEF 40% of best.
takeaway: Cannot finish sentences or PEF 33–50% of best means acute severe asthma.

stem:
A 68-year-old man has a persistent cough and coughing up small amounts of blood. He has smoked 30 cigarettes daily for 40 years.

Which diagnosis requires urgent consideration?
why_correct: Haemoptysis and persistent cough in a heavy smoker are concerning features requiring assessment for lung cancer.
why_wrong: B. Migraine does not explain these respiratory symptoms. C. IBS affects the gastrointestinal tract. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause haemoptysis. E. Viral rhinitis does not explain persistent haemoptysis in this context.
pearl: Unexplained haemoptysis in an adult aged 40 or over warrants a suspected lung cancer pathway referral; in a heavy smoker with persistent cough, lung cancer must be excluded promptly.
thinking: Older heavy smoker ↓ Persistent cough ↓ Haemoptysis is a red flag ↓ Malignancy must be excluded ↓ Lung cancer
exam_trap: E, viral rhinitis — the only other respiratory option, but it is a self-limiting nasal illness and does not cause persistent cough with haemoptysis.
takeaway: Haemoptysis in an older smoker is lung cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 60-year-old man has a persistent cough, weight loss and a hoarse voice. He has a long smoking history.

Which complication of a lung tumour can cause hoarseness?

options.A: Phrenic nerve involvement by the tumour
options.E: Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel

why_correct: A lung tumour, particularly in the mediastinum, can involve the recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause vocal cord palsy and hoarseness.
why_wrong: A. Phrenic nerve involvement causes diaphragmatic paralysis, not hoarseness. B. Sympathetic chain involvement causes Horner syndrome. D. Optic nerve pathology causes visual disturbance. E. Median nerve pathology causes sensory and motor symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Hoarseness with a lung tumour suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, more often left-sided because the left nerve loops under the aortic arch; it signals mediastinal spread.
thinking: Smoker with cough and weight loss ↓ Likely lung cancer ↓ New hoarse voice suggests vocal cord palsy ↓ Mediastinal nerve involvement ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: A, phrenic nerve involvement — another mediastinal nerve that tumours invade, but it paralyses the hemidiaphragm and causes breathlessness, not hoarseness.
takeaway: Lung cancer with hoarseness means recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.

stem:
A 44-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty swallowing. Endoscopy reveals a smooth narrowing of the oesophagus with no obvious mass.

Which condition is a possible cause?
why_correct: A benign oesophageal stricture can cause progressive dysphagia due to narrowing of the oesophageal lumen.
why_wrong: A. Candidiasis produces white plaques and odynophagia rather than a smooth stricture. C. Appendicitis does not cause oesophageal narrowing. D. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear after vomiting causing haematemesis. E. Varices appear as submucosal veins and do not typically cause progressive dysphagia.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia always needs endoscopy; a smooth stricture without a mass is often peptic from long-standing reflux, but biopsies are still taken to exclude malignancy.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia ↓ Endoscopy shows smooth luminal narrowing ↓ No mass seen ↓ Benign fibrotic narrowing ↓ Benign oesophageal stricture
exam_trap: A, oesophageal candidiasis — an endoscopic oesophageal diagnosis, but it shows white plaques and causes painful swallowing, not a smooth narrowing.
takeaway: Smooth narrowing without a mass on endoscopy suggests a benign, often peptic, stricture.

stem:
A 70-year-old man presents with a new painful groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Which type of hernia is most likely?
why_correct: A femoral hernia typically presents below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and has a relatively high risk of complications.
why_wrong: A. Epigastric hernias occur in the upper midline abdominal wall. B. Umbilical hernias occur at the umbilicus. D. Hiatus hernias occur through the diaphragm. E. Incisional hernias occur at previous surgical incision sites.
pearl: Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, have a narrow neck and a high risk of strangulation, so they should be repaired promptly rather than observed.
thinking: Groin lump ↓ Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ Femoral canal territory ↓ Painful, raising concern for complication ↓ Femoral hernia
exam_trap: E, incisional hernia — a common hernia in older adults, but it arises at a previous surgical scar, which is not described, and is not defined by the pubic tubercle.
takeaway: Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle means femoral hernia; repair early.

stem:
A 28-year-old man develops a new episode of painless bright-red rectal bleeding. He has no anal pain.

Which diagnosis is a common cause of painless bright-red rectal bleeding?
why_correct: Haemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red bleeding on the paper or in the pan in younger adults. In adults aged 50 or over, new unexplained rectal bleeding needs colorectal cancer assessment (FIT-guided, per NICE NG12) before being attributed to haemorrhoids.
why_wrong: A. Anal fissures typically cause severe pain during and after defecation. B. Acute pancreatitis causes severe upper abdominal pain and does not cause rectal bleeding. D. Gastric ulcers cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which presents as melaena or haematemesis rather than bright-red rectal blood. E. Oesophagitis causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms and does not usually cause bright-red rectal bleeding.
pearl: Haemorrhoids cause painless bright-red blood on the paper or in the pan; an anal fissure gives similar blood but with sharp pain on and after defecation.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Painless bright-red rectal bleeding ↓ No anal pain argues against fissure ↓ Bright red suggests a distal source ↓ Haemorrhoids
exam_trap: A, anal fissure — also causes bright-red bleeding in young adults, but it typically causes severe pain during and after defecation, which he does not have.
takeaway: Bright-red rectal bleeding: painless suggests haemorrhoids, painful suggests fissure.

stem:
A 57-year-old man develops sudden painless rectal bleeding. He is haemodynamically stable and has no abdominal pain.

Which source should be considered?
why_correct: Diverticular bleeding can cause sudden, painless, sometimes substantial lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Perforated ulcer causes an acute abdomen and upper GI pathology. C. Pancreatitis causes severe upper abdominal pain. D. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain rather than isolated painless rectal bleeding. E. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain and may cause haematuria.
pearl: Diverticular disease is a leading cause of sudden painless lower GI bleeding in older adults; most bleeds settle spontaneously, and haemodynamic status guides the urgency of management.
thinking: Adult in his late 50s ↓ Sudden painless rectal bleeding ↓ Stable with no abdominal pain ↓ Lower GI vascular source ↓ Diverticular bleeding
exam_trap: A, perforated peptic ulcer — peptic ulcers can bleed, but perforation causes sudden severe abdominal pain and peritonism, not painless rectal bleeding.
takeaway: Sudden painless lower GI bleeding in an older adult: think diverticular disease.

stem:
A 41-year-old woman has very heavy menstrual bleeding. Ultrasound shows a submucosal uterine fibroid.

Which symptom is particularly associated with submucosal fibroids?
why_correct: Fibroids, particularly those distorting the uterine cavity such as submucosal fibroids, can cause heavy menstrual bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Jaundice indicates hepatobiliary disease. B. Haemoptysis is a respiratory symptom. C. Polyuria has urinary/metabolic causes. D. Sudden monocular blindness requires urgent ophthalmological/vascular assessment.
pearl: Submucosal fibroids distort the uterine cavity and cause heavy menstrual bleeding and subfertility out of proportion to their size; hysteroscopic resection may be an option.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding ↓ Ultrasound shows a submucosal fibroid ↓ Distorted cavity with larger bleeding surface ↓ Heavy menstrual bleeding
exam_trap: D, sudden monocular blindness — the most alarming symptom offered, but it reflects ocular or vascular disease and has no link with uterine fibroids.
takeaway: Submucosal fibroids classically cause heavy menstrual bleeding.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding 3 years after the menopause.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Any vaginal bleeding after menopause requires appropriate assessment because endometrial pathology, including cancer, must be excluded.
why_wrong: A. Ovulation does not normally occur after menopause. B. Menstrual bleeding should have ceased after menopause. C. Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle ovulatory pain. E. Menstruation does not resume after the menopause.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding in women aged 55 or over needs a suspected cancer pathway referral; transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness is a usual first investigation.
thinking: Menopause 3 years ago ↓ New vaginal bleeding ↓ Menses do not resume after menopause ↓ Endometrial pathology must be excluded ↓ Postmenopausal bleeding
exam_trap: E, resumption of normal menses — tempting if the bleeding is assumed hormonal, but periods do not return years after menopause; any bleeding is abnormal.
takeaway: Any bleeding after the menopause is postmenopausal bleeding and needs urgent assessment.

stem:
A 57-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding. She is overweight and has a history of type 2 diabetes.

Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding is the key presenting symptom of endometrial cancer, and obesity and type 2 diabetes are associated risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid cancer does not explain this presentation. B. Renal cell carcinoma can cause haematuria but not typically postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. C. Testicular cancer cannot explain postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. D. Pancreatic cancer has a different typical presentation.
pearl: Unopposed oestrogen drives endometrial cancer: obesity, diabetes, nulliparity, late menopause and tamoxifen raise risk, and postmenopausal bleeding is the usual presenting symptom.
thinking: Postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Obesity and type 2 diabetes ↓ Unopposed oestrogen and insulin resistance ↓ Endometrial source ↓ Endometrial cancer
exam_trap: B, renal cell carcinoma — linked with obesity and causes bleeding, but the bleeding is haematuria, not vaginal bleeding after the menopause.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding plus obesity or diabetes: think endometrial cancer.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Her blood pressure is 165/105 mmHg.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A seizure associated with hypertension in pregnancy, particularly after 20 weeks, should be treated as eclampsia until proven otherwise.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not typically cause generalised tonic-clonic seizures. B. A seizure in pregnancy with severe hypertension should not automatically be attributed to epilepsy. C. Vasovagal syncope does not usually cause a sustained generalised seizure. D. Hypoglycaemia is a differential but does not explain the hypertensive context.
pearl: Treat a seizure with hypertension after 20 weeks as eclampsia: give IV magnesium sulfate, control blood pressure and plan delivery once stable; magnesium, not standard antiepileptics, is first line.
thinking: Pregnant at 32 weeks ↓ Generalised tonic-clonic seizure ↓ Severe hypertension at 165/105 mmHg ↓ Pre-eclampsia with seizure ↓ Eclampsia
exam_trap: B, epilepsy — tempting for any tonic-clonic seizure, but severe hypertension in the third trimester makes eclampsia the diagnosis to treat until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Seizure plus hypertension after 20 weeks is eclampsia: magnesium sulfate first.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman notices that one nipple has recently become inverted. She has no history of breastfeeding.

What should be considered?
why_correct: New nipple inversion, particularly in a non-lactating woman, is a suspicious breast feature requiring assessment.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. B. Fibromyalgia does not cause structural breast changes. C. Lactation does not explain new nipple inversion in this context. D. Candidiasis affects mucosal surfaces.
pearl: New nipple inversion or retraction, unlike long-standing inversion, can signal underlying breast cancer and needs urgent triple assessment: examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: Woman aged 58 ↓ Recent, new nipple inversion ↓ Not related to lactation ↓ Possible tethering of ducts by tumour ↓ Breast malignancy
exam_trap: C, normal lactation — a benign nipple-related answer, but she is not breastfeeding and lactation does not cause new inversion.
takeaway: New nipple inversion is suspicious for breast cancer until assessed.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents with spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge. There is no obvious breast infection.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: An intraductal papilloma can cause spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge, although malignancy also needs appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Mastitis usually causes pain, erythema and systemic symptoms. B. Fibroadenoma presents as a painless mobile lump without discharge. C. Prolactinoma causes bilateral milky discharge, not unilateral bloody discharge. E. Fibromyalgia does not cause nipple discharge.
pearl: Intraductal papilloma is the commonest cause of spontaneous single-duct bloody nipple discharge, but triple assessment is needed because ductal carcinoma can present the same way.
thinking: Spontaneous nipple discharge ↓ Unilateral and bloody ↓ No infection ↓ Benign ductal lesion most common ↓ Intraductal papilloma
exam_trap: C, galactorrhoea from prolactinoma — it causes nipple discharge, but typically bilateral and milky, not unilateral and bloody.
takeaway: Unilateral bloody nipple discharge suggests intraductal papilloma, but exclude cancer.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman is diagnosed with a fragility fracture after falling from standing height. Her bone density is reduced.

Which diagnosis best describes the underlying skeletal disorder?
why_correct: Osteoporosis is characterised by reduced bone strength and increased risk of fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. Osteomalacia results from defective mineralisation of bone. B. Osteoarthritis affects joints rather than primarily reducing bone strength. D. Septic arthritis is an infected joint. E. RA is an inflammatory autoimmune joint disease.
pearl: A fracture from standing height or less is a fragility fracture and signals osteoporosis; assess fracture risk, optimise calcium and vitamin D, and consider bisphosphonate treatment.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Fracture from a standing-height fall ↓ Fragility fracture ↓ Reduced bone density ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: A, osteomalacia — also weakens bone and causes fractures, but it is a mineralisation defect, usually from vitamin D deficiency, with bone pain and abnormal bone biochemistry.
takeaway: Fragility fracture plus low bone density means osteoporosis.

stem:
A 22-year-old man presents with fever, headache and neck stiffness. He has a widespread non-blanching purpuric rash.

What organism is particularly associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Meningococcal infection can cause meningitis with rapidly progressive meningococcal septicaemia and a non-blanching rash.
why_wrong: A. Candida causes opportunistic fungal infections. B. H. pylori causes gastric infection. C. E. coli can cause meningitis in specific groups but is not the classic cause of this presentation in a young adult. D. S. epidermidis is associated particularly with prosthetic-device infections.
pearl: Suspected meningococcal disease with a non-blanching rash: give parenteral benzylpenicillin in the community without delay and transfer urgently; never wait for investigations.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Fever, headache and neck stiffness suggest meningitis ↓ Non-blanching purpuric rash suggests septicaemia ↓ Classic meningococcal disease ↓ Neisseria meningitidis
exam_trap: C, Escherichia coli — a recognised meningitis organism, but mainly in neonates; in a young adult with a purpuric rash, meningococcus is the classic cause.
takeaway: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 56-year-old man has progressive weakness of the hands. Examination reveals muscle wasting and fasciculations.

Which type of neurological lesion is most consistent with these findings?
why_correct: Muscle wasting, fasciculations and weakness are characteristic of lower motor neuron involvement.
why_wrong: B. UMN lesions typically cause increased tone and reflexes. C. Occipital lesions primarily affect vision. D. Cerebellar lesions primarily cause coordination problems. E. Basal ganglia disease produces movement disorders.
pearl: Wasting and fasciculations mark lower motor neuron involvement; if upper motor neuron signs coexist with no sensory loss, think motor neurone disease.
thinking: Progressive hand weakness ↓ Muscle wasting ↓ Fasciculations ↓ Anterior horn cell or peripheral nerve pattern ↓ Lower motor neuron lesion
exam_trap: B, upper motor neuron lesion — weakness is shared, but UMN lesions cause spasticity and hyperreflexia without early wasting or fasciculations.
takeaway: Wasting plus fasciculations means a lower motor neuron lesion.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman develops sudden weakness and numbness affecting her right arm and leg. She also has difficulty finding and producing words.

Which feature would most strongly support a cortical cerebral lesion?
why_correct: Aphasia indicates dysfunction of the language-dominant (usually left) cerebral cortex, which is consistent with right-sided weakness, and is a cortical sign that a subcortical or peripheral lesion would not produce.
why_wrong: A. Isolated foot drop suggests common peroneal nerve or L5 root pathology. B. Isolated calf wasting suggests a lower motor neuron or peripheral process. D. Peripheral nerve pain does not localise to the cerebral cortex. E. An isolated reduced ankle reflex suggests S1 root or peripheral nerve disease.
pearl: Cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect or visual field loss localise a stroke to the cortex and help separate anterior circulation strokes from lacunar strokes, which lack them.
thinking: Right arm and leg weakness and numbness ↓ Word-finding and production difficulty ↓ Language sits in the dominant, usually left, cortex ↓ Cortical sign ↓ Aphasia
exam_trap: E, loss of ankle reflex only — a specific-sounding neurological sign, but it points to S1 root or peripheral nerve disease, not a cerebral cortical lesion.
takeaway: Aphasia is a cortical sign localising to the dominant hemisphere.

stem:
A 61-year-old man develops difficulty speaking after a stroke. He understands what is being said but produces slow, effortful speech with relatively few words.

Which type of aphasia is most likely?
why_correct: Broca aphasia causes non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
why_wrong: A. Wernicke aphasia causes fluent but impaired, often nonsensical speech with poor comprehension. B. Dysarthria affects articulation rather than language formulation. C. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. E. Amnesia concerns memory rather than language production.
pearl: Broca aphasia is non-fluent, effortful speech with good comprehension (frontal lobe); Wernicke aphasia is fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension (temporal lobe).
thinking: Speech difficulty after stroke ↓ Comprehension preserved ↓ Slow, effortful speech with few words ↓ Expressive, non-fluent aphasia ↓ Broca aphasia
exam_trap: B, dysarthria — tempting because speech is slow and laboured, but dysarthria is a disorder of articulation, not of producing language.
takeaway: Broca is broken speech with intact understanding; Wernicke is fluent nonsense.

stem:
A 72-year-old man suddenly develops inability to understand spoken language and produces fluent but nonsensical speech.

Which brain region is most likely affected?
why_correct: Wernicke's area lies in the dominant temporal region and is involved in language comprehension.
why_wrong: B. The cerebellum coordinates movement. C. The occipital lobe primarily processes vision. D. The non-dominant parietal lobe does not produce classic Wernicke aphasia. E. The spinal cord cannot cause cortical aphasia.
pearl: Wernicke area lies in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, typically within the middle cerebral artery territory; damage gives fluent speech with poor comprehension.
thinking: Sudden onset suggests stroke ↓ Cannot understand spoken language ↓ Fluent but nonsensical speech ↓ Receptive (Wernicke) aphasia ↓ Dominant temporal lobe
exam_trap: D, non-dominant parietal lobe only — a cortical answer, but non-dominant parietal lesions cause neglect and spatial problems, not receptive aphasia.
takeaway: Fluent nonsense with poor comprehension localises to the dominant temporal lobe.

stem:
A 76-year-old man becomes acutely confused over a day while being treated for pneumonia. His family reports that he was cognitively well beforehand.

What is the key feature distinguishing delirium from dementia?
correct_answer: B. Acute onset with fluctuating attention
why_correct: Delirium develops acutely and characteristically causes fluctuating attention and awareness.
why_wrong: A. Gradual decline is characteristic of dementia. C. Delirium often has an underlying precipitant such as infection or medication. D. Stable impairment is more consistent with dementia. E. Impaired attention is a defining feature of delirium.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating and centred on inattention; screen with a validated tool such as the 4AT and look for the precipitant, such as infection, drugs, retention, constipation or pain.
thinking: Confusion developing over a day ↓ Cognitively well beforehand ↓ Clear precipitant in pneumonia ↓ Hallmark of delirium ↓ Acute onset with fluctuating attention
exam_trap: C, no identifiable precipitating factors — tempting if delirium is thought idiopathic, but it usually has a cause, here pneumonia, which should be treated.
takeaway: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention; dementia is gradual and progressive.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman reports feeling as though she is watching herself from outside her body during periods of severe stress.

Which symptom is this?
why_correct: Depersonalisation is a feeling of detachment or unreality concerning one's own self or body.
why_wrong: A. A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus. B. Thought insertion is the belief that thoughts have been placed into one's mind by an external source. C. A delusion is a fixed false belief. E. Echolalia is repetition of another person's words.
pearl: Depersonalisation is feeling detached from oneself; derealisation is feeling the surroundings are unreal. Both are common with stress or anxiety, and insight is preserved.
thinking: Episodes during severe stress ↓ Feels as though watching herself from outside her body ↓ An 'as if' sense of detachment from the self ↓ Not a perception of something external ↓ Depersonalisation
exam_trap: A, hallucination — the experience sounds perceptual, but a hallucination is a perception without a stimulus; she describes an 'as if' feeling of detachment from her own self.
takeaway: Detached from self is depersonalisation; the world feeling unreal is derealisation.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia has become increasingly withdrawn. He has little spontaneous speech, reduced emotional expression and has stopped seeing friends.

Which type of symptom is this?
why_correct: Reduced motivation, emotional expression, speech and social engagement are characteristic negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
why_wrong: A. Panic symptoms are acute episodes of intense anxiety. B. Obsessions are intrusive repetitive thoughts. C. Positive symptoms include hallucinations and delusions. D. Dissociative symptoms involve disruption in normally integrated consciousness, memory or identity.
pearl: Negative symptoms of schizophrenia, such as alogia, blunted affect, avolition and social withdrawal, respond poorly to antipsychotics and drive much long-term disability.
thinking: Schizophrenia ↓ Little spontaneous speech ↓ Reduced emotional expression ↓ Social withdrawal ↓ Negative symptom
exam_trap: C, positive symptom — the familiar schizophrenia category, but positive symptoms are added experiences such as hallucinations and delusions, not losses of function.
takeaway: Negative symptoms are losses; positive symptoms are additions such as hallucinations.

stem:
A 16-year-old girl has not started menstruating. Examination shows normal breast development but little pubic and axillary hair. Investigations suggest a lack of functional ovaries.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) causes primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development, from peripheral aromatisation of testicular testosterone, but scant pubic and axillary hair because androgen-dependent hair growth fails; there are testes rather than functional ovaries and no uterus.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis presents with pelvic pain and/or subfertility in women who menstruate, not primary amenorrhoea. B. Turner syndrome causes ovarian failure with absent or poor breast development and usually normal pubic hair from adrenal androgens, the opposite of this picture. C. Pregnancy should be considered in sexually active adolescents but does not explain primary amenorrhoea with scant pubic hair and absent ovaries. E. PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes irregular or absent ovulation with hyperandrogenism, not absent ovaries with scant body hair.
pearl: Complete androgen insensitivity: 46,XY with testes, normal breasts from aromatised testosterone, scant pubic and axillary hair and no uterus, presenting as primary amenorrhoea.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea at 16 ↓ Normal breast development ↓ Scant pubic and axillary hair ↓ No functional ovaries ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: B, Turner syndrome — classic for primary amenorrhoea with ovarian failure, but it gives poor breast development and usually normal pubic hair, the reverse of this picture.
takeaway: Breasts present, body hair scant and primary amenorrhoea: think androgen insensitivity.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement and has not developed other expected pubertal changes. His height is below that of most peers but his growth pattern has remained consistent.

What is an important initial consideration?
why_correct: Absence of expected pubertal development by this age warrants assessment for delayed puberty.
why_wrong: A. Cushing syndrome has a different clinical pattern and does not specifically cause absent testicular development. C. Precocious puberty involves unusually early pubertal development. D. Acromegaly occurs after growth plates have largely fused. E. Hyperthyroidism does not explain absent testicular enlargement.
pearl: In boys, absent testicular enlargement by about 14 years defines delayed puberty; constitutional delay with steady growth is commonest, but hypogonadism and chronic illness must be excluded.
thinking: Boy aged 16 ↓ No testicular enlargement ↓ No other pubertal changes ↓ Short but growing consistently ↓ Delayed puberty
exam_trap: C, precocious puberty — the other puberty-timing option, but it means unusually early development, whereas this boy has none at 16.
takeaway: No testicular enlargement by around 14 years in a boy means delayed puberty.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents with a painful, red area of breast tissue three weeks after starting breastfeeding. She has a temperature of 38.5°C.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Breastfeeding-associated breast pain, erythema and systemic symptoms are typical of lactational mastitis.
why_wrong: A. Intraductal papilloma commonly causes nipple discharge. C. Fibrocystic change can cause cyclical breast discomfort but not an acute febrile presentation. D. Breast cancer does not typically present with an acute febrile inflammatory illness. E. Fibroadenoma is usually a painless discrete lump.
pearl: In lactational mastitis, continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected breast; add flucloxacillin if infection is likely or symptoms fail to settle, and look for an abscess if not improving.
thinking: Three weeks into breastfeeding ↓ Painful red area of breast ↓ Fever of 38.5°C ↓ Inflammation of the lactating breast ↓ Lactational mastitis
exam_trap: D, breast cancer — inflammatory cancer can mimic infection, but an acute febrile illness in early breastfeeding is mastitis; cancer is considered if it fails to resolve.
takeaway: A painful, red, febrile breast while breastfeeding is mastitis; keep feeding.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman notices spontaneous blood-stained discharge from one nipple. There is no fever or breast inflammation.

Which lesion is a recognised cause of this presentation?
why_correct: An intraductal papilloma can cause spontaneous, often blood-stained, unilateral nipple discharge.
why_wrong: A. A galactocele is a milk-retention cyst associated with lactation. C. Fat necrosis typically follows trauma and presents as a firm lump, not spontaneous bloody discharge. D. A breast abscess is painful and inflammatory. E. Fibroadenoma typically presents as a painless breast lump.
pearl: Spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct most often comes from an intraductal papilloma near the areola; assessment is still needed because ductal carcinoma can present similarly.
thinking: Spontaneous nipple discharge ↓ From one nipple ↓ Blood-stained ↓ No fever or inflammation ↓ Intraductal papilloma
exam_trap: D, subareolar breast abscess — near the nipple and may discharge, but it is painful and inflamed, and this woman has no fever or inflammation.
takeaway: Spontaneous bloody discharge from one nipple is classically an intraductal papilloma.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman presents with a new breast lump. It is hard, irregular and poorly mobile. There is associated skin tethering.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: The features are suspicious for breast malignancy
options.B: No assessment is required if there is no pain
options.C: The features are diagnostic of fibroadenoma
options.D: The lump is necessarily a cyst
options.E: The lump is necessarily an abscess

correct_answer: A. The features are suspicious for breast malignancy
why_correct: A new hard, irregular, poorly mobile breast lump with skin tethering has suspicious features and requires urgent breast assessment.
why_wrong: B. Breast cancer can be painless. C. Fibroadenomas are typically smooth and mobile. D. A simple cyst is typically smooth and fluctuant. E. Abscesses usually cause pain and inflammatory changes.
pearl: Hard, irregular, fixed lumps with skin tethering, nipple change or axillary nodes are suspicious; refer on a suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment: examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: New breast lump at 52 ↓ Hard and irregular ↓ Poorly mobile ↓ Skin tethering ↓ Suspicious for breast malignancy
exam_trap: C, diagnostic of fibroadenoma — a common breast lump, but fibroadenomas are smooth, rubbery and mobile, typically in younger women, not hard and tethered.
takeaway: A hard, irregular, tethered breast lump is cancer until triple assessment says otherwise.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman develops severe loin pain and fever. She has rigors and appears unwell. Imaging shows a ureteric stone with proximal urinary tract dilatation.

What is the most important concern?
why_correct: Infection proximal to an obstructed urinary tract can rapidly become life-threatening and requires urgent urological management.
why_wrong: B. Obstruction makes this complicated; infection behind an obstruction needs urgent decompression. C. Fever and systemic illness make uncomplicated renal colic inappropriate as the diagnosis. D. Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not cause this clinical picture. E. Cystitis does not explain an obstructed upper urinary tract with systemic illness.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent; antibiotics alone are not enough.
thinking: Ureteric stone ↓ Proximal dilatation means obstruction ↓ Fever and rigors mean infection ↓ Infection behind obstruction risks urosepsis ↓ Infected obstructed urinary tract
exam_trap: B, uncomplicated pyelonephritis — fever and loin pain fit, but obstruction makes it complicated; without decompression it can rapidly progress to septic shock.
takeaway: Fever plus an obstructing stone needs urgent decompression, not antibiotics alone.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no vaginal discharge, flank pain or systemic symptoms.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria and frequency without systemic or upper urinary tract features are typical of a lower UTI.
why_wrong: A. Glomerulonephritis causes renal findings such as haematuria and proteinuria rather than isolated dysuria. B. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever, systemic illness and flank pain. C. PID is usually associated with pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness and/or abnormal vaginal discharge. D. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain.
pearl: In a non-pregnant woman with typical lower UTI symptoms and no upper tract or systemic features, the diagnosis is clinical, and a short course of nitrofurantoin is the usual UK first-line choice.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Dysuria and frequency ↓ No vaginal discharge, so vaginitis less likely ↓ No flank pain or systemic features ↓ Lower urinary tract infection
exam_trap: B, acute pyelonephritis — also a UTI, but it needs fever, systemic upset or flank pain, all absent here.
takeaway: Dysuria and frequency without fever or flank pain mean lower UTI.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman has dysuria, urinary frequency and fever. She also has marked tenderness in the costovertebral angle.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, urinary symptoms and flank or costovertebral-angle tenderness suggest infection of the kidney.
why_wrong: B. Stress incontinence causes leakage. C. Cystitis usually lacks systemic illness and flank tenderness. D. Stones cause colicky pain but do not by themselves explain fever and infection. E. Candidiasis causes vulvovaginal itching and discharge rather than renal-angle tenderness.
pearl: Acute pyelonephritis needs an antibiotic that reaches renal tissue, so nitrofurantoin is unsuitable; send urine for culture, and admit if septic, vomiting or not improving.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency ↓ Fever adds systemic features ↓ Costovertebral angle tenderness ↓ Upper urinary tract infection ↓ Acute pyelonephritis
exam_trap: C, uncomplicated cystitis — shares the dysuria and frequency, but fever and renal-angle tenderness show the infection has reached the kidney.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms plus fever and loin tenderness mean pyelonephritis.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops persistent nausea, itching and increasing confusion despite appropriate medical management.

Which complication may indicate the need to consider renal replacement therapy?
why_correct: Significant uraemic complications are among the situations in which renal replacement therapy may need to be considered.
why_wrong: A. Mild oedema can often be managed medically. B. An isolated creatinine value is not by itself an indication for dialysis. D. Controlled hypertension is not an indication. E. Chronic anaemia alone does not automatically require renal replacement therapy.
pearl: Reasons to consider dialysis in CKD include uraemic complications such as encephalopathy, pericarditis or intractable symptoms, plus refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia or acidosis.
thinking: CKD ↓ Persistent nausea and itching ↓ Increasing confusion ↓ Despite appropriate medical management, so refractory ↓ Uraemic complications
exam_trap: B, mild isolated creatinine elevation — a number feels decisive, but dialysis decisions rest on symptoms and complications, not a single mild creatinine rise.
takeaway: Refractory uraemic complications are a reason to consider renal replacement therapy.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea several days after returning from abroad. She is drinking normally and has no signs of dehydration.

What is the most important initial management principle?
why_correct: Maintaining hydration is central to management of acute diarrhoeal illness when there is no evidence of severe dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction increases the risk of dehydration. B. There is no evidence of a surgical abdomen. C. Corticosteroids are not routine treatment for infectious diarrhoea. E. Insulin has no role.
pearl: Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting; maintaining oral fluid intake is the mainstay, with oral rehydration solution for those at risk, and stool culture if bloody, severe or persistent.
thinking: Diarrhoea after travel abroad ↓ Likely infective ↓ Drinking normally, not dehydrated ↓ Ongoing losses must be replaced ↓ Maintain adequate fluid intake
exam_trap: B, immediate emergency surgery — the severe pain tempts, but nothing described suggests a surgical abdomen; this is a diarrhoeal illness managed medically.
takeaway: Acute infective diarrhoea is managed first by keeping the patient hydrated.

stem:
A 45-year-old man has episodic wheeze and cough that are worse when he is exposed to house dust. Between episodes, his respiratory examination is normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Variable respiratory symptoms triggered by environmental exposure with normal findings between episodes are characteristic of asthma.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary fibrosis causes persistent rather than highly variable symptoms. B. Pleural effusion causes persistent breathlessness and reduced breath sounds. C. Bronchiectasis usually causes chronic productive cough. D. Lung cancer commonly causes persistent respiratory symptoms.
pearl: Asthma is diagnosed from variable symptoms supported by objective evidence of airway inflammation or variable obstruction, such as FeNO, bronchodilator reversibility or peak flow variability.
thinking: Episodic wheeze and cough ↓ Triggered by house dust ↓ Normal examination between episodes ↓ Variable, reversible airway obstruction ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: C, bronchiectasis — a chronic airway disease with cough, but it causes persistent daily productive sputum rather than episodic, trigger-driven wheeze.
takeaway: Episodic, trigger-driven wheeze with normal findings between attacks suggests asthma.

stem:
A 23-year-old man develops sudden severe pain and swelling of the left side of his scrotum. He has no urinary symptoms and the pain began abruptly while he was asleep.

What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
why_correct: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain without urinary symptoms is highly concerning for testicular torsion, a time-critical surgical emergency.
why_wrong: A. An inguinal hernia may cause groin or scrotal swelling but the abrupt severe testicular presentation requires torsion to be excluded. B. Hydrocele is generally painless. C. An epididymal cyst is usually painless. E. Varicocele usually develops gradually and causes a dragging discomfort.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis needing urgent surgical exploration; do not delay for ultrasound, as the chance of saving the testis falls sharply within hours.
thinking: Young man ↓ Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain ↓ Onset during sleep ↓ No urinary symptoms to suggest infection ↓ Testicular torsion
exam_trap: E, varicocele — another left-sided scrotal swelling, but it develops gradually with a dragging ache, not sudden severe pain.
takeaway: Sudden severe testicular pain is torsion until surgery proves otherwise.

stem:
A 65-year-old man has swelling and pain in his right calf following several weeks of reduced mobility.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Unilateral calf swelling and pain with a provoking factor such as immobility are characteristic features that should raise suspicion of DVT.
why_wrong: A. Gout typically causes acute inflammatory arthritis. C. Osteoarthritis causes joint-related mechanical pain. D. Varicose eczema causes chronic inflammatory skin changes. E. Cellulitis can cause unilateral swelling and erythema but does not explain the thrombotic risk context by itself.
pearl: For suspected DVT use the two-level Wells score: if likely, arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if it is delayed; if unlikely, start with a D-dimer.
thinking: Older man ↓ Several weeks of reduced mobility ↓ Unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ Venous stasis as a provoking factor ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: E, cellulitis — can cause unilateral leg swelling and pain, but no erythema or fever is described, and recent immobility points to venous thrombosis.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling after immobility is DVT until excluded.

stem:
A 56-year-old man presents with sudden onset of weakness affecting his right face and arm. His speech is slurred.

What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.C: Activate the local acute stroke pathway
options.D: Reassure him that symptoms are likely migraine

correct_answer: C. Activate the local acute stroke pathway
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms are highly concerning for acute stroke and require immediate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Routine referral would delay time-critical assessment. B. There is no evidence of bacterial infection. D. Stroke must be considered urgently rather than assumed to be migraine. E. Rehabilitation may be required later but is not the initial priority.
pearl: Sudden facial and arm weakness with speech disturbance is FAST-positive: activate the stroke pathway at once because reperfusion treatments are time-dependent, and check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Right face and arm weakness ↓ Slurred speech ↓ FAST-positive, likely stroke ↓ Activate the local acute stroke pathway
exam_trap: D, reassure that it is likely migraine — migraine aura can cause focal symptoms, but sudden focal weakness must be treated as stroke; delay loses the treatment window.
takeaway: FAST-positive symptoms: activate the stroke pathway immediately.

stem:
A 68-year-old man develops sudden loss of vision in his right eye lasting 10 minutes. His vision then returns completely to normal.

What is this episode commonly called?
why_correct: Transient monocular visual loss due to retinal or optic circulation is termed amaurosis fugax and can be a manifestation of transient ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment generally causes persistent visual symptoms. C. Optic neuritis typically causes subacute painful visual loss. D. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. E. Conjunctivitis causes redness and discharge.
pearl: Amaurosis fugax is a TIA affecting the eye, often from carotid emboli; arrange urgent specialist TIA assessment with carotid imaging and start aspirin unless contraindicated.
thinking: Older man ↓ Sudden monocular visual loss ↓ Lasts 10 minutes ↓ Complete recovery suggests transient ischaemia ↓ Amaurosis fugax
exam_trap: A, retinal detachment — causes sudden monocular loss, but it is usually preceded by floaters and flashes and persists rather than resolving completely.
takeaway: Transient monocular blindness is amaurosis fugax: manage as a TIA.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman develops weakness that becomes worse after repeated movements but improves after resting. Examination is otherwise normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fatigable weakness that improves with rest is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson's causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes exertional limb pain rather than fatigable muscle weakness. C. MS produces neurological deficits separated in time and space. D. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with UMN/LMN signs.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis classically causes fatigable ptosis, diplopia and proximal weakness; check acetylcholine receptor antibodies and image the chest for thymoma.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Weakness worsens with repeated movement ↓ Improves after rest ↓ Examination otherwise normal ↓ Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: C, multiple sclerosis — common in young women and causes fatigue, but it produces deficits separated in time and space, not fatigable weakness that recovers with rest.
takeaway: Weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest is myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 74-year-old man suddenly develops difficulty speaking and weakness of his right arm. Which clinical feature would make a stroke particularly likely?

options.A: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
options.B: Gradual onset of symptoms over several months
options.C: Bilateral chronic joint pain and morning stiffness

correct_answer: A. Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
why_correct: Stroke classically presents with sudden focal neurological dysfunction.
why_wrong: B. Gradual progression is not typical of acute stroke. C. Chronic joint pain and stiffness are unrelated. D. Itching is unrelated. E. Constipation and bloating do not indicate acute focal cerebral ischaemia.
pearl: Stroke is a sudden focal loss of neurological function; always check capillary glucose because hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke, and image urgently to exclude haemorrhage.
thinking: Older man ↓ Speech difficulty and right arm weakness ↓ Abrupt onset ↓ Focal deficit fitting a vascular territory ↓ Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
exam_trap: B, gradual onset over several months — a neurological history, but slow progression suggests a tumour or degenerative disease rather than stroke.
takeaway: Sudden onset of a focal neurological deficit is the hallmark of stroke.

stem:
A 60-year-old man suddenly develops weakness and sensory loss affecting the left side of his body. He also has left-sided visual field loss.

Which vascular territory is most likely involved?
correct_answer: A. Right middle cerebral artery territory
why_correct: A right hemispheric lesion can produce contralateral weakness, sensory loss and visual field deficit, commonly within the MCA territory.
