pearl: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss with high glucose and ketones in a young person is type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise; assess urgently for DKA.
thinking: Adolescent with thirst and polyuria ↓ Weight loss ↓ Markedly high glucose ↓ Ketones indicate insulin deficiency ↓ Type 1 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: B, type 2 diabetes mellitus — it is increasingly seen in young people, but ketosis with weight loss in an adolescent points to insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia with ketones and weight loss in a young person means type 1 diabetes.

stem: A 54-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the left face and arm, more marked than in the left leg, with neglect of the left side of space. Which vascular territory is most likely affected?
why_correct: Contralateral face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness, with neglect of the opposite side (a non-dominant parietal cortical sign), localises to the right middle cerebral artery territory.
why_wrong: B. A left anterior cerebral artery occlusion would cause right-sided weakness predominantly affecting the leg. C. A left posterior cerebral artery occlusion typically causes a right homonymous hemianopia rather than left-sided weakness. D. Basilar artery occlusion causes brainstem signs, such as cranial nerve palsies, bilateral deficits or reduced consciousness, rather than unilateral cortical neglect. E. A right posterior cerebral artery occlusion mainly causes a left homonymous hemianopia rather than face and arm weakness.
pearl: Face and arm weakness greater than leg points to the MCA territory; neglect is a non-dominant parietal sign, so left-sided weakness with neglect means right MCA.
thinking: Left face and arm weakness ↓ Leg less affected ↓ Pattern of middle cerebral artery ↓ Neglect means non-dominant parietal lobe ↓ Right middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: B, left anterior cerebral artery — candidates confuse sides and territories, but ACA strokes cause contralateral leg-predominant weakness, and a left lesion affects the right side.
takeaway: Face and arm more than leg with neglect localises to the non-dominant MCA.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has difficulty finding words and understanding spoken language after an acute neurological event. What term best describes this deficit?
why_correct: Aphasia is an impairment of language, including speaking, understanding, reading or writing.
why_wrong: B. Apraxia is difficulty carrying out learned purposeful movements despite adequate strength. C. Dysarthria is impaired articulation due to motor dysfunction. D. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. E. Ataxia is impaired coordination.
pearl: Aphasia is a disorder of language, affecting expression, comprehension, reading or writing; dysarthria is a disorder of articulation.
thinking: Acute neurological event ↓ Word-finding difficulty ↓ Impaired comprehension of speech ↓ Language itself is affected ↓ Aphasia
exam_trap: C, dysarthria — it is a common speech problem after stroke, but it affects articulation, not word finding or comprehension.
takeaway: Problems finding or understanding words mean aphasia, not dysarthria.

stem: A 70-year-old man has difficulty articulating words, but his language comprehension and word selection are intact. What is the most likely deficit?
why_correct: Dysarthria is impaired speech articulation caused by dysfunction of the muscles or neurological pathways involved in speech.
why_wrong: A. Hemianopia is loss of part of the visual field. B. Ataxia concerns coordination. C. Dysphagia concerns swallowing. E. Aphasia is a language disorder.
pearl: Dysarthria is a motor disorder of articulation with intact language; aphasia is a language disorder affecting word choice or comprehension.
thinking: Difficulty articulating words ↓ Comprehension intact ↓ Word selection intact ↓ Language normal, mechanics impaired ↓ Dysarthria
exam_trap: E, aphasia — speech difficulty in an older man suggests stroke-related aphasia, but intact comprehension and word selection rule out a language disorder.
takeaway: Slurred speech with normal language is dysarthria.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops sudden loss of vision in the right eye. There is no eye pain. What diagnosis should be considered urgently?
why_correct: Sudden painless monocular visual loss is a medical emergency and retinal vascular occlusion is an important cause.
why_wrong: A. Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically causes a painful red eye with haloes, headache and vomiting. B. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters rather than sudden profound visual loss. C. Chronic open-angle glaucoma causes gradual peripheral visual-field loss. E. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring of vision.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss suggests retinal artery occlusion, an eye stroke; it needs emergency assessment, and in older patients giant cell arteritis must be considered.
thinking: Sudden loss of vision in one eye ↓ No eye pain ↓ Abrupt painless loss suggests a vascular cause ↓ Ischaemia of the retina ↓ Retinal artery occlusion
exam_trap: A, acute angle-closure glaucoma — it is a classic eye emergency, but it causes a painful red eye with haloes and vomiting, not painless loss.
takeaway: Sudden painless monocular visual loss is a retinal vascular emergency.

stem: A 62-year-old man reports intermittent dizziness when turning his head. Examination reveals a carotid bruit. Which diagnosis should be considered before attributing the symptoms to benign positional vertigo?
why_correct: Neurological or vascular causes should be considered when dizziness is accompanied by concerning vascular or neurological features.
why_wrong: B. A vestibular schwannoma typically causes progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus rather than head-turn dizziness with a carotid bruit. C. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. D. Vestibular neuronitis causes a single prolonged episode of acute vertigo, often after a viral illness. E. Functional dizziness should not be diagnosed when vascular findings such as a carotid bruit need to be investigated.
pearl: Before labelling dizziness as benign positional vertigo, look for vascular or neurological features; a carotid bruit warrants assessment for cerebrovascular disease.
thinking: Older man with dizziness ↓ Episodes on head turning ↓ Carotid bruit on examination ↓ Evidence of vascular disease ↓ Cerebrovascular disease
exam_trap: D, acute vestibular neuronitis — it is a common cause of vertigo, but it causes a single prolonged episode, not intermittent head-turn dizziness with a bruit.
takeaway: Dizziness with vascular signs such as a carotid bruit needs cerebrovascular assessment.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has painful oral ulcers that recur every few months. They are small, round and have a grey-white base with an erythematous border. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent small painful ulcers with a grey-white base and erythematous halo are typical aphthous ulcers.
why_wrong: A. Oral cancer usually presents as a persistent non-healing lesion. C. Herpes zoster causes painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. D. Oral candidiasis produces removable or adherent white plaques. E. Tonsillitis causes inflamed tonsils and sore throat.
pearl: Recurrent aphthous ulcers are small, round, painful ulcers with a grey-white base and red halo that heal on their own; any oral ulcer that fails to heal needs urgent referral to exclude cancer.
thinking: Recurrent painful oral ulcers ↓ Every few months ↓ Small and round ↓ Grey-white base with red border ↓ Aphthous ulcers
exam_trap: A, oral cancer — oral ulcers raise cancer concern, but cancer typically presents as a persistent non-healing lesion rather than recurrent healing ulcers.
takeaway: Recurrent small painful ulcers that heal are aphthous; a persistent ulcer needs referral.

stem: A 33-year-old woman develops painful swelling of the parotid glands, fever and malaise. She has not been vaccinated against mumps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral or unilateral parotid swelling with systemic symptoms is characteristic of mumps.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis causes localized skin and soft-tissue inflammation. C. Dental abscess usually causes localized dental pain and swelling. D. Otitis externa affects the external ear canal. E. Tonsillitis primarily affects the tonsils.
pearl: Mumps causes painful parotid swelling with fever and malaise in unvaccinated people; it is notifiable, and complications include orchitis or oophoritis and meningitis.
thinking: Painful parotid swelling ↓ Fever and malaise ↓ Not vaccinated against mumps ↓ Viral parotitis ↓ Mumps
exam_trap: C, dental abscess — it causes facial swelling and pain, but it is localised to a tooth and does not cause parotid swelling.
takeaway: Painful parotid swelling with fever in an unvaccinated adult is mumps.

stem: A 68-year-old man has gradually worsening difficulty swallowing and a hoarse voice. He has a long smoking history. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia and persistent hoarseness in a smoker are concerning for laryngeal cancer.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa does not cause progressive dysphagia. B. Conjunctivitis does not cause dysphagia or hoarseness. C. Tension headache does not cause voice changes. D. Gastritis does not explain persistent hoarseness with dysphagia.
pearl: Persistent hoarseness, especially in a smoker, needs urgent ENT assessment for laryngeal cancer; associated dysphagia increases concern.
thinking: Long smoking history ↓ Progressive dysphagia ↓ Persistent hoarse voice ↓ Lesion affecting the larynx ↓ Laryngeal malignancy
exam_trap: D, gastritis — it is a common upper GI complaint, but it does not explain persistent hoarseness with progressive dysphagia.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker needs urgent ENT assessment for laryngeal cancer.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has facial pain and purulent nasal discharge for 12 days. Symptoms initially improved but then became significantly worse. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent symptoms with a pattern of initial improvement followed by worsening can indicate acute bacterial sinusitis.
why_wrong: A. Viral rhinosinusitis usually improves within about 10 days; worsening after initial improvement suggests bacterial infection. B. Tension-type headache does not cause purulent nasal discharge. C. Migraine does not cause persistent purulent nasal discharge. E. Allergic rhinitis typically causes itchy eyes, sneezing and watery discharge.
pearl: Sinusitis that worsens after initial improvement (double sickening), or persists without improving, suggests bacterial infection, which may warrant antibiotics.
thinking: Facial pain and purulent discharge ↓ Symptoms for 12 days ↓ Initial improvement ↓ Then significant worsening ↓ Acute bacterial sinusitis
exam_trap: A, acute viral rhinosinusitis — it is the commonest cause of sinus symptoms, but it usually improves; worsening after initial improvement suggests bacterial infection.
takeaway: Double sickening in sinusitis suggests a bacterial cause.

stem: A 23-year-old woman develops ear pain after repeatedly using cotton buds. Examination shows an inflamed, tender external auditory canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Ear canal inflammation and pain following local trauma or moisture exposure are characteristic of otitis externa.
why_wrong: A. Otitis media involves the middle ear and typically follows an upper respiratory infection. B. Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged vertigo without external canal inflammation. C. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and hearing symptoms. D. Mastoiditis causes post-auricular swelling and tenderness.
pearl: Otitis externa is inflammation of the ear canal, commonly triggered by cotton buds or water; treat with topical drops and advise keeping the ear dry.
thinking: Repeated cotton bud use ↓ Ear pain ↓ Inflamed, tender external canal ↓ Trauma to the canal skin ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: A, otitis media — it is the commonest cause of ear pain, but it affects the middle ear and usually follows a respiratory infection, not canal trauma.
takeaway: Painful inflamed ear canal after cotton buds is otitis externa.

stem: A 65-year-old man develops gradually worsening difficulty hearing conversations, particularly in noisy environments. He has worked with loud machinery for many years. What type of hearing loss is most likely?
why_correct: Long-term occupational noise exposure damages the cochlea and causes sensorineural hearing loss.
why_wrong: A. This is unrelated to hearing. B. Eustachian tube dysfunction causes conductive rather than sensorineural loss. D. Conductive loss results from problems transmitting sound through the external or middle ear. E. Otitis externa causes acute ear canal symptoms.
pearl: Noise-induced hearing loss is sensorineural and typically bilateral, with difficulty hearing in background noise; audiometry classically shows a notch around 4 kHz. Ear protection is the key prevention.
thinking: Older man with gradual hearing difficulty ↓ Worse in background noise ↓ Years of loud machinery damage cochlear hair cells ↓ Sensorineural hearing loss
exam_trap: D, conductive hearing loss — tempting as a common, fixable cause, but noise damages the cochlea rather than sound transmission through the external or middle ear.
takeaway: Long-term loud noise damages the cochlea: think sensorineural, not conductive, loss.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with recurrent nosebleeds. He is taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Which blood test is particularly relevant?
why_correct: The INR measures the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and is relevant when bleeding occurs.
why_wrong: B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. C. Amylase can support assessment of pancreatitis. D. HbA1c assesses longer-term glycaemic control. E. TSH assesses thyroid function.
pearl: Bleeding on warfarin needs an urgent INR: a supratherapeutic INR may explain the bleeding and guides whether to withhold warfarin or reverse it with vitamin K.
thinking: Recurrent nosebleeds ↓ Taking warfarin for AF ↓ Warfarin effect is measured by the INR ↓ A raised INR increases bleeding risk ↓ Check the INR
exam_trap: B, troponin — tempting because he has a cardiac condition, but troponin measures myocardial injury and says nothing about anticoagulation or bleeding risk.
takeaway: Any bleeding in a patient on warfarin: check the INR first.

stem:
A woman gives birth vaginally. Shortly afterwards she develops heavy vaginal bleeding. Her uterus feels soft and boggy on abdominal examination.

What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage and typically presents with heavy bleeding and a soft, poorly contracted uterus.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer does not cause acute heavy postpartum bleeding in this pattern. B. Abruption occurs before delivery and is associated with abdominal pain and bleeding. C. Retained placental tissue can cause PPH but is not suggested by a boggy uterus alone. E. Uterine rupture is an obstetric emergency, usually associated with severe pain, fetal compromise and maternal instability.
pearl: Remember the 4 Ts of PPH: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Atony is the commonest cause; start with uterine massage and uterotonics such as oxytocin.
thinking: Heavy bleeding shortly after vaginal birth ↓ Primary postpartum haemorrhage ↓ Soft, boggy uterus means poor contraction ↓ Uterine atony
exam_trap: C, retained placenta — a real cause of PPH within the 4 Ts, but the stem gives a soft, boggy uterus, the hallmark of atony rather than retained tissue.
takeaway: Primary PPH with a soft, boggy uterus is atony until proven otherwise: rub up a contraction.

stem:
During a vaginal delivery, the baby's head delivers but then retracts against the mother's perineum and the shoulders do not deliver with normal traction.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Perform an episiotomy as the only intervention
options.D: Pull firmly on the baby's head

why_correct: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency. The McRoberts manoeuvre is the initial manoeuvre used to help release the impacted anterior shoulder.
why_wrong: A. Fundal pressure can worsen impaction and should be avoided. B. Episiotomy may facilitate internal manoeuvres but does not itself release the impacted shoulder. D. Excessive traction on the head risks brachial plexus injury. E. Delay increases the risk of fetal hypoxia.
pearl: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, then McRoberts (hyperflexing the hips) with suprapubic pressure; never use fundal pressure or excessive traction on the head.
thinking: Head delivers then retracts (turtle sign) ↓ Shoulders do not deliver with normal traction ↓ Shoulder dystocia ↓ First manoeuvre to free the anterior shoulder ↓ McRoberts manoeuvre
exam_trap: D, pulling firmly on the head — instinctive when delivery stalls, but excessive traction does not free the impacted shoulder and risks brachial plexus injury.
takeaway: Turtle sign means shoulder dystocia: call for help and start with McRoberts, never fundal pressure.

stem:
A child has an incidental cardiac murmur. Examination reveals a fixed, widely split second heart sound.

Which congenital heart defect is most likely?
why_correct: A fixed, widely split second heart sound is characteristic of an atrial septal defect because right-sided filling remains relatively increased throughout the respiratory cycle.
why_wrong: A. VSD typically produces a pansystolic murmur. B. Tetralogy commonly causes cyanosis and a harsh ejection systolic murmur. C. PDA classically causes a continuous machinery murmur. E. Coarctation causes upper/lower limb blood-pressure differences and weak femoral pulses.
pearl: ASD gives a soft ejection systolic flow murmur at the upper left sternal edge with fixed splitting of S2; children are often asymptomatic, so it is frequently found incidentally.
thinking: Incidental murmur in a child ↓ Fixed, widely split S2 ↓ Split does not vary with respiration ↓ Persistently increased right-sided flow ↓ Atrial septal defect
exam_trap: A, VSD — the commonest congenital heart defect and a frequent incidental murmur, but it gives a pansystolic murmur, not fixed splitting of the second heart sound.
takeaway: Fixed splitting of S2 points to an atrial septal defect.

stem:
A child has a loud pansystolic murmur heard best at the lower left sternal edge.

Which congenital heart defect is most likely?
why_correct: A ventricular septal defect typically produces a pansystolic murmur due to blood flow across the ventricular septum during systole.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur. B. ASD is associated with fixed splitting of S2. D. Coarctation produces characteristic pulse and blood-pressure abnormalities. E. PDA causes a continuous murmur.
pearl: VSD is the commonest congenital heart defect; small defects give a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, and many close spontaneously.
thinking: Loud pansystolic murmur ↓ Heard best at the lower left sternal edge ↓ Flow across the ventricular septum in systole ↓ VSD
exam_trap: B, ASD — another left-to-right shunt, but ASD gives a soft flow murmur higher up with fixed splitting of S2, not a loud pansystolic murmur.
takeaway: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge in a child: think VSD.

stem:
A child has a continuous "machinery" murmur heard beneath the left clavicle.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A continuous machinery murmur is characteristic of a patent ductus arteriosus.
why_wrong: A. Coarctation is associated with reduced femoral pulses. B. ASD produces a systolic flow murmur with fixed splitting of S2. C. VSD produces a pansystolic murmur. E. Tetralogy usually produces an ejection systolic murmur from right ventricular outflow obstruction.
pearl: PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle; it is more common in preterm infants and may be accompanied by a collapsing pulse.
thinking: Murmur continuous through systole and diastole ↓ Machinery quality ↓ Beneath the left clavicle ↓ Persistent aorta-to-pulmonary artery flow ↓ PDA
exam_trap: A, coarctation — can cause a murmur over the left upper chest and back, but its clue is weak or delayed femoral pulses, not a continuous machinery murmur.
takeaway: Continuous machinery murmur under the left clavicle means patent ductus arteriosus.

stem:
A child with congenital heart disease develops episodes of marked cyanosis, particularly during crying. The child instinctively squats after exertion.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanotic episodes due to right ventricular outflow obstruction. Squatting can increase systemic vascular resistance and reduce right-to-left shunting.
why_wrong: A. VSD is generally acyanotic unless severe pulmonary vascular disease develops. B. PDA is not typically associated with episodic cyanosis. C. ASD is usually acyanotic in childhood. E. Coarctation primarily causes systemic hypertension and reduced lower-limb perfusion.
pearl: Tetralogy of Fallot causes hypercyanotic spells, often triggered by crying; squatting raises systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting across the VSD.
thinking: Congenital heart disease with episodic cyanosis ↓ Spells triggered by crying ↓ Squats after exertion to raise systemic resistance ↓ Right ventricular outflow obstruction with shunt ↓ Tetralogy of Fallot
exam_trap: A, VSD — part of tetralogy, but an isolated VSD is a left-to-right shunt and acyanotic in childhood unless severe pulmonary vascular disease develops.
takeaway: Cyanotic spells relieved by squatting are classic for tetralogy of Fallot.

stem:
A patient has a painful, swollen and erythematous olecranon bursa with fever.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute localised swelling, erythema, pain and fever over a bursa suggest infection.
why_wrong: A. Tendinopathy causes pain related to tendon use rather than an acutely inflamed bursa with fever. B. Osteoarthritis affects joints rather than producing an acutely infected bursa. D. Fibromyalgia does not cause focal inflammatory swelling. E. Rheumatoid disease can cause bursitis but the acute febrile presentation suggests infection.
pearl: A hot, swollen bursa with fever is septic until proven otherwise; aspirate for Gram stain and culture before antibiotics where possible. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism.
thinking: Swollen olecranon bursa ↓ Painful and erythematous ↓ Systemic fever ↓ Infection of the bursa ↓ Septic bursitis
exam_trap: E, rheumatoid arthritis — RA can cause olecranon bursitis, but an acutely inflamed bursa with fever points to infection.
takeaway: Hot, red olecranon bursa with fever: septic bursitis until the aspirate says otherwise.

stem:
A pregnant woman is exposed to a child with a mild febrile illness and a fine rash. She has not been vaccinated against rubella.

Why is rubella infection particularly important in pregnancy?

options.B: It is a leading cause of abruption
options.D: It can cause fetal congenital abnormalities

correct_answer: D. It can cause fetal congenital abnormalities
why_correct: Maternal rubella infection, particularly early in pregnancy, can cause congenital rubella syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Encephalitis is a rare complication of rubella and is not the reason it matters in pregnancy. B. Rubella is not a recognised cause of placental abruption. C. Maternal pneumonitis is a recognised risk of varicella, not rubella, in pregnancy. E. Rubella does not precipitate pre-eclampsia.
pearl: Congenital rubella syndrome risk is highest in early pregnancy: cataracts, sensorineural deafness and heart defects. MMR is live, so a non-immune woman is vaccinated after delivery.
thinking: Pregnant and unvaccinated against rubella ↓ Contact with fever and fine rash ↓ Possible rubella infection ↓ Virus crosses the placenta, worst early on ↓ Fetal congenital abnormalities
exam_trap: C, maternal pneumonitis — a genuine pregnancy danger, but of varicella, not rubella; rubella matters because of congenital rubella syndrome.
takeaway: Rubella in pregnancy matters for the fetus: congenital rubella syndrome, worst early on.

stem:
A 3-week-old infant remains visibly jaundiced. Blood tests show an elevated conjugated bilirubin.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Breast milk jaundice; continue feeding and review at 6 weeks
options.B: Prolonged physiological jaundice; recheck bilirubin in 2 weeks
options.D: Needs urgent assessment for cholestatic liver disease
options.E: Gilbert syndrome unmasked by poor feeding; reassure parents

correct_answer: D. Needs urgent assessment for cholestatic liver disease
why_correct: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant is pathological and requires assessment for causes of neonatal cholestasis, including biliary atresia.
why_wrong: A. Breast milk jaundice is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not explain a raised conjugated fraction. B. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is not physiological, and delaying assessment risks missing biliary atresia. C. Haemolysis produces predominantly unconjugated bilirubin, which is what phototherapy treats. E. Gilbert syndrome causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, so reassurance is inappropriate with a raised conjugated fraction.
pearl: Prolonged neonatal jaundice needs a split bilirubin; a raised conjugated fraction must be investigated urgently because the outcome in biliary atresia depends on early surgery.
thinking: Still jaundiced at 3 weeks ↓ Prolonged neonatal jaundice ↓ Conjugated bilirubin raised ↓ Cholestasis, including biliary atresia ↓ Urgent assessment
exam_trap: A, breast milk jaundice — a common cause of prolonged jaundice in a well baby, but it is unconjugated; a raised conjugated fraction is never benign.
takeaway: Conjugated jaundice in a baby is always pathological: refer urgently, think biliary atresia.

stem:
A child has persistent joint swelling and morning stiffness lasting several weeks. There is no history of trauma or infection.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent inflammatory joint symptoms in a child, particularly morning stiffness and swelling, suggest juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Reactive arthritis follows a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, and there is no history of infection. C. Benign nocturnal limb pains (growing pains) do not cause joint swelling or morning stiffness. D. Transient synovitis is a short-lived hip effusion that settles within days, rather than persistent arthritis with morning stiffness. E. Hypermobility causes activity-related joint pain without persistent swelling or inflammatory morning stiffness.
pearl: JIA is arthritis starting before age 16, persisting at least 6 weeks, with no other cause; children need regular eye screening because uveitis is often asymptomatic.
thinking: Child with persistent joint swelling ↓ Morning stiffness over several weeks ↓ No trauma or preceding infection ↓ Chronic inflammatory arthritis ↓ Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
exam_trap: A, reactive arthritis — also causes joint swelling, but it follows a gut or genitourinary infection, which the stem excludes.
takeaway: Persistent inflammatory joint swelling in a child without trauma or infection: think JIA.

stem:
A newborn is found to have persistent jaundice, poor feeding, constipation and hypotonia.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Congenital hypothyroidism can present with prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, hypotonia and constipation. Newborn screening allows early diagnosis and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Hirschsprung disease causes delayed meconium passage and bowel obstruction. C. Phenylketonuria is usually detected through newborn screening and does not typically present with this early pattern. D. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting. E. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia may cause salt wasting and ambiguous genitalia, depending on the form.
pearl: Congenital hypothyroidism is detected by the newborn blood spot test; prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, constipation and a large tongue are clinical clues. Early levothyroxine protects development.
thinking: Persistent jaundice ↓ Poor feeding and constipation ↓ Hypotonia ↓ Global slowing from thyroid hormone deficiency ↓ Congenital hypothyroidism
exam_trap: A, Hirschsprung disease — tempting because of constipation, but it presents with delayed meconium and obstruction, and does not explain jaundice and hypotonia.
takeaway: Prolonged neonatal jaundice with hypotonia and constipation: check thyroid function.

stem:
A patient develops fatigue, nausea, dark urine and jaundice several weeks after unprotected sexual intercourse.

Which infection should be considered?
why_correct: Hepatitis B can be sexually transmitted and acute infection can cause a flu-like prodrome followed by jaundice and dark urine.
why_wrong: A. Disseminated gonococcal infection causes arthritis, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions rather than acute hepatitis. B. HIV seroconversion causes a glandular-fever-like illness with rash, but a jaundiced hepatitis picture is not characteristic. C. Chlamydial perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome) causes right upper quadrant pain but not typically jaundice and dark urine. D. Hepatitis C is less efficiently sexually transmitted and acute infection is usually asymptomatic.
pearl: Hepatitis B spreads sexually, by blood and vertically; acute infection shows HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc. Offer testing and vaccination to sexual partners and close contacts.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse weeks earlier ↓ Prodrome of fatigue and nausea ↓ Dark urine and jaundice ↓ Sexually transmitted acute hepatitis ↓ Acute hepatitis B
exam_trap: D, hepatitis C — also a blood-borne hepatitis, but sexual transmission is inefficient and acute infection is usually asymptomatic rather than jaundiced.
takeaway: Acute jaundice weeks after unprotected sex: think acute hepatitis B.

stem:
A pregnant woman who is not known to have had chickenpox is exposed to a child with chickenpox.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give the MMR vaccine within 72 hours of contact
options.B: Reassure her, as chickenpox is usually mild in adults
options.C: Give the varicella vaccine within 5 days of contact
options.D: Start aciclovir now without checking immunity
options.E: Assess exposure and check varicella antibodies

correct_answer: E. Assess exposure and check varicella antibodies
why_correct: Varicella infection can cause significant maternal and fetal complications. A susceptible pregnant woman with significant exposure should have her immunity assessed and receive appropriate specialist advice.
why_wrong: A. MMR is a live vaccine, is contraindicated in pregnancy and does not protect against varicella. B. Varicella can cause serious maternal pneumonitis and fetal varicella syndrome, so reassurance alone is inappropriate. C. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. D. Immunity should be checked first; women with varicella antibodies need no antiviral prophylaxis.
pearl: A pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox with uncertain immunity needs urgent varicella IgG testing; if non-immune she needs specialist post-exposure prophylaxis, as maternal varicella can cause severe pneumonitis.
thinking: Pregnant, no known chickenpox ↓ Contact with a child with chickenpox ↓ Risk of maternal pneumonitis and fetal harm ↓ Confirm significant exposure and immunity ↓ Check varicella antibodies
exam_trap: D, start aciclovir now — prophylaxis may be needed, but many adults are already immune, so check varicella antibodies first; immune women need no treatment.
takeaway: Chickenpox contact in pregnancy: check varicella IgG before deciding on prophylaxis.

stem:
A newborn has sensorineural hearing loss, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly.

Which congenital infection should be considered?
why_correct: Congenital CMV can cause sensorineural hearing loss, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and neurological abnormalities.
why_wrong: B. Congenital toxoplasmosis classically causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse intracranial calcification; sensorineural deafness is the hallmark of congenital CMV. C. Parvovirus B19 causes fetal anaemia and hydrops rather than this syndrome. D. Group B streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis, not a congenital syndrome with deafness. E. Congenital varicella syndrome causes cicatricial skin scarring and limb hypoplasia.
pearl: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss; it can also cause petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and microcephaly.
thinking: Newborn with sensorineural deafness ↓ Petechiae ↓ Hepatosplenomegaly ↓ Congenital viral infection ↓ Cytomegalovirus
exam_trap: B, toxoplasmosis — shares congenital infection features such as hepatosplenomegaly, but its hallmark is chorioretinitis and hydrocephalus; deafness points to CMV.
takeaway: Congenital infection with sensorineural deafness: think CMV first.

stem:
A newborn has hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis.

Which congenital infection is most likely?
why_correct: The combination of hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis is classically associated with congenital toxoplasmosis.
why_wrong: A. Congenital syphilis has a different clinical presentation. B. Congenital rubella has features including cataracts, hearing loss and cardiac abnormalities. C. Congenital varicella can cause limb and skin abnormalities. D. CMV can cause intracranial calcification and hearing loss but the classic combination here is toxoplasmosis.
pearl: Congenital toxoplasmosis has a classic triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse intracranial calcification. Maternal infection may come from undercooked meat or cat faeces.
thinking: Newborn with hydrocephalus ↓ Intracranial calcifications ↓ Chorioretinitis ↓ Classic triad ↓ Congenital toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: D, CMV — also causes intracranial calcification, but typically with microcephaly and deafness; hydrocephalus with chorioretinitis is the toxoplasmosis triad.
takeaway: Hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and calcification together: congenital toxoplasmosis.

stem:
A newborn develops a widespread rash, hepatosplenomegaly and nasal discharge.

Which congenital infection should be considered?
why_correct: Congenital syphilis can cause rash, hepatosplenomegaly and nasal discharge ("snuffles").
why_wrong: A. Toxoplasmosis classically causes chorioretinitis and neurological abnormalities. B. Rubella is associated with congenital cardiac, ocular and auditory abnormalities. C. Pertussis is a respiratory infection. D. Mumps is associated with parotitis.
pearl: Early congenital syphilis causes snuffles, a rash that can involve the palms and soles, and hepatosplenomegaly; antenatal screening allows maternal treatment with penicillin.
thinking: Newborn with widespread rash ↓ Hepatosplenomegaly ↓ Nasal discharge (snuffles) ↓ Early congenital syphilis
exam_trap: B, rubella — can cause a neonatal rash and hepatosplenomegaly, but its hallmarks are cataracts, deafness and heart defects, not snuffles.
takeaway: Neonatal snuffles with rash and hepatosplenomegaly: congenital syphilis.

stem:
A 66-year-old man is invited for an NHS ultrasound screening examination.

Which condition is being screened for?
why_correct: The NHS Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening Programme offers screening to men aged 65.
why_wrong: B. There is no NHS screening programme for carotid stenosis in asymptomatic people. C. There is no NHS population screening programme for renal cancer. D. Gallbladder cancer is not screened for in the NHS. E. There is no NHS population screening programme for peripheral arterial disease.
pearl: The NHS AAA Screening Programme offers men a one-off abdominal ultrasound in the year they turn 65; older men who were not screened can self-refer.
thinking: Older man ↓ Invited for NHS ultrasound screening ↓ One-off aortic scan offered to men around 65 ↓ Abdominal aortic aneurysm
exam_trap: E, peripheral arterial disease — shares atherosclerotic risk factors with AAA, but there is no NHS population screening programme for it.
takeaway: NHS ultrasound screening for older men is for abdominal aortic aneurysm.

stem:
A 72-year-old man undergoes abdominal ultrasound for another reason and is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 3.5 cm.

He has no abdominal or back pain.

Which description best fits this presentation?
why_correct: An abdominal aortic aneurysm discovered incidentally in an asymptomatic patient is an asymptomatic AAA.
why_wrong: B. Acute mesenteric ischaemia causes severe abdominal pain, often with relatively limited early examination findings. C. Rupture usually causes sudden severe abdominal/back pain with haemodynamic instability. D. Renal colic causes severe flank-to-groin pain and urinary symptoms. E. Aortic dissection has a different acute clinical presentation.
pearl: Small asymptomatic AAAs are managed with ultrasound surveillance and cardiovascular risk reduction; symptoms, rapid growth or a large diameter (around 5.5 cm) prompt referral for repair.
thinking: Incidental finding on ultrasound ↓ Aorta measures 3.5 cm, so aneurysmal ↓ No abdominal or back pain ↓ Asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm
exam_trap: C, ruptured AAA — the dreaded complication, but rupture causes sudden severe pain and shock, whereas this patient is pain-free with an incidental finding.
takeaway: An incidental, pain-free AAA is asymptomatic: surveillance and risk-factor control.

stem:
A child develops a high fever, severe sore throat, drooling and difficulty breathing. The child is sitting upright and does not want to lie down.

What is the most important immediate principle?

options.A: Take a throat swab and start oral penicillin V today
options.B: Give oral dexamethasone and observe on the ward for 4 hours
options.C: Keep the child calm and get urgent airway support
options.D: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor and torch
options.E: Lie the child flat and give high-flow oxygen

correct_answer: C. Keep the child calm and get urgent airway support
why_correct: Epiglottitis can cause sudden complete upper-airway obstruction. The child should be kept calm and managed urgently by an experienced airway team.
why_wrong: A. A throat swab may precipitate obstruction, and oral antibiotics are inappropriate in a potential airway emergency. B. Oral dexamethasone and observation is management for croup, not suspected epiglottitis. D. Throat examination can precipitate complete airway obstruction. E. Lying the child flat may worsen obstruction and distress; the child should stay in their position of comfort.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, do not examine the throat or upset the child; keep them upright with a parent and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway.
thinking: High fever and severe sore throat ↓ Drooling, sitting upright ↓ Difficulty breathing ↓ Suspected epiglottitis, airway at risk ↓ Keep calm, urgent airway support
exam_trap: D, examining the throat with a tongue depressor — instinctive for a sore throat, but it can precipitate complete airway obstruction in epiglottitis.
takeaway: Drooling, upright, febrile child: do not examine the throat; get airway experts now.

stem:
An infant with bronchiolitis is breathing rapidly and is taking less than half of their usual feeds.

What is the main immediate concern?
why_correct: Increased work of breathing can significantly impair feeding in bronchiolitis, increasing the risk of dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency is not an acute consequence of bronchiolitis. B. Reflux does not explain reduced intake caused by respiratory distress. C. Cow's milk protein allergy does not explain acute feeding difficulty during a respiratory infection. E. Thyrotoxicosis does not explain the acute feeding difficulty.
pearl: Markedly reduced feeding in bronchiolitis is a key reason to consider admission; support hydration with nasogastric or IV fluids, and give oxygen if saturations are low.
thinking: Infant with bronchiolitis ↓ Tachypnoea increases work of breathing ↓ Too breathless to feed well ↓ Taking under half usual feeds ↓ Risk of dehydration
exam_trap: B, gastro-oesophageal reflux — common in infants with feeding problems, but here poor intake is explained by respiratory distress from bronchiolitis.
takeaway: In bronchiolitis, poor feeding means dehydration risk: assess hydration and consider admission.

stem:
A child has fever, headache and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash. The child is becoming drowsy.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.C: Immune thrombocytopenia needing a blood count
options.E: Viral illness; safety-net and review in 24 hours

correct_answer: D. Possible meningococcal disease; treat immediately
why_correct: Fever, altered consciousness and a rapidly developing non-blanching rash are red flags for meningococcal disease.
why_wrong: A. Scarlet fever causes a fine blanching sandpaper rash and does not explain drowsiness with a spreading non-blanching rash. B. IgA vasculitis causes a purpuric rash on the legs and buttocks but not fever with drowsiness. C. ITP causes petechiae in a well child, not fever and reduced consciousness. E. Fever with a non-blanching rash and drowsiness must not be managed as a simple viral illness.
pearl: Fever with a non-blanching rash and drowsiness is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; give parenteral benzylpenicillin in the community or IV ceftriaxone in hospital without delay.
thinking: Fever and headache ↓ Rapidly spreading non-blanching rash ↓ Becoming drowsy ↓ Meningococcal septicaemia or meningitis ↓ Treat immediately
exam_trap: C, ITP needing a blood count — explains petechiae, but children with ITP are well; fever, drowsiness and a spreading rash demand immediate antibiotics.
takeaway: Fever plus non-blanching rash plus drowsiness: antibiotics now, investigations later.

stem:
A university student has fever, sore throat and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Examination reveals splenomegaly.

Which advice is particularly important?

options.A: Avoid contact sports until the spleen settles
options.B: Take amoxicillin for 7 days to shorten the illness
options.C: Stay off university for 6 weeks to prevent spread
options.D: Start oral prednisolone to shrink the spleen
options.E: Follow a low-protein diet until the liver tests settle

correct_answer: A. Avoid contact sports until the spleen settles
why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis can cause splenomegaly, increasing the risk of splenic rupture with abdominal trauma.
why_wrong: B. Amoxicillin does not treat EBV and commonly causes a rash in infectious mononucleosis. C. Exclusion from university is not required, as spread requires close contact such as kissing. D. Corticosteroids are reserved for complications such as airway obstruction, not routine splenomegaly. E. Dietary protein restriction is not indicated in infectious mononucleosis.
pearl: In infectious mononucleosis, advise avoiding contact sports and heavy lifting for several weeks because of splenic rupture risk; amoxicillin given in error often causes a widespread rash.
thinking: Young adult with fever and sore throat ↓ Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Splenomegaly ↓ Infectious mononucleosis ↓ Avoid contact sports
exam_trap: B, amoxicillin for 7 days — tempting for a sore throat, but EBV is viral and amoxicillin commonly triggers a rash in glandular fever.
takeaway: Glandular fever with splenomegaly: no contact sports until the spleen settles.

stem:
A person with advanced HIV develops headache and focal neurological symptoms. Brain imaging shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

Which opportunistic infection is a classic consideration?
why_correct: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an important opportunistic infection in advanced HIV and can cause multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions.
why_wrong: A. Scabies affects the skin. B. Cystitis affects the urinary tract. C. Influenza does not characteristically produce multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions. E. Otitis externa affects the external ear.
pearl: In advanced HIV, multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis; the main differential is primary CNS lymphoma, which is more often a single lesion.
thinking: Advanced HIV ↓ Headache and focal neurology ↓ Multiple ring-enhancing lesions ↓ Classic opportunistic CNS infection ↓ Toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: C, influenza — a common infection that can cause headache, but it does not produce multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions.
takeaway: Advanced HIV with multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions: cerebral toxoplasmosis.

stem:
A traveller returning from a malaria-endemic area develops fever, confusion and jaundice.

Why is this presentation particularly concerning?

options.C: It suggests hepatitis A from contaminated food
options.D: It suggests travellers' diarrhoea with dehydration
options.E: It indicates ovale malaria relapsing from liver stages

correct_answer: B. Severe falciparum malaria is possible
why_correct: Neurological disturbance and organ dysfunction in a traveller with suspected malaria are red flags for severe malaria, particularly falciparum malaria.
why_wrong: A. Confusion and jaundice are features of severe malaria, which is usually due to falciparum rather than uncomplicated vivax infection. C. Hepatitis A can cause jaundice, but fever with confusion in a returning traveller must prompt exclusion of severe falciparum malaria. D. Travellers' diarrhoea does not explain jaundice and confusion. E. Ovale relapses cause milder disease and do not typically cause cerebral malaria and organ dysfunction.
pearl: Fever in a traveller returning from a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise; confusion or jaundice suggests severe falciparum malaria needing urgent IV artesunate.
thinking: Returned from malaria-endemic area ↓ Fever ↓ Confusion and jaundice indicate organ dysfunction ↓ Features of severe malaria ↓ Severe falciparum malaria
exam_trap: C, hepatitis A — explains jaundice after travel, but fever with confusion in a returning traveller must be treated as severe falciparum malaria until excluded.
takeaway: Febrile traveller with confusion or jaundice: severe falciparum malaria until proven otherwise.

stem:
A person develops fatigue, nausea, dark urine and jaundice after recent travel and consumption of contaminated food.

Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Hepatitis A is commonly transmitted by the faecal–oral route and can cause an acute hepatitis syndrome with jaundice and dark urine.
why_wrong: A. HIV does not characteristically cause this acute jaundiced hepatitis syndrome. B. Gonorrhoea is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection. C. Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted infection. D. Hepatitis C is primarily blood-borne.
pearl: Hepatitis A is spread by the faecal–oral route and causes an acute, self-limiting hepatitis that never becomes chronic; vaccination protects travellers.
thinking: Recent travel ↓ Contaminated food ↓ Fatigue, nausea, dark urine and jaundice ↓ Faecal–oral acute hepatitis ↓ Hepatitis A
exam_trap: D, hepatitis C — a viral hepatitis, but it is blood-borne, usually asymptomatic when acute and not acquired from food.
takeaway: Jaundice after travel and contaminated food or water: hepatitis A.

stem:
A patient with an uncertain vaccination history presents with a contaminated wound.

What should determine whether tetanus prophylaxis is required?

options.C: Blood group and current antibiotic use
options.D: Whether the wound is painful or bleeding
options.E: Penicillin allergy status and wound site

correct_answer: A. Immunisation history and wound type
why_correct: Tetanus prevention after injury depends on both the wound characteristics and the individual's vaccination history.
why_wrong: B. Cholesterol and blood pressure have no bearing on tetanus risk. C. Blood group and antibiotic use do not determine the need for tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin. D. Pain or bleeding does not determine tetanus risk. E. Penicillin allergy and wound site do not determine whether tetanus prophylaxis is required.
pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds, such as those contaminated with soil or containing devitalised tissue, need an immediate dose of tetanus vaccine if immunisation is incomplete or uncertain; human tetanus immunoglobulin is added for high-risk wounds and for tetanus-prone wounds when immunisation status is uncertain.
thinking: Contaminated wound ↓ Tetanus-prone ↓ Vaccination history uncertain ↓ Need depends on wound risk and immunity ↓ Immunisation history and wound type
exam_trap: E, penicillin allergy and wound site — tempting because antibiotics may be considered, but they do not decide whether tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed.
takeaway: Tetanus prophylaxis is decided by wound risk plus immunisation status.

stem:
A 7-year-old boy develops sudden inability to pass urine with lower abdominal discomfort. He has severe constipation.

What is an important possible contributor?
why_correct: Severe constipation can cause bladder outlet dysfunction and contribute to urinary retention in children.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not explain urinary retention. B. Hay fever does not cause urinary obstruction. D. Hyperthyroidism does not typically cause acute urinary retention. E. Otitis media is unrelated.
pearl: Constipation is a common, often overlooked cause of urinary problems in children, including retention, UTI and wetting; treating the constipation often resolves them.
thinking: Child with sudden urinary retention ↓ Lower abdominal discomfort ↓ Severe constipation ↓ Loaded rectum obstructs the bladder outlet ↓ Faecal impaction
exam_trap: D, hyperthyroidism — a systemic disorder that alters bowel habit, but it causes loose stools and does not obstruct the bladder outlet.
takeaway: Urinary retention in a constipated child: think faecal impaction and treat the bowel.

stem:
A child has chronic diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and poor weight gain. Coeliac disease is confirmed.

Which condition is particularly associated with coeliac disease?
why_correct: Coeliac disease has an established association with other autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. Haemophilia is an inherited coagulation disorder. B. The association is particularly with autoimmune type 1 diabetes. D. Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder. E. Cystic fibrosis is a separate inherited disorder.
pearl: Coeliac disease clusters with other autoimmune conditions, especially type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease; people with type 1 diabetes should be tested for coeliac disease.
thinking: Confirmed coeliac disease ↓ Autoimmune enteropathy ↓ Clusters with other autoimmune disease ↓ Type 1 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: B, type 2 diabetes only — tempting because diabetes is right, but the association is with autoimmune type 1 diabetes, not type 2.
takeaway: Coeliac disease and type 1 diabetes travel together: test for one when you find the other.

stem:
A competent 15-year-old asks their doctor not to disclose confidential information to their parents.

What should the doctor generally do?

options.A: Tell the parents, as they have parental responsibility
options.B: Contact the school nurse to share the information
options.C: Respect confidentiality unless there is a safeguarding risk
options.D: Ask the parents to consent on the child's behalf
options.E: Defer the consultation until a parent is able to attend

correct_answer: C. Respect confidentiality unless there is a safeguarding risk
why_correct: A competent young person can have confidentiality rights. Information should not routinely be disclosed to parents without consent unless there is a justified reason, such as a safeguarding concern.
why_wrong: A. Parental responsibility does not override the confidentiality of a competent young person without a justified reason. B. The school has no entitlement to confidential medical information. D. A competent 15-year-old can consent to their own care. E. Delaying care to involve parents is not required and may deter the young person from seeking help.
pearl: A competent young person is owed confidentiality like an adult; encourage them to involve their parents, but disclose without consent only when there is a serious risk of harm.
thinking: Competent 15-year-old ↓ Asks for confidentiality from parents ↓ Duty of confidentiality applies ↓ Can be breached only for serious risk ↓ Respect it unless safeguarding risk
exam_trap: A, tell the parents — tempting because they hold parental responsibility, but this does not override a competent young person's confidentiality without good reason.
takeaway: A competent teenager's confidentiality is respected unless there is a safeguarding risk.

stem:
A patient attends with their partner, who answers every question and refuses to leave the room.

What is an important step if domestic abuse is a concern?

options.A: Tell the partner everything discussed previously
options.B: Ensure an opportunity to speak to the patient alone
options.E: Ask the partner to answer all questions

correct_answer: B. Ensure an opportunity to speak to the patient alone
why_correct: Speaking with the patient privately allows confidential assessment and may facilitate disclosure of domestic abuse or other safeguarding concerns.
why_wrong: A. Confidential information should not be disclosed inappropriately. C. Immediate discharge without assessment may compromise safety. D. Aggressive confrontation may increase risk. E. This prevents confidential assessment.
pearl: If domestic abuse is suspected, create a safe opportunity to see the patient alone, ask directly and sensitively, document carefully and signpost to support services.
thinking: Partner answers every question ↓ Partner refuses to leave the room ↓ Possible coercive control ↓ Disclosure needs privacy ↓ Speak to the patient alone
exam_trap: D, confronting the partner — feels protective, but confrontation can escalate risk to the patient; the priority is a safe private conversation.
takeaway: Suspected domestic abuse: always find a way to see the patient alone.

stem:
A junior doctor is handing over several patients at the end of a shift.

Which information is particularly important to communicate?

options.A: Full past medical history of each patient
options.C: Names, bed numbers and ward locations
options.D: Tasks already completed during the shift
options.E: Social history and family contact details

correct_answer: B. Current concerns and outstanding tasks
why_correct: Safe handover should communicate relevant clinical information, current risks and tasks requiring follow-up.
why_wrong: A. A full past history adds cognitive load without highlighting current risks. C. Identifiers alone are insufficient for safe continuity of care. D. Outstanding tasks matter more than completed ones. E. These details do not convey current clinical risk or required actions.
pearl: Good handover focuses on unwell patients, outstanding jobs and what to do if things change; structured tools such as SBAR keep it concise and safe.
thinking: End of shift ↓ Responsibility passes to another doctor ↓ They need the current risks and pending actions ↓ Current concerns and outstanding tasks
exam_trap: C, names, bed numbers and ward locations — essential identifiers, but on their own they say nothing about risk or what still needs doing.
takeaway: Hand over what is worrying and what is outstanding, not everything that has happened.

stem:
A junior doctor reviews a deteriorating patient but is uncertain about the appropriate management.

What should they do?

options.A: Wait until the next ward round

why_correct: Doctors should recognise the limits of their competence and seek senior assistance when a patient's condition or management exceeds their experience.
why_wrong: A. Deterioration requires timely action. B. Discharge is inappropriate without adequate assessment. C. Managing beyond one's competence can put the patient at risk. D. Abnormal observations require appropriate clinical response.
pearl: Recognising the limits of your competence is a GMC duty; escalate a deteriorating patient promptly, ideally using a structured tool such as SBAR, while starting ABCDE care.
thinking: Patient deteriorating ↓ Junior doctor uncertain of management ↓ Beyond current competence ↓ Delay could cause harm ↓ Seek senior help
exam_trap: A, wait until the next ward round — tempting to avoid disturbing seniors, but deterioration needs timely escalation, not delay.
takeaway: Unsure about a deteriorating patient? Escalate to a senior now.

stem:
After administering an injection, a doctor is left holding the used needle.

What should they do?

options.A: Recap it with two hands, then discard
options.B: Put it straight into a sharps bin
options.C: Place it in a yellow clinical waste bag
options.D: Leave it on the trolley to dispose of later

correct_answer: B. Put it straight into a sharps bin
why_correct: Used sharps should be disposed of promptly and safely in an appropriate sharps container to reduce needlestick injuries.
why_wrong: A. Two-handed recapping is a common cause of needlestick injury. C. Clinical waste bags can be pierced by sharps. D. An exposed needle left on a trolley creates a hazard. E. Bending needles increases needlestick risk.
pearl: Dispose of sharps at the point of use straight into a sharps bin and never recap; after a needlestick, encourage bleeding, wash and report urgently to occupational health.
thinking: Used needle in hand ↓ Needlestick injury risk ↓ Recapping, bending or delay add risk ↓ Immediate disposal at point of use ↓ Sharps bin
exam_trap: A, recapping with two hands — a habit some have seen, but two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injury.
takeaway: Used needles go straight into a sharps bin: never recap.

stem:
A patient reports that penicillin caused nausea and diarrhoea several years ago.

How should this history be interpreted?

options.A: It suggests a delayed hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: It indicates a severe IgE-mediated allergy
options.C: It suggests intolerance rather than allergy
options.E: It is evidence of anaphylaxis requiring adrenaline

correct_answer: C. It suggests intolerance rather than allergy
why_correct: Gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and diarrhoea are common adverse effects and do not by themselves establish an immune-mediated penicillin allergy.
why_wrong: A. Delayed hypersensitivity typically causes rash or other immune features, not isolated gastrointestinal upset. B. Nausea and diarrhoea do not indicate IgE-mediated allergy. D. Gastrointestinal intolerance does not contraindicate beta-lactams. E. These symptoms are not anaphylaxis.
pearl: Many recorded penicillin allergies are not true allergies; gastrointestinal upset is intolerance, so document the reaction accurately to avoid needlessly withholding penicillins.
thinking: Penicillin caused nausea and diarrhoea ↓ These are common pharmacological side effects ↓ Gastrointestinal upset alone is not an immune reaction ↓ Intolerance, not allergy
exam_trap: D, contraindicates all beta-lactams — feels like the safe choice, but mislabelling intolerance as allergy leads to broader, less effective antibiotics.
takeaway: Nausea or diarrhoea with penicillin is intolerance, not allergy.

stem:
A patient has symptoms strongly suggestive of a viral upper respiratory tract infection without features suggesting bacterial infection.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.C: No antibiotics; symptomatic and safety-netting advice
options.D: Oral prednisolone to shorten the illness

correct_answer: C. No antibiotics; symptomatic and safety-netting advice
why_correct: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections, and unnecessary prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance and adverse effects.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated viral illness. B. Antibiotics are not indicated to prevent secondary infection in viral URTI. D. Corticosteroids are not indicated for viral URTI. E. Broad-spectrum antibiotics without indication cause adverse effects and drive resistance.
pearl: Most URTIs are viral and self-limiting; give no antibiotics, explain the expected course and self-care, and safety-net for red flags.
thinking: URTI symptoms ↓ Features strongly suggest a viral cause ↓ No bacterial features ↓ Antibiotics add harm without benefit ↓ No antibiotics; self-care and safety-netting
exam_trap: A, immediate amoxicillin with safety-netting — sounds cautious, but antibiotics do not help viral URTI and drive resistance and side effects.
takeaway: Viral URTI: no antibiotics, just self-care and clear safety-netting.

stem:
A patient has chronic knee osteoarthritis causing pain and reduced mobility.

Which is an important core component of management?

options.C: Exercise and weight management where appropriate

correct_answer: C. Exercise and weight management where appropriate
why_correct: Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and weight management can improve symptoms in people who are overweight or obese.
why_wrong: A. Maintaining appropriate activity is important. B. Long-term systemic corticosteroids are not routine treatment for osteoarthritis. D. Antibiotics do not treat osteoarthritis. E. Prolonged inactivity can worsen function.
pearl: Core osteoarthritis management for everyone is information, therapeutic exercise and weight loss if overweight; medicines are adjuncts, not the foundation.
thinking: Chronic knee osteoarthritis ↓ Pain and reduced mobility ↓ Core treatment needed for all ↓ Strengthen muscles and reduce joint load ↓ Exercise and weight management
exam_trap: E, prolonged bed rest — seems to rest the joint, but inactivity weakens muscles and worsens pain and function.
takeaway: Exercise and weight loss are core treatment for knee osteoarthritis.

stem: Which patient has an established risk factor for osteoporosis?

options.A: A person on long-term inhaled salbutamol
options.B: A person with a BMI of 32
options.D: A person on long-term oral prednisolone
options.E: A person taking regular thiazide diuretics

correct_answer: D. A person on long-term oral prednisolone
why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid use is an important risk factor for osteoporosis and fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is not an osteoporosis risk factor. B. Higher body weight is associated with greater bone density; low BMI is the risk factor. C. Metformin is not a recognised osteoporosis risk factor. E. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and are not an osteoporosis risk factor.
pearl: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are a major osteoporosis risk factor; fracture risk tools such as FRAX include steroid use, and bone protection should be considered early.
thinking: Looking for an osteoporosis risk factor ↓ Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation and increase resorption ↓ Long-term oral prednisolone ↓ Established risk factor
exam_trap: B, BMI of 32 — tempting as obesity seems unhealthy, but higher body weight is linked to greater bone density; low BMI is the risk factor.
takeaway: Long-term oral steroids are a key osteoporosis risk factor: think bone protection.

stem:
A 55-year-old patient has gradually worsening shoulder pain, particularly when lifting the arm above the head. There is pain and weakness with active shoulder movement.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Rotator cuff disorders commonly cause shoulder pain and difficulty with overhead movements, often with weakness.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand and wrist. C. Tennis elbow causes lateral elbow pain. D. De Quervain tenosynovitis causes radial wrist pain. E. Achilles rupture affects the ankle.
pearl: Rotator cuff disorders cause a painful arc on abduction and pain on resisted movement; marked weakness, especially after injury, suggests a tear needing imaging.
thinking: Gradually worsening shoulder pain ↓ Worse lifting the arm overhead ↓ Pain and weakness on active movement ↓ Rotator cuff pathology ↓ Rotator cuff disorder
exam_trap: A, carpal tunnel syndrome — a common upper-limb complaint, but it causes hand numbness and tingling, not shoulder pain on overhead movement.
takeaway: Shoulder pain on overhead activity with weakness: rotator cuff disorder.

stem:
A patient has lower back pain radiating down the posterior aspect of the leg and into the foot. The pain is worsened by coughing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Radicular pain radiating from the lower back into the leg, particularly when worsened by coughing or straining, is typical of sciatica.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the upper limb. C. PMR causes proximal shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness. E. Hand osteoarthritis does not cause leg radicular pain.
pearl: Sciatica is radicular leg pain, often worse with coughing or straining; always ask about saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction to exclude cauda equina syndrome.
thinking: Low back pain ↓ Radiates down the back of the leg into the foot ↓ Worse with coughing ↓ Nerve root irritation ↓ Sciatica
exam_trap: A, fibromyalgia — causes chronic pain, but it is widespread, not a radiating leg pain made worse by coughing.
takeaway: Back pain radiating into the foot and worse on coughing is sciatica; screen for cauda equina.

stem:
A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops firm subcutaneous nodules over pressure points.

What are these most likely to represent?
why_correct: Rheumatoid nodules are an extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis and commonly occur over pressure points.
why_wrong: A. Ganglion cysts are fluctuant cysts arising from joints or tendon sheaths. B. Tophi are urate deposits in chronic gout. D. Xanthomata are yellowish lipid deposits associated with hyperlipidaemia. E. Calcinosis cutis is associated with systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, usually non-tender lumps over pressure points such as the elbows, and are associated with seropositive, more severe disease.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Firm subcutaneous nodules ↓ Over pressure points ↓ Extra-articular RA feature ↓ Rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: B, tophaceous gout — tophi also form over the elbows and fingers, but they occur in chronic gout; in known RA, firm nodules are rheumatoid nodules.
takeaway: Firm nodules over pressure points in RA are rheumatoid nodules.

stem:
A patient with knee osteoarthritis develops a soft swelling behind the knee.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A Baker cyst is a fluid-filled swelling in the popliteal region and can occur secondary to knee joint disease.
why_wrong: A. Dupuytren disease affects the palmar fascia. B. Achilles rupture affects the posterior ankle. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the wrist. D. Olecranon bursitis causes swelling over the elbow.
pearl: A Baker cyst is a popliteal swelling linked to knee arthritis; rupture can mimic DVT with calf pain and swelling, so DVT may need excluding with ultrasound.
thinking: Knee osteoarthritis ↓ Joint fluid tracks posteriorly ↓ Soft swelling behind the knee ↓ Popliteal cyst ↓ Baker cyst
exam_trap: D, olecranon bursitis — a common fluid-filled swelling, but it lies over the elbow, not behind the knee.
takeaway: Soft popliteal swelling in knee arthritis is a Baker cyst; rupture can mimic DVT.

stem:
A patient with diabetes develops a chronic foot ulcer that probes deeply and has surrounding tenderness. They develop fever.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic diabetic foot ulcers can extend to underlying bone and cause osteomyelitis.
why_wrong: A. Migraine is unrelated. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve. C. Osteoarthritis does not cause an infected chronic ulcer. E. Fibromyalgia does not cause a local infected ulcer.
pearl: A diabetic foot ulcer that probes to bone strongly suggests osteomyelitis; arrange an X-ray (MRI if still suspected) and urgent referral to the multidisciplinary foot team.
thinking: Diabetes with chronic foot ulcer ↓ Ulcer probes deeply ↓ Surrounding tenderness and fever ↓ Infection has reached bone ↓ Osteomyelitis
exam_trap: C, osteoarthritis — affects the bones and joints of the foot, but it does not cause fever or a deep infected ulcer.
takeaway: Diabetic foot ulcer that probes deeply with fever: osteomyelitis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A child has irregular patches of hair loss with hairs of different lengths. They admit repeatedly pulling their hair when anxious.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent hair pulling causing irregular areas of hair loss is characteristic of trichotillomania.
why_wrong: B. Androgenetic alopecia follows a characteristic patterned distribution. C. Tinea capitis may cause scaling and broken hairs and requires consideration of fungal infection. D. Telogen effluvium causes diffuse shedding. E. Alopecia areata typically produces smooth, discrete patches.
pearl: Trichotillomania gives irregular patches with broken hairs of varying lengths on a normal scalp; manage with behavioural approaches and address any underlying anxiety.
thinking: Child with irregular patches of hair loss ↓ Hairs of different lengths ↓ Admits pulling hair when anxious ↓ Self-induced hair loss ↓ Trichotillomania
exam_trap: E, alopecia areata — also causes patchy hair loss in children, but its patches are smooth and discrete, not irregular with broken hairs of mixed length.
takeaway: Irregular patches, hairs of varying length and pulling behaviour: trichotillomania.

stem:
A patient with systemic sclerosis develops progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough.

Which pulmonary complication should be considered?
why_correct: Systemic sclerosis is associated with interstitial lung disease, which can cause progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis is unrelated. B. Pulmonary embolism is possible in many patients but is not the characteristic systemic sclerosis lung complication. C. Bronchiectasis is not the defining pulmonary complication here. D. Pneumothorax causes acute symptoms rather than this progressive pattern.
pearl: Interstitial lung disease is a leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis; pulmonary arterial hypertension is the other major lung complication to look for.
thinking: Systemic sclerosis ↓ Progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ Persistent dry cough ↓ Fibrotic lung involvement ↓ Interstitial lung disease
exam_trap: B, pulmonary embolism in every case — PE causes breathlessness, but usually acutely; progressive dyspnoea with dry cough in systemic sclerosis suggests ILD.
takeaway: Systemic sclerosis with progressive dyspnoea and dry cough: think interstitial lung disease.

stem:
A patient with suspected giant cell arteritis develops sudden visual disturbance in one eye.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Arrange temporal artery biopsy before steroids
options.B: Treat as an emergency to prevent visual loss
options.C: Start oral aspirin and review in clinic within a week
options.D: Refer to rheumatology clinic within 2 weeks for review
options.E: Await ESR and CRP before treating

correct_answer: B. Treat as an emergency to prevent visual loss
why_correct: Visual symptoms in suspected GCA require urgent assessment and treatment because visual loss can become permanent.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids should not be delayed while awaiting biopsy. C. Aspirin is not the treatment, and delay risks permanent visual loss. D. A 2-week referral is too slow for visual symptoms. E. Treatment should not wait for blood results.
pearl: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms is an emergency: give high-dose corticosteroids immediately and arrange same-day ophthalmology review; biopsy or ultrasound can follow.
thinking: Suspected giant cell arteritis ↓ Sudden visual disturbance in one eye ↓ Threat of ischaemic optic neuropathy ↓ Visual loss may become permanent ↓ Treat as an emergency
exam_trap: A, temporal artery biopsy before steroids — tempting to secure the diagnosis, but biopsy remains useful after steroids start, and delay risks permanent blindness.
takeaway: GCA with visual symptoms: steroids immediately, do not wait for tests.

stem:
A patient with known myasthenia gravis develops increasing difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath.

What is the most important concern?

options.C: Functional dysphagia with associated panic attacks
options.E: Pulmonary embolism related to recent immobility

correct_answer: D. Myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure
why_correct: Bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness in myasthenia can progress to life-threatening respiratory failure and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. A stricture does not explain breathlessness in a patient with known myasthenia gravis. B. Hyperventilation is a diagnosis of exclusion and dangerous to assume here. C. Functional dysphagia does not explain progressive bulbar and respiratory weakness. E. Pulmonary embolism does not explain bulbar weakness with dysphagia.
pearl: In suspected myasthenic crisis, monitor forced vital capacity rather than relying on saturations, which fall late, and involve critical care early; bulbar weakness raises aspiration risk.
thinking: Known myasthenia gravis ↓ Worsening dysphagia (bulbar weakness) ↓ Breathlessness (respiratory muscle weakness) ↓ Impending ventilatory failure ↓ Myasthenic crisis
exam_trap: E, pulmonary embolism — a cause of acute breathlessness, but it does not explain worsening swallowing, which points to bulbar weakness.
takeaway: Myasthenia with dysphagia and breathlessness: myasthenic crisis; check FVC and escalate.

stem:
A young adult with neurological symptoms develops double vision due to impaired coordinated horizontal eye movements.

Which neurological disorder is classically associated with internuclear ophthalmoplegia?
why_correct: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is classically associated with multiple sclerosis in younger adults.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson disease does not classically cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia. C. Motor neurone disease does not characteristically cause this finding. D. Bell's palsy affects the facial nerve. E. Myasthenia can mimic ocular motility disorders but does not cause a central MLF lesion.
pearl: In INO the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct while the abducting eye shows nystagmus; bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Young adult with neurological symptoms ↓ Diplopia from impaired horizontal gaze ↓ Internuclear ophthalmoplegia ↓ MLF lesion, typically demyelinating ↓ Multiple sclerosis
exam_trap: E, myasthenia gravis only — can mimic almost any eye movement disorder, but it is not an MLF lesion; a true INO in a young adult suggests MS.
takeaway: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult: think multiple sclerosis.

stem:
A patient has a resting tremor, rigidity and progressively slower movements.

Which clinical feature is central to the diagnosis of Parkinson disease?
why_correct: Bradykinesia is a core motor feature of Parkinson disease, alongside features such as rigidity and resting tremor.
why_wrong: A. Sudden blindness is unrelated. C. Hyperreflexia alone does not establish Parkinson disease. D. Isolated sensory loss is not characteristic of Parkinson disease. E. Acute flaccid paralysis suggests an acute neurological or peripheral process.
pearl: Parkinsonism requires bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity; asymmetrical onset and a good levodopa response support idiopathic Parkinson disease.
thinking: Resting tremor ↓ Rigidity ↓ Progressively slower movements ↓ Bradykinesia is essential for parkinsonism ↓ Bradykinesia
exam_trap: C, hyperreflexia as the only finding — suggests an upper motor neurone lesion, not the extrapyramidal syndrome of Parkinson disease.
takeaway: No bradykinesia, no parkinsonism: it is the core diagnostic feature.

stem:
A patient with Parkinson disease develops constipation and reduced sense of smell.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: These suggest an alternative diagnosis to Parkinson disease
options.B: These are side effects of levodopa

correct_answer: C. Parkinson disease has non-motor features
why_correct: Parkinson disease can cause non-motor features including constipation and reduced sense of smell.
why_wrong: A. Constipation and anosmia are recognised features of Parkinson disease. B. Reduced smell is not a levodopa side effect and often precedes treatment. D. These features are common in idiopathic Parkinson disease and do not indicate MSA. E. Reduced smell does not indicate Alzheimer's disease.
pearl: Non-motor features of Parkinson disease include anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and later cognitive decline; some precede motor signs by years.
thinking: Known Parkinson disease ↓ Constipation ↓ Reduced sense of smell ↓ Recognised non-motor features ↓ Parkinson disease has non-motor features
exam_trap: B, side effects of levodopa — constipation can worsen with medication, but reduced smell is not a drug effect and often predates treatment.
takeaway: Anosmia and constipation are non-motor features of Parkinson disease, not drug side effects.

stem:
A patient develops facial pain, purulent nasal discharge and nasal obstruction that have persisted for more than 10 days without improvement.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent symptoms with purulent nasal discharge and facial pain, particularly without improvement, are compatible with acute bacterial sinusitis.
why_wrong: A. Migraine can cause facial or head pain but does not cause persistent purulent nasal discharge. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock-like pain without nasal symptoms. D. Allergic rhinitis typically causes sneezing, itching and watery discharge. E. Cluster headache causes brief attacks with watery ipsilateral rhinorrhoea, not persistent purulent discharge.
pearl: Most acute sinusitis is viral and settles; bacterial infection becomes more likely when symptoms persist beyond about 10 days without improvement or worsen after initial improvement.
thinking: Facial pain and nasal obstruction ↓ Purulent nasal discharge ↓ Persisting over 10 days without improvement ↓ Suggests bacterial infection ↓ Acute bacterial sinusitis
exam_trap: D, persistent allergic rhinitis — also causes long-lasting obstruction, but with sneezing, itch and watery discharge rather than facial pain and purulent discharge.
takeaway: Sinus symptoms beyond 10 days without improvement suggest bacterial sinusitis.

stem:
A patient is struck on the nose during sport and develops pain, swelling and nasal deformity.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Trauma followed by nasal pain, swelling and deformity is typical of a nasal fracture.
why_wrong: A. Sinusitis does not usually cause immediate deformity after injury. B. Allergic rhinitis is not caused by acute trauma. D. Epistaxis describes bleeding and does not explain the structural deformity. E. Nasal polyps are non-traumatic mucosal lesions.
pearl: In a nasal fracture, always exclude a septal haematoma, which needs urgent drainage; reassess deformity once swelling settles, as manipulation is best done within about two weeks.
