thinking: Blow to the nose during sport ↓ Pain and swelling ↓ Visible nasal deformity ↓ Structural bony injury ↓ Nasal fracture
exam_trap: D, epistaxis alone — common after nasal trauma, but bleeding does not explain the deformity, which indicates a fracture.
takeaway: Nasal trauma with deformity is a fracture; always check for a septal haematoma.

stem:
A patient develops severe ear pain after regularly swimming. Moving the outer ear makes the pain worse.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Otitis externa commonly follows water exposure and causes pain that is worsened by manipulation of the pinna or tragus.
why_wrong: A. Mastoiditis causes post-auricular tenderness and swelling. B. Acoustic neuroma usually causes progressive unilateral hearing symptoms. C. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus. E. Otitis media affects the middle ear and does not characteristically cause pain on moving the external ear.
pearl: Otitis externa is common in swimmers, and pain on moving the pinna or tragus is the key sign; treat with topical ear drops and consider necrotising otitis externa in diabetic or immunocompromised patients.
thinking: Regular swimming ↓ Moisture macerates the ear canal ↓ Severe ear pain ↓ Worse on moving the outer ear ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: E, otitis media — also causes severe ear pain, but tenderness on moving the pinna or tragus localises the problem to the ear canal.
takeaway: Ear pain worse on moving the pinna after swimming: otitis externa.

stem:
A patient has recurrent itchy, crusted eyelid margins with a gritty sensation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins can cause crusting, irritation and a gritty sensation.
why_wrong: B. Acute glaucoma causes severe painful visual disturbance. C. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. D. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss rather than eyelid-margin inflammation. E. Retinal detachment causes visual field symptoms.
pearl: Blepharitis is chronic and recurrent; the mainstay is regular lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid-margin cleaning, and it often coexists with dry eye.
thinking: Recurrent symptoms ↓ Itchy, crusted eyelid margins ↓ Gritty sensation ↓ Eyelid margin inflammation ↓ Blepharitis
exam_trap: D, optic neuritis — an eye diagnosis, but it causes painful visual loss, not itchy, crusted lid margins.
takeaway: Crusted, itchy lid margins with grittiness: blepharitis, treated with lid hygiene.

stem:
A patient reports gritty, burning eyes that become worse after prolonged computer use. There is no significant loss of vision.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Grittiness and burning, particularly with prolonged screen use, are common symptoms of dry eye disease.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss. B. Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden severe visual loss. C. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and field loss. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe pain and visual disturbance.
pearl: Screen use reduces blinking and worsens dry eye; manage with lubricating drops, regular screen breaks and conscious blinking, and review urgently if pain or visual loss develops.
thinking: Gritty, burning eyes ↓ Worse after prolonged screen use ↓ No significant visual loss ↓ Tear film problem ↓ Dry eye disease
exam_trap: E, acute angle-closure glaucoma — causes eye pain, but it is severe with blurred vision, haloes and a red eye, not gritty discomfort after screen use.
takeaway: Gritty, burning eyes worse with screens and normal vision: dry eye disease.

stem:
A child's eyes do not appear to point in the same direction.

What is the clinical term for this finding?
why_correct: Strabismus refers to misalignment of the eyes.
why_wrong: A. Binocular diplopia means double vision, which is a symptom rather than the term for misalignment. C. Nystagmus is involuntary rhythmic eye movement. D. Hypermetropia is long-sightedness; it can contribute to squint but is not the term for misalignment. E. Amblyopia is reduced visual development.
pearl: A child with a persistent squint needs ophthalmology or orthoptic referral, because untreated strabismus can cause amblyopia; the corneal light reflex and cover test detect it.
thinking: Child's eyes point in different directions ↓ Ocular misalignment ↓ Clinical term for misalignment ↓ Strabismus
exam_trap: E, amblyopia — closely linked because squint can cause it, but amblyopia is reduced visual development in an eye, not the misalignment itself.
takeaway: Misaligned eyes is strabismus; refer early to prevent amblyopia.

stem:
A child has difficulty focusing on near objects and experiences eye strain when reading.

Which refractive error may cause this?
why_correct: Hypermetropia can make near focusing more difficult, particularly when accommodation is insufficient.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment causes acute visual symptoms. B. Myopia primarily causes difficulty with distance vision. C. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss. D. Cataract causes lens opacity and progressive visual impairment.
pearl: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) makes near focusing effortful, causing eye strain and headaches when reading; it is corrected with convex (plus) lenses.
thinking: Child struggles to focus on near objects ↓ Eye strain when reading ↓ Excess accommodation needed ↓ Image focuses behind the retina ↓ Hypermetropia
exam_trap: B, myopia — the most familiar refractive error in children, but short-sightedness blurs distance vision while near vision is usually good.
takeaway: Difficulty with near vision and strain on reading: hypermetropia.

stem:
A patient has recurrent episodes of lower abdominal discomfort and bloating associated with bowel habit changes. There is no fever or systemic illness.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Diverticular disease can cause recurrent abdominal symptoms without the systemic inflammatory features of acute diverticulitis.
why_wrong: A. Obstruction causes vomiting, distension and failure to pass stool or flatus. B. Chronic pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back and steatorrhoea. C. Ischaemic colitis causes sudden abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea. D. Complicated diverticulitis causes persistent pain with fever and systemic inflammation.
pearl: Diverticular disease means symptoms from diverticula without acute inflammation; diverticulitis adds fever, persistent localised pain and raised inflammatory markers.
thinking: Recurrent lower abdominal discomfort ↓ Bloating and change in bowel habit ↓ No fever or systemic illness ↓ No acute inflammation ↓ Symptomatic diverticular disease
exam_trap: D, acute complicated diverticulitis — part of the same disease spectrum, but it causes fever and systemic upset, which are absent here.
takeaway: Diverticular symptoms without fever or systemic upset: diverticular disease, not diverticulitis.

stem:
An older patient develops progressive abdominal distension, constipation and vomiting. Abdominal imaging shows marked colonic dilatation.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive constipation and abdominal distension with colonic dilatation suggest large bowel obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Small bowel obstruction shows dilated small bowel loops rather than marked colonic dilatation. C. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting without colonic dilatation or constipation. D. Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea and vomiting without colonic dilatation. E. IBS does not cause marked bowel dilatation from mechanical obstruction.
pearl: Large bowel obstruction in older patients is most often due to colorectal cancer or volvulus; CT confirms the cause and level, and caecal dilatation signals perforation risk.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Progressive distension and constipation ↓ Vomiting ↓ Marked colonic dilatation on imaging ↓ Large bowel obstruction
exam_trap: B, small bowel obstruction — also causes distension and vomiting, but imaging shows dilated small bowel loops, not marked colonic dilatation.
takeaway: Progressive distension, constipation and colonic dilatation: large bowel obstruction.

stem:
Several people develop vomiting and watery diarrhoea within a short period after attending the same event.

What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Acute vomiting and diarrhoea affecting several people over a short period strongly suggest an infectious outbreak.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease is chronic and immune-mediated. C. Colorectal cancer does not typically cause an acute cluster of illness. D. Crohn disease is a chronic inflammatory condition. E. IBS is not an infectious illness.
pearl: A cluster of acute vomiting and diarrhoea after a shared event suggests infectious gastroenteritis, often norovirus or food-borne; suspected food poisoning must be notified to the local health protection team.
thinking: Several people unwell ↓ All attended the same event ↓ Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea ↓ Common infectious source ↓ Infectious gastroenteritis
exam_trap: E, irritable bowel syndrome — causes diarrhoea, but it is chronic and non-infectious and cannot explain an acute cluster of illness.
takeaway: Acute vomiting and diarrhoea in a cluster after a shared event: infectious gastroenteritis.

stem:
A patient develops fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea after eating inadequately cooked poultry.

Which organism is a recognised cause?
why_correct: Salmonella can cause acute febrile gastroenteritis and is associated with contaminated or inadequately cooked food, including poultry.
why_wrong: A. H. pylori is associated with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. C. C. tetani causes tetanus, not gastroenteritis. D. Candida is not a typical cause of acute foodborne gastroenteritis. E. Giardia typically causes prolonged diarrhoea and malabsorption, often after contaminated water.
pearl: Salmonella and Campylobacter are classic causes of febrile gastroenteritis from undercooked poultry; most cases settle with fluids alone, without antibiotics.
thinking: Undercooked poultry ↓ Fever ↓ Abdominal cramps and diarrhoea ↓ Invasive bacterial food poisoning ↓ Salmonella
exam_trap: E, Giardia lamblia — a recognised cause of diarrhoea, but it is usually waterborne and causes prolonged bloating and malabsorption rather than acute febrile illness.
takeaway: Febrile gastroenteritis after undercooked poultry: think Salmonella or Campylobacter.

stem:
A traveller develops prolonged foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss after drinking untreated water.

Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Giardia commonly causes prolonged diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption following contaminated water exposure.
why_wrong: A. Salmonella typically causes acute inflammatory gastroenteritis. B. Streptococcus pyogenes is not a typical cause of this syndrome. C. Shigella commonly causes acute diarrhoea, often with blood and fever. D. Influenza does not cause this characteristic prolonged gastrointestinal illness.
pearl: Giardiasis causes prolonged, foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea with bloating and weight loss after untreated water; confirm with stool testing and treat with metronidazole.
thinking: Traveller drank untreated water ↓ Prolonged diarrhoea ↓ Foul-smelling stool and bloating ↓ Weight loss from malabsorption ↓ Giardia lamblia
exam_trap: C, Shigella — a cause of travellers' diarrhoea, but it causes acute, often bloody diarrhoea with fever rather than prolonged malabsorption.
takeaway: Prolonged foul diarrhoea and bloating after untreated water: Giardia.

stem:
A patient with a known gastric ulcer suddenly develops severe abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen.

What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen in a patient with peptic ulcer disease suggests perforation and peritonitis.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids do not cause acute abdominal pain. B. IBS does not cause peritonism. D. Constipation does not cause a rigid acute abdomen. E. Lactose intolerance causes gastrointestinal symptoms after lactose ingestion, not peritonitis.
pearl: Perforated peptic ulcer causes sudden severe pain and a board-like rigid abdomen; an erect chest X-ray may show free air under the diaphragm, and CT is more sensitive.
thinking: Known gastric ulcer ↓ Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Rigid abdomen means peritonitis ↓ Ulcer has breached the gut wall ↓ Perforation
exam_trap: B, IBS — causes abdominal pain, but it never produces peritonism or a rigid abdomen.
takeaway: Peptic ulcer plus sudden pain and a rigid abdomen: perforation until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with longstanding peptic ulcer disease develops recurrent large-volume vomiting and early satiety.

Which complication may explain these symptoms?
why_correct: Gastric outlet obstruction can cause recurrent vomiting, early satiety and difficulty emptying the stomach.
why_wrong: A. Reflux causes heartburn and regurgitation rather than large-volume vomiting and early satiety. C. Achalasia causes dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food and is not a complication of peptic ulcer disease. D. Small bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, distension and constipation. E. Cyclical vomiting syndrome causes stereotyped discrete episodes with well intervals and is not a complication of ulcer disease.
pearl: Gastric outlet obstruction gives large-volume vomiting of undigested food, early satiety and a succussion splash, with a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
thinking: Longstanding peptic ulcer disease ↓ Scarring at the pylorus or duodenum ↓ Stomach cannot empty ↓ Large-volume vomiting and early satiety ↓ Gastric outlet obstruction
exam_trap: D, small bowel obstruction — causes vomiting, but with colicky pain and distension, and it is not a typical complication of peptic ulcer disease.
takeaway: Peptic ulcer history plus large-volume vomiting and early satiety: gastric outlet obstruction.

stem:
A patient reports recurrent upper abdominal discomfort, early fullness after eating and indigestion.

Which term best describes this symptom complex?
why_correct: Dyspepsia refers to a group of upper gastrointestinal symptoms including epigastric discomfort, early satiety and postprandial fullness.
why_wrong: A. Haemoptysis is coughing blood. B. Odynophagia is painful swallowing. C. Tenesmus is the sensation of incomplete bowel evacuation. E. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
pearl: Dyspepsia is an umbrella term for upper GI symptoms such as epigastric discomfort, fullness, early satiety and indigestion; always screen for red flags such as dysphagia, weight loss and anaemia.
thinking: Upper abdominal discomfort ↓ Early fullness after eating and indigestion ↓ A cluster of upper GI symptoms, not a swallowing problem ↓ Dyspepsia
exam_trap: E, dysphagia — sounds similar and is also an upper GI symptom, but it means difficulty swallowing; nothing in the stem describes food sticking or swallowing trouble.
takeaway: Dyspepsia is a symptom complex; dysphagia and odynophagia are swallowing problems.

stem:
A patient has persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit. They complain of headaches and itching after a hot shower.

Which disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Increased red-cell mass can cause hyperviscosity symptoms, and aquagenic pruritus is a recognised feature of polycythaemia vera.
why_wrong: B. Thrombocytopenia means a low platelet count. C. Haemophilia causes bleeding due to clotting-factor deficiency. D. Iron deficiency causes low haemoglobin. E. Aplastic anaemia causes bone-marrow failure and cytopenias.
pearl: Persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit with itching after a warm bath or shower should prompt consideration of polycythaemia vera, usually confirmed by JAK2 mutation testing.
thinking: Persistently high haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Headaches suggest hyperviscosity ↓ Aquagenic pruritus is a classic myeloproliferative clue ↓ Polycythaemia
exam_trap: E, aplastic anaemia — a marrow disorder that may tempt, but it causes low counts across all cell lines, the opposite of a raised haemoglobin and haematocrit.
takeaway: High haemoglobin and haematocrit plus aquagenic itch: think polycythaemia vera.

stem:
A pregnant woman has concerns after handling cat litter.

Which infection is of particular relevance?
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii can be transmitted through exposure to infected cat faeces or contaminated soil and is important during pregnancy because congenital infection can occur.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is an external ear infection. B. Tetanus is not specifically associated with cat litter. D. Influenza is transmitted primarily through respiratory exposure. E. Scabies is caused by mites and spreads mainly through close skin contact.
pearl: Toxoplasmosis is caught from cat faeces, soil and undercooked meat; pregnant women should avoid emptying cat litter or wear gloves and wash hands, and eat meat well cooked.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Exposure to cat litter (cat faeces) ↓ Toxoplasma gondii is shed in cat faeces and can cross the placenta ↓ Toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: B, tetanus — dirt and soil exposure can bring tetanus to mind, but tetanus needs a contaminated wound and is not specifically linked to cat litter or congenital infection.
takeaway: Cat litter in pregnancy means toxoplasmosis risk: gloves and hand hygiene.

stem:
A pregnant woman who is not known to be immune is exposed to rubella.

What is the major concern?
why_correct: Maternal rubella infection, particularly early in pregnancy, can cause congenital rubella syndrome with serious fetal consequences.
why_wrong: A. Rubella is not a cause of peptic ulcer disease. B. Renal colic is unrelated. C. Rubella does not cause congenital appendicitis. D. Scabies is a mite infestation unrelated to congenital rubella.
pearl: Rubella in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome with deafness, cataracts and heart defects; MMR is live, so non-immune women are vaccinated after delivery, not during pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant, not known to be immune ↓ Exposed to rubella ↓ Virus crosses the placenta, with greatest risk early in pregnancy ↓ Congenital rubella syndrome
exam_trap: D, neonatal scabies — the only other infection-sounding option, but scabies is a mite infestation spread by skin contact and has no link to rubella.
takeaway: The danger of rubella in pregnancy is to the fetus: congenital rubella syndrome.

stem:
A pregnant woman asks whether seasonal influenza vaccination is appropriate.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
options.C: Only women with diabetes should be vaccinated
options.D: All vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy
options.E: Vaccination must always be delayed until after delivery

correct_answer: A. Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
why_correct: Seasonal influenza vaccination is offered during pregnancy because pregnant women have increased risk of complications from influenza and vaccination also provides protection to the infant after birth.
why_wrong: B. The recommended influenza vaccines do not cause influenza infection. C. The recommendation is not restricted to women with diabetes. D. Some vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, but not all. E. Vaccination should not routinely be postponed until after delivery.
pearl: Inactivated influenza vaccine is offered to all pregnant women during flu season at any stage of pregnancy; it protects the mother and passes antibodies that protect the baby in early infancy.
thinking: Pregnant woman asks about flu vaccine ↓ Pregnancy raises the risk of severe influenza ↓ Inactivated vaccine is safe at any gestation ↓ Vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
exam_trap: D, all vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — tempting caution, but only live vaccines are avoided; inactivated influenza vaccine is actively recommended.
takeaway: Offer inactivated flu vaccine to every pregnant woman in flu season.

stem: Which vaccine type is generally avoided during pregnancy because it contains live attenuated organisms?
why_correct: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy as a precaution because of theoretical fetal risk.
why_wrong: B. Toxoid vaccines use inactivated toxins. C. Inactivated vaccines do not contain replicating live organisms. D. Recombinant subunit vaccines contain selected antigenic components. E. Conjugate vaccines contain antigen linked to a carrier protein.
pearl: Live vaccines such as MMR, varicella and BCG are generally avoided in pregnancy; inactivated, toxoid and subunit vaccines can be given when indicated.
thinking: Pregnancy ↓ Concern is a vaccine organism that can replicate ↓ Only live attenuated vaccines contain replicating organisms ↓ Live attenuated vaccine
exam_trap: B, toxoid vaccine — 'toxin' sounds risky in pregnancy, but toxoids are inactivated toxins that cannot replicate and are not routinely avoided.
takeaway: In pregnancy avoid live vaccines; inactivated vaccines are generally acceptable.

stem:
A child develops an itchy rash consisting of crops of vesicles and crusted lesions at different stages.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox characteristically causes successive crops of itchy vesicles, pustules and crusted lesions at different stages.
why_wrong: B. Scarlet fever produces a fine, sandpaper-like rash. C. Measles causes a maculopapular rash rather than crops of vesicles. D. Rubella causes a maculopapular rash. E. Impetigo causes superficial bacterial skin lesions, often with honey-coloured crusts.
pearl: Chickenpox lesions appear in successive crops, so papules, vesicles and crusts are seen together; a child remains infectious until all lesions have crusted over.
thinking: Child with itchy rash ↓ Vesicles and crusts present together ↓ Lesions at different stages = successive crops ↓ Varicella
exam_trap: E, impetigo — also causes crusting, but it gives localised honey-coloured crusts rather than widespread itchy crops of vesicles at different stages.
takeaway: Itchy vesicles in crops at different stages = chickenpox.

stem:
A new screening test is being assessed for a disease. Of 100 people who definitely have the disease, 95 test positive.

What does this result primarily describe?
why_correct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive: true positives ÷ all people with the disease.
why_wrong: A. Positive predictive value is the probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. B. Specificity measures correctly identified people without the disease. C. Prevalence is the proportion of the population with the disease. E. Negative predictive value is the probability that a person with a negative test does not have the disease.
pearl: Sensitivity is calculated only among people who truly have the disease; a highly sensitive test rarely misses disease, so a negative result helps rule it out.
thinking: Group studied = 100 people who definitely have the disease ↓ 95 test positive ↓ True positives ÷ all with disease ↓ Sensitivity
exam_trap: A, positive predictive value — also involves positive tests, but PPV starts from those who test positive and asks how many truly have the disease; here the starting group is the diseased.
takeaway: Start with the diseased: sensitivity. Start with positive tests: PPV.

stem:
A GP practice records 20 new cases of type 2 diabetes during one calendar year among its registered population.

Which epidemiological measure is being described?
why_correct: Incidence measures new cases occurring in a population over a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Prevalence describes existing cases at a particular time or over a period. B. Case fatality describes deaths among people with a particular disease. C. Specificity describes diagnostic test performance. E. Sensitivity describes diagnostic test performance.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases over a defined period in a population at risk; prevalence counts all existing cases. In chronic diseases prevalence builds up as new cases accumulate.
thinking: 20 cases recorded ↓ They are new diagnoses ↓ Over a defined period of one calendar year ↓ Incidence
exam_trap: A, prevalence — the commonest confusion, but prevalence includes all existing cases, old and new; counting only new diagnoses over a year is incidence.
takeaway: New cases over time = incidence; all current cases = prevalence.

stem:
A survey finds that 8% of adults in a town currently have asthma.

Which epidemiological measure is being reported?
why_correct: Prevalence describes the proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or during a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity concerns detection of people with disease. B. Relative risk compares disease risk between groups. C. Specificity concerns correctly identifying people without disease. E. Incidence measures new cases.
pearl: Prevalence is a snapshot of everyone with the condition at a point or period, regardless of when it began; cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence, not incidence.
thinking: Survey of a town population ↓ 8% currently have asthma ↓ Existing cases as a proportion at one time ↓ Prevalence
exam_trap: E, incidence — tempting because it is also a measure of disease frequency, but incidence counts only new cases over time; 'currently have' signals existing cases.
takeaway: 'Currently have' a condition signals prevalence.

stem:
A cohort study compares two groups. The risk of developing a disease is 10% in the exposed group and 5% in the unexposed group.

What is the relative risk?
why_correct: Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed = 10% ÷ 5% = 2.
why_wrong: A. This would represent the reverse ratio. B. A relative risk of 1 indicates equal risk. D. This is not the ratio of the two risks. E. This is also not the ratio.
pearl: Relative risk compares risk in the exposed with risk in the unexposed: above 1 means higher risk with exposure, 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower risk.
thinking: Cohort study ↓ Risk 10% in exposed, 5% in unexposed ↓ RR = exposed ÷ unexposed ↓ 10 ÷ 5 = 2
exam_trap: A, 0.5 — the result of dividing the wrong way round (unexposed ÷ exposed); the exposed group always goes on top.
takeaway: Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed.

stem:
A treatment produces an absolute risk reduction of 10%.

What is the approximate number needed to treat to prevent one additional event?
why_correct: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction. An ARR of 0.10 gives an NNT of 10.
why_wrong: A. Would require an ARR of 100%. B. Would correspond to an ARR of 20%. D. Would correspond to an ARR of 5%. E. Would correspond to an ARR of 1%.
pearl: NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction; express the ARR as a decimal first, and round any fractional NNT up to the next whole patient.
thinking: Absolute risk reduction given as 10% ↓ Convert the percentage to a decimal: 0.10 ↓ NNT = 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.10 ↓ 10
exam_trap: E, 100 — the result of treating 10% as if it were 1% when converting the percentage; 1 ÷ 0.10 gives 10, not 100.
takeaway: NNT = 1 ÷ ARR, with the ARR written as a decimal.

stem:
A case-control study reports an odds ratio of 3 for exposure to a particular factor and development of a disease.

What does this indicate?

options.A: 3% of exposed people develop the disease
options.B: The relative risk of disease in the exposed group is 3
options.C: Three people must be exposed for one extra case of the disease
options.D: The exposure is proven to cause the disease
options.E: The odds of disease are 3 times higher in the exposed

correct_answer: E. The odds of disease are 3 times higher in the exposed
why_correct: An odds ratio of 3 indicates that the odds of the outcome are three times as high in the exposed group relative to the comparison group.
why_wrong: A. An odds ratio is not an absolute risk or prevalence. B. A case-control study cannot directly estimate relative risk; the odds ratio approximates it only when the disease is rare. C. This describes a number needed to harm. D. An association does not by itself establish causation.
pearl: Case-control studies start from the outcome and look back at exposure, so they yield odds ratios; the odds ratio approximates relative risk only when the disease is rare.
thinking: Case-control design ↓ Groups chosen by outcome, so risk cannot be measured directly ↓ Odds ratio compares odds by exposure ↓ Odds of disease 3 times higher in the exposed
exam_trap: B, relative risk of 3 — tempting because the OR often approximates the RR, but a case-control study cannot measure risk directly and the approximation holds only for rare diseases.
takeaway: Case-control studies give an odds ratio, not a relative risk or proof of causation.

stem:
A study reports a relative risk of 1.4 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9–2.1.

Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The exposure significantly increases the risk by 40%
options.B: The study proves there is no difference between the groups
options.C: The p-value for this result is below the 0.05 threshold
options.D: It is not statistically significant at the 5% level
options.E: The interval shows a clinically important harm from exposure

correct_answer: D. It is not statistically significant at the 5% level
why_correct: For a relative risk, a 95% confidence interval that includes 1 is compatible with no association at the conventional 5% significance level.
why_wrong: A. The interval includes 1, so the increase is not statistically significant. B. Failure to demonstrate statistical significance does not prove the null hypothesis. C. An interval including 1 corresponds to p above 0.05. E. The interval includes a range of possible effects, including no effect.
pearl: For ratios such as relative risk or odds ratio, the value of no effect is 1; if the 95% confidence interval includes 1, the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level.
thinking: Relative risk 1.4 ↓ 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1 ↓ Interval includes 1, the value of no effect ↓ Not statistically significant at the 5% level
exam_trap: A, a significant 40% increase — the point estimate does suggest a 40% rise, but the interval includes 1, so the result is compatible with no effect and is not significant.
takeaway: Ratio CI including 1, or difference CI including 0: not significant.

stem:
A researcher concludes that a new treatment is effective when in reality there is no true treatment effect.

What type of error has occurred?
why_correct: A Type I error is a false-positive conclusion: rejecting a true null hypothesis.
why_wrong: B. Recall bias concerns inaccurate recollection of past exposures or events. C. Type II error is failing to detect a true effect. D. Selection bias results from systematic differences in who enters or remains in a study. E. Confounding occurs when another factor distorts an observed association.
pearl: A type I error is a false positive: finding an effect that is not really there, with its probability set by alpha. A type II error is a false negative, often from too small a sample.
thinking: Conclusion: the treatment works ↓ Reality: no true effect ↓ A true null hypothesis has been rejected ↓ Type I error
exam_trap: C, type II error — the other statistical error, but type II means missing a real effect (false negative); here a non-existent effect was claimed (false positive).
takeaway: Type I error = false positive; type II error = false negative.

stem: What does increasing the statistical power of a study primarily do?

options.A: Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
options.B: Reduces the probability of a type I error
options.D: Increases the true effect size of the treatment being tested
options.E: Lowers the significance level required for a result

correct_answer: A. Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
why_correct: Statistical power is the probability of detecting a specified true effect, commonly expressed as 1 − β.
why_wrong: B. The type I error rate is set by the chosen alpha, not by power. C. Confounding requires appropriate study design or analysis. D. Power does not change the true effect size. E. The significance level is chosen independently of power.
pearl: Power (1 − β) is the chance of detecting a true effect of a given size; it rises mainly with larger sample size, larger effect size and less variability.
thinking: Power = 1 − β ↓ β is the chance of missing a true effect ↓ Higher power means fewer false negatives ↓ Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
exam_trap: B, reduces type I error — tempting because power and error rates are linked, but the type I error rate is fixed by the chosen alpha; power reduces type II error.
takeaway: More power means fewer type II errors, not fewer type I errors.

stem: What is the main purpose of randomisation in a clinical trial?

options.A: To keep participants and assessors blind to allocation
options.B: To make results generalisable to the wider population
options.C: To balance known and unknown confounders between groups
options.D: To increase the statistical power of the trial
options.E: To reduce loss to follow-up in each group

correct_answer: C. To balance known and unknown confounders between groups
why_correct: Random allocation helps create comparable groups and reduces confounding by indication and other baseline differences.
why_wrong: A. Keeping participants and assessors unaware of allocation is blinding, a separate methodological feature. B. Generalisability depends on who is recruited, not on randomisation. D. Power depends mainly on sample size and effect size. E. Randomisation does not reduce loss to follow-up.
pearl: Randomisation is the only method that balances unknown as well as known confounders between groups; allocation concealment protects it, and blinding is a separate safeguard.
thinking: Purpose of random allocation ↓ Chance alone decides group membership ↓ Known and unknown baseline factors spread evenly ↓ Balances confounders between groups
exam_trap: A, keeping participants and assessors blind — randomisation and blinding often appear together, but blinding hides allocation once made; randomisation decides allocation and balances confounders.
takeaway: Randomisation balances confounders; blinding protects against bias after allocation.

stem:
In a randomised trial, participants and investigators are unaware of which treatment each participant receives.

What methodological feature is being used?
why_correct: Blinding prevents participants and/or investigators from knowing treatment allocation and can reduce certain forms of bias.
why_wrong: A. Matching pairs participants according to selected characteristics. B. Intention-to-treat concerns how trial participants are analysed after allocation. D. Randomisation determines how participants are allocated. E. Stratification involves dividing participants according to important characteristics before analysis or allocation.
pearl: Blinding stops knowledge of allocation influencing behaviour, care or outcome assessment; when both participants and investigators are unaware, the trial is double-blind.
thinking: Randomised trial ↓ Participants and investigators do not know who receives which treatment ↓ Knowledge of the treatment received is hidden after allocation ↓ Blinding
exam_trap: D, randomisation — present in every RCT, but randomisation determines how allocation is made; keeping people unaware of that allocation is blinding.
takeaway: Unaware of treatment received = blinding; chance allocation = randomisation.

stem:
A study finds that coffee drinking is associated with lung cancer. Further analysis shows that smokers are much more likely to drink coffee.

What concept may explain part of the observed association?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both the exposure and outcome and may distort the observed relationship between coffee consumption and lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Randomisation is a method used to reduce confounding in trials. B. Sensitivity concerns diagnostic testing. C. Specificity concerns diagnostic testing. D. Blinding concerns knowledge of treatment allocation.
pearl: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome without lying on the causal pathway; it can be handled by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification or multivariable analysis.
thinking: Coffee associated with lung cancer ↓ Smokers drink more coffee ↓ Smoking itself causes lung cancer ↓ A third factor distorts the association: confounding
exam_trap: A, randomisation — it is the best tool against confounding, so it tempts, but it is a method of prevention, not the concept that explains this distorted association.
takeaway: A factor linked to both exposure and outcome is a confounder.

stem:
Researchers randomly allocate patients with hypertension to receive either a new drug or standard treatment and compare blood pressure after six months.

What type of study is this?
why_correct: Participants are randomly allocated to intervention and comparison groups and outcomes are subsequently compared.
why_wrong: B. In a cohort study the investigators observe rather than allocate the exposure. C. Case-control studies start with outcome status. D. Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome at a single time point. E. Allocation here was random, so it is not a non-randomised trial.
pearl: The defining feature of an RCT is that investigators allocate the intervention by chance; in observational studies such as cohorts, exposure is not assigned by the investigator.
thinking: Investigators assign the treatment ↓ Allocation is random ↓ Outcomes compared after follow-up ↓ Randomised controlled trial
exam_trap: B, prospective cohort study — it also follows groups forward over time, but in a cohort the exposure is observed, not allocated by the investigators.
takeaway: Investigator randomly allocates the intervention = RCT.

stem:
A doctor is handing over a deteriorating patient to the on-call team.

Which information is particularly important to include?

options.A: Full admission history and complete past medical history
options.B: Diagnosis, drug chart and next of kin details
options.C: Admission diagnosis and planned discharge date
options.D: Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan

correct_answer: D. Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan
why_correct: Safe handover should communicate the information required for continuity of care, including current concerns, pending tasks and what to do if the patient deteriorates.
why_wrong: A. Extensive background can obscure the important handover points. B. These details do not convey current risk or what to do if the patient deteriorates. C. The original diagnosis may not describe the current risk. E. Identification alone is insufficient.
pearl: A safe handover focuses on what the next team needs: current condition, outstanding jobs and what to do if things worsen. Structured tools such as SBAR help.
thinking: Deteriorating patient ↓ On-call team must act after handover ↓ They need current state, pending tasks and an escalation plan ↓ Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan
exam_trap: A, full admission and past medical history — feels thorough, but excessive background buries the critical points; the team needs current risk and clear actions.
takeaway: Hand over the present and the plan: status, jobs, escalation.

stem:
A woman has had unprotected sexual intercourse and wants to reduce the risk of pregnancy.

Which is a recognised form of emergency contraception?
why_correct: The copper IUD is an effective form of emergency contraception and can also provide ongoing contraception.
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics have no contraceptive role. C. Barrier cream alone is not a recognised emergency contraceptive method. D. Routine combined contraception is not itself an emergency method after intercourse. E. Methotrexate is not an emergency contraceptive.
pearl: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive and also provides ongoing contraception; the oral options are levonorgestrel and ulipristal acetate.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Wants to reduce pregnancy risk now ↓ Needs a recognised emergency method ↓ Copper intrauterine device
exam_trap: E, methotrexate — associated with ending an early pregnancy, so it may tempt, but it is used for ectopic pregnancy and is not an emergency contraceptive.
takeaway: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception.

stem:
A woman reports menstrual bleeding that is significantly heavier than usual and interferes with her daily activities.

Which term is commonly used for this problem?
why_correct: Heavy menstrual bleeding refers to excessive menstrual bleeding that affects a woman's physical, social, emotional or material quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Irregular bleeding refers to variable cycle timing rather than volume. B. Dysmenorrhoea, primary or secondary, means painful menstruation. D. Intermenstrual bleeding occurs between periods. E. Amenorrhoea means absence of menstruation.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on quality of life rather than measured blood loss; ask about flooding, clots and changing protection, and check a full blood count.
thinking: Periods much heavier than usual ↓ Interferes with daily activities ↓ The problem is volume, not pain or timing ↓ Heavy menstrual bleeding
exam_trap: D, intermenstrual bleeding — another abnormal bleeding pattern, but it means bleeding between periods; here the periods themselves are heavier.
takeaway: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on the woman's life.

stem:
A 24-year-old who previously had regular periods has had no menstruation for four months.

What should be excluded first?
why_correct: Pregnancy is the commonest and most important initial cause to exclude in a person with secondary amenorrhoea who could become pregnant.
why_wrong: A. Cataract does not cause amenorrhoea. B. Otitis externa is unrelated. C. Iron overload is not the initial consideration in this presentation. D. Appendicitis does not explain persistent amenorrhoea.
pearl: In anyone with secondary amenorrhoea who could be pregnant, do a pregnancy test first, before investigating causes such as PCOS, thyroid disease or hyperprolactinaemia.
thinking: Previously regular periods ↓ No menstruation for four months: secondary amenorrhoea ↓ The commonest cause must be ruled out first ↓ Pregnancy
exam_trap: C, iron overload — haemochromatosis can rarely cause hypogonadism and amenorrhoea, but it is uncommon and never the first thing to exclude.
takeaway: Secondary amenorrhoea: always exclude pregnancy first.

stem:
A woman who is 9 weeks pregnant develops vaginal bleeding and cramping. Ultrasound confirms that the pregnancy is no longer viable.

What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Pregnancy loss before fetal viability is classified as miscarriage.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterine cavity. B. Placenta praevia concerns placental location in later pregnancy. C. Placental abruption occurs later in pregnancy, usually with placental separation. E. Postpartum haemorrhage occurs after delivery.
pearl: Miscarriage is loss of a pregnancy before viability; in early pregnancy bleeding, ultrasound establishes viability and location, which also helps exclude ectopic pregnancy.
thinking: 9 weeks pregnant ↓ Vaginal bleeding and cramping ↓ Ultrasound confirms the pregnancy is no longer viable ↓ Miscarriage
exam_trap: A, ectopic pregnancy — the key alternative in early pregnancy bleeding and pain, but it means implantation outside the uterus; the stem describes an ultrasound-confirmed non-viable pregnancy.
takeaway: Pregnancy lost before viability = miscarriage.

stem:
A 61-year-old has headaches, facial plethora and itching after a hot shower. Blood tests show an elevated haemoglobin and haematocrit.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder causing increased red-cell production; aquagenic pruritus is a recognised symptom.
why_wrong: A. Acute leukaemia commonly causes marrow failure and blasts. B. Iron deficiency causes reduced haemoglobin. D. Thalassaemia trait typically causes microcytosis rather than this acquired erythrocytosis. E. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia.
pearl: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm usually driven by a JAK2 mutation; it raises thrombosis risk and is managed with venesection and low-dose aspirin, sometimes cytoreduction.
thinking: Headaches and facial plethora ↓ Itching after a hot shower ↓ Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Polycythaemia vera
exam_trap: A, acute leukaemia — another marrow malignancy, but it causes marrow failure with anaemia, infection and bleeding, not raised haemoglobin with plethora.
takeaway: Plethora, aquagenic itch and high haematocrit: polycythaemia vera.

stem:
A newborn is found to have prolonged jaundice, poor feeding and hypotonia. Screening suggests thyroid hormone deficiency.

Why is early treatment important?
why_correct: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism can cause irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment, so early detection and treatment are important.
why_wrong: A. Congenital cataracts have different causes. B. Hypoglycaemic seizures are not the key complication of congenital hypothyroidism. C. Prolonged jaundice is a feature but kernicterus is not the reason early thyroxine is critical. E. Adrenal crisis relates to congenital adrenal hyperplasia, not thyroid hormone deficiency.
pearl: Congenital hypothyroidism is picked up on the newborn blood spot test; prompt levothyroxine prevents irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment. Prolonged jaundice is a recognised clue.
thinking: Newborn with prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, hypotonia ↓ Screening suggests thyroid hormone deficiency ↓ Thyroid hormone is essential for early brain development ↓ Prevent impaired neurodevelopment
exam_trap: C, preventing kernicterus — tempting because jaundice is in the stem, but kernicterus is not the reason early thyroxine is critical; untreated hypothyroidism harms brain development.
takeaway: Congenital hypothyroidism: early levothyroxine protects neurodevelopment.

stem:
A newborn screening programme identifies an infant with persistently elevated phenylalanine.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Phenylketonuria is caused by impaired metabolism of phenylalanine, resulting in elevated blood phenylalanine concentrations.
why_wrong: A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia involves inherited adrenal steroid synthesis defects. B. Congenital hypothyroidism involves deficient thyroid hormone production. C. Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR dysfunction. E. Down syndrome is caused by chromosome 21 abnormalities.
pearl: Phenylketonuria is detected on the newborn blood spot screen; a low-phenylalanine diet from early infancy prevents intellectual disability, with tight control needed before and during pregnancy.
thinking: Newborn screening ↓ Persistently raised phenylalanine ↓ Impaired phenylalanine metabolism ↓ Phenylketonuria
exam_trap: B, congenital hypothyroidism — also detected on the newborn blood spot, but it is picked up through raised TSH, not raised phenylalanine.
takeaway: Raised phenylalanine on newborn screening = phenylketonuria.

stem:
A parent is heterozygous for an autosomal dominant condition.

What is the probability that each pregnancy will inherit the condition?
why_correct: A heterozygous affected parent has a 50% chance of transmitting the pathogenic allele in each pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. This is not the expected Mendelian probability. B. 25% applies to a different inheritance scenario, such as two carrier parents for an autosomal recessive condition. D. This is not the expected probability for a heterozygous affected parent. E. A heterozygous parent does not transmit the allele to every child.
pearl: Each child of a heterozygous parent with an autosomal dominant condition has a 50% chance of inheriting it, independent of what happened in previous pregnancies.
thinking: Autosomal dominant condition ↓ Parent heterozygous: one affected allele ↓ Each pregnancy receives one of the two alleles ↓ 50%
exam_trap: B, 25% — the familiar figure for two carrier parents of an autosomal recessive condition, but one heterozygous dominant parent gives 50% per pregnancy.
takeaway: Autosomal dominant, one affected parent: 50% risk each pregnancy.

stem:
A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition and her partner is unaffected.

What is the probability that each male child will be affected?
why_correct: Each son receives his X chromosome from his mother. A carrier mother has a 50% chance of transmitting the affected X chromosome to each son.
why_wrong: A. There is no standard 10% probability here. B. This does not represent the probability for an individual male child. D. The probability is not 75%. E. A carrier mother will not transmit the affected X chromosome to every son.
pearl: A carrier mother of an X-linked recessive condition passes it to half her sons (affected) and half her daughters (carriers); affected fathers never pass it to sons.
thinking: X-linked recessive, carrier mother ↓ Unaffected father gives his Y to every son ↓ Each son gets either maternal X with equal chance ↓ 50%
exam_trap: B, 25% — the chance that any one child, before its sex is known, is an affected boy, but the question asks about each male child, for whom the risk is 50%.
takeaway: Carrier mother: each son 50% affected, each daughter 50% carrier.

stem:
A competent adult tells their doctor about a sensitive medical problem and asks that the information not be shared with their family.

What should the doctor generally do?

options.C: Tell all members of the clinical team regardless of relevance

why_correct: Competent adults are entitled to confidentiality. Information should only be shared where there is an appropriate justification.
why_wrong: A. A spouse has no automatic right to confidential medical information. B. Employers do not automatically have access to confidential clinical information. C. Information should be shared only with those who need it for appropriate care. D. Public disclosure would breach confidentiality.
pearl: Confidentiality applies to family and spouses too; disclosure without consent needs a clear justification, such as a legal requirement or a serious risk of harm to others.
thinking: Competent adult ↓ Shares sensitive information ↓ Asks that family are not told ↓ No justification to disclose: respect confidentiality
exam_trap: A, tell the patient's spouse — feels natural for a close family member, but spouses have no automatic right to a competent adult's medical information.
takeaway: Family have no automatic right to a competent patient's information.

stem:
A competent adult is being assessed for capacity to make a particular medical decision.

Which ability is required?

options.A: Ability to have no mental health diagnosis
options.B: Ability to make the decision the doctor considers sensible
options.C: Ability to agree with the doctor's recommendation
options.D: Ability to remember every detail of their medical history
options.E: Ability to understand the relevant information

correct_answer: E. Ability to understand the relevant information
why_correct: Capacity requires the person to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, and communicate the decision.
why_wrong: A. Having a mental health diagnosis does not automatically mean lack of capacity. B. Capacity is not determined by whether the decision appears sensible. C. A person can have capacity while making a decision the clinician disagrees with. D. Remembering every detail is unnecessary.
pearl: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific; the functional test asks whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information, and communicate a decision.
thinking: Capacity assessment for one decision ↓ Decision-specific functional test ↓ Understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate ↓ Ability to understand the relevant information
exam_trap: B, making a decision the doctor considers sensible — tempting when a choice seems risky, but an unwise decision does not on its own mean a lack of capacity.
takeaway: Capacity: understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate.

stem:
A competent adult refuses a recommended operation because they believe the risks outweigh the benefits.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Assess capacity formally because the refusal seems unwise
options.B: Seek the family's consent to proceed with the operation instead
options.C: Refer to the courts for authorisation to perform the operation
options.D: Respect the refusal, ensuring they are fully informed
options.E: Ask a second surgeon to see them and persuade them to agree

correct_answer: D. Respect the refusal, ensuring they are fully informed
why_correct: A person with capacity is entitled to make decisions that others consider unwise.
why_wrong: A. Capacity is presumed, and an unwise decision alone does not justify questioning it. B. Family members cannot consent on behalf of a competent adult. C. Courts cannot override a competent adult's refusal of treatment. E. Pressuring the patient to agree undermines voluntary decision-making.
pearl: A competent adult may refuse any treatment, even life-saving treatment, whatever their reasons; make sure they are fully informed, document the discussion and leave the door open.
thinking: Competent adult ↓ Refuses recommended surgery after weighing risks ↓ A seemingly unwise decision does not remove capacity ↓ Respect the refusal, ensuring they are fully informed
exam_trap: A, formally assess capacity because the refusal seems unwise — tempting caution, but capacity is presumed and an unwise decision alone does not justify doubting it.
takeaway: A refusal by a person with capacity must be respected, even if it seems unwise.

stem:
A patient receiving regular morphine for advanced cancer develops persistent constipation.

Which medication is commonly prescribed alongside regular opioid treatment to prevent or treat opioid-induced constipation?
why_correct: Constipation is a common adverse effect of opioids, so regular laxative treatment is often required.
why_wrong: A. Antacids do not adequately treat opioid-induced constipation. B. Anticoagulants do not treat constipation. D. Antihistamines are not appropriate treatment. E. Antibiotics do not prevent opioid-induced constipation.
pearl: Tolerance does not develop to opioid constipation, so prescribe a regular laxative, typically a stimulant with or without a softener, whenever starting regular strong opioids.
thinking: Regular morphine ↓ Opioids slow gut motility ↓ Constipation persists because no tolerance develops ↓ A laxative
exam_trap: A, an antacid only — opioids can cause GI upset, but antacids treat acid symptoms and do nothing for opioid-induced constipation.
takeaway: Regular opioid? Prescribe a regular laxative alongside it.

stem: Which lifestyle measure can help reduce osteoporosis risk?
why_correct: Regular weight-bearing and resistance exercise can support bone health and reduce fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Immobility promotes bone loss. B. Smoking is a risk factor for osteoporosis. C. Excessive alcohol consumption increases fracture risk. D. Adequate calcium intake is important for bone health.
pearl: Weight-bearing and resistance exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D, stopping smoking and moderating alcohol all help protect bone and reduce fracture risk.
thinking: Osteoporosis prevention ↓ Bone strengthens under mechanical load ↓ The other options all promote bone loss ↓ Weight-bearing exercise
exam_trap: D, avoiding all dietary calcium — may tempt anyone worried about kidney stones, but adequate calcium intake is needed for bone health.
takeaway: Load the bones, stop smoking, limit alcohol: osteoporosis prevention.

stem:
An older housebound patient has diffuse bone discomfort and proximal muscle weakness. Blood tests suggest vitamin D deficiency.

Which factor increases the risk?
why_correct: Limited sunlight exposure reduces cutaneous vitamin D synthesis and is a risk factor for vitamin D deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Adequate dietary intake reduces deficiency risk. B. Mobility itself is not a risk factor. C. Weight-bearing exercise supports bone health. E. Outdoor activity generally increases sunlight exposure.
pearl: Housebound people, those who cover their skin and people with darker skin are at higher risk of vitamin D deficiency; UK advice supports daily supplements for at-risk groups.
thinking: Older and housebound ↓ Bone pain with proximal weakness suggests osteomalacia ↓ Vitamin D is made in skin exposed to sunlight ↓ Limited sunlight exposure
exam_trap: B, normal mobility — tempting because mobility is mentioned in the scenario, but normal mobility is protective; the risk comes from staying indoors with little sunlight.
takeaway: Housebound means little sunlight: high risk of vitamin D deficiency.

stem:
A patient with prolonged diarrhoea develops tremor and muscle cramps. Blood tests show a low magnesium concentration.

Which electrolyte abnormality can be associated with hypomagnesaemia?
why_correct: Hypomagnesaemia commonly coexists with hypokalaemia and can make hypokalaemia difficult to correct.
why_wrong: A. Hypomagnesaemia does not characteristically cause hypercalcaemia. B. Hyperphosphataemia is not the characteristic association. C. It does not characteristically cause hypernatraemia. E. There is no characteristic isolated hyperchloraemia.
pearl: Hypokalaemia that will not correct should prompt a magnesium check; magnesium deficiency drives renal potassium loss, so both need replacing.
thinking: Prolonged diarrhoea ↓ Low magnesium with tremor and cramps ↓ Magnesium deficiency promotes renal potassium wasting ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: A, hypercalcaemia — calcium and magnesium disturbances are linked, but hypomagnesaemia is associated with hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia.
takeaway: Refractory hypokalaemia: check and replace magnesium.

stem:
A patient develops severe hyponatraemia and becomes confused and drowsy.

What is the main immediate concern?
why_correct: Severe or rapidly developing hyponatraemia can cause cerebral oedema and neurological symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency does not explain acute neurological deterioration. B. Pulmonary fibrosis is unrelated. C. Cataracts do not develop as an acute complication. D. Renal stones are not the principal acute concern.
pearl: Confusion or drowsiness in severe hyponatraemia reflects brain swelling as water moves into cells; it is an emergency needing senior input and carefully controlled hypertonic saline.
thinking: Severe hyponatraemia ↓ Low plasma osmolality draws water into brain cells ↓ Confusion and drowsiness ↓ Cerebral oedema
exam_trap: D, renal stones — an electrolyte-related complication that may come to mind, but stones are not an acute risk of hyponatraemia; brain swelling is.
takeaway: Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia means cerebral oedema risk: treat urgently.

stem:
A patient has chronic severe hyponatraemia.

Why must correction be carefully controlled?

options.A: To reduce the risk of cerebral oedema
options.B: To avoid precipitating acute heart failure
options.C: To avoid hypokalaemia from saline infusion
options.E: To prevent acute kidney injury from saline

correct_answer: D. To avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome
why_correct: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, a potentially severe neurological complication.
why_wrong: A. Cerebral oedema is the risk of rapidly correcting chronic hypernatraemia, not hyponatraemia. B. Fluid overload is a consideration but not the reason correction rate is limited. C. Hypokalaemia is not the main reason for controlled correction. E. Saline does not cause acute kidney injury in this context.
pearl: In chronic hyponatraemia the brain has adapted, so raise sodium slowly with close monitoring; overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination, which can be irreversible.
thinking: Chronic severe hyponatraemia ↓ Brain cells have adapted to low osmolality ↓ A rapid rise in sodium damages them ↓ Avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome
exam_trap: A, reduce the risk of cerebral oedema — that is the danger of low sodium itself and of fast correction of hypernatraemia; too-fast correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes demyelination.
takeaway: Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

stem:
A patient develops marked polyuria after a pituitary operation. Urine is very dilute.

Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Damage to the hypothalamic-pituitary system can reduce ADH secretion, causing central diabetes insipidus.
why_wrong: A. Excess aldosterone causes sodium retention and potassium loss. B. Excess PTH causes hypercalcaemia. C. This does not cause diabetes insipidus. E. Excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Polyuria with dilute urine after pituitary surgery suggests cranial diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency); monitor fluid balance and sodium, and treat with desmopressin.
thinking: Pituitary operation ↓ Marked polyuria ↓ Very dilute urine = water not being reabsorbed ↓ Reduced antidiuretic hormone secretion
exam_trap: A, excess aldosterone — a hormone acting on the kidney, but aldosterone excess retains sodium and causes hypokalaemia, not large volumes of dilute urine.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria after pituitary surgery = cranial diabetes insipidus.

stem: Which feature of a thyroid nodule should raise concern for malignancy?
why_correct: Hoarseness may indicate recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and is a concerning feature in a thyroid mass.
why_wrong: A. Constipation is non-specific. B. Ankle swelling has many possible causes but is not a characteristic thyroid cancer warning sign. C. Increased appetite is not a typical warning sign of thyroid malignancy. D. Fatigue is non-specific.
pearl: Red flags in a thyroid lump include hoarseness or voice change, rapid growth, stridor, a hard fixed mass and cervical lymphadenopathy; these need urgent referral.
thinking: Thyroid nodule ↓ Malignancy can invade nearby structures ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement causes voice change ↓ Hoarseness
exam_trap: D, mild fatigue — may tempt as a thyroid-related symptom, but fatigue is non-specific and not a warning sign of malignancy in a nodule.
takeaway: Thyroid lump with hoarseness: suspect malignancy and refer urgently.

stem:
A 15-year-old has never menstruated. She has normal breast development and a normal female external appearance. Examination identifies a shortened vagina.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome) causes congenital absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper vagina, presenting as primary amenorrhoea with a shortened vagina but normal ovarian function, breast development and pubic hair.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis requires functioning endometrium and causes pelvic pain and/or infertility rather than primary amenorrhoea with a short vagina. B. PMOS (formerly PCOS) may cause menstrual irregularity but does not cause congenital absence of the uterus or a shortened vagina. D. Fibroids are acquired benign uterine tumours and do not cause primary amenorrhoea in a 15-year-old. E. PID is an acquired ascending infection and does not cause primary amenorrhoea or a shortened vagina.
pearl: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breasts and external genitalia but a short vagina points to MRKH: the ovaries work normally, so puberty occurs, but the uterus and upper vagina are absent.
thinking: Never menstruated at 15 ↓ Normal breasts and external appearance, so ovarian oestrogen is present ↓ Shortened vagina suggests an absent upper genital tract ↓ Müllerian agenesis
exam_trap: B, PMOS (formerly PCOS) — the commonest cause of menstrual disturbance tempts, but it does not cause a congenitally short vagina or absent uterus.
takeaway: Normal puberty, no periods and a short vagina: think Müllerian agenesis.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has stopped having periods for 8 months. Pregnancy is excluded. FSH is repeatedly elevated.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Loss of ovarian function before the usual age of menopause can cause amenorrhoea with elevated FSH.
why_wrong: A. PMOS (formerly PCOS) typically has normal or low FSH with a raised LH:FSH ratio. B. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea causes low or normal FSH. C. Prolactinoma causes low or normal gonadotrophins. D. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from intrauterine adhesions with normal FSH.
pearl: Amenorrhoea with a persistently raised FSH before the usual age of menopause suggests premature ovarian insufficiency; hormone replacement is offered to protect bone and cardiovascular health.
thinking: 8 months without periods, pregnancy excluded ↓ FSH repeatedly high = ovaries failing, not the pituitary ↓ Age 34, well before usual menopause ↓ Premature ovarian insufficiency
exam_trap: B, functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea — common in young women, but the problem is central, so FSH is low or normal rather than raised.
takeaway: High FSH means ovarian failure; low or normal FSH points to a central cause.

stem:
A woman has profuse, offensive vaginal discharge. Examination shows a yellow-green discharge and an inflamed cervix.

Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Trichomoniasis can cause a frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge and an inflamed, sometimes “strawberry”, cervix.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes causes painful grouped vesicles or ulcers. B. Candidiasis typically causes thick, white discharge with vulval irritation. C. Genital warts are caused by HPV and produce papillomatous lesions. E. Syphilis classically causes a painless chancre in primary infection.
pearl: Trichomonas vaginalis gives a frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge, sometimes with a strawberry cervix; treat with metronidazole and ensure sexual partners are treated too.
thinking: Profuse, offensive discharge ↓ Yellow-green colour ↓ Inflamed cervix ↓ Sexually transmitted protozoan infection: trichomoniasis
exam_trap: B, vulvovaginal candidiasis — common and causes discharge, but it is typically thick, white and non-offensive with itch, not yellow-green with cervicitis.
takeaway: Offensive yellow-green discharge with an inflamed cervix means trichomoniasis.

stem:
A young woman with untreated chlamydia develops lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness.

What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Ascending chlamydial infection can cause PID, which may subsequently lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe unilateral pain and is not a complication of chlamydia. B. Appendicitis is not a complication of chlamydia and does not cause cervical motion tenderness. C. Endometriosis is not caused by chlamydial infection. E. Interstitial cystitis causes bladder pain and frequency.
pearl: Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness in a sexually active woman is PID until proven otherwise; exclude pregnancy and treat empirically early, as delay increases tubal damage.
thinking: Untreated chlamydia ↓ Infection ascends from the cervix to the upper genital tract ↓ Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness ↓ Pelvic inflammatory disease
exam_trap: A, adnexal torsion — acute pelvic pain tempts, but the stem gives untreated chlamydia and cervical motion tenderness, pointing to ascending infection.
takeaway: Untreated chlamydia plus pelvic pain and cervical excitation means PID.

stem:
A 72-year-old man develops progressive lower urinary tract symptoms and has an abnormal, hard, irregular prostate on examination.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: An irregular or hard prostate in an older man with urinary symptoms raises concern for prostate malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Hydrocele causes painless scrotal swelling. B. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain. C. Renal colic causes acute flank-to-groin pain. D. Acute prostatitis usually presents with systemic infection and a painful prostate.
pearl: A prostate that feels malignant on rectal examination warrants urgent suspected cancer referral; a normal PSA does not override a suspicious examination.
thinking: Older man with progressive urinary symptoms ↓ Prostate hard and irregular ↓ Benign enlargement is smooth; infection is tender ↓ Prostate cancer
exam_trap: D, acute prostatitis — also causes urinary symptoms, but it presents acutely with fever and a tender, boggy prostate, not a hard, irregular one.
takeaway: Smooth enlarged prostate suggests BPH; hard irregular prostate suggests cancer.

stem:
A patient has painless visible haematuria and an incidental renal mass on imaging.

Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Renal cell carcinoma can present with painless haematuria and a renal mass.
why_wrong: B. Prostate cancer arises from the prostate and does not present as a renal mass. C. Testicular cancer presents as a testicular mass. D. Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension and headache rather than haematuria. E. Neuroblastoma is a childhood tumour.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria with a renal mass should be treated as renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise; the classic triad of haematuria, flank pain and mass is seen in only a minority.
thinking: Painless visible haematuria ↓ Renal mass on imaging ↓ Commonest primary malignancy of the kidney ↓ Renal cell carcinoma
exam_trap: B, prostate adenocarcinoma — haematuria tempts a urological cancer, but it does not produce a renal mass; the kidney lesion localises the tumour.
takeaway: Haematuria plus a renal mass means renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops marked peripheral oedema.

What is the main mechanism?

options.A: Raised hydrostatic pressure from heart failure
options.E: Venous obstruction from deep vein thrombosis

correct_answer: B. Low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia
why_correct: Heavy urinary protein loss causes hypoalbuminaemia, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and promoting oedema.
why_wrong: A. Heart failure is not the mechanism of nephrotic oedema. C. Lymphatic obstruction is not the mechanism. D. Sepsis-related capillary leak is not the cause of nephrotic oedema. E. DVT causes unilateral swelling, not generalised nephrotic oedema.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome combines heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; loss of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure so fluid moves into the tissues, with renal sodium retention adding to it.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome ↓ Heavy urinary protein loss ↓ Serum albumin falls ↓ Low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia
exam_trap: A, raised hydrostatic pressure from heart failure — oedema is classically cardiac, but nothing here suggests heart failure; the driver is protein loss.
takeaway: Nephrotic oedema is driven by hypoalbuminaemia lowering oncotic pressure.

stem:
A patient develops haematuria, hypertension and reduced renal function. Urinalysis shows red-cell casts.

Which process is most likely?
why_correct: Red-cell casts strongly indicate bleeding from inflamed glomeruli and are characteristic of nephritic presentations.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration alone does not produce this urinary finding. B. Prostate enlargement does not cause red-cell casts. D. Cystitis can cause haematuria but does not produce red-cell casts. E. Renal stones may cause haematuria but not red-cell casts.
pearl: Red-cell casts form in the renal tubules and mean bleeding from inflamed glomeruli; with hypertension and falling renal function they signal a nephritic picture needing urgent renal assessment.
thinking: Haematuria, hypertension and reduced renal function ↓ Red-cell casts = blood of glomerular origin ↓ Nephritic syndrome ↓ Glomerular inflammation
exam_trap: E, renal stone obstruction — causes haematuria and can impair function, but bleeding arises below the glomerulus, so red-cell casts do not form.
takeaway: Red-cell casts mean glomerular bleeding: think glomerulonephritis.

stem:
An elderly patient develops acute kidney injury after several days of vomiting while taking an ACE inhibitor and an NSAID.

Which medication combination contributes to increased AKI risk?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs can impair renal haemodynamics, particularly during hypovolaemia, increasing the risk of AKI.
why_wrong: A. These do not form the classic AKI-risk combination. B. This is not the typical medication combination causing acute renal hypoperfusion. D. These topical/oral agents do not produce the characteristic interaction. E. These do not characteristically produce this renal haemodynamic effect.
pearl: ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs both reduce glomerular filtration; with dehydration they can precipitate AKI, so advise pausing them during vomiting or diarrhoea (sick day guidance).
thinking: Days of vomiting = hypovolaemia ↓ NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole ↓ ACE inhibitor relaxes the efferent arteriole ↓ Filtration falls: ACE inhibitor and NSAID
exam_trap: E, paracetamol and topical emollient — paracetamol is a familiar drug to worry about, but at normal doses it does not impair renal haemodynamics.
takeaway: Volume depletion plus ACE inhibitor plus NSAID is a classic recipe for AKI.

stem:
A patient with established chronic kidney disease asks about long-term complications.

Which complication is particularly important?

options.D: Increased bone density in all patients

why_correct: CKD is associated with substantially increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
why_wrong: A. CKD does not provide immunity to infection. B. Hypertension is common in CKD. C. CKD increases rather than reduces cardiovascular risk. D. CKD can cause mineral and bone disorders rather than universally increasing bone density.
pearl: Cardiovascular disease, rather than end-stage renal failure, is the leading cause of death in CKD; control blood pressure, offer statin therapy and address other risk factors.
thinking: Established CKD ↓ Hypertension, accelerated atherosclerosis and vascular calcification ↓ Most patients are more likely to die of CVD than reach dialysis ↓ Increased cardiovascular risk
exam_trap: C, reduced risk of cardiovascular disease — mirrors the correct answer to catch quick readers, but CKD raises cardiovascular risk rather than lowering it.
takeaway: CKD is a major cardiovascular risk factor; manage it as one.

stem:
A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency.

Why is prompt assessment and management important?

options.A: Pregnancy raises the risk of UTI complications
options.B: Dysuria in pregnancy usually indicates candidiasis
options.C: UTI in pregnancy is a common cause of pre-eclampsia
options.D: Pregnancy reduces the effectiveness of antibiotics
options.E: Urinary symptoms are an early sign of miscarriage

correct_answer: A. Pregnancy raises the risk of UTI complications
why_correct: UTIs in pregnancy require appropriate assessment and treatment because infection can progress and is associated with maternal and pregnancy complications.
why_wrong: B. Dysuria should not be attributed to candidiasis without assessment for UTI. C. UTI is not a common cause of pre-eclampsia. D. Pregnancy does not reduce antibiotic effectiveness. E. Urinary symptoms are not a sign of miscarriage.
pearl: Ureteric dilatation and urinary stasis in pregnancy make ascending infection and pyelonephritis more likely, so UTI in pregnancy needs a urine culture and prompt pregnancy-safe antibiotics.
thinking: Pregnant with dysuria and frequency ↓ Pregnancy causes ureteric dilatation and stasis ↓ Infection ascends more readily, with maternal and fetal consequences ↓ Pregnancy raises the risk of UTI complications
exam_trap: C, UTI as a common cause of pre-eclampsia — sounds like a plausible pregnancy complication, but pre-eclampsia is placental in origin, not caused by UTI.
takeaway: Treat UTI in pregnancy promptly; it ascends easily to pyelonephritis.

stem:
A pregnant woman has no urinary symptoms, but urine testing identifies significant bacteriuria.

Why is this clinically important?

options.B: It needs no treatment unless urinary symptoms develop
options.C: It suggests that gestational diabetes has developed
options.D: It is a likely contaminant that can be disregarded
options.E: It should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis

correct_answer: E. It should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis
why_correct: Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy reduces the risk of progression to symptomatic urinary infection and pyelonephritis.
why_wrong: A. Pre-eclampsia is characterised by hypertension and organ involvement, not bacteriuria. B. Pregnancy is an exception to the usual approach of not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. C. Bacteriuria does not diagnose diabetes. D. Significant bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated, not disregarded.
pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened for at booking and treated in pregnancy, unlike in most non-pregnant adults, because untreated it can progress to pyelonephritis.
thinking: Pregnant, no urinary symptoms ↓ Significant bacteriuria on testing ↓ Pregnancy favours ascending infection ↓ Treat to prevent pyelonephritis
exam_trap: B, no treatment unless symptoms develop — correct for most non-pregnant adults, which is why it tempts, but pregnancy is a key exception.
takeaway: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated.

stem:
An older man with known benign prostatic enlargement develops painful inability to pass urine.

What is the immediate management?
why_correct: Acute urinary retention requires prompt bladder decompression, usually with catheterisation.
why_wrong: A. Untreated retention can cause significant complications. B. Immediate prostatectomy is not the routine initial treatment. D. Fluid restriction does not relieve obstruction. E. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless infection is present.
pearl: Acute urinary retention needs prompt catheterisation; record the residual volume, look for precipitants such as constipation or drugs, and consider an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter.
thinking: Known benign prostatic enlargement ↓ Painful inability to pass urine ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Decompress the bladder: urinary catheterisation
exam_trap: E, oral antibiotics in every case — infection can precipitate retention, but antibiotics do not relieve the obstruction and are not routinely needed.
takeaway: Painful retention: catheterise first, then find the cause.

stem:
A patient with bacterial meningitis undergoes lumbar puncture.

Which CSF pattern is most typical?

options.A: High neutrophils, high protein and low glucose
options.B: Low neutrophils, low protein and high glucose
options.C: High lymphocytes, low protein and high glucose
options.D: No cells with very high glucose

correct_answer: A. High neutrophils, high protein and low glucose
why_correct: Bacterial meningitis typically produces a neutrophil-predominant CSF response, raised protein and reduced glucose.
why_wrong: B. This is not the typical bacterial pattern. C. A lymphocyte-predominant pattern is more typical of several viral and other causes. D. This is not compatible with bacterial meningitis. E. Red cells alone do not diagnose bacterial meningitis.
pearl: Bacterial meningitis gives cloudy CSF with neutrophils, high protein and low glucose relative to serum; never delay antibiotics to obtain an LP in an unwell patient.
