pearl: Myasthenic crisis is weakness severe enough to threaten breathing; monitor forced vital capacity rather than oxygen saturations, as hypoxia is a late sign, and involve critical care early.
thinking: Known myasthenia gravis ↓ Weakness worsening over several days ↓ Bulbar involvement: dysphagia and dysarthria ↓ D, respiratory failure
exam_trap: A, brainstem stroke — bulbar signs can suggest it, but gradual worsening in known myasthenia points to myasthenic crisis threatening respiration.
takeaway: Bulbar weakness in myasthenia signals impending crisis: monitor breathing with FVC.

stem:
A patient is found to have a solitary thyroid nodule on examination.

Which investigation is generally used first to assess the thyroid structure?
why_correct: Ultrasound is the key initial imaging investigation for characterising a thyroid nodule and assessing features that may require further investigation.
why_wrong: A. CT is not first-line for characterising a thyroid nodule. B. Chest X-ray does not characterise a thyroid nodule. D. An isotope uptake scan assesses function and is used mainly when TSH is suppressed, not as the first structural assessment. E. Colonoscopy examines the large bowel.
pearl: A thyroid nodule is assessed with thyroid function tests and ultrasound; ultrasound features guide whether fine-needle aspiration cytology is needed.
thinking: Solitary thyroid nodule ↓ Structure needs characterising ↓ Ultrasound defines features and guides FNA ↓ C, thyroid ultrasound
exam_trap: D, radioisotope uptake scan — a thyroid-specific test, but it assesses function and is reserved mainly for nodules with suppressed TSH, not first structural assessment.
takeaway: Thyroid nodule: ultrasound first for structure, then FNA if features warrant it.

stem:
A patient with a thyroid nodule develops a firm cervical lymph node.

Why is this finding clinically important?

options.A: It suggests reactive lymphadenitis from thyroiditis
options.B: It suggests the nodule is an autonomous toxic adenoma
options.C: It indicates a benign colloid goitre
options.D: It may indicate nodal spread of thyroid cancer
options.E: It is a typical feature of Graves disease

correct_answer: D. It may indicate nodal spread of thyroid cancer
why_correct: Cervical lymphadenopathy in a patient with a thyroid nodule can be a concerning feature for malignancy.
why_wrong: A. A firm node with a thyroid nodule should not be attributed to reactive change without excluding malignancy. B. Toxic adenomas are not associated with cervical lymphadenopathy. C. Lymphadenopathy does not establish benign disease. E. Graves disease is an autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism and does not explain a firm node with a nodule.
pearl: A thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy raises concern for malignancy, especially papillary carcinoma, which typically spreads to neck nodes; refer urgently.
thinking: Thyroid nodule ↓ Firm cervical lymph node ↓ Thyroid cancer can spread to neck nodes ↓ D, possible nodal spread of thyroid cancer
exam_trap: A, reactive lymphadenitis — reactive nodes are common, but a firm node with a thyroid nodule must be treated as possible metastasis until excluded.
takeaway: Thyroid nodule plus a firm neck node is suspicious for cancer: refer urgently.

stem:
A person with diabetes has reduced sensation in both feet.

Why is regular foot inspection important?

options.A: It eliminates the need for footwear
options.B: It improves nerve conduction in the feet
options.C: It reduces the need for glycaemic control
options.E: Injuries may go unnoticed and ulcerate

correct_answer: E. Injuries may go unnoticed and ulcerate
why_correct: Loss of protective sensation means minor trauma may go unnoticed and progress to ulceration or infection.
why_wrong: A. Appropriate footwear remains important. B. Inspection does not improve nerve function. C. Glycaemic control remains important. D. It does not reverse kidney disease.
pearl: Loss of protective sensation is a key risk for diabetic foot ulcers; daily self-inspection, suitable footwear and regular foot review help catch injuries early.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Reduced sensation in both feet ↓ Minor injuries cause no pain and go unnoticed ↓ E, injuries may go unnoticed and ulcerate
exam_trap: B, improving nerve conduction — inspection sounds therapeutic, but it does not change nerve function; it detects damage the patient cannot feel.
takeaway: Numb diabetic feet must be checked daily because injuries go unfelt.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman notices a new, painless breast lump.

What is the most appropriate next step?
why_correct: A new breast lump in an adult requires clinical assessment and appropriate breast imaging/investigation to exclude malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy is unrelated. B. A new breast lump should not simply be assumed benign. D. Cervical screening does not investigate a breast lump. E. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection.
pearl: A new breast lump in a woman of this age needs urgent referral on a suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: 48-year-old woman ↓ New painless breast lump ↓ Malignancy must be excluded ↓ C, urgent breast assessment
exam_trap: B, reassurance without examination — tempting because most breast lumps are benign, but a new lump cannot be dismissed without examination and imaging.
takeaway: New breast lump: urgent referral for triple assessment.

stem:
A woman has a breast lump with local skin tethering.

What does skin tethering suggest?
why_correct: Skin tethering can occur when a breast malignancy involves or pulls on supporting tissues and is therefore a concerning clinical feature.
why_wrong: A. Skin tethering is not a feature of normal breast nodularity. B. Mastitis usually presents with inflammatory features rather than tethering. C. Fibroadenomas are mobile and well circumscribed and do not tether the skin. D. Simple cysts are smooth and do not tether the skin.
pearl: Skin tethering, dimpling or peau d'orange over a breast lump suggests malignancy infiltrating the supporting ligaments or skin and needs urgent assessment.
thinking: Breast lump ↓ Skin tethered over it ↓ Tumour pulling on supporting tissues or skin ↓ E, possible underlying breast malignancy
exam_trap: C, mobile fibroadenoma — the classic benign breast lump, but fibroadenomas are mobile and well circumscribed and do not tether the skin.
takeaway: A breast lump that tethers the skin is suspicious for cancer.

stem:
A woman has spontaneous unilateral bloody nipple discharge from a single duct.

What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.A: It is usually duct ectasia; reassure and discharge
options.B: It suggests a prolactinoma; check serum prolactin
options.C: It needs assessment for an underlying lesion
options.D: It suggests periductal mastitis needing antibiotics
options.E: It is typical of hormonal changes

correct_answer: C. It needs assessment for an underlying lesion
why_correct: Spontaneous unilateral bloody or serous discharge, particularly from a single duct, is a concerning breast symptom requiring assessment.
why_wrong: A. Spontaneous single-duct bloody discharge should not be attributed to duct ectasia without assessment. B. Prolactinoma causes bilateral milky galactorrhoea, not unilateral bloody discharge. D. Periductal mastitis usually causes pain and inflammatory changes. E. Bloody single-duct discharge is not a hormonal finding and does not exclude malignancy.
pearl: Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct or bloodstained nipple discharge needs breast assessment; intraductal papilloma is a common cause, but carcinoma must be excluded.
thinking: Spontaneous nipple discharge ↓ Unilateral, single duct, bloody ↓ Suggests an intraductal lesion ↓ C, assess for an underlying lesion
exam_trap: A, duct ectasia — a common benign cause of nipple discharge, but spontaneous single-duct bloody discharge cannot be dismissed without assessment.
takeaway: Bloody single-duct nipple discharge needs assessment for an underlying lesion.

stem:
A woman develops a persistent eczematous, crusted lesion involving the nipple and areola.

Which condition should be considered?
correct_answer: A. Paget disease of the breast
why_correct: Persistent unilateral eczematous changes involving the nipple should raise concern for Paget disease, which is associated with underlying breast carcinoma.
why_wrong: B. Bruising does not produce this characteristic persistent lesion. C. Periductal mastitis causes periareolar inflammation or abscess rather than a persistent eczematous nipple lesion. D. Intraductal papilloma typically causes nipple discharge without eczematous skin change. E. Mondor disease causes a tender cord-like superficial vein rather than a nipple lesion.
pearl: Paget disease of the nipple begins on the nipple and spreads to the areola, whereas eczema usually starts on the areola; it signals underlying breast carcinoma.
thinking: Persistent nipple and areola lesion ↓ Eczematous and crusted ↓ Not resolving ↓ A, Paget disease of the breast
exam_trap: C, periductal mastitis — affects the periareolar area, but it causes inflammation or abscess, not a persistent eczematous crusted nipple lesion.
takeaway: Persistent eczema-like change of the nipple: think Paget disease and refer.

stem:
A woman with suspected ovarian malignancy develops increasing abdominal distension and ascites.

What is a possible mechanism?
why_correct: Ovarian cancer can spread within the peritoneal cavity and produce malignant ascites.
why_wrong: A. Corneal infection is unrelated. C. Bone formation does not explain ascites. D. Thyroid disease is not the usual explanation in this clinical context. E. Middle-ear infection does not cause malignant ascites.
pearl: Ovarian cancer often presents late with bloating and distension from peritoneal spread and malignant ascites; persistent bloating in a woman warrants assessment including CA125.
thinking: Suspected ovarian malignancy ↓ Increasing distension with ascites ↓ Peritoneal seeding produces fluid ↓ B, peritoneal involvement by malignancy
exam_trap: D, thyroid hormone deficiency — severe hypothyroidism can rarely cause effusions, but with suspected ovarian cancer, ascites reflects peritoneal spread.
takeaway: Ascites in ovarian cancer reflects peritoneal spread.

stem: Which factor increases the risk of endometrial cancer?
why_correct: Obesity is associated with increased endometrial cancer risk, partly through increased peripheral oestrogen production.
why_wrong: A. Lower lifetime oestrogen exposure does not increase risk in the same way. B. Combined hormonal contraception is associated with reduced endometrial cancer risk. C. Early menopause generally reduces lifetime oestrogen exposure. D. Lack of oestrogen exposure is not the characteristic risk factor.
pearl: Endometrial cancer risk rises with unopposed oestrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, tamoxifen and oestrogen-only HRT; the combined pill is protective.
thinking: Endometrial cancer is oestrogen-driven ↓ Adipose tissue converts androgens to oestrogen ↓ Unopposed oestrogen stimulates the endometrium ↓ E, obesity
exam_trap: B, long-term combined pill — sounds like hormone exposure, but its progestogen protects the endometrium, so it reduces endometrial cancer risk.
takeaway: Unopposed oestrogen, especially from obesity, raises endometrial cancer risk.

stem: What is the main purpose of HPV vaccination?

options.A: To prevent HPV-related cancers and genital warts
options.B: To prevent genital herpes and other sexual infections
options.D: To clear existing cervical HPV infection
options.E: To replace the need for cervical screening

correct_answer: A. To prevent HPV-related cancers and genital warts
why_correct: HPV vaccination protects against important HPV types responsible for cervical and several other HPV-related diseases.
why_wrong: B. Genital herpes is caused by herpes simplex virus, and HPV vaccine does not protect against other STIs. C. The vaccine is preventive and does not treat existing warts. D. Vaccination does not clear established HPV infection. E. Vaccinated people should still attend cervical screening.
pearl: HPV vaccination is preventive: it protects against high-risk types causing cervical, anal and other cancers and against wart-causing types; it does not treat established infection.
thinking: HPV causes cancers and genital warts ↓ Vaccine induces immunity before exposure ↓ Prevents rather than treats infection ↓ A, prevent HPV-related cancers and warts
exam_trap: E, replacing cervical screening — tempting because the vaccine prevents most cervical cancers, but it does not cover every high-risk type, so screening continues.
takeaway: HPV vaccine prevents disease; vaccinated people still need cervical screening.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman has a persistent vulval ulcer that has not healed.

What should be considered?
why_correct: A persistent unexplained vulval ulcer or lesion in an older woman requires assessment to exclude malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Cystitis does not usually cause a persistent vulval ulcer. C. Persistent ulceration is not a normal feature of ageing. D. Appendicitis is unrelated. E. Otitis media is unrelated.
pearl: A persistent vulval ulcer or lump in an older woman needs referral to exclude vulval cancer; lichen sclerosus is an important predisposing condition.
thinking: 72-year-old woman ↓ Persistent vulval ulcer that has not healed ↓ Malignancy must be excluded ↓ A, vulval malignancy
exam_trap: C, normal ageing — atrophic change is common after menopause, but a non-healing ulcer is never normal and must be assessed for malignancy.
takeaway: A non-healing vulval ulcer in an older woman needs assessment for cancer.

stem:
A man with long-standing diabetes develops persistent erectile dysfunction.

Which mechanism can contribute?

options.C: Low testosterone caused by long-term metformin

correct_answer: B. Diabetic vascular disease and neuropathy
why_correct: Diabetes can cause endothelial/vascular dysfunction and neuropathy, both of which can contribute to erectile dysfunction.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes does not cause hyperprolactinaemia. C. Metformin is not a recognised cause of low testosterone and erectile dysfunction. D. Peyronie disease causes penile curvature and is not the typical diabetic mechanism. E. Thyrotoxicosis is not the usual explanation in a patient with long-standing diabetes.
pearl: Diabetes causes erectile dysfunction through endothelial and vascular disease plus autonomic neuropathy; erectile dysfunction can be an early marker of cardiovascular disease.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ Persistent erectile dysfunction ↓ Endothelial damage plus autonomic neuropathy ↓ B, diabetic vascular disease and neuropathy
exam_trap: C, low testosterone from metformin — testosterone deficiency can cause erectile dysfunction, but metformin is not a recognised cause; the mechanism is vascular and neuropathic.
takeaway: Erectile dysfunction in diabetes is vascular and neuropathic.

stem:
A woman has very irregular menstrual cycles and is having difficulty conceiving.

What mechanism may contribute to infertility?
why_correct: Irregular or absent ovulation can reduce the opportunity for conception and is an important cause of female infertility.
why_wrong: A. Middle-ear dysfunction is unrelated. B. Corneal disease is unrelated. C. Bone formation is unrelated. D. Red blood cell production does not directly explain infertility.
pearl: Irregular cycles suggest anovulation, a common cause of female subfertility; polycystic ovary syndrome is the most frequent underlying cause.
thinking: Very irregular menstrual cycles ↓ Difficulty conceiving ↓ Ovulation irregular or absent ↓ E, irregular or absent ovulation
exam_trap: D, increased red-cell production — a physiological-sounding distractor with no role in conception; very irregular cycles point to anovulation as the cause of subfertility.
takeaway: Irregular cycles with difficulty conceiving point to anovulation.

stem:
A postmenopausal woman has vaginal dryness and discomfort during intercourse.

What is a common cause?
why_correct: Reduced oestrogen after menopause can cause vaginal and vulvovaginal dryness, irritation and discomfort during intercourse.
why_wrong: B. Candidiasis is less common after menopause and causes itching and discharge rather than dryness. C. Bacterial vaginosis causes a fishy-smelling discharge rather than dryness. D. Pelvic inflammatory disease causes pelvic pain and discharge, mainly in younger women. E. Cervical ectropion causes discharge or contact bleeding, not vaginal dryness.
pearl: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes vaginal dryness, dyspareunia and urinary symptoms; lubricants, moisturisers and topical vaginal oestrogen are effective.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman ↓ Vaginal dryness and painful intercourse ↓ Oestrogen loss thins the vaginal epithelium ↓ A, genitourinary syndrome of menopause
exam_trap: B, recurrent candidiasis — a common vaginal complaint, but it is less frequent after menopause and causes itch and discharge rather than dryness.
takeaway: Postmenopausal vaginal dryness and dyspareunia: genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

stem: Why does loss of oestrogen after menopause increase fracture risk?

options.B: It causes all fractures through trauma alone

why_correct: Reduced oestrogen increases bone turnover and contributes to loss of bone mineral density.
why_wrong: A. Menopause does not cause osteomyelitis. B. Reduced bone density can increase fracture risk even after relatively minor trauma. C. Oestrogen loss does not increase bone formation. D. Calcium absorption is not completely prevented.
pearl: Oestrogen restrains bone resorption; after menopause, resorption outpaces formation, causing osteoporosis and fragility fractures from minimal trauma.
thinking: Menopause ↓ Oestrogen loss increases bone turnover and resorption ↓ Bone mineral density falls ↓ E, accelerated bone loss
exam_trap: D, preventing calcium absorption completely — calcium handling matters for bone, but absorption is not abolished; the key change is accelerated bone loss.
takeaway: Postmenopausal oestrogen loss accelerates bone loss and fragility fractures.

stem: A woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. Which benign condition can cause this symptom?
why_correct: Atrophic changes after menopause are a common benign cause of postmenopausal bleeding, although malignancy must be excluded.
why_wrong: A. Endometrial cancer is a malignant, not benign, cause of postmenopausal bleeding. B. Cervical cancer is a malignant, not benign, cause. C. Ovulation does not normally occur after menopause. E. Menstruation has ceased after menopause, so bleeding should not be attributed to it.
pearl: Atrophy is a common benign cause of postmenopausal bleeding, but every postmenopausal bleed needs referral to exclude endometrial cancer before atrophy is accepted.
thinking: Postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Question asks for a benign cause ↓ Oestrogen loss thins vaginal and endometrial tissue ↓ D, vaginal or endometrial atrophy
exam_trap: A, endometrial adenocarcinoma — the must-exclude cause of postmenopausal bleeding, but it is malignant, and the question asks for a benign cause.
takeaway: Atrophy is a common benign cause of postmenopausal bleeding, but cancer must be excluded.

stem: What is the main purpose of population breast screening?

options.B: To detect breast cancer at an earlier stage
options.C: To replace assessment of symptomatic breast lumps
options.D: To diagnose every benign breast lump

correct_answer: B. To detect breast cancer at an earlier stage
why_correct: Screening aims to identify breast cancer before it presents symptomatically, allowing earlier diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Screening does not prevent all breast cancer. C. A symptomatic breast lump still requires appropriate clinical assessment. D. Screening is not designed to diagnose every benign lump. E. Breast screening does not diagnose ovarian cancer.
pearl: Breast screening by mammography aims to detect cancer earlier, before symptoms; a woman with a symptomatic lump needs referral regardless of recent screening.
thinking: Population screening of people without symptoms ↓ Mammography finds cancers before they present ↓ Earlier stage allows better outcomes ↓ B, detect cancer earlier
exam_trap: A, preventing all breast cancer — screening sounds preventive, but it detects existing cancers earlier rather than stopping them developing.
takeaway: Screening detects breast cancer earlier; it does not prevent it.

stem:
A patient with breast cancer develops enlarged axillary lymph nodes.

What does this finding potentially represent?

options.A: A normal finding in all breast cancers

why_correct: Breast cancer commonly drains to axillary lymph nodes, which can therefore contain regional metastatic disease.
why_wrong: A. Not every patient with breast cancer has involved nodes. B. Axillary nodes represent regional rather than automatically distant disease. C. Thyroid disease is not the usual explanation in this context. D. Renal failure does not explain regional axillary lymphadenopathy.
pearl: The axilla is the main lymphatic drainage of the breast; axillary nodal status is one of the most important prognostic factors and guides treatment.
thinking: Breast cancer ↓ Breast lymph drains mainly to the axilla ↓ Enlarged axillary nodes ↓ E, regional lymphatic spread
exam_trap: B, definite distant metastasis — node involvement does mean spread, but axillary nodes represent regional disease, not distant metastasis.
takeaway: Axillary nodes in breast cancer represent regional, not distant, spread.

stem:
A 70-year-old patient develops persistent rectal bleeding with no obvious benign explanation.

What important diagnosis should be excluded?
why_correct: Persistent rectal bleeding, especially in an older adult, requires assessment for colorectal cancer as well as other causes.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids are a benign cause, and the stem states there is no obvious benign explanation. B. Anal fissure is a benign cause usually associated with painful defaecation. C. Solitary rectal ulcer is benign and uncommon, and is not the key diagnosis to exclude. E. Proctalgia fugax causes fleeting rectal pain without bleeding.
pearl: Persistent unexplained rectal bleeding in an older adult needs investigation for colorectal cancer; do not attribute it to haemorrhoids without proper assessment.
thinking: 70-year-old ↓ Persistent rectal bleeding ↓ No obvious benign explanation ↓ D, exclude colorectal cancer
exam_trap: A, internal haemorrhoids — the commonest cause of rectal bleeding, but the stem excludes an obvious benign cause, and age makes cancer the must-exclude diagnosis.
takeaway: Persistent rectal bleeding in an older adult: exclude colorectal cancer.

stem:
A patient with colorectal cancer develops multiple lesions in the liver.

What route commonly allows colorectal cancer to reach the liver?
why_correct: Venous drainage from much of the large bowel enters the portal circulation, making the liver a common site of metastatic spread.
why_wrong: A. Cerebrospinal fluid seeding is not the usual route. B. Lymphatic spread goes to regional nodes and does not explain the usual route to the liver. C. Coronary arteries do not provide the usual route. E. The auditory canal has no relevant route.
pearl: Colorectal cancer spreads to the liver via the portal venous system, making the liver the commonest site of distant metastasis.
thinking: Colorectal cancer ↓ Bowel venous blood drains into the portal vein ↓ The liver is the first capillary bed reached ↓ D, portal venous circulation
exam_trap: B, lymphatics via the thoracic duct — colorectal cancer does spread lymphatically, but to regional nodes; liver metastases arise via portal venous blood.
takeaway: Colorectal cancer reaches the liver through the portal vein.

stem:
A patient with colorectal cancer develops abdominal distension, vomiting and inability to pass stool or flatus.

What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Distension with vomiting and failure to pass stool or flatus is characteristic of intestinal obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Paralytic ileus is not the expected complication of an obstructing colorectal tumour. B. Perforation causes peritonism rather than this obstructive picture. D. Gastroenteritis causes diarrhoea rather than failure to pass stool or flatus. E. Opioid constipation does not usually cause absolute constipation with vomiting and distension.
pearl: Colorectal cancer, especially left-sided, is a common cause of large bowel obstruction in adults; a competent ileocaecal valve can create a dangerous closed loop.
thinking: Colorectal cancer ↓ Distension and vomiting ↓ Unable to pass stool or flatus ↓ C, large bowel obstruction
exam_trap: A, paralytic ileus — also causes distension and failure to pass flatus, but follows surgery or metabolic upset; an obstructing tumour causes mechanical obstruction.
takeaway: Colorectal cancer with distension and absolute constipation: large bowel obstruction.

stem: Which infection is associated with an increased risk of anal cancer?
why_correct: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types is associated with anal cancer.
why_wrong: A. Rhinovirus commonly causes the common cold. B. HSV type 2 causes genital herpes but is not an established cause of anal cancer. D. Hepatitis A primarily affects the liver. E. Influenza is a respiratory infection.
pearl: Persistent high-risk HPV infection, mainly types 16 and 18, causes most anal cancers, as well as cervical, vulval, penile and oropharyngeal cancers.
thinking: Anal cancer ↓ Squamous epithelium of the anal canal ↓ Persistent high-risk HPV drives dysplasia ↓ C, human papillomavirus
exam_trap: B, HSV type 2 — a sexually transmitted genital virus, but it causes recurrent ulcers, not anal cancer; high-risk HPV is the oncogenic virus.
takeaway: Persistent high-risk HPV infection causes most anal cancers.

stem:
A patient with peptic ulcer disease vomits fresh blood.

What complication has occurred?
why_correct: Haematemesis indicates bleeding from the upper gastrointestinal tract.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is a skin infection. B. UTI does not cause haematemesis. D. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain. E. Glaucoma affects the eye.
pearl: Haematemesis means bleeding from the upper GI tract; peptic ulcer is the commonest cause, and the Glasgow-Blatchford score helps risk-stratify these patients.
thinking: Peptic ulcer disease ↓ Vomiting fresh blood ↓ Bleeding source in the upper GI tract ↓ C, upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: B, lower urinary tract infection — a distractor with no link to vomited blood; with a known ulcer and haematemesis, the ulcer has bled into the upper GI tract.
takeaway: Haematemesis in peptic ulcer disease is upper GI bleeding: resuscitate and risk-stratify.

stem:
A patient with presumed IBS develops unexplained weight loss.

Why is this important?

options.A: It is an expected feature of long-standing IBS
options.B: It is a red flag that warrants reconsidering the diagnosis
options.C: It confirms coeliac disease as the underlying cause of symptoms
options.D: It reflects dietary restriction and supports the IBS diagnosis
options.E: It indicates acute appendicitis needing urgent surgical review

correct_answer: B. It is a red flag that warrants reconsidering the diagnosis
why_correct: Unexplained weight loss should prompt consideration of an alternative or additional diagnosis rather than simply attributing symptoms to IBS.
why_wrong: A. Significant unexplained weight loss is not a feature of IBS, however long-standing. C. Weight loss is non-specific and does not establish coeliac disease; serology and biopsy are needed. D. Weight loss should not be attributed to dietary restriction without excluding other causes, and it does not support IBS. E. Weight loss is not a feature of appendicitis, which presents acutely with abdominal pain.
pearl: IBS should be diagnosed only without red flags; unexplained weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia or onset in later life require investigation for other causes.
thinking: Presumed IBS ↓ New unexplained weight loss ↓ Not a feature of IBS ↓ B, red flag that warrants reconsidering the diagnosis
exam_trap: D, dietary restriction supports IBS — people with IBS do restrict foods, but weight loss should never be attributed to diet before excluding organic disease.
takeaway: Unexplained weight loss is a red flag that does not fit IBS.

stem:
A patient develops fatigue, nausea, dark urine and jaundice.

Which system is primarily affected in acute viral hepatitis?
why_correct: Viral hepatitis causes inflammation of the liver and can produce jaundice, dark urine and systemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid disease does not cause the typical hepatitis presentation. B. Retinal disease causes visual symptoms. C. Joint disease does not explain jaundice. D. Middle-ear disease causes auditory symptoms.
pearl: Acute viral hepatitis causes jaundice with dark urine, often after a prodrome of fatigue and nausea; check liver function, clotting and viral hepatitis serology.
thinking: Fatigue and nausea ↓ Dark urine and jaundice ↓ Hepatocellular inflammation impairs bilirubin handling ↓ E, liver
exam_trap: A, thyroid gland — thyroid disease can cause fatigue, but not jaundice or dark urine; this combination points to the liver.
takeaway: Jaundice with dark urine and malaise: think liver, including viral hepatitis.

stem: Which factor substantially increases the risk of abdominal aortic aneurysm?
why_correct: Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
why_wrong: A. Regular exercise is not a major AAA risk factor. C. Seasonal allergies are unrelated. D. Hypertension is a recognised risk factor; low blood pressure is not. E. Risk increases with age rather than young age.
pearl: Smoking is the strongest modifiable AAA risk factor; others include male sex, older age, hypertension and family history. The NHS offers men a one-off screening ultrasound at 65.
thinking: Abdominal aortic aneurysm ↓ Smoking damages the aortic wall ↓ Strongest modifiable risk factor ↓ B, smoking
exam_trap: D, low blood pressure alone — blood pressure is relevant, but hypertension, not low blood pressure, is the recognised AAA risk factor.
takeaway: Smoking is the key modifiable risk factor for AAA.

stem:
A patient with long-standing Raynaud phenomenon develops tight, shiny skin over the fingers and recurrent digital ulcers.

What should be considered?
correct_answer: D. An underlying connective tissue disease
why_correct: Severe or complicated Raynaud phenomenon, particularly with digital ulcers and skin changes, can occur secondary to connective tissue disease.
why_wrong: A. Otitis media affects the middle ear. B. Dehydration does not cause sclerodactyly or digital ulcers. C. IBS does not cause digital ulcers or sclerodermatous skin changes, and malabsorption is not a feature of IBS. E. Cataract affects the eye.
pearl: Raynaud phenomenon with digital ulcers or sclerodactyly suggests secondary Raynaud, classically systemic sclerosis; check autoantibodies and consider rheumatology referral.
thinking: Long-standing Raynaud phenomenon ↓ Tight, shiny finger skin (sclerodactyly) ↓ Recurrent digital ulcers ↓ D, underlying connective tissue disease
exam_trap: B, dehydration causing skin atrophy — tight skin may suggest a simple skin problem, but dehydration does not cause sclerodactyly or digital ulcers.
takeaway: Raynaud with sclerodactyly or digital ulcers: think systemic sclerosis.

stem: Why is a scaphoid fracture clinically important even when the initial X-ray appears normal?
why_correct: The scaphoid has a vulnerable blood supply, so fractures can result in avascular necrosis, particularly of the proximal fragment.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated. C. Pneumonia is unrelated. D. Cataract is unrelated. E. Appendicitis is unrelated.
pearl: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, so fractures risk proximal pole avascular necrosis; with suspected fracture and a normal X-ray, immobilise and arrange further imaging.
thinking: Suspected scaphoid fracture ↓ Initial X-ray may be normal ↓ Retrograde blood supply to the proximal pole ↓ B, risk of avascular necrosis
exam_trap: A, hyperthyroidism — like the other distractors, unrelated; the danger of a missed scaphoid fracture is avascular necrosis and non-union.
takeaway: Suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal X-ray: immobilise and image further.

stem: A patient falls onto an outstretched hand and develops pain over the lateral elbow, particularly with forearm rotation. What fracture is most likely?
why_correct: Radial head fractures commonly follow a fall onto an outstretched hand and cause lateral elbow pain, especially with pronation and supination.
why_wrong: B. Clavicle fracture causes shoulder pain. C. Olecranon fracture causes posterior elbow pain. D. Scaphoid fracture causes wrist/snuffbox tenderness. E. Humeral shaft fracture causes upper-arm pain.
pearl: Radial head fractures follow a fall onto an outstretched hand and cause lateral elbow pain worse on rotation; X-ray may show only a joint effusion (fat pad sign).
thinking: Fall onto an outstretched hand ↓ Lateral elbow pain ↓ Worse with forearm rotation ↓ A, radial head fracture
exam_trap: D, scaphoid fracture — the classic outstretched-hand injury, but it causes wrist and snuffbox tenderness, not lateral elbow pain on rotation.
takeaway: Outstretched-hand fall with lateral elbow pain on rotation: radial head fracture.

stem: A man falls directly onto his elbow and develops posterior elbow pain and difficulty extending the elbow. What injury is most likely?
why_correct: A direct blow to the elbow can fracture the olecranon and impair elbow extension.
why_wrong: B. Colles fracture affects the distal radius. C. Clavicle injury affects the shoulder. D. Radial head injury causes lateral elbow pain and pain with rotation. E. Scaphoid injury causes wrist pain.
pearl: Olecranon fractures usually follow a direct fall onto the elbow; triceps pull displaces the fragment, so weak or absent active extension suggests a displaced fracture.
thinking: Direct fall onto the elbow ↓ Posterior elbow pain ↓ Difficulty extending; triceps mechanism disrupted ↓ A, olecranon fracture
exam_trap: D, radial head fracture — another elbow fracture after a fall, but it causes lateral pain worse on rotation and typically follows an outstretched-hand fall.
takeaway: Direct blow to the elbow with impaired extension: olecranon fracture.

stem: A 24-year-old man sustains a shoulder injury playing rugby. His arm is held slightly abducted and externally rotated, with a prominent squared-off shoulder contour. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An anterior shoulder dislocation classically presents with the arm abducted and externally rotated and loss of the normal rounded shoulder contour.
why_wrong: A. Frozen shoulder causes restricted movement without acute deformity. B. Clavicle fracture causes focal clavicular tenderness. C. Posterior dislocation typically presents with the arm held adducted and internally rotated. D. Rotator cuff tear causes weakness and pain rather than this deformity.
pearl: Anterior dislocation is the commonest shoulder dislocation; check axillary nerve function (regimental badge sensation) before and after reduction.
thinking: Young man, rugby injury ↓ Arm abducted and externally rotated ↓ Squared-off shoulder contour ↓ E, anterior shoulder dislocation
exam_trap: C, posterior dislocation — another acute dislocation, but the arm is held adducted and internally rotated, classically after a seizure or electric shock.
takeaway: Abducted, externally rotated arm with a squared shoulder: anterior dislocation.

stem: A patient has a painful shoulder following a seizure. The arm is held adducted and internally rotated. What injury should be suspected?
why_correct: Posterior shoulder dislocation is classically associated with seizures and electrical injury and presents with internal rotation and adduction.
why_wrong: A. Anterior dislocation usually causes abduction and external rotation. B. Olecranon fracture affects the elbow. C. Scaphoid fracture affects the wrist. E. Clavicle fracture produces clavicular tenderness.
pearl: Posterior shoulder dislocation classically follows seizures or electric shock and is easily missed on an AP X-ray (light-bulb sign), so obtain an axillary or lateral view.
thinking: Shoulder pain after a seizure ↓ Arm held adducted and internally rotated ↓ Violent muscle contraction drives the head posteriorly ↓ D, posterior shoulder dislocation
exam_trap: A, anterior dislocation — far commoner overall, but it holds the arm abducted and externally rotated; seizures classically cause posterior dislocation.
takeaway: Shoulder pain after a seizure with internal rotation: posterior dislocation.

stem: A patient has shoulder pain that is particularly troublesome when raising the arm overhead. There is a painful arc of movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain during elevation of the arm, particularly through the mid-range, is characteristic of subacromial impingement.
why_wrong: A. Olecranon bursitis causes swelling over the elbow. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms. D. Scaphoid fracture causes wrist pain. E. Dupuytren disease causes fixed flexion deformities of the fingers.
pearl: Subacromial impingement causes a painful arc on abduction, typically mid-range; management includes analgesia, physiotherapy and sometimes a subacromial steroid injection.
thinking: Shoulder pain worse with overhead activity ↓ Painful arc of movement ↓ Rotator cuff compressed under the acromion ↓ C, subacromial impingement
exam_trap: A, olecranon bursitis — another upper-limb overuse condition, but it causes swelling at the elbow, not shoulder pain on elevation.
takeaway: A painful arc on shoulder abduction suggests subacromial impingement.

stem: A patient develops pain over the medial elbow associated with repetitive wrist flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Medial epicondylitis, or golfer's elbow, affects the common flexor tendon origin at the medial epicondyle.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve at the wrist. B. Lateral epicondylitis affects the lateral epicondyle and extensor tendons. C. Scaphoid fracture causes wrist pain. D. Olecranon fracture is an acute bony injury.
pearl: Golfer's elbow is medial epicondyle pain at the flexor origin, worse on resisted wrist flexion; tennis elbow is lateral, worse on resisted wrist extension.
thinking: Medial elbow pain ↓ Repetitive wrist flexion ↓ Common flexor origin overloaded ↓ E, medial epicondylitis
exam_trap: B, lateral epicondylitis — the commoner elbow tendinopathy, but it causes lateral pain linked to wrist extension; medial pain with flexion is golfer's elbow.
takeaway: Medial is golfer's elbow (flexors); lateral is tennis elbow (extensors).

stem: A man develops a soft, fluctuant swelling directly over the tip of his elbow after repeatedly leaning on his desk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Repetitive pressure over the olecranon can cause inflammation and swelling of the olecranon bursa.
why_wrong: A. Radial head fracture causes acute lateral elbow pain after trauma. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the wrist/hand. D. Dupuytren disease affects the palmar fascia. E. Tennis elbow causes lateral elbow pain without a fluctuant swelling.
pearl: Olecranon bursitis often follows repeated pressure on the elbow; if the bursa is hot, red and tender, consider septic bursitis and aspirate for culture.
thinking: Repeatedly leaning on the elbow ↓ Soft, fluctuant swelling ↓ Directly over the olecranon tip ↓ B, olecranon bursitis
exam_trap: E, tennis elbow — a common work-related elbow problem, but it causes lateral pain on wrist extension without a fluctuant swelling.
takeaway: Fluctuant swelling over the elbow tip after repeated pressure: olecranon bursitis.

stem: A patient sustains a finger injury and subsequently develops inability to actively extend the proximal interphalangeal joint. What deformity is characteristic?
why_correct: Boutonnière deformity results from disruption of the central slip of the extensor mechanism, producing PIP flexion.
why_wrong: A. Swan-neck deformity involves PIP hyperextension and DIP flexion. B. Dupuytren contracture produces palmar fascial contractures. D. Trigger finger causes catching or locking. E. Mallet finger involves inability to extend the DIP joint.
pearl: A boutonnière deformity may take days to appear after a PIP joint injury; splint the PIP joint in extension early, because a missed central slip rupture leads to a fixed deformity.
thinking: Finger injury ↓ Cannot actively extend the PIP joint ↓ Central slip of the extensor mechanism disrupted ↓ PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension ↓ Boutonnière deformity
exam_trap: E, mallet finger — also an extensor tendon injury after trauma, but it affects the DIP joint through the terminal tendon, not the PIP joint.
takeaway: Central slip injury = PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension = boutonnière.

stem: Which deformity is characterised by hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal joint and flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint?
why_correct: Swan-neck deformity consists of PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion.
why_wrong: A. Boutonnière deformity causes PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension. C. Trigger finger causes catching or locking. D. Mallet finger causes DIP flexion from extensor tendon injury. E. Dupuytren disease produces fixed flexion contractures.
pearl: Swan-neck deformity is classically seen in rheumatoid arthritis and can also follow an untreated mallet finger; it is the mirror image of boutonnière deformity.
thinking: PIP joint hyperextended ↓ DIP joint flexed ↓ Imbalance of extensor and volar plate forces at the PIP ↓ Swan-neck deformity
exam_trap: A, boutonnière deformity — the classic paired finger deformity, but it is the reverse: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension.
takeaway: Swan neck: PIP up, DIP down; boutonnière: PIP down, DIP up.

stem: An overweight pregnant woman develops burning and numbness over the outer aspect of her thigh without weakness. Which nerve is most likely involved?
why_correct: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing sensory symptoms over the lateral thigh without motor deficit.
why_wrong: B. The genitofemoral nerve supplies skin over the genital region and upper anterior thigh, not the lateral thigh. C. Femoral nerve lesions can cause quadriceps weakness. D. Common peroneal nerve dysfunction affects the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, with foot drop. E. Sciatic nerve problems produce broader lower-limb symptoms.
pearl: Meralgia paraesthetica is a purely sensory syndrome from compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the anterior superior iliac spine; obesity, pregnancy and tight belts are classic triggers.
thinking: Burning and numbness over the lateral thigh ↓ No weakness, so a purely sensory nerve ↓ Weight gain and pregnancy compress it at the groin ↓ Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
exam_trap: C, femoral nerve — also supplies the thigh, but it serves the anterior thigh and its lesions cause quadriceps weakness; this patient has lateral sensory symptoms only.
takeaway: Lateral thigh sensory symptoms with no weakness: think lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

stem: A patient with longstanding carpal tunnel syndrome develops weakness of thumb opposition. Which muscle group is primarily affected?
why_correct: The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles responsible for thumb opposition.
why_wrong: B. Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve. C. Deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve. D. Hypothenar muscles are supplied mainly by the ulnar nerve. E. Interossei are mainly supplied by the ulnar nerve.
pearl: In carpal tunnel syndrome, thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction and opposition indicate motor involvement of the median nerve and favour referral for surgical decompression.
thinking: Longstanding carpal tunnel syndrome ↓ Median nerve compressed at the wrist ↓ Recurrent motor branch supplies the thenar muscles ↓ Weak opposition ↓ Thenar muscles
exam_trap: D, hypothenar muscles — another intrinsic hand group, but supplied mainly by the ulnar nerve, which does not pass through the carpal tunnel.
takeaway: Median nerve at the wrist = thenar muscles; ulnar nerve = hypothenar and interossei.

stem: A 74-year-old woman sustains a vertebral fracture after lifting a light shopping bag. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.E: Septic arthritis of a facet joint

why_correct: A fracture occurring after minimal trauma in an older adult is characteristic of a fragility fracture and should prompt assessment for osteoporosis.
why_wrong: B. Lifting a light bag is minimal trauma, not a high-energy mechanism. C. Muscle strain does not cause a vertebral fracture. D. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. E. Facet joint septic arthritis is an infective process with fever and does not explain a fracture after minimal trauma.
pearl: A fracture from minimal trauma, such as lifting a light object or a fall from standing height, is a fragility fracture and should trigger osteoporosis assessment and fracture-prevention treatment.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Vertebral fracture after lifting a light bag ↓ Minimal force caused a fracture ↓ Bone is weak ↓ Osteoporotic fragility fracture
exam_trap: B, high-energy traumatic spinal fracture — the word fracture suggests major trauma, but lifting a light bag is minimal force, which is exactly what defines a fragility fracture.
takeaway: Fracture from minimal trauma in an older adult = fragility fracture until proven otherwise.

stem: Which finding in an adult with an acute asthma attack indicates life-threatening disease?

options.B: Ability to speak in full sentences

why_correct: A silent chest may indicate critically reduced airflow and impending respiratory failure.
why_wrong: A. Mild wheeze alone does not indicate life-threatening asthma. B. Speaking in full sentences suggests less severe respiratory compromise. D. Mild cough is nonspecific. E. A normal respiratory rate is not a marker of severe airflow obstruction.
pearl: A silent chest means so little air is moving that wheeze disappears; with exhaustion, cyanosis or confusion it signals life-threatening asthma needing senior and critical care input.
thinking: Acute asthma attack ↓ Wheeze needs airflow to be heard ↓ No breath sounds = minimal airflow ↓ Impending respiratory failure ↓ Silent chest
exam_trap: E, normal respiratory rate — can look reassuring, but a tiring patient may slow down; life-threatening asthma is recognised by a silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort and exhaustion.
takeaway: In acute asthma a quiet chest is ominous, not reassuring.

stem: A patient with asthma has a peak expiratory flow of 35% of their personal best during an acute attack. What does this indicate?
why_correct: A markedly reduced peak flow during an acute attack indicates significant airflow obstruction.
why_wrong: A. This degree of reduction is not normal variation. B. 35% of personal best is substantially reduced. C. The clinical context indicates an acute exacerbation. D. Peak flow reduction in asthma reflects airflow obstruction rather than restriction.
pearl: Always compare peak flow with the patient's best or predicted value; in an acute attack, PEF between a third and a half of best indicates acute severe asthma, and below a third is life-threatening.
thinking: Known asthma, acute attack ↓ PEF 35% of personal best ↓ Marked fall in expiratory flow ↓ Severe airflow obstruction
exam_trap: D, restrictive lung disease — peak flow can fall in many conditions, but during an asthma attack the fall reflects airway narrowing, not reduced lung volumes.
takeaway: A large fall in PEF from personal best during an attack means severe obstruction; act on it.

stem: A patient has fever, productive cough and focal bronchial breathing over the right lower chest. What is the most likely underlying process?
why_correct: Fever, productive cough and focal bronchial breathing are typical of pulmonary consolidation.
why_wrong: B. Pneumothorax usually causes reduced breath sounds. C. Pleural effusion typically causes reduced breath sounds and stony dullness. D. Asthma causes widespread wheeze rather than focal bronchial breathing. E. PE does not usually cause focal bronchial breathing.
pearl: Bronchial breathing, dullness to percussion and increased vocal resonance over one area are the classic signs of consolidation; confirm with chest X-ray and assess severity with CURB-65.
thinking: Fever and productive cough = infection ↓ Focal bronchial breathing ↓ Sound conducted through solid lung ↓ Consolidation ↓ Lobar pneumonia
exam_trap: C, pleural effusion only — also gives basal signs, but an effusion causes stony dullness with reduced breath sounds, not bronchial breathing.
takeaway: Focal bronchial breathing with fever means consolidation: think lobar pneumonia.

stem: A patient with confirmed pulmonary embolism develops a small amount of haemoptysis. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Gastric ulceration with swallowed blood mistaken for haemoptysis
options.D: Pulmonary oedema from acute left ventricular failure
options.E: Oesophageal rupture with blood tracking into the mediastinum

correct_answer: B. Pulmonary infarction with alveolar haemorrhage
why_correct: A peripheral pulmonary embolus can cause pulmonary infarction and associated haemoptysis.
why_wrong: A. Gastric ulceration causes haematemesis or melaena; the blood would not originate from the lungs. C. Nasal trauma causes epistaxis. D. Pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure can cause pink frothy sputum but is not the typical mechanism of haemoptysis in PE. E. Oesophageal rupture causes severe chest pain and mediastinitis, not this typical PE-related haemoptysis.
pearl: Haemoptysis with pleuritic chest pain in PE points to a peripheral embolus causing pulmonary infarction; large central emboli more often present with collapse and shock.
thinking: Confirmed PE ↓ Embolus blocks a peripheral pulmonary artery ↓ Distal lung tissue infarcts ↓ Blood leaks into alveoli ↓ Pulmonary infarction with alveolar haemorrhage
exam_trap: D, pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure — PE strains the heart and oedema can give pink frothy sputum, but small-volume haemoptysis in PE comes from infarcted lung.
takeaway: Haemoptysis in PE reflects pulmonary infarction from a peripheral clot.

stem: A 72-year-old man has progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough. Examination reveals fine end-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive exertional dyspnoea, dry cough and fine bibasal inspiratory crackles are characteristic of pulmonary fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. COPD typically causes productive cough, wheeze and coarse rather than fine end-inspiratory crackles. B. PE generally presents more acutely. C. Asthma typically causes variable wheeze and reversible airflow obstruction. D. Pneumothorax causes acute unilateral symptoms.
pearl: Fine, velcro-like bibasal end-inspiratory crackles with a dry cough and progressive breathlessness suggest pulmonary fibrosis; look for finger clubbing and confirm with high-resolution CT.
thinking: Older adult with progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ Persistent dry cough ↓ Fine end-inspiratory bibasal crackles ↓ Interstitial fibrosis pattern ↓ Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
exam_trap: A, COPD — common in older adults with cough and breathlessness, but it typically gives a productive cough, wheeze and coarse crackles rather than fine velcro crackles.
takeaway: Dry cough plus fine bibasal velcro crackles = pulmonary fibrosis; HRCT confirms.

stem: A 19-year-old has fever, sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy. Infectious mononucleosis is suspected. Which antibiotic is particularly associated with a widespread rash if given to this patient?
why_correct: Giving amoxicillin or ampicillin during acute EBV infection commonly produces a widespread maculopapular rash.
why_wrong: B. Metronidazole is used against anaerobic organisms and some protozoa. C. Flucloxacillin is an antistaphylococcal penicillin and is not the classic association. D. Nitrofurantoin is used mainly for urinary infections. E. Doxycycline is not characteristically associated with this EBV-related rash.
pearl: Avoid amoxicillin when glandular fever is possible; the rash it triggers during EBV infection is often not a true penicillin allergy, so think before labelling the patient allergic.
thinking: Young adult with fever, sore throat and nodes ↓ Infectious mononucleosis suspected ↓ Aminopenicillins in EBV trigger a widespread rash ↓ Amoxicillin
exam_trap: C, flucloxacillin — also a penicillin, so it tempts, but the classic rash association in EBV is with aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin and ampicillin.
takeaway: Sore throat that could be glandular fever: avoid amoxicillin.

stem: Which clinical feature particularly supports a diagnosis of peritonsillar abscess?
why_correct: Inability or difficulty opening the mouth is a characteristic feature of peritonsillar abscess.
why_wrong: A. Ankle oedema suggests systemic or venous disease. B. Photophobia is associated with several ocular and neurological conditions. D. Calf swelling raises concern for venous disease. E. Haematuria suggests urinary tract pathology.
pearl: Quinsy causes severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, a muffled hot-potato voice and uvular deviation away from the swelling; it needs same-day ENT assessment for drainage and antibiotics.
thinking: Suspected peritonsillar abscess ↓ Pus collects beside the tonsil ↓ Inflammation spreads to the nearby medial pterygoid muscle ↓ Painful, limited mouth opening ↓ Trismus
exam_trap: B, photophobia — a feature of meningitis, another acute febrile illness, but it is not a feature of a peritonsillar collection; trismus is.
takeaway: Sore throat plus trismus and uvular deviation = quinsy until proven otherwise.

stem: Why is a cholesteatoma clinically important?

options.A: It causes only temporary ear blockage
options.B: It is caused by excess earwax
options.D: It is primarily a disorder of the retina

correct_answer: E. It can erode surrounding structures
why_correct: Cholesteatoma can progressively erode bone and cause serious local complications.
why_wrong: A. It can cause significant complications beyond blockage. B. It is not simply impacted cerumen. C. Cholesteatoma does not reliably resolve spontaneously. D. It is an ear condition.
pearl: Persistent foul-smelling ear discharge with hearing loss and debris or a retraction pocket in the attic suggests cholesteatoma; refer to ENT, as it can erode ossicles and cause facial palsy or intracranial infection.
thinking: Keratinising squamous epithelium trapped in the middle ear ↓ Keeps expanding ↓ Erodes ossicles, bone and nearby structures ↓ It can erode surrounding structures
exam_trap: A, causes only temporary ear blockage — early symptoms such as discharge and hearing loss can seem minor, but cholesteatoma keeps growing and destroying bone.
takeaway: Cholesteatoma is progressive and destructive; refer to ENT for surgery.

stem: A patient develops stridor following neck surgery. Bilateral vocal cord palsy is suspected. What is the major immediate concern?
why_correct: Bilateral vocal cord dysfunction can severely narrow the airway and cause stridor.
why_wrong: A. Intestinal obstruction causes abdominal symptoms. C. Hyperglycaemia does not cause this acute airway presentation. D. Renal failure does not explain acute stridor. E. Visual loss is unrelated.
pearl: Stridor after thyroid or neck surgery is an emergency: consider bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy or a compressing neck haematoma, and call senior anaesthetic help immediately.
thinking: Recent neck surgery ↓ New stridor ↓ Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves both cords near the midline ↓ Glottic narrowing ↓ Airway obstruction
exam_trap: C, hyperglycaemia — post-operative metabolic problems are common, but they do not cause stridor; noisy breathing after neck surgery is an airway problem first.
takeaway: Stridor after neck surgery = airway threat until proven otherwise.

stem: A child develops a harsh, high-pitched noise predominantly during inspiration. What is this sound called?
why_correct: Stridor is a harsh inspiratory sound caused by upper-airway narrowing.
why_wrong: A. Wheeze is usually a musical sound associated with lower-airway narrowing. B. Bronchial breathing is a transmitted breath sound associated with consolidation. C. Crackles are discontinuous sounds associated with fluid or airway/alveolar opening. D. A pleural rub results from inflamed pleural surfaces.
pearl: Stridor localises narrowing to the larynx or trachea; in a child keep them calm, do not examine the throat if epiglottitis is possible, and get urgent senior help.
thinking: Harsh, high-pitched sound ↓ Mainly on inspiration ↓ Extrathoracic upper-airway narrowing ↓ Stridor
exam_trap: A, wheeze — also high-pitched, but it is musical, mainly expiratory and arises from lower-airway narrowing, as in asthma or bronchiolitis.
takeaway: Harsh inspiratory noise = stridor (upper airway); musical expiratory noise = wheeze.

stem: Which symptom is particularly associated with nasal polyps?
why_correct: Nasal polyps can obstruct airflow to the olfactory region and commonly cause hyposmia or anosmia.
why_wrong: A. Dysuria is painful urination. C. Sudden deafness is an auditory problem. D. Diplopia is a visual/neurological symptom. E. Haemoptysis is coughing blood.
pearl: Bilateral nasal polyps cause blockage and loss of smell; a unilateral polyp, or one with bleeding or crusting, is a red flag for tumour and needs urgent ENT assessment.
thinking: Polyps fill the nasal cavity ↓ Airflow cannot reach the olfactory cleft ↓ Smell reduced or lost ↓ Reduced sense of smell
exam_trap: C, sudden unilateral deafness — nasal disease can affect the ear via the Eustachian tube, but sudden deafness is a sensorineural problem unrelated to polyps.
takeaway: Nasal blockage with reduced smell suggests polyps; unilateral polyps need urgent review.

stem: Why does a nasal septal haematoma require prompt treatment?

options.A: It frequently leads to cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea
options.C: It obstructs the Eustachian tube, causing otitis media
options.D: It can cause ischaemic necrosis of septal cartilage

correct_answer: D. It can cause ischaemic necrosis of septal cartilage
why_correct: A septal haematoma can disrupt cartilage nutrition and lead to septal cartilage necrosis and deformity.
why_wrong: A. CSF rhinorrhoea reflects skull base injury, not a septal haematoma. B. It does not cause cataracts. C. A septal haematoma does not obstruct the Eustachian tube or cause otitis media. E. It does not cause renal failure.
pearl: After nasal trauma always inspect the septum: a boggy, swollen septum needs same-day incision and drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis, abscess and saddle-nose deformity.
thinking: Nasal trauma ↓ Blood lifts the perichondrium off the septal cartilage ↓ Cartilage loses its nutrient supply ↓ Ischaemic necrosis of septal cartilage
exam_trap: A, CSF rhinorrhoea — also follows facial trauma, but it reflects a skull base fracture, not a septal haematoma.
takeaway: Septal haematoma needs same-day drainage to save the cartilage.

stem: A 35-year-old woman develops gradually progressive hearing loss. Examination of the external ear and tympanic membrane is normal. What type of hearing loss is characteristic of otosclerosis?
why_correct: Otosclerosis involves abnormal fixation of the stapes and typically causes conductive hearing loss.
why_wrong: A. Otosclerosis classically produces conductive rather than purely sensorineural loss. B. Central hearing loss is due to central auditory pathway pathology. C. This is not an auditory diagnosis. D. This is not an auditory diagnosis.
pearl: Otosclerosis typically causes progressive conductive hearing loss in young adults with a normal-looking tympanic membrane, often with a family history and worsening in pregnancy.
thinking: Young adult with gradual hearing loss ↓ Normal ear canal and drum ↓ Abnormal bone fixes the stapes footplate ↓ Sound not transmitted through the middle ear ↓ Conductive hearing loss
exam_trap: A, sensorineural only — tempting because the drum looks normal, as in most sensorineural loss, but stapes fixation blocks sound conduction.
takeaway: Normal drum plus progressive conductive loss in a young adult = otosclerosis.

stem: A patient wakes with sudden complete hearing loss in one ear. The external ear and tympanic membrane appear normal. What type of hearing loss should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden hearing loss with a normal external and middle ear suggests sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
why_wrong: B. Eustachian tube dysfunction causes conductive symptoms rather than sudden complete sensorineural loss. C. Otitis externa causes an inflamed painful ear canal. D. Otosclerosis causes gradually progressive conductive hearing loss. E. Wax causes conductive hearing loss and should usually be visible.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency: refer urgently, as early treatment, usually with corticosteroids, gives the best chance of recovery.
thinking: Sudden complete hearing loss in one ear ↓ Normal canal and drum, so no conductive cause seen ↓ Problem lies in the cochlea or nerve ↓ Sudden sensorineural hearing loss
exam_trap: E, conductive loss from wax — the commonest cause of a blocked ear, but wax would be visible on otoscopy, and this ear canal is normal.
takeaway: Sudden unilateral hearing loss with a normal-looking ear = urgent ENT referral.

stem: Which condition typically causes conductive rather than sensorineural hearing loss?
why_correct: Otosclerosis interferes with transmission of sound through the middle ear and causes conductive hearing loss.
why_wrong: B. Ménière disease causes sensorineural hearing loss. C. Acoustic nerve pathology causes sensorineural hearing loss. D. Vestibular schwannoma causes sensorineural hearing loss. E. Presbycusis is age-related sensorineural hearing loss.
pearl: Tuning forks separate the types: in conductive loss bone conduction beats air on the affected side and Weber lateralises to that ear; in sensorineural loss Weber goes to the better ear.
thinking: Conductive loss = problem in the canal or middle ear ↓ The other options affect the cochlea or nerve ↓ Otosclerosis fixes the stapes ↓ Otosclerosis
exam_trap: D, vestibular schwannoma — a classic cause of unilateral hearing loss, but it compresses the cochlear nerve and causes sensorineural loss.
takeaway: Otosclerosis is conductive; Ménière disease, schwannoma and presbycusis are sensorineural.

stem: A 78-year-old man has gradually progressive bilateral hearing loss, particularly affecting high-frequency sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Presbycusis is age-related sensorineural hearing loss, typically affecting high frequencies initially.
why_wrong: B. Cholesteatoma usually causes conductive hearing loss and chronic discharge. C. Otitis externa affects the external auditory canal. D. Otosclerosis usually causes conductive hearing loss. E. Nasal polyps affect the nasal passages.
pearl: Presbycusis is bilateral, symmetrical, gradual high-frequency sensorineural loss; asymmetric or unilateral loss should prompt investigation for another cause such as vestibular schwannoma.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Gradual, bilateral hearing loss ↓ High frequencies affected first ↓ Age-related cochlear degeneration ↓ Presbycusis
exam_trap: D, otosclerosis — also gradual and progressive, but it typically starts in younger adults and causes conductive, not high-frequency sensorineural, loss.
takeaway: Older adult with symmetrical high-frequency loss = presbycusis; asymmetry needs investigation.

stem: A patient with age-related macular degeneration develops rapid worsening of central vision and new distortion of straight lines. What process characterises the wet form?
correct_answer: A. Abnormal choroidal blood vessel growth
why_correct: Neovascular or wet AMD involves abnormal blood vessel growth beneath the retina, which can leak and damage the macula.
why_wrong: B. Drusen and geographic atrophy characterise dry (non-neovascular) AMD. C. Optic nerve inflammation causes optic neuritis. D. Corneal ulceration is an anterior ocular condition. E. Lens opacity causes cataract.
pearl: Sudden distortion of straight lines or rapid central vision loss in AMD suggests the wet form; refer urgently to ophthalmology, as anti-VEGF injections can preserve vision if started early.
thinking: Known AMD ↓ Rapid central loss with distortion (metamorphopsia) ↓ Leakage or bleeding under the macula ↓ Abnormal choroidal blood vessel growth
exam_trap: B, drusen with geographic atrophy — a real AMD finding, but it defines the dry form, which progresses slowly rather than causing rapid distortion.
takeaway: New distortion in AMD = suspect wet AMD and refer urgently for anti-VEGF.

stem: A young adult develops painful loss of vision in one eye, particularly when moving the eye. Which additional finding is characteristic of optic neuritis?

options.A: Fixed flexion deformity of the fingers

why_correct: Optic neuritis commonly causes painful visual loss with impaired colour perception.
why_wrong: A. Finger contracture is a musculoskeletal finding. C. Purulent ear discharge indicates ear disease. D. Haematuria indicates urinary tract pathology. E. Ankle oedema is unrelated.
pearl: Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss, reduced colour vision (red desaturation) and a relative afferent pupillary defect; it may be the first presentation of multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Painful unilateral visual loss, worse on eye movement ↓ Inflamed optic nerve ↓ Colour perception affected early ↓ Reduced colour vision
exam_trap: A, fixed flexion deformity of the fingers — candidates linking optic neuritis to a systemic disease may look for a body sign, but this is Dupuytren-type contracture and unrelated.
takeaway: Painful eye movement plus red desaturation = optic neuritis; think MS.

stem: A patient has significant unilateral optic nerve dysfunction. When light is moved from the normal eye to the affected eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate. What is this finding called?

options.E: Efferent defect from third nerve palsy

why_correct: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) is seen on the swinging light test when reduced afferent transmission from one eye, classically from optic nerve or severe retinal disease, makes both pupils dilate when light is moved to the affected eye.
why_wrong: A. Argyll Robertson pupils are small, irregular pupils that accommodate but react poorly to light. B. Horner syndrome causes miosis, mild ptosis and anhidrosis, with normal pupillary light responses. C. A Holmes-Adie pupil is a dilated tonic pupil with a poor light response and slow, sustained near response. E. A third nerve palsy causes an efferent defect with ptosis, a dilated unreactive pupil and a 'down and out' eye, not an afferent defect.
pearl: The swinging light test detects asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal disease; a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) is a key sign in optic neuritis.
thinking: Unilateral optic nerve dysfunction ↓ Less light signal from the affected eye ↓ Light swung to that eye: both pupils dilate ↓ Relative afferent pupillary defect
exam_trap: E, efferent defect from third nerve palsy — pupil dilatation suggests it, but an efferent defect affects only the involved pupil; in an RAPD both pupils respond together.
takeaway: Both pupils dilate when light swings to one eye = RAPD = optic nerve disease.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with severe unilateral testicular pain that began suddenly one hour ago. The affected testis is high-riding. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Sudden severe testicular pain with a high-riding testis is classic for testicular torsion, which requires urgent surgery to preserve the testis.
why_wrong: A. Urine culture: Does not diagnose or treat torsion. C. Oral antibiotics: Appropriate for some infections, not torsion. D. Reassurance: Torsion is a surgical emergency. E. Scrotal ultrasound before treatment: Imaging should not delay urgent surgical management when clinical suspicion is high.
pearl: Suspected testicular torsion is a surgical emergency: the testis is most likely to be saved if detorted early, so imaging must not delay scrotal exploration.
thinking: Young man with sudden severe testicular pain ↓ High-riding testis ↓ Testicular torsion ↓ Ischaemia is time-critical ↓ Immediate surgical exploration
exam_trap: E, scrotal ultrasound before treatment — feels like careful practice, but scanning wastes time when clinical suspicion of torsion is high.
takeaway: Clinical suspicion of torsion = theatre, not scan.

stem: A 68-year-old man has progressive difficulty recalling recent events. His family reports that he repeatedly asks the same questions. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive impairment of recent memory is a typical early feature of Alzheimer disease.
why_wrong: A. Panic disorder: Causes recurrent panic attacks rather than progressive memory loss. C. Parkinson disease: Primarily presents with motor features, although cognitive impairment can occur. D. Acute psychosis: Characterised by symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions. E. Delirium: Has acute onset and fluctuating attention.
pearl: Alzheimer disease typically begins with insidious loss of recent memory over months to years; always screen for reversible contributors such as hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency and depression.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Progressive loss of recent memory ↓ Repeats the same questions ↓ Gradual course, no acute fluctuation ↓ Alzheimer disease
exam_trap: E, delirium — also causes memory problems in older people, but it is acute, fluctuating and impairs attention rather than progressing gradually.
takeaway: Gradual progressive recent memory loss = dementia; acute fluctuating confusion = delirium.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has intrusive thoughts that her hands are contaminated. She repeatedly washes them for several hours each day despite recognising that the behaviour is excessive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intrusive unwanted thoughts accompanied by repetitive compulsive behaviour are characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
why_wrong: A. PTSD: Requires a traumatic event followed by characteristic re-experiencing and avoidance symptoms. C. Generalised anxiety disorder: Causes excessive worry across several areas rather than compulsive rituals. D. Mania: Causes elevated or irritable mood with increased activity and other characteristic features. E. Psychosis: Involves symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations.
pearl: OCD combines obsessions (intrusive thoughts recognised as one's own) with compulsions performed to relieve anxiety; first-line treatment is CBT with exposure and response prevention, with an SSRI if needed.
thinking: Intrusive contamination thoughts ↓ Repeated hand-washing to relieve them ↓ Recognises it is excessive ↓ Obsessions plus compulsions ↓ OCD
exam_trap: C, generalised anxiety disorder — anxiety is central to both, but GAD is diffuse worry about many things without ritualised compulsions.
takeaway: Obsessions plus compulsions with insight = OCD.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with a painless lump in his neck that has been gradually increasing in size. Which feature would most increase concern for malignancy?

options.D: Bilateral small cervical nodes during a cold
options.E: Reduction in size over several days

why_correct: A hard, fixed and persistent lymph node is concerning for malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Tenderness during a viral illness: More typical of reactive lymphadenopathy. C. Soft consistency: More commonly associated with benign causes. D. Bilateral small nodes during a cold: Commonly occurs with acute infection. E. Reduction in size: Suggests a reactive process.
pearl: A persistent, painless, enlarging neck lump in an adult, especially if hard or fixed, needs urgent assessment for malignancy such as head and neck cancer or lymphoma.
thinking: Adult with a painless, slowly enlarging neck lump ↓ Malignant infiltration makes tissue hard ↓ Tumour tethers to surrounding structures ↓ Hard and fixed consistency
exam_trap: B, tenderness during a viral illness — a painful lump can feel more worrying, but tenderness usually means reactive inflammation; malignant nodes are typically painless.
takeaway: Hard, fixed, painless, persistent node = suspicious; tender, soft or shrinking = reactive.

stem: A newborn develops jaundice at 12 hours of age. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: It is most likely breast milk jaundice
options.B: It needs review if it persists beyond 14 days
options.D: It should be regarded as pathological

correct_answer: D. It should be regarded as pathological
why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is considered pathological and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Breast milk jaundice: Occurs later and does not explain jaundice at 12 hours. B. Review at 14 days: Jaundice within the first 24 hours needs urgent assessment, not delayed review. C. Physiological jaundice: Typically develops after the first 24 hours. E. It is normal after feeding: Early jaundice is not considered a normal post-feeding finding.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise; measure serum bilirubin urgently rather than judging by eye, and consider haemolysis or sepsis.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Jaundice at 12 hours of age ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours ↓ Haemolysis or sepsis likely ↓ Pathological
exam_trap: C, physiological jaundice — the commonest neonatal jaundice, but it appears after the first 24 hours, never at 12 hours.
takeaway: Jaundice under 24 hours old = pathological; check serum bilirubin urgently.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss and diarrhoea. Blood tests show a low haemoglobin and low ferritin. She has no obvious source of blood loss. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Coeliac disease can cause malabsorption and iron-deficiency anaemia, sometimes without prominent gastrointestinal symptoms.
why_wrong: B. Acute appendicitis: Causes acute abdominal pain rather than chronic malabsorption. C. Haemorrhoids: May cause rectal bleeding but do not explain diarrhoea and malabsorption. D. Gallstone disease: Does not typically cause iron deficiency. E. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: Does not cause malabsorption.
pearl: Test for coeliac disease with tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA in unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or chronic diarrhoea; the patient must be eating gluten when tested.
thinking: Young adult with diarrhoea, weight loss and fatigue ↓ Iron deficiency without blood loss ↓ Poor iron absorption in the duodenum ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: C, haemorrhoids — bleeding is a common cause of iron loss, but no blood loss is reported, and haemorrhoids do not explain diarrhoea and weight loss.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency, especially with diarrhoea: test for coeliac disease.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a persistent white patch on the lateral border of her tongue that cannot be scraped away. She has smoked for many years. What is the most appropriate concern?

options.D: Recurrent minor aphthous ulcer of the tongue
options.E: Herpes simplex infection of the tongue

why_correct: A persistent non-scrapable white oral lesion, particularly in a smoker, may represent leukoplakia and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Geographic tongue: Produces migrating erythematous areas with white borders. C. Pseudomembranous candidiasis: Produces white plaques that can be scraped away. D. Aphthous ulcer: Produces a discrete, self-healing ulcer rather than a persistent white plaque. E. Herpes simplex infection: Usually produces painful vesicles or ulcers.
pearl: Any persistent oral white or red patch that cannot be scraped off needs specialist assessment and usually biopsy; red patches (erythroplakia) carry an even higher malignant risk.
thinking: Persistent white patch on the tongue ↓ Cannot be scraped off, so not thrush ↓ Lateral tongue in a long-term smoker ↓ Potentially malignant lesion ↓ Leukoplakia
exam_trap: C, pseudomembranous candidiasis — a common white oral lesion, but candida plaques scrape away; this patch does not.
takeaway: Persistent non-scrapable white oral patch = leukoplakia until biopsied.

stem: A 59-year-old woman presents with a new breast lump. It is hard, irregular and fixed to the underlying tissue. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Re-examine in 6 weeks before deciding on referral
options.B: Reassure her that it is probably benign
options.D: Prescribe oral antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
options.E: Urgent referral to a breast assessment service

correct_answer: E. Urgent referral to a breast assessment service
why_correct: A new hard, irregular or fixed breast lump requires urgent assessment for possible malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Re-examination in 6 weeks: Would delay urgent assessment of a suspicious lump. B. Reassure: The clinical features are concerning. C. Hormone replacement therapy: Has no role in evaluating a breast lump. D. Antibiotics: There is no evidence of infection, and this would delay urgent assessment.
pearl: Refer a suspicious breast lump via the suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography and/or ultrasound) and biopsy.
thinking: New breast lump in an older woman ↓ Hard, irregular and fixed ↓ Features of carcinoma ↓ Urgent referral to a breast assessment service
exam_trap: A, re-examine in 6 weeks — reasonable for some cyclical lumps in younger women, but a hard, fixed lump at 59 needs urgent assessment now.
takeaway: Suspicious breast lump = urgent referral for triple assessment.

stem: A 55-year-old man has progressive difficulty swallowing food. He reports that food sometimes feels stuck behind his sternum. Which symptom is particularly concerning for oesophageal malignancy?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia is an important alarm symptom requiring urgent assessment for oesophageal cancer.
why_wrong: A. Occasional hiccups: Non-specific and not a typical cancer red flag. B. Increased thirst: Suggests a metabolic or endocrine issue rather than oesophageal obstruction. C. Mild bloating: Non-specific. D. Increased urinary frequency: Suggests a urinary/metabolic cause.
pearl: Dysphagia is a red-flag symptom: refer for urgent upper GI endoscopy via the suspected cancer pathway, especially when it is progressive or accompanied by weight loss.
thinking: Middle-aged man ↓ Food sticks behind the sternum ↓ Swallowing worsening over time ↓ Mechanical narrowing, possibly tumour ↓ Progressive dysphagia
exam_trap: A, occasional hiccups — can accompany oesophageal lesions, but they are non-specific; progressive dysphagia is the alarm feature.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia = urgent endoscopy to exclude oesophageal cancer.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with a new headache accompanied by scalp tenderness. She has no visual symptoms. Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange outpatient temporal artery biopsy before treatment
