options.B: Arrange routine audiology and an ENT outpatient review
options.C: Urgent treatment for suspected giant cell arteritis
options.D: Treat with topical antifungal medication for scalp tinea
options.E: Start a triptan for presumed migraine and review in a week

correct_answer: C. Urgent treatment for suspected giant cell arteritis
why_correct: New headache with scalp tenderness and raised inflammatory markers in an older adult is concerning for giant cell arteritis, where prompt treatment is important to reduce the risk of visual complications.
why_wrong: A. Biopsy before treatment: Glucocorticoids should not be delayed while awaiting temporal artery biopsy, as GCA can cause irreversible visual loss. B. Routine audiology and ENT review: Does not address the suspected inflammatory vascular condition. D. Topical antifungal for scalp tinea: Has no relevance to raised inflammatory markers and suspected GCA. E. Start a triptan: The presentation is not typical of migraine, and delay risks visual loss.
pearl: In suspected giant cell arteritis start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and refer urgently; biopsy or ultrasound can follow, as findings persist for a short time after steroids start.
thinking: Older adult with new headache and scalp tenderness ↓ Raised inflammatory markers ↓ Suspected giant cell arteritis ↓ Risk of sudden visual loss ↓ Urgent treatment
exam_trap: A, outpatient temporal artery biopsy before treatment — confirms the diagnosis, but delaying steroids risks irreversible blindness.
takeaway: Suspected GCA: steroids now, confirm the diagnosis afterwards.

stem: A 26-year-old man develops a widespread rash after starting amoxicillin for suspected bacterial pharyngitis. He has marked fatigue and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which underlying infection is most likely?
why_correct: A widespread rash following amoxicillin in a patient with a mononucleosis-like illness is strongly associated with EBV infection.
why_wrong: A. Malaria: Causes febrile episodes rather than this characteristic rash association. B. Influenza: Does not characteristically cause this amoxicillin-associated rash. C. Hepatitis A: Causes an acute hepatitis syndrome rather than this presentation. E. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis would respond to amoxicillin and does not explain the characteristic amoxicillin-associated rash with marked fatigue.
pearl: A rash after amoxicillin in a patient with sore throat, lymphadenopathy and fatigue suggests glandular fever; confirm with a Monospot test and advise avoiding contact sports for now.
thinking: Young adult with pharyngitis ↓ Marked fatigue and cervical nodes ↓ Widespread rash after amoxicillin ↓ Classic EBV reaction ↓ Epstein–Barr virus infection
exam_trap: E, group A streptococcal infection — the reason amoxicillin was given, but strep throat responds to it and does not explain the rash with marked fatigue.
takeaway: Amoxicillin rash during a sore throat illness = think EBV.

stem: A 42-year-old man has acute severe pain and swelling of his knee. He has a fever. What investigation is essential to distinguish septic arthritis from other causes of an acutely swollen joint?
why_correct: Synovial fluid aspiration allows assessment for infection, including microscopy and culture, and is essential when septic arthritis is suspected.
why_wrong: B. Bone density scan: Assesses bone mineral density rather than joint infection. C. Colonoscopy: Does not investigate acute joint infection. D. Spirometry: Assesses respiratory function. E. Chest X-ray: Does not assess the joint.
pearl: In an acutely hot swollen joint, aspirate before antibiotics where possible and send fluid for Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy; septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days.
thinking: Acute hot swollen knee ↓ Fever ↓ Septic arthritis must be excluded ↓ Need synovial fluid for microscopy, culture and crystals ↓ Joint aspiration
exam_trap: E, chest X-ray — may form part of a general sepsis work-up, but it cannot assess the joint; only synovial fluid confirms or excludes septic arthritis.
takeaway: Hot swollen joint: aspirate it; septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old woman develops painful swelling of the thumb and wrist after repetitive lifting of her baby. Pain is particularly provoked by moving the thumb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain around the radial wrist associated with repetitive thumb use is typical of De Quervain tenosynovitis.
why_wrong: A. Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow): Causes lateral elbow pain. C. Dupuytren contracture: Causes palmar fascial thickening and finger contractures. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome: Causes numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution. E. Trigger finger: Causes painful catching or locking of a finger.
pearl: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons; Finkelstein's test reproduces pain over the radial styloid.
thinking: Repetitive lifting with thumb use ↓ Pain and swelling at the radial wrist ↓ Worse on thumb movement ↓ First extensor compartment tendons inflamed ↓ De Quervain tenosynovitis
exam_trap: D, carpal tunnel syndrome — also linked to repetitive wrist use, but it causes numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution, not radial tendon pain.
takeaway: Radial wrist pain on thumb movement with positive Finkelstein's test = De Quervain.

stem: A 45-year-old man has pain over the outer aspect of his elbow that is worse when gripping objects and extending his wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lateral elbow pain aggravated by wrist extension and gripping is typical of lateral epicondylitis.
why_wrong: A. Golfer's elbow: Causes medial rather than lateral elbow pain. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome: Causes hand sensory symptoms. C. Frozen shoulder: Causes painful restriction of shoulder movement. D. De Quervain tenosynovitis: Causes radial wrist/thumb pain.
pearl: Tennis elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle; most cases settle with activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy.
thinking: Pain over the outer elbow ↓ Worse with gripping and wrist extension ↓ Common extensor origin overloaded ↓ Lateral epicondylitis ↓ Tennis elbow
exam_trap: A, golfer's elbow — the paired overuse condition, but it affects the medial epicondyle and is provoked by wrist flexion.
takeaway: Lateral elbow pain on wrist extension = tennis elbow; medial on flexion = golfer's.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has burning pain and tingling over the outer aspect of her thigh. There is no weakness and the symptoms do not extend below the knee. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing sensory symptoms over the outer thigh without weakness.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome: Causes multiple neurological deficits and possible bladder/bowel dysfunction. B. Femoral neuropathy: Can cause weakness of knee extension and broader sensory loss. C. Sciatica: Usually follows a lumbosacral nerve-root distribution and may extend below the knee. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome: Affects the hand.
pearl: Meralgia paraesthetica is a clinical diagnosis: sensory symptoms over the anterolateral thigh with normal power, reflexes and back examination, usually managed by removing the compression.
thinking: Burning and tingling over the outer thigh ↓ No weakness ↓ Stops above the knee, so not a root pattern ↓ Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve ↓ Meralgia paraesthetica
exam_trap: C, sciatica — leg pain with tingling suggests a nerve root, but sciatica usually radiates below the knee in a dermatomal pattern.
takeaway: Outer-thigh sensory symptoms above the knee with normal power = meralgia paraesthetica.

stem: A 68-year-old man has painful enlargement of the skull and progressive hearing difficulty. X-rays show thickened, deformed bones. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Paget disease causes abnormal bone remodelling and can lead to bone enlargement, deformity and hearing loss when the skull is affected.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes inflammatory joint disease. C. Fibromyalgia: Causes widespread pain without structural bone enlargement. D. Osteoporosis: Causes reduced bone density and fragility fractures rather than enlarged deformed bones. E. Gout: Causes acute inflammatory arthritis and tophi.
pearl: Paget disease typically shows a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate; skull involvement can cause hearing loss, and bisphosphonates treat bone pain.
thinking: Older man with a painful enlarging skull ↓ Progressive hearing loss ↓ X-ray: thickened, deformed bone ↓ Disordered remodelling ↓ Paget disease of bone
exam_trap: D, osteoporosis — the commonest bone disease of older adults, but it thins bone and causes fragility fractures rather than enlarged, thickened bones.
takeaway: Enlarged deformed bones with an isolated raised ALP = Paget disease.

stem: A 27-year-old man develops severe pain and swelling in his ankle after stepping awkwardly during a football match. He is unable to continue playing. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Start therapeutic anticoagulation for six weeks
options.B: Arrange urgent MRI of the ankle before any examination
options.C: Clinical assessment to decide if imaging is needed
options.D: Apply a below-knee cast without further assessment

correct_answer: C. Clinical assessment to decide if imaging is needed
why_correct: Acute ankle injuries require clinical assessment, including consideration of whether fracture imaging criteria are met.
why_wrong: A. Therapeutic anticoagulation: There is no indication in an acute ankle injury. B. Urgent MRI: MRI is not a first-line test, and examination should guide whether any imaging is needed. D. Below-knee cast without assessment: Immobilisation should follow assessment and, where indicated, imaging to define the injury. E. Colonoscopy: Unrelated.
pearl: Use the Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray is needed only with bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of a malleolus, or inability to weight-bear both immediately and when examined.
thinking: Acute twisting ankle injury ↓ Pain, swelling, stopped playing ↓ Fracture possible but not certain ↓ Examine and apply the Ottawa rules ↓ Clinical assessment decides imaging
exam_trap: B, urgent MRI before examination — sounds thorough, but MRI is not first line and examination should decide whether any imaging is needed.
takeaway: Ankle injury: examine and apply the Ottawa rules before ordering an X-ray.

stem: A 22-year-old woman develops jaundice and dark urine after taking an oxidant medication. She is known to have G6PD deficiency. What process is most likely occurring?
why_correct: G6PD deficiency predisposes to oxidative haemolysis following certain medications or infections.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency: Does not explain acute jaundice and dark urine. B. Bone marrow infiltration: Causes broader cytopenias. C. Vitamin B12 deficiency: Causes macrocytic anaemia and neurological symptoms. E. Platelet destruction: Causes thrombocytopenia and bleeding.
pearl: In G6PD deficiency, oxidant drugs such as primaquine, dapsone and nitrofurantoin, fava beans and infection can trigger acute haemolysis; the blood film may show bite cells and Heinz bodies.
thinking: Known G6PD deficiency ↓ Oxidant drug exposure ↓ Red cells cannot cope with oxidative stress ↓ Jaundice and dark urine ↓ Haemolysis
exam_trap: E, platelet destruction — drug reactions can cause immune thrombocytopenia, but that produces bleeding and purpura, not jaundice and dark urine.
takeaway: G6PD deficiency plus an oxidant trigger = acute haemolysis.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents with visible haematuria and severe loin pain that comes in waves. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Colicky loin pain with haematuria is characteristic of a ureteric stone.
why_wrong: B. Benign prostatic enlargement: Causes lower urinary tract symptoms. C. Bladder cancer: Classically causes painless haematuria. D. Prostatitis: Usually causes pelvic/perineal pain, urinary symptoms and sometimes fever. E. Acute cystitis: Usually causes dysuria, frequency and urgency.
pearl: Suspected ureteric colic is confirmed with non-contrast CT KUB; an obstructing stone with signs of infection needs urgent decompression.
thinking: Visible haematuria ↓ Severe loin pain coming in waves ↓ Colic from ureteric obstruction ↓ Stone damages the urothelium ↓ Ureteric stone
exam_trap: C, bladder cancer — visible haematuria in an older man is a cancer red flag, but bladder cancer is classically painless; colicky loin pain points to a stone.
takeaway: Haematuria with colicky loin pain = stone; painless visible haematuria = think cancer.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with blood and protein in his urine following a recent upper respiratory infection. His blood pressure is elevated. Which type of renal disease is most likely?
why_correct: Haematuria, proteinuria and hypertension are characteristic of a nephritic picture.
why_wrong: A. Urinary retention: Causes inability to pass urine rather than glomerular abnormalities. C. Renal colic: Causes severe colicky pain. D. Cystitis: Causes lower urinary symptoms. E. Nephrotic syndrome: Is characterised predominantly by heavy proteinuria and oedema.
pearl: Haematuria within days of an upper respiratory infection suggests IgA nephropathy, whereas post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically appears a couple of weeks after the infection.
thinking: Recent upper respiratory infection ↓ Blood and protein in the urine ↓ Raised blood pressure ↓ Glomerular inflammation ↓ Nephritic syndrome
exam_trap: E, nephrotic syndrome — also a glomerular disease with proteinuria, but it is defined by heavy proteinuria, low albumin and oedema rather than haematuria and hypertension.
takeaway: Haematuria plus hypertension = nephritic; heavy proteinuria plus oedema = nephrotic.

stem: A 44-year-old woman develops widespread swelling of her ankles and eyelids. Blood tests show low serum albumin and urine testing shows marked proteinuria. Which mechanism best explains the oedema?
why_correct: Heavy urinary protein loss reduces serum albumin, lowering plasma oncotic pressure and promoting oedema.
why_wrong: A. Increased bone mineralisation: Unrelated. B. Increased bile secretion: Does not explain generalised oedema. D. Increased red cell production: Does not cause oedema. E. Reduced airway resistance: Unrelated.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, often with hyperlipidaemia; it also raises the risk of venous thrombosis and infection.
thinking: Ankle and eyelid swelling ↓ Marked proteinuria ↓ Low serum albumin ↓ Less albumin holding fluid in vessels ↓ Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
exam_trap: B, increased bile secretion — swelling might prompt thoughts of liver disease, but bile secretion does not cause oedema; albumin lost in the urine does.
takeaway: Nephrotic oedema: urinary albumin loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure.

stem: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has persistently raised blood pressure. Which complication should be routinely screened for using urine testing?
why_correct: Diabetes can cause albuminuria and chronic kidney disease, so urinary albumin assessment is an important part of diabetic complication screening.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral arterial disease: Is assessed by foot examination and pulses, not urine testing. B. Otitis externa: Is not a routine diabetic complication screen. D. Acute appendicitis: Is not a diabetic complication. E. Diabetic retinopathy: Is screened for with retinal photography, not urine testing.
pearl: People with diabetes should have their urine albumin:creatinine ratio and eGFR checked at least annually; albuminuria is an early sign of kidney damage and a reason to tighten blood pressure control.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes ↓ Raised blood pressure adds renal risk ↓ Early kidney damage shows as albuminuria ↓ Urine albumin testing ↓ Diabetic kidney disease
exam_trap: E, diabetic retinopathy — also part of routine diabetic screening, but it is detected by retinal photography, not urine testing.
takeaway: Diabetes screening: urine ACR for kidneys, retinal photos for eyes, foot checks for feet.

stem: A 70-year-old woman develops increasing breathlessness. Examination reveals reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. Which investigation is most appropriate initially?
why_correct: A pleural effusion is suspected clinically; chest X-ray is an appropriate initial investigation to confirm it.
why_wrong: A. Spirometry assesses airflow and lung function rather than confirming an effusion. B. Echocardiography may help investigate a cardiac cause but does not initially confirm the pleural effusion. D. Bronchoscopy is not the initial investigation for a suspected pleural effusion. E. CTPA is primarily for suspected pulmonary embolism.
pearl: Stony dullness with reduced breath sounds suggests a pleural effusion; after chest X-ray, ultrasound guides aspiration, and pleural fluid analysis separates transudate from exudate.
thinking: Breathlessness ↓ Basal dullness and reduced breath sounds ↓ Pleural effusion suspected ↓ Confirm quickly and simply ↓ Chest X-ray
exam_trap: E, CT pulmonary angiogram — breathlessness raises PE, but the examination points to an effusion, which a chest X-ray confirms first.
takeaway: Suspected pleural effusion: chest X-ray first, then ultrasound-guided aspiration.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful red eyes, joint pain and shortness of breath. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary and extrapulmonary manifestations such as uveitis and arthralgia is characteristic of sarcoidosis.
why_wrong: A. COPD does not cause hilar lymphadenopathy or uveitis. B. Tuberculosis can cause lymphadenopathy but the overall pattern is less characteristic. C. Asthma does not cause bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. E. Pulmonary embolism does not explain chronic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
pearl: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with uveitis, arthralgia or erythema nodosum is classic, and serum ACE and calcium may be raised.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Recurrent painful red eyes (uveitis) ↓ Joint pain and breathlessness ↓ Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy ↓ Sarcoidosis
exam_trap: B, tuberculosis — causes hilar nodes and must be excluded, but nodes are usually unilateral, and the recurrent multisystem eye and joint pattern fits sarcoidosis better.
takeaway: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy plus eye, joint or skin features = sarcoidosis.

stem: A 28-year-old man has recurrent episodes of coughing and wheezing. He reports that symptoms are particularly troublesome after exposure to cats. Between episodes he is completely well. Which physiological abnormality is most characteristic of asthma?

options.D: Increased residual volume as the defining abnormality
options.E: Reduced diffusion capacity as the defining abnormality

why_correct: Asthma is characterised by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation.
why_wrong: B. Reduced total lung capacity indicates restrictive disease. C. Fixed airflow obstruction is more characteristic of established COPD. D. Increased residual volume can occur with air trapping but is not the defining feature. E. Reduced diffusion capacity is not the defining physiological abnormality in asthma.
pearl: Asthma is defined by variability: symptoms and peak flow fluctuate, worsen with triggers such as allergens and improve with bronchodilators, whereas COPD obstruction is largely fixed.
thinking: Episodic cough and wheeze ↓ Triggered by cats ↓ Completely well between episodes ↓ Obstruction comes and goes ↓ Variable airflow obstruction
exam_trap: C, fixed airflow obstruction — obstruction is the right idea, but fixed obstruction characterises established COPD; asthma is variable and reversible.
takeaway: Asthma = variable, reversible obstruction; COPD = largely fixed obstruction.

stem: A 56-year-old man has persistent hoarseness for 5 weeks. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history. What is the most appropriate action?
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness, particularly in a smoker, is a red flag for laryngeal malignancy and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Speech therapy should not replace assessment for a possible underlying lesion. B. Antibiotics are inappropriate without evidence of bacterial infection. C. Reflux may cause hoarseness but should not be assumed in this high-risk presentation. D. Prolonged hoarseness with cancer risk factors should not simply be observed.
pearl: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older adult, especially a smoker, needs a suspected cancer referral to ENT so the larynx can be directly visualised.
thinking: Hoarseness persisting for weeks ↓ Heavy smoking history ↓ No infective explanation ↓ Laryngeal cancer must be excluded ↓ Urgent ENT assessment
exam_trap: C, proton-pump inhibitor only — reflux can cause hoarseness, but treating empirically in a high-risk smoker delays diagnosis of laryngeal cancer.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker = urgent ENT to visualise the larynx.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with acute severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. Imaging shows dilated small bowel loops. Which finding would most strongly suggest strangulated bowel obstruction?

options.A: Passage of normal stools and flatus
options.B: Severe continuous pain with systemic deterioration
options.E: Colicky pain with vomiting and distension

correct_answer: B. Severe continuous pain with systemic deterioration
why_correct: Strangulation causes compromised blood supply and may produce severe continuous pain, systemic toxicity and eventual peritonitis.
why_wrong: A. Continued normal stool and flatus makes complete obstruction less likely. C. Mild discomfort is not suggestive of strangulation. D. Increased appetite does not support bowel obstruction. E. Colicky pain with vomiting and distension is typical of uncomplicated mechanical obstruction.
pearl: In bowel obstruction, constant pain, fever, tachycardia, peritonism or a rising lactate suggest strangulation, which needs urgent surgery rather than conservative management.
thinking: Small-bowel obstruction on imaging ↓ Strangulation means the bowel's blood supply is compromised ↓ Ischaemic bowel gives constant rather than colicky pain ↓ Ischaemia and toxins cause systemic upset ↓ Severe continuous pain with systemic deterioration
exam_trap: E, colicky pain with vomiting and distension — these are the textbook features of obstruction, but they describe simple mechanical obstruction, not strangulation.
takeaway: Obstruction with constant pain and systemic upset = strangulation until proven otherwise.

stem: A 67-year-old woman has abdominal pain, bloating and altered bowel habit. CT shows diverticula in the sigmoid colon but no abscess or perforation. What is the most likely finding?
why_correct: Colonic diverticula without evidence of acute inflammation or complications indicate diverticular disease.
why_wrong: A. Perforation would produce evidence of perforation and often peritonitis. B. An abscess would show a localised collection. C. Toxic megacolon is a severe colonic complication associated with inflammatory or infective colitis. E. Diverticula themselves do not establish colorectal cancer.
pearl: Diverticulosis means diverticula are present, diverticular disease means they cause symptoms, and diverticulitis means inflammation; altered bowel habit in an older adult still warrants exclusion of colorectal cancer.
thinking: Pain, bloating and altered bowel habit ↓ CT: sigmoid diverticula ↓ No abscess or perforation ↓ Symptomatic diverticula without complications ↓ Diverticular disease
exam_trap: E, colorectal cancer — altered bowel habit in an older woman is a red flag, but the CT shows diverticula only; cancer must be excluded, not assumed.
takeaway: Symptomatic diverticula without inflammation = diverticular disease; inflamed = diverticulitis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with fatigue and shortness of breath. Her haemoglobin is 86 g/L and her mean cell volume is low. Which blood test is most useful to confirm iron deficiency?
why_correct: Ferritin reflects body iron stores and is the most useful routine test for confirming iron deficiency, although it can rise with inflammation.
why_wrong: B. TSH assesses thyroid function. C. Amylase is associated with pancreatic injury. D. Vitamin B12 deficiency typically causes macrocytosis. E. Troponin assesses myocardial injury.
pearl: Ferritin is the best single routine test for iron deficiency, but it rises with inflammation; once confirmed, always look for the cause, such as heavy periods, diet, coeliac disease or GI bleeding.
thinking: Fatigue and breathlessness ↓ Anaemia with low MCV ↓ Iron deficiency most likely ↓ Confirm depleted iron stores ↓ Ferritin
exam_trap: D, vitamin B12 — a standard anaemia test, but B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis, not a low MCV.
takeaway: Low-MCV anaemia: ferritin confirms iron deficiency, then find the cause.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with painful swelling of the scrotum. The affected testis is high-riding and lies horizontally. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours

why_correct: A high-riding, horizontally lying testis with acute pain is highly suggestive of testicular torsion, which requires urgent surgical management.
why_wrong: A. Torsion can cause irreversible testicular ischaemia. B. Antibiotics are appropriate for suspected epididymo-orchitis, not torsion. C. Analgesia does not treat the underlying torsion. E. Delaying assessment risks testicular loss.
pearl: A high-riding testis with a horizontal lie and absent cremasteric reflex favour torsion; epididymo-orchitis is usually more gradual with urinary symptoms, but if in doubt, explore.
thinking: Young man with acute painful scrotal swelling ↓ High-riding testis ↓ Horizontal lie ↓ Testicular torsion ↓ Immediate surgical assessment
exam_trap: B, oral antibiotics and review — appropriate for epididymo-orchitis, but treating presumed infection here risks losing a torted testis.
takeaway: Acute scrotum in a young male: torsion until proven otherwise; urology now.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents with severe colicky pain radiating from his loin to his groin. He is restless and unable to find a comfortable position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with marked restlessness is typical of renal/ureteric colic.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulitis usually causes left lower quadrant pain. C. Appendicitis usually produces right lower abdominal pain after initial central pain. D. Pancreatitis typically causes persistent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. E. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain.
pearl: Patients with renal colic cannot keep still, unlike peritonitis where they lie motionless; NSAIDs are first-line analgesia if not contraindicated, with non-contrast CT KUB to confirm.
thinking: Severe colicky pain ↓ Radiates from loin to groin ↓ Restless, cannot get comfortable ↓ Ureteric spasm around an obstruction ↓ Ureteric stone
exam_trap: C, acute appendicitis — lower abdominal pain may confuse, but patients with appendicitis lie still; restless writhing with loin-to-groin radiation means colic.
takeaway: Loin-to-groin colic with restlessness = ureteric stone.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has frequent loose stools containing blood and mucus. She has urgency and lower abdominal discomfort. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea with urgency is characteristic of ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong: A. GORD causes reflux symptoms rather than bloody diarrhoea. C. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption and diarrhoea but not typically bloody stools. D. IBS does not cause rectal bleeding. E. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain.
pearl: Ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum and extends continuously; bloody diarrhoea with urgency needs stool culture to exclude infection and referral for endoscopic assessment.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Frequent loose stools with blood and mucus ↓ Urgency ↓ Inflamed colonic mucosa ↓ Ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: D, irritable bowel syndrome — fits urgency and lower abdominal discomfort, but IBS does not cause blood in the stool.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea with urgency: think ulcerative colitis after excluding infection.

stem: A newborn becomes visibly jaundiced at 12 hours of age. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is considered pathological until proven otherwise and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Early neonatal jaundice should not be ignored. B. Physiological jaundice generally develops after the first 24 hours. D. Gilbert syndrome does not explain significant jaundice at 12 hours of life. E. Breast milk jaundice occurs later.
pearl: Early-onset neonatal jaundice is commonly due to haemolysis, such as rhesus or ABO incompatibility or G6PD deficiency; check serum bilirubin promptly and assess for sepsis.
thinking: Visible jaundice at 12 hours ↓ Physiological jaundice starts after day one ↓ Early onset implies excess bilirubin production, often haemolysis ↓ Pathological neonatal jaundice
exam_trap: B, physiological neonatal jaundice — the commonest type, but it does not appear within the first 24 hours of life.
takeaway: Day-one jaundice is pathological; physiological jaundice appears later.

stem: A 6-year-old child has fever, sore throat, a bright-red “strawberry” tongue and a fine sandpaper-like rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, sore throat, strawberry tongue and a fine sandpaper rash are classic features of scarlet fever caused by group A Streptococcus.
why_wrong: A. Rubella usually causes a milder maculopapular rash with lymphadenopathy. C. Kawasaki disease causes prolonged fever with mucosal changes, conjunctivitis, rash and lymphadenopathy, but the classic sandpaper rash and sore throat point to scarlet fever. D. Measles typically causes cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash. E. Infectious mononucleosis commonly causes pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy but not the characteristic sandpaper rash.
pearl: Scarlet fever is a notifiable group A streptococcal infection treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin; the child should stay off school until 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
thinking: Child with fever and sore throat ↓ Strawberry tongue ↓ Fine sandpaper-like rash ↓ Group A streptococcal toxin ↓ Scarlet fever
exam_trap: C, Kawasaki disease — also causes a strawberry tongue and rash, but it needs prolonged fever with conjunctivitis and extremity changes, not sore throat with a sandpaper rash.
takeaway: Sore throat + strawberry tongue + sandpaper rash = scarlet fever; treat with penicillin V.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has persistent cough, weight loss and haemoptysis. A chest X-ray shows a central hilar mass. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A central lung mass in a heavy smoker with systemic symptoms and haemoptysis is highly suggestive of bronchogenic carcinoma; small-cell carcinoma commonly arises centrally.
why_wrong: A. Sarcoidosis typically causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy rather than a unilateral central mass. B. Pulmonary embolism usually presents acutely with breathlessness and/or pleuritic chest pain. D. Bronchiectasis causes chronic productive cough and recurrent infections rather than a central mass. E. Community-acquired pneumonia usually produces an acute infective presentation.
pearl: Small-cell and squamous cell carcinomas typically arise centrally, whereas adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral; small-cell cancer is linked to SIADH and ectopic ACTH.
thinking: Heavy smoker ↓ Cough, weight loss and haemoptysis ↓ Central hilar mass on X-ray ↓ Central bronchogenic carcinoma ↓ Small-cell lung cancer
exam_trap: A, pulmonary sarcoidosis — linked to the hilum, but it causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in younger adults, not a unilateral mass with haemoptysis in a heavy smoker.
takeaway: Smoker with haemoptysis, weight loss and a hilar mass = lung cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 74-year-old man has progressive breathlessness and a persistent cough. He has a long smoking history. Spirometry shows a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio. Which pattern is present?
why_correct: A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio indicates airflow obstruction, as seen in COPD and asthma.
why_wrong: B. A reduced ratio is abnormal. C. Upper airway obstruction may alter flow-volume loops but is not defined simply by a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio. D. Restriction is characterised primarily by reduced lung volumes. E. Diffusion impairment is assessed separately.
pearl: A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio confirms airflow obstruction; in COPD it persists after a bronchodilator, whereas asthma usually shows significant reversibility.
thinking: Long smoking history ↓ Progressive breathlessness and cough ↓ FEV₁ reduced more than FVC ↓ Low FEV₁/FVC ratio ↓ Obstructive lung disease
exam_trap: D, restrictive lung disease — also causes breathlessness with abnormal spirometry, but restriction reduces both values, so the ratio is normal or high.
takeaway: Low FEV₁/FVC = obstruction; low FVC with a normal or high ratio = restriction.

stem: A 65-year-old man with cirrhosis becomes confused and develops asterixis. There is no focal neurological deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Confusion and asterixis in a patient with advanced liver disease are characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson disease is a chronic movement disorder. B. Multiple sclerosis does not typically present with this acute confusional state. C. Migraine does not explain asterixis. D. A lacunar stroke would produce a focal deficit such as pure motor or sensory loss and does not cause asterixis.
pearl: In hepatic encephalopathy look for a precipitant such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, sedatives or electrolyte disturbance; treat with lactulose, adding rifaximin to prevent recurrence.
thinking: Known cirrhosis with new confusion ↓ Asterixis (flapping tremor) ↓ No focal deficit ↓ Toxins bypass the failing liver ↓ Hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: D, lacunar ischaemic stroke — confusion in an older man raises stroke, but lacunar strokes cause focal deficits and not asterixis.
takeaway: Cirrhosis plus confusion and a flap = hepatic encephalopathy; find the precipitant.

stem: A 69-year-old man develops sudden difficulty speaking and weakness of his right arm. Which feature would most strongly suggest an acute stroke rather than a peripheral nerve lesion?

options.A: Gradual onset of weakness over several months
options.B: Symptoms that occur after exercise and resolve with rest
options.C: Isolated numbness of a single fingertip only
options.D: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
options.E: Pain and tingling in the hand on moving the wrist

correct_answer: D. Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological dysfunction is a classic presentation of acute stroke and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Gradual progression over months is not typical of an acute stroke. B. Exertional symptoms that resolve with rest do not suggest an acute cerebrovascular event. C. Isolated fingertip numbness is more suggestive of a local peripheral nerve problem. E. Movement-related wrist pain and tingling suggest a local musculoskeletal or nerve problem.
pearl: Use FAST in the community and ROSIER in the emergency department to recognise stroke; sudden focal deficits need immediate brain imaging to guide thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
thinking: Older man ↓ Sudden speech difficulty ↓ Sudden right arm weakness ↓ Central pattern, not a single nerve ↓ Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
exam_trap: C, isolated fingertip numbness — any new neurological symptom may seem worrying, but a tiny isolated area suggests a local digital nerve problem, not stroke.
takeaway: Sudden focal deficit = stroke until proven otherwise; image immediately.

stem: A 67-year-old man taking a thiazide diuretic develops confusion. Blood tests show a sodium concentration of 119 mmol/L. Which neurological complication is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Severe acute hyponatraemia can cause cerebral oedema and neurological complications including seizures.
why_wrong: A. Haematuria is a urinary tract finding. C. Jaundice indicates hepatobiliary disease. D. Cataract is unrelated to acute hyponatraemia. E. Peripheral oedema is not the characteristic acute neurological complication.
pearl: Thiazides are a common cause of hyponatraemia in older adults; severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs urgent specialist-guided treatment, avoiding over-rapid correction of sodium.
thinking: Thiazide diuretic ↓ Sodium 119 mmol/L with confusion ↓ Water shifts into brain cells ↓ Cerebral oedema ↓ Seizure
exam_trap: E, peripheral oedema — fluid problems seem linked to sodium disorders, but oedema is not the acute neurological danger; cerebral oedema causing seizures is.
takeaway: Severe hyponatraemia threatens the brain: watch for seizures and correct carefully.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with confusion and weakness. Her sodium is 118 mmol/L. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely responsible for her neurological symptoms?
why_correct: Severe hyponatraemia can cause cerebral dysfunction, including confusion, seizures and reduced consciousness.
why_wrong: B. Mild hypomagnesaemia would not usually produce this picture. C. Mild hypercalcaemia is unlikely to cause this acute neurological presentation. D. Hyperkalaemia is primarily dangerous because of its cardiac effects. E. Mild hyperchloraemia is not a typical cause of acute confusion.
pearl: Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly: raising sodium too fast risks osmotic demyelination syndrome, which can cause quadriparesis, dysarthria and dysphagia days later.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Confusion and weakness ↓ Sodium 118 mmol/L ↓ Water enters and swells brain cells ↓ Severe hyponatraemia
exam_trap: C, mild hypercalcaemia — a recognised cause of confusion in older adults, but mild elevation rarely causes this picture, and the strikingly low sodium explains it.
takeaway: Confusion with very low sodium: hyponatraemia is the cause; correct carefully.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is confused and clinically euvolaemic. Her serum sodium and serum osmolality are low, but her urine osmolality and urine sodium are inappropriately high. Thyroid and adrenal function are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine with high urinary sodium, after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, is the pattern of SIADH, caused by inappropriate ADH-driven water retention.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia with a normal or high-normal sodium. B. Type 1 diabetes causes hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis rather than euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria with dilute urine and a high-normal or raised sodium. E. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria and oedema, giving a hypervolaemic picture.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: confirm euvolaemia, normal thyroid and adrenal function and no diuretic use; manage with fluid restriction and by treating the cause, such as drugs, lung disease or malignancy.
thinking: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia ↓ Low serum osmolality ↓ Urine inappropriately concentrated with high sodium ↓ Thyroid and adrenal function normal ↓ SIADH
exam_trap: D, diabetes insipidus — also an ADH disorder, but it is the opposite: absent ADH action gives dilute urine and a high-normal or raised sodium.
takeaway: Euvolaemic low sodium with concentrated urine and normal thyroid and adrenals = SIADH.

stem: A 34-year-old man has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and jaundice. Blood tests during attacks show haemolysis. Which inherited condition causes intermittent haemolysis due to defects in red-cell membrane proteins?
why_correct: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects in red-cell membrane proteins and produces extravascular haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia due to marrow failure. C. Haemophilia A is a factor VIII deficiency. D. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia. E. Von Willebrand disease causes impaired haemostasis.
pearl: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant; look for spherocytes on the film, splenomegaly, gallstones and a family history; parvovirus B19 can trigger an aplastic crisis.
thinking: Recurrent jaundice with haemolysis ↓ Inherited cause ↓ Faulty red-cell membrane proteins ↓ Rigid spherical cells destroyed in the spleen ↓ Hereditary spherocytosis
exam_trap: A, aplastic anaemia — a haematological cause of anaemia, but it is marrow failure with pancytopenia, not haemolysis with jaundice.
takeaway: Inherited membrane defect with haemolysis and spherocytes = hereditary spherocytosis.

stem: A 66-year-old man has persistent hoarseness, dysphagia and a neck mass. Which diagnosis should be urgently excluded?
why_correct: Persistent hoarseness with dysphagia and cervical lymphadenopathy is concerning for head and neck cancer.
why_wrong: A. Reflux can cause hoarseness but should not be assumed in the presence of red-flag features. C. Viral pharyngitis is generally acute and self-limiting. D. Allergic rhinitis does not explain a neck mass. E. Otitis externa affects the external ear canal.
pearl: Head and neck cancers are strongly linked to smoking and alcohol, and HPV for oropharyngeal cancer; persistent hoarseness, dysphagia or a neck lump warrants a suspected cancer referral.
thinking: Older man ↓ Persistent hoarseness ↓ Dysphagia ↓ Neck mass, possibly nodal spread ↓ Head and neck malignancy
exam_trap: A, simple reflux without further assessment — reflux can cause hoarseness, but assuming it in the presence of a neck mass and dysphagia misses cancer.
takeaway: Hoarseness, dysphagia and a neck lump together = suspect head and neck cancer.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with painless visible haematuria. He has smoked for 40 years. Urine culture is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Reassure and repeat urinalysis in 6 months

why_correct: Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker is a red flag for urinary tract malignancy and requires urgent investigation.
why_wrong: A. Renal biopsy is not the initial investigation for suspected urinary tract cancer. B. Anticoagulation does not treat the cause and may worsen bleeding. C. There is no evidence of UTI. D. Visible haematuria requires investigation rather than reassurance.
pearl: Unexplained visible haematuria in an older adult needs a suspected cancer referral for cystoscopy and upper tract imaging; smoking is the main risk factor for bladder cancer.
thinking: Older long-term smoker ↓ Painless visible haematuria ↓ Urine culture negative ↓ Bladder or renal cancer possible ↓ Urgent urological assessment
exam_trap: C, prescribe antibiotics — UTI is a common cause of haematuria, but the culture is negative, and treating blindly delays a cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria without infection = urgent urology referral.

stem: A 7-year-old child has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea and weight loss. Blood tests show anaemia and raised inflammatory markers. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, weight loss and systemic inflammation suggest inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease.
why_wrong: A. Constipation does not explain systemic inflammation and weight loss. B. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea rather than inflammatory features. D. Reflux causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms, not bloody diarrhoea. E. Coeliac disease can cause diarrhoea and poor growth but typically does not cause bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: Children with inflammatory bowel disease often have growth failure or delayed puberty as well as gut symptoms; refer to paediatric gastroenterology for endoscopy.
thinking: Child with recurrent abdominal pain ↓ Bloody diarrhoea and weight loss ↓ Anaemia and raised inflammatory markers ↓ Chronic inflammatory bowel disease ↓ Crohn disease
exam_trap: E, coeliac disease — a common cause of diarrhoea and poor growth in children, but it does not typically cause bloody diarrhoea with raised inflammatory markers.
takeaway: Child with bloody diarrhoea, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers: think IBD.

stem: A 42-year-old woman develops proximal muscle weakness and difficulty climbing stairs. She has a heliotrope rash around the eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Proximal muscle weakness accompanied by a heliotrope rash is characteristic of dermatomyositis.
why_wrong: A. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness but not a characteristic inflammatory rash. C. MS causes neurological deficits disseminated in time and space. D. Peripheral neuropathy usually produces distal sensory and motor abnormalities. E. Osteoarthritis causes joint symptoms rather than inflammatory proximal muscle weakness.
pearl: Adult dermatomyositis is associated with underlying malignancy, so screen for cancer; look for a raised creatine kinase, Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash.
thinking: Proximal weakness, difficulty climbing stairs ↓ Heliotrope rash around the eyes ↓ Inflammatory myopathy with skin signs ↓ Dermatomyositis
exam_trap: A, myasthenia gravis — can cause proximal weakness, but it is fatigable, often with ptosis, and has no inflammatory rash.
takeaway: Proximal weakness plus heliotrope rash = dermatomyositis; screen for cancer.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty swallowing and weight loss. Endoscopy identifies an irregular oesophageal mass. Which symptom combination is particularly concerning for oesophageal cancer?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia accompanied by unexplained weight loss is a major alarm presentation for oesophageal malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Occasional hiccups are nonspecific. C. Postprandial heartburn is common and nonspecific. D. Nausea alone is nonspecific. E. Bloating is not a typical presentation of oesophageal cancer.
pearl: In the UK, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, linked to reflux and Barrett's oesophagus, is more common than squamous carcinoma; dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy.
thinking: Progressive difficulty swallowing ↓ Unexplained weight loss ↓ Mechanical obstruction with systemic effect ↓ Alarm combination ↓ Dysphagia with weight loss
exam_trap: C, heartburn after large meals — reflux is a risk factor for adenocarcinoma, but postprandial heartburn alone is common and non-specific, not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Dysphagia plus weight loss = oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and poor growth. Blood tests show low haemoglobin and low ferritin. Which investigation is most appropriate for suspected coeliac disease?
why_correct: IgA tissue transglutaminase is the standard first-line serological test for suspected coeliac disease, with total IgA also assessed.
why_wrong: A. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury. B. Stool culture investigates infective diarrhoea and does not diagnose coeliac disease. D. Anti-gliadin antibody testing is no longer recommended because of poor sensitivity and specificity. E. Occult blood testing does not diagnose coeliac disease.
pearl: Test IgA tTG together with total IgA while the child is still eating gluten; IgA deficiency gives a false negative, so an IgG-based test is then needed.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain and poor growth ↓ iron deficiency suggests malabsorption ↓ suspected coeliac disease ↓ first-line serology: IgA tissue transglutaminase
exam_trap: D, IgG anti-gliadin antibodies — sounds like a coeliac antibody test, but anti-gliadin testing is outdated, with poor sensitivity and specificity, and is not recommended.
takeaway: Suspected coeliac disease: IgA tTG plus total IgA, on a gluten-containing diet.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops severe pain and swelling around the ankle after stepping on a nail. He has diabetes. The wound is contaminated. Which aspect of his history is particularly important when assessing his need for tetanus protection?

options.A: Most recent HbA1c and glucose control
options.B: Most recent fasting serum cholesterol level
options.E: ABO blood group and red-cell antibody screen

why_correct: Tetanus prophylaxis after a potentially contaminated wound depends on the wound characteristics and the person's vaccination history.
why_wrong: A. Glycaemic control affects wound healing but does not determine tetanus prophylaxis. B. Cholesterol does not affect tetanus prophylaxis. C. Previous appendicectomy has no bearing on tetanus immunity. E. Blood group does not determine tetanus prophylaxis.
pearl: Tetanus prophylaxis after a tetanus-prone wound depends on wound risk and immunisation status: an incompletely or uncertainly immunised patient needs a vaccine dose and may also need human tetanus immunoglobulin.
thinking: Puncture wound from a nail ↓ contaminated wound = tetanus-prone ↓ need for vaccine or immunoglobulin depends on prior immunisation ↓ take the tetanus vaccination history
exam_trap: A, HbA1c and glucose control — diabetes rightly raises concern about wound healing and infection, but it does not determine tetanus prophylaxis.
takeaway: Tetanus-prone wound: decide on prophylaxis from wound risk plus vaccination history.

stem: A 22-year-old sexually active man develops dysuria and a purulent urethral discharge. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Dysuria with purulent urethral discharge is typical of urethritis, commonly caused by gonorrhoea or chlamydia.
why_wrong: B. Syphilis classically causes a painless chancre initially. C. Herpes causes painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions. D. Candidiasis more commonly causes genital itching and discharge. E. Acute hepatitis B primarily causes systemic and hepatic disease.
pearl: Test men with urethritis by NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; if gonorrhoea is suspected, take a urethral swab for culture and sensitivities before treatment, and arrange partner notification.
thinking: Young sexually active man ↓ dysuria with purulent urethral discharge ↓ urethritis ↓ commonest sexually transmitted causes: chlamydia or gonorrhoea
exam_trap: C, primary genital herpes — also causes dysuria, but it produces painful vesicles or ulcers rather than a purulent urethral discharge.
takeaway: Purulent urethral discharge with dysuria means urethritis: think gonorrhoea or chlamydia.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a painless swelling in the neck. Examination reveals several enlarged cervical lymph nodes. He reports night sweats and unexplained weight loss. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Trial of an oral antihistamine for two weeks
options.C: Reassure and review the nodes in three months
options.D: Routine dental review for an oral source of infection
options.E: Topical antibiotic to the overlying neck skin

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for possible malignancy
why_correct: Persistent lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats requires urgent investigation for malignancy, including lymphoma.
why_wrong: A. Antihistamines do not explain or investigate persistent lymphadenopathy. C. Waiting three months is inappropriate given the red-flag systemic symptoms. D. Dental disease can cause local lymphadenopathy but does not adequately explain night sweats and weight loss. E. A topical antibiotic is inappropriate without evidence of a local bacterial skin infection.
pearl: Lymphadenopathy with night sweats and weight loss (B symptoms) suggests lymphoma; refer urgently on a suspected cancer pathway, as an excision or core biopsy is needed for diagnosis.
thinking: Painless neck swelling ↓ several enlarged cervical nodes ↓ night sweats and weight loss = B symptoms ↓ possible lymphoma or other malignancy ↓ urgent assessment
exam_trap: C, reassure and review in three months — watchful waiting suits reactive nodes after an infection, but systemic B symptoms make it unsafe here.
takeaway: Lymphadenopathy plus night sweats or weight loss needs urgent cancer assessment.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has progressive difficulty swallowing. She reports that food initially sticks in the chest but she can now only tolerate liquids. Which pattern is most concerning for an obstructing oesophageal lesion?
why_correct: Mechanical obstruction classically causes dysphagia initially to solids and later to liquids as the obstruction worsens.
why_wrong: A. Dysphagia to liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder. B. Food-related discomfort alone is nonspecific. D. Hiccups are nonspecific. E. Positional symptoms are more suggestive of reflux.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia starting with solids is a mechanical obstruction pattern; dysphagia is an alarm symptom needing urgent upper GI endoscopy to exclude oesophageal cancer.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia ↓ food sticks in the chest ↓ now tolerating only liquids ↓ narrowing lumen = mechanical obstruction ↓ solids progressing to liquids
exam_trap: A, liquids progressing to solids — this reverses the pattern; difficulty with liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia.
takeaway: Solids then liquids means stricture or tumour; both from the outset suggests motility.

stem: A 59-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence presents with jaundice, ascites and confusion. What complication of chronic liver disease is most likely responsible for the confusion?
why_correct: Confusion in a patient with advanced liver disease and decompensation is characteristic of hepatic encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Acute glaucoma causes painful visual symptoms. B. Uraemic encephalopathy requires significant renal failure, which is not described here. C. Hypothyroidism causes chronic cognitive slowing rather than acute confusion in this context. D. Parkinson disease is a chronic movement disorder.
pearl: Hepatic encephalopathy is usually triggered by a precipitant such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, electrolyte disturbance or sedatives; find and treat it, and give lactulose.
thinking: Chronic alcohol dependence ↓ jaundice and ascites = decompensated cirrhosis ↓ new confusion ↓ gut-derived toxins such as ammonia reach the brain ↓ hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: B, uraemic encephalopathy — also causes confusion in a sick patient, but nothing suggests renal failure, whereas liver decompensation is obvious.
takeaway: Confusion in decompensated cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy until proven otherwise.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with infertility, irregular periods and excess facial hair. Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Premature ovarian insufficiency with raised gonadotrophin levels
options.D: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome with a 46,XY karyotype
options.E: Hypopituitarism with secondary hypogonadism and low gonadotrophins

why_correct: Irregular ovulation with clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism) and subfertility is the typical presentation of PMOS (formerly PCOS), the commonest cause of anovulatory infertility.
why_wrong: A. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes oestrogen deficiency with raised gonadotrophins and amenorrhoea, not excess facial hair. B. Turner syndrome causes ovarian failure with short stature and primary amenorrhoea, not hyperandrogenism. D. Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) presents with primary amenorrhoea and sparse body hair, not hirsutism. E. Hypopituitarism with secondary hypogonadism reduces gonadotrophin stimulation and causes amenorrhoea without hyperandrogenism.
pearl: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is diagnosed when two of three features are present: irregular or absent ovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology, after excluding other causes.
thinking: Young woman with infertility ↓ irregular periods = anovulation ↓ excess facial hair = hyperandrogenism ↓ both cardinal features together ↓ PMOS (formerly PCOS)
exam_trap: A, premature ovarian insufficiency — also causes irregular periods and subfertility, but oestrogen deficiency does not produce hirsutism.
takeaway: Irregular cycles plus hirsutism in a young woman: PMOS (formerly PCOS).

stem: A 82-year-old man is admitted with pneumonia. He becomes acutely confused and repeatedly tries to leave the ward. His attention fluctuates. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.C: Ignore the confusion because it is expected in older age
options.D: Assess for and treat underlying causes of delirium

correct_answer: D. Assess for and treat underlying causes of delirium
why_correct: Acute fluctuating confusion with impaired attention suggests delirium, which should prompt identification and treatment of precipitating factors such as infection, pain, dehydration or medication effects.
why_wrong: A. Delirium is usually due to an underlying medical problem rather than requiring psychiatric admission. B. Antidepressants do not treat acute delirium. C. Acute confusion is not a normal consequence of ageing. E. Dementia is generally chronic and progressive.
pearl: Delirium has an acute onset, fluctuating course and inattention; screen with a tool such as the 4AT, treat the cause, and use non-drug measures before considering sedation.
thinking: Older man with pneumonia ↓ acute confusion ↓ fluctuating attention ↓ delirium ↓ identify and treat precipitants such as infection, drugs and dehydration
exam_trap: E, diagnose dementia — confusion in an older adult tempts this label, but dementia is gradual; acute fluctuating inattention means delirium.
takeaway: Acute fluctuating confusion in hospital is delirium: find and treat the cause.

stem: A 45-year-old man has persistent nasal congestion, facial pressure and reduced sense of smell for several months. Examination reveals bilateral nasal polyps. Which condition is most strongly associated with nasal polyps?
why_correct: Nasal polyps commonly occur in chronic rhinosinusitis and cause persistent nasal obstruction and reduced smell.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis does not cause nasal polyps. B. Renal failure is unrelated. C. Peptic ulcer disease is unrelated. D. Aortic stenosis does not cause nasal obstruction.
pearl: Bilateral nasal polyps usually reflect chronic rhinosinusitis and are first treated with intranasal corticosteroids; a unilateral polyp or bleeding needs urgent ENT review to exclude tumour.
thinking: Months of nasal blockage ↓ facial pressure and reduced smell ↓ bilateral nasal polyps ↓ chronic sinonasal mucosal inflammation ↓ chronic rhinosinusitis
exam_trap: C, peptic ulcer disease — the only option with a chronic mucosal flavour, but it has no link to nasal polyps; persistent nasal symptoms point to the sinuses.
takeaway: Bilateral nasal polyps mean chronic rhinosinusitis; a unilateral polyp is a red flag.

stem: A 68-year-old man has fatigue and bone pain. Blood tests show anaemia and raised total protein. Which initial investigation is particularly useful when multiple myeloma is suspected?
why_correct: Serum protein electrophoresis can identify a monoclonal protein associated with multiple myeloma.
why_wrong: B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. C. Thyroid tests do not investigate a monoclonal paraprotein. D. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury. E. An isotope bone scan is unhelpful because myeloma lesions are lytic and often show no increased uptake.
pearl: When myeloma is suspected, request serum protein electrophoresis with a serum free light chain assay; light-chain-only myeloma can be missed by electrophoresis alone.
thinking: Older man with bone pain and fatigue ↓ anaemia ↓ raised total protein suggests excess immunoglobulin ↓ possible monoclonal paraprotein ↓ serum protein electrophoresis
exam_trap: E, isotope bone scan — bone pain makes this tempting, but myeloma lesions are lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so bone scans often miss them.
takeaway: Suspected myeloma: protein electrophoresis plus serum free light chains.

stem: A 57-year-old man has progressive dysphagia, weight loss and persistent reflux symptoms. Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is a major alarm presentation for oesophageal malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid cancer presents with a neck mass or compressive neck symptoms. B. Testicular cancer usually presents as a testicular mass. C. Renal cell carcinoma commonly presents with haematuria or systemic symptoms. E. Prostate cancer primarily affects the prostate and may cause urinary symptoms.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom at any age; long-standing reflux raises the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma through Barrett oesophagus, so refer urgently for endoscopy.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia ↓ weight loss ↓ persistent reflux, a risk factor via Barrett oesophagus ↓ alarm features ↓ oesophageal cancer
exam_trap: A, thyroid cancer — a neck malignancy can compress the oesophagus, but it usually presents with a neck lump, and reflux is not a risk factor.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss: oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with persistent hoarseness, difficulty swallowing and a neck mass. He has a long history of smoking. Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent hoarseness with dysphagia and a neck mass in a smoker is concerning for laryngeal or upper aerodigestive tract malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Colorectal cancer primarily causes bowel-related symptoms and does not explain this presentation. B. Prostate cancer primarily causes urinary or metastatic symptoms. C. Testicular cancer presents with a testicular lesion. E. Renal cell carcinoma does not typically present with persistent hoarseness.
pearl: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker needs urgent laryngoscopy; an accompanying neck mass suggests nodal spread and warrants a suspected head and neck cancer referral.
thinking: Long-term smoker ↓ persistent hoarseness = laryngeal involvement ↓ dysphagia and neck mass suggest local or nodal spread ↓ laryngeal cancer
exam_trap: E, renal cell carcinoma — it can metastasise widely, but it does not typically cause hoarseness, dysphagia and a neck mass.
takeaway: Smoker with persistent hoarseness and a neck lump: think laryngeal cancer.

stem: A 41-year-old man develops severe low back pain after lifting a heavy object. He has no weakness, sensory loss, bladder symptoms or systemic features. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Arrange an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine
options.B: Refer for urgent spinal surgical opinion
options.C: Bed rest for one week with analgesia
options.D: Advise staying active and offer analgesia

correct_answer: D. Advise staying active and offer analgesia
why_correct: Uncomplicated acute mechanical low back pain without red flags is generally managed conservatively, including maintaining activity and appropriate analgesia.
why_wrong: A. Imaging is not required without red flags. B. There is no indication for surgical referral without neurological deficit or red flags. C. Bed rest delays recovery and causes deconditioning. E. There is no evidence of malignancy.
pearl: Do not image low back pain without red flags; advise staying active, and NICE advises against paracetamol alone, with an oral NSAID usually first choice if suitable.
thinking: Back pain after lifting ↓ no weakness, sensory loss or bladder symptoms ↓ no systemic features ↓ no red flags = mechanical back pain ↓ stay active with analgesia
exam_trap: A, urgent MRI of the lumbar spine — severe pain tempts imaging, but without red flags MRI does not change management and may show irrelevant changes.
takeaway: Back pain without red flags: no imaging, keep active, give analgesia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with painful urination, urinary frequency and lower abdominal discomfort. A pregnancy test is positive. What diagnosis should be considered particularly important because of pregnancy?
correct_answer: B. Urinary tract infection in pregnancy
why_correct: Urinary symptoms during pregnancy require assessment because untreated urinary infection can progress to complications including pyelonephritis.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause dysuria. C. Bladder pain syndrome is a chronic diagnosis of exclusion; infection must be excluded first, and it carries no specific pregnancy-related risk. D. Otitis externa is an ear condition. E. Migraine does not cause urinary symptoms.
pearl: In pregnancy, always send a urine culture for suspected UTI and treat promptly, as infection can progress to pyelonephritis; avoid trimethoprim in the first trimester.
thinking: Dysuria, frequency and lower abdominal pain ↓ urinary tract infection ↓ positive pregnancy test ↓ higher risk of pyelonephritis and complications ↓ UTI in pregnancy
exam_trap: C, interstitial cystitis — causes bladder pain and frequency, but it is a chronic diagnosis of exclusion and infection must be ruled out first.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms in pregnancy: culture the urine and treat UTI promptly.

stem: A 4-year-old child has fever, lethargy, neck stiffness and photophobia. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?
why_correct: Fever with neck stiffness and altered general condition is highly concerning for meningitis.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa causes ear canal pain rather than meningism. C. Migraine is less likely with fever and marked systemic illness. D. Constipation does not cause meningism and fever. E. Croup causes barking cough and stridor.
pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, start IV ceftriaxone promptly; never delay antibiotics for a lumbar puncture, which is withheld if there are signs of raised intracranial pressure or shock.
thinking: Young child with fever ↓ neck stiffness and photophobia = meningism ↓ lethargy shows systemic illness ↓ meningitis
exam_trap: C, migraine — photophobia can tempt this, but fever, neck stiffness and lethargy in a child point to meningitis.
takeaway: Fever with neck stiffness and photophobia in a child is meningitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 3-year-old child has a barking cough and stridor at rest. He is becoming increasingly distressed. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Urgent assessment and treatment for severe croup
options.B: Encourage the child to lie flat
options.C: Send the child home without assessment
options.D: Examine the throat repeatedly with a tongue depressor

correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment and treatment for severe croup
why_correct: Stridor at rest indicates more severe upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: B. Distressed children with upper-airway obstruction should generally be kept comfortable rather than unnecessarily agitated or positioned inappropriately. C. Stridor at rest is an emergency warning sign. D. Repeated throat examination can increase distress and potentially worsen airway obstruction. E. Antihistamines do not provide appropriate treatment for severe croup.
pearl: Stridor at rest means severe croup: give a corticosteroid and nebulised adrenaline, with oxygen if needed, keep the child calm on a parent's lap, and avoid examining the throat.
thinking: Barking cough = croup ↓ stridor at rest ↓ increasing distress ↓ significant upper airway obstruction ↓ urgent assessment and treatment for severe croup
exam_trap: D, repeated throat examination — seems like thorough assessment, but upsetting a child with a narrowed airway can precipitate complete obstruction.
takeaway: Croup with stridor at rest is severe: treat urgently and keep the child calm.

stem:
A 6-year-old boy develops sudden severe abdominal pain and vomiting. He draws his knees up and becomes intermittently distressed. His parent reports that his stools contain blood and mucus.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and blood/mucus-containing stool are characteristic of intussusception.
why_wrong: A. Gastroenteritis usually causes diarrhoea and vomiting without this characteristic pattern. B. Constipation does not typically cause this acute presentation. C. Appendicitis usually causes progressively localising abdominal pain rather than episodic colic with blood and mucus. D. Pyloric stenosis occurs in young infants and causes projectile vomiting.
pearl: Intussusception is commonest in infants and toddlers, so in older children consider a pathological lead point; ultrasound shows a target sign, and air enema reduction is first-line if the child is stable.
thinking: Child with sudden abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ intermittent colicky distress with knees drawn up ↓ blood and mucus in the stool ↓ intussusception
exam_trap: A, gastroenteritis — vomiting and abnormal stool tempt this, but episodic colic with blood and mucus suggests bowel telescoping, not infection.
takeaway: Colicky pain plus blood and mucus in the stool in a child: intussusception.

stem:
A 7-year-old child has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. During one episode he develops severe pain, draws his knees up and then becomes temporarily settled before another episode begins.

What feature most strongly suggests an intestinal obstruction rather than simple gastroenteritis?

options.B: Low-grade fever and frequent loose stools
options.D: Reduced appetite and mild lethargy for days
options.E: A single episode of non-bilious vomiting

why_correct: Colicky pain occurring in waves is characteristic of intestinal obstruction because of repeated contractions against the obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Nausea and mild diffuse tenderness are non-specific. B. Low-grade fever with loose stools is more in keeping with gastroenteritis. D. Reduced appetite and lethargy occur in many gastrointestinal illnesses. E. A single episode of vomiting does not establish obstruction.
pearl: Colicky pain coming in waves reflects peristalsis against a blockage; colic with bilious vomiting, distension or blood in the stool in a child needs urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Recurrent abdominal pain ↓ severe episodes with knees drawn up ↓ settles between episodes ↓ waves of peristalsis against a blockage ↓ colicky, intermittent pain
exam_trap: E, a single non-bilious vomit — vomiting occurs in obstruction, but one non-bilious episode is non-specific and common in gastroenteritis.
takeaway: Waves of colicky pain with calm intervals suggest obstruction.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has persistent hoarseness for 5 weeks. He has a long history of cigarette smoking.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Voice rest and review in 6 weeks if still hoarse
options.C: Urgent referral for suspected laryngeal cancer
options.D: Oral antibiotics for presumed chronic laryngitis

correct_answer: C. Urgent referral for suspected laryngeal cancer
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness, particularly in a smoker, is a red flag for laryngeal malignancy and warrants urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Antihistamines do not address the cancer red flag. B. Hoarseness has already persisted for 5 weeks in a smoker and needs urgent suspected-cancer referral rather than further observation. D. Antibiotics are inappropriate without evidence of bacterial infection and would delay assessment. E. Speech therapy should not substitute for assessment of a potentially serious cause.
pearl: Persistent unexplained hoarseness in an older adult, particularly a smoker, needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngoscopy rather than repeated review or empirical treatment.
thinking: Hoarseness for over a month ↓ older long-term smoker ↓ no clear benign cause ↓ red flag for laryngeal cancer ↓ urgent referral
exam_trap: B, voice rest and review in 6 weeks — reasonable for short-lived hoarseness, but persistence in a smoker means delay could miss laryngeal cancer.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker: urgent laryngoscopy, not watchful waiting.

stem:
A patient with capacity refuses a recommended operation after the surgeon explains the risks and benefits. The patient understands the information and consistently maintains the decision.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Ask the patient's family to overrule the decision
options.D: Proceed with surgery because it is medically beneficial
options.E: Sedate the patient and perform the operation

why_correct: A capacitous adult has the right to refuse treatment, even when clinicians consider the treatment medically beneficial.
why_wrong: A. Family members cannot overrule a capacitous patient's decision. C. A court order is not routinely required for a capacitous refusal. D. Medical benefit does not override a valid refusal. E. Performing treatment covertly or against a capacitous refusal would be unlawful.
pearl: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, even life-saving treatment, for reasons others consider unwise; document the discussion and leave the door open for them to change their mind.
thinking: Adult patient ↓ given risks and benefits ↓ understands and consistently refuses ↓ has capacity ↓ valid refusal must be respected
exam_trap: C, obtain a court order — feels like a safe escalation, but courts are not needed to accept a capacitous refusal; they are for genuine disputes over capacity.
takeaway: A capacitous refusal must be respected, even if it seems unwise.

stem:
A doctor is asked to perform a procedure that they have never been trained to perform and do not consider themselves competent to undertake.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Perform it without informing the patient
options.B: Ask a medical student to perform it
options.C: Explain the limitation and seek appropriate senior help
options.D: Perform the procedure because they are a doctor
options.E: Attempt the procedure after watching an online video

correct_answer: C. Explain the limitation and seek appropriate senior help
why_correct: Doctors should work within the limits of their competence and seek assistance or supervision when required.
why_wrong: A. The patient should not be subjected to an unrecognised competence risk. B. Delegating an unfamiliar procedure to a less-qualified person is inappropriate. D. Being a doctor does not imply competence in every procedure. E. An online video does not constitute appropriate training or supervision.
pearl: GMC guidance requires doctors to recognise and work within the limits of their competence; declining and seeking senior help or supervision protects patient safety.
thinking: Procedure never trained in ↓ not competent to do it ↓ patient safety comes first ↓ be honest about the limitation ↓ seek senior help or supervision
exam_trap: D, perform it because they are a doctor — reflects pressure to cope, but a medical qualification does not confer competence in every procedure.
takeaway: Work within your competence and ask for senior help.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman has episodes of cold, painful fingers that change from white to blue and then red when she comes indoors after being outside in cold weather.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic colour changes of the digits triggered by cold or stress are characteristic of Raynaud phenomenon.
why_wrong: A. DVT usually causes unilateral limb swelling and pain. B. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory symptoms rather than episodic colour changes. C. Osteoarthritis causes joint symptoms rather than vascular colour changes. D. Cellulitis causes persistent erythema, warmth and swelling.
pearl: Raynaud phenomenon causes white, then blue, then red digits; onset later in adult life or features such as digital ulcers or rashes should prompt screening for connective tissue disease.
thinking: Cold triggers symptoms ↓ painful fingers ↓ white then blue then red ↓ vasospasm, ischaemia then reperfusion ↓ Raynaud phenomenon
exam_trap: B, peripheral neuropathy — finger pain and numbness tempt this, but neuropathy does not cause episodic, cold-triggered colour changes.
takeaway: White, blue, then red fingers on cold exposure: Raynaud phenomenon.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman has abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. Blood tests show iron-deficiency anaemia. She has no rectal bleeding.

Which investigation is most appropriate for suspected coeliac disease?
why_correct: Coeliac disease should be investigated initially with appropriate coeliac serology while the patient is consuming gluten.
why_wrong: A. Occult blood testing does not diagnose coeliac disease. B. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury. C. Colonoscopy is not the initial investigation for suspected coeliac disease. E. A plain abdominal radiograph does not diagnose coeliac disease.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia is a recognised reason to test for coeliac disease; check IgA tTG with total IgA, and refer adults with positive serology for duodenal biopsy.
thinking: Bloating and diarrhoea ↓ iron-deficiency anaemia without bleeding suggests malabsorption ↓ suspected coeliac disease ↓ first test is serology on a gluten-containing diet
exam_trap: C, colonoscopy as the first test — tempting for diarrhoea with anaemia, but coeliac disease affects the small bowel and serology comes first.
takeaway: Suspected coeliac disease: serology first, then duodenal biopsy if positive.

stem:
A 64-year-old man has calf pain when walking that settles after a few minutes of rest. He has a long history of smoking.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intermittent claudication is exertional limb pain caused by arterial insufficiency and is strongly associated with smoking.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes inflammatory skin changes. B. Hip osteoarthritis causes joint-related pain and may not have this vascular pattern. D. DVT usually causes persistent swelling and pain rather than reproducible exertional symptoms. E. Acute limb ischaemia causes sudden severe symptoms and threatens limb viability.
pearl: Intermittent claudication is reproducible calf pain on walking, relieved by rest; confirm PAD with the ankle–brachial pressure index, and stopping smoking is the key intervention.
thinking: Older smoker ↓ calf pain on walking ↓ settles with rest ↓ reproducible exertional ischaemia ↓ peripheral arterial disease
exam_trap: E, acute limb ischaemia — also arterial, but it causes sudden constant pain with pallor and pulselessness, not predictable exertional pain.
takeaway: Exertional calf pain relieved by rest in a smoker: claudication from PAD.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has progressive difficulty climbing stairs and lifting objects overhead. Examination shows symmetrical proximal muscle weakness. She has no sensory loss.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness without sensory loss is characteristic of an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis.
why_wrong: B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve distribution in the hand. C. Migraine does not cause persistent proximal muscle weakness. D. Osteoarthritis causes joint pain and stiffness rather than symmetrical proximal weakness. E. Peripheral neuropathy commonly produces sensory abnormalities.
