Chlamydia partner notification is not a diabetes-screening strategy. E. Fertility assessment is not the immediate purpose of partner notification.
pearl: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so partner notification finds and treats infected contacts, prevents reinfection of the index patient and reduces complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease.
thinking: Chlamydia diagnosed ↓ Partners often asymptomatic ↓ Untreated partners transmit and reinfect ↓ Treat infected partners and reduce transmission
exam_trap: E, routine fertility testing for partners — chlamydia can affect fertility, which tempts, but notification exists to test and treat contacts, not for fertility work-up.
takeaway: Partner notification exists to treat contacts and break the chain of transmission.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with painful, swollen joints and a new skin rash several days after developing a sore throat. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Migratory inflammatory arthritis following a recent streptococcal throat infection is a classic feature of acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects older adults with proximal girdle pain and stiffness, not post-pharyngitis arthritis with rash. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without inflammatory arthritis. D. Gout usually causes an acute monoarthritis in older adults and is not triggered by a sore throat. E. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and not triggered by a recent throat infection.
pearl: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and causes migratory polyarthritis, carditis and rashes such as erythema marginatum; diagnosis uses the Jones criteria with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
thinking: Recent sore throat ↓ Possible streptococcal infection ↓ Painful swollen joints plus new rash ↓ Post-streptococcal immune reaction ↓ Acute rheumatic fever
exam_trap: D, acute polyarticular gout — swollen painful joints suggest crystal arthritis, but gout is unusual in a young woman, is not triggered by a sore throat and does not cause a rash.
takeaway: Arthritis and rash after a sore throat: think acute rheumatic fever.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a photosensitive facial rash across her cheeks and nose. She also reports joint pains and fatigue. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A photosensitive malar rash with arthralgia and systemic symptoms is suggestive of SLE.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes mechanical joint symptoms and not a photosensitive rash. C. Psoriatic arthritis is associated with scaly psoriatic plaques, not a photosensitive malar rash. D. Cellulitis is an acute localised bacterial skin infection. E. Facial seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy scale involving the nasolabial folds and is not photosensitive or associated with arthralgia.
pearl: A photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, with arthralgia and fatigue, suggests SLE; ANA is a sensitive screening test, while anti-dsDNA is more specific.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Photosensitive rash over cheeks and nose ↓ Joint pain and fatigue ↓ Multisystem autoimmune picture ↓ Systemic lupus erythematosus
exam_trap: E, seborrhoeic dermatitis — another common rash in the same facial area, but it is greasy and scaly, involves the nasolabial folds and causes no joint pain or fatigue.
takeaway: Photosensitive malar rash plus arthralgia and fatigue: think SLE and check ANA.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has a painless ulcer beneath the ball of his foot. Examination reveals reduced sensation to light touch. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A painless plantar ulcer in a person with diabetes and loss of protective sensation is characteristic of a neuropathic foot ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Arterial ulcers are typically painful and associated with poor perfusion. C. Venous ulcers usually occur around the gaiter region. D. A sacral pressure ulcer would occur over the sacrum, not the plantar foot. E. Cellulitis causes inflammatory skin changes rather than a chronic painless plantar ulcer.
pearl: Neuropathic diabetic ulcers form painlessly over pressure points such as the metatarsal heads; any diabetic foot ulcer needs urgent referral to the multidisciplinary foot service.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Painless ulcer under ball of foot = pressure point ↓ Reduced sensation ↓ Loss of protective sensation ↓ Diabetic neuropathic ulcer
exam_trap: A, arterial ulcer — also common on the diabetic foot, but arterial ulcers are typically painful with signs of poor perfusion, not painless with sensory loss.
takeaway: A painless plantar ulcer with sensory loss in diabetes is neuropathic; refer to the foot team.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has severe pain in her hip after a minor fall. X-ray confirms a fracture. Which factor is most likely to have contributed?
why_correct: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is strongly suggestive of underlying osteoporosis or reduced bone strength.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause fragility fractures. C. Asthma itself does not directly explain a low-trauma fracture. D. Hyperthyroidism can affect bone health, but osteoporosis is the direct condition associated with fragility fracture. E. Otitis media is unrelated.
pearl: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less is a fragility fracture and suggests osteoporosis; after hip fracture, assess bone health and falls risk to prevent the next fracture.
thinking: 72-year-old woman ↓ Minor fall ↓ Hip fracture = low-trauma fracture ↓ Reduced bone strength ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: D, hyperthyroidism alone — a genuine risk factor for bone loss, but it acts through reduced bone density; the direct explanation for a fragility fracture is osteoporosis.
takeaway: Low-trauma fracture in an older adult means osteoporosis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is found to have a vertebral compression fracture after minimal trauma. Which investigation may be used to assess bone mineral density?
why_correct: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry is used to assess bone mineral density.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy assesses the gastrointestinal tract. C. Audiometry assesses hearing. D. Spirometry assesses lung function. E. ECG assesses cardiac electrical activity.
pearl: DXA measures bone mineral density, reported as a T-score; a T-score of −2.5 or below defines osteoporosis, and a vertebral fragility fracture should prompt bone health assessment.
thinking: 70-year-old woman ↓ Vertebral compression fracture ↓ Minimal trauma = fragility fracture ↓ Suspected osteoporosis ↓ DXA scan
exam_trap: D, spirometry — a familiar routine test in older adults, but it measures lung function; bone mineral density is measured by DXA.
takeaway: Bone mineral density is measured by DXA; a fragility fracture should trigger it.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with persistent fatigue and widespread muscle aches. Examination is normal and inflammatory markers are normal. She has poor sleep and feels exhausted despite resting. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Widespread pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance and absence of objective inflammatory findings are typical of fibromyalgia.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis causes an acutely inflamed joint and systemic illness. C. Giant cell arteritis occurs mainly in older adults and causes headache and vascular symptoms. D. Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and may cause local or systemic inflammatory features. E. Gout causes an acute inflamed joint.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis of chronic widespread pain with fatigue and unrefreshing sleep; a normal examination and normal blood tests, including inflammatory markers, support it.
thinking: Widespread muscle aches ↓ Fatigue and poor sleep ↓ Normal examination ↓ Normal inflammatory markers ↓ Fibromyalgia
exam_trap: C, giant cell arteritis — aches and fatigue may suggest it, but it affects older adults, causes headache and raises inflammatory markers, which are normal here.
takeaway: Widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep with normal tests suggests fibromyalgia.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Which public-health measure is particularly important?
why_correct: Tuberculosis can be transmitted to close contacts, so contact tracing and appropriate assessment are important.
why_wrong: A. ECG monitoring is not the key public-health intervention. B. Dairy restriction is not a standard TB-control measure. D. Salt restriction is unrelated to TB transmission. E. Appendectomy has no role.
pearl: TB is a notifiable disease in the UK; notify, start treatment and arrange contact tracing to identify latent and active infection in close contacts.
thinking: Pulmonary TB diagnosed ↓ Spread by airborne droplets ↓ Close contacts at risk ↓ Public health priority ↓ Assessment of close contacts
exam_trap: B, avoiding all dairy products — echoes the historical link between TB and unpasteurised milk, but dairy avoidance is not a control measure for pulmonary TB.
takeaway: Pulmonary TB: notify and trace close contacts.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with fever, severe sore throat and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. She is markedly fatigued. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Fever, severe pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and marked fatigue are typical of infectious mononucleosis.
why_wrong: A. Acute sinusitis causes facial pain and nasal symptoms rather than severe pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and marked fatigue. C. Migraine does not cause severe pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. D. Appendicitis causes abdominal symptoms. E. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms.
pearl: Glandular fever (EBV) causes fever, severe pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and fatigue in teenagers; amoxicillin may trigger a rash, and contact sports should be avoided because of splenic rupture risk.
thinking: Teenager ↓ Fever and severe sore throat ↓ Tender cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Marked fatigue ↓ Infectious mononucleosis
exam_trap: A, acute bacterial sinusitis — a febrile upper respiratory infection, but it causes facial pain and nasal symptoms rather than severe pharyngitis, nodes and profound fatigue.
takeaway: Teenager with sore throat, neck nodes and marked fatigue: think glandular fever.

stem: A 39-year-old woman develops watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps after returning from abroad. She has no fever or blood in the stool and remains well hydrated. What is the most appropriate general advice?

options.A: Start a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin
options.B: Maintain oral fluids and monitor symptoms

correct_answer: B. Maintain oral fluids and monitor symptoms
why_correct: Most uncomplicated traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting, with hydration being the mainstay of management.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not routinely needed for mild, afebrile, non-bloody traveller's diarrhoea in a well-hydrated patient. C. Stopping oral intake increases dehydration risk. D. There is no indication for emergency surgery. E. Corticosteroids are not indicated.
pearl: Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting; oral rehydration is the mainstay, and antibiotics are reserved for severe, febrile or bloody illness or vulnerable patients.
thinking: Watery diarrhoea after travel ↓ No fever or blood ↓ Well hydrated ↓ Uncomplicated and self-limiting ↓ Maintain oral fluids and monitor
exam_trap: A, a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin — antibiotics feel active for travel-related illness, but mild afebrile non-bloody diarrhoea does not need them and they add resistance and side-effect risk.
takeaway: Uncomplicated traveller's diarrhoea: fluids and observation, not routine antibiotics.

stem: A 77-year-old man becomes confused and agitated after admission to hospital. He repeatedly tries to get out of bed and is unable to focus on questions. What is an important initial step?

options.A: Start an antidepressant for presumed agitated depression
options.C: Arrange discharge home the same day with family support
options.D: Look for and treat an underlying physical cause
options.E: Refer to the memory clinic for dementia assessment

correct_answer: D. Look for and treat an underlying physical cause
why_correct: Acute confusion with impaired attention suggests delirium, which commonly has an underlying precipitant requiring identification and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Antidepressants do not treat acute delirium. B. Fluid restriction may worsen dehydration and delirium. C. Discharge without assessment may be unsafe. E. Acute confusion should not be labelled dementia; the acute cause must be addressed first.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention; search for and treat causes such as infection, drugs, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, pain and metabolic disturbance.
thinking: Older man, newly admitted ↓ Acute confusion and agitation ↓ Unable to focus = inattention ↓ Delirium ↓ Look for and treat the underlying cause
exam_trap: E, memory clinic referral for dementia — cognitive impairment makes it tempting, but acute inattentive confusion is delirium and its cause must be treated first.
takeaway: Acute confusion in hospital is delirium until proven otherwise: find the cause.

stem: A 70-year-old man with advanced dementia is unable to understand, retain or weigh information about a proposed procedure. What should be assessed?

options.A: His previous employment and occupational history
options.B: His most recent Mini-Mental State Examination score
options.D: His ability to drive safely and his DVLA licence status
options.E: Whether he has a formal dementia diagnosis

correct_answer: C. Whether he has decision-specific capacity
why_correct: Capacity is assessed for the particular decision at the time it needs to be made.
why_wrong: A. Employment history is irrelevant. B. A cognitive screening score does not determine decision-specific capacity. D. Driving ability is a separate issue. E. A diagnosis of dementia does not by itself determine capacity.
pearl: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision- and time-specific; a person lacks capacity if, due to an impairment of mind or brain, they cannot understand, retain, weigh or communicate the decision.
thinking: Advanced dementia ↓ Cannot understand, retain or weigh information ↓ Capacity is decision-specific ↓ Assess capacity for this decision
exam_trap: E, whether he has a formal dementia diagnosis — a diagnosis seems relevant, but no diagnosis alone proves incapacity; capacity is judged for the specific decision.
takeaway: Capacity is decision-specific; a diagnosis alone never proves incapacity.

stem: A 45-year-old patient refuses a recommended treatment after demonstrating understanding of the benefits, risks and alternatives. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Respect the refusal if the patient has capacity
options.B: Ask a relative to overrule the patient
options.C: Discharge the patient from all medical care
options.D: Treat the patient against their wishes automatically

correct_answer: A. Respect the refusal if the patient has capacity
why_correct: A capacitous adult has the right to refuse treatment, even when the decision carries significant risk.
why_wrong: B. Relatives do not normally override a capacitous adult. C. Refusal of one treatment does not mean refusal of all care. D. Treatment without valid consent is generally unlawful. E. The patient should continue to receive appropriate information and care.
pearl: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, even if the decision seems unwise or risks death; document the discussion, keep offering support and leave the door open.
thinking: Adult patient ↓ Understands benefits, risks and alternatives ↓ Has capacity ↓ Refuses treatment ↓ Respect the refusal
exam_trap: B, ask a relative to overrule — involving family feels caring, but relatives have no power to override a capacitous adult's refusal.
takeaway: A capacitous adult can refuse treatment, even unwisely; respect it and keep caring.

stem: A doctor realises that they have made a significant error in a patient's care. What is an important professional response?

options.A: Be open with the patient under the duty of candour
options.B: Avoid documenting the incident in the clinical record
options.C: Amend the clinical notes to reflect the intended care
options.D: Wait for the outcome before telling the patient anything
options.E: Attribute the error to another member of the clinical team

correct_answer: A. Be open with the patient under the duty of candour
why_correct: Professional practice requires openness and honesty when things go wrong, with appropriate disclosure and documentation.
why_wrong: B. Accurate documentation is important. C. Altering records is inappropriate. D. Delaying disclosure of a significant error is inappropriate. E. Blaming others does not fulfil professional responsibilities.
pearl: The professional duty of candour means telling the patient promptly when something goes wrong, apologising, explaining what will be done, and reporting the incident so lessons are learned.
thinking: Doctor recognises a significant error ↓ Patient's care affected ↓ Professional duty of openness ↓ Be open with the patient under the duty of candour
exam_trap: D, wait for the outcome before telling the patient — seems to spare worry, but disclosure must be prompt whatever the eventual outcome.
takeaway: When things go wrong: tell the patient promptly, apologise, document and report.

stem: A junior doctor is asked to perform a procedure they have never been trained to perform. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Pretend to have performed the procedure previously
options.B: Explain the limitation and seek appropriate supervision
options.C: Perform it independently to gain experience
options.D: Ask a medical student to supervise

correct_answer: B. Explain the limitation and seek appropriate supervision
why_correct: Doctors should work within their competence and seek appropriate help or supervision when needed.
why_wrong: A. Misrepresenting competence is unsafe and unprofessional. C. Performing an unfamiliar procedure without appropriate supervision may put the patient at risk. D. A medical student is not an appropriate supervisor. E. The appropriate response is to seek support, not abandon all clinical work.
pearl: Doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence; asking for help or supervision is a professional strength, not a weakness.
thinking: Junior doctor ↓ Asked to do an untrained procedure ↓ Outside competence ↓ Patient safety comes first ↓ Explain and seek supervision
exam_trap: C, perform it independently to gain experience — learning matters, but doing an untrained procedure unsupervised puts the patient at risk.
takeaway: Outside your competence: say so and seek supervision.

stem: A doctor is concerned that a colleague is repeatedly arriving at work smelling strongly of alcohol and appears impaired while caring for patients. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Post about it on social media
options.B: Speak to the colleague privately and take no further action
options.C: Treat it as a private health matter for the colleague
options.D: Discuss the colleague's behaviour with the patients affected
options.E: Raise the concern through formal clinical channels

correct_answer: E. Raise the concern through formal clinical channels
why_correct: Patient safety takes priority, and concerns about a colleague's fitness to practise should be raised appropriately.
why_wrong: A. Social media is not an appropriate route. B. An impaired colleague caring for patients is a patient-safety issue that needs escalation, not just a private conversation. C. A credible patient-safety concern is not a private matter. D. Discussing confidential concerns with patients is inappropriate.
pearl: If a colleague may be putting patients at risk, raise the concern promptly through local channels such as the clinical lead or medical director; patient safety outweighs loyalty.
thinking: Colleague repeatedly smells of alcohol ↓ Appears impaired while caring for patients ↓ Immediate patient-safety risk ↓ Raise through formal channels
exam_trap: B, speak privately and take no further action — feels supportive and collegial, but an impaired doctor treating patients is a safety risk that must be escalated.
takeaway: Impaired colleague treating patients: escalate formally; patient safety comes first.

stem: A 71-year-old woman reports gradually worsening central vision and difficulty reading. Examination shows bilateral central retinal changes without acute pain or redness. What condition is most likely?
why_correct: Age-related macular degeneration commonly causes progressive central visual impairment in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes inflammation and discharge rather than progressive central visual loss. B. Retinal detachment usually presents suddenly with flashes, floaters or a field defect. C. Acute angle closure causes a painful red eye. E. Open-angle glaucoma causes peripheral field loss rather than central retinal changes.
pearl: AMD causes gradual central visual loss with distortion; sudden distortion or deterioration suggests wet AMD, which needs rapid referral for anti-VEGF treatment.
thinking: 71-year-old ↓ Gradual central vision loss, difficulty reading ↓ Bilateral central retinal changes ↓ No pain or redness ↓ Age-related macular degeneration
exam_trap: E, primary open-angle glaucoma — also gradual, painless and bilateral in older adults, but it causes peripheral field loss, not central visual loss.
takeaway: Gradual central vision loss in an older adult is AMD; glaucoma takes peripheral vision first.

stem: A 72-year-old woman develops sudden painless monocular visual loss. She has hypertension and atrial fibrillation. Which vascular event is most consistent with this presentation?
why_correct: Sudden painless monocular visual loss can result from retinal arterial occlusion, particularly in patients with vascular risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Uveitis causes a painful photophobic red eye. B. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters rather than profound sudden visual loss. C. Conjunctivitis does not cause profound visual loss. D. Cataract develops gradually.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with vascular risk factors suggests retinal artery occlusion, a stroke equivalent; refer immediately, look for embolic sources such as AF and carotid disease, and consider giant cell arteritis.
thinking: Sudden painless monocular visual loss ↓ AF and hypertension = embolic and vascular risk ↓ Embolus to the retinal artery ↓ Retinal artery occlusion
exam_trap: B, posterior vitreous detachment — a common sudden painless eye event in older adults, but it causes flashes and floaters rather than profound visual loss.
takeaway: Sudden painless monocular loss with vascular risk: retinal artery occlusion, an eye stroke.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops progressive difficulty swallowing and has lost 8 kg unintentionally. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Reassure and review in one year
options.C: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor

why_correct: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm presentation requiring urgent investigation for serious oesophageal or upper gastrointestinal disease.
why_wrong: B. Delaying investigation risks missing significant disease. C. An empirical PPI trial delays urgent investigation of alarm symptoms. D. Physiotherapy is unrelated. E. Allergic rhinitis does not explain progressive dysphagia and weight loss.
pearl: Dysphagia, especially with weight loss, requires a suspected cancer pathway referral for urgent upper GI endoscopy; never mask alarm symptoms with an empirical PPI trial.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia ↓ 8 kg unintentional weight loss ↓ Alarm features ↓ Possible oesophageal or gastric cancer ↓ Urgent upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: C, trial of a proton pump inhibitor — suits uncomplicated dyspepsia, but progressive dysphagia with weight loss demands urgent endoscopy, not empirical treatment.
takeaway: Dysphagia with weight loss: urgent endoscopy, not a PPI trial.

stem: A 64-year-old man has persistent iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious dietary cause. He has no overt gastrointestinal bleeding. What should be considered?
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, particularly in an adult, can result from occult gastrointestinal blood loss and warrants appropriate investigation.
why_wrong: A. Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia, not iron deficiency. B. Migraine does not cause iron deficiency. C. Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is distinct from true iron deficiency and does not explain iron loss. E. B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia, not iron deficiency.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women needs investigation for GI blood loss, including coeliac serology and upper and lower GI investigation, to exclude gastric and colorectal cancer.
thinking: 64-year-old man ↓ Persistent iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No dietary cause, no overt bleeding ↓ Occult blood loss suspected ↓ Gastrointestinal blood loss
exam_trap: C, anaemia of chronic kidney disease — a common anaemia in older adults, but it reflects reduced erythropoietin, not true iron loss, so it does not explain iron deficiency.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older man: investigate the GI tract for occult bleeding.

stem: A 48-year-old man has severe loin pain, fever and rigors. He has known ureteric obstruction. What complication should be suspected?

options.D: Mechanical back pain from muscle strain
options.E: Osteoarthritis of the lumbar facet joints

why_correct: Fever and systemic illness in a patient with urinary obstruction suggest an infected obstructed system, which requires urgent management.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache is unrelated. B. Loin pain, rigors and known ureteric obstruction indicate a complicated upper-tract infection, not uncomplicated lower UTI. D. Mechanical back pain from muscle strain does not explain fever and rigors. E. Facet joint osteoarthritis does not cause fever and urinary obstruction.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent.
thinking: Known ureteric obstruction ↓ Severe loin pain ↓ Fever and rigors ↓ Infection behind the obstruction ↓ Infected obstructed urinary system
exam_trap: B, uncomplicated lower UTI — infection is present, but loin pain, rigors and known obstruction make this a complicated upper-tract emergency.
takeaway: Fever with an obstructed kidney needs antibiotics and urgent drainage.

stem: A 74-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is prescribed ibuprofen regularly for osteoarthritis. Which renal effect is a concern?

options.A: Increased erythropoietin production by the kidney
options.B: Permanent improvement in renal function over time
options.C: Increased glomerular filtration via afferent dilatation
options.D: Reduced renal blood flow and worsening function

correct_answer: D. Reduced renal blood flow and worsening function
why_correct: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing renal vasodilation and potentially worsening kidney function, particularly in vulnerable patients.
why_wrong: A. CKD is associated with reduced rather than increased erythropoietin production. B. NSAIDs do not improve renal function. C. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation and so reduce, rather than increase, glomerular filtration. E. NSAIDs can contribute to AKI.
pearl: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole; in CKD, especially with ACE inhibitors or diuretics, this can cut filtration and cause acute kidney injury, so prefer safer analgesic options.
thinking: CKD ↓ Regular ibuprofen ↓ Prostaglandin inhibition ↓ Afferent arteriolar constriction ↓ Reduced renal blood flow and worsening function
exam_trap: C, increased filtration via afferent dilatation — names the right vessel, but NSAIDs remove prostaglandin-driven afferent dilatation and so reduce, not increase, filtration.
takeaway: NSAIDs narrow the afferent arteriole and worsen renal function in CKD.

stem: A 42-year-old woman notices spontaneous bloody discharge from one nipple. There is no obvious infection. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.E: Repeat examination after her next period

correct_answer: A. Refer for breast clinic assessment
why_correct: Spontaneous bloody nipple discharge requires appropriate breast assessment because it can be associated with significant breast pathology.
why_wrong: B. Proton pump inhibitors have no relevance. C. The symptom warrants assessment. D. There is no evidence of infection, so antibiotics are not indicated. E. Spontaneous bloody discharge needs referral rather than delayed re-examination.
pearl: Spontaneous bloody nipple discharge from one breast needs breast clinic assessment; intraductal papilloma is a common cause, but carcinoma must be excluded with triple assessment.
thinking: Spontaneous bloody discharge ↓ From one nipple, no infection ↓ Possible papilloma or carcinoma ↓ Refer for breast clinic assessment
exam_trap: D, flucloxacillin for periductal mastitis — mastitis can cause discharge, but there are no signs of infection and bloody discharge must not be treated empirically.
takeaway: Spontaneous bloody nipple discharge needs breast clinic assessment.

stem: A 31-year-old woman discovers a painless lump in her neck. It has persisted for 6 weeks and has not responded to treatment for a presumed throat infection. What should be considered?

options.A: Benign branchial cyst managed with reassurance and no follow-up
options.B: Reactive viral lymphadenitis managed with reassurance
options.D: Recurrent tonsillitis requiring a further antibiotic course

correct_answer: E. Persistent cervical lymphadenopathy needing review
why_correct: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy requires assessment for causes including malignancy and infection.
why_wrong: A. A persistent new neck lump in an adult needs assessment rather than an assumed benign diagnosis without follow-up. B. Persistence beyond the expected course warrants reassessment rather than reassurance. C. Migraine does not cause cervical lymphadenopathy. D. A lump persisting despite treatment needs assessment for persistent lymphadenopathy rather than more antibiotics.
pearl: A neck node persisting for weeks or failing to settle after an infection needs reassessment and investigation, considering lymphoma, metastatic cancer, TB and other causes.
thinking: Painless neck lump ↓ Persisting 6 weeks ↓ Not settled after treatment for presumed throat infection ↓ Unexplained persistent node ↓ Persistent lymphadenopathy needing review
exam_trap: D, recurrent tonsillitis needing more antibiotics — the throat-infection history tempts, but a painless lump persisting despite treatment needs assessment, not further antibiotics.
takeaway: A neck lump that persists after infection needs review, not more antibiotics.

stem: A 66-year-old man develops a painless enlarging mass in his neck. He has no fever or other symptoms of acute infection. What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Start oral corticosteroids and review in a month's time
options.B: Treat as reactive nodes with a course of antibiotics
options.C: Reassure him without examination, as the mass is painless
options.D: Enlarging neck mass needs assessment for malignancy
options.E: Review the mass if it becomes painful or tender over time

correct_answer: D. Enlarging neck mass needs assessment for malignancy
why_correct: A persistent unexplained neck mass in an adult is a potential malignancy and requires appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids can alter clinical findings and are not an appropriate substitute for assessment. B. Infection cannot safely be assumed without features of infection or assessment. C. Reassurance without investigation may delay diagnosis. E. Pain is not required for malignancy.
pearl: A painless enlarging neck mass in an older adult is cancer until proven otherwise, often metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma or lymphoma; refer urgently and avoid steroids or antibiotics that delay diagnosis.
thinking: 66-year-old ↓ Painless neck mass ↓ Enlarging ↓ No features of infection ↓ Assess for malignancy
exam_trap: B, treat as reactive nodes with antibiotics — reactive nodes are common, but with no features of infection an enlarging painless mass must be assessed, not treated blind.
takeaway: Painless enlarging neck mass in an older adult: refer urgently to exclude malignancy.

stem: A 57-year-old man has pain and stiffness in his hands that is worse after use and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts around 10 minutes. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Mechanical joint pain with brief morning stiffness is typical of osteoarthritis.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects the shoulder and hip girdles. B. Reactive arthritis follows an infection and is an inflammatory arthritis. C. Rheumatoid arthritis usually causes prolonged morning stiffness and inflammatory symptoms. E. Septic arthritis causes an acutely painful, inflamed joint.
pearl: Osteoarthritis pain worsens with use and eases with rest, with brief morning stiffness of under about half an hour; inflammatory arthritis such as RA causes prolonged stiffness that eases with activity.
thinking: 57-year-old ↓ Hand pain worse with use, eased by rest ↓ Morning stiffness around 10 minutes ↓ Mechanical, non-inflammatory pattern ↓ Osteoarthritis
exam_trap: C, rheumatoid arthritis — also affects the hands, but it causes prolonged morning stiffness that improves with activity, not brief stiffness and pain on use.
takeaway: Pain worse with use and short morning stiffness means osteoarthritis, not inflammatory arthritis.

stem: A 36-year-old woman develops recurrent episodes of painful, swollen fingers and toes. She also has scaly plaques over her elbows and knees. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Inflammatory joint symptoms in a patient with psoriasis are suggestive of psoriatic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia does not cause swollen joints. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes nerve-compression symptoms. D. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative rather than inflammatory arthritis. E. Gout causes acute crystal arthritis rather than this persistent inflammatory pattern associated with psoriasis.
pearl: Psoriatic arthritis may cause dactylitis, enthesitis, DIP joint disease and nail changes such as pitting and onycholysis; ask people with psoriasis about joint symptoms.
thinking: Painful swollen fingers and toes ↓ Recurrent episodes ↓ Scaly plaques on elbows and knees = psoriasis ↓ Inflammatory arthritis with psoriasis ↓ Psoriatic arthritis
exam_trap: E, gout — recurrent painful swollen digits can mimic gout flares, but the psoriatic plaques point to psoriatic arthritis, which characteristically swells whole digits.
takeaway: Inflammatory arthritis in someone with psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of her fingers, with the entire digit becoming swollen. She also has psoriasis. What is the characteristic joint finding?
why_correct: Diffuse swelling of an entire finger or toe, giving a "sausage digit" appearance, is dactylitis and is associated with psoriatic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Tophi are deposits of urate associated with chronic gout. C. Swan-neck deformity is a characteristic deformity that can occur in rheumatoid arthritis. D. Heberden nodes are bony swellings at DIP joints in osteoarthritis. E. Boutonnière deformity is associated with disruption of the extensor mechanism.
pearl: Dactylitis, a diffusely swollen sausage digit from combined tenosynovitis and joint inflammation, is a hallmark of psoriatic arthritis and other spondyloarthritides.
thinking: Psoriasis ↓ Recurrent painful finger swelling ↓ Entire digit swollen = sausage digit ↓ Dactylitis
exam_trap: A, tophi — painful finger swellings suggest crystal disease, but tophi are discrete urate deposits of chronic gout, not diffuse whole-digit swelling.
takeaway: Whole-digit sausage swelling with psoriasis is dactylitis.

stem: A 43-year-old woman develops a new pigmented mole that has become asymmetrical, developed irregular borders and contains several different shades of brown and black. What is the most concerning diagnosis?
why_correct: Asymmetry, irregular borders and multiple colours are important warning features of melanoma.
why_wrong: B. Seborrhoeic keratoses are usually benign, often stuck-on appearing lesions. C. Dermatofibroma is typically a firm benign dermal nodule. D. Tinea corporis causes annular scaly lesions. E. Vitiligo causes depigmented patches rather than a changing pigmented lesion.
pearl: Use the ABCDE features (asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter, evolution) to spot melanoma; a changing pigmented lesion warrants urgent suspected-cancer referral.
thinking: New pigmented mole ↓ Asymmetry, irregular border and several colours ↓ Classic ABCDE warning features ↓ Melanoma
exam_trap: B, seborrhoeic keratosis — it is common and can be pigmented and multicoloured, but it looks stuck-on and is not a new mole evolving asymmetry and irregular borders.
takeaway: A changing, asymmetrical, multicoloured mole is melanoma until proven otherwise.

stem: A 67-year-old woman reports several episodes of fresh blood mixed with her stool. She has no anal pain. What condition should be considered?
why_correct: Rectal bleeding, particularly when mixed with stool and without anal pain, requires assessment for colorectal pathology including cancer.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause rectal bleeding. C. Reflux does not cause rectal bleeding. D. Anal fissure typically causes painful defaecation and bright-red blood. E. Peptic ulcer disease usually causes upper gastrointestinal bleeding, which may produce melaena.
pearl: In an older adult, rectal bleeding mixed with stool and without anal pain points to a source above the anus; colorectal cancer must be excluded before blaming haemorrhoids.
thinking: 67-year-old with rectal bleeding ↓ Blood mixed with stool ↓ No anal pain, so fissure unlikely ↓ Colonic source must be excluded ↓ Colorectal cancer
exam_trap: D, anal fissure — it causes bright-red bleeding, but with sharp pain on defaecation and blood on the surface; painless blood mixed into stool at 67 suggests colorectal pathology.
takeaway: Painless blood mixed into the stool in an older adult needs colorectal cancer excluded.

stem: A 52-year-old man notices a change in the shape of his stools and has developed persistent constipation alternating with loose stools. He has no previous bowel disorder. What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Start oral corticosteroids for presumed inflammatory colitis
options.B: Increase dietary fibre and review the symptoms in a year
options.C: Persistent change in bowel habit needs assessment
options.D: Wait for rectal bleeding to develop before investigating
options.E: Diagnose IBS and start an antispasmodic such as mebeverine

correct_answer: C. Persistent change in bowel habit needs assessment
why_correct: A persistent new change in bowel habit can indicate significant bowel pathology and should not automatically be attributed to IBS.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids are not appropriate without an established diagnosis. B. A persistent new bowel-habit change needs assessment, not a year's delay. D. Significant bowel disease can occur without bleeding. E. IBS is a diagnosis made in an appropriate clinical context after considering alarm features.
pearl: A new, persistent change in bowel habit in a middle-aged or older adult is a red flag for colorectal cancer; it should be investigated rather than labelled as IBS.
thinking: 52-year-old with no prior bowel disorder ↓ New change in stool shape and alternating habit ↓ Persistent new change is an alarm feature ↓ Persistent change in bowel habit needs assessment
exam_trap: E, diagnose IBS and start mebeverine — the alternating pattern sounds like IBS, but new-onset symptoms at 52 are an alarm feature and IBS is diagnosed only after excluding red flags.
takeaway: New-onset bowel habit change later in life is investigated, not assumed to be IBS.

stem: A 49-year-old man reports painless bright-red bleeding after defaecation. Examination identifies enlarged haemorrhoids. Which symptom is particularly typical of haemorrhoids?
why_correct: Haemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red bleeding associated with defaecation.
why_wrong: B. Haemoptysis is coughing blood from the respiratory tract. C. Haematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding. D. Melaena usually indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than haemorrhoids. E. Dysphagia concerns the upper gastrointestinal tract.
pearl: Haemorrhoids typically cause painless bright-red blood on the paper or dripping into the pan after defaecation; significant pain suggests a fissure or thrombosed haemorrhoid instead.
thinking: Painless bleeding after defaecation ↓ Enlarged haemorrhoids on examination ↓ Bleeding from vascular cushions in the anal canal ↓ Bright-red rectal bleeding
exam_trap: D, black tarry stools — it is a form of gastrointestinal bleeding so may tempt, but melaena reflects digested blood from an upper GI source, not the anal canal.
takeaway: Haemorrhoids bleed bright red and painlessly; melaena points to an upper GI source.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has severe pelvic pain during intercourse and painful periods. She has no fever or abnormal vaginal discharge. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia are characteristic symptoms of endometriosis.
why_wrong: A. Cystitis causes dysuria and urinary frequency. B. Candidiasis causes itching and superficial discomfort. D. PID more commonly causes pelvic pain with infection-related symptoms such as abnormal discharge or fever. E. Bacterial vaginosis causes discharge and odour rather than cyclical deep pelvic pain.
pearl: Dysmenorrhoea with deep dyspareunia in a woman of reproductive age points to endometriosis; diagnosis is often delayed for years, so take these symptoms seriously.
thinking: Painful periods ↓ Deep pain during intercourse ↓ No fever or discharge, so infection less likely ↓ Ectopic endometrial tissue causing cyclical pain ↓ Endometriosis
exam_trap: D, pelvic inflammatory disease — it also causes pelvic pain and deep dyspareunia, but the absence of fever and abnormal discharge and the link to periods favour endometriosis.
takeaway: Dysmenorrhoea plus deep dyspareunia without infective features suggests endometriosis.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding one year after her last menstrual period. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
why_correct: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment because it can be a presenting symptom of endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Candidiasis causes itching and discharge rather than postmenopausal bleeding. C. A Bartholin abscess causes a painful vulval swelling. D. Ovulation does not normally cause bleeding after menopause. E. Menstruation has ceased after menopause.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; it needs prompt gynaecological assessment, usually starting with transvaginal ultrasound of endometrial thickness.
thinking: 54-year-old ↓ Bleeding a year after the last period ↓ This is postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Most important serious cause to exclude ↓ Endometrial cancer
exam_trap: E, normal menstruation — a return of periods may seem possible, but 12 months of amenorrhoea defines menopause, so any bleeding now is postmenopausal and needs investigation.
takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs endometrial cancer excluded.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent postmenopausal bleeding. Examination reveals a visible lesion arising from the cervix. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Treat with an antifungal cream only
options.C: Reassurance because cervical lesions are always benign

why_correct: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding requires appropriate assessment for significant cervical pathology, including malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Antifungal treatment is inappropriate without evidence of candidiasis. B. HRT is not treatment for an unexplained cervical lesion. C. Cervical lesions are not invariably benign. D. Persistent postmenopausal bleeding should not simply be observed.
pearl: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding must be assessed urgently for cervical cancer; a cervical screening test is not the right tool for a symptomatic, visible lesion.
thinking: 58-year-old with recurrent postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Visible lesion on the cervix ↓ Possible cervical malignancy ↓ Urgent gynaecological assessment
exam_trap: C, reassurance because cervical lesions are always benign — polyps and ectropion are common, but no visible lesion with postmenopausal bleeding can be assumed benign without assessment.
takeaway: A visible cervical lesion with postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent gynaecological referral.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a new unilateral headache and scalp tenderness. He also reports pain when chewing. Which blood test is particularly useful when assessing for giant cell arteritis?
why_correct: CRP is an inflammatory marker commonly used alongside ESR when assessing suspected giant cell arteritis.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. Amylase may be raised in pancreatic disease. D. Liver function tests are used in assessment of hepatobiliary disease. E. Antinuclear antibodies are used in connective tissue disease, not giant cell arteritis.
pearl: In suspected giant cell arteritis, check CRP and ESR but start high-dose glucocorticoids without waiting for results or biopsy, because vision is at risk.
thinking: Older adult with new unilateral headache ↓ Scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ Suspected giant cell arteritis ↓ Inflammatory markers support the diagnosis ↓ C-reactive protein
exam_trap: E, antinuclear antibodies — autoimmune tests feel relevant to a vasculitis, but ANA is used for connective tissue disease; GCA is supported by raised CRP and ESR.
takeaway: Suspected GCA: check CRP and ESR, but start steroids without waiting.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after minor injuries. His platelet count is normal. Which type of disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Excessive bleeding despite a normal platelet count suggests a problem with platelet function or the coagulation system.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis affects bone strength rather than haemostasis. B. Hyperthyroidism due to Graves disease does not typically cause this bleeding pattern. C. B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia and does not explain a bleeding tendency with a normal platelet count. D. Secondary polycythaemia raises the haematocrit and does not explain recurrent mucosal bleeding.
pearl: Mucosal bleeding such as epistaxis with a normal platelet count suggests a platelet function or coagulation defect, most commonly von Willebrand disease; check a clotting screen and von Willebrand studies.
thinking: Recurrent nosebleeds ↓ Prolonged bleeding after minor injury ↓ Platelet count normal, so not thrombocytopenia ↓ Defect of platelet function or coagulation ↓ Platelet or clotting disorder
exam_trap: D, secondary polycythaemia due to smoking — it is a haematological condition so may tempt, but it raises the haematocrit rather than impairing haemostasis.
takeaway: Bleeding tendency with a normal platelet count points to a function or clotting defect.

stem: A 28-year-old man has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of his knee without preceding trauma. His serum urate is normal during the acute episode. What is an important principle?

options.A: Normal urate during a flare excludes gout
options.B: Knee involvement makes gout very unlikely
options.C: Normal urate during a flare does not exclude gout
options.D: Gout in men under 30 is usually due to renal failure
options.E: Joint aspiration is unhelpful when urate is normal

correct_answer: C. Normal urate during a flare does not exclude gout
why_correct: Serum urate can be normal during an acute gout flare, so the diagnosis should not be excluded solely on this basis.
why_wrong: A. A normal level during an acute attack does not rule out gout. B. Gout can affect large joints, including the knee. D. Hyperuricaemia has multiple causes and is not usually due to renal failure. E. Synovial fluid crystal analysis remains diagnostic regardless of serum urate.
pearl: Serum urate can fall during an acute gout flare, so recheck it once the flare has settled; joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent urate crystals is diagnostic.
thinking: Recurrent painful knee swelling without trauma ↓ Gout remains possible in a young man ↓ Urate may fall during an acute flare ↓ Normal urate during a flare does not exclude gout
exam_trap: A, normal urate excludes gout — it seems logical that gout needs a high urate, but levels often fall during flares; recheck after the flare and aspirate the joint for crystals.
takeaway: Normal urate in a flare does not exclude gout; recheck later or aspirate.

stem: A 69-year-old woman is diagnosed with a hip fracture after a low-energy fall. Which underlying condition is particularly relevant to consider?
why_correct: A fragility fracture after a low-energy fall should prompt consideration of osteoporosis.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without causing fragility fractures. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve at the wrist. D. Gout causes inflammatory arthritis. E. Hyperthyroidism can contribute to bone loss but is not the primary condition suggested by this presentation.
pearl: A hip fracture from a fall from standing height or less is a fragility fracture; it should trigger bone health assessment and treatment to prevent further fractures.
thinking: 69-year-old woman ↓ Hip fracture after a low-energy fall ↓ Healthy bone should withstand this force ↓ Fragility fracture implies weak bone ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: E, hyperthyroidism only — it can reduce bone density so may tempt, but it is a secondary contributor; the condition a fragility fracture directly indicates is osteoporosis.
takeaway: A low-energy hip fracture is a fragility fracture: think osteoporosis.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has progressive difficulty swallowing solid food but can swallow liquids normally. What mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Dysphagia initially affecting solids suggests a mechanical obstruction within the oesophagus.
why_wrong: A. Gastroenteritis does not cause progressive dysphagia. C. Gastric outlet obstruction occurs beyond the oesophagus. D. Oropharyngeal weakness causes difficulty initiating swallowing. E. Functional diarrhoea does not affect swallowing.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia to solids suggests a mechanical stricture or tumour, while solids and liquids affected from the outset suggests a motility disorder. New dysphagia needs urgent endoscopy.
thinking: 61-year-old with progressive dysphagia ↓ Solids affected, liquids still pass ↓ Narrowed oesophageal lumen ↓ Structural cause such as stricture or cancer ↓ Mechanical obstruction
exam_trap: D, oropharyngeal weakness — a recognised dysphagia mechanism, but it causes difficulty initiating swallowing with coughing or choking, not progressive solid-food dysphagia.
takeaway: Progressive solids-first dysphagia means mechanical obstruction until proven otherwise.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with coeliac disease continues to eat gluten before undergoing diagnostic blood tests. Why is this important?

options.A: Gluten prevents blood from clotting during venepuncture
options.B: Gluten avoidance can cause falsely negative serology
options.C: Gluten intake causes false-positive serum pregnancy tests
options.D: Gluten intake increases serum troponin to diagnostic levels
options.E: Gluten exposure is needed for accurate HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing

correct_answer: B. Gluten avoidance can cause falsely negative serology
why_correct: Coeliac serology is most informative while the patient is consuming gluten.
why_wrong: A. Gluten does not prevent normal coagulation. C. Gluten does not cause false-positive pregnancy tests. D. Gluten does not characteristically increase troponin. E. HLA typing is genetic and unaffected by gluten intake.
pearl: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy are only reliable while the patient is eating gluten; advise gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing.
thinking: Coeliac testing planned ↓ Antibodies are produced in response to gluten ↓ Avoiding gluten lets antibody levels fall ↓ Gluten avoidance can cause falsely negative serology
exam_trap: E, gluten exposure needed for HLA typing — it tempts because gluten matters for coeliac tests, but HLA-DQ2/DQ8 is genetic and unaffected by diet; serology depends on gluten.
takeaway: Patients must keep eating gluten until coeliac testing is complete.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and dark urine. Which underlying condition should be considered?
why_correct: Painless obstructive jaundice is an important presentation of pancreatic or biliary malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without dark urine. D. Biliary colic is painful and does not usually cause persistent painless jaundice. E. Migraine causes neurological symptoms rather than obstructive jaundice.
pearl: Painless obstructive jaundice in an older adult suggests pancreatic head or biliary malignancy; a palpable non-tender gallbladder makes gallstones unlikely. Arrange urgent imaging.
thinking: 70-year-old with jaundice ↓ Dark urine suggests conjugated, obstructive picture ↓ Painless, so stones less likely ↓ Malignant bile duct obstruction ↓ Pancreatic or biliary malignancy
exam_trap: D, biliary colic from gallstones — stones are a common cause of obstructive jaundice, but they usually cause pain; painless jaundice in an older adult suggests malignancy.
takeaway: Painless obstructive jaundice in older adults is pancreatic or biliary cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 48-year-old man develops severe central abdominal pain followed by rigid abdominal muscles and marked tenderness. What condition should be suspected?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with guarding and rigidity suggests peritoneal inflammation.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic does not typically cause generalized rigidity. C. IBS does not cause peritonism. D. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. E. Functional dyspepsia does not cause peritoneal signs.
pearl: Board-like rigidity, guarding and marked tenderness indicate peritonitis, often from a perforated viscus; resuscitate, give analgesia and seek urgent surgical review.
thinking: Severe central abdominal pain ↓ Followed by rigid abdominal muscles ↓ Marked tenderness ↓ Signs of peritoneal irritation ↓ Peritonitis
exam_trap: A, biliary colic — it causes severe abdominal pain, but it is right upper quadrant pain without generalised rigidity; rigidity signals peritoneal inflammation.
takeaway: Abdominal rigidity and guarding mean peritonitis and need urgent surgical review.

stem: A 26-year-old man twists his knee while playing football. He subsequently develops locking of the knee and pain along the joint line. What injury should be considered?
why_correct: Joint-line pain with mechanical locking after a twisting injury is typical of a meniscal tear.
why_wrong: A. Plantar fasciitis affects the plantar heel. B. Achilles rupture affects the ankle. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the wrist and hand. D. Tennis elbow affects the lateral elbow.
pearl: A twisting injury on a weight-bearing knee followed by locking and joint-line tenderness suggests a meniscal tear; MRI confirms it when needed.
thinking: Twisting knee injury playing football ↓ Mechanical locking ↓ Joint-line pain ↓ Torn meniscal fragment blocking movement ↓ Meniscal tear
exam_trap: B, Achilles rupture — a common sports injury in young adults, but it affects the heel and ankle and causes loss of push-off power, not knee locking.
takeaway: Twisting injury plus locking and joint-line pain means meniscal tear.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has gradually increasing shoulder pain and marked difficulty moving her shoulder in several directions. Passive and active movement are both restricted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Frozen shoulder causes painful restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute inflammatory joint attacks. B. Tennis elbow affects the lateral elbow. D. Achilles tendinopathy affects the ankle. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) restricts both active and passive movement, especially external rotation; it is more common in middle age and in people with diabetes.
thinking: 58-year-old with gradually worsening shoulder pain ↓ Restriction in several directions ↓ Active and passive movement both limited ↓ Capsular stiffening ↓ Frozen shoulder
exam_trap: A, gout — it may tempt as a cause of joint pain and stiffness, but it causes acute, intensely inflamed attacks, not gradual global loss of shoulder movement.
takeaway: Loss of both active and passive shoulder movement suggests frozen shoulder.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops shoulder pain after repeatedly lifting heavy objects. There is painful movement of the shoulder, particularly when lifting the arm. What type of problem is most likely?
why_correct: Shoulder pain associated with overhead or lifting activities commonly results from rotator cuff pathology.
why_wrong: B. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain. C. Achilles rupture affects the lower leg and ankle. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. E. Meniscal injury affects the knee.
pearl: Rotator cuff disorders cause pain on lifting or abducting the arm, often with a painful arc, while passive range is largely preserved, which helps distinguish them from frozen shoulder.
thinking: Shoulder pain after repetitive heavy lifting ↓ Pain worse on raising the arm ↓ Overloaded cuff tendons under the acromion ↓ Rotator cuff disorder
exam_trap: E, meniscal tear — like cuff disease it is an overuse or sports soft-tissue injury, but it occurs in the knee, so it cannot explain shoulder pain on lifting.
takeaway: Shoulder pain on lifting or abduction after overuse suggests rotator cuff pathology.

stem: A 74-year-old man has severe back pain following a minor fall. An X-ray shows a vertebral compression fracture. Which condition is an important underlying risk factor?
why_correct: Osteoporosis weakens bone and can cause vertebral compression fractures after minimal trauma.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a peripheral nerve disorder. B. IBS does not cause bone fragility. C. Migraine does not cause vertebral fractures. D. Gout does not typically cause fragility fractures.
pearl: A vertebral compression fracture after minimal trauma is a fragility fracture; treat the pain, assess bone health and consider whether causes such as myeloma or metastases need excluding.
thinking: 74-year-old man ↓ Severe back pain after a minor fall ↓ Vertebral compression fracture on X-ray ↓ Minimal trauma suggests fragile bone ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: D, gout — a common metabolic condition in older men, but it causes inflammatory arthritis, not bone fragility or compression fractures.
takeaway: Vertebral fracture from minor trauma signals osteoporosis, in men as well as women.

stem: A 76-year-old woman develops a new unilateral headache and pain when chewing. She also reports transient visual blurring. What complication of giant cell arteritis is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Giant cell arteritis can compromise the ophthalmic circulation and cause permanent visual loss, making urgent recognition and treatment essential.
why_wrong: A. Cataracts do not develop within hours from GCA. B. Corneal abrasion is unrelated to the underlying vasculitis. D. Retinal detachment is not the characteristic complication. E. Otitis externa is unrelated to GCA.
pearl: Visual symptoms in suspected giant cell arteritis are an emergency: give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and refer urgently to ophthalmology, as visual loss is often irreversible.
thinking: 76-year-old with new unilateral headache ↓ Jaw claudication ↓ Transient visual blurring ↓ Ischaemia of the optic nerve circulation ↓ Permanent visual loss
exam_trap: D, retinal detachment from trauma — it is a sight-threatening emergency, but it follows flashes and floaters and is not a complication of the arteritis in GCA.
takeaway: GCA with visual symptoms needs immediate steroids to prevent permanent blindness.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting several seconds, triggered by turning over in bed. She has no hearing loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief, position-triggered episodes of vertigo without hearing loss are characteristic of BPPV.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular migraine can cause longer episodes and is associated with migraine features. B. Vestibular schwannoma usually causes progressive unilateral hearing loss. D. Ménière disease causes longer episodes with hearing symptoms and tinnitus. E. Labyrinthitis causes prolonged vertigo, often with hearing symptoms.
pearl: BPPV causes brief vertigo provoked by head movement; confirm with the Dix-Hallpike test and treat with the Epley manoeuvre rather than vestibular sedatives.
thinking: Recurrent vertigo lasting seconds ↓ Triggered by turning over in bed ↓ No hearing loss ↓ Positional inner-ear cause ↓ Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
exam_trap: D, Ménière disease — also recurrent vertigo, but attacks last minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, which are absent here.
takeaway: Seconds-long positional vertigo without hearing loss is BPPV.

stem: A 43-year-old man develops sudden unilateral hearing loss over several hours. There is no earwax or other obvious external-ear cause. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Wait several months before seeking help

why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a time-sensitive condition requiring prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. Delaying assessment can delay potentially beneficial treatment. B. The cause must be assessed rather than assumed to be benign. C. Ear drops do not treat sensorineural hearing loss. E. Sudden hearing loss is not normal ageing.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency; once wax and external causes are excluded, refer urgently, as early steroid treatment may improve recovery.
thinking: Sudden unilateral hearing loss over hours ↓ No wax or external-ear cause ↓ Likely sensorineural ↓ Time-sensitive treatment window ↓ Urgent assessment is required
exam_trap: C, treat routinely with ear drops — drops suit wax or otitis externa, but these have been excluded; sudden sensorineural loss needs urgent ENT assessment.
takeaway: Sudden unexplained hearing loss needs urgent same-day ENT assessment.

stem: A 4-month-old infant with bronchiolitis is feeding poorly and has increasing respiratory effort. Which finding is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Apnoea is a serious feature in an infant with bronchiolitis and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Cough is expected in bronchiolitis. B. Nasal congestion is common. D. Rhinorrhoea is common in viral respiratory infections. E. Some reduction in feeding can occur, although significant feeding difficulty is concerning.
pearl: In bronchiolitis, apnoea, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis or persistently low oxygen saturations are red flags needing emergency referral; young infants are most at risk.
thinking: 4-month-old with bronchiolitis ↓ Poor feeding and rising work of breathing ↓ Look for red-flag features ↓ Apnoea signals exhaustion ↓ Apnoeic episodes
exam_trap: E, slight reduction in appetite — feeding matters in bronchiolitis, but a mild drop is expected; markedly reduced intake or apnoea is what signals danger.
takeaway: Apnoea in an infant with bronchiolitis is a red flag for emergency care.

stem: A 2-year-old child develops sudden severe coughing and wheezing while playing with small toys. What is the most important initial consideration?
why_correct: Sudden respiratory symptoms during play with small objects should raise immediate concern about foreign-body aspiration.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis does not cause sudden wheezing after playing with an object. B. Croup produces characteristic barking cough and stridor. C. Bronchiolitis usually follows viral symptoms. D. Asthma is not typically triggered by a sudden choking event.
pearl: Sudden choking, coughing or wheeze in a toddler, especially while playing with small objects, suggests an inhaled foreign body; bronchoscopy may be needed even if symptoms settle.
thinking: 2-year-old ↓ Sudden onset of coughing and wheeze ↓ Playing with small toys at the time ↓ Choking-type event ↓ Inhaled foreign body
exam_trap: B, croup — common at this age with noisy breathing, but it follows a coryzal illness with barking cough and stridor, not a sudden onset during play.
takeaway: Sudden cough and wheeze while playing with small objects means foreign body.

stem: A 2-year-old child has a seizure during a fever. The seizure lasts 25 minutes. What is the most appropriate classification?
why_correct: A febrile seizure lasting more than 5 minutes requires emergency management because of the risk of status epilepticus.
why_wrong: A. A simple febrile seizure is brief (under 15 minutes) and generalised. B. Syncope is not a prolonged convulsive state. C. Rigors with febrile delirium are not a seizure and do not explain a 25-minute convulsion. E. Breath-holding episodes occur in specific circumstances and do not explain a prolonged convulsion.
pearl: Any febrile seizure lasting more than 5 minutes needs emergency treatment as for status epilepticus; a seizure this long is never classed as a simple febrile seizure.
thinking: 2-year-old ↓ Seizure during a fever ↓ Lasts 25 minutes ↓ Far beyond a brief simple febrile seizure ↓ Prolonged febrile seizure
exam_trap: A, typical simple febrile seizure — the age and fever fit, but simple seizures are brief and generalised; 25 minutes makes it prolonged and an emergency.
takeaway: A long febrile seizure is not simple; over 5 minutes needs emergency treatment.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. He is growing normally, has no weight loss or rectal bleeding, and examination is normal. Which feature would be a red flag requiring further assessment?
why_correct: Weight loss is an alarm feature in a child with recurrent abdominal pain.
why_wrong: A. Mild intermittent pain alone is not necessarily a red flag. B. Stress-related symptoms can occur in functional abdominal pain. C. Symptoms associated with school can occur with functional disorders. E. Normal growth is reassuring.
pearl: Most recurrent abdominal pain in children is functional, but weight loss, faltering growth, rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms or persistent vomiting suggest organic disease.
thinking: Child with recurrent abdominal pain ↓ Growing well with normal examination ↓ Which feature would change this ↓ Weight loss suggests organic disease ↓ Unintentional weight loss
exam_trap: B, symptoms associated with stress — it may seem worrying, but a link to stress is typical of functional abdominal pain and is not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Weight loss turns childhood recurrent abdominal pain into a red-flag presentation.

stem: A 3-year-old child has diarrhoea and vomiting. He is thirsty and has dry mucous membranes but remains alert and is drinking. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: Oral rehydration is appropriate for children with mild-to-moderate dehydration who can drink.
why_wrong: A. Restricting fluids would worsen dehydration. B. Antidiarrhoeal medicines are generally not appropriate in young children. C. Antibiotics are not routinely required for uncomplicated gastroenteritis. E. Insulin does not treat dehydration from gastroenteritis.
pearl: Children with gastroenteritis and clinical dehydration who are alert and can drink should have oral rehydration solution, given little and often; IV fluids are for shock or ORS failure.
thinking: 3-year-old with diarrhoea and vomiting ↓ Thirst and dry mucous membranes ↓ Alert and drinking, no shock ↓ Mild-to-moderate dehydration ↓ Oral rehydration solution
exam_trap: C, immediate IV antibiotics — an unwell child may seem to need urgent intervention, but most gastroenteritis is viral and the priority is oral rehydration.
takeaway: Alert, drinking, dehydrated child: oral rehydration solution first.

stem: A 4-year-old child with gastroenteritis becomes lethargic, has markedly reduced urine output and cannot keep fluids down. What is the main concern?
why_correct: Lethargy, oliguria and inability to maintain oral intake are concerning features of significant dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Post-infective lactose intolerance causes ongoing loose stools, not acute lethargy and oliguria. C. Allergic rhinitis does not cause oliguria. D. Otitis externa does not explain the presentation. E. Constipation does not explain the acute systemic findings.
pearl: Red-flag signs in a dehydrated child include lethargy or altered responsiveness, reduced urine output, tachycardia and sunken eyes; inability to keep fluids down needs urgent escalation.
thinking: Child with gastroenteritis ↓ Lethargy ↓ Markedly reduced urine output ↓ Cannot keep fluids down ↓ Significant dehydration
exam_trap: A, post-infective lactose intolerance — it does follow gastroenteritis, but it causes persistent loose stools, not acute lethargy, oliguria and inability to keep fluids down.
takeaway: Lethargy and oliguria in gastroenteritis signal significant dehydration.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had constipation for 8 months, starting around the time of toilet training. He withholds stool, passes large, hard stools and frequently soils his underwear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: A. Functional constipation with overflow soiling
why_correct: Constipation starting around toilet training with withholding behaviour and large hard stools is functional constipation; faecal impaction lets softer stool leak around it, causing overflow soiling (NICE CG99).
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and faltering growth but does not best explain withholding and overflow soiling. C. Hirschsprung disease usually presents from birth with delayed meconium, and soiling is uncommon. D. Intussusception is an acute obstructive emergency with colicky pain and vomiting. E. Appendicitis is an acute illness with abdominal pain and fever, not months of constipation.
pearl: Overflow soiling in a constipated child is not deliberate: loose stool leaks around an impacted mass. Disimpaction with macrogol, then maintenance laxatives and toileting, is the mainstay.
thinking: Constipation for 8 months ↓ Began around toilet training ↓ Withholding with large hard stools ↓ Soiling from leakage around impacted stool ↓ Functional constipation with overflow soiling
exam_trap: C, Hirschsprung disease — it causes chronic constipation, but usually presents from birth with delayed meconium; onset at toilet training with withholding is functional.
takeaway: Constipation starting at toilet training with withholding and soiling is functional.

stem: A 6-year-old child has constipation and abdominal pain. He is otherwise well and growing normally. Which initial management is most appropriate?

options.D: Arrange urgent abdominal X-ray and blood tests
options.E: Dietary fibre changes alone without a laxative

correct_answer: A. Regular toileting and laxative treatment
why_correct: Behavioural measures, regular toileting and appropriate laxative treatment form the basis of management of childhood constipation.
why_wrong: B. Chemotherapy has no role. C. Fluid restriction can worsen constipation. D. Investigations are not needed for idiopathic constipation in a well, normally growing child. E. Dietary measures alone are not recommended as first-line treatment.
pearl: In idiopathic childhood constipation, start a laxative (macrogol first line) with behavioural measures such as scheduled toileting and a reward system; diet changes alone are not enough.
thinking: 6-year-old with constipation and abdominal pain ↓ Otherwise well and growing normally ↓ No red flags, so idiopathic ↓ Laxatives plus behavioural measures ↓ Regular toileting and laxative treatment
exam_trap: E, dietary fibre changes alone — diet advice feels gentler and is part of care, but it is not recommended as sole first-line treatment; a laxative is needed.
takeaway: Treat childhood constipation with laxatives plus toileting, not diet alone.

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after accidentally swallowing a button battery. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Give an antacid and review the child again in 48 hours
options.B: Discharge and check stools for the battery passing
options.C: Give an antidiarrhoeal and observe for passage at home
options.D: Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
options.E: Induce vomiting with ipecacuanha to expel the battery

correct_answer: D. Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
why_correct: Button batteries can cause serious tissue injury, particularly when lodged in the oesophagus, and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Antacids do not prevent battery-related tissue damage, and delay is dangerous. B. Discharge without imaging can miss oesophageal impaction and severe injury. C. Antidiarrhoeals have no role. E. Inducing vomiting is unsafe.
pearl: A swallowed button battery can cause severe oesophageal burns within hours; get an urgent X-ray, and a battery lodged in the oesophagus needs emergency endoscopic removal.
thinking: Child has swallowed a button battery ↓ A lodged battery causes rapid tissue injury ↓ Its position determines management ↓ Imaging needed now ↓ Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
exam_trap: B, discharge and check stools — reasonable for many harmless swallowed objects, but a battery stuck in the oesophagus can perforate within hours; it must be imaged.
takeaway: A swallowed button battery needs an urgent X-ray, never watchful waiting.

stem: A 7-year-old child develops a widespread rash consisting of small, itchy, fluid-filled blisters. Several lesions have already crusted. What is an appropriate infection-control measure?

options.A: Return to school as soon as some lesions crust
options.B: Give the siblings oral aciclovir to prevent them catching it
options.C: Isolate until the fever has settled
options.E: Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts

correct_answer: E. Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
why_correct: Chickenpox can cause serious complications in susceptible pregnant people and immunocompromised individuals.
why_wrong: A. The child remains infectious until all lesions have crusted. B. Routine antiviral prophylaxis is not given to healthy siblings. C. Infectivity continues until all lesions crust, not just until fever settles. D. Shared personal items can facilitate transmission.
pearl: Chickenpox is infectious until all lesions have crusted over; keep the child off school until then and away from susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised people, who risk severe disease.
thinking: Child with itchy vesicular rash ↓ Lesions at different stages, some crusted ↓ Chickenpox ↓ Serious risk to vulnerable contacts ↓ Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
exam_trap: A, return when some lesions crust — crusting does mark the end of infectivity, but only once all lesions have crusted, not just some.
takeaway: Chickenpox is infectious until every lesion has crusted; protect vulnerable contacts.

stem: A 6-year-old child develops a bright-red rash on both cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs. The child is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slapped-cheek facial rash followed by a lacy body rash is characteristic of parvovirus B19 infection.
why_wrong: A. Meningococcal disease causes acute systemic illness and a non-blanching rash. C. Cellulitis is usually localized. D. Impetigo produces crusted superficial lesions. E. Measles usually causes fever with a widespread maculopapular rash and respiratory symptoms.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek) is usually mild, and children are no longer infectious once the rash appears; it matters most in pregnancy and in people with haemolytic anaemias.
thinking: 6-year-old, otherwise well ↓ Bright-red rash on both cheeks ↓ Followed by lacy rash on the limbs ↓ Classic parvovirus B19 pattern ↓ Slapped cheek syndrome
exam_trap: E, measles — also a childhood viral rash, but it causes a febrile, unwell child with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis and a spreading maculopapular rash.
takeaway: Slapped cheeks then a lacy limb rash in a well child means parvovirus B19.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has recurrent urinary tract infections and dysuria. Which advice can help reduce the risk of recurrent lower urinary tract infections?

options.B: Restrict fluid intake to reduce voiding
options.C: Void promptly when the bladder is full

correct_answer: C. Void promptly when the bladder is full
why_correct: Regularly emptying the bladder and avoiding prolonged urinary retention can form part of advice for preventing recurrent UTIs.
why_wrong: A. Unnecessary catheterisation increases infection risk. B. Fluid restriction is inappropriate. D. Unsupervised antibiotics promote adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. E. Deliberately avoiding urination does not reduce UTI risk.
pearl: Self-care advice for recurrent UTIs includes good hydration and not delaying voiding; these measures come before considering preventive antibiotics.
thinking: Recurrent lower UTIs ↓ Bacteria multiply in urine held in the bladder ↓ Regular emptying flushes them out ↓ Void promptly when the bladder is full
exam_trap: B, restrict fluid intake — fewer voids may sound like less irritation, but concentrated urine and infrequent emptying favour bacterial growth; good hydration is advised.
takeaway: Prevent recurrent UTIs with good hydration and prompt, regular bladder emptying.

stem: A 67-year-old man has urinary hesitancy, weak urinary stream and difficulty starting urination. What is the most likely underlying problem?
why_correct: Hesitancy and weak urinary flow are typical lower urinary tract symptoms caused by bladder outlet obstruction, commonly from benign prostatic enlargement.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia. B. Overactive bladder causes storage symptoms such as urgency and frequency rather than hesitancy and a weak stream. C. Appendicitis does not cause chronic obstructive urinary symptoms. D. Renal colic causes acute flank pain.
pearl: Lower urinary tract symptoms divide into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, straining) and storage (urgency, frequency, nocturia); voiding symptoms in older men usually reflect benign prostatic enlargement.
thinking: 67-year-old man ↓ Hesitancy and weak stream ↓ Voiding symptoms of outlet obstruction ↓ Commonest cause in older men ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
