exam_trap: B, overactive bladder — a common cause of urinary symptoms in older people, but it causes storage symptoms such as urgency and frequency, not hesitancy or a weak stream.
takeaway: Hesitancy and a weak stream in an older man point to benign prostatic enlargement.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has dysuria but also develops vaginal discharge and pelvic discomfort. What diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Renal colic from a ureteric stone

why_correct: Dysuria accompanied by vaginal discharge and pelvic symptoms should prompt consideration of an STI rather than assuming a simple UTI.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes severe flank pain. C. Uncomplicated UTI does not usually cause vaginal discharge. D. Interstitial cystitis causes chronic bladder pain and urgency but not vaginal discharge. E. Osteoarthritis is unrelated.
pearl: Dysuria with vaginal discharge or pelvic pain should prompt STI testing (chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT) and consideration of PID, not just a urine dipstick for UTI.
thinking: 23-year-old with dysuria ↓ Also vaginal discharge ↓ Pelvic discomfort ↓ Features beyond simple cystitis ↓ Sexually transmitted infection
exam_trap: C, uncomplicated lower UTI — dysuria fits, but simple cystitis does not cause vaginal discharge; discharge with pelvic pain suggests an STI and possible PID.
takeaway: Dysuria with vaginal discharge means testing for STIs, not assuming a UTI.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with chlamydia. She has a regular sexual partner who has no symptoms. What is an important part of management?

options.A: Treat the partner if symptoms develop
options.B: Test the partner in 6 months if still asymptomatic
options.C: Advise abstinence for six months after treatment

correct_answer: D. Partner notification, testing and treatment
why_correct: Sexual partners should be appropriately notified and tested, and treated where indicated, to reduce reinfection and onward transmission.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms risks ongoing transmission. B. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so delayed testing risks reinfection and onward transmission. C. Prolonged abstinence is unnecessary; sex is avoided only until treatment is completed. E. Emollients do not treat chlamydia.
pearl: In chlamydia, partner notification is essential: current partners should be tested and treated without waiting for their results, and sex avoided until both have completed treatment.
thinking: Confirmed chlamydia ↓ Regular partner without symptoms ↓ Chlamydia is often asymptomatic ↓ An untreated partner means reinfection ↓ Partner notification, testing and treatment
exam_trap: A, treat the partner if symptoms develop — the partner looks well, but chlamydia is usually silent, so waiting for symptoms allows reinfection and onward spread.
takeaway: Treat chlamydia partners regardless of symptoms to prevent reinfection.

stem: A 48-year-old man develops severe weakness after taking a new medication. Blood tests show a markedly raised potassium level. Which cardiac complication is the major immediate concern?
why_correct: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause dangerous cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis is inflammatory and not caused by hyperkalaemia. C. Endocarditis is an infective valvular disease unrelated to potassium. D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a structural inherited condition, not an effect of hyperkalaemia. E. Aortic dissection is a vascular emergency unrelated to hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Severe hyperkalaemia is a cardiac emergency: get an ECG, give IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells.
thinking: Weakness after a new medicine ↓ Markedly raised potassium ↓ Disturbed myocardial membrane potential ↓ Risk of conduction block and ventricular arrhythmia ↓ Life-threatening arrhythmia
exam_trap: A, acute pericarditis — it can cause ECG changes, but it is an inflammatory condition; hyperkalaemia threatens the heart through conduction failure and arrhythmia.
takeaway: Severe hyperkalaemia kills through arrhythmia: ECG, IV calcium, then shift potassium.

stem: A 73-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has persistent nausea, reduced appetite and increasing fatigue. His renal function has deteriorated significantly. Which complication of advanced kidney disease can contribute to these symptoms?
why_correct: Accumulation of uraemic toxins in advanced kidney failure can cause nausea, anorexia, fatigue and other systemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa causes local ear symptoms. B. Hyperthyroidism produces a different systemic pattern. C. Iron overload does not explain the typical uraemic syndrome. E. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye.
pearl: Symptomatic uraemia (nausea, anorexia, fatigue, pruritus, confusion) in advanced CKD is a key trigger to discuss dialysis or conservative kidney management.
thinking: CKD with significant deterioration ↓ Nausea, poor appetite and fatigue ↓ Retained nitrogenous waste ↓ Uraemic syndrome ↓ Uraemia
exam_trap: C, iron overload — it may tempt because iron is part of anaemia care in CKD, but overload does not cause this picture; uraemic toxins explain the symptoms.
takeaway: Nausea, anorexia and fatigue in advanced CKD suggest uraemia.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with asthma uses her salbutamol inhaler several times every day. She is otherwise stable. What does this suggest?

options.A: Salbutamol should replace all preventer treatment
options.B: She no longer needs asthma review
options.D: Her asthma control may be inadequate

correct_answer: D. Her asthma control may be inadequate
why_correct: Frequent reliance on a reliever inhaler suggests poor asthma control and should prompt review of treatment and adherence.
why_wrong: A. Reliever treatment does not replace appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment. B. Frequent symptoms are a reason for review, not discharge from follow-up. C. Salbutamol use does not diagnose diabetes. E. Frequent reliever use suggests ongoing symptoms.
pearl: Needing a short-acting reliever several times a day indicates uncontrolled asthma; check inhaler technique, adherence and triggers before stepping up anti-inflammatory treatment.
thinking: Asthma ↓ Salbutamol used several times every day ↓ Frequent reliever use reflects ongoing symptoms ↓ Review technique, adherence and treatment ↓ Her asthma control may be inadequate
exam_trap: A, salbutamol should replace preventer treatment — it relieves symptoms quickly, but relying on it alone leaves airway inflammation untreated and increases attack risk.
takeaway: Frequent reliever use means poor asthma control and needs review.

stem: A 64-year-old woman taking warfarin presents with unexplained bruising. Her INR is significantly above her therapeutic range. What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR next month
options.B: Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
options.C: Start low-dose aspirin 75 mg once daily routinely
options.D: Increase the warfarin dose and recheck the INR in a week

correct_answer: B. Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
why_correct: A markedly elevated INR increases bleeding risk and requires assessment and appropriate adjustment of anticoagulation.
why_wrong: A. A significantly elevated INR with bruising should not be left for a month. C. Aspirin can further increase bleeding risk and is not routinely added. D. Increasing warfarin would further increase anticoagulation. E. Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding, not bruising alone.
pearl: With a high INR, management depends on bleeding: minor bleeding may need warfarin withheld and vitamin K, while major bleeding needs prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Unexplained bruising ↓ INR well above range ↓ Assess bleeding severity and adjust treatment ↓ Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
exam_trap: E, give prothrombin complex concentrate immediately — it rapidly reverses warfarin, but it is reserved for major bleeding; bruising alone does not justify it.
takeaway: High INR: assess bleeding first, then withhold warfarin or reverse accordingly.

stem: A doctor realises that they have made an error in a patient's prescription. The medication has not yet been administered. What should they do?

options.A: Correct it at the next routine ward round
options.B: Correct the error promptly and inform the team
options.D: Take no action because no harm has occurred
options.E: Ask the pharmacist to amend it quietly

correct_answer: B. Correct the error promptly and inform the team
why_correct: Prompt recognition and correction of errors reduces the risk of harm and supports safe clinical practice.
why_wrong: A. Delaying action could allow the medication to be administered. C. Deleting evidence without appropriate documentation is unsafe. D. An error still requires appropriate action even if harm has not yet occurred. E. The prescriber should correct the error and the team must be informed so the incident is handled openly.
pearl: When you find a prescribing error, correct it immediately, inform the team, document it and report it through local incident reporting even if no harm occurred, as near misses drive learning.
thinking: Prescribing error found ↓ Drug not yet given ↓ Risk remains until corrected ↓ Act now and be open with the team ↓ Correct the error promptly and inform the team
exam_trap: D, take no action because no harm occurred — no patient was hurt, but the error remains live; it must be corrected and handled openly as a near miss.
takeaway: Correct errors immediately and be open, even when no harm has occurred.

stem: A patient is unconscious and requires an urgent life-saving procedure. There is no available advance decision refusing treatment. What principle generally applies?

options.A: Consent should first be obtained from an IMCA
options.B: Treatment requires written consent from the next of kin
options.C: Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
options.D: Treatment should wait until a relative can consent
options.E: A court order is needed before the procedure can proceed

correct_answer: C. Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
why_correct: Necessary emergency treatment can be provided when the patient lacks capacity and delay would put them at significant risk, subject to relevant legal and clinical requirements.
why_wrong: A. An IMCA does not give consent, and waiting would cause dangerous delay. B. Relatives cannot consent for an adult and written consent is not required in an emergency. D. Waiting for relatives may cause dangerous delay. E. A court order is not needed for necessary emergency treatment.
pearl: In an emergency, an adult who lacks capacity can be given necessary treatment in their best interests without consent; relatives cannot consent for them unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
thinking: Unconscious patient lacks capacity ↓ Urgent life-saving treatment needed ↓ No advance decision refusing it ↓ Delay would cause serious harm ↓ Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
exam_trap: B, written consent from the next of kin — involving family feels proper, but relatives cannot consent for an adult, and seeking it must not delay emergency treatment.
takeaway: Treat incapacitated patients in emergencies in their best interests; relatives cannot consent.

stem: A patient asks the doctor not to disclose their diagnosis to their adult daughter. The patient has capacity. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Ask another patient to tell the daughter
options.B: Tell the daughter because she is a close relative
options.C: Disclose the diagnosis automatically because the daughter is next of kin
options.E: Post the diagnosis in the family group chat

why_correct: Confidential patient information should not be disclosed to relatives without appropriate consent or another valid justification.
why_wrong: A. This would still breach confidentiality. B. Being a relative does not automatically provide access to confidential information. C. Next-of-kin status does not automatically override a capacitous patient's confidentiality. E. Electronic disclosure to a group would be inappropriate.
pearl: A patient with capacity decides who is told about their health; next-of-kin status gives relatives no automatic right to confidential information.
thinking: Patient has capacity ↓ Asks for the diagnosis to be kept from the daughter ↓ No overriding justification described ↓ Respect the patient's confidentiality
exam_trap: C, disclose because the daughter is next of kin — next of kin sounds like a legal right, but it gives no entitlement to confidential information without consent.
takeaway: Next of kin has no automatic right to a capacitous patient's information.

stem: A patient receiving a blood transfusion develops fever, chills and back pain. What is the immediate action?
why_correct: A suspected acute transfusion reaction requires the transfusion to be stopped immediately and the patient assessed according to the local transfusion-reaction protocol.
why_wrong: A. Further blood should not be administered until the reaction has been assessed. B. Increasing the rate could worsen a serious reaction. C. These symptoms may indicate a significant transfusion reaction. E. Intravenous access is needed for ongoing assessment and treatment.
pearl: In an acute transfusion reaction, stop the transfusion, keep the line open, assess ABCDE and recheck patient and unit identity; fever with back pain raises concern for ABO incompatibility.
thinking: Transfusion in progress ↓ Fever, chills and back pain ↓ Possible acute haemolytic reaction ↓ Stop further exposure first ↓ Stop the transfusion
exam_trap: E, remove all intravenous access — removing the source seems logical, but the cannula is needed for fluids and treatment; stop the blood, keep the line.
takeaway: Transfusion reaction: stop the transfusion, keep IV access, assess urgently.

stem: Before administering a unit of blood, which information is particularly important to check against the patient and blood component?

options.B: The patient's ward name and bed number
options.C: The patient's next of kin details

correct_answer: A. Patient identity and compatibility details
why_correct: Correct patient identification and compatibility checks are essential to prevent potentially fatal transfusion errors.
why_wrong: B. Ward and bed number are not reliable patient identifiers. C. Next-of-kin details do not confirm identity or compatibility. D. Occupation is irrelevant to transfusion identification. E. Food preference is irrelevant.
pearl: Wrong blood in the patient is a leading cause of serious transfusion harm; positive bedside identity checks against the wristband and blood component prevent ABO-incompatible transfusion.
thinking: Unit of blood ready ↓ Biggest risk is giving the wrong blood ↓ Bedside check against the patient ↓ Patient identity and compatibility details
exam_trap: B, ward name and bed number — commonly used to locate patients, but patients move beds; they are not reliable identifiers for transfusion.
takeaway: Positive patient identification at the bedside prevents fatal transfusion errors.

stem: A patient has a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding. Before using it for feeding, what is important?

options.A: Ask the patient whether the tube feels correctly positioned
options.B: Check position by testing aspirate with litmus paper
options.C: Confirm position with the air 'whoosh' test
options.D: Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
options.E: Use the tube without checking because it was inserted by a doctor

correct_answer: D. Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
why_correct: Incorrectly positioned feeding tubes can cause serious harm, including pulmonary aspiration. Position must be confirmed according to the relevant protocol before use.
why_wrong: A. Patient sensation cannot reliably confirm tube position. B. Litmus paper is not a safe method for confirming tube position. C. Auscultation of injected air is unreliable and should not be used. E. Professional status does not remove the need for safety checks.
pearl: Confirm nasogastric tube position before first use with aspirate pH testing, using X-ray if no suitable aspirate is obtained; never rely on litmus paper or the air whoosh test.
thinking: NG tube inserted for feeding ↓ Misplacement in the lung can be fatal ↓ Reliable confirmation needed ↓ Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
exam_trap: C, the air whoosh test — it is a traditional bedside check, but auscultation is unreliable and is no longer acceptable for confirming tube position.
takeaway: Confirm NG tube position by aspirate pH or X-ray before feeding.

stem: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a patient whose blood-borne virus status is unknown. What should they do first?

options.B: Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
options.C: Continue working without reporting the minor incident
options.D: Suck the wound clean, cover it and report it later
options.E: Finish the shift and report it if symptoms develop

correct_answer: B. Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
why_correct: Immediate first aid and prompt occupational-health assessment are important because post-exposure management may be time-sensitive.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics have no role in preventing blood-borne viral infection. C. Even an apparently minor incident should be reported and assessed appropriately. D. The wound should not be sucked, and delayed reporting risks missing time-sensitive prophylaxis. E. Blood-borne infections may initially be asymptomatic and prophylaxis is time-sensitive.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water without scrubbing or sucking, and report immediately to occupational health or the emergency department.
thinking: Needlestick injury ↓ Source blood-borne virus status unknown ↓ First aid limits exposure ↓ Prophylaxis is time-sensitive ↓ Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
exam_trap: E, finish the shift and report if symptoms develop — it seems minor, but blood-borne infection may be silent and HIV PEP works best when started within hours.
takeaway: Needlestick: bleed it, wash it, report it immediately.

stem: A healthcare worker has a needlestick injury potentially involving HIV exposure. Why is urgent assessment important?

options.A: A tetanus vaccine booster effectively treats HIV exposure
options.B: PEP should wait until the source patient's result is back
options.C: Seroconversion symptoms typically appear within 24 hours

correct_answer: E. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive
why_correct: Significant occupational exposure may require urgent assessment for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus vaccination does not prevent HIV. B. PEP should not be delayed while awaiting source testing when the exposure is significant. C. Acute HIV infection may be asymptomatic and seroconversion illness occurs weeks later. D. Antibiotics do not prevent HIV.
pearl: HIV PEP should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure; do not wait for source test results when the exposure is significant.
thinking: Needlestick with possible HIV exposure ↓ PEP works best when started early ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive
exam_trap: B, PEP should wait for the source result — it seems to avoid unnecessary drugs, but delay reduces effectiveness; start PEP and stop it if the source tests negative.
takeaway: Start HIV PEP as early as possible; do not wait for source results.

stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted with a persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats. What infection-control principle is particularly important?

options.A: Routine contact with other patients on the ward
options.B: Sharing a room with other vulnerable patients
options.C: No precautions until the diagnosis is confirmed
options.E: Turning off the ventilation in the patient's room

correct_answer: D. Respiratory isolation and infection control
why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate isolation and infection-control measures because transmission can occur through airborne particles.
why_wrong: A. Unrestricted contact increases transmission risk. B. Vulnerable patients may be at greater risk. C. Precautions may be necessary while diagnosis is being established. E. Appropriate ventilation is an important infection-control measure.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs a single room with respiratory precautions until infectivity is assessed; suspected multidrug-resistant TB needs a negative-pressure room.
thinking: Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats ↓ Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission risk ↓ Protect other patients and staff ↓ Respiratory isolation and infection control
exam_trap: C, no precautions until confirmed — waiting for proof seems proportionate, but confirmation takes time and transmission occurs meanwhile; isolate on suspicion.
takeaway: Isolate suspected pulmonary TB on suspicion, not confirmation.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis. What is an important public-health action?

options.A: Advise the patient to avoid dairy products
options.C: Notify TB services for contact tracing
options.D: Prescribe an antitussive for the cough
options.E: Advise the patient that household contacts do not need assessment

correct_answer: C. Notify TB services for contact tracing
why_correct: Active TB requires coordinated public-health management, including assessment of relevant contacts.
why_wrong: A. Dairy avoidance is not the central public-health intervention. B. TB treatment requires an appropriate course rather than stopping when symptoms improve. D. Treatment addresses the infection, not simply the cough. E. Household and other relevant contacts may require assessment.
pearl: TB is a notifiable disease in the UK; notification triggers contact tracing, and treatment requires a full multi-drug course with adherence support.
thinking: Active pulmonary TB ↓ Infectious to close contacts ↓ Notifiable disease ↓ Contacts need screening ↓ Notify TB services for contact tracing
exam_trap: E, household contacts do not need assessment — they may be well, but close contacts are at highest risk and may have latent or active TB needing screening.
takeaway: Active TB is notifiable and needs contact tracing.

stem: A patient with a new sexually transmitted infection asks whether their recent sexual partners need to know. What is an important principle?

options.A: Partners need informing if they develop symptoms
options.B: Partners will be told the patient's identity by the clinic
options.C: Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
options.D: The patient has to tell partners personally
options.E: Partner notification is unnecessary if symptoms have resolved

correct_answer: C. Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
why_correct: Partner notification is an important part of STI management and helps prevent onward transmission and complications.
why_wrong: A. Many STIs are asymptomatic, so notification should not depend on symptoms. B. Provider-led notification can be anonymous and protects the patient's confidentiality. D. Partners can also be notified by the clinic, so the patient does not have to do it personally. E. Resolution of symptoms does not necessarily mean the infection has cleared or that partners are safe.
pearl: Partner notification is a routine part of STI care; it can be patient-led or provider-led, and provider-led notification keeps the index patient anonymous.
thinking: New STI diagnosis ↓ Partners may be infected without symptoms ↓ Untreated partners transmit and reinfect ↓ Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
exam_trap: A, inform partners if they develop symptoms — it seems proportionate, but many STIs are asymptomatic, so waiting allows onward spread and complications.
takeaway: Notify STI partners regardless of symptoms; anonymity can be preserved.

stem: A traveller develops severe watery diarrhoea during a holiday abroad but remains alert and able to drink. What is an important initial management measure?
why_correct: Replacing water and electrolytes is the key initial treatment for uncomplicated diarrhoeal illness when the patient can drink safely.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged fasting is unnecessary. C. Antibiotics are not routinely required for uncomplicated diarrhoea. D. Chemotherapy has no role in routine infectious diarrhoea. E. Fluid restriction increases dehydration risk.
pearl: Rehydration is the cornerstone of managing travellers' diarrhoea; oral rehydration solution replaces water and electrolytes, and most cases are self-limiting.
thinking: Traveller with watery diarrhoea ↓ Large fluid and electrolyte losses ↓ Alert and able to drink ↓ Oral route is safe ↓ Oral rehydration solution
exam_trap: C, routine intravenous antibiotics — severe diarrhoea abroad may feel infective and serious, but most cases are self-limiting and rehydration is the priority.
takeaway: Rehydrate first in travellers' diarrhoea; use ORS if the patient can drink.

stem: A patient is suspected of having meningococcal meningitis and is rapidly deteriorating. What is the key principle?

options.A: Discharge if the patient remains conscious
options.B: Wait for lumbar puncture results before antibiotics
options.C: Delay antibiotics until a CT head is reported
options.D: Give oral amoxicillin and review next day
options.E: Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations

correct_answer: E. Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed.
why_wrong: A. Consciousness does not exclude serious meningitis. B. Waiting for lumbar puncture results can cause dangerous treatment delay. C. Imaging should not delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease. D. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inadequate for suspected meningococcal disease.
pearl: In suspected meningococcal disease, give parenteral antibiotics immediately; in primary care, give IM or IV benzylpenicillin before urgent transfer if this does not delay it.
thinking: Suspected meningococcal meningitis ↓ Rapid deterioration ↓ Delay increases mortality ↓ Investigations must not hold up treatment ↓ Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
exam_trap: B, wait for lumbar puncture results — LP helps confirm the diagnosis, but it must never delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease: give antibiotics immediately; never wait for tests.

stem: A patient has a deep contaminated wound after stepping on a dirty metal object. What factor is particularly important when assessing the need for tetanus prevention?

options.A: Whether the patient has a penicillin allergy
options.B: Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
options.C: The patient's eye colour and skin complexion
options.D: Whether the patient ate breakfast that morning
options.E: The patient's ABO blood group and rhesus status

correct_answer: B. Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
why_correct: Tetanus prevention depends on the type of wound and the patient's previous immunisation status.
why_wrong: A. Penicillin allergy affects antibiotic choice, not tetanus prophylaxis. C. Eye colour and complexion are irrelevant. D. Food intake is irrelevant. E. Blood group does not determine tetanus prophylaxis.
pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds include deep, puncture or soil-contaminated wounds; the need for a vaccine booster and human tetanus immunoglobulin depends on wound risk and vaccination history.
thinking: Deep wound from a dirty metal object ↓ Contaminated, so tetanus-prone ↓ Protection depends on prior immunity ↓ Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
exam_trap: A, penicillin allergy — it seems relevant to antibiotic cover for dirty wounds, but it does not determine the need for tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
takeaway: Tetanus prophylaxis depends on wound risk and vaccination history.

stem: A hospital ward has several patients with diarrhoea caused by *Clostridioides difficile*. Which measure is particularly important for reducing transmission?

options.A: Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
options.B: Using alcohol hand gel as the only measure in every circumstance
options.C: Allowing unrestricted movement between affected patients and vulnerable patients
options.D: Sharing equipment between affected and unaffected patients without cleaning

correct_answer: A. Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
why_correct: *C. difficile* spores can persist in the environment, so appropriate hand hygiene and effective environmental cleaning are important infection-control measures.
why_wrong: B. Alcohol hand rub is not reliably sporicidal against *C. difficile* spores. C. Unrestricted contact can increase transmission. D. Shared contaminated equipment can facilitate transmission. E. Appropriate infection-control precautions should be maintained.
pearl: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores; use soap and water handwashing, isolation, gloves and aprons and sporicidal (chlorine-based) cleaning, alongside antibiotic review.
thinking: Ward outbreak of C. difficile diarrhoea ↓ The organism forms resistant spores ↓ Spores survive alcohol and persist on surfaces ↓ Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
exam_trap: B, alcohol gel as the only measure — it is standard ward hand hygiene, but it does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water and sporicidal cleaning are needed.
takeaway: C. difficile: soap and water, not alcohol gel, plus sporicidal cleaning.

stem: A 26-year-old woman wants to start a combined oral contraceptive pill. Which factor is an important contraindication?
why_correct: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in women with migraine with aura because of the increased risk of ischaemic stroke.
why_wrong: A. Dysmenorrhoea is not a contraindication. C. Previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery is not a contraindication. D. Age 26 alone is not a contraindication. E. Mild acne is not a contraindication.
pearl: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk; progestogen-only methods or a copper IUD are suitable alternatives.
thinking: Wants the combined pill ↓ Oestrogen raises thrombotic risk ↓ Migraine with aura already raises stroke risk ↓ Combined risk unacceptable ↓ Migraine with aura
exam_trap: A, dysmenorrhoea — painful periods may seem a reason for caution, but the combined pill is often used to treat dysmenorrhoea and is not contraindicated.
takeaway: Migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception.

stem: A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill asks what to do if she develops severe chest pain and breathlessness. What should she do?

options.A: Wait several weeks for a routine review
options.C: Take an antacid and ignore the symptoms

why_correct: Severe chest pain and breathlessness may indicate pulmonary embolism, which requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Potential thromboembolism should not be managed through delayed routine review. B. An additional contraceptive pill does not treat suspected thromboembolism. C. Reflux should not be assumed in the presence of potentially serious symptoms. D. Fluid restriction is inappropriate.
pearl: Women on combined hormonal contraception must know VTE warning signs: calf pain or swelling, chest pain and breathlessness need urgent assessment for DVT or pulmonary embolism.
thinking: Taking the combined pill ↓ Increased venous thromboembolism risk ↓ Severe chest pain and breathlessness ↓ Possible pulmonary embolism ↓ Seek urgent medical assessment
exam_trap: C, take an antacid — chest pain is often indigestion, but on the combined pill severe pain with breathlessness must be treated as thrombotic until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Chest pain and breathlessness on the combined pill: urgent assessment for PE.

stem: A 32-year-old woman wants a long-acting reversible contraceptive method and does not want to take a daily tablet. Which is an example of a long-acting reversible contraceptive?
why_correct: Intrauterine devices and implants are long-acting reversible contraceptive methods.
why_wrong: A. The combined pill requires regular daily use. B. The progestogen-only pill requires regular administration. C. Fertility-awareness methods are not long-acting reversible contraception. E. Condoms are user-dependent barrier contraception.
pearl: LARC methods (copper IUD, hormonal IUS, implant and injection) do not depend on daily use, so their typical-use effectiveness is far higher than pills or condoms.
thinking: Wants long-acting reversible method ↓ Does not want a daily tablet ↓ LARC includes intrauterine methods, implant and injection ↓ Intrauterine device
exam_trap: B, progestogen-only pill — it is oestrogen-free and suits many women, but it is taken daily, so it is not long-acting reversible contraception.
takeaway: LARC means IUD, IUS, implant or injection, never a pill.

stem: A woman using a combined oral contraceptive pill develops severe abdominal pain and jaundice. What should be considered?

options.A: Hormonal acne vulgaris of the face

why_correct: New significant abdominal pain and jaundice require clinical assessment rather than being attributed automatically to contraception.
why_wrong: A. Acne does not explain jaundice and abdominal pain. B. Tension headache does not explain jaundice. D. Jaundice is not a normal expected effect. E. Otitis externa is unrelated.
pearl: The combined pill can rarely cause cholestatic jaundice and is linked to gallstones and hepatic vein thrombosis; new jaundice means stopping it and assessing urgently.
thinking: Taking the combined pill ↓ Severe abdominal pain ↓ New jaundice ↓ Not an expected side effect ↓ A serious hepatobiliary problem
exam_trap: D, a normal effect of contraception — mild side effects are common on the pill, but jaundice with severe pain is never normal and needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Jaundice on the combined pill is never normal: stop it and investigate.

stem: A pregnant woman has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure and severe hypertension. What obstetric emergency should be considered?
why_correct: Eclampsia is the occurrence of a seizure associated with pre-eclampsia.
why_wrong: B. Placenta praevia causes painless vaginal bleeding. C. Syncope does not explain a generalised seizure with severe hypertension. D. Hyperemesis causes vomiting, not typically seizures. E. Gestational diabetes does not characteristically cause seizures.
pearl: Eclampsia is treated with IV magnesium sulfate to control and prevent seizures, plus blood pressure control; delivery is planned once the woman is stabilised.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Generalised tonic-clonic seizure ↓ Severe hypertension ↓ Seizure on a background of pre-eclampsia ↓ Eclampsia
exam_trap: C, physiological syncope — fainting is common in pregnancy and can cause brief jerks, but it does not cause a tonic-clonic seizure with severe hypertension.
takeaway: Seizure plus hypertension in pregnancy is eclampsia: give magnesium sulfate.

stem: A newborn becomes cyanosed shortly after birth and has severe respiratory distress. What is an important principle?

options.A: Warm the baby and reassess colour at the next feed
options.C: Urgent assessment for cardiac and other causes
options.D: Cyanosis is a normal transitional finding in newborns
options.E: Review at the routine six-to-eight-week baby check

correct_answer: C. Urgent assessment for cardiac and other causes
why_correct: Significant central cyanosis in a newborn is abnormal and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Cold exposure does not adequately explain central cyanosis with severe respiratory distress. B. Antibiotics alone are inappropriate without identifying the cause. D. Persistent central cyanosis with respiratory distress is not a normal transitional finding. E. Delaying assessment risks missing a life-threatening condition.
pearl: Central cyanosis in a newborn is never normal; assess urgently for cardiac causes such as duct-dependent congenital heart disease, and for respiratory, infective or metabolic causes.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Central cyanosis soon after birth ↓ Severe respiratory distress ↓ Possible cardiac, respiratory or infective cause ↓ Urgent assessment for cardiac and other causes
exam_trap: D, cyanosis is a normal transitional finding — blue hands and feet can be normal early on, but central cyanosis with severe distress is not.
takeaway: Central cyanosis in a newborn needs urgent assessment; acrocyanosis alone is normal.

stem: A 7-year-old child has recurrent abdominal pain around school days but remains well, has normal growth and has no nocturnal symptoms or blood in the stool. What is an appropriate approach?

options.A: Consider functional abdominal pain after assessment
options.B: Diagnose appendicitis and refer to the surgical team urgently
options.C: Start a gluten-free diet without first testing for coeliac
options.D: Perform an emergency diagnostic laparotomy the same day
options.E: Arrange urgent colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer

correct_answer: A. Consider functional abdominal pain after assessment
why_correct: Recurrent abdominal pain without alarm features and with normal growth can be functional.
why_wrong: B. Appendicitis usually causes an acute progressive illness. C. A gluten-free diet before testing is inappropriate and can mask coeliac disease. D. Emergency surgery is inappropriate without evidence of an acute surgical abdomen. E. Colorectal cancer would be highly unusual and is not suggested by this presentation.
pearl: Functional abdominal pain is common in school-age children; diagnose it after excluding red flags such as weight loss, faltering growth, nocturnal symptoms or blood in the stool.
thinking: 7-year-old with recurrent abdominal pain ↓ Linked to school days ↓ Normal growth, no night symptoms or blood ↓ No red flags ↓ Consider functional abdominal pain after assessment
exam_trap: C, gluten-free diet without testing — coeliac disease is a fair thought in recurrent abdominal pain, but removing gluten before testing gives falsely negative results.
takeaway: Recurrent abdominal pain without red flags in a child is usually functional.

stem: A woman with PMOS (formerly PCOS) asks about a long-term health implication. Which is associated with PMOS (formerly PCOS)?

options.A: Reduced long-term risk of metabolic disease
options.B: Reduced risk of gestational diabetes in pregnancy
options.C: Protection against endometrial cancer in later life
options.D: Reduced long-term risk of cardiovascular disease

correct_answer: E. Increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia
why_correct: Chronic anovulation in PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure of the endometrium, increasing the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Metabolic complications such as obesity, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance are more common in PMOS (formerly PCOS). B. PMOS (formerly PCOS) increases, rather than reduces, the risk of gestational and type 2 diabetes. C. PMOS (formerly PCOS) increases endometrial cancer risk through unopposed oestrogen; it is not protective. D. Cardiovascular risk factors are increased in PMOS (formerly PCOS), not reduced.
pearl: PMOS (formerly PCOS) carries long-term risks of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, type 2 and gestational diabetes and cardiovascular risk factors; ensure regular withdrawal bleeds.
thinking: Chronic anovulation ↓ Little progesterone from ovulation ↓ Unopposed oestrogen on the endometrium ↓ Endometrial overgrowth ↓ Increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia
exam_trap: C, protection against endometrial cancer — the combined pill often used in PMOS is protective, which may confuse, but the condition itself raises endometrial cancer risk.
takeaway: Anovulation in PMOS means unopposed oestrogen and endometrial hyperplasia risk.

stem: A patient's serum sodium is 118 mmol/L and they are confused. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Sodium within the normal reference range for age
options.B: Mild hypernatraemia requiring oral water intake
options.C: Isolated hyperkalaemia needing a repeat blood sample
options.D: Moderate hyponatraemia for routine outpatient review

correct_answer: E. Severe hyponatraemia needing urgent assessment
why_correct: A sodium of 118 mmol/L represents severe hyponatraemia, and confusion may indicate significant neurological effects.
why_wrong: A. Normal serum sodium is approximately 135–145 mmol/L at any adult age. B. The sodium is low, not high. C. Potassium is a separate electrolyte. D. A sodium of 118 mmol/L with confusion is severe and needs urgent assessment.
pearl: Hyponatraemia with confusion is severe and symptomatic; manage urgently with senior input and correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
thinking: Sodium 118 mmol/L ↓ Well below the normal range ↓ Patient is confused ↓ Neurological symptoms indicate severity ↓ Severe hyponatraemia needing urgent assessment
exam_trap: D, moderate hyponatraemia for routine review — it correctly identifies low sodium, but a level this low with confusion is severe and needs urgent care.
takeaway: Confusion with low sodium is severe hyponatraemia: urgent, careful correction.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has pain and stiffness at the base of her thumb, particularly when opening jars. There is no systemic illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Mechanical pain at the thumb base, particularly with gripping activities, is typical of thumb-base osteoarthritis.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia does not cause isolated mechanical thumb-base pain. C. Gout causes acute inflammatory attacks. D. Rheumatoid arthritis usually causes inflammatory symmetrical joint disease. E. Septic arthritis would usually cause acute inflammation and systemic features.
pearl: Thumb-base (first carpometacarpal) osteoarthritis causes pain on gripping and pinching, often with squaring of the thumb base; it is common in middle-aged and older women.
thinking: 55-year-old woman ↓ Pain and stiffness at the thumb base ↓ Worse with gripping such as opening jars ↓ No systemic illness ↓ Hand osteoarthritis
exam_trap: D, rheumatoid arthritis — it commonly affects the hands, but it causes symmetrical inflammatory swelling of the MCP and PIP joints, not isolated mechanical thumb-base pain.
takeaway: Thumb-base pain on gripping in middle age suggests osteoarthritis.

stem: A 61-year-old man reports progressive difficulty seeing at night and increasing glare from headlights. Vision has gradually deteriorated over several years. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Gradual painless visual deterioration with glare and difficulty in low-light conditions is typical of cataract.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment typically presents acutely with flashes, floaters or a visual-field defect. C. Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden visual loss. D. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes painful red eye and acute visual symptoms. E. Conjunctivitis does not cause progressive loss of vision.
pearl: Cataract causes gradual painless blurring, glare from lights and poor night vision; refer for surgery when it affects quality of life rather than on a visual acuity cut-off alone.
thinking: 61-year-old with years of gradual visual decline ↓ Difficulty seeing at night ↓ Glare from headlights ↓ Painless lens opacity ↓ Cataract
exam_trap: A, retinal detachment — it causes visual loss in older adults, but it is sudden, with flashes, floaters or a curtain, not a gradual decline over years.
takeaway: Gradual painless blurred vision with glare suggests cataract.

stem: A patient has a positive screening test for a disease. The test has a high specificity. What does high specificity mean?

options.A: A low rate of false-positive results
options.B: The test is always positive in disease
options.E: A low rate of true-negative results

correct_answer: A. A low rate of false-positive results
why_correct: A highly specific test correctly identifies people without the disease, so false-positive results are uncommon.
why_wrong: B. That relates more closely to sensitivity. C. Specificity is not determined by disease prevalence. D. Specificity says nothing about disease severity. E. High specificity means a high, not low, true-negative rate.
pearl: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative; a highly specific test gives few false positives, so a positive result helps rule the disease in (SpPIn).
thinking: High specificity ↓ Correctly identifies those without disease ↓ Few healthy people test positive ↓ A low rate of false-positive results
exam_trap: B, always positive in disease — it describes a test that detects every case, which is high sensitivity, not specificity.
takeaway: High specificity means few false positives: a positive helps rule in.

stem: A diagnostic test has very high sensitivity. Which statement is correct?

options.A: A negative result makes the disease less likely
options.B: A positive result confirms the disease
options.D: The test also has high specificity
options.E: The test rarely produces false positives

correct_answer: A. A negative result makes the disease less likely
why_correct: Highly sensitive tests detect most people who have the disease, so a negative result can be useful for ruling it out in appropriate settings.
why_wrong: B. A highly sensitive test can still have false-positive results. C. Sensitivity does not depend on disease prevalence. D. Sensitivity and specificity are separate test characteristics. E. Few false positives reflect high specificity, not sensitivity.
pearl: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive; a highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule the disease out (SnNOut).
thinking: Very high sensitivity ↓ Detects nearly everyone with the disease ↓ Few false negatives ↓ A negative result makes the disease less likely
exam_trap: E, rarely produces false positives — it sounds like a feature of any good test, but few false positives reflects high specificity, not sensitivity.
takeaway: High sensitivity means few false negatives: a negative helps rule out.

stem: A clinical study reports a relative risk of 1. What does this mean?

options.C: Risk is the same in both groups
options.D: The exposure halves the risk of disease
options.E: The disease is twice as common in one group

correct_answer: C. Risk is the same in both groups
why_correct: A relative risk of 1 indicates equal risk in the exposed and comparison groups.
why_wrong: A. A relative risk of 1 is the null value and does not indicate a significant effect. B. A protective exposure would give a relative risk below 1. D. Halving the risk would correspond to a relative risk of 0.5. E. A relative risk of 2 would indicate twice the risk.
pearl: Relative risk is the risk in the exposed group divided by the risk in the unexposed group; 1 means no difference, below 1 a protective effect and above 1 increased risk.
thinking: Relative risk compares exposed with unexposed ↓ It is a ratio of two risks ↓ A ratio of 1 means they are equal ↓ Risk is the same in both groups
exam_trap: A, the result is statistically significant — a reported figure may look like a finding, but RR of 1 is the null value; significance depends on the confidence interval.
takeaway: A relative risk of 1 means no difference in risk between groups.

stem: A trial reports a 95% confidence interval for an odds ratio of 0.72–1.34. What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.A: The result is statistically significant at 5%
options.B: The study demonstrates the treatment has no effect
options.C: The result is compatible with no association
options.D: The treatment increases the odds by about 34%
options.E: The treatment reduces the odds of the outcome by 28%

correct_answer: C. The result is compatible with no association
why_correct: For an odds ratio, 1 represents no association. Because the interval crosses 1, the result is compatible with no association.
why_wrong: A. The interval crosses 1, so the result is not statistically significant. B. Crossing 1 does not prove that no effect exists. D. 1.34 is only the upper limit of the interval, not the estimated effect. E. 0.72 is only the lower limit of the interval and a benefit is not established.
pearl: For ratios such as odds ratios, a 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level; it does not prove there is no effect.
thinking: Odds ratio 95% CI 0.72 to 1.34 ↓ Null value for a ratio is 1 ↓ The interval includes 1 ↓ Not statistically significant ↓ The result is compatible with no association
exam_trap: B, demonstrates no effect — a non-significant result is often misread as proof of no effect, but the interval still allows meaningful benefit or harm.
takeaway: A ratio CI crossing 1 is non-significant, not proof of no effect.

stem: A researcher wants to compare the incidence of a disease in people exposed and unexposed to a suspected risk factor over several years. Which study design is particularly suitable?
why_correct: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed groups over time and can compare disease incidence.
why_wrong: A. A case report describes an individual case. B. Qualitative interviews explore experiences rather than directly measuring disease incidence. D. A case series describes a group of cases without an appropriate comparison group. E. A cross-sectional study assesses exposure and outcome at a particular point rather than following incidence over time.
pearl: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed groups forward to measure incidence and relative risk; case-control studies start from the outcome and suit rare diseases.
thinking: Compare exposed and unexposed people ↓ Measure new cases (incidence) ↓ Over several years ↓ Follow groups forward in time ↓ Cohort study
exam_trap: E, cross-sectional survey — it also relates exposure and disease, but only at one point in time, so it measures prevalence, not incidence.
takeaway: Comparing incidence by exposure over time needs a cohort study.

stem: A 67-year-old man with COPD becomes increasingly breathless and confused. His oxygen saturation is low. What is the most appropriate principle when giving oxygen?

options.C: Give oxygen only if he asks for it
options.D: Give unlimited high-flow oxygen without monitoring
options.E: Give controlled oxygen and assess for hypercapnia

correct_answer: E. Give controlled oxygen and assess for hypercapnia
why_correct: Some patients with COPD are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, so oxygen should be appropriately controlled and the patient assessed.
why_wrong: A. Hypoxaemia requires treatment. B. Confusion may be caused or worsened by respiratory failure. C. Treatment should be based on clinical need. D. Uncontrolled oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients.
pearl: In COPD with risk of hypercapnia, give controlled oxygen via a Venturi mask to a target of 88–92% and check an arterial blood gas; confusion may reflect rising CO2.
thinking: COPD with breathlessness and confusion ↓ Low saturations need oxygen ↓ Risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure ↓ Controlled oxygen and assess for hypercapnia
exam_trap: A, withhold oxygen completely — fear of CO2 retention tempts, but hypoxaemia kills; the answer is controlled oxygen with monitoring, never withholding it.
takeaway: COPD and hypoxia: never withhold oxygen, control it and check the blood gas.

stem: A 24-year-old woman develops wheeze, chest tightness and breathlessness after exposure to a cat. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Episodic wheeze and chest tightness triggered by an allergen are typical of asthma.
why_wrong: B. Pneumothorax usually causes sudden chest pain and unilateral reduced breath sounds. C. Pleural effusion causes reduced breath sounds and is not typically episodic. D. Pulmonary fibrosis causes progressive rather than episodic symptoms. E. Pulmonary embolism can cause breathlessness but is not typically triggered reproducibly by cat exposure with wheeze.
pearl: Episodic wheeze, chest tightness and breathlessness triggered by an allergen such as cat dander is classic asthma; variability and reversibility are its hallmarks.
thinking: Young adult with wheeze and chest tightness ↓ Clear trigger: cat exposure ↓ Episodic, allergen-driven airway narrowing ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: E, pulmonary embolism — causes acute breathlessness in a young woman, but wheeze with a reproducible allergen trigger points to asthma, not PE.
takeaway: Wheeze plus an allergen trigger in a young adult is asthma until shown otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old man has persistent hoarseness for more than three weeks. He is a smoker. What is the appropriate concern?
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness, particularly in a smoker, requires assessment for laryngeal cancer.
why_wrong: A. Cataract affects vision. C. Otitis externa affects the ear canal. D. Persistent hoarseness requires investigation rather than being automatically attributed to a viral infection. E. Gout causes inflammatory arthritis.
pearl: Persistent unexplained hoarseness, especially in a smoker, needs urgent ENT assessment for laryngeal cancer rather than reassurance.
thinking: Hoarseness for more than three weeks ↓ Smoker in middle age ↓ Red flag for laryngeal malignancy ↓ Laryngeal malignancy must be excluded
exam_trap: D, simple transient viral infection only — viral laryngitis is common, but it settles quickly; persistent hoarseness in a smoker must not be dismissed.
takeaway: Hoarseness that persists, especially in a smoker, is laryngeal cancer until excluded.

stem: A patient with hearing loss asks why the clinician wants to examine the ears and arrange hearing assessment rather than simply prescribing antibiotics. What is the reason?

options.A: Antibiotics restore most types of hearing loss
options.B: Treatment depends on the cause of hearing loss
options.C: Hearing loss is usually caused by infection
options.D: Hearing tests are reserved for children

correct_answer: B. Treatment depends on the cause of hearing loss
why_correct: Conductive, sensorineural and mixed hearing loss have different causes and management.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not restore hearing in most causes. C. Most hearing loss is not caused by acute infection. D. Hearing assessment helps characterise the deficit at any age. E. Many causes of hearing loss are persistent.
pearl: Hearing loss may be conductive, sensorineural or mixed; otoscopy, tuning-fork tests and audiometry identify the type, which then directs treatment.
thinking: Patient with hearing loss ↓ Many causes: wax, effusion, age-related, noise and others ↓ Antibiotics help only infective causes ↓ Treatment depends on the cause
exam_trap: C, hearing loss is usually caused by infection — infection is a familiar cause, but most hearing loss is not infective, so antibiotics without assessment are wrong.
takeaway: Characterise hearing loss before treating it; antibiotics are not a default.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking, urinary urgency and cognitive impairment. MRI shows enlarged ventricles without another clear explanation. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: The combination of gait disturbance, urinary dysfunction and cognitive impairment is characteristic of normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
why_wrong: B. Motor neurone disease (ALS) primarily causes progressive motor weakness. C. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor but not this classic triad. D. Primary progressive multiple sclerosis has a different pattern of neurological deficits. E. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes vertical gaze palsy and early falls, not ventricular enlargement.
pearl: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus gives the triad of gait disturbance, urinary urgency or incontinence and cognitive decline with enlarged ventricles; it is a potentially reversible cause of dementia.
thinking: Progressive gait difficulty ↓ Urinary urgency and cognitive impairment ↓ Enlarged ventricles without another cause ↓ Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
exam_trap: C, Parkinson's disease — gait disturbance tempts, but Parkinson's causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor and does not explain the triad with enlarged ventricles.
takeaway: Gait, urine and cognition plus enlarged ventricles: think normal-pressure hydrocephalus.

stem: A 31-year-old man hears voices commenting on his actions and believes that strangers are secretly monitoring him. What syndrome is most likely?
why_correct: Hallucinations and delusional beliefs are characteristic features of psychosis.
why_wrong: A. Panic disorder causes episodic intense fear and autonomic symptoms. C. GAD causes excessive worry. D. A specific phobia involves marked fear of a particular object or situation. E. OCD involves intrusive thoughts and compulsions, with preserved reality testing.
pearl: Psychosis means loss of contact with reality, shown by hallucinations and delusions; voices commenting on actions and persecutory beliefs are classic features.
thinking: Voices commenting on his actions ↓ Belief that strangers are secretly monitoring him ↓ Hallucinations plus persecutory delusions ↓ Psychosis
exam_trap: E, OCD — intrusive thoughts can seem like fixed beliefs, but in OCD reality testing is preserved and there are no hallucinations.
takeaway: Hallucinations plus delusions mean psychosis; preserved reality testing points away from it.

stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks alcohol heavily develops tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea 12 hours after stopping alcohol. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea occurring after cessation of heavy alcohol use are typical features of alcohol withdrawal.
why_wrong: A. Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia rather than this autonomic picture. B. Hyperthyroidism causes more persistent symptoms. D. Opioid toxicity causes sedation and respiratory depression. E. Meningitis would usually produce fever and meningeal features.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal begins within hours of the last drink with tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea, and can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, so it needs active management.
thinking: Heavy alcohol use ↓ Stopped drinking about 12 hours earlier ↓ Tremor, sweating, anxiety and nausea: autonomic overactivity ↓ Alcohol withdrawal
exam_trap: A, Wernicke encephalopathy — also linked to heavy drinking, but causes confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia rather than this autonomic picture.
takeaway: Autonomic overactivity hours after stopping heavy drinking is alcohol withdrawal.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has severe low mood and says she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most important immediate priority?

options.A: Arrange a routine review in six months
options.B: Ignore the statement unless she has already attempted suicide
options.C: Focus only on her physical examination
options.D: Reassure her that suicidal thoughts are always harmless
options.E: Assess her immediate suicide risk and safety

correct_answer: E. Assess her immediate suicide risk and safety
why_correct: Suicidal thoughts require prompt assessment of immediate risk, protective factors and safety needs.
why_wrong: A. A routine delayed review is inappropriate when there may be immediate risk. B. Risk assessment is required before an attempt occurs. C. Physical assessment alone does not address the immediate safety concern. D. Suicidal thoughts cannot safely be dismissed.
pearl: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk; assess intent, plans, means, protective factors and immediate safety, and act on what you find.
thinking: Severe low mood ↓ Thoughts of ending her life disclosed ↓ Possible immediate danger ↓ Assess her immediate suicide risk and safety
exam_trap: B, ignore the statement unless she has already attempted suicide — past attempts raise risk, but their absence never makes suicidal thoughts safe to ignore.
takeaway: Any disclosure of suicidal thoughts needs an immediate risk and safety assessment.

stem: A 72-year-old man taking warfarin starts a new antibiotic. A few days later he develops nosebleeds and extensive bruising. What should be considered?

options.C: Iron deficiency from chronic occult blood loss
options.D: An interaction reducing the effect of warfarin
options.E: Vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism

correct_answer: A. An interaction increasing warfarin's effect
why_correct: Some antibiotics can increase anticoagulant effect and bleeding risk in patients taking warfarin.
why_wrong: B. Hypoglycaemia does not cause nosebleeds and bruising. C. Iron deficiency does not explain the acute bruising and bleeding. D. Increased bleeding suggests excessive rather than reduced anticoagulation. E. Vitamin D deficiency is unrelated to bleeding.
pearl: Several antibiotics, such as clarithromycin, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, can raise the INR; check the INR when a patient on warfarin starts one.
thinking: Warfarin plus a new antibiotic ↓ Days later: nosebleeds and extensive bruising ↓ Over-anticoagulation suggested ↓ Interaction increasing warfarin's effect
exam_trap: D, an interaction reducing warfarin's effect — interactions can go either way, but bleeding and bruising mean too much anticoagulation, not too little.
takeaway: New bleeding on warfarin after an antibiotic: suspect a raised INR from interaction.

stem: A patient develops diarrhoea shortly after starting an antibiotic. What complication should be considered if the diarrhoea is significant or persistent?
why_correct: Antibiotic exposure is an important risk factor for C. difficile infection, particularly when diarrhoea develops during or after treatment.
why_wrong: A. Microscopic colitis is associated with drugs such as PPIs and NSAIDs rather than being the key concern after antibiotics. C. Osteoporosis is unrelated to acute diarrhoea after antibiotics. D. IBS is a chronic functional disorder and is not the serious complication to consider after starting an antibiotic. E. Migraine does not explain persistent diarrhoea.
pearl: Diarrhoea during or after antibiotics should prompt stool testing for C. difficile; broad-spectrum agents such as clindamycin, cephalosporins and quinolones carry particular risk.
thinking: Recent antibiotic exposure ↓ Significant or persistent diarrhoea ↓ Disrupted gut flora allows C. difficile overgrowth ↓ C. difficile infection
exam_trap: A, collagenous microscopic colitis — causes watery diarrhoea and is drug-associated, but mainly with PPIs and NSAIDs; after antibiotics, C. difficile is the key concern.
takeaway: Antibiotics followed by diarrhoea: test for C. difficile.

stem: A 66-year-old man has a painless enlargement of his skull and increasing difficulty finding correctly fitting hats. What condition should be considered?
why_correct: Paget disease can cause abnormal enlargement and deformity of affected bones, including the skull.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis affects joints rather than causing skull enlargement. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without bony enlargement. D. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. E. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory polyarthritis.
pearl: Paget disease causes disordered bone remodelling; look for skull enlargement, bone pain, deafness and an isolated raised ALP with normal calcium.
thinking: Older man ↓ Painless skull enlargement; hats no longer fit ↓ Abnormal bone remodelling and enlargement ↓ Paget disease of bone
exam_trap: A, osteoarthritis — common in older adults and causes bony change, but it affects joints and does not enlarge the skull.
takeaway: Enlarging skull or increasing hat size in an older adult: think Paget disease.

stem: A patient with chronic diarrhoea develops weakness and a low potassium concentration. What is a likely explanation?
why_correct: Chronic diarrhoea can cause significant gastrointestinal potassium loss and hypokalaemia.
why_wrong: A. Retinal disease is unrelated. C. Haemoglobin production does not cause hypokalaemia. D. Bone density does not explain potassium loss. E. Vitamin D does not directly explain this presentation.
pearl: Diarrhoeal fluid is rich in potassium, so chronic diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia with weakness, cramps and arrhythmia risk; check U&Es and an ECG.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea ↓ Weakness with a low serum potassium ↓ Diarrhoeal fluid carries potassium out of the body ↓ Gastrointestinal potassium loss
exam_trap: E, excess vitamin D — causes hypercalcaemia and can cause weakness, but does not explain low potassium; the diarrhoea is the obvious source of loss.
takeaway: Chronic diarrhoea plus weakness: think hypokalaemia from GI loss.

stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops persistent itching without a primary skin rash. What is a possible explanation?
why_correct: Generalised pruritus can occur in advanced chronic kidney disease without a primary dermatological rash.
why_wrong: A. Atopic eczema causes itchy inflamed, often flexural, eczematous skin, so a primary rash would be present. B. Psoriasis produces visible scaly plaques. D. Tinea causes characteristic localised annular fungal lesions. E. Pityriasis rosea produces a herald patch followed by oval scaly lesions.
pearl: CKD-associated pruritus causes generalised itch without a primary rash, often with only scratch marks; it is common in advanced CKD and in patients on dialysis.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ Persistent generalised itching ↓ No primary skin rash to explain it ↓ CKD-associated pruritus
exam_trap: A, atopic eczema flare — itch is its hallmark, but eczema produces visible inflamed skin; itch without a primary rash points to a systemic cause.
takeaway: Itch without a rash in advanced CKD is CKD-associated pruritus.

stem: A 69-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops swollen ankles and increasing breathlessness. Which medication class is commonly used to help manage fluid overload?
why_correct: Loop diuretics can promote renal sodium and water excretion and are used to manage fluid overload when appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Antidiarrhoeals reduce bowel motility. C. Bisphosphonates affect bone metabolism. D. Antacids treat gastrointestinal symptoms. E. Antihistamines treat allergic symptoms.
pearl: Loop diuretics such as furosemide remain effective in reduced kidney function and are the mainstay for fluid overload in CKD; monitor weight, renal function and potassium.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ Ankle swelling and increasing breathlessness ↓ Salt and water overload ↓ Loop diuretics
exam_trap: C, bisphosphonates — familiar drugs in older patients, but they act on bone metabolism and do nothing for salt and water overload.
takeaway: Fluid overload in CKD is treated with loop diuretics and close monitoring.

stem: A patient develops excessive urination after a head injury. Blood glucose is normal. The urine is very dilute. What hormone deficiency can cause this?
why_correct: Central diabetes insipidus can occur after head injury due to impaired ADH production or release.
why_wrong: A. Insulin deficiency causes hyperglycaemia with osmotic diuresis, but blood glucose is normal. B. ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency with fatigue and hypotension rather than dilute polyuria. C. Growth hormone deficiency affects body composition and energy, not urine concentration. E. TSH deficiency causes secondary hypothyroidism.
pearl: Central diabetes insipidus can follow head injury, pituitary surgery or tumours; ADH deficiency causes large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose.
thinking: Head injury ↓ Excessive urination with normal glucose ↓ Very dilute urine ↓ Failure of ADH production or release ↓ Antidiuretic hormone deficiency
exam_trap: A, insulin — its deficiency causes polyuria, but through glucose-driven osmotic diuresis; normal glucose with dilute urine points to ADH.
takeaway: Dilute polyuria after head injury with normal glucose: ADH deficiency.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a painless, firm lump within one testicle. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Reassure as a probable epididymal cyst

correct_answer: C. Urgent assessment for testicular cancer
why_correct: A painless firm intratesticular mass in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise; NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral, with urgent scrotal ultrasound.
why_wrong: A. Delaying reassessment could delay the diagnosis of testicular cancer. B. An epididymal cyst is separate from the testis; a firm intratesticular lump must be investigated. D. Epididymo-orchitis is usually painful with inflammatory features, and antibiotics would delay diagnosis of a painless mass. E. A painless intratesticular mass needs a suspected cancer pathway referral, not a routine referral.
pearl: A firm painless lump within the testis is cancer until proven otherwise; refer on a suspected cancer pathway with urgent scrotal ultrasound.
thinking: Young man ↓ Painless, firm lump ↓ Arising within the testis itself ↓ Urgent assessment for testicular cancer
exam_trap: B, reassure as a probable epididymal cyst — cysts are common and benign, but lie separate from the testis; a firm intratesticular lump must be investigated.
takeaway: Intratesticular lump in a young man: urgent ultrasound and suspected cancer referral.

stem: During labour, a fetal hand is felt alongside the presenting part. What is this an example of?
why_correct: A limb presenting alongside another fetal presenting part is a compound presentation.
why_wrong: A. Cord prolapse involves the umbilical cord descending ahead of the presenting part. C. Occipitoposterior position describes the orientation of the fetal head, not a limb alongside the presenting part. D. Footling breech presentation means a foot presents first, rather than a hand alongside the head. E. Placenta praevia concerns placental location.
pearl: Compound presentation is a fetal limb, usually a hand, lying alongside the presenting part, most often the head; distinguish it from cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency.
thinking: Labour in progress ↓ Fetal hand felt on examination ↓ Lying alongside the presenting part ↓ Compound presentation
exam_trap: A, cord prolapse — also something felt beside the presenting part, but that is umbilical cord, not a limb; a hand alongside it is compound presentation.
takeaway: A limb beside the presenting part is compound presentation; cord beside it is cord prolapse.

stem: A newborn becomes lethargic and feeds poorly. The infant feels cold and has an abnormal temperature. What is the appropriate concern?
why_correct: Poor feeding, lethargy and temperature abnormality in a newborn can be signs of serious infection and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Physiological jaundice does not cause lethargy, poor feeding and temperature instability. B. These are concerning rather than reassuring neonatal features. C. Transient tachypnoea causes early respiratory distress after birth rather than lethargy and temperature instability. E. Reflux causes effortless regurgitation in a thriving baby, not lethargy and abnormal temperature.
pearl: Neonatal infection often presents non-specifically: poor feeding, lethargy and temperature instability, including hypothermia, all demand urgent assessment.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Lethargy and poor feeding ↓ Feels cold with abnormal temperature ↓ Non-specific signs of serious illness ↓ Possible neonatal infection
exam_trap: B, normal newborn behaviour after birth — newborns sleep a lot, but lethargy, poor feeding and temperature instability are red flags, never normal.
takeaway: In a newborn, abnormal temperature plus poor feeding means infection until proven otherwise.

stem: A 6-year-old child has recurrent abdominal pain around the umbilicus. Growth is normal, examination is normal and there are no red-flag features. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Recurrent abdominal pain without alarm features and with normal growth and examination is commonly functional.
why_wrong: B. Appendicitis causes an acute evolving illness with localising signs, not recurrent pain with a normal examination. C. Peritonitis causes significant tenderness and systemic illness. D. Obstruction usually causes vomiting, distension and inability to pass stool or flatus. E. Inflammatory bowel disease usually causes red flags such as weight loss, poor growth, diarrhoea or rectal bleeding.
pearl: Recurrent periumbilical pain in a thriving child with normal examination and no red flags is usually functional; explain, reassure and avoid over-investigation.
thinking: 6-year-old with recurrent periumbilical pain ↓ Normal growth and examination ↓ No red-flag features ↓ Functional abdominal pain
exam_trap: E, inflammatory bowel disease — causes recurrent pain, but usually with red flags such as weight loss, poor growth, diarrhoea or rectal bleeding, all absent here.
takeaway: Recurrent pain with normal growth, normal examination and no red flags is functional.

stem: A child develops a widespread itchy rash after taking a new antibiotic. There is no breathing difficulty, facial swelling or circulatory compromise. What should be considered?
why_correct: A new rash following medication exposure without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise suggests a drug-related skin reaction rather than anaphylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Anaphylaxis requires features of significant airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. B. Kawasaki disease causes prolonged fever with conjunctival, mucosal and extremity changes. C. Henoch–Schönlein purpura causes a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and legs rather than an itchy rash after a drug. E. Meningococcal septicaemia causes a non-blanching rash in an unwell child.
pearl: An itchy rash after a new drug without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise is a drug reaction, not anaphylaxis; stop the drug and record the reaction.
thinking: Child starts a new antibiotic ↓ Widespread itchy rash ↓ No breathing difficulty, facial swelling or circulatory compromise ↓ Drug-related rash
exam_trap: A, anaphylaxis — the drug-rash link tempts, but anaphylaxis requires airway, breathing or circulation compromise, which is explicitly absent.
takeaway: Skin features alone after a drug suggest a drug rash; anaphylaxis needs ABC compromise.

stem: A child develops a rash consisting of small fluid-filled lesions at different stages of development. Some lesions are crusted while others are fresh vesicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Crops of itchy vesicles at different stages are characteristic of chickenpox.
why_wrong: A. Measles causes a widespread maculopapular rash rather than crops of vesicles. B. Scarlet fever causes a fine, rough-textured rash. C. Impetigo causes superficial erosions and golden crusts. D. Erythema nodosum causes tender subcutaneous nodules.
pearl: Chickenpox produces itchy crops of lesions at different stages — papules, vesicles and crusts together — usually starting on the trunk and face.
thinking: Child with a vesicular rash ↓ Lesions at different stages ↓ Fresh vesicles alongside crusted ones ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: C, impetigo — also crusts, but the crusts are golden and follow superficial erosions; crops of vesicles at different stages are typical of chickenpox.
takeaway: Vesicles and crusts at different stages together point to chickenpox.

stem: A child develops fever, sore throat and a rash that feels rough to touch. The tongue is red and prominent papillae are visible. What is this tongue appearance called?
why_correct: A red tongue with prominent papillae in the context of scarlet fever is classically described as a strawberry tongue.
why_wrong: A. Fissured tongue has grooves or fissures. B. Black hairy tongue produces dark elongated papillae. D. Geographic tongue produces irregular depapillated areas. E. A smooth tongue lacks the prominent papillae described.
pearl: Scarlet fever combines fever, sore throat, a sandpaper-like rash and a strawberry tongue; it is caused by group A streptococcus and is a notifiable disease in England.
thinking: Fever and sore throat ↓ Rash rough to touch ↓ Red tongue with prominent papillae ↓ Strawberry tongue
exam_trap: D, geographic tongue — another distinctive tongue pattern, but it shows smooth depapillated patches, the opposite of prominent papillae.
takeaway: Sandpaper rash plus strawberry tongue means scarlet fever.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has intermittent calf pain after walking a fixed distance. The pain disappears after resting for several minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Predictable exertional calf pain relieved by rest is characteristic of intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes persistent inflammatory skin changes. B. Acute limb ischaemia causes sudden severe symptoms and threatened limb viability. C. Venous disease causes chronic swelling and skin changes rather than classic exertional calf pain. D. DVT usually causes swelling and pain rather than predictable exertional symptoms.
pearl: Intermittent claudication is reproducible calf pain after walking a predictable distance, relieved by rest; it signals peripheral arterial disease, so check pulses and ABPI.
thinking: Calf pain on walking ↓ Fixed, predictable distance ↓ Relieved by rest within minutes ↓ Intermittent claudication
exam_trap: D, deep vein thrombosis — also causes calf pain, but with persistent swelling and tenderness, not pain that reliably comes with exertion and settles with rest.
takeaway: Exertional calf pain relieved by rest is claudication: assess for peripheral arterial disease.

stem: A 69-year-old man develops sudden difficulty speaking but remains able to understand what is being said to him. Which cortical function is most likely affected?
why_correct: Difficulty producing language with relatively preserved comprehension suggests expressive language impairment.
why_wrong: B. Comprehension is preserved, which argues against receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia. C. Visuospatial impairment causes neglect or spatial disorientation rather than difficulty producing speech. D. Memory impairment does not cause expressive language difficulty. E. Hearing impairment does not directly cause loss of language production.
pearl: Expressive (Broca's) aphasia gives non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension; it localises to the dominant, usually left, inferior frontal lobe.
thinking: Sudden onset suggests a vascular event ↓ Difficulty speaking ↓ Understanding preserved ↓ Expressive aphasia ↓ Language production
exam_trap: B, language comprehension — aphasia tempts as a whole, but receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia impairs understanding, which is preserved here.
takeaway: Understands but cannot speak fluently: expressive (Broca's) aphasia.

stem: A patient is suspected of having bacterial meningitis. What principle should guide antibiotic treatment?

options.A: Avoid antibiotics because meningitis is always viral
