pearl: Cerebellar signs include ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia; a cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes signs on the same side.
thinking: Progressive difficulty coordinating movements ↓ Slurred speech (dysarthria) ↓ Unsteady gait ↓ Cerebellum
exam_trap: C, peripheral sensory nerve — sensory loss can cause an unsteady gait, but it does not cause slurred speech or cerebellar-type limb incoordination.
takeaway: Ataxia plus dysarthria localises to the cerebellum.

stem: A 47-year-old woman develops weakness that is worse when she repeatedly uses the affected muscles. Sensation is normal. Which anatomical site is primarily affected in myasthenia gravis?
why_correct: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting neuromuscular transmission at the neuromuscular junction.
why_wrong: A. Cerebellar disease causes coordination problems. B. Optic nerve disease causes visual impairment. C. Kidney disease does not explain fatigable skeletal muscle weakness. D. Posterior column disease primarily affects proprioception and vibration.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis is antibody-mediated, usually against acetylcholine receptors, at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and diplopia, and normal sensation.
thinking: Weakness worse with repeated use ↓ Fatigability ↓ Sensation normal ↓ Neuromuscular junction
exam_trap: D, spinal cord posterior columns — a neurological site, but posterior column disease causes loss of proprioception and vibration sense, not fatigable weakness.
takeaway: Fatigable weakness with normal sensation: neuromuscular junction, think myasthenia.

stem: A 34-year-old man reports numbness and tingling in both feet. Examination shows reduced vibration sensation and reduced ankle reflexes. What type of problem is most likely?
why_correct: Distal sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes is typical of peripheral neuropathy.
why_wrong: B. Upper motor neuron lesions usually produce brisk reflexes. C. Migraine does not cause persistent distal sensory loss. D. Myasthenia affects motor transmission without sensory loss. E. Cerebellar disease causes incoordination rather than a distal sensory neuropathy pattern.
pearl: Length-dependent peripheral neuropathy starts in the feet with reduced vibration sense and depressed ankle reflexes; common causes include diabetes, alcohol and B12 deficiency.
thinking: Numbness and tingling in both feet ↓ Reduced vibration sensation ↓ Reduced ankle reflexes ↓ Peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: B, upper motor neuron lesion — it can cause bilateral leg symptoms, but it produces brisk reflexes, not reduced ankle reflexes.
takeaway: Distal sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes: peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of acute arthritis and is found to have hard nodules around several finger joints. What are these nodules most likely to represent?
why_correct: Tophi are deposits of monosodium urate associated with longstanding gout.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid nodules are associated with rheumatoid arthritis rather than chronic urate deposition. B. Ganglia are fluid-filled structures commonly found around joints and tendons. D. Sebaceous cysts are skin-associated cysts. E. Lipomas are benign fatty tissue lumps.
pearl: Tophi are urate deposits of chronic gout, often around finger joints, the ears and elbows; they indicate the need for long-term urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent acute arthritis ↓ Hard nodules around finger joints ↓ Chronic urate crystal deposition ↓ Tophi
exam_trap: A, rheumatoid nodules — firm nodules near joints are a recognised RA feature, but recurrent acute arthritis attacks point to gout.
takeaway: Recurrent acute arthritis with hard periarticular nodules: tophaceous gout.

stem: A 67-year-old man has a painful swollen big toe following several days of heavy alcohol intake and dietary excess. What mechanism underlies gout?

options.C: Bacterial invasion of the joint in every case

correct_answer: E. Deposition of monosodium urate crystals
why_correct: Gout results from inflammatory responses to monosodium urate crystal deposition.
why_wrong: A. Cholesterol deposition is not the mechanism of gout. B. Calcium oxalate is not the usual cause of gout. C. Bacterial infection causes septic arthritis. D. Autoimmune mechanisms are important in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis.
pearl: Gout is inflammation triggered by monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; alcohol and dietary excess can precipitate attacks.
thinking: Painful swollen big toe ↓ Heavy alcohol and dietary excess ↓ Urate precipitates in the joint ↓ Deposition of monosodium urate crystals
exam_trap: C, bacterial invasion of the joint — septic arthritis must be excluded in a hot joint, but it is not the mechanism of gout.
takeaway: Gout: monosodium urate crystals, needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

stem: A 69-year-old man has acute pain and swelling of the knee. Synovial fluid contains calcium pyrophosphate crystals. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease causes acute inflammatory arthritis known as pseudogout.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. C. Bursitis affects a bursa rather than the joint itself. D. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis.
pearl: Pseudogout is acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, classically of an older adult's knee; crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, often with chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.
thinking: Older man with acute knee pain and swelling ↓ Joint aspirated ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate crystals seen ↓ Pseudogout
exam_trap: D, gout — it is the other crystal arthritis, but it is caused by monosodium urate, not calcium pyrophosphate.
takeaway: Pyrophosphate crystals mean pseudogout; urate crystals mean gout.

stem: A 41-year-old man has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of several fingers, with sausage-like swelling of entire digits. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Dactylitis is diffuse swelling of an entire digit and is associated with conditions including psoriatic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Erythema nodosum causes tender subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins. B. Clubbing is enlargement of the distal fingers with altered nail curvature. C. Koilonychia refers to spoon-shaped nails. D. Cyanosis is bluish discoloration from increased deoxygenated haemoglobin.
pearl: Dactylitis, sausage-like swelling of a whole digit, is typical of spondyloarthritis, especially psoriatic arthritis, so look for psoriasis and nail pitting.
thinking: Painful swelling of several fingers ↓ Whole digits swollen like sausages ↓ Inflammation of joints and tendon sheaths together ↓ Dactylitis
exam_trap: B, clubbing — another finger sign, but it is painless bulbous enlargement of the fingertip with nail changes, not whole-digit swelling.
takeaway: Sausage digit means dactylitis: think psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 24-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain and vomiting after returning from a holiday abroad. Several friends who ate the same meal have similar symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Multiple people developing acute gastrointestinal symptoms after sharing food strongly suggests foodborne illness.
why_wrong: B. Migraine does not explain a cluster of gastrointestinal illness. C. Appendicitis would not typically affect several people who ate the same meal. D. Renal colic is not a foodborne illness. E. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain.
pearl: Several people falling ill after a shared meal indicates foodborne illness; suspected food poisoning is notifiable in England, so inform the local health protection team.
thinking: Abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ After a shared meal ↓ Several companions affected at the same time ↓ Food poisoning
exam_trap: C, appendicitis — severe abdominal pain in a young man suggests it, but a cluster of people ill after the same meal points to a shared food source.
takeaway: A cluster of gastrointestinal illness after a shared meal means food poisoning: notify.

stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after a suspected foodborne infection. Several days later, he becomes pale, tired and passes very little urine. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea followed by anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury is characteristic of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency from blood loss develops gradually and does not cause reduced urine output. B. Henoch–Schönlein purpura causes a purpuric rash, joint and abdominal pain rather than this post-diarrhoeal picture. D. Intussusception causes colicky pain and redcurrant-jelly stool rather than pallor and oliguria days later. E. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a throat or skin infection, not bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: HUS typically follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157; antibiotics and antimotility agents are generally avoided in suspected cases.
thinking: Bloody diarrhoea after foodborne infection ↓ Days later, pale and tired from anaemia ↓ Very little urine from acute kidney injury ↓ Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
exam_trap: A, iron deficiency from blood loss — pallor after bloody diarrhoea seems to fit, but it develops slowly and does not explain reduced urine output.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea followed by pallor and oliguria in a child: HUS.

stem: A child recovering from bloody diarrhoea develops pallor, bruising and reduced urine output. Which three abnormalities characterise haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

options.A: Aplastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.B: Haemolytic anaemia, neutropenia and acute kidney injury
options.C: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.D: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytosis and acute kidney injury
options.E: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute liver failure

correct_answer: C. Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
why_correct: This triad is characteristic of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
why_wrong: A. The anaemia in HUS is haemolytic, not aplastic. B. Neutropenia is not part of the triad. D. Platelets are low, not raised, in HUS. E. The organ injury in HUS is renal, not hepatic.
pearl: HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy: haemolytic anaemia with red cell fragments on the blood film, low platelets and acute kidney injury.
thinking: Recovering from bloody diarrhoea ↓ Pallor from haemolysis and bruising from low platelets ↓ Reduced urine from kidney injury ↓ Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
exam_trap: E, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute liver failure — two parts are right, but the organ injured in HUS is the kidney, not the liver.
takeaway: HUS triad: haemolytic anaemia, low platelets and acute kidney injury.

stem: A 26-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhoea after returning from a region with poor sanitation. She is extremely thirsty and has marked dehydration. Which organism is classically associated with severe watery diarrhoea?
why_correct: Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea that can rapidly produce severe dehydration.
why_wrong: B. Tuberculosis usually causes chronic disease. C. Streptococcus pyogenes commonly causes throat and skin infections. D. Meningococcus causes invasive meningococcal disease. E. Staphylococcus aureus can cause various infections and food poisoning but is not the classic cause of massive watery diarrhoea described here.
pearl: Cholera causes profuse, painless rice-water diarrhoea that can cause life-threatening dehydration within hours; oral rehydration solution is the mainstay, with IV fluids if severe.
thinking: Return from an area with poor sanitation ↓ Profuse watery diarrhoea ↓ Marked dehydration and thirst ↓ Vibrio cholerae
exam_trap: E, Staphylococcus aureus — a classic food-poisoning organism, but its toxin mainly causes rapid-onset vomiting, not massive watery diarrhoea.
takeaway: Profuse rice-water diarrhoea with severe dehydration after travel: cholera.

stem: A 25-year-old man develops diarrhoea while travelling abroad. He has no blood in the stool and remains systemically well. What is an important initial management principle?

options.B: Restrict fluids to reduce stool volume

why_correct: Most uncomplicated traveller's diarrhoea is managed initially with adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not routinely needed for mild traveller's diarrhoea in a well patient. B. Fluid restriction risks dehydration. C. A systemically well patient can usually rehydrate orally without admission. D. Metronidazole is for specific infections such as giardiasis, not empirical use.
pearl: Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting; oral fluids and electrolytes are the mainstay, with antibiotics reserved for severe illness, dysentery or high-risk patients.
thinking: Diarrhoea while travelling ↓ No blood in the stool ↓ Systemically well ↓ Maintain adequate oral hydration
exam_trap: A, routine empirical ciprofloxacin — antibiotics can shorten severe traveller's diarrhoea, but they are not routine in a well patient and add resistance and side-effect risks.
takeaway: Mild traveller's diarrhoea in a well patient: rehydrate, no routine antibiotics.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops recurrent bloating, abdominal discomfort and foul-smelling diarrhoea after returning from a camping trip where he drank untreated stream water. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Untreated freshwater exposure followed by persistent bloating and malabsorptive diarrhoea is typical of giardiasis.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain. C. Renal colic causes severe flank-to-groin pain. D. Acute cholecystitis causes persistent right upper quadrant pain and systemic inflammation. E. Peptic ulcer disease typically causes dyspepsia or upper GI pain.
pearl: Giardiasis follows drinking untreated water and causes bloating, flatulence and foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea; confirm on stool testing and treat with metronidazole.
thinking: Drank untreated stream water ↓ Recurrent bloating and abdominal discomfort ↓ Foul-smelling malabsorptive diarrhoea ↓ Giardiasis
exam_trap: E, peptic ulcer disease — upper abdominal discomfort and bloating overlap, but it does not cause foul-smelling diarrhoea after drinking untreated water.
takeaway: Untreated water followed by bloating and foul, greasy diarrhoea: Giardia.

stem: A newborn has repeated episodes of vomiting, lethargy and poor feeding after feeds are introduced. The infant appears well between episodes. Which category of disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent unexplained deterioration associated with feeding in a newborn can indicate an inherited metabolic disorder.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents at 2–8 weeks with projectile vomiting in a hungry baby rather than lethargy. B. Reflux causes effortless regurgitation in a thriving infant without lethargy. C. Cow's milk protein allergy causes vomiting, eczema or bloody stools rather than recurrent lethargic decompensation. E. Neonatal abstinence syndrome causes irritability, tremor and high-pitched crying after in-utero opioid exposure.
pearl: A newborn who repeatedly deteriorates with vomiting and lethargy after feeds, but is well between episodes, may have an inborn error of metabolism; check glucose, ammonia and blood gas and seek urgent specialist advice.
thinking: Newborn with repeated vomiting and lethargy ↓ Episodes linked to feeds ↓ Well between episodes, suggesting metabolic decompensation ↓ Inherited metabolic disorder
exam_trap: A, pyloric stenosis — it causes repeated vomiting after feeds, but it presents at a few weeks old with projectile vomiting in a hungry baby, not lethargy.
takeaway: Feed-related vomiting with lethargy in a newborn: think inborn error of metabolism.

stem: A newborn develops prolonged jaundice, poor feeding and lethargy. Which feature would make an inherited metabolic disorder particularly concerning?

options.A: Normal urine and stool with no symptoms

why_correct: Feed-associated deterioration can be a clue to metabolic disorders in neonates.
why_wrong: A. Absence of symptoms makes a serious metabolic disorder less likely. B. Crying alone is nonspecific. C. Normal feeding and growth are reassuring. E. Hiccups alone are common and nonspecific.
pearl: Prolonged jaundice with poor feeding and lethargy that worsen after feeds suggests a metabolic disorder such as galactosaemia; prolonged neonatal jaundice always needs investigation.
thinking: Newborn with prolonged jaundice ↓ Poor feeding and lethargy ↓ Deterioration linked to feeds suggests a substrate-triggered metabolic disease ↓ Symptoms beginning after feeds
exam_trap: E, brief hiccups after feeds — also feed-related, but hiccups are common and harmless in newborns and carry no metabolic significance.
takeaway: In a sick newborn, deterioration after feeds is a clue to inherited metabolic disease.

stem: A 9-year-old child has recurrent wheeze and chronic productive cough. The child also has poor growth and frequent chest infections. Which investigation may be particularly relevant when cystic fibrosis is suspected?
why_correct: Sweat chloride testing is an important diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Faecal occult blood testing does not diagnose cystic fibrosis. C. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. D. Exercise ECG is not a diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis. E. D-dimer assesses thrombotic risk in appropriate clinical contexts.
pearl: Sweat chloride testing is the key diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis; suspect it with recurrent chest infections, chronic productive cough, poor growth or malabsorption, even after newborn screening.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze and chronic productive cough ↓ Frequent chest infections ↓ Poor growth ↓ Sweat chloride testing
exam_trap: A, faecal occult blood testing — gut involvement is part of CF, but occult blood testing does not assess it or diagnose cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: Suspected cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride test.

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is offered a screening test for a fetal chromosomal condition. She asks whether a positive result proves that the fetus has the condition. What is the correct explanation?

options.A: No; it estimates risk; diagnostic testing may follow
options.B: No; but a repeat screening test will confirm the result
options.C: Yes; a higher-chance result confirms the diagnosis outright
options.D: Yes; positive screening results are diagnostic in themselves
options.E: No; but a detailed anomaly scan at 20 weeks will confirm it

correct_answer: A. No; it estimates risk; diagnostic testing may follow
why_correct: Screening estimates the probability of a condition; diagnostic testing is used when definitive confirmation is required.
why_wrong: B. Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis. C. A higher-chance result estimates probability and does not confirm the diagnosis. D. Screening is not equivalent to diagnosis and false-positive results occur. E. Ultrasound findings can support suspicion but do not confirm a chromosomal diagnosis; diagnostic testing such as CVS or amniocentesis is required.
pearl: Antenatal screening for chromosomal conditions gives a chance estimate; a higher-chance result leads to an offer of further testing, with CVS or amniocentesis needed for a diagnosis.
thinking: Pregnant woman offered screening ↓ Screening estimates chance, not certainty ↓ False positives occur ↓ No; it estimates risk; diagnostic testing may follow
exam_trap: E, the 20-week anomaly scan will confirm it — ultrasound markers can raise suspicion, but only invasive testing such as CVS or amniocentesis confirms a chromosomal diagnosis.
takeaway: Screening gives a chance; CVS or amniocentesis gives a diagnosis.

stem: A 38-year-old man has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and jaundice. Imaging shows multiple stones within the bile ducts. What condition is present?
why_correct: Stones within the common bile duct or biliary tree are termed choledocholithiasis.
why_wrong: A. Cholelithiasis refers to stones in the gallbladder rather than the bile ducts. C. Nephrolithiasis refers to kidney stones. D. Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder. E. Sialolithiasis refers to salivary gland stones.
pearl: Choledocholithiasis presents with biliary pain plus obstructive jaundice and can be complicated by cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis; duct stones are usually removed by ERCP.
thinking: Recurrent abdominal pain with jaundice ↓ jaundice means bile flow is blocked ↓ imaging places the stones within the bile ducts ↓ duct stones = choledocholithiasis
exam_trap: A, Cholelithiasis — the commonest gallstone term, so it tempts, but it means stones in the gallbladder; stones lying in the bile ducts are choledocholithiasis.
takeaway: Gallbladder stones = cholelithiasis; bile duct stones = choledocholithiasis.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting around 30 minutes, associated with tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss in one ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic vertigo associated with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus is characteristic of Ménière's disease.
why_wrong: B. BPPV causes brief positional episodes without characteristic hearing loss. C. Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged vertigo without the characteristic fluctuating hearing loss. D. Otosclerosis usually causes progressive conductive hearing loss rather than episodic vertigo. E. Otitis externa causes ear canal pain and inflammation.
pearl: Ménière's disease is the triad of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, often with aural fullness.
thinking: Recurrent vertigo lasting about 30 minutes ↓ tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss in one ear ↓ episodic vertigo with cochlear symptoms ↓ Ménière's disease
exam_trap: B, Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — common and recurrent, but attacks last seconds, are triggered by head position and have no hearing loss or tinnitus.
takeaway: Vertigo for minutes to hours plus hearing loss and tinnitus: think Ménière's disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman develops recurrent episodes of a spinning sensation when she rolls over in bed. Examination is otherwise normal. Which bedside test is commonly used to provoke symptoms in suspected BPPV?
why_correct: The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre is used to assess for posterior canal BPPV.
why_wrong: A. The Epley manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV rather than being the diagnostic test. B. The head impulse test assesses vestibulo-ocular reflex function in acute vestibular syndrome. C. The Semont manoeuvre is a treatment manoeuvre rather than the standard diagnostic test. E. Romberg assesses proprioception and balance but does not provoke BPPV.
pearl: In posterior canal BPPV, the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre provokes vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus after a short latency; the Epley manoeuvre then treats it.
thinking: Recurrent spinning on rolling over in bed ↓ examination otherwise normal ↓ suspected posterior canal BPPV ↓ provoke it with the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre
exam_trap: A, Epley manoeuvre — the best-known BPPV manoeuvre, but it is the repositioning treatment; the bedside test that provokes symptoms is the Dix-Hallpike.
takeaway: Dix-Hallpike provokes and diagnoses BPPV; the Epley manoeuvre treats it.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with sudden hearing loss in one ear that developed over several hours. There is no obvious obstruction in the ear canal. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Prescribe ear drops for wax without examination
options.B: Ignore the symptom if there is no pain
options.C: Treat as an urgent ENT problem
options.E: Reassure and review in one year

correct_answer: C. Treat as an urgent ENT problem
why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss requires urgent assessment because early treatment may be time-sensitive.
why_wrong: A. Wax should not be assumed without evidence of obstruction. B. Absence of pain does not make sudden hearing loss benign. D. Presbycusis is gradual and age-related. E. Delayed assessment risks missing a time-sensitive condition.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss without an obvious cause is an ENT emergency; early specialist assessment allows time-sensitive treatment such as steroids to be considered.
thinking: Unilateral hearing loss developing over hours ↓ no canal obstruction, so not wax ↓ likely sudden sensorineural hearing loss ↓ treat as an urgent ENT problem
exam_trap: D, Diagnose presbycusis — tempting at 63, but presbycusis is gradual and usually symmetrical; loss over hours in one ear needs urgent ENT assessment.
takeaway: Sudden unexplained hearing loss is an urgent referral, not a wait-and-see problem.

stem: A 45-year-old man has chronic nasal obstruction, facial pressure and reduced sense of smell. Symptoms have persisted for several months. What condition should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent nasal symptoms with facial pressure and reduced smell are typical features of chronic rhinosinusitis.
why_wrong: A. Rhinitis medicamentosa follows prolonged topical decongestant use and does not typically cause facial pressure and loss of smell. C. Viral rhinitis resolves within days to weeks. D. Ménière's disease causes episodic vertigo and hearing symptoms. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric shock-like facial pain without nasal symptoms.
pearl: Chronic rhinosinusitis means sinonasal symptoms persisting beyond about three months, such as blockage, discharge, facial pressure and reduced smell; look for nasal polyps.
thinking: Nasal obstruction, facial pressure and reduced smell ↓ symptoms persisting for several months ↓ chronic sinonasal inflammation ↓ chronic rhinosinusitis
exam_trap: A, Rhinitis medicamentosa — causes chronic congestion, but needs prolonged topical decongestant use and does not typically cause facial pressure and loss of smell.
takeaway: Months of blockage, facial pressure and reduced smell point to chronic rhinosinusitis.

stem: A child is suspected of having aspirated a small toy. He is coughing but remains able to speak and breathe. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Give food to push the object down
options.B: Blindly sweep the mouth with fingers
options.C: Lie the child flat and leave him alone
options.D: Immediately perform abdominal thrusts despite effective coughing
options.E: Encourage coughing and assess the child

correct_answer: E. Encourage coughing and assess the child
why_correct: An effectively coughing child should be encouraged to cough while being closely assessed.
why_wrong: A. Food should not be used to dislodge an airway foreign body. B. Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper. C. The child requires active observation and appropriate escalation if deterioration occurs. D. Abdominal thrusts are not indicated when the child has an effective cough.
pearl: A child with a suspected inhaled foreign body who is coughing effectively should be encouraged to cough and watched closely; back blows and thrusts are for an ineffective cough.
thinking: Suspected aspirated toy ↓ child can cough, speak and breathe ↓ the cough is effective ↓ encourage coughing and assess the child
exam_trap: D, Immediate abdominal thrusts — part of choking management, but only once the cough becomes ineffective; with an effective cough they are unnecessary and risk harm.
takeaway: Effective cough: encourage and observe. Ineffective cough: back blows, then thrusts.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of palpitations, sweating and a feeling of impending doom. Her ECG is normal between episodes. She has no syncope or exertional symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent sudden episodes of intense fear accompanied by autonomic symptoms, with no evidence of an underlying cardiac cause, are characteristic of panic attacks.
why_wrong: B. Aortic stenosis typically causes exertional symptoms and a characteristic murmur. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness, oedema and exercise intolerance. D. PE can cause acute dyspnoea and chest pain but would not typically cause recurrent stereotyped episodes with this pattern. E. Ventricular tachycardia is a cardiac arrhythmia and would usually produce an abnormal rhythm during an episode.
pearl: Panic attacks are sudden surges of intense fear with autonomic symptoms that peak within minutes; exclude arrhythmia and other organic causes before attributing palpitations to panic.
thinking: Recurrent palpitations, sweating and impending doom ↓ normal ECG between episodes ↓ no syncope or exertional symptoms ↓ panic attacks
exam_trap: E, Ventricular tachycardia — palpitations and dread fit, but VT is a dangerous arrhythmia that tends to cause presyncope or syncope; fear-driven episodes without cardiac features fit panic.
takeaway: Episodic fear with autonomic symptoms and no cardiac findings suggests panic attacks.

stem: A patient with OCD spends several hours each day washing their hands because of an intrusive fear of contamination. Which feature most strongly distinguishes a compulsion from an ordinary habit?

options.A: It is repeated at the same time each day
options.C: It relieves distress caused by an obsession
options.D: It is performed more quickly than usual
options.E: It is tied to a routine such as mealtimes

correct_answer: C. It relieves distress caused by an obsession
why_correct: Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules, often to reduce distress.
why_wrong: A. Regular timing describes a routine rather than a compulsion. B. Automatic behaviour without awareness is typical of a habit; compulsions are driven by an obsession. D. Speed is not a defining feature. E. Linking washing to routines such as mealtimes is normal hygiene.
pearl: Compulsions are repetitive acts driven by an obsession to neutralise anxiety; they bring brief relief but reinforce the cycle. CBT with exposure and response prevention is first-line.
thinking: Intrusive contamination fear (obsession) ↓ hours of handwashing in response ↓ the act is done to reduce obsessional distress ↓ that link defines a compulsion
exam_trap: B, It happens automatically without thought — tempting because both are repetitive, but automatic, unthinking behaviour is a habit; compulsions are driven by an obsession.
takeaway: A compulsion is driven by an obsession and done to reduce distress; a habit is not.

stem: A 40-year-old man develops recurrent intrusive thoughts that he might accidentally harm his children. He finds the thoughts extremely distressing and has no wish to act on them. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Thought insertion indicating a psychotic illness

correct_answer: D. Ego-dystonic obsessional thoughts, not intent
why_correct: Unwanted intrusive thoughts can occur in OCD and are often inconsistent with the person's wishes and values.
why_wrong: A. Thought insertion is the belief that thoughts are placed by an external agency, whereas he recognises these thoughts as his own. B. The thoughts are unwanted and he has no wish to act on them, so they do not represent homicidal ideation. C. PTSD intrusions are re-experiencing of a traumatic event. E. Overvalued ideas are firmly held and acceptable to the person, not distressing unwanted intrusions.
pearl: Ego-dystonic intrusive harm thoughts in OCD are unwanted and distressing, and do not reflect intent; the person resists them. Do not mistake them for homicidal ideation.
thinking: Recurrent thoughts of harming his children ↓ the thoughts are extremely distressing ↓ no wish or intent to act ↓ ego-dystonic obsessional thoughts, not intent
exam_trap: B, Homicidal ideation requiring urgent safeguarding — the content sounds alarming, but the thoughts are unwanted, distressing and without intent, which marks them as obsessional.
takeaway: Unwanted, distressing harm thoughts that the person resists are obsessions, not intent.

stem: A 28-year-old man develops nightmares, hypervigilance and avoidance after being assaulted. He has difficulty sleeping and becomes distressed when passing the location of the assault. Which feature is particularly characteristic of PTSD?
why_correct: Intrusive memories, nightmares or flashbacks are characteristic re-experiencing symptoms of PTSD.
why_wrong: A. Progressive memory loss suggests a cognitive disorder. B. Compulsive washing suggests OCD. C. Elevated mood suggests mania rather than PTSD. D. Isolated hallucinations do not define PTSD.
pearl: PTSD after trauma combines re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance and hyperarousal; trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line in the UK.
thinking: Assault followed by nightmares ↓ avoidance and hypervigilance ↓ distress at reminders of the trauma ↓ re-experiencing the event is the hallmark of PTSD
exam_trap: D, Auditory hallucinations in isolation — some trauma survivors describe perceptual disturbance, but isolated hallucinations do not define PTSD; re-experiencing the trauma does.
takeaway: PTSD hallmark: re-experiencing the trauma through flashbacks or nightmares.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with depression reports that she has lost interest in activities she previously enjoyed. What term describes this symptom?
why_correct: Anhedonia is loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyable activities.
why_wrong: A. Flight of ideas is rapid movement between connected thoughts, typically seen in mania. C. Echolalia is repetition of another person's words. D. Derealisation is a sense that the external world is unreal. E. Confabulation involves producing fabricated information, often without deliberate deception.
pearl: Anhedonia, loss of interest or pleasure, is a core symptom of depression alongside persistent low mood; ask about it directly in every mood assessment.
thinking: Patient with depression ↓ no longer enjoys previously enjoyed activities ↓ loss of interest or pleasure ↓ anhedonia
exam_trap: D, Derealisation — also a subjective change in experience, but it is a sense that the world is unreal, not a loss of enjoyment or interest.
takeaway: Loss of interest or pleasure is anhedonia, a core symptom of depression.

stem: A 41-year-old man with depression reports early-morning waking and waking several hours earlier than usual. Which symptom pattern is commonly associated with depression?

options.A: Reduced need for sleep with increased energy
options.D: Sleep paralysis as the defining feature

why_correct: Early-morning waking can occur in depressive illness, particularly with biological symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Reduced need for sleep with increased energy is characteristic of mania or hypomania. C. Dream recall is not a diagnostic feature of depression. D. Sleep paralysis is associated with sleep disorders rather than being a defining feature of depression. E. Alcohol-related sleep does not define depression.
pearl: Early-morning waking, mood worse in the morning, and loss of appetite and weight are biological (somatic) features suggesting more severe depression.
thinking: Known depression ↓ waking hours earlier than usual ↓ a biological symptom of depressive illness ↓ early-morning awakening
exam_trap: A, Reduced need for sleep with increased energy — also a sleep change, but feeling rested on little sleep is a feature of mania or hypomania, not depression.
takeaway: Depression: early-morning waking with tiredness. Mania: little sleep without tiredness.

stem: A patient with bipolar disorder has become increasingly energetic, sleeps only three hours a night without feeling tired, and is spending excessively. What symptom is particularly suggestive of mania?
why_correct: A reduced need for sleep, rather than simply insomnia with tiredness, is characteristic of mania.
why_wrong: A. Appetite change is nonspecific. C. Slowed speech is more associated with depression. D. Increased sleep is more consistent with depressive illness. E. Social withdrawal is not characteristic of mania.
pearl: In mania, a reduced need for sleep without fatigue is a key early warning sign, alongside elevated or irritable mood, overactivity and reckless spending.
thinking: Bipolar disorder with increasing energy ↓ only three hours' sleep yet not tired ↓ excessive spending ↓ reduced need for sleep points to mania
exam_trap: A, Loss of appetite alone — appetite may fall in mania, but it is non-specific; the distinctive feature is needing little sleep without feeling tired.
takeaway: Sleeping little yet feeling energetic signals mania, not simple insomnia.

stem: A 30-year-old man repeatedly eats very large amounts of food rapidly and feels unable to control his eating. He does not regularly vomit or use laxatives afterwards. His BMI is increasing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent episodes of binge eating without regular compensatory behaviours are characteristic of binge-eating disorder.
why_wrong: A. Anorexia is characterised by restriction and significantly low body weight. C. Prader–Willi syndrome is a genetic disorder with hyperphagia from childhood and learning disability. D. A specific phobia involves a circumscribed fear. E. Bulimia includes regular compensatory behaviours.
pearl: Binge-eating disorder involves recurrent loss-of-control binges without regular compensatory behaviours, so weight often rises, unlike bulimia.
thinking: Recurrent rapid eating of large amounts ↓ feels unable to control eating ↓ no regular vomiting or laxatives; BMI rising ↓ binge-eating disorder
exam_trap: E, Bulimia nervosa — shares recurrent binges with loss of control, but requires regular compensatory behaviours such as vomiting or laxatives, which he does not use.
takeaway: Binges without regular compensation = binge-eating disorder; with compensation = bulimia.

stem: A 22-year-old university student has become increasingly withdrawn and believes that strangers on the bus are communicating secret messages specifically to him. What type of symptom is this?
why_correct: A fixed false belief that is not consistent with available evidence, such as believing strangers are sending personally directed secret messages, is a delusion.
why_wrong: A. A compulsion is a repetitive behaviour or mental act. B. An obsession is an intrusive unwanted thought, image or urge. C. A phobia is an excessive fear of a specific object or situation. D. Confabulation involves filling memory gaps with fabricated information.
pearl: A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with conviction despite contrary evidence and out of keeping with cultural background; new delusions in a young adult raise concern for psychosis.
thinking: Increasingly withdrawn young man ↓ believes strangers send him secret messages ↓ belief is fixed and not based on evidence ↓ delusion
exam_trap: B, Obsession — both involve persistent thoughts, but obsessions are recognised as one's own and unwanted; he holds this belief as true, so it is a delusion.
takeaway: Fixed false belief held with conviction = delusion; unwanted intrusive thought = obsession.

stem: A 30-year-old woman sees a coat hanging in a dark room and briefly mistakes it for a person. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: An illusion is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus.
why_wrong: A. A hallucination occurs without an external stimulus. B. Confabulation is the production of fabricated information, usually associated with memory impairment. C. An obsession is an intrusive thought, image or urge. D. A delusion is a false fixed belief.
pearl: An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus, common in poor light, fatigue or delirium; a hallucination is a perception without any external stimulus.
thinking: A real object is present (a coat) ↓ the room is dark ↓ briefly misperceived as a person ↓ misinterpretation of a real stimulus = illusion
exam_trap: A, Hallucination — she 'sees' a person, but a real stimulus (the coat) is being misread; hallucinations occur without any external stimulus.
takeaway: Real stimulus misread = illusion; no stimulus at all = hallucination.

stem: A 29-year-old man with psychosis believes that the television presenter is speaking directly to him through coded messages. What type of delusion is this?
why_correct: A delusion of reference involves believing that otherwise ordinary events or communications have a special personal significance.
why_wrong: B. Delusions of poverty involve an unfounded belief of being financially ruined or without resources. C. Nihilistic delusions involve beliefs that oneself, others or the world do not exist or have ceased to exist. D. Grandiose delusions involve exaggerated beliefs about power, identity or importance. E. Delusions of guilt involve excessive or unfounded guilt.
pearl: Delusions of reference involve believing that ordinary events, such as television or radio broadcasts, carry special messages meant personally for the patient.
thinking: Psychosis ↓ believes a TV presenter speaks directly to him ↓ an ordinary event given special personal meaning ↓ delusion of reference
exam_trap: D, Delusion of grandeur — being singled out by a broadcaster may sound special, but the core belief is personal significance in ordinary events, which is reference.
takeaway: Ordinary events seen as personal messages = delusion of reference.

stem: A 34-year-old woman believes that she has extraordinary powers and can control world events. Which type of delusion is this?
why_correct: Grandiose delusions involve an exaggerated belief in one's importance, power or abilities.
why_wrong: A. Delusions of reference involve assigning personal significance to external events. B. Persecutory delusions involve beliefs that others are intending harm. D. Delusions of guilt involve excessive or unfounded guilt. E. Nihilistic delusions involve beliefs about non-existence or destruction.
pearl: Grandiose delusions, such as having special powers or controlling world events, are typical of mania with psychotic features but also occur in schizophrenia.
thinking: Belief in extraordinary powers ↓ believes she controls world events ↓ exaggerated sense of power and importance ↓ delusion of grandeur
exam_trap: A, Delusion of reference — linking herself to world events may seem referential, but she believes she causes them through special power, which is grandiose.
takeaway: Belief in exceptional power, identity or importance = grandiose delusion.

stem: A 32-year-old man with psychosis believes that the government is following him and intends to kill him despite no supporting evidence. What type of delusion is this?
why_correct: A fixed belief that others are deliberately threatening or intending harm is a persecutory delusion.
why_wrong: A. Guilt delusions involve excessive or unfounded guilt. C. Reference delusions involve assigning special personal meaning to external events. D. Nihilistic delusions concern non-existence or destruction. E. Grandiose delusions involve exceptional power or importance.
pearl: Persecutory delusions, the belief that others intend harm, are the commonest delusions in schizophrenia; always assess the risk to the patient and to others.
thinking: Psychosis ↓ believes the government is following him ↓ believes they intend to kill him, without evidence ↓ persecutory delusion
exam_trap: C, Delusion of reference — being watched may seem referential, but the core belief is that others intend to harm him, which defines persecution.
takeaway: Fixed belief that others intend harm = persecutory delusion.

stem: A 42-year-old man with severe depression believes that he has committed unforgivable crimes and deserves to be punished, despite evidence that he has done nothing wrong. What type of delusion is this?
why_correct: An excessive, fixed and unfounded belief of having committed serious wrongdoing is a delusion of guilt.
why_wrong: B. Persecutory delusions involve beliefs of being threatened or harmed by others. C. Nihilistic delusions concern non-existence or destruction. D. Grandiose delusions concern exceptional power or importance. E. Reference delusions involve special personal significance assigned to external events.
pearl: Delusions of guilt, like nihilistic and poverty delusions, are mood-congruent features of psychotic depression, which needs urgent psychiatric assessment and risk review.
thinking: Severe depression ↓ believes he committed unforgivable crimes ↓ belief fixed despite evidence of no wrongdoing ↓ delusion of guilt
exam_trap: B, Persecutory delusion — 'deserves to be punished' suggests threat, but he blames himself rather than believing others are unjustly targeting him.
takeaway: Unfounded conviction of serious wrongdoing in depression = delusion of guilt.

stem: A 31-year-old man with schizophrenia believes that other people can hear his private thoughts. What is this symptom most commonly called?
why_correct: Thought broadcasting is the belief that other people can hear one's thoughts.
why_wrong: A. Thought insertion is the belief that thoughts are being placed in the mind by an external agency. C. Thought withdrawal is the belief that thoughts are being removed from the mind. D. Delusional perception is a delusion arising from a normal perception. E. Thought blocking is sudden interruption of the flow of thought or speech.
pearl: Thought broadcasting, insertion and withdrawal are thought-alienation symptoms and are first-rank symptoms classically associated with schizophrenia.
thinking: Schizophrenia ↓ believes others can hear his private thoughts ↓ his own thoughts felt to be shared with others ↓ thought broadcasting
exam_trap: A, Thought insertion — another thought-alienation symptom, but it means alien thoughts are placed into the mind, not that others can hear his own thoughts.
takeaway: Others hear my thoughts = broadcasting; thoughts put in = insertion; taken out = withdrawal.

stem: A patient suddenly stops speaking during a conversation and appears unable to continue the train of thought. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: Thought blocking is a sudden interruption in the flow of thought, often experienced as thoughts disappearing abruptly.
why_wrong: B. Flight of ideas is rapid shifting between thoughts. C. Echolalia is repetition of another person's speech. D. Thought broadcasting is the belief that others can hear one's thoughts. E. A neologism is a newly created or idiosyncratic word.
pearl: Thought blocking is an abrupt stop in the train of thought, often linked to schizophrenia; distinguish it from absence seizures and simple distraction.
thinking: Sudden stop in mid-conversation ↓ unable to continue the train of thought ↓ abrupt interruption of thought flow ↓ thought blocking
exam_trap: D, Thought broadcasting — another thought-related symptom of psychosis, but it is a belief that others hear one's thoughts, not an abrupt halt in thinking and speech.
takeaway: Sudden halt in thought and speech mid-sentence = thought blocking.

stem: A 27-year-old man with mania rapidly moves from one topic to another, with each new idea loosely connected to the previous one. What is this called?
why_correct: Flight of ideas is rapid shifting between thoughts, with understandable but often superficial connections, and is particularly associated with mania.
why_wrong: A. Echolalia is repetition of another person's words. B. Thought broadcasting is a belief that others can hear one's thoughts. C. Thought blocking is an abrupt interruption of thought. D. Confabulation concerns fabricated information associated with memory impairment.
pearl: Flight of ideas is rapid, pressured shifting between topics with understandable links such as puns or rhymes; it is a hallmark of mania.
thinking: Known mania ↓ rapid movement from one topic to another ↓ each new idea loosely linked to the last ↓ flight of ideas
exam_trap: C, Thought blocking — also a disturbance of thought flow, but it is a sudden stop, the opposite of the rapid, accelerated shifting seen in mania.
takeaway: Mania with rapid, loosely linked topic jumps = flight of ideas.

stem: A 26-year-old man repeatedly uses a made-up word that has no recognised meaning and insists that it describes an object. What is this called?
why_correct: A neologism is a newly created word or expression that has an idiosyncratic meaning to the patient.
why_wrong: A. Echolalia involves repeating another person's words. B. Flight of ideas is rapid movement between thoughts. C. Thought blocking is interruption of thought. D. A delusion of reference involves assigning personal significance to external events.
pearl: A neologism is a new word, or an existing word given a private meaning, and is a feature of formal thought disorder, typically in schizophrenia.
thinking: Repeatedly uses a made-up word ↓ the word has no recognised meaning ↓ insists it names an object ↓ neologism
exam_trap: A, Echolalia — another abnormal speech feature, but echolalia repeats words just spoken by someone else; inventing new words is a neologism.
takeaway: An invented word with a private meaning = neologism.

stem: A patient with delirium is agitated and repeatedly tries to leave the ward. What should be addressed first?

options.D: Identify and treat the underlying cause

correct_answer: D. Identify and treat the underlying cause
why_correct: Delirium is usually secondary to an underlying medical, medication-related or other precipitating cause that should be identified and managed.
why_wrong: A. Delirium should not automatically be labelled dementia. B. Antidepressants do not treat delirium. C. Long-term antipsychotic treatment does not address the underlying cause. E. CBT is not the immediate treatment for acute delirium.
pearl: Delirium signals an underlying problem such as infection, drugs, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation or pain; finding and treating the cause is central to management.
thinking: Agitated patient with delirium ↓ delirium is secondary to an underlying precipitant ↓ treating the cause allows recovery ↓ identify and treat the underlying cause
exam_trap: C, Start long-term antipsychotic treatment — agitation tempts sedation, but antipsychotics are only for short-term use in severe distress or risk and do not treat the cause.
takeaway: In delirium, look for and treat the cause before reaching for sedation.

stem: A 66-year-old man develops sudden severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. He has repeated vomiting and cannot pass stool or flatus. What syndrome is most likely?
why_correct: Abdominal pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation are characteristic features of intestinal obstruction.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause acute complete obstruction. B. Chronic constipation does not explain this acute obstructive syndrome. C. Functional dyspepsia causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms. D. GORD causes reflux symptoms rather than intestinal obstruction.
pearl: Bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation; manage with drip and suck, imaging (usually CT) and urgent surgical review.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ distension and repeated vomiting ↓ no stool or flatus passed ↓ acute intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Chronic constipation — failure to pass stool tempts it, but absolute constipation with vomiting, distension and acute pain is obstruction, not constipation.
takeaway: Pain, distension, vomiting and no flatus = intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old man with abdominal distension and vomiting has a CT scan showing a transition point in the small bowel. What does the transition point indicate?

options.A: Change from dilated to collapsed bowel
options.B: The site of a localised bowel perforation
options.C: The normal position of the ileocaecal valve
options.D: A segment of bowel wall thickening from colitis
options.E: A region of adynamic ileus without obstruction

correct_answer: A. Change from dilated to collapsed bowel
why_correct: A transition point is where dilated bowel proximally changes to relatively collapsed bowel distally, supporting mechanical obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Perforation is shown by free gas rather than a change in bowel calibre. C. The ileocaecal valve is a normal anatomical structure and is not synonymous with a transition point. D. Bowel wall thickening is not defined by a change in calibre. E. Ileus causes diffuse dilatation without a transition point.
pearl: A transition point on CT, with dilated bowel proximally and collapsed bowel distally, confirms mechanical obstruction and localises the cause, such as adhesions or a hernia.
thinking: Distension and vomiting ↓ CT shows a transition point ↓ calibre changes from dilated to collapsed bowel ↓ mechanical obstruction at that site
exam_trap: E, A region of adynamic ileus without obstruction — ileus also causes distension and vomiting, but it produces diffuse dilatation without a transition point.
takeaway: Transition point = dilated to collapsed bowel, marking mechanical obstruction.

stem: A 48-year-old man has chronic constipation and suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting and marked distension. What should this change in symptoms suggest?
why_correct: Sudden severe pain, vomiting and marked distension are red flags for an acute obstructive or other surgical abdominal process.
why_wrong: A. Reflux does not explain the symptoms. B. Sudden severe pain, vomiting and marked distension are not features of uncomplicated constipation. C. Functional dyspepsia does not cause this acute obstructive picture. E. IBS does not cause acute severe obstruction.
pearl: A sudden change from chronic constipation to severe pain, vomiting and distension is a red flag for obstruction, for example from tumour or volvulus, and needs urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Background chronic constipation ↓ sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ vomiting and marked distension ↓ acute intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Exacerbation of simple constipation — the background history tempts it, but acute severe pain with vomiting and marked distension is not simple constipation.
takeaway: New vomiting, distension and severe pain in a constipated patient: think obstruction.

stem: A 54-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain with guarding and rebound tenderness. What does this examination finding suggest?
why_correct: Guarding and rebound tenderness indicate irritation of the peritoneum and can occur with serious intra-abdominal pathology.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not produce abdominal guarding. C. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms rather than generalized peritoneal signs. D. Simple constipation does not usually cause peritoneal signs. E. Reflux does not cause guarding and rebound tenderness.
pearl: Guarding and rebound tenderness signal peritonitis, from causes such as perforation or appendicitis, and the patient needs urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Severe abdominal pain ↓ guarding on palpation ↓ rebound tenderness ↓ inflamed peritoneum = peritoneal irritation
exam_trap: D, Simple constipation — common and can be painful, but it does not produce guarding or rebound; these signs mean peritoneal irritation.
takeaway: Guarding plus rebound tenderness = peritonism: get urgent surgical review.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with acute flank pain and visible blood in her urine. She has no fever. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute severe flank pain with haematuria and no evidence of infection is typical of a ureteric stone.
why_wrong: A. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever and systemic illness. B. Polycystic kidney disease causes chronic renal manifestations rather than typical acute colic. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria and oedema. E. Cystitis usually causes dysuria, frequency and urgency rather than severe colicky flank pain.
pearl: Renal colic causes sudden severe loin-to-groin pain with haematuria; NSAIDs are first-line analgesia and non-contrast CT KUB confirms the stone.
thinking: Acute, severe flank pain ↓ visible blood in the urine ↓ no fever, so infection less likely ↓ ureteric stone
exam_trap: A, Acute pyelonephritis — flank pain with abnormal urine tempts it, but pyelonephritis usually brings fever and systemic illness, which are absent.
takeaway: Acute flank pain plus haematuria without fever = ureteric stone.

stem: A woman develops heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery. The placenta has been delivered but appears incomplete. What cause of postpartum haemorrhage should be considered?
why_correct: Retained placental tissue can prevent effective uterine contraction and cause postpartum haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy occurs outside the uterus in early pregnancy. C. Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden collapse, hypoxia and coagulopathy. D. Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and does not cause significant postpartum haemorrhage. E. Hyperemesis causes severe vomiting during pregnancy.
pearl: Postpartum haemorrhage causes follow the 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin; an incomplete placenta means retained tissue that must be removed.
thinking: Heavy bleeding after delivery ↓ placenta delivered but incomplete ↓ retained fragments stop the uterus contracting well ↓ retained placental tissue
exam_trap: C, Amniotic fluid embolism — a dramatic obstetric emergency with bleeding, but it presents with sudden collapse, hypoxia and coagulopathy, not an incomplete placenta.
takeaway: Postpartum haemorrhage with an incomplete placenta: retained tissue, the Tissue of the 4 Ts.

stem: A 5-day-old newborn is feeding poorly and has a temperature of 38.2°C. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Fever and poor feeding in a neonate are important signs of possible serious infection and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Fever in a neonate should not be attributed to overwrapping; serious infection must be excluded. B. Fever is not a normal neonatal finding. C. Colic does not cause fever. E. Breastfeeding does not normally cause fever and poor feeding.
pearl: Any fever in a baby under 3 months is a red flag for serious bacterial infection; a febrile, poorly feeding neonate needs urgent assessment and a full septic screen.
thinking: 5-day-old neonate ↓ temperature of 38.2°C, a fever ↓ feeding poorly ↓ possible serious neonatal infection
exam_trap: A, Overheating from excessive wrapping — a common reassuring explanation, but fever in a neonate must never be put down to wrapping before infection is excluded.
takeaway: Fever in a baby under 3 months is serious infection until proven otherwise.

stem: A child with a barking cough develops increasing stridor at rest and difficulty breathing. What does this indicate?

options.A: Mild croup suitable for home care

why_correct: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Stridor at rest indicates at least moderate croup and is not suitable for home management. B. Bronchiolitis affects infants and causes wheeze and crackles rather than stridor. C. Asthma causes expiratory wheeze rather than inspiratory stridor. D. Allergic rhinitis does not cause stridor.
pearl: In croup, stridor at rest with increasing work of breathing signals significant airway narrowing; give oral dexamethasone and, if severe, nebulised adrenaline with senior help.
thinking: Barking cough suggests croup ↓ stridor now present at rest ↓ increasing difficulty breathing ↓ severe upper-airway obstruction
exam_trap: A, Mild croup suitable for home care — the barking cough suggests croup, but stridor at rest with breathing difficulty is not mild and needs hospital assessment.
takeaway: Croup with stridor at rest is not mild: assess urgently in hospital.

stem: A 74-year-old woman suddenly develops difficulty producing speech. She understands what is being said to her but can only produce a few words. What type of aphasia is most likely?
why_correct: Difficulty producing language despite relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of expressive aphasia.
why_wrong: A. Dysphonia is a disorder of voice quality. B. Receptive aphasia primarily impairs understanding of language. C. Dysarthria is impaired articulation rather than impaired language formulation. D. Amnesia concerns memory rather than language production.
pearl: Expressive (Broca's) aphasia gives non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, typically from a dominant frontal lobe lesion such as stroke.
thinking: Sudden onset of speech difficulty ↓ can produce only a few words ↓ understands what is said ↓ expressive aphasia
exam_trap: C, Dysarthria — also limits speech output, but dysarthria is impaired articulation with intact language; she cannot produce language, which is aphasia.
takeaway: Non-fluent speech with preserved understanding = expressive (Broca's) aphasia.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has recurrent unilateral headaches accompanied by transient visual disturbance. What feature would be particularly concerning for a secondary headache disorder?

options.B: Previous identical headaches over many years
options.C: Photophobia and phonophobia during each episode
options.E: Improvement after a period of sleep or rest

correct_answer: A. Sudden onset peaking within seconds
why_correct: A thunderclap headache is a red flag for serious secondary causes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage.
why_wrong: B. A stable recurrent pattern is more suggestive of a primary headache disorder. C. Photophobia and phonophobia are common in migraine. D. Nausea commonly accompanies migraine. E. Improvement with sleep or rest can occur with migraine.
pearl: A thunderclap headache, reaching maximum intensity almost instantly, needs emergency assessment for subarachnoid haemorrhage, whatever the previous headache history.
thinking: Recurrent unilateral headache with visual aura suggests migraine ↓ look for features that break the pattern ↓ sudden onset peaking within seconds ↓ red flag for a secondary cause
exam_trap: C, Photophobia and phonophobia — they sound worrying, but they are typical migraine features; the red flag is the speed of onset.
takeaway: Thunderclap onset is a red flag even in someone with known migraine.

stem: A 24-year-old man suddenly loses consciousness, becomes stiff and then develops rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. He is confused afterwards. What is the most likely seizure type?
why_correct: Loss of consciousness followed by tonic stiffening, clonic jerking and a postictal period is characteristic of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure.
why_wrong: A. Focal impaired awareness seizures cause altered awareness with automatisms rather than generalised stiffening and jerking of all limbs. B. Atonic seizures involve sudden loss of tone. C. Myoclonic seizures consist primarily of brief jerks. E. Absence seizures are brief and lack tonic-clonic activity.
pearl: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures cause sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening then clonic jerking, often with tongue biting, followed by postictal confusion.
thinking: Sudden loss of consciousness ↓ tonic stiffening ↓ rhythmic jerking of all four limbs ↓ postictal confusion ↓ generalised tonic-clonic seizure
exam_trap: C, Myoclonic seizure — also produces jerking, but myoclonic jerks are brief, often with preserved awareness, without prior stiffening or postictal confusion.
takeaway: Stiffening, then jerking of all limbs, then confusion = generalised tonic-clonic seizure.

stem: A 20-year-old man has a seizure for the first time. He has now recovered fully and is alert. What is an important next step?

options.B: Diagnose epilepsy on the basis of this event
options.C: Arrange GP review if a second seizure occurs
options.E: Advise he may continue driving meanwhile

correct_answer: D. Refer for specialist first-seizure review
why_correct: A first suspected seizure requires appropriate assessment to determine the cause and risk of recurrence before a definitive diagnosis or long-term treatment decision.
why_wrong: A. Antiseizure medication is not usually started before specialist assessment. B. A single seizure does not automatically establish epilepsy. C. A first seizure needs prompt specialist assessment rather than waiting for recurrence. E. He must stop driving and inform the DVLA after a first seizure.
pearl: After a first suspected seizure, refer urgently to a first-seizure specialist and advise the patient to stop driving and inform the DVLA; drug treatment is a specialist decision.
thinking: First seizure ↓ now fully recovered ↓ cause and recurrence risk not yet known ↓ refer for specialist first-seizure review
exam_trap: A, Start levetiracetam before discharge — seems protective, but antiseizure drugs are not usually started after one seizure before specialist assessment.
takeaway: First seizure: urgent specialist referral and driving advice, not immediate drugs.

stem: A 19-year-old woman reports brief episodes of sudden muscle jerks shortly after waking. She remains conscious throughout. What seizure type is most likely?
why_correct: Myoclonic seizures cause brief, sudden muscle jerks with preserved awareness.
why_wrong: A. Focal impaired-awareness seizures involve impaired awareness. B. Absence seizures primarily cause brief impaired awareness. C. Tonic-clonic seizures involve loss of consciousness and sustained motor activity. E. Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of muscle tone.
pearl: Morning myoclonic jerks in a young person suggest juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; sodium valproate is generally avoided in anyone who could become pregnant.
thinking: Young woman ↓ brief sudden muscle jerks ↓ occur shortly after waking ↓ consciousness preserved ↓ myoclonic seizure
exam_trap: C, Generalised tonic-clonic seizure — the jerking tempts it, but GTCS involves loss of consciousness and sustained activity; brief jerks with awareness are myoclonic.
takeaway: Brief jerks soon after waking with preserved awareness = myoclonic seizures.

stem: A 42-year-old woman develops weakness of one side of the body after a seizure. The weakness resolves over several hours. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: Temporary focal weakness following a seizure is known as Todd's paresis.
why_wrong: B. Multiple sclerosis causes neurological episodes separated in time and space rather than a typical immediate postictal weakness. C. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness. D. Myasthenia causes fluctuating fatigable weakness rather than a postictal focal deficit. E. Guillain-Barré causes progressive peripheral weakness.
pearl: Todd's paresis is temporary focal weakness after a seizure that usually resolves within hours, occasionally longer; a persisting deficit needs assessment for stroke.
thinking: Seizure first ↓ then weakness of one side of the body ↓ resolves over several hours ↓ Todd's paresis
exam_trap: B, Multiple sclerosis — causes transient focal deficits, but they are not tied to a seizure; one-sided weakness immediately after a seizure is Todd's paresis.
takeaway: Transient one-sided weakness after a seizure = Todd's paresis.

stem: A 67-year-old man suddenly becomes unable to understand spoken language. He speaks fluently but his words make little sense. What type of aphasia is most likely?
why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech accompanied by impaired comprehension is characteristic of receptive aphasia.
why_wrong: A. Dysphonia is impaired voice quality. B. Expressive aphasia primarily impairs speech production with relatively preserved comprehension. C. Dysarthria is impaired articulation. D. Mutism is absence of speech rather than fluent but impaired language.
pearl: Receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia gives fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension, often without awareness of errors; it localises to the dominant temporal lobe.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ cannot understand spoken language ↓ speech fluent but makes little sense ↓ receptive aphasia
exam_trap: B, Expressive aphasia — also an aphasia after stroke, but it causes non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension, the reverse of this picture.
takeaway: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor understanding = receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia.

stem: A 71-year-old man develops difficulty swallowing after a stroke. He coughs repeatedly while drinking water. What complication is he at increased risk of?
why_correct: Dysphagia with coughing during swallowing suggests aspiration risk, which can lead to aspiration pneumonia.
why_wrong: B. Dysphagia does not directly cause renal failure. C. Otitis externa is unrelated. D. Stroke can increase DVT risk through immobility, but coughing with swallowing specifically indicates aspiration risk. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: After a stroke, screen swallowing before giving oral food, fluids or medicines; coughing on drinking suggests aspiration and needs speech and language therapy assessment.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ new difficulty swallowing ↓ coughing while drinking water ↓ fluid entering the airway ↓ aspiration pneumonia risk
exam_trap: D, Deep vein thrombosis only — immobility after stroke does raise DVT risk, but coughing on swallowing specifically signals aspiration.
takeaway: Post-stroke dysphagia with coughing on drinking = aspiration risk: swallow screen first.

stem: A 69-year-old woman develops sudden difficulty walking, slurred speech and severe unsteadiness. Limb coordination is impaired. Which part of the brain is particularly associated with coordination?
why_correct: The cerebellum is important for coordination, balance and smooth execution of movement.
why_wrong: A. The hypothalamus regulates autonomic and endocrine functions. B. The medulla contains important autonomic centres but is not the principal site for coordination. C. The pituitary is an endocrine gland. E. The frontal lobes are involved in executive function and voluntary motor control but are not the principal coordination centre.
pearl: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus, slurred speech and past-pointing; sudden onset suggests a posterior circulation stroke.
thinking: Sudden difficulty walking and severe unsteadiness ↓ slurred speech ↓ impaired limb coordination ↓ cerebellum
exam_trap: B, Medulla only — brainstem strokes can also cause unsteadiness and slurred speech, but the structure principally responsible for coordination is the cerebellum.
takeaway: Ataxia, slurred speech and incoordination point to the cerebellum.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of both legs with loss of sensation below the umbilicus. She also has difficulty passing urine. What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: Bilateral weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction suggest spinal cord involvement and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy affects the facial nerve. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve in the hand. C. Migraine does not cause a sensory level and urinary retention. E. Tension headache does not cause spinal neurological deficits.
pearl: Bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction indicate a spinal cord lesion; arrange urgent MRI of the spine and specialist assessment.
thinking: Sudden weakness of both legs ↓ sensory loss below the umbilicus (a sensory level) ↓ difficulty passing urine ↓ spinal cord compression
exam_trap: C, Migraine — can cause transient neurological symptoms, but never a sensory level with bilateral leg weakness and urinary difficulty.
takeaway: Bilateral leg weakness plus sensory level plus bladder change = cord lesion: urgent MRI.

stem: A 41-year-old woman develops weakness of both legs several days after a viral illness. Examination shows reduced reflexes. What neurological pattern is most characteristic of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
why_correct: Guillain-Barré classically causes progressive symmetrical weakness that may ascend from the legs.
why_wrong: B. Brief impaired awareness suggests a seizure disorder. C. Resting tremor is associated with Parkinson's disease. D. Unilateral painful visual loss can occur with optic neuritis. E. Isolated facial weakness suggests a facial nerve disorder.
pearl: Guillain–Barré syndrome causes progressive, symmetrical, ascending weakness with reduced reflexes after an infection; monitor FVC because respiratory muscles can fail.
thinking: Recent viral illness ↓ weakness of both legs ↓ reduced reflexes ↓ ascending symmetrical weakness of Guillain–Barré
exam_trap: E, Isolated facial weakness — facial weakness can occur in GBS, but alone it suggests a facial nerve disorder; the hallmark is ascending symmetrical limb weakness.
takeaway: Post-infective ascending symmetrical weakness with reduced reflexes = Guillain–Barré.

stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD becomes acutely confused and increasingly breathless. His oxygen saturation is low. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Acute worsening breathlessness, hypoxaemia and confusion in severe respiratory disease may indicate respiratory failure.
why_wrong: B. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency and does not explain hypoxaemia. C. Hepatic encephalopathy occurs in liver failure. D. Stroke causes focal deficits rather than hypoxaemia with breathlessness. E. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion but does not explain low oxygen saturation and breathlessness.
pearl: Confusion, worsening breathlessness and hypoxaemia in COPD suggest acute respiratory failure; check arterial blood gases and give controlled oxygen, targeting 88–92%.
thinking: COPD patient ↓ increasingly breathless ↓ low oxygen saturation ↓ new confusion from hypoxaemia or hypercapnia ↓ acute respiratory failure
exam_trap: D, Acute ischaemic stroke — new confusion in an older man tempts it, but stroke causes focal deficits and does not explain hypoxaemia and breathlessness.
takeaway: Confused, breathless, hypoxic COPD patient: think respiratory failure and get an ABG.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. His leg is swollen and painful on the same side. What underlying condition is particularly relevant?
why_correct: A painful swollen leg can indicate DVT, which is an important source of pulmonary emboli.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not explain acute unilateral leg swelling with possible embolic symptoms. B. Hand cellulitis is unrelated. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. D. Cataract affects the eye.
pearl: Most pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thrombosis in the leg; a swollen, painful leg with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain strongly supports PE.
thinking: Sudden breathlessness ↓ pleuritic chest pain ↓ swollen, painful leg ↓ DVT as the source of pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: B, Cellulitis of the hand — infection causes swelling and pain, but the hand is irrelevant here; a swollen leg with chest symptoms points to DVT.
takeaway: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness with a swollen leg: think DVT with PE.

stem: A 73-year-old woman develops sudden weakness and difficulty speaking. She is assessed in the emergency department shortly after symptom onset. What should be considered immediately?
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficits require urgent assessment for acute stroke.
why_wrong: A. Sinusitis does not explain sudden focal neurological symptoms. B. Dementia causes progressive cognitive decline rather than sudden focal neurological deficit. C. Migraine can mimic stroke but must not be assumed without assessment. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute speech disturbance.
pearl: Sudden focal neurological deficit is stroke until proven otherwise; urgent brain imaging decides eligibility for time-critical thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ weakness and difficulty speaking ↓ seen shortly after onset ↓ acute stroke, a time-critical emergency
exam_trap: C, Migraine prophylaxis only — migraine with aura can mimic stroke, but sudden weakness and speech difficulty must be treated as stroke until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Sudden focal deficit: treat as acute stroke and image urgently.

stem: A 59-year-old woman develops sudden monocular loss of vision lasting 10 minutes before completely resolving. What vascular event should be considered?
why_correct: Transient monocular visual loss can result from retinal ischaemia and may be a vascular warning symptom.
why_wrong: A. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters rather than a transient complete loss of vision. B. Chronic open-angle glaucoma causes gradual, painless peripheral field loss. C. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss evolving over days rather than a 10-minute episode. D. Allergic conjunctivitis causes itchy red eyes without loss of vision.
pearl: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) is a TIA equivalent, often from carotid emboli; it needs urgent TIA assessment including carotid imaging.
thinking: Sudden loss of vision in one eye ↓ lasts about 10 minutes ↓ resolves completely ↓ transient retinal ischaemia
exam_trap: C, Acute demyelinating optic neuritis — causes monocular visual loss, but it is painful and evolves over days rather than resolving within minutes.
takeaway: Brief monocular visual loss = amaurosis fugax: manage as a TIA.

stem: A 46-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the right side of his face, arm and leg. He also has difficulty speaking. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden unilateral weakness involving the face, arm and leg together with speech disturbance strongly suggests an acute stroke.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy does not typically cause sudden hemiparesis with aphasia. C. Bell's palsy causes isolated lower motor neuron facial weakness. D. Migraine can cause neurological symptoms but stroke must be urgently considered. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve distribution in the hand.
pearl: Sudden one-sided face, arm and leg weakness with speech disturbance fits a stroke; a positive FAST screen means emergency transfer to a stroke unit.
thinking: Sudden onset in a 46-year-old ↓ weakness of the right face, arm and leg together ↓ difficulty speaking ↓ stroke
exam_trap: C, Bell's palsy — the facial weakness tempts it, but Bell's affects the face alone; arm and leg weakness with speech difficulty means stroke.
takeaway: Sudden face, arm and leg weakness with speech change = stroke.

stem: A 10-year-old boy develops widespread itchy wheals shortly after eating a food. He is otherwise well, with no breathing difficulty or circulatory symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.C: Intramuscular adrenaline immediately in every case

why_correct: Isolated urticaria without features of anaphylaxis can be treated symptomatically with an antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not treat allergic urticaria. B. Insulin has no role. C. Adrenaline is required for anaphylaxis, not uncomplicated isolated urticaria. D. Antifungal treatment is inappropriate.
pearl: Isolated urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation problems is treated with a non-sedating oral antihistamine; adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis.
thinking: Itchy wheals after a food ↓ no breathing difficulty ↓ no circulatory symptoms ↓ isolated urticaria, not anaphylaxis ↓ antihistamine
exam_trap: C, Intramuscular adrenaline immediately in every case — lifesaving in anaphylaxis, but isolated urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation involvement does not need it.
