stem: A woman with longstanding cyclical pelvic pain is having difficulty conceiving. Which condition can be associated with both symptoms?
why_correct: Endometriosis can cause pelvic pain and is associated with reduced fertility.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not explain this combination. B. Plantar fasciitis is unrelated. C. Cataract is unrelated. D. Otitis externa is unrelated to fertility.
pearl: Endometriosis links pelvic pain with subfertility through adhesions, distorted pelvic anatomy and inflammation; ask about fertility plans, since hormonal treatments are contraceptive.
thinking: Longstanding cyclical pelvic pain ↓ Difficulty conceiving ↓ One condition explaining both ↓ Endometriosis
exam_trap: A, migraine — it can be cyclical with periods, which tempts, but it explains neither pelvic pain nor subfertility; endometriosis explains both.
takeaway: Cyclical pelvic pain plus subfertility points to endometriosis.

stem: A woman with PMOS (formerly PCOS) is found to have obesity and insulin resistance. Which long-term condition is she at increased risk of developing?
why_correct: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is associated with insulin resistance, especially with obesity, and carries an increased risk of impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. Addisonian crisis results from adrenal insufficiency. B. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia and is not linked to PMOS (formerly PCOS). C. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and is not caused by insulin resistance or PMOS (formerly PCOS). E. Diabetes insipidus is due to ADH deficiency or resistance and is unrelated to insulin resistance.
pearl: PMOS (formerly PCOS) carries an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, especially with obesity; offer regular glycaemic screening and weight-management support.
thinking: PMOS (formerly PCOS) ↓ Obesity ↓ Insulin resistance ↓ Impaired glucose tolerance over time ↓ Type 2 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: C, type 1 diabetes — diabetes is the right theme, which tempts, but type 1 is autoimmune beta-cell destruction and is not driven by insulin resistance.
takeaway: PMOS (formerly PCOS) with obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes.

stem: Which symptom is characteristic of the menopausal transition?
why_correct: Vasomotor symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats are common during the menopausal transition.
why_wrong: A. Haemoptysis is coughing up blood. B. Haematuria is blood in the urine. C. Purulent sputum suggests respiratory infection. E. Loin-to-groin pain suggests renal colic.
pearl: Vasomotor symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats are the hallmark of the menopausal transition; in women over 45 with typical symptoms, the diagnosis is clinical without FSH testing.
thinking: Menopausal transition ↓ Falling oestrogen ↓ Disturbed thermoregulation ↓ Vasomotor symptoms ↓ Hot flushes
exam_trap: B, haematuria — a symptom in midlife that may tempt, but it signals urinary tract pathology needing assessment and is not a feature of the menopause.
takeaway: Hot flushes and night sweats are typical of the menopausal transition.

stem: A healthy 24-year-old woman wants reliable contraception and has no contraindications to oestrogen. Which option contains both an oestrogen and a progestogen?
why_correct: The combined oral contraceptive contains both an oestrogen and a progestogen.
why_wrong: A. The LNG-IUS releases a progestogen only. C. The copper IUD is non-hormonal. D. The progestogen-only pill contains progestogen without oestrogen. E. DMPA is a progestogen-only injection.
pearl: Combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring) contains an oestrogen and a progestogen; the IUS, implant, injection and progestogen-only pill contain progestogen only.
thinking: Wants reliable contraception ↓ No contraindication to oestrogen ↓ Method containing oestrogen and progestogen ↓ Combined oral contraceptive pill
exam_trap: A, levonorgestrel IUS — a highly reliable hormonal method, which tempts, but it releases progestogen only; the combined pill contains both hormones.
takeaway: Only combined methods contain both oestrogen and progestogen.

stem: A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive asks about an important serious adverse effect. Which risk is increased?
why_correct: Combined hormonal contraception containing oestrogen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.
why_wrong: A. It does not cause appendicitis. C. Renal colic is not a typical adverse effect. D. Cataract is not the characteristic serious adverse effect. E. Otitis externa is unrelated.
pearl: Oestrogen-containing contraception raises VTE risk, so take a personal and family history and use UKMEC to check contraindications such as previous VTE.
thinking: Combined oral contraceptive ↓ Oestrogen increases clotting factors ↓ Hypercoagulable state ↓ Venous thromboembolism
exam_trap: D, cataract in all users — sounds like a plausible long-term drug effect, but it is not a recognised serious risk; VTE is the key serious adverse effect.
takeaway: Combined hormonal contraception increases the risk of VTE.

stem: A woman has had unprotected sexual intercourse and does not wish to become pregnant. What is the appropriate principle?

options.D: Emergency contraception is ineffective after any unprotected intercourse
options.E: Wait until the next menstrual period before considering it

why_correct: Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse, with the appropriate method chosen according to timing and circumstances.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics do not prevent pregnancy. C. Insulin has no role. D. Emergency contraception has recognised indications after unprotected intercourse. E. Waiting may reduce available options and effectiveness.
pearl: Emergency contraception options are the copper IUD (most effective), ulipristal and levonorgestrel; offer it as soon as possible, choosing the method by timing and circumstances.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Pregnancy not wanted ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Consider emergency contraception promptly
exam_trap: E, waiting until the next period — may seem sensible to see whether pregnancy occurs, but delay narrows the options and reduces effectiveness; act promptly.
takeaway: Offer emergency contraception as soon as possible after unprotected sex.

stem: Which contraceptive method provides long-term contraception and is placed inside the uterus?
why_correct: Intrauterine contraceptive methods are inserted into the uterine cavity and provide long-term contraception.
why_wrong: A. The combined pill is taken orally. B. The condom is a barrier method. C. The implant is inserted under the skin. E. The patch is applied to the skin.
pearl: The copper IUD and hormonal IUS are long-acting reversible contraceptives placed in the uterus; LARC methods are more effective than user-dependent methods.
thinking: Long-term contraception ↓ Placed inside the uterus ↓ Copper device or levonorgestrel system ↓ Intrauterine device or system
exam_trap: C, contraceptive implant — also long-acting and reversible, which tempts, but it sits under the skin of the upper arm, not inside the uterus.
takeaway: The IUD and IUS are the intrauterine long-acting methods.

stem: A sexually active 21-year-old has dysuria and urethral discharge but no testicular pain. Which sexually transmitted infection is commonly associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Chlamydia commonly causes urethritis, which may present with dysuria and urethral discharge.
why_wrong: A. Varicella causes chickenpox and shingles. B. Hepatitis A primarily causes acute hepatitis. D. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis. E. Influenza is a respiratory viral infection.
pearl: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK and is often asymptomatic; test with a NAAT, treat with doxycycline and arrange partner notification.
thinking: Sexually active young adult ↓ Dysuria and urethral discharge ↓ Urethritis ↓ Commonest bacterial STI ↓ Chlamydia
exam_trap: B, hepatitis A — it can be sexually transmitted, which may tempt, but it causes acute hepatitis, not urethritis; chlamydia causes dysuria and discharge.
takeaway: Dysuria with urethral discharge in a young adult suggests chlamydial urethritis.

stem: Untreated chlamydia infection in a woman can ascend into the upper genital tract. Which complication can result?
why_correct: Ascending chlamydial infection can cause PID and subsequent reproductive complications.
why_wrong: B. Bacterial vaginosis is a lower genital tract dysbiosis, not ascending chlamydial infection. C. Ectropion is a benign cervical finding. D. Candidiasis is a fungal infection unrelated to chlamydia. E. Endometriosis is not caused by infection.
pearl: Ascending chlamydia can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, leading to tubal damage, infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain, often after silent infection.
thinking: Untreated chlamydia ↓ Ascends from the cervix ↓ Infects the uterus and tubes ↓ Pelvic inflammatory disease
exam_trap: B, bacterial vaginosis — another common genital condition, which tempts, but it is a vaginal dysbiosis rather than an ascending chlamydial infection.
takeaway: Untreated chlamydia can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease.

stem: A woman with previous untreated PID is having difficulty conceiving. Which complication of PID can explain this?
why_correct: PID can cause scarring of the fallopian tubes, resulting in tubal-factor infertility.
why_wrong: A. PMOS (formerly PCOS) is an endocrine disorder unrelated to PID. B. Premature ovarian insufficiency is not caused by PID. C. Hyperprolactinaemia is an endocrine cause of infertility unrelated to PID. E. Endometriosis is not a complication of PID.
pearl: PID scars and blocks the fallopian tubes, causing tubal-factor infertility and raising ectopic pregnancy risk; the risk rises with each episode.
thinking: Previous untreated PID ↓ Tubal inflammation and scarring ↓ Blocked or damaged tubes ↓ Tubal-factor infertility
exam_trap: E, endometriosis — it also causes pelvic adhesions and infertility, which tempts, but it is not a complication of PID; infection damages the tubes.
takeaway: PID causes infertility through tubal scarring and blockage.

stem: A neonate is suspected of having sepsis. What is the appropriate management principle?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and review by the GP in 24 hours
options.B: Wait for blood culture results before antibiotics
options.C: Give IV antibiotics if the CRP at 18 hours is raised
options.D: Urgent assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour
options.E: Treat with a single dose of IM antibiotics and discharge

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour
why_correct: Neonatal sepsis can progress rapidly and requires urgent assessment and appropriate antimicrobial management.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected neonatal sepsis. B. Antibiotics must not be delayed for culture results. C. Waiting for a later CRP delays treatment of suspected sepsis. E. A single dose followed by discharge is unsafe.
pearl: Suspected neonatal sepsis needs urgent assessment, a blood culture and IV antibiotics within an hour of the decision to treat; never wait for blood test or culture results.
thinking: Neonate ↓ Suspected sepsis ↓ Subtle signs, rapid deterioration ↓ Do not delay for tests ↓ Urgent assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour
exam_trap: C, IV antibiotics if CRP at 18 hours is raised — CRP does guide later decisions, which tempts, but it must not delay starting antibiotics in suspected sepsis.
takeaway: Suspected neonatal sepsis: IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

stem: Which newborn has the greatest risk of respiratory distress syndrome?
why_correct: Surfactant production increases with gestational age, so very premature infants are at greatest risk.
why_wrong: A. It is not an adult disorder caused by neonatal surfactant deficiency. B. Post-term infants are not typically at increased risk because of surfactant deficiency. D. Respiratory distress syndrome is a neonatal condition. E. Term infants generally have adequate surfactant.
pearl: Respiratory distress syndrome is caused by surfactant deficiency and is commonest in very premature infants; antenatal corticosteroids before preterm birth reduce the risk.
thinking: Surfactant production rises with gestation ↓ Very premature lungs lack surfactant ↓ Alveolar collapse ↓ Very premature infant
exam_trap: E, healthy term infant — term babies can have breathing problems such as transient tachypnoea, which tempts, but they usually have adequate surfactant.
takeaway: The more premature the baby, the higher the risk of RDS.

stem: A newborn has a visible opening involving the upper lip and palate. What congenital abnormality is present?
why_correct: A congenital gap in the upper lip and palate is characteristic of cleft lip and palate.
why_wrong: A. Hydrocephalus involves excess cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system. B. DDH affects the hip joint. D. Talipes is a congenital foot deformity. E. Hypospadias is an abnormal urethral opening in the penis.
pearl: Cleft lip and palate are often seen on antenatal scan or at birth; the palate must be inspected at the newborn examination, and care is led by a specialist multidisciplinary cleft team.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Visible opening in the upper lip ↓ Extending into the palate ↓ Failure of facial fusion ↓ Cleft lip and palate
exam_trap: E, hypospadias — another congenital fusion defect checked at the newborn examination, which tempts, but it affects the penis, not the lip and palate.
takeaway: A gap in the upper lip and palate at birth is cleft lip and palate.

stem: A newborn with a cleft palate has difficulty creating suction during feeding. What is the main immediate problem?
why_correct: A cleft palate can prevent effective oral suction and make feeding difficult.
why_wrong: A. Glue ear is a later complication rather than the immediate problem. B. Speech problems emerge later. C. Dental problems emerge later. E. Airway obstruction is associated with Pierre Robin sequence rather than the suction difficulty described.
pearl: Babies with a cleft palate cannot form an oral seal, so feeding is the immediate problem; specialist cleft nurses support with squeezable bottles and special teats while weight is monitored.
thinking: Newborn with cleft palate ↓ Cannot seal the oral cavity ↓ Unable to generate suction ↓ Difficulty feeding effectively
exam_trap: A, otitis media with effusion — common in cleft palate, which tempts, but it is a later complication; the immediate newborn problem is ineffective feeding.
takeaway: The immediate problem in a newborn with cleft palate is feeding.

stem: A newborn becomes jittery and lethargic. Blood glucose is very low. What is the immediate concern?
why_correct: Jitteriness and lethargy are recognised manifestations of neonatal hypoglycaemia, which requires prompt management.
why_wrong: B. Neonatal abstinence syndrome causes jitteriness but does not explain a very low glucose. C. Hypocalcaemia can cause jitteriness, but the documented low glucose is the immediate concern. D. Sepsis should be considered as an underlying cause, but the immediate concern is the hypoglycaemia. E. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy follows perinatal asphyxia.
pearl: Neonatal hypoglycaemia can cause jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy and seizures; risk is higher in preterm and growth-restricted babies and infants of diabetic mothers.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Jittery and lethargic ↓ Very low blood glucose ↓ Brain depends on glucose ↓ Neonatal hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: D, neonatal sepsis — it can cause lethargy and low glucose, which tempts, but the measured hypoglycaemia is the immediate concern to treat while sepsis is considered.
takeaway: A jittery, lethargic newborn with low glucose needs the hypoglycaemia treated now.

stem: A patient reports that a mole has recently changed in size, shape and colour. Which feature is particularly concerning?

options.D: A lesion that disappears within minutes

why_correct: Change in a pigmented lesion's size, shape or colour is an important warning sign for melanoma.
why_wrong: A. Symmetry is generally less suspicious than asymmetry. B. Absence of pigmentation does not define melanoma risk. D. A lesion disappearing within minutes is more consistent with a transient process such as urticaria. E. Long-term stability is less concerning.
pearl: Change in size, shape or colour is a major feature of the weighted seven-point checklist and the E of ABCDE; an evolving mole needs urgent referral.
thinking: Mole ↓ Recent change in size, shape and colour ↓ Evolution ↓ Major warning sign for melanoma ↓ Evolution of the lesion
exam_trap: B, absence of pigmentation — amelanotic melanoma exists, which tempts, but lack of pigment alone does not define risk; change over time is the key warning sign.
takeaway: A changing mole is the most important warning sign for melanoma.

stem: A patient is suspected of having necrotising fasciitis. What is the appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent senior surgical assessment and treatment
options.B: Oral flucloxacillin and clinical review in 48 hours
options.C: Mark the erythema with a pen and review in 24 hours
options.D: MRI of the affected area before any surgical referral
options.E: IV antibiotics on the medical ward and review tomorrow

correct_answer: A. Urgent senior surgical assessment and treatment
why_correct: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive surgical emergency requiring urgent multidisciplinary management, including surgical assessment.
why_wrong: B. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for necrotising infection. C. Delay can result in rapid deterioration. D. Imaging should not delay surgical assessment. E. Antibiotics without urgent surgical debridement are inadequate.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to the visible skin changes is the classic early clue to necrotising fasciitis; it is a surgical emergency needing urgent debridement alongside IV antibiotics and resuscitation.
thinking: Suspected necrotising fasciitis ↓ Rapidly spreading, life-threatening soft-tissue infection ↓ Antibiotics cannot reach necrotic tissue ↓ Urgent surgical debridement is definitive ↓ Urgent senior surgical assessment and treatment
exam_trap: E, IV antibiotics on the ward and review tomorrow — IV antibiotics are needed, so it looks adequate, but without urgent surgical debridement the infection progresses within hours.
takeaway: Necrotising fasciitis: do not wait or image first; get senior surgeons involved now.

stem: An older adult develops gradually worsening painless blurring of vision without eye pain or redness. What is a common cause?
why_correct: Cataracts typically cause gradual, painless deterioration in vision.
why_wrong: B. Orbital cellulitis causes pain, swelling and systemic features. C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes painful red eye and visual disturbance. D. Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden visual loss. E. Corneal abrasion is usually painful.
pearl: Cataract is the commonest cause of gradual, painless blurring of vision in older adults; glare and difficulty driving at night are typical, and surgery is offered when vision affects daily life.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Gradual, not sudden, onset ↓ Painless with no redness ↓ Lens opacity blurring vision ↓ Cataract
exam_trap: D, Retinal artery occlusion — it is also painless, which tempts, but it causes sudden profound visual loss rather than gradual blurring.
takeaway: Gradual, painless blurring in an older adult is cataract; sudden painless loss suggests a vascular cause.

stem: An elderly patient develops progressive difficulty reading and recognising faces, with central rather than peripheral visual loss. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Age-related macular degeneration primarily affects the macula and therefore causes central visual impairment.
why_wrong: B. Glaucoma typically causes progressive peripheral field loss, with central vision preserved until late. C. Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness and peripheral (tunnel) field loss. D. Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes rather than progressive central loss. E. A pituitary adenoma causes bitemporal, peripheral field loss.
pearl: Age-related macular degeneration damages the macula, so reading and recognising faces fail first; sudden distortion or rapid central loss suggests wet AMD and needs urgent referral.
thinking: Elderly patient ↓ Difficulty reading and recognising faces ↓ Central rather than peripheral loss ↓ Macular pathology ↓ Age-related macular degeneration
exam_trap: B, Chronic open-angle glaucoma — also common and gradual in older people, but it erodes the peripheral field first and spares central vision until late.
takeaway: Central visual loss points to the macula (AMD); peripheral loss points to glaucoma.

stem: A patient with asthma remains symptomatic despite being prescribed an inhaled medication. What should be checked before simply escalating treatment?

options.A: Serum total and specific IgE levels
options.B: Full blood count and serum ferritin

why_correct: Incorrect inhaler technique or poor adherence can lead to inadequate asthma control and should be addressed before unnecessary escalation.
why_wrong: A. IgE levels do not explain poor control in a patient already on treatment and are not the first check. B. FBC and ferritin do not assess the commonest causes of poor asthma control. C. A chest radiograph is not routinely needed before treatment escalation. E. Allergen testing may identify triggers but does not replace checking technique and adherence first.
pearl: Before stepping up asthma treatment, check inhaler technique, adherence and trigger exposure; poor technique is common, and escalating without fixing it adds side effects without improving control.
thinking: Asthma still symptomatic ↓ Already prescribed inhaled treatment ↓ Commonest reasons for poor control are technique and adherence ↓ Fix these before escalating ↓ Check inhaler technique and adherence
exam_trap: E, Skin-prick testing — identifying triggers seems thorough, but it does not address the commonest reason for poor control, which is how the inhaler is being used.
takeaway: Poor asthma control: check technique and adherence before adding drugs.

stem: A smoker with COPD asks which intervention can most importantly alter the course of their disease. What should be addressed?
why_correct: Smoking cessation is a key intervention for people with COPD and can slow further loss of lung function.
why_wrong: A. Appropriate physical activity and pulmonary rehabilitation are beneficial. B. Vaccination is an important part of preventive care. D. Long-term antibiotics are not required for every patient. E. Bed rest worsens deconditioning.
pearl: Smoking cessation is the most effective way to slow the accelerated decline in lung function in COPD; offer behavioural support with medication at every opportunity.
thinking: Smoker with COPD ↓ Asks what alters the course of the disease ↓ Continued smoking drives faster lung function decline ↓ Stopping slows that decline ↓ Smoking cessation
exam_trap: D, Long-term antibiotics for everyone — prophylactic antibiotics are used in selected patients with frequent exacerbations, but not for all, and they do not halt disease progression.
takeaway: In COPD, stopping smoking is the intervention that most changes the disease course.

stem: A patient with COPD finds that breathing out slowly through partially closed lips helps their breathlessness. What is this technique called?

options.A: Forced expiration against a closed glottis

why_correct: Pursed-lip breathing involves slow expiration through partially closed lips and can help some patients with COPD manage breathlessness.
why_wrong: A. This describes a Valsalva-type manoeuvre. C. The Heimlich manoeuvre is used for choking. D. The Valsalva manoeuvre involves forced expiration against a closed airway. E. Hyperventilation is rapid or excessive ventilation.
pearl: Pursed-lip breathing slows expiration and creates back-pressure that splints the small airways open, reducing air trapping and easing breathlessness in COPD.
thinking: COPD with breathlessness ↓ Slow exhalation through partly closed lips ↓ Back-pressure keeps small airways open ↓ Less air trapping ↓ Pursed-lip breathing
exam_trap: D, Valsalva manoeuvre — it also involves expiratory effort, but it is forced straining against a closed airway, not gentle exhalation through the lips.
takeaway: Breathing out slowly through pursed lips in COPD reduces air trapping.

stem: An adult has community-acquired pneumonia. Which factor forms part of the CURB-65 severity assessment?
why_correct: CURB-65 includes Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure and age ≥65 years.
why_wrong: A. Hearing loss is not included. B. Rash is not part of the score. C. Visual acuity is not included. E. Weight loss is not part of CURB-65.
pearl: CURB-65 gives one point each for confusion, raised urea, raised respiratory rate, low blood pressure and age 65 or over; it helps decide whether pneumonia can be managed at home or needs admission.
thinking: Community-acquired pneumonia ↓ Severity assessed with CURB-65 ↓ C stands for Confusion ↓ Others are urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age ↓ Confusion
exam_trap: E, Weight loss — it suggests significant illness and may worry the clinician, but CURB-65 uses only acute physiological markers and age.
takeaway: CURB-65 is Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure and age 65 or over.

stem: Which respiratory finding contributes to the CURB-65 score?
why_correct: A respiratory rate of at least 30 breaths per minute is one component of CURB-65.
why_wrong: B. Pleuritic pain is not part of the score. C. Cough is not part of the score. D. A respiratory rate of 12/min does not meet the CURB-65 respiratory criterion. E. Oxygen saturation is not itself a CURB-65 component.
pearl: The respiratory criterion in CURB-65 is a respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute or more; oxygen saturation is not scored but still matters for oxygen therapy and admission decisions.
thinking: Asked for the respiratory CURB-65 component ↓ R stands for respiratory rate ↓ Only a raised rate scores ↓ Symptoms and saturation are not scored ↓ Respiratory rate ≥30/min
exam_trap: E, Oxygen saturation of 99% — saturation feels like the obvious respiratory marker, but it is not a CURB-65 component, and 99% is normal anyway.
takeaway: The R in CURB-65 is a respiratory rate of 30 or more, not oxygen saturation.

stem: A patient is being assessed for suspected pulmonary embolism. Which finding contributes to the Wells score for PE?

options.C: Oxygen saturation below 94% on room air

correct_answer: B. Clinical signs of deep-vein thrombosis
why_correct: Clinical signs of DVT are one of the components of the Wells PE score.
why_wrong: A. Age is a PERC criterion, not a Wells PE criterion. C. Hypoxia is not a component of the Wells PE score. D. D-dimer, age-adjusted or not, is a separate test interpreted after the Wells score. E. Oestrogen use features in the PERC rule but not in the Wells PE score.
pearl: The two-level Wells PE score gives most weight to clinical signs of DVT and to PE being the most likely diagnosis; the score then decides whether D-dimer or imaging comes next.
thinking: Suspected PE ↓ Wells score estimates pre-test probability ↓ Includes DVT signs, PE most likely, tachycardia, immobility, previous VTE, haemoptysis, cancer ↓ DVT signs score highly ↓ Clinical signs of DVT
exam_trap: D, Raised age-adjusted D-dimer — it is part of the PE pathway, which tempts, but it is a test interpreted after the Wells score, not a component of it.
takeaway: Wells PE scores clinical features; D-dimer is the next step, not part of the score.

stem: A patient has breathlessness and reduced breath sounds at the right lung base. Which additional examination finding would most support a pleural effusion?
why_correct: Fluid in the pleural space gives stony dullness to percussion, with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the effusion.
why_wrong: A. Wheeze indicates narrowing of the lower airways. B. Inspiratory stridor indicates upper airway obstruction. D. Nasal congestion is unrelated to pleural disease. E. Hyperresonance indicates excess air, as in pneumothorax.
pearl: A pleural effusion gives stony dullness, reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the affected base; reduced breath sounds with hyperresonance instead suggest pneumothorax.
thinking: Breathlessness with reduced basal breath sounds ↓ Consider effusion, consolidation, collapse, pneumothorax ↓ Fluid gives the dullest percussion note ↓ Stony dullness indicates fluid ↓ Stony dullness to percussion
exam_trap: E, Hyperresonance — reduced breath sounds also occur in pneumothorax, so it tempts, but hyperresonance means air in the pleural space, not fluid.
takeaway: Reduced breath sounds with stony dullness is effusion; with hyperresonance it is pneumothorax.

stem: A patient has a witnessed generalised seizure followed by several minutes of confusion and drowsiness. What is this period called?
why_correct: Confusion and drowsiness following a seizure are characteristic of the postictal state.
why_wrong: A. An aura occurs before or at the beginning of some seizures. B. This is not the term for post-seizure confusion. C. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness due to reduced cerebral perfusion. D. Remission means reduction or disappearance of disease activity.
pearl: A period of confusion and drowsiness after an event supports an epileptic seizure over syncope, after which recovery is usually rapid and complete.
thinking: Witnessed generalised seizure ↓ Followed by minutes of confusion and drowsiness ↓ Brain recovering after seizure activity ↓ Helps distinguish seizure from syncope ↓ Postictal state
exam_trap: C, Syncope — it also causes transient loss of consciousness, but recovery is usually quick without prolonged confusion; the confusion points to a seizure.
takeaway: Prolonged confusion after an event favours seizure; rapid recovery favours syncope.

stem: A patient has had a recent epileptic seizure and asks whether they can immediately resume driving. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: They may drive once they have had a normal EEG
options.B: Driving is permitted if the seizure occurred at night
options.C: They may drive once antiepileptic treatment is started
options.D: Driving restrictions apply under DVLA guidance
options.E: They may drive after 48 hours if they feel well

correct_answer: D. Driving restrictions apply under DVLA guidance
why_correct: Seizures can impair driving safety, and patients must follow the applicable DVLA medical standards.
why_wrong: A. A normal EEG does not lift DVLA driving restrictions. B. Seizures during sleep are still subject to DVLA rules and do not permit immediate driving. C. Starting antiepileptic treatment does not by itself permit driving. E. Feeling well after 48 hours does not satisfy DVLA requirements.
pearl: After a seizure, the patient must stop driving and inform the DVLA; notifying is the patient's legal responsibility, and the doctor should advise clearly and document that advice.
thinking: Recent epileptic seizure ↓ Asks about driving straight away ↓ Further seizures endanger patient and public ↓ DVLA medical standards set the rules ↓ Driving restrictions apply under DVLA guidance
exam_trap: A, Normal EEG — a normal result seems reassuring, but a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy and does not lift DVLA restrictions.
takeaway: After a seizure: stop driving, tell the DVLA, and document the advice given.

stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease reports episodes where their feet seem temporarily "stuck to the floor" when starting to walk. What is this called?
why_correct: Freezing is a recognised Parkinsonian gait phenomenon in which the patient temporarily feels unable to initiate or continue walking.
why_wrong: A. Chorea consists of involuntary irregular movements. C. Hemiplegia is paralysis of one side of the body. D. Ataxia is impaired coordination. E. Festination is involuntary acceleration with short shuffling steps once walking, not an inability to start.
pearl: Freezing of gait is a sudden, brief inability to start or continue walking in Parkinson's disease, often at doorways or on turning, and is an important cause of falls.
thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ Feet feel stuck to the floor ↓ Difficulty initiating walking ↓ Episodic and transient ↓ Freezing of gait
exam_trap: E, Festinating gait — also Parkinsonian and gait-related, but festination is involuntary hurrying with short steps once walking, not being unable to start.
takeaway: Stuck feet on starting is freezing; hurrying short steps once moving is festination.

stem: A young adult with multiple sclerosis develops a new neurological deficit lasting several days. What does this pattern suggest?
why_correct: A new neurological episode lasting beyond a brief transient period can represent an MS relapse, after excluding alternative explanations such as infection.
why_wrong: B. Migraine can cause neurological symptoms but should not automatically be assumed. C. Otitis externa does not explain a new neurological deficit. D. Dehydration does not characteristically cause a focal neurological episode lasting several days. E. Vasovagal episodes are usually brief.
pearl: An MS relapse is a new or worsening neurological deficit lasting more than 24 hours without fever; exclude infection such as a UTI, which can cause a pseudo-relapse.
thinking: Known MS ↓ New neurological deficit ↓ Lasts several days, not minutes ↓ Pattern of a new demyelinating episode, once infection is excluded ↓ A relapse
exam_trap: B, Migraine in every case — migraine aura can cause focal symptoms, but it lasts minutes to an hour, not days, and should not be assumed in known MS.
takeaway: A new deficit lasting days in MS is a relapse once infection is excluded.

stem: A patient develops intermittent drooping of the eyelids that becomes worse later in the day and improves after rest. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Fatigable ptosis that worsens with use and improves with rest is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
why_wrong: A. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye. B. Conjunctivitis causes ocular irritation and discharge. D. Cataract causes gradual visual blurring. E. Retinal detachment causes visual disturbance rather than fatigable ptosis.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, with ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day or on sustained upgaze; acetylcholine receptor antibodies support the diagnosis.
thinking: Intermittent ptosis ↓ Worse later in the day ↓ Improves after rest ↓ Fatigable neuromuscular junction weakness ↓ Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: A, Acute glaucoma — an eye emergency, which tempts in an eye-focused stem, but it causes a painful red eye with visual loss, not fatigable ptosis.
takeaway: Fatigable ptosis that improves with rest suggests myasthenia gravis.

stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome develops worsening breathlessness and difficulty counting aloud in one breath. What complication is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Guillain–Barré syndrome can progress to respiratory muscle weakness and respiratory failure, requiring urgent assessment.
why_wrong: B. Facial weakness occurs in GBS but does not explain falling breath capacity. C. Bronchospasm causes wheeze and does not reduce single-breath counting through muscle weakness. D. A pleural effusion is not an expected GBS complication and would not explain this pattern. E. Hyperventilation does not explain a reduced single-breath count in progressive GBS.
pearl: In Guillain–Barré syndrome, monitor vital capacity serially; oxygen saturation may stay normal until late, so a falling capacity should prompt early critical care involvement.
thinking: Guillain–Barré syndrome, ascending weakness ↓ Worsening breathlessness ↓ Cannot count in one breath, falling vital capacity ↓ Diaphragm and intercostal weakness ↓ Respiratory muscle weakness
exam_trap: E, Anxiety-related hyperventilation — distress is common in GBS, but anxiety does not reduce the single-breath count; this is neuromuscular respiratory failure.
takeaway: In GBS, measure vital capacity; oxygen saturation falls late.

stem: A patient requests an intimate examination. What should the clinician consider?

options.B: Allowing any unrelated person to observe without consent

why_correct: For intimate examinations, clinicians should consider the use of a chaperone and respect the patient's privacy and dignity.
why_wrong: B. Observers should not be present without appropriate justification and consent. C. Patients should receive appropriate information. D. Examination details must remain confidential. E. The procedure should be explained and consent obtained.
pearl: Offer a chaperone for every intimate examination, whatever the sex of patient and doctor; explain the examination, obtain consent, and record who was present or that the offer was declined.
thinking: Intimate examination ↓ Patient dignity, comfort and safety ↓ Explain and obtain consent ↓ A chaperone protects patient and clinician ↓ Offer an appropriate chaperone
exam_trap: B, Allowing any unrelated person to observe — it may look like having a witness, but observers need justification and consent; a chaperone is an appropriate, trained person.
takeaway: Always offer a chaperone for intimate examinations and document the offer.

stem: A patient is considering an operation. What information should form part of the consent discussion?

options.B: Every possible theoretical complication regardless of relevance
options.C: No information if the operation is routine

correct_answer: D. Material risks and reasonable alternatives
why_correct: Valid consent requires appropriate information about material risks, benefits and reasonable alternatives relevant to the patient's decision.
why_wrong: A. Risks and alternatives are also relevant. B. Information should be relevant and proportionate rather than an indiscriminate list of every theoretical possibility. C. Routine procedures still require valid consent. E. Consent should support the patient's decision rather than simply present the clinician's preference.
pearl: Since Montgomery (2015), doctors must discuss material risks, those a reasonable person in the patient's position or this particular patient would consider significant, plus reasonable alternatives, including no treatment.
thinking: Patient considering an operation ↓ Valid consent needs an informed decision ↓ Montgomery: risks material to this patient ↓ Plus reasonable alternatives ↓ Material risks and reasonable alternatives
exam_trap: B, Every theoretical complication — an exhaustive list seems safest, but consent should focus on what matters to this patient rather than overwhelm with irrelevant detail.
takeaway: Consent means discussing material risks and reasonable alternatives, including doing nothing.

stem: A doctor notices a factual error in a patient's paper medical record. What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Cover it with correction fluid and write the correct entry over it
options.B: Rewrite the whole page and discard the original
options.C: Leave it uncorrected to preserve the integrity of the original record
options.D: Cross it out heavily so the original cannot be read
options.E: Correct it transparently without obscuring the original entry

correct_answer: E. Correct it transparently without obscuring the original entry
why_correct: Medical records should remain an accurate and auditable account, so corrections should be transparent and appropriately dated.
why_wrong: A. Correction fluid obscures the original entry and destroys the audit trail. B. Discarding the original page removes part of the record. C. A known factual error should be corrected, not left. D. Obliterating the original entry so it cannot be read destroys the audit trail.
pearl: Correct a paper record by drawing a single line through the error so it stays legible, then add the correct entry with date, time, signature and reason; never erase or conceal entries.
thinking: Factual error in paper notes ↓ Record must stay accurate and auditable ↓ Original must remain readable ↓ Single line, signed and dated correction ↓ Correct it transparently
exam_trap: D, Cross it out heavily — it feels like removing the error clearly, but obliterating the original destroys the audit trail and may look like concealment.
takeaway: Strike through errors once, keep them legible, and sign and date the correction.

stem: A patient is choosing between two reasonable treatment options with different benefits and risks. What approach is appropriate?

options.B: Allowing the clinician's preference to determine the decision automatically

why_correct: Shared decision-making combines clinical evidence with the patient's values, preferences and circumstances.
why_wrong: A. Unrelated people have no decision-making authority. B. The clinician's preference alone should not determine a choice between reasonable options. D. Patients should be appropriately involved in decisions about their care. E. Relevant risks should be discussed.
pearl: Shared decision-making means explaining the options with their benefits and risks, exploring what matters to the patient, and reaching a decision together.
thinking: Two reasonable treatment options ↓ Different benefits and risks ↓ Best choice depends on the patient's values ↓ Combine evidence with preferences ↓ Shared decision-making
exam_trap: B, Clinician's preference decides — doctors can offer a recommendation, but between reasonable options the patient's values should guide the choice.
takeaway: When options are reasonable, decide with the patient, not for them.

stem: A doctor needs to tell a patient that an investigation has confirmed cancer. What is an important communication principle?

options.B: Give the diagnosis while the patient is leaving the hospital

correct_answer: A. Provide information clearly and sensitively
why_correct: Serious diagnoses should be communicated clearly, honestly and sensitively, allowing the patient appropriate opportunity to ask questions.
why_wrong: B. Important information should be communicated in an appropriate setting. C. Jargon can make understanding more difficult. D. Patients should have an opportunity to ask questions. E. False reassurance undermines honest communication.
pearl: When breaking bad news, choose a private setting, find out what the patient knows, give a warning shot, explain clearly, pause, respond to emotion and agree next steps (SPIKES).
thinking: Confirmed cancer ↓ Serious, life-changing news ↓ Honesty, clarity and empathy ↓ Allow questions and offer support ↓ Provide information clearly and sensitively
exam_trap: E, Give false reassurance — it may feel kind, but it undermines trust and informed decisions; honesty delivered with compassion is required.
takeaway: Break bad news honestly, clearly and kindly in an appropriate setting.

stem: A 3-month-old infant has bruising on the trunk without a satisfactory explanation. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Review again once the infant starts to crawl
options.B: Treat the bruising as a safeguarding concern
options.C: Reassure the parents and arrange GP follow-up
options.D: Attribute it to a viral illness and observe
options.E: Accept that bruising follows normal handling

correct_answer: B. Treat the bruising as a safeguarding concern
why_correct: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is unusual and requires appropriate safeguarding assessment.
why_wrong: A. Assessment should not be delayed. C. Reassurance without safeguarding assessment is unsafe. D. A viral illness does not adequately explain unexplained bruising. E. Non-mobile infants do not normally acquire bruising through ordinary handling.
pearl: Bruising in a baby who is not yet mobile is rare and must be treated as a safeguarding concern; follow local child protection procedures and involve senior paediatric staff.
thinking: 3-month-old infant ↓ Not independently mobile ↓ Truncal bruising without adequate explanation ↓ Possible non-accidental injury ↓ Treat as a safeguarding concern
exam_trap: E, Bruising from normal handling — a carer may offer this explanation, but non-mobile infants rarely bruise from ordinary care.
takeaway: Those who do not cruise rarely bruise: unexplained bruising in a non-mobile baby is safeguarding.

stem: A clinician has concerns that a child may be experiencing abuse. What is important when documenting the assessment?

options.C: Alter the notes if the concern is later disproved
options.D: Delete concerning information after discussing it with colleagues
options.E: Record objective findings and relevant statements accurately

correct_answer: E. Record objective findings and relevant statements accurately
why_correct: Accurate contemporaneous documentation is essential when safeguarding concerns arise.
why_wrong: A. Objective observations should be distinguished from interpretation. B. Injuries and relevant findings should be documented. C. Records should not be retrospectively altered to conceal information. D. Relevant documentation should not be deleted.
pearl: In suspected abuse, document clearly and contemporaneously: record findings objectively, use body maps, quote the words of the child or carer verbatim, and note who was present.
thinking: Concern about child abuse ↓ Records may be used in protection or legal proceedings ↓ Must be accurate and objective ↓ Facts and exact statements, not assumptions ↓ Record objective findings and statements accurately
exam_trap: A, Record only the clinician's assumptions — clinical opinion has a place, but it must be separated from objective findings; assumptions alone are unreliable.
takeaway: Document safeguarding findings objectively, with exact words and body maps.

stem: A patient privately tells a clinician that their partner is physically abusing them. What is an appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Advise couples counselling with the partner present
options.B: Report it to the police without the patient's consent
options.C: Tell the patient they should leave the relationship today
options.D: Arrange to speak with the partner about the allegation
options.E: Listen, assess immediate safety and discuss support

correct_answer: E. Listen, assess immediate safety and discuss support
why_correct: The clinician should respond sensitively, assess immediate risk and help the patient access appropriate support.
why_wrong: A. Joint counselling can increase risk and is not recommended. B. For a competent adult, police involvement without consent is not the initial approach unless there is serious risk to others or a legal duty. C. The clinician should support rather than dictate personal decisions. D. Confronting an alleged abuser may increase risk.
pearl: When an adult discloses domestic abuse, listen and take it seriously, assess immediate safety and any risk to others, and offer referral to specialist domestic abuse support services.
thinking: Private disclosure of abuse ↓ Competent adult ↓ Respond sensitively, without judgement ↓ Assess immediate risk ↓ Listen, assess safety and discuss support
exam_trap: B, Report to the police without consent — it seems protective, but for a competent adult it is not the default unless there is serious risk to others or a legal duty.
takeaway: Disclosure of abuse: listen, assess safety and offer support, respecting adult autonomy.

stem: An elderly patient is at risk of delirium during hospital admission. Which intervention may help reduce the risk?

options.A: Nurse the patient in a single dark side room
options.B: Give night-time sedation to promote sleep
options.D: Keep glasses and hearing aids in storage

correct_answer: C. Promote orientation, hydration and sleep
why_correct: Addressing reversible risk factors such as dehydration, sensory impairment, sleep disruption and disorientation can help prevent delirium.
why_wrong: A. Isolation in a darkened room increases disorientation. B. Sedatives can precipitate or worsen delirium. D. Removing sensory aids increases disorientation. E. Immobility increases delirium risk; appropriate mobilisation is beneficial.
pearl: Delirium is often preventable: provide glasses and hearing aids, orientation cues, hydration, nutrition, good sleep, early mobilisation and pain control, and avoid unnecessary sedatives.
thinking: Older inpatient at risk of delirium ↓ Many reversible risk factors ↓ Disorientation, dehydration, poor sleep ↓ Multicomponent non-drug prevention ↓ Promote orientation, hydration and sleep
exam_trap: B, Night-time sedation — better sleep helps, which makes it tempting, but sedatives can precipitate or worsen delirium.
takeaway: Prevent delirium with orientation, hydration, sleep and mobility, not sedatives.

stem: A patient twists their ankle while playing football. There is lateral ankle pain and swelling, but they can walk and there is no obvious deformity. What is the most likely injury?
why_correct: An inversion-type injury with lateral ankle pain and swelling is commonly caused by a ligament sprain.
why_wrong: A. Lisfranc injuries affect the midfoot rather than causing lateral ankle pain. C. Achilles rupture causes posterior ankle pain and weak plantarflexion. D. A bimalleolar fracture usually prevents weight-bearing and may cause deformity. E. A tibial plateau fracture causes knee pain and swelling.
pearl: The Ottawa ankle rules guide X-ray: image if there is bony tenderness at the malleoli or the patient cannot bear weight; otherwise lateral pain and swelling after a twist is usually a ligament sprain.
thinking: Twisting injury playing football ↓ Lateral ankle pain and swelling ↓ Able to walk, no deformity ↓ Significant fracture less likely ↓ Ankle ligament sprain
exam_trap: D, Bimalleolar fracture — swelling after a twist raises fracture concern, but walking without deformity makes this unstable fracture unlikely.
takeaway: A weight-bearing lateral ankle injury without deformity is usually a sprain; apply the Ottawa rules.

stem: A patient is suspected of having an Achilles tendon rupture. Which bedside test may support the diagnosis?
why_correct: In the Thompson test, absence or marked reduction of plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed suggests Achilles tendon rupture.
why_wrong: B. Kernig testing is associated with meningeal irritation. C. Weber testing assesses hearing. D. Allen testing assesses hand circulation. E. Romberg testing assesses balance and proprioception.
pearl: In the Simmonds–Thompson test, squeezing the calf with the patient prone normally plantarflexes the foot; absent movement suggests Achilles rupture, often with a palpable gap and a reported snap.
thinking: Suspected Achilles rupture ↓ Need a bedside test of tendon continuity ↓ Squeeze the calf, watch the foot ↓ No plantarflexion means rupture ↓ Thompson test
exam_trap: C, Weber test — the name also appears in ankle fracture classification, which tempts, but the Weber tuning-fork test assesses hearing.
takeaway: Calf squeeze with no plantarflexion means Achilles rupture (Thompson test).

stem: A patient has a painless swelling over the olecranon after repeatedly leaning on their elbows. They are otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Gout of the first MTP joint

why_correct: Repeated pressure over the olecranon can cause inflammation and swelling of the olecranon bursa.
why_wrong: A. Achilles rupture affects the ankle. B. Septic arthritis affects a joint and is typically painful with restricted movement. C. Gout classically affects the first MTP joint. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes neurological symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Olecranon bursitis from repeated pressure is usually painless and aseptic; warmth, redness, pain or fever suggests septic bursitis, which needs aspiration and antibiotics.
thinking: Swelling over the olecranon ↓ Repeated leaning on elbows ↓ Painless and otherwise well ↓ Bursa inflamed by friction ↓ Olecranon bursitis
exam_trap: B, Septic arthritis — swelling near a joint tempts, but septic arthritis is painful with restricted movement and the patient is usually unwell.
takeaway: Painless swelling over the point of the elbow after leaning is olecranon bursitis.

stem: A patient with longstanding gout has firm nodules around the ears and finger joints. What are these lesions called?
why_correct: Tophi are deposits of monosodium urate associated with chronic gout.
why_wrong: B. Rheumatoid nodules are associated with rheumatoid arthritis. C. Xanthomas contain lipid and are associated with disorders such as hyperlipidaemia. D. Heberden nodes are bony swellings at distal interphalangeal joints in osteoarthritis. E. Lipomas are benign fatty tumours.
pearl: Tophi are urate deposits seen in chronic gout, classically on the ear helix, fingers and around joints; they reflect long-standing hyperuricaemia and support urate-lowering treatment.
thinking: Long-standing gout ↓ Firm nodules on ears and fingers ↓ Monosodium urate deposits ↓ Sign of chronic disease ↓ Tophi
exam_trap: B, Rheumatoid nodules — also firm nodules near joints, but they occur in rheumatoid arthritis, usually over extensor surfaces, not with gout.
takeaway: Nodules on the ear in a patient with gout are tophi.

stem: A patient has symmetrical hand pain. Which feature of the history is most suggestive of inflammatory arthritis?

options.A: Pain only after a long walk
options.E: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour

correct_answer: E. Morning stiffness lasting over an hour
why_correct: Early-morning stiffness lasting more than 30–60 minutes is characteristic of inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Pain mainly after activity such as a long walk suggests mechanical joint disease. B. Pain only after trauma suggests injury rather than inflammatory arthritis. C. Brief stiffness after inactivity (gelling) is typical of osteoarthritis. D. Inflammatory synovitis is usually painful, so painless swelling is not the typical pattern.
pearl: Inflammatory arthritis causes prolonged early-morning stiffness that eases with activity, whereas osteoarthritis causes brief stiffness after rest and pain that worsens with use.
thinking: Symmetrical hand pain ↓ Inflammatory or mechanical? ↓ Prolonged early-morning stiffness ↓ Eases as the day goes on ↓ Morning stiffness lasting over an hour
exam_trap: C, Stiffness lasting 30 seconds after sitting — stiffness hints at arthritis, but brief gelling after rest is typical of osteoarthritis, not inflammation.
takeaway: Long morning stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis; brief gelling suggests osteoarthritis.

stem: Which condition can occur as an extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Rheumatoid nodules are a recognised extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis is unrelated. B. Renal colic is unrelated. D. Otitis externa is unrelated. E. Cataract is not a characteristic extra-articular manifestation.
pearl: Extra-articular features of rheumatoid arthritis include nodules, interstitial lung disease, scleritis, dry eyes, anaemia, vasculitis and Felty's syndrome; nodules are linked with seropositive disease.
thinking: Rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Systemic disease beyond the joints ↓ Subcutaneous nodules over pressure areas ↓ Recognised extra-articular feature ↓ Rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: E, Cataract in every patient — eye involvement does occur in RA, but as dry eye or scleritis; cataract is neither universal nor characteristic.
takeaway: Rheumatoid nodules are a classic extra-articular feature of rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. She has known gallstones. Which is a common cause of acute pancreatitis?
why_correct: Gallstones are one of the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis, alongside alcohol.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulosis is not a common cause. B. Appendicitis does not commonly cause acute pancreatitis. C. Haemorrhoids are unrelated. E. Ulcerative colitis is not a common cause.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol cause most acute pancreatitis; after gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy is advised early, usually during the same admission or soon after, to prevent recurrence.
thinking: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back ↓ Vomiting ↓ Acute pancreatitis ↓ Known gallstones ↓ Gallstones
exam_trap: B, Appendicitis — a common surgical cause of abdominal pain, but it does not cause pancreatitis or epigastric pain radiating to the back.
takeaway: Gallstones and alcohol cause most acute pancreatitis.

stem: Which combination is most characteristic of acute pancreatitis?

options.B: Right iliac fossa pain and haematuria
options.C: Severe epigastric pain and raised lipase

correct_answer: C. Severe epigastric pain and raised lipase
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis typically causes severe upper abdominal pain, often radiating to the back, with elevated pancreatic enzymes.
why_wrong: A. Suggests urinary infection. B. Suggests urinary or appendiceal pathology rather than pancreatitis. D. Suggests venous thromboembolism. E. Suggests possible biliary or pancreatic malignancy rather than acute pancreatitis.
pearl: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed by typical epigastric pain radiating to the back with markedly raised serum lipase or amylase; lipase is the more specific test.
thinking: Severe epigastric pain ↓ Often radiates to the back with vomiting ↓ Pancreatic enzymes leak into the blood ↓ Raised lipase ↓ Severe epigastric pain and raised lipase
exam_trap: E, Painless jaundice and weight gain — pancreatic disease can cause jaundice, but painless jaundice suggests pancreatic head cancer, usually with weight loss.
takeaway: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase means acute pancreatitis.

stem: Which is another common cause of acute pancreatitis?
why_correct: Excessive alcohol consumption is a major cause of acute pancreatitis.
why_wrong: A. Hay fever is unrelated. B. Migraine does not cause pancreatitis. C. Iron deficiency does not commonly cause pancreatitis. D. Osteoarthritis is unrelated.
pearl: GET SMASHED lists causes of pancreatitis; gallstones and alcohol dominate, with others including hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, ERCP, drugs and trauma.
thinking: Asked for a common cause of acute pancreatitis ↓ Two causes dominate ↓ Gallstones and alcohol ↓ Alcohol excess
exam_trap: C, Iron deficiency — a common condition, which may tempt, but it does not cause pancreatitis; metabolic causes include hypercalcaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia.
takeaway: Alongside gallstones, alcohol is the other major cause of acute pancreatitis.

stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis becomes hypotensive, confused and oliguric. What does this suggest?

options.C: Mild pancreatitis needing oral fluids and analgesia

correct_answer: E. Severe pancreatitis with organ dysfunction
why_correct: Hypotension, altered mental state and reduced urine output indicate significant physiological deterioration.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic does not cause shock, confusion and oliguria. B. Opioids may cause drowsiness but do not explain hypotension with oliguria. C. These features indicate organ dysfunction, not mild disease. D. Chronic pancreatitis with malabsorption does not cause acute shock and oliguria.
pearl: Severe acute pancreatitis is defined by persistent organ failure; hypotension, confusion and oliguria demand fluid resuscitation, close monitoring and early critical care input.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ Hypotension, confusion and oliguria ↓ Circulatory, neurological and renal dysfunction ↓ Systemic inflammatory response ↓ Severe pancreatitis with organ dysfunction
exam_trap: B, Opioid side-effects — opioids can cause drowsiness, which tempts, but they do not explain hypotension with oliguria.
takeaway: Shock, confusion and oliguria in pancreatitis mean severe disease: resuscitate and escalate.

stem: A patient with appendicitis initially develops central abdominal pain that later localises to the right iliac fossa. What explains this pattern?

options.A: Migration of visceral to parietal pain
options.B: Referred pain via the right phrenic nerve
options.C: Movement of a faecolith along the colon
options.D: Spasm of the small bowel mesentery

correct_answer: A. Migration of visceral to parietal pain
why_correct: Early appendiceal inflammation causes poorly localised visceral pain; subsequent parietal peritoneal irritation localises the pain to the right iliac fossa.
why_wrong: B. Phrenic-mediated referred pain is felt at the shoulder tip. C. Faecolith movement does not explain the migration of pain. D. Mesenteric spasm does not account for localisation to the right iliac fossa. E. Bile duct obstruction causes right upper quadrant pain and jaundice.
pearl: Appendicitis pain starts periumbilically because midgut visceral pain is poorly localised, then moves to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
thinking: Early central abdominal pain ↓ Visceral midgut pain, poorly localised ↓ Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum ↓ Somatic, well-localised RIF pain ↓ Migration of visceral to parietal pain
exam_trap: B, Referred pain via the phrenic nerve — referred pain is a real mechanism, but phrenic irritation refers to the shoulder tip, not the right iliac fossa.
takeaway: Central then RIF pain in appendicitis is visceral pain becoming parietal.

stem: A patient develops sudden severe abdominal pain followed by a rigid abdomen. What diagnosis should be considered?

options.B: Acute exacerbation of irritable bowel syndrome
options.E: Renal colic from an obstructing ureteric stone

why_correct: Sudden severe pain followed by generalised peritoneal irritation is a red flag for perforation.
why_wrong: B. IBS does not cause peritonism. C. Biliary colic causes colicky pain without a rigid abdomen. D. Gastroenteritis does not cause generalised peritonism. E. Renal colic causes restlessness and loin pain without peritonism.
pearl: Sudden severe pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen suggests perforation; an erect chest X-ray may show free air under the diaphragm, though CT is more sensitive.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Rigid abdomen, generalised peritonism ↓ Contents leaking into the peritoneal cavity ↓ Surgical emergency ↓ Perforated viscus with peritonitis
exam_trap: E, Renal colic — it also causes sudden severe pain, but patients writhe and the abdomen stays soft; rigidity means peritonitis.
takeaway: Sudden pain with a rigid abdomen means perforation until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient with longstanding reflux develops progressive difficulty swallowing. What is the significance?

options.A: An expected feature of uncomplicated reflux
options.B: A reason to double the PPI and review in 3 months
options.C: A sign of functional dysphagia needing reassurance
options.D: An alarm feature requiring further assessment
options.E: A feature of anxiety-related globus sensation

correct_answer: D. An alarm feature requiring further assessment
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia in a patient with reflux requires investigation because significant oesophageal pathology, including malignancy, must be considered.
why_wrong: A. Progressive dysphagia is not a reassuring feature of reflux. B. Escalating PPI without investigation would delay diagnosis. C. Progressive dysphagia should not be labelled functional without investigation. E. Globus is a non-progressive sensation and does not explain progressive dysphagia.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia is an alarm feature at any age; with long-standing reflux think of peptic stricture or oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and refer for urgent upper GI endoscopy.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ Risk of Barrett's oesophagus and stricture ↓ New progressive dysphagia ↓ Possible malignancy ↓ An alarm feature requiring further assessment
exam_trap: B, Double the PPI and review in 3 months — treating reflux seems logical, but it delays endoscopy and the diagnosis of possible cancer.
takeaway: Dysphagia is a red flag: refer for urgent endoscopy rather than simply increasing the PPI.

stem: A patient is suspected of having C. difficile infection in hospital. What infection-control principle is particularly important?

options.C: Share equipment between patients without cleaning
options.D: Move the patient into a communal dining area
options.E: Encourage unrestricted contact with other patients

correct_answer: A. Appropriate isolation and infection-control precautions
why_correct: C. difficile can spread in healthcare settings, so appropriate infection-control measures are essential.
why_wrong: B. Hand hygiene is important. C. Shared contaminated equipment can spread infection. D. Communal areas may increase transmission risk. E. Unrestricted contact may facilitate transmission.
pearl: With suspected C. difficile, isolate promptly, use gloves and aprons, and wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill the spores.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile in hospital ↓ Spores spread via hands, equipment and environment ↓ Risk of ward outbreaks ↓ Isolation and contact precautions ↓ Appropriate isolation and infection-control precautions
exam_trap: D, Moving the patient to a communal dining area — normal activity may seem good for wellbeing, but a patient with suspected C. difficile should be isolated, not mixing.
takeaway: Suspected C. difficile: isolate and wash hands with soap and water.

stem: A patient with Bell's palsy cannot fully close one eye. What complication is particularly important to prevent?
why_correct: Incomplete eyelid closure can cause exposure and drying of the cornea, potentially leading to corneal injury.
why_wrong: A. It does not directly cause cataract. C. Optic neuritis affects the optic nerve rather than eyelid closure. D. Bell's palsy does not directly cause retinal detachment. E. It does not cause acute angle-closure glaucoma.
pearl: In Bell's palsy with incomplete eye closure, protect the cornea with lubricating drops and ointment and tape the eye closed at night; a painful red eye needs urgent ophthalmology review.
thinking: Bell's palsy ↓ Orbicularis oculi weakness ↓ Eye cannot close fully ↓ Cornea exposed and dries ↓ Corneal damage from exposure
exam_trap: C, Optic neuritis — it is a nerve-related eye problem, which tempts, but it involves the optic nerve and is unrelated to facial nerve palsy.
takeaway: In Bell's palsy, protect the cornea when the eye cannot close.

stem: A 72-year-old develops a unilateral tremor that is most noticeable when the hand is resting and improves during voluntary movement. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: A resting tremor is a classic feature of Parkinson's disease, particularly when accompanied by bradykinesia or rigidity.
why_wrong: A. Essential tremor is usually an action or postural tremor. B. Cerebellar tremor is typically intention-related. C. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory and/or motor deficits rather than a classic resting tremor. E. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness.
pearl: Parkinson's tremor is typically an asymmetric, pill-rolling resting tremor that lessens with movement; the diagnosis rests on bradykinesia with tremor or rigidity.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Unilateral tremor ↓ Worst at rest ↓ Improves with voluntary movement ↓ Parkinson's disease
exam_trap: A, Essential tremor — the commonest tremor disorder, but it is a bilateral postural or action tremor, not a resting tremor.
takeaway: Resting tremor suggests Parkinson's; postural tremor essential tremor; intention tremor cerebellar disease.

stem: A patient has fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen towards the end of the day. Which feature would support myasthenia gravis?
why_correct: Myasthenia gravis affects neuromuscular transmission and typically causes fatigable weakness without pupillary involvement.
why_wrong: B. Joint swelling is unrelated. C. Reflexes are generally preserved. D. Fixed dilated pupils suggest another neurological or toxic process. E. Sensory loss is not typical of myasthenia.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis spares the pupils, sensation and reflexes; ptosis with a dilated pupil suggests a third nerve palsy, which may be compressive and needs urgent imaging.
thinking: Fluctuating ptosis and diplopia ↓ Worse later in the day ↓ Neuromuscular junction disorder ↓ Pupils, sensation and reflexes spared ↓ Normal pupils
exam_trap: D, Fixed dilated pupils — eye signs seem to fit ptosis and diplopia, but pupil involvement points to a third nerve palsy or toxic cause, not myasthenia.
takeaway: Fatigable ptosis with normal pupils suggests myasthenia gravis.

stem: A patient develops severe headache and neck stiffness after a thunderclap headache. What complication of subarachnoid haemorrhage does the neck stiffness represent?
why_correct: Blood within the subarachnoid space can irritate the meninges and produce neck stiffness.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy does not cause meningism. B. Biliary obstruction is unrelated. D. The clinical setting strongly suggests meningeal irritation rather than simple muscle strain. E. Joint inflammation does not explain neck stiffness in this context.
pearl: Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with a sudden thunderclap headache peaking within minutes; meningism can take hours to develop, so its absence early does not exclude SAH.
thinking: Thunderclap headache ↓ Subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ Blood in the subarachnoid space ↓ Irritates the meninges ↓ Meningeal irritation
exam_trap: D, Muscle strain only — neck stiffness is often musculoskeletal, but after a thunderclap headache it must be attributed to meningeal irritation.
takeaway: Neck stiffness after a thunderclap headache is meningism from blood: think SAH.

stem: A patient suddenly develops facial weakness, arm weakness and speech difficulty. What should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden facial, arm and speech abnormalities are classic warning signs of acute stroke.
why_wrong: B. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes localised hand sensory symptoms. C. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute neurological deficits. D. Migraine can cause neurological symptoms in some patients, but sudden focal deficits require urgent stroke assessment. E. Gastroenteritis does not cause focal neurological weakness.
pearl: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) identifies likely stroke; treat as an emergency, check blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a mimic, and arrange urgent brain imaging.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Facial and arm weakness ↓ Speech difficulty ↓ Focal deficit, FAST positive ↓ Acute stroke
exam_trap: D, Migraine — some migraines cause focal deficits, which tempts, but sudden facial, arm and speech deficits must be managed as stroke first.
takeaway: Sudden face, arm or speech deficit is stroke until proven otherwise.

stem: Which symptom can occur as a non-motor manifestation of Parkinson's disease?
why_correct: Constipation is a recognised non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease.
why_wrong: B. Haematemesis suggests upper GI bleeding. C. Jaundice suggests hepatobiliary disease. D. Haemoptysis suggests respiratory or cardiovascular pathology. E. Haematuria suggests urinary tract pathology.
pearl: Non-motor features of Parkinson's include constipation, loss of smell, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, postural hypotension and dementia; some precede motor symptoms by years.
thinking: Parkinson's affects more than movement ↓ Autonomic involvement of the gut ↓ Slowed bowel transit ↓ Recognised non-motor feature ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: B, Haematemesis — it is a gastrointestinal symptom, which tempts, but it indicates upper GI bleeding, not Parkinson's disease.
takeaway: Constipation, loss of smell and REM sleep disorder are non-motor features of Parkinson's.

stem: Which is a core symptom of depression?

options.A: Increased energy and reduced need for sleep

why_correct: Persistent low mood is one of the core symptoms of a depressive episode.
why_wrong: A. Increased energy with reduced need for sleep suggests mania or hypomania. B. Painless jaundice suggests hepatobiliary disease. D. Facial weakness suggests a neurological disorder. E. Calf pain is not a core depressive symptom.
pearl: The core symptoms of depression are persistent low mood and anhedonia; also ask about energy, sleep, appetite and concentration, and always assess suicide risk.
thinking: Asked for a core depressive symptom ↓ Core features are low mood and loss of interest ↓ Present most days over weeks ↓ Persistent low mood
exam_trap: A, Increased energy and reduced need for sleep — mood-related, which tempts, but these describe mania or hypomania, the opposite pole.
takeaway: Persistent low mood and anhedonia are the core symptoms of depression.

stem: A patient reports that activities they previously enjoyed no longer give them pleasure. What is this symptom called?
why_correct: Anhedonia means reduced ability to experience pleasure and is a core symptom of depression.
why_wrong: A. Echolalia is repetition of another person's words. C. Ataxia refers to impaired coordination. D. Paraesthesia refers to abnormal sensations such as tingling. E. Dysphasia is impaired language function.
pearl: Anhedonia, loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, is a core symptom of depression; ask directly what the patient used to enjoy and whether that has changed.
thinking: Previously enjoyed activities ↓ No longer give pleasure ↓ Loss of the capacity for enjoyment ↓ Core symptom of depression ↓ Anhedonia
exam_trap: E, Dysphasia — the medical-sounding term tempts, but dysphasia is impaired language function, not loss of pleasure.
takeaway: Loss of pleasure in usual activities is anhedonia.

stem: A patient firmly believes that the television broadcaster is sending secret personal messages specifically to them, despite evidence to the contrary. What is this most likely to represent?
why_correct: A fixed false belief that is maintained despite evidence against it is a delusion.
why_wrong: A. A compulsion is a repetitive act or mental ritual. B. A phobia is an excessive fear of a particular object or situation. C. A hallucination is a perception occurring without an external stimulus. D. A panic attack is an acute episode of intense fear with physical symptoms.
pearl: A delusion is a fixed false belief held despite contrary evidence and out of keeping with cultural background; believing the television sends personal messages is a delusion of reference.
thinking: Firm belief ↓ Television sending personal messages ↓ Held despite contrary evidence ↓ Abnormal belief, not perception ↓ Delusion
exam_trap: C, Hallucination — the television makes it seem perceptual, but there is no false perception; the abnormality is the belief about real broadcasts.
takeaway: False perception is a hallucination; a fixed false belief is a delusion.

stem: A patient taking a combined oral contraceptive pill has missed pills. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Stop the pill and rely on condoms until the next period starts
options.B: Take two pills each day for the remainder of the pack to catch up
options.C: It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
options.D: Emergency contraception is needed after one missed pill
options.E: No further action is needed if fewer than three pills were missed

correct_answer: C. It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
why_correct: The need for additional precautions or emergency contraception depends on the specific circumstances of the missed pills.
why_wrong: A. Stopping the pill is unnecessary and leaves the patient unprotected. B. Doubling doses for the rest of the pack is not recommended. D. Emergency contraception is not automatically required after one missed pill. E. Missing two or more pills can require additional precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
pearl: Missed combined pill advice depends on how many pills were missed and where in the pack; one missed pill usually needs only taking it now, while more may need extra precautions or emergency contraception.
thinking: Combined oral contraceptive ↓ Missed pills ↓ Risk depends on number missed and week of pack ↓ Determines need for condoms or emergency contraception ↓ It depends on how many and when
exam_trap: E, No action if fewer than three missed — it sounds like a familiar rule, but missing two or more pills can require extra precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
takeaway: Missed pill advice hinges on how many were missed and where in the pack.

stem: A woman has had unprotected intercourse and is concerned about pregnancy. What is the key principle?

options.A: Emergency contraception is effective only after pregnancy is established
options.C: It is only available to women over 40
options.D: Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible
options.E: Emergency contraception is never needed after unprotected intercourse

correct_answer: D. Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible
why_correct: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so appropriate options should be considered promptly.
why_wrong: A. Emergency contraception is intended to prevent pregnancy before an established pregnancy. B. Emergency contraception does not permanently prevent fertility. C. Age does not create such a restriction. E. It can be appropriate after unprotected intercourse.
pearl: Emergency contraception options are the copper IUD, the most effective, and oral ulipristal or levonorgestrel; all should be used as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Concern about pregnancy ↓ Emergency contraception is time-sensitive ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Consider it as soon as possible
exam_trap: A, Effective only after pregnancy is established — it confuses emergency contraception with abortion; it prevents pregnancy and does not work once pregnancy is established.
takeaway: Offer emergency contraception promptly; the copper IUD is the most effective option.

stem: A 38-year-old woman who smokes asks about starting a combined hormonal contraceptive. Why does smoking matter?

options.A: Smoking causes immediate infertility in every woman
options.C: Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
options.D: Smoking eliminates the risk of venous thrombosis
options.E: Smoking makes combined contraception completely risk-free

correct_answer: C. Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
why_correct: Smoking contributes to cardiovascular risk, particularly as age and smoking intensity increase, and this is relevant when considering combined hormonal contraception.
why_wrong: A. It does not cause immediate infertility in every woman. B. Smoking does not abolish contraceptive efficacy. D. Smoking does not protect against thrombosis. E. Smoking does not make contraception safer.
pearl: Combined hormonal contraception adds thrombotic and arterial risk; UKMEC advises against it in smokers aged 35 or over, so progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods are preferred.
thinking: Woman aged 38 ↓ Smoker ↓ Combined hormones raise venous and arterial risk ↓ Age and smoking add to that risk ↓ Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
exam_trap: B, Smoking prevents all contraceptive effects — smoking clearly matters, which tempts, but it raises cardiovascular risk rather than reducing efficacy.
takeaway: Smokers aged 35 or over should generally avoid combined hormonal contraception.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has irregular periods followed by 12 months without menstruation. She has no other concerning features. What does this most likely represent?
why_correct: Menopause is clinically defined retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhoea when there is no other obvious cause, in the appropriate age group.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer can cause abnormal bleeding but does not explain this typical menopausal transition by itself. B. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. D. PID typically causes pelvic pain and genital tract symptoms. E. Ectopic pregnancy presents with pregnancy-related symptoms and potentially pain or bleeding.
pearl: Menopause is diagnosed clinically in women over 45 after 12 months without periods; FSH testing is not usually needed in this age group.
thinking: Woman aged 52 ↓ Irregular periods, then none ↓ 12 months of amenorrhoea ↓ No other concerning features ↓ Menopause
exam_trap: A, Cervical cancer — cancer worries tempt, but it causes abnormal bleeding, not amenorrhoea; bleeding after the menopause would need investigation.
takeaway: Over 45 with 12 months of amenorrhoea, menopause is a clinical diagnosis.

stem: Which medication exposure is an important risk factor for osteoporosis?

options.C: Long-term dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use
options.D: Short-term topical emollient use for eczema
options.E: Long-term thiazide diuretic therapy for hypertension

why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment increases bone loss and fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is not a recognised osteoporosis risk factor. C. Calcium channel blockers are not a recognised osteoporosis risk factor. D. Emollients do not cause osteoporosis. E. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and are not a risk factor.
pearl: Long-term systemic corticosteroids are a major cause of osteoporosis and fragility fracture; consider bone protection early when prolonged courses are expected, especially in older adults.
thinking: Asked for a drug cause of osteoporosis ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and calcium absorption ↓ Long-term systemic use ↓ Raised fracture risk ↓ Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy
exam_trap: E, Thiazide diuretics — diuretics feature in bone questions, which tempts, but thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and are not an osteoporosis risk factor.
takeaway: Long-term systemic steroids cause osteoporosis: think about bone protection.
